papers.title: LLM-Integrated Bayesian State Space Models for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Forecasting in the real world requires integrating structured time-series data with unstructured textual information, but existing methods are architecturally limited by fixed input/output horizons and are unable to model or quantify uncertainty. We address this challenge by introducing LLM-integrated Bayesian State space models (LBS), a novel probabilistic framework for multimodal temporal forecasting. At a high level, LBS consists of two components: (1) a state space model (SSM) backbone that captures the temporal dynamics of latent states from which both numerical and textual observations are generated and (2) a pretrained large language model (LLM) that is adapted to encode textual inputs for posterior state estimation and decode textual forecasts consistent with the latent trajectory. This design enables flexible lookback and forecast windows, principled uncertainty quantification, and improved temporal generalization thanks to the well-suited inductive bias of SSMs toward modeling dynamical systems. Experiments on the TextTimeCorpus benchmark demonstrate that LBS improves the previous state-of-the-art by 13.20% while providing human-readable summaries of each forecast. Our work is the first to unify LLMs and SSMs for joint numerical and textual prediction, offering a novel foundation for multimodal temporal reasoning.
papers.summary: Real-world forecasting often needs to combine numeric time series with unstructured text, but existing methods are tied to fixed input and output horizons and cannot model or quantify uncertainty. LLM-integrated Bayesian state space models (`LBS`) pair a state space model (SSM) backbone, which captures the dynamics of latent states that generate both numerical and textual observations, with a pretrained large language model adapted to encode text for posterior state estimation and to decode textual forecasts consistent with the latent trajectory. This design allows flexible lookback and forecast windows and principled uncertainty quantification, and the SSM's inductive bias toward dynamical systems is argued to aid temporal generalization. On the `TextTimeCorpus` benchmark it **improves on the previous state of the art by 13.20%** while also producing human-readable summaries of each forecast.

papers.title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
papers.abstract: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.
papers.summary: Streaming data systems are optimized for moving data, not for GPU-heavy work such as running large language model inference inside a pipeline for unsupervised pattern finding or content moderation. The authors build a system on `Google Cloud Dataflow` for hybrid streaming machine learning workloads, combining co-designed autoscaling over heterogeneous worker pools with prefix-aware batching. They report **1.5x to 2x higher throughput** for streaming pipelines that call LLMs at similar latency, along with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency than existing streaming data processing systems.

papers.title: The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus: harmonising 128 aviation-safety source codes into one deduplicated cross-national accident dataset
papers.abstract: National aviation-investigation databases are deep but territorial; global compilations such as the Aviation Safety Network and the Bureau of Aircraft Accidents Archives are hand-curated, apply their own inclusion thresholds, and publish no per-record lineage. The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus harmonizes 279,485 occurrences and 131,882 attached narratives from 128 source codes -- national accident-investigation authorities, occurrence-reporting systems and four global compilations. Records are mapped into one schema; each normalized record reduces to exactly one key from an ordered ladder -- event signature, registration and date, rounded position and date, or source and native identifier -- so a missing field never creates a link, and the key is the occurrence identifier. Records the ladder cannot reach are scored in a blocked pass into an explicit merge table and applied only within an automatically approved score band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking; one provenance row per contributing source -- its native identifier and URL -- is retained, with attribution and licence terms per source code. Linkage error is measured on five adjudicated samples totalling 200 pairs. A recorded uniform random draw of 60 from the 3,441 merges the automatic band applies as it ships found no error; the exact two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on its false-merge rate is 6.0%, or 205 pairs. The measured error covers the scored band only; the ladder's deterministic joins are not adjudicated. The corpus has no exposure denominators and inherits the under-reporting of its sources. It is offered as a base for cross-national safety statistics, source-disagreement studies and narrative text mining; a frozen, DOI-referenced snapshot accompanies the live API.
papers.summary: National aviation accident databases are deep but territorial, while global compilations apply their own inclusion thresholds and publish no per-record lineage. The corpus harmonizes 279,485 occurrences and 131,882 narratives from 128 source codes into one schema, reducing each record to a single key from an ordered ladder so that a missing field never creates a link, and scoring the remaining candidates in a blocked pass that is applied automatically only within an approved band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking, and one provenance row per contributing source is retained with attribution and licence terms. A random audit of 60 automatic merges found no errors, giving an **exact 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound of 6.0% on the false-merge rate**, though the deterministic ladder joins are not adjudicated and the corpus inherits the under-reporting of its sources.

papers.title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability scores an explanation of a sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature by asking a model to predict, token by token, where the feature fires on evaluation examples or to judge whether marked tokens fit it. We find that the evaluation data standard pipelines build can be scored without reading the explanation. On Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing runs for 500 random GPT-2 small features, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and a rule that says "yes" when the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers (recomputed from the stored per-item verdicts, on marks rebuilt from the pipeline's code); a rule reading only the mark count reaches 0.969. The cue changes form across pipelines: current delphi always marks the same slot in its fuzzing negatives, and full-context runs mark negatives with more tokens. OpenAI's simulation benchmark lists each neuron's top-activating sequences first; a rule that predicts activity on the first five scores 0.227 in pooled correlation against 0.160 for GPT-4's published simulator (post hoc). We give closed forms for what such rules can score; show that one scorer's simulation scores are higher on stored snippets than on natural windows but not shown to be reordered; and build windows that remove the position cue, derive but do not build negatives that remove the mark cues, and separate the sequence cue by decomposition. On natural-text windows cut at random offsets, the best fixed-offset prior shared by all features scores 0.015. On them, that scorer, a typed decision model (Jev), reaches a pooled correlation of 0.331 over 49 features, against 0.013 with shuffled explanations, and an open 8B simulator with the original read-out reads the explanation there (0.194 against 0.019). Scores should be reported beside the best explanation-free rule on the same items.
papers.summary: Automated interpretability scores an explanation of a sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature by having a model predict token by token where the feature fires, or judge whether marked tokens fit it. The authors show that the evaluation data standard pipelines build can be scored without reading the explanation at all: on `Neuronpedia` fuzzing runs for 500 random `GPT-2 small` features, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and **a rule that says yes whenever the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers**. The cue changes form across pipelines, with `delphi` always marking the same slot in its fuzzing negatives, and because OpenAI's simulation benchmark lists each neuron's top-activating sequences first, a rule that predicts activity on the first five outscores the published `GPT-4` simulator. On natural-text windows cut at random offsets the position cue nearly vanishes and scorers must actually read the explanation, so the authors recommend reporting every score beside the best explanation-free rule on the same items.

papers.title: The Best Second Opinion Is Right Where the Primary Is Wrong: Partner Selection for Selective Span Tagging
papers.abstract: A span tagger that ranks its outputs by risk can defer the riskiest ones to a person, and a second model can sharpen this ranking. Which second model should it be? Partner selection is conditional, not global: the best second opinion is the model that is right where the primary is wrong. Across eight tagger types, three seeds and three English benchmarks (576 evaluated primary-partner pairings), choosing the partner by held-out accuracy on the primary's errors recovers 82% of the best partner's gain, against 69-70% for span F1 or a random pick. Frozen before a fourth dataset was chosen, the rule replicated there (Spearman 0.40 vs. 0.04 for span F1). Partner value is also directional. The predictive distribution is the second opinion: hard labels discard half of a partner's value, and scoring the served label improves 94% of pairings. Fixed before the fourth dataset was chosen, this score also replicated there. For LoRA-tuned decoders, independently trained partners beat every readout of the primary network. Applied zero-shot to 51 MASSIVE locales, every primary has a helpful trained partner in every locale, and the preferred partner follows competence.
papers.summary: A span tagger that ranks its outputs by risk can defer the riskiest ones to a person, and a second model can sharpen that ranking, but it is unclear which second model to pick. The authors argue partner selection is conditional rather than global: the best partner is whichever model is accurate on the primary's own mistakes. Across eight tagger types, three seeds and three English benchmarks, or 576 primary-partner pairings, **choosing the partner by held-out accuracy on the primary's errors recovers 82% of the best partner's gain**, against 69-70% for span F1 or a random pick, and the rule replicated on a fourth dataset chosen after it was frozen. Using the partner's predictive distribution rather than hard labels improves 94% of pairings, independently trained partners beat every readout of a LoRA-tuned primary, and applied zero-shot to 51 `MASSIVE` locales every primary has a helpful trained partner in every locale.

papers.title: Exposure Is Not Commitment: Double-Stratified Evaluation of Latent Monitors for Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using language agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and a growing literature probes model internals to catch unsafe actions before they execute, with sharply conflicting results. We argue much of the conflict is an evaluation artifact, and propose a double-stratification protocol: separate injection exposure from behavioral commitment, in both the evaluation and the training population. On the primary Qwen AgentDojo grid, monitors trained on the naive mixed unsafe-versus-rest contrast mostly learn exposure: they flag exposed trajectories whether or not the agent complies, and barely predict which cases turn unsafe. Retrained on exposed cases only, the same probe families predict the model's own unsafe tool call up to two steps early, the maximum the three-step trajectories admit (logistic AUROC 0.853, matched by a trained TF-IDF text baseline at 0.855). Mistral-7B reaches 0.896 and OLMo-2-7B 0.912; their naive contrasts learn different things: inverted exposure ranking on one, both axes on the other. Representations separate on exposure (probe 1.000 versus trained text 0.908) and where visible context is sanitized or unavailable. Training contrast alone reproduces the shape of recent pre-action-probe negative results, one candidate explanation for the conflict: the signal exists, but the model's own zero-shot forecast and NLA verbalizations do not reliably recover it. An unstratified AUROC overstates what a latent monitor knows, and what a naive contrast learns is population-dependent: evaluations should stratify both.
papers.summary: Tool-using language agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and studies that probe model internals to catch unsafe actions before they execute have reported sharply conflicting results. The authors argue much of the conflict is an evaluation artifact and propose a double-stratification protocol that separates injection exposure from behavioral commitment in both the evaluation set and the training population. On the primary `Qwen` `AgentDojo` grid, monitors trained on the naive unsafe-versus-rest contrast mostly learn whether an injection was present rather than whether the agent complied, but **retrained on exposed cases only, the same probe families predict the model's own unsafe tool call up to two steps early with AUROC 0.853**, a figure a trained TF-IDF text baseline matches at 0.855. `Mistral-7B` and `OLMo-2-7B` reach 0.896 and 0.912, and the authors conclude that an unstratified AUROC overstates what a latent monitor knows and that what a naive contrast learns depends on the population.

papers.title: Artifact Distillation: Training-Free Transfer from Frontier to Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Closing the gap between frontier and smaller language models is usually approached by distillation: fine-tuning the small model (student) on a frontier model's (teacher) outputs, which binds transfer to training compute and leaves the transferred knowledge largely opaque. We propose Artifact Distillation: a teacher solves training instances and externalizes its problem-solving procedure into an artifact bank that a student queries at inference time, with no gradient updates. Across four LiveBench tasks, a bank written by Claude Opus 4.5 lets Claude Haiku 4.5 outperform unaided Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning (0.707 vs. 0.647) at 60% of its cost, and reach Sonnet 4.5's level on table joining at 89% of its cost. The same raw bank raises Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800, showing that transfer is not confined to the teacher's model family.
papers.summary: Closing the gap between frontier and small language models is usually done by distillation, fine-tuning the student on the teacher's outputs, which ties transfer to training compute and leaves the transferred knowledge opaque. In `Artifact Distillation`, the teacher solves training instances and externalizes its problem-solving procedure into an artifact bank that the student queries at inference time with no gradient updates. Across four `LiveBench` tasks, a bank written by `Claude Opus 4.5` lets **`Claude Haiku 4.5` outperform unaided `Claude Sonnet 4.5` on spatial reasoning (0.707 vs. 0.647) at 60% of its cost**, and reach the level of `Claude Sonnet 4.5` on table joining at 89% of its cost. The same raw bank raises the pooled score of `Qwen3.5-27B` from 0.730 to 0.800, showing the transfer is not confined to the teacher's model family.

papers.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning for Reasoning Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks, where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long chain-of-thought data serves as a crucial foundation for eliciting and enhancing their reasoning abilities. Despite rapid progress in both improving and analyzing reasoning-oriented SFT, the field still lacks a systematic survey that consolidates its fast-growing literature. To fill this gap, we present a comprehensive review of recent advancements in reasoning SFT, examining the literature through the dual lenses of methodological design and analytical investigation. First, we review methodological improvements across the SFT pipeline and categorize them into data-centric approaches and algorithm-centric innovations. Second, we reorganize analytical studies along three dimensions: data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights. Finally, by synthesizing current research focuses and remaining bottlenecks, we outline promising future directions for reasoning SFT. We hope this survey deepens the understanding of reasoning SFT and paves the way for advanced reasoning models.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long chain-of-thought data is a central step in eliciting the abilities of large reasoning models, but the fast-growing literature on reasoning-oriented SFT has lacked a consolidated overview. The survey reviews methodological work across the SFT pipeline, splitting it into data-centric approaches and algorithm-centric innovations, and reorganizes analytical studies along **three dimensions: data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights**. It closes by synthesizing current research focuses and remaining bottlenecks into a set of future directions for reasoning SFT.

papers.title: Rank-Aware Differentially Private Release of Listwise Preferences for LLM Alignment
papers.abstract: Listwise preference feedback offers richer supervision for large language model (LLMs) alignment than pairwise comparisons, but a full ranking also reveals more sensitive user preferences. Existing privacy-preserving alignment methods focus mainly on pairwise feedback, while listwise alignment under local differential privacy (LDP) remains unexplored. Extending LDP to this listwise domain raises a critical challenge: the high sensitivity of the full ranking space demands excessive noise, neutralizing the benefits of listwise supervision. To address this challenge, we analyze the interaction between supervision granularity and privacy noise in downstream training, and introduce a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatizes listwise preference data into a low-sensitivity granularity suitable for downstream alignment. The mechanism leverages ranking information to sample a fixed-size binary partition, concentrating the noise near borderline items instead of perturbing all items uniformly as randomized response (RR) does. Empirical evaluations on downstream LLM alignment tasks show that our mechanism consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets. The code is available at https://github.com/tdsai-lab/RAEM.
papers.summary: Listwise preference feedback gives richer supervision for large language model alignment than pairwise comparisons, but a full ranking also reveals more about a user's preferences, and listwise alignment under local differential privacy (LDP) had not been studied. Privatizing the full ranking space naively demands so much noise that the benefit of listwise supervision disappears. The authors analyze how supervision granularity interacts with privacy noise in downstream training and introduce a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatizes listwise data into a fixed-size binary partition of low sensitivity, concentrating noise near borderline items rather than perturbing every item uniformly as randomized response (RR) does. On downstream alignment tasks the mechanism **consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets**.

papers.title: Prompt-agnostic Language Models
papers.abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: https://github.com/FSadrieh/prompt-agnostic-llms. Model checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/prompt-agnostic-language-models.
papers.summary: Large language models remain sensitive to how a prompt is phrased, and the usual remedy, manual prompt optimization at inference time, adds overhead and does not scale. The authors instead build robustness in during instruction tuning, and show that when several paraphrases of each prompt are mixed into training their gradients interfere, with **57% of trainable parameters showing sign conflicts** and naive averaging discarding roughly a fifth of the gradient magnitude. Two gradient-merging methods, `Prompt-TIES` and `Prompt-DARE`, apply interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging to the per-paraphrase gradients. Across four models from two families at two scales, the interaction between phrasing and specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and the merging methods nearly halve that variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to accuracy, whereas other train-time approaches based on data construction, consistency regularization, or contrastive alignment improve raw performance but do not reliably reduce it.

papers.title: An Introduction to Large Language Models for Scientists and Professionals
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.
papers.summary: Effective and responsible use of large language models requires understanding how they work, where they fail, and how their outputs should be evaluated, a gap for many scientists and professionals who use them daily. Written as the basis for a lecture in a master's program on artificial intelligence in medicine at the University of Turin, the book explains tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies without mathematical detail, with particular attention to hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, privacy, governance, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. More advanced chapters cover Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. **A substantial hands-on exercise walks the reader through running a local model with `Ollama` and `Open WebUI` to interrogate a collection of scientific papers**, stressing evidence retrieval, source verification, and the difference between plausible language and supported conclusions, with no programming knowledge required.

papers.title: From Geometry to Behavior: How Instruction Exposure Unlocks Latent Rhetorical Directions in LLMs
papers.abstract:
Language models do not merely memorize facts; they absorb rhetorical strategies from pretraining data, including the human tendency to reason by analogy. We ask: is this absorbed capability geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning, and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time?
  We extract an "Analogy Vector" from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it enables steerable explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), improving harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts. A small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality.
  Our central finding, from seven matched base-instruct pairs, is a gradient of behavioral accessibility: the analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models (strict pretraining/IT separation) show flat steering landscapes: present but behaviorally inert. Qwen-2.5 base models (instruction data woven into pretraining) are already partially accessible before any explicit fine-tuning; base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaches 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma, providing geometric corroboration of the behavioral gradient. This challenges the binary "base vs instruct" framing: the relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model has received across its full training pipeline. We position activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool that reveals how instruction exposure organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space.
papers.summary: Language models absorb rhetorical strategies such as reasoning by analogy from pretraining data, and the authors ask whether that capability is geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time. They extract an analogy direction from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it steers explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models from the `Gemma-2`, `Llama-3.1`, and `Qwen-2.5` families spanning 2B to 32B parameters, raising a harmonic-mean quality score from 3.22 to 3.94 for `Gemma-2-9B-IT` on 300 held-out prompts, with a small human study validating the LLM judge. Across seven matched base-instruct pairs, **the direction exists in every base model but its behavioral accessibility under linear steering scales continuously with how much instruction exposure the model received across its full training pipeline**. `Gemma-2` base models, trained with strict separation between pretraining and instruction tuning, show flat steering landscapes, while `Qwen-2.5` base models, which saw instruction data woven into pretraining, are already partially steerable, with base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector at 0.94-0.97 for `Qwen-2.5` versus 0.37-0.66 for `Gemma-2`.

papers.title: Where Planning Changes the Outcome of Orbital Games
papers.abstract:
This paper introduces OrbitalGym, a simulation environment for studying when planning algorithms or system design determine the outcome of adversarial orbital encounters. In an orbital game, two non-cooperative teams of satellites maneuver during rendezvous and proximity operations to win a differential-reward objective. Advances in terrestrial game playing have prompted many methods for orbital games, but studies typically evaluate one method in one scenario, often against a passive or random defender. It is unclear whether better planning matters once vehicle capability (maneuverability, sensing, communications) and adversarial responses are considered.
  OrbitalGym is a JAX-based environment supporting varying numbers of agents, state representations (position, velocity, attitude, fuel), explicit or implicit communication, and proximity or conical field-of-view sensors. It compiles games to batched GPU code, enabling large-scale parallel simulation of policies across many configurations. This identifies regimes where policy choice affects outcomes and regimes where system capability dominates.
  We study two close-range games: pursuit-evasion, where one spacecraft tries to capture another, and lady-bandit-guard, where a guard prevents an attacker from reaching a protected asset. We compare PD, LQR, model predictive path integral control, and Monte Carlo tree search over ratios of thrust and propellant, initial separation, game duration, sensor capability, and the definition of capture. In pursuit-evasion the propellant ratio decides most encounters: against five of six evader policies, pursuer policy changes capture probability by 10 percent or more in at most 15 of 90 capability configurations. In lady-bandit-guard, policy matters more: against bandits able to reach the asset, a better guard policy raises defense probability by at least 10 percent in 56 to 74 of 90 configurations.
papers.summary: Work on adversarial orbital encounters, where non-cooperative teams of satellites maneuver during rendezvous and proximity operations, usually evaluates one planning method in one scenario against a passive or random opponent, leaving open whether better planning matters once vehicle capability and adversarial responses are considered. `OrbitalGym` is a JAX-based environment that compiles multi-agent orbital games to batched GPU code, supporting varying agent counts, state representations, communication modes, and sensor models, so policies can be evaluated in parallel across many configurations. Comparing PD, LQR, model predictive path integral control, and Monte Carlo tree search in pursuit-evasion and lady-bandit-guard games over a grid of capability settings, the authors find that **in pursuit-evasion the propellant ratio decides most encounters**, with pursuer policy shifting capture probability by 10 percent or more in at most 15 of 90 configurations. In lady-bandit-guard, policy matters more, as a better guard policy raises defense probability by at least 10 percent in 56 to 74 of 90 configurations.

papers.title: One Confidence Threshold, Unequal Coverage: Language Gaps in Typed Decision Interfaces and How Translating Inputs Reduces Them
papers.abstract: Deployed classifiers often act on a prediction only when its confidence clears a threshold and pass the rest to a person. We ask whether one threshold serves all languages equally on typed decision interfaces, APIs that return a probability for each option of a fixed multiple-choice question. In a confirmatory study with a written analysis plan, three vendors' interfaces classified 1,000 MASSIVE items, each in 51 languages, with a threshold of 0.9. Even when a request is answered correctly in both English and another language, the English version clears the threshold more often, by 8.6-11.7 percentage points on average. Observed coverage, the share of requests handled automatically, is lower than English's in every other language, while the requests the gate handles are rarely wrong. The gap remains when every language is reweighted to the same accuracy, and a standard calibration metric (ECE) does not detect it on one interface. In exploratory analyses, English's coverage stays higher when each language gets its own threshold fitted to the same 5% error target. Translating inputs into English nearly closes the gap at 0.9 but leaves English ahead at that error target. Requests written natively in African languages show a gap in the same direction when English is their human translation. We recommend reporting per-language coverage at the operating threshold.
papers.summary: Deployed classifiers often act on a prediction only when its confidence clears a threshold and hand the rest to a person, and the authors ask whether one threshold serves all languages equally on typed decision interfaces, meaning APIs that return a probability for each option of a fixed multiple-choice question. In a confirmatory study with a written analysis plan, three vendors' interfaces classified 1,000 `MASSIVE` items in each of 51 languages at a threshold of 0.9. **Even when a request is answered correctly in both English and another language, the English version clears the threshold 8.6-11.7 percentage points more often on average**, so automated coverage is lower than English's in every other language, the gap survives reweighting every language to the same accuracy, and a standard calibration metric fails to detect it on one interface. Translating inputs into English nearly closes the gap at the 0.9 threshold, and the authors recommend reporting per-language coverage at the operating threshold.

papers.title: GenAI as an 'Invisible Hand' in Opinion Dynamics: Evidence from a Group-Level Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Recent arguments suggest that genAI can act as an invisible hand that gradually shapes social structures, such as collective beliefs and norms. The argument is that if millions of people repeatedly consult genAI tools, their generated outcomes quietly shape what becomes acceptable, reasonable or conventional. We study this in the context of collective opinion dynamics, i.e., how groups form opinions around controversial dynamics. We present the findings of a simulation including 50,000 group discussions across 50 controversial statements, three LLMs, and different social configurations. We vary two characteristics of LLM interaction-agreeableness and personalization-and compare the influence of genAI in homogeneous and heterogeneous groups. Our findings indicate that profile-specific personalization increases LLM influence when models adopt a non-neutral stance, i.e., when they agree or disagree with the user. Furthermore, we find that neutral LLMs have a stronger effect in homogeneous groups. Based on our simulation, we generate a set of hypotheses to specify how, why and when AI-related features and social configurations jointly shape collective opinion making.
papers.summary: If millions of people repeatedly consult generative AI tools, their outputs may quietly shape what a society treats as acceptable, reasonable, or conventional, and the authors test this idea in the setting of collective opinion dynamics. They simulate 50,000 group discussions across 50 controversial statements with three LLMs, varying the model's agreeableness and personalization and comparing homogeneous and heterogeneous groups. **Profile-specific personalization increases LLM influence when the model adopts a non-neutral stance**, agreeing or disagreeing with the user, while neutral LLMs have a stronger effect in homogeneous groups. The simulation results are distilled into hypotheses about how, why, and when AI features and social configurations jointly shape collective opinion formation.

papers.title: Cassette-Editor: A Video Editing Agent That Edits the Way You Do
papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly work by calling tools on a persistent artifact, such as a code repository, and the result of each call shapes their next step. Video editing is a demanding case of this pattern: what a frame shows depends on how every clip is trimmed, retimed, cropped, and nested, so knowledge about the footage holds only for particular uses of it, and an invalid edit can leave the timeline structurally broken. Existing video editing agents keep their edits valid with critic agents, reviewers, or restricted output formats. We present Cassette-Editor, a video editing agent with a deliberately simple interface: one tool reads the project and one tool writes to it. Every write passes through the same executor, rules, and commit service as the user's manual edits, and either commits atomically or is rejected with located diagnostics and repair options, while the model keeps the creative choices and decides how to recover. Reads relate stored analysis of the footage to each use of it on the timeline. In a controlled experiment, a real model is shown 277 of its own committed edits after damaging them. It corrected nearly every call with full or minimal feedback, but locating each problem cut the input tokens a correction needed to less than half, and its corrections dropped other values the model had written in one case rather than seven.
papers.summary: Language agents increasingly work by calling tools on a persistent artifact, and video editing is a demanding case because what a frame shows depends on how every clip is trimmed, retimed, cropped, and nested, so an invalid edit can leave the timeline structurally broken. Instead of critic agents, reviewers, or restricted output formats, `Cassette-Editor` exposes one tool to read the project and one to write to it, and routes every write through the same executor, rules, and commit service as a user's manual edits, so it either commits atomically or is rejected with located diagnostics and repair options while the model keeps the creative choices and decides how to recover. Reads relate stored analysis of the footage to each use of it on the timeline. In a controlled experiment where a model was shown 277 of its own committed edits after they were damaged, it corrected nearly every call with full or minimal feedback, but **locating each problem cut the input tokens a correction needed to less than half** and reduced the cases where a correction dropped other values the model had written from seven to one.

papers.title: Two-Colour Zig-Zag Numberlink on Rectangles: A Forbidden-Pattern Characterization, a Constructive Polynomial-Time Algorithm, and a Lean Verification
papers.abstract: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell. The problem is NP-complete when the number of pairs is un- bounded (Adcock et al.). For a single pair it is the Hamiltonian path problem in rectangular grid graphs, solved by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter. Two pairs on a rectangle form the paired 2-disjoint path cover problem. We settle the case of two pairs on rectangles with the endpoints anywhere in the grid. If both sides of the rectangle are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if no entry of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs. The catalogue consists of a parity condition, an alternation condition on the border, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. If a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side. The characterization is construc- tive. Solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together, in time O((R+C) RC). Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4. The finite case analyses, which are window certificates for the corner configurations and a check of all irreducible instances with sides 11-22, are carried out by the Lean compiler via native decide. We describe the algorithm, the catalogue, the proof structure, the compromises made in the formalization, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C that produce identical output.
papers.summary: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell, a problem that is NP-complete for unboundedly many pairs and reduces to Hamiltonian paths in rectangular grid graphs for a single pair. The authors settle the two-pair case on rectangles with endpoints anywhere: **when both sides are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if none of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs**, consisting of a parity condition, a border alternation condition, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. When a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side, and solutions are built constructively in O((R+C)RC) time by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together. Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic program are verified in `Lean 4`, with the finite case analyses discharged by native decide, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C produce identical output.

papers.title: Bouba Beats Kiki, and Other Regularities in the Subjective Preferences of LLMs
papers.abstract:
Users engage with large language models on tasks that are purely objective ("When was Netflix founded?"), purely subjective ("What should I name my child?") or anywhere in-between. We have rich tools for evaluating model accuracy with respect to objective criteria. However, when it comes to subjective aspects of a task, we do not have similarly developed methodology at hand. In this paper, we take some early steps towards framing the question of subjective evaluation. Rather than measure how often a model is right or wrong on a question, we instead ask, how do models make choices among multiple viable responses without a clear winner?
  To study this question, we restrict our focus to short-form content, and consider comparison tasks among three such content types: numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. We identify 29 aspects of these short-form examples covering many areas of syntax and semantics (length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix, spoken sound, etc.). We show first that models tend to have strong and reproducible preferences for or against some of these aspects. Second, we show that variations in how the model is asked to express a preference may cause some of these aspects to activate or deactivate in the model's selection. Third, we show that overall preference distributions among pairs may vary radically based on seemingly-unimportant variations in the nature of the question posed to the model, raising new questions about manipulation. And finally, we show that, if models are used both to create lists of alternatives and to rank them, there are unexpected interactions between the two stages that may also drive the models' stated preferences.
papers.summary: Users bring large language models everything from purely objective questions to purely subjective ones, yet while accuracy against objective criteria is well instrumented, there is little methodology for studying how a model chooses among several viable answers with no clear winner. The authors restrict attention to short-form content, running comparison tasks over numbers, baby names, and fictional cities, and identify 29 aspects of such items spanning syntax and semantics, including length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix, and spoken sound. **Models show strong and reproducible preferences for or against some of these aspects**, and which aspects activate depends on how the model is asked to express a preference. Overall preference distributions can shift radically with seemingly unimportant changes to the question, raising questions about manipulation, and when a model both generates the list of alternatives and ranks them, the two stages interact in unexpected ways that also shape its stated preferences.

papers.title: Network Topology Does Not Matter: The Breakdown of Classical Consensus in LLM Populations
papers.abstract: As multi-agent language model networks become widely deployed, predicting their collective behavior is a critical challenge. Classical distributed consensus theory relies on network topology to predict convergence, structurally assuming that agent updates are convex combinations, population means are conserved, and weights are content-independent. In this work, we demonstrate that these foundational assumptions fail for large language models (LLMs). By deterministically extracting continuous credence from token-level probabilities across eight instruction-tuned models and 73,080 controlled exchanges, we directly measure the empirical LLM update operator. We find that LLMs systematically violate convexity by updating outside the hull of observed opinions, exhibiting active repulsion (negative weights) that fundamentally breaks row-stochastic modeling and standard bounded-confidence repairs. Scaling these empirically fitted operators to simulations of 10,000 agents reveals that algebraic connectivity explains almost none of the final outcome variance. Instead, population dynamics are governed entirely by the model's internal update bias and message framing. Consequently, populations of several models, including those with up to 7B parameters, reliably compound small local drifts to reach confident agreement on objectively false claims regardless of their network structure. Our results prove that classical graph-theoretic metrics are inadequate for LLM populations, highlighting a profound deployment risk where multi-agent deliberation predictably saturates in collective delusion.
papers.summary: Classical distributed consensus theory predicts the convergence of multi-agent networks from their topology, assuming that each agent's update is a convex combination of observed opinions, that population means are conserved, and that weights do not depend on content. By deterministically extracting continuous credences from token-level probabilities across eight instruction-tuned models and 73,080 controlled exchanges, the authors directly measure the empirical update operator of large language models and find that **LLMs systematically update outside the hull of observed opinions, showing active repulsion with negative weights** that breaks row-stochastic modeling and standard bounded-confidence repairs. Scaling the fitted operators to simulations of 10,000 agents, algebraic connectivity explains almost none of the variance in final outcomes, which are governed instead by the model's internal update bias and message framing. Populations of several models, including ones with up to 7B parameters, reliably compound small local drifts into confident agreement on objectively false claims regardless of network structure.

papers.title: The Coordination Tax and the Heterogeneity Dividend: Break-Even Conditions for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM pipelines built on interoperability protocols such as the Open Floor Protocol (OFP) or A2A are usually justified on capability grounds, with their runtime cost treated as an overhead of unknown size. Comparing such a pipeline with one model call is underspecified, because a pipeline can give each role a different model. We give a closed-form model that sets the coordination tax (decomposition overhead plus per-handoff protocol cost) against the heterogeneity dividend from routing work to a cheaper model, with a break-even threshold and a feasibility bound, $\alpha < 1/r$, and measure every term, with OFP as the protocol under test, on 135 HumanEval and ClassEval tasks in 2430 runs of six architectures with Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. The protocol adds 7.2 ms per handoff, 0.11% of pipeline wall time. Decomposition does not pay on these tasks: a planner-coder-reviewer pipeline costs 3.22x as much as a single strong call, takes 3.24x as long, and solves no more tasks. Moving planner and reviewer to the cheap model cuts the pipeline's cost to 0.39x but changes pass@1 by -6.7 points, leaving it dearer, slower and less accurate than the single call, and the break-even forecast misses by -19% because the cheap roles inflate token volume. The saving lies in choosing a model per task instead: an oracle choice between the two single calls solves 94.3% of runs at half the strong call's cost per solved task.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM pipelines built on interoperability protocols such as the Open Floor Protocol (OFP) or A2A are usually justified on capability grounds with their runtime cost treated as an overhead of unknown size, and comparing one to a single model call is underspecified because each role can be given a different model. The authors give a closed-form model that sets the coordination tax, meaning decomposition overhead plus per-handoff protocol cost, against the heterogeneity dividend from routing work to a cheaper model, with a break-even threshold and a feasibility bound of alpha below 1/r, and measure every term with OFP on 135 `HumanEval` and `ClassEval` tasks across 2,430 runs of six architectures using `Claude Opus 5.5` and `Claude Haiku 5.5`. The protocol itself adds only 7.2 ms per handoff, but **a planner-coder-reviewer pipeline costs 3.22x as much as a single strong call, takes 3.24x as long, and solves no more tasks**, and moving the planner and reviewer to the cheap model cuts cost to 0.39x while dropping pass@1 by 6.7 points. The saving lies instead in choosing a model per task, since an oracle choice between the two single calls solves 94.3% of runs at half the strong call's cost per solved task.

papers.title: DuQUAD: A Dual-View Framework with Quality-Aware Evidence Pruning for Multi-Document Question Answering
papers.abstract: Large language models with retrieval-augmented generation systematically underutilize evidence in the middle of multi-document contexts, a phenomenon known as Lost in the Middle. Existing mitigation strategies, such as document reordering and attention steering, can reduce boundary bias but remain brittle in noisy settings, where inaccurate relevance estimation and spurious documents still obscure useful evidence in central positions. We propose DuQUAD, a multi-document QA framework that mitigates positional bias through dual-view reasoning and quality-aware evidence pruning. DuQUAD combines a Local Agent guided by a Structural Fusion Score with a Global Agent that reasons over the full document set, providing both targeted evidence recovery and broad contextual understanding. The framework further filters candidate evidence using explicit quality scoring and refines it at the sentence level to reduce noise. DuQUAD consistently outperforms strong Lost-in-the-Middle mitigation baselines, including hybrid retrieval and reranking, multi-agent reasoning, and context optimization methods, improving accuracy by 3.0% on average over the strongest competing baseline and gold evidence recall by 9.4%, while substantially reducing computational cost compared to existing multi-agent frameworks.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented language models tend to ignore evidence placed in the middle of long multi-document contexts, and existing fixes such as reordering or attention steering break down when retrieval is noisy and irrelevant documents crowd out useful ones. `DuQUAD` pairs a Local Agent, which uses a Structural Fusion Score to recover targeted evidence, with a Global Agent that reasons over the whole document set, then applies explicit quality scoring and sentence-level refinement to prune spurious passages. Against hybrid retrieval, reranking, multi-agent, and context-optimization baselines, it improves accuracy by **3.0% on average over the strongest competitor** and raises gold evidence recall by 9.4%, while costing less compute than prior multi-agent frameworks.

papers.title: Search-Guided Reasoning Trace Curation for Verilog Generation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved Verilog generation. However, most training pipelines distill natural-language reasoning traces whose intermediate design decisions are weakly structured and are primarily selected according to the correctness of the final generated RTL. We present MCTS-SFT, a verifier-guided framework for curating reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Verilog generation models. MCTS-SFT formulates trace construction as search over intermediate reasoning states and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to propagate functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts to earlier design decisions. Within this framework, we introduce Plan-MCTS, which searches over compact hardware-design plans that explicitly represent interfaces, timing, state, behavior, and update rules. We further study plan-preserving supervision, in which the searched structured state is retained as part of the downstream SFT target. Our experiments find that Plan-MCTS achieves the highest functional trace yield, with 84.2% correct traces compared with 81.9% for one-shot structured planning and 82.0% for unguided tree exploration. For identical Plan-MCTS trajectories and Verilog outputs, retaining the explicit searched plan during SFT raises pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%, demonstrating that the representation of intermediate design decisions materially affects downstream learning. In a separate 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision improves pass@10 over full-response chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 points while reducing downstream generation length by approximately 50% on VerilogEval-v2. These results demonstrate that structured hardware planning, verifier-guided search, and explicit intermediate-state supervision provide complementary mechanisms for constructing more effective and token-efficient training data for Verilog generation.
papers.summary: Training data for Verilog generation is usually distilled from natural-language reasoning traces that are only filtered by whether the final register-transfer-level code passes, leaving intermediate design decisions loosely structured. `MCTS-SFT` treats trace construction as a search over intermediate reasoning states and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to push functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts back to earlier decisions, and the `Plan-MCTS` variant searches over compact hardware plans covering interfaces, timing, state, behavior, and update rules. `Plan-MCTS` yields 84.2% functionally correct traces versus about 82% for one-shot planning or unguided search, and **keeping the searched plan in the supervised fine-tuning target lifts pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%** on identical trajectories. In a separate 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision beats full chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 pass@10 points on `VerilogEval-v2` while roughly halving generation length.

papers.title: Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration for Spectral Compression of Dense Retrieval Embeddings
papers.abstract: Spectral compression reduces the storage and scoring costs of dense retrieval by projecting embeddings onto a smaller principal subspace. However, its corpus-derived weighting rules tie all retained directions to a shared spectral trend, without directly accounting for their individual contributions to relevance. To address this, we propose Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration (RRC), a closed-form method for refining spectral weights using relevance judgments. RRC estimates margin-based weights from the means and variances of positive--negative score contributions along each retained direction. It retains directions with positive estimated weights, decomposes their log weights into a fitted power-law trend and a residual, and adds the residual to the compressor's log weights on this support. This allows relevance judgments to adjust individual directions while preserving the compressor's overall spectral trend. RRC applies to PCA, Whitening, and SpecTemp, and incorporates the corrections into the existing transformation shared by documents and queries, without iterative model training or an additional inference stage. Experiments with three encoders on nine datasets covering conventional and reasoning-intensive retrieval show that SpecTemp + RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on the BEIR group and BRIGHT at every target dimension. On the five evaluated BRIGHT datasets, it improves over SpecTemp by an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points at 768 dimensions. The gains also persist under scalar and product quantization, improving the trade-off between per-document storage and retrieval effectiveness. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rrc-spectral-compression-B5CE/
papers.summary: Spectral compression shrinks dense retrieval embeddings by projecting onto a principal subspace, but the corpus-derived weights it assigns to retained directions follow a shared spectral trend and ignore how much each direction actually contributes to relevance. Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration (`RRC`) is a closed-form correction that estimates margin-based weights per direction from the means and variances of positive-versus-negative score contributions, fits a power-law trend to their log weights, and adds only the residual to the compressor's weights so the overall spectral shape is preserved. It plugs into `PCA`, Whitening, and `SpecTemp` without retraining or an extra inference stage. Across three encoders and nine datasets, `SpecTemp` plus `RRC` is the most effective compressor on the `BEIR` group and `BRIGHT` at every target dimension, **gaining an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points over `SpecTemp` at 768 dimensions on `BRIGHT`**, with the gains holding under scalar and product quantization.

papers.title: Towards Myocardial Infarction Diagnosis: An Investigation into Machine Learning and Deep Learning Algorithms using ECG Data
papers.abstract: Myocardial Infarction (MI) is a severe and potentially fatal cardiac condition caused by myocardial injury due to ischemia, and timely detection can substantially reduce its mortality. Electrocardiography (ECG) is the primary diagnostic modality for MI, but manual interpretation is susceptible to human error. In this work, we propose Visionary V2, a multi-step, adaptive filtration method for ECG signal normalization, and use it to study machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches to MI detection on the PTB Diagnostic ECG Database using all 15 available leads. On statistical features extracted from the filtered signals, such as the R-R interval, a Bagging ensemble of decision trees reaches 96.6% accuracy, compared with 87.7% when the signals are processed with BioSPPy. We further generate an image dataset from the filtered signals, on which a custom ResNet-50 misclassifies only 1 of 7,000 validation images and a custom CNN reaches an F1 score of about 98.7%. Finally, we apply LIME, Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients to verify that the image models attend to the ECG waveform rather than the background. These results indicate that careful signal normalization combined with ML and DL models can support fast and accurate automated MI screening.
papers.summary: Manual electrocardiogram (ECG) reading for myocardial infarction (MI) is error-prone, and the authors argue that signal normalization is a neglected step in automated detection. They introduce `Visionary V2`, a multi-step adaptive filtering method, and use it to compare machine learning and deep learning classifiers on all 15 leads of the `PTB Diagnostic ECG Database`, both on hand-crafted statistical features such as R-R intervals and on images rendered from the filtered signals. A bagging ensemble of decision trees reaches 96.6% accuracy on features from the new filter versus 87.7% with `BioSPPy` preprocessing, and on the image dataset **a custom `ResNet-50` misclassifies only 1 of 7,000 validation images** while a custom CNN reaches an F1 of about 98.7%. LIME, Grad-CAM, and Integrated Gradients are used to check that the image models attend to the waveform rather than the background.

papers.title: Moment-Guided Optimizers for Noisy Deep Learning: MGO-SC as a Simple Consistency Gate for Adam-Style Updates
papers.abstract: Adaptive optimizers are widely used in deep learning, yet their behavior can degrade under heavy stochasticity and label noise where the sign and magnitude of gradients can be unstable. We study MGO-SC (Moment-Guided Optimizer with Sign-Consistency), a lightweight modification of Adam-style methods that derives a coordinate-wise consistency gate from the magnitude of a sign exponential moving average (EMA): coordinates whose gradient sign is stable are trusted, while coordinates whose sign fluctuates are down-weighted. We show that the naive form of this gate, which can only shrink updates, loses effective step size and underperforms when the learning rate is matched to the baseline. We therefore introduce a mean-preserving variant that reallocates trust across coordinates without changing the net per-tensor step magnitude. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, under a matched learning rate and decoupled weight decay, mean-preserving MGO-SC consistently improves over its AdamW baseline across clean, symmetric, and asymmetric label noise (e.g., +1.4 points at 40% symmetric noise; paired bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero; Wilcoxon p<0.01), while adding no second-order information or per-sample filtering. We report matched-seed effect sizes, nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired significance tests, and we release code and raw logs.
papers.summary: Adam-style optimizers can degrade under heavy stochasticity and label noise, where the sign and magnitude of per-coordinate gradients become unstable. `MGO-SC` (Moment-Guided Optimizer with Sign-Consistency) adds a coordinate-wise gate derived from the magnitude of a sign exponential moving average (EMA), trusting coordinates whose gradient sign is stable and down-weighting those that flip; because the naive gate can only shrink updates and loses effective step size at a matched learning rate, the authors introduce a mean-preserving variant that reallocates trust across coordinates without changing the net per-tensor step. On `CIFAR-10` with `ResNet-18` under matched learning rate and decoupled weight decay, the mean-preserving version **consistently beats `AdamW` across clean, symmetric, and asymmetric label noise, including +1.4 points at 40% symmetric noise**, with bootstrap confidence intervals and Wilcoxon tests reported and code and raw logs released.

papers.title: Generation, Not Selection: LLM Proposals for Certified Access-Control Policy Mining
papers.abstract: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) policy mining---recovering a compact, auditable policy from an access log---is posed as minimum set cover and solved greedily, which enjoys an $s^{*}(1+\ln m)$ guarantee. That guarantee is \emph{conditional} on a precondition the literature never states: the candidate pool handed to greedy must contain the optimal rules. Generation, not selection, is the binding constraint, and existing generators are purely \emph{syntactic}---they surface a rule only when enough log records witness it, so they fail on precisely the rare exception rules that fill a heavy-tailed policy. We replace the generator with a language model proposing rules \emph{semantically}, from attribute names, and keep the combinatorial selector to carry the guarantee: every proposal is filtered against the observed denials, so soundness is independent of the proposal mechanism and an unreliable proposer can only waste candidates, never grant access. Over five seeds on each of two enterprise domains, adding semantic proposal to a syntactic miner dominates it on \emph{ten of ten} runs---strictly better on seven---with near-optimal policies ($9.2$--$9.6$ rules against $s^{*}=9$, versus $11.2$--$14.6$) and false grants cut four- to sevenfold. Replacing the syntactic miner rather than augmenting it wins only where witnesses are scarce. An anonymization ablation isolates the mechanism: opaque attribute names cost two thirds of the model's rule recovery while leaving the syntactic baselines provably unmoved, and cost nothing where witnesses are plentiful. Semantic knowledge and log evidence are substitutes.
authors: Gautam Kumar (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur
Shamik Sural (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur
papers.summary: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) policy mining recovers a compact rule set from an access log by greedy set cover, but the familiar approximation guarantee only holds if the candidate pool already contains the optimal rules, and existing syntactic generators only propose rules that enough log records witness, so they miss the rare exception rules that dominate heavy-tailed policies. The authors keep the combinatorial selector for its guarantee but replace the generator with a language model that proposes rules semantically from attribute names, filtering every proposal against observed denials so an unreliable proposer can waste candidates but never grant unauthorized access. Over five seeds on two enterprise domains, adding semantic proposals to a syntactic miner wins on **ten of ten runs, yielding 9.2 to 9.6 rules against an optimum of 9 versus 11.2 to 14.6 for the baseline**, with false grants cut four- to sevenfold. An anonymization ablation shows that opaque attribute names remove two thirds of the model's rule recovery while leaving syntactic baselines unchanged, indicating semantic knowledge and log evidence act as substitutes.

papers.title: Learning Graph Beliefs for Active Radio Mapping With Decision-Certified Multi-Step Sensing
papers.abstract: Radio maps provide essential wireless propagation knowledge for network optimization and autonomous platforms. Acquiring dense measurements, however, is prohibitively costly, requiring active sampling to prioritize informative measurements. Existing active sampling methods typically rely on variances from prescribed spatial models or learned pointwise uncertainty, which may not fully capture the spatial correlation of different measurements. This paper proposes GraphBARC, a graph-structured active radio map construction framework that integrates learned spatial modeling with analytical Bayesian inference. A graph network learns correlated node and edge factors using only acquired measurements, inducing a joint full-map belief that supports analytical observation updates without retraining. Rather than immediate one-step acquisition, it adopts a nonmyopic sensing strategy that evaluates joint map-wide Bayes risk reduction over feasible multi-step routes, accounting for information redundancy among planned measurements. We reuse candidate responses and derive residual-based bounds directly on route-value differences, retaining shared response-error structure to avoid uniformly high-accuracy evaluation. An error-aware continuation bound screens unpromising prefixes, after which only responses needed for unresolved comparisons are refined. We further establish a computable decision-gap bound and show that certified exclusions remain valid during refinement. Experiments show that GraphBARC reduces mean root-mean-square error (RMSE) by over 16% relative to the evaluated baselines and core planning time by 56% compared with the fixed-accuracy, unpruned implementation.
papers.summary: Building radio maps for wireless network optimization requires dense measurements that are costly to collect, and existing active sampling methods rely on prescribed spatial models or pointwise uncertainty that miss correlations between measurements. `GraphBARC` learns node and edge factors with a graph network from acquired measurements alone, inducing a joint full-map belief that supports analytical Bayesian updates without retraining, and plans nonmyopic multi-step sensing routes by evaluating map-wide Bayes risk reduction while accounting for redundancy among planned measurements. Residual-based bounds on route-value differences, an error-aware continuation bound for screening prefixes, and a computable decision-gap bound let it certify route exclusions during refinement. Experiments show **over 16% lower RMSE than the evaluated baselines** and a 56% reduction in core planning time compared with a fixed-accuracy unpruned implementation.

papers.title: What a Weight Update Buys: Leverage Across Training Stages
papers.abstract: Post-training moves a language model's weights by about a thousandth of their norm and changes its behavior sharply; pretraining moves them by a third and buys a slow drift. We introduce leverage, an exact measure of what a unit of weight change buys: the Fisher quadratic form of an update, computed with one forward-mode pass per direction, divided by the same form for random directions of the same size at the same checkpoint. Leverage orders released Olmo-3, T\"ulu-3, Zephyr, and OLMo-2 checkpoints over four orders of magnitude: pretraining windows sit at the random level on prose, SFT five times above it, RL-Zero and RLVR at 400-1,500, and DPO at 400-23,000. With this instrument we find that pretraining accumulates into noise: windows of 30k to 1M steps are no more consequential on prose than random directions of their size, as a noisy quadratic model of SGD predicts. We find that training precision changes what an update looks like: training bf16 parameters without an fp32 master copy freezes 36-99% of coordinates, lowers leverage up to sevenfold, and creates an alignment between update magnitudes and the diagonal Fisher that fp32 training does not show. We derive and verify a law for reuse: the sign-flip null predicts the relative damage of random drop-and-rescale (DARE) at keep rate $p$ as $(1-p)/(p\,\rho_{\mathrm{sign}})$, within a factor of two of measurement wherever DARE succeeds. Two controls make these readings reliable: every controlled SFT and DPO trajectory with fp32 master weights loses leverage as it moves, and two re-runs of a released DPO stage from its anchor with its published recipe land within 1% of the released displacement and 4% of its leverage, where a plain recipe reads five to six times lower; leaving one component out traces the level to the length-normalized loss and its batch size of 128 together.
papers.summary: Post-training shifts a language model's weights by roughly a thousandth of their norm yet changes behavior sharply, while pretraining moves them by a third and produces only slow drift. The authors define leverage as the Fisher quadratic form of a weight update, computed with one forward-mode pass per direction, divided by the same quantity for random directions of equal size at the same checkpoint, and apply it to released `Olmo-3`, `Tulu-3`, `Zephyr`, and `OLMo-2` checkpoints. **Leverage spans four orders of magnitude: pretraining windows of 30k to 1M steps sit at the random level on prose, supervised fine-tuning about five times above, RL-Zero and RLVR at 400 to 1,500, and DPO at 400 to 23,000.** They also find that training bf16 parameters without an fp32 master copy freezes 36 to 99% of coordinates and cuts leverage up to sevenfold, and derive a sign-flip law predicting the damage from random drop-and-rescale (`DARE`) merging within a factor of two wherever `DARE` works.

papers.title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.
papers.summary: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training suffers from uneven routing that creates compute and communication hot spots, and existing placement and replication fixes add expert copies that compete with token buffers for scarce GPU memory. `LRMoE` plans retention quotas and expert placement during the forward pass under memory constraints while keeping all routed computation, then during backpropagation uses a load recalibration metric to estimate each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and keeps only pairs within quota, distributing them across eligible expert instances with capacity-aware routing. Physical compaction turns the retained pairs into smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and buffer demand. On `Qwen3-30B-A3B` and `GLM4.5-106B-A12B`, it **cuts cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2 to 44.8% relative to `SYMI`**.

papers.title: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery
papers.abstract: Modern image generators can produce complex visual artifacts, including diagrams, interfaces, and records that combine text, graphics, and layout to convey detailed information. They may refuse requests for overtly harmful imagery yet still generate artifacts that guide dangerous actions or support deception. We call the risk arising from what such images enable, rather than only what they depict, functional visual harm (FVH). Existing safety benchmarks focus largely on overtly harmful content, such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving image generators' safety alignment against FVH insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce FVH-Bench, comprising 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. The 11 evaluated image generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently generate artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions. High scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability further indicate that these outputs can support the intended harmful purposes. A further analysis finds that existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of FVH, indicating gaps in their ability to recognize harmful visual functions. Together, these findings show that evaluating image-generator safety alignment requires considering not only what images depict, but also what they may enable.
papers.summary: Image generators now produce diagrams, interfaces, and document-like records that convey detailed information, so they can refuse overtly harmful imagery yet still output artifacts that guide dangerous actions or enable deception, a risk the authors call functional visual harm (FVH). `FVH-Bench` contains 669 prompts spanning five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains, scored on refusal, how fully the targeted harmful function is realized, and how usable the resulting artifact is. **The 11 evaluated generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently produce artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful function**, and existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of such outputs. The results argue that safety evaluation for image generation must consider what images enable, not only what they depict.

papers.title: Threshold Compatibility and Support-Selection Diagnostics in Neural Discovery of Partial Differential Equations
papers.abstract: Accurate regression need not yield the correct equation after support selection. For a median/sample-standard-deviation threshold in neural PDE discovery, we derive an exact two-signal retention boundary and a complete-vector perturbation bound. Exact advection-diffusion libraries lose diffusion despite coefficient recovery to numerical precision. True-support refits of forty saved sparse states reduce diffusion error without restoring all derivative accuracy. A fixed sequential threshold ridge comparator recovers exact support in sixty ideal controls but selects extra terms in every learned state. All-fold correct-support candidates are rejected by conditional validation; post hoc energy pooling preserves their higher minimum loss in all sixty states. Supplied-support estimates outperform unchanged selected equations in all 240 physical-residual comparisons on four unused analytic trajectories. With coefficients, observation points and weights fixed, exact replacement of the learned library and target reverses their learned-row ordering in 59/60 states. Weighting both losses also fails the specified Burgers diffusion-benefit criterion at every tested budget.
