These finite diagnostics distinguish threshold incompatibility, refit damage and score rejection; they establish neither automatic correction nor general recovery or predictive stability.
papers.summary: Accurate regression in neural discovery of partial differential equations does not guarantee that thresholding recovers the correct equation. For the common median-over-sample-standard-deviation threshold, the authors derive an exact two-signal retention boundary and a complete-vector perturbation bound, and run a battery of finite diagnostics on advection-diffusion and Burgers libraries. **Exact advection-diffusion libraries drop the diffusion term even when coefficients are recovered to numerical precision**, refits on the true support only partially repair derivative accuracy, a fixed sequential threshold ridge comparator recovers exact support in all sixty ideal controls but adds extra terms in every learned state, and conditional validation rejects correct-support candidates in all sixty cases. The diagnostics separate threshold incompatibility, refit damage, and score rejection but explicitly establish no automatic correction or general recovery guarantee.

papers.title: Predicate Neuron: Differentiable Quantization of Predicate Relations in Gradient-based Learning
papers.abstract: In machine learning, symbolic reasoning approaches often rely on static architectures that hinder integration into deep neural networks and gradient-based optimization. To address this, we introduce the Native Predicate Neuron, a differentiable logic-reasoning neural module that enriches standard architectures with symbolic reasoning capabilities via first-order logic quantization. The proposed neuron models relational logic by learning to alternate between operations using a single trainable parameter. It features a tailored gradient mechanism with a dual-nature formulation: executing hard logical operations during training while maintaining differentiability for backpropagation. By quantizing both its input and choice state, the Predicate Neuron approximates continuous and non-continuous functions, effectively resolving discontinuities that standard deep learning architectures struggle with. We evaluate the Predicate Neuron across Fully-Connected, Convolutional, Recurrent, and Transformer architectures on benchmarks like MNIST and Wikitext. Results show that incorporating Predicate Neurons accelerates convergence, boosts accuracy, and lowers loss in general, with particularly strong improvements in tasks requiring monotonic reasoning or handling discontinuities. Overall, the Predicate Neuron natively integrates into standard neural networks to enable fuzzy logic operations and is available in Keras and PyTorch.
papers.summary: Symbolic reasoning modules usually rely on static architectures that are hard to embed in gradient-trained networks. The Native `Predicate Neuron` is a differentiable logic module that quantizes first-order logic relations, learning to switch between logical operations through a single trainable parameter, and uses a dual-nature gradient scheme that executes hard logical operations in the forward pass while staying differentiable for backpropagation. By quantizing both its inputs and its operation choice, it can approximate discontinuous as well as continuous functions. Evaluated inside fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent, and Transformer architectures on benchmarks including `MNIST` and `Wikitext`, **adding Predicate Neurons speeds convergence, raises accuracy, and lowers loss, with the largest gains on tasks involving monotonic reasoning or discontinuities**, and implementations are released for Keras and PyTorch.

papers.title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.
papers.summary: Enterprise retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must answer over documents written by many teams over time, where metadata and fast-changing facts live outside the documents themselves. The authors build a quarterly snapshot of `SEC EDGAR` with 167,050 filings, 508,714 embedded risk-factor chunks, and a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges, then compare text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design using the same model and temperature, scored by an LLM judge over 20 questions asked three times each. **GraphRAG answered 16 of 20 questions correctly on all three attempts versus 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG**, losing only on structured aggregation, while vector RAG failed the single-document category it was expected to win because company attribution cannot be recovered from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods came from text-to-SQL conflating people who share a surname, a failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading text structurally prevents, and the authors claim no generality beyond this corpus, model, and question set.

papers.title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
papers.abstract: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.
papers.summary: When a single calibration parameter cannot reproduce a physical model's behavior across all operating conditions because of model discrepancy, global calibration averages over contexts and loses accuracy. The authors build a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods with Gaussian kernels centered on a target context, inflating the covariance to absorb context uncertainty, reflecting at domain boundaries, and optionally correcting for uneven context sampling, then approximate the whole family with a conditional normalizing flow trained by amortized variational inference. In a twin experiment on the `Branin-Hoo` function, localization reduces aggregate predictive errors relative to a global posterior under both uniform and skewed context distributions. Applied to the k-epsilon turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model with atmospheric surface forcing as context, **localized calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to both deterministic and global-posterior calibration**, though both experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

papers.title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
papers.abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.
papers.summary: Many language model uses end in a typed decision among a closed set of options, and reading option probabilities from a single forward pass is fast but unreliable on multi-step cases like arithmetic, counting, or date comparison, while thinking first is accurate but costs seconds. `ThinkJev` builds both modes from one open hybrid-thinking model: System 1 reads the option-letter probabilities when the model answers directly, and System 2 reads the same letters after thinking on the same cached prompt, so escalation repeats no work and a single sampled thought yields the answer under every thinking budget. Without any training, a statistical test on labeled dev data decides where System 1 may answer alone under a target error rate; **at a 5% target, `Qwen3.5-27B` answers 24.5% of 8,359 test decisions directly with a realized error of 3.9%**, and stopping thoughts early once the answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy versus 82.7% for always thinking while using 72% of the thought tokens. On the public items of `JevBench`, the 27B model thinks on 29.4% of items and is not distinguishable in accuracy from two thinking APIs.

papers.title: Selective Transfer Learning for Groundwater Level Anomaly Forecasting: Accuracy-Risk Trade-offs
papers.abstract: This work studies context-aware selective transfer learning for multi-well groundwater anomaly forecasting in the Netherlands. Source-domain pretraining can raise average accuracy but is not uniformly reliable: it degrades performance on a substantial fraction of heterogeneous wells. Context-Aware Selective Learning (CASL) uses calibration-trained, constrained contextual blending of frozen no-transfer and fixed-transfer parents. Global Convex Blend uses the same parents with one calibration-fitted weight per seed. The corrected task requires nine consecutive observed monthly inputs and an exact three-calendar-month target, without interpolation. Evaluation covers 457 wells and 13,718 test windows under five predefined seeds, with the four-cell maxsim0.60 source pool frozen using Always-TL validation RMSE alone. Fixed transfer harms 18.38-51.86% of wells. CASL has 0.424-1.084% lower RMSE than No TL, partially rescuing 97.53-99.50% and fully rescuing 23.46-43.78% of fixed-harmed wells. Partial rescue can arise structurally from convex blending and does not establish contextual superiority. Global Convex Blend protects more wells in four seeds, while CASL has slightly lower pooled RMSE in four. Neither dominates: the results support an accuracy-risk trade-off on the fixed split, not rolling deployment validity.
papers.summary: Pretraining on source wells can raise average accuracy for groundwater anomaly forecasting but harms a large share of heterogeneous target wells, so the authors study when to apply transfer. Context-Aware Selective Learning (`CASL`) learns a constrained contextual blend of frozen no-transfer and fixed-transfer parent models on calibration data, and is compared with a Global Convex Blend that fits one weight per seed, on a corrected task requiring nine consecutive observed monthly inputs and an exact three-month-ahead target. Across 457 Dutch wells and 13,718 test windows over five seeds, **fixed transfer harms 18.38 to 51.86% of wells**, while `CASL` lowers RMSE by 0.424 to 1.084% versus no transfer and partially rescues 97.53 to 99.50% of harmed wells. Neither blending scheme dominates, partial rescue can arise structurally from convex blending alone, and the authors frame the result as an accuracy-risk trade-off on a fixed split rather than evidence of deployment validity.

papers.title: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Large-Scale Study of Oversight Directives in Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Agent skills, reusable instruction packages centred on a SKILL.md file, extend AI agents on demand, and a single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it. Some lines are oversight-loosening directives: they tell the agent to proceed without approval, to bypass checks with --no-verify, or to keep working without checking in. Although such directives can remove a checkpoint from every agent that loads them, no prior work has examined them. We present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills. We split skills into units (sentences, bullets, table cells, and code lines), develop a codebook that labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism, and scope, label 2,097 units by hand, and train a detector to scale the analysis. Our results show that about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive. These directives most often loosen oversight through permission flags, and most of them (70.1%) apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI. Compared with skills that have the same amount of oversight language, skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive, an association that holds across all our robustness checks, and they do not compensate with more tightening. Loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by their adopters: 2.4% of the skill families that carry loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills, and 1.1% of distinct loosening units for half of all loosening occurrences. Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4, while the LLM behind them, prompted with our codebook instead, catches 61% at a precision of 0.71.
papers.summary: Agent skills are reusable instruction packages built around a SKILL.md file, and a single line in a widely copied skill that tells the agent to proceed without approval, bypass checks with --no-verify, or avoid checking in can remove an oversight checkpoint from every agent that loads it. The authors analyze 1.53 million English skills from `GitSkills`, split them into sentence, bullet, table-cell, and code-line units, hand-label 2,097 units with a codebook covering polarity, mechanism, and scope, and train a detector to scale up. **About one in seventeen skills, roughly 88,000, contains an oversight-loosening directive**, most often via permission flags, and 70.1% apply unconditionally rather than only in contexts like CI. Skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7 to 1.8 times the odds of containing such a directive without adding compensating tightening, loosening spreads mainly through a few upstream skill families, and open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of these directives at precision below 0.4, whereas the same LLM prompted with the codebook catches 61% at precision 0.71.

papers.title: Anisotropic Trust Region Warping for Prior-Data Fitted Networks in Bayesian Optimisation
papers.abstract: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) replace the hyperparameter refitting of Gaussian Process (GP) surrogates in Bayesian optimisation with a single forward pass, at the cost of a prior that is fixed at meta-training time. We show empirically that a PFN's predictive log-likelihood falls increasingly behind that of a refitted GP as the objective function's lengthscale grows beyond the mode of the PFN's meta-training prior, and that this deficit carries over to optimisation performance. To correct the mismatch without retraining the network, we introduce Anisotropic Trust Region (ATR) warping. Per-dimension lengthscales are estimated by kernel target alignment, and an affine rescaling of the input space maps the objective onto the lengthscale the PFN expects, with a trust region around the anchor determining which observations are retained, leaving the PFN's $\mathcal{O}(d \cdot N^2)$ inference cost unchanged. On functions drawn from a Mat\'ern-3/2 kernel, ATR warping improves optimisation performance of the PFN at both extremes of the lengthscale range. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/Trust-Region-Warping-For-PFNs.
papers.summary: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) replace Gaussian Process (GP) hyperparameter refitting in Bayesian optimisation with a single forward pass, but their prior is frozen at meta-training time. The authors show empirically that a PFN's predictive log-likelihood falls further behind a refitted GP as the objective's lengthscale grows beyond the mode of the meta-training prior, and that this gap carries into optimisation performance. Anisotropic Trust Region (`ATR`) warping estimates per-dimension lengthscales by kernel target alignment, applies an affine rescaling so the objective matches the lengthscale the PFN expects, and uses a trust region around an anchor to decide which observations to retain, leaving inference cost unchanged. **On functions drawn from a Matern-3/2 kernel, ATR warping improves PFN optimisation performance at both extremes of the lengthscale range** without retraining the network.

papers.title: Poisoned Skills: Propagating Jailbreaks Through Agent Markdown Files
papers.abstract: Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., SKILL.md), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.
papers.summary: Agent frameworks let users supply Markdown files such as SKILL.md that are assembled into the agent's system prompt at initialization, and the authors ask whether a jailbreak embedded in such a file propagates into prohibited behavior. They build a `LangChain` question-answering agent whose system prompt comes from a user-provided Markdown file, embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a `GPTFUZZER`-based attack, and test seven open-weight models on 270 forbidden questions across nine harm categories. **A benign system prompt yields a mean attack success rate (ASR) of 0.5%, while the injected skill file raises it to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models.** Two obfuscation strategies, zero-width-character stealth payloads and grapheme-to-phoneme phonetic payloads, do no better than plain text, with the phonetic variant dropping mean ASR to 30%, suggesting vulnerability depends more on the model than on the payload encoding.

papers.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.
papers.summary: Large language models show promise on research-level problems, but no comprehensive collection of such problems exists and evaluating on them is difficult. `OpenFrontiers` pairs a structured corpus of 12,151 open research problems across disciplines, recording statements, context, and progress, with a retrospective mathematics benchmark of 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each formalized as a Lean 4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews, with an `HQ-50` subset filtered by quality score. Formal proofs are graded by two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on `HQ-50` under a standardized budget, **closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems**, while live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of already published solutions.

papers.title: EUReCA: End-to-End Unified CBCT Reconstruction Across Clinical Acquisitions
papers.abstract: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for image-guided radiotherapy, but reducing the number of projections to lower dose and scan time makes reconstruction increasingly ill-posed. We present EUReCA (End-to-end Unified REconstruction across Clinical Acquisitions), a geometry-aware feed-forward model for variable-view clinical linac CBCT. For a given acquisition trajectory, EUReCA accepts 8-100 projections with a single set of weights, without view-count-specific retraining; the same architecture and training recipe extend unchanged to other clinical trajectories. It combines learned projection features with an in-frame Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstruction. The model encodes each projection with a shared multiscale backbone, back-projects features into multiresolution 3D grids using the acquisition geometry, aggregates variable numbers of views at fixed computational cost, and refines the volume with a global 3D transformer and multilevel decoder. On simulated data, EUReCA achieved 29.9-33.2 dB PSNR with 10-100 views and outperformed all applicable feed-forward baselines; it also exceeded iterative optimization-based methods while running orders of magnitude faster. On 15 measured patient CBCT scans evaluated against vendor reconstructions, EUReCA achieved the best performance at every tested view count. These results suggest that geometry-aware, measurement-anchored feed-forward reconstruction can provide a practical and flexible foundation for variable-view linac CBCT.
papers.summary: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) guides radiotherapy, but cutting the number of X-ray projections to reduce dose makes reconstruction ill-posed, and existing learned methods need retraining for each view count. `EUReCA` is a geometry-aware feed-forward model that encodes each projection with a shared multiscale backbone, back-projects features into 3D grids using the acquisition geometry, and refines the volume with a global 3D transformer alongside an in-frame Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstruction. **A single set of weights handles 8 to 100 projections without view-specific retraining**, reaching 29.9 to 33.2 dB PSNR on simulated data while beating feed-forward baselines and much slower iterative methods. On 15 measured patient scans compared against vendor reconstructions it scored best at every tested view count.

papers.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
papers.abstract: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.
papers.summary: Because large language models are pretrained on uncurated web scrapes, an attacker can plant poisoned documents in the training data. The authors pretrain `Qwen3` models at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters from scratch with a small fraction of poisoned text, then post-train them into command-line agents using a clean pipeline, and report this as the first demonstration that pretraining poisoning alone can implant a remote code execution backdoor in a deployed agent. **Poisoning just 0.1% of the corpus gives the 4B agent a roughly 92% attack success rate (ASR)**, with the agent running the attacker-chosen command when a trigger appears and behaving normally otherwise. Success grows with model scale and stays above zero even at a 0.0005% poison rate.

papers.title: Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Drafters
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is used to reduce the inference cost of language models. One-step diffusion drafters propose a block of multiple tokens in parallel, reducing the sequential cost of speculative decoding. On-policy distillation trains these drafters using verifier feedback on their own proposals. However, parallel drafting makes this feedback difficult to use: the drafter predicts each token without observing the preceding tokens sampled within the same block, while the verifier conditions its prediction on those tokens. Different sampled prefixes therefore give different verifier targets for the same drafter prediction. We show that distilling against these targets separately can suppress tokens that are plausible after some prefixes but unlikely after others, harming draft acceptance. We explain the effects of this mismatch and introduce Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation (MDraft), a new parallel drafter distillation method which samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes. We use all the drafts to collect information from the verifier, allowing support from alternative prefixes to influence the training target. The resulting algorithm improves the acceptance length of a parallel drafter beyond the level of pre-training, and alleviates the effects of the distributional mismatch. MDraft changes only training, retaining the drafter's architecture and inference procedure, allowing the resulting drafter to be used as-is in place of the pretrained checkpoint. Experiments on a suite of mathematical, coding, and conversational tasks show longer accepted drafts than prior distillation methods.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding with one-step diffusion drafters proposes a whole block of tokens in parallel, but training such drafters on verifier feedback is awkward: the drafter predicts each token without seeing the other tokens sampled in the same block, while the verifier conditions on them, so different sampled prefixes yield conflicting targets for the same prediction. Distilling against those targets separately can suppress tokens that are plausible after some prefixes but not others, hurting acceptance. Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation (`MDraft`) samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes, changing only the training procedure so the drafter remains a drop-in replacement for the pretrained checkpoint. **Accepted draft lengths rise above the pretrained drafter's level** and beyond prior distillation methods on math, coding, and conversational tasks.

papers.title: Selective and Hybrid-State Communication for Latent Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Efficient communication remains a major bottleneck in large language model multiagent systems. Latent communication reduces repeated natural-language exchange by transferring internal model states between agents, but these transfers remain costly and are typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations. We address this problem from two complementary perspectives. We introduce SelectKV, a boundary-aware method that selectively communicates KV states while protecting inherited context, and HyLaMAS, which extends latent collaboration to hybrid linear-attention models by communicating both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace. Across six benchmarks, SelectKV reduces communicated KV positions and logical KV payload by 9.7-9.9%, with accuracy unchanged on two benchmarks, within one percentage point on three, and six points lower on HumanEval+. Across Qwen3.5 model scales, HyLaMAS reduces decoded output tokens by 53-80% and achieves 1.16-2.78x speedups relative to text-based multi-agent communication. Together, these independently evaluated methods represent two complementary approaches to efficient latent-state communication across conventional Transformer and hybrid model architectures.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems built on large language models spend much of their budget re-exchanging natural language, and latent communication that transfers internal model states instead has so far been tied to conventional key-value (KV) cache representations. Two methods are proposed: `SelectKV` selectively transmits KV states while protecting context the receiving agent already inherited, and `HyLaMAS` extends latent collaboration to hybrid linear-attention models by sharing both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace. Across six benchmarks `SelectKV` trims communicated KV positions and payload by 9.7 to 9.9%, with accuracy unchanged or within a point on five benchmarks and six points lower on `HumanEval+`. **The hybrid-model method cuts decoded output tokens by 53 to 80% and yields 1.16 to 2.78x speedups** over text-based communication across `Qwen3.5` model scales.

papers.title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
papers.abstract:
Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities.
  We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture.
  We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything
papers.summary: Training and evaluating web agents requires websites that are diverse, executable, and resettable, but hand-built mirrors need per-site engineering and generated sites drift from the real ones they imitate. `WebAnything` automatically reconstructs reusable environments from real URLs: an Explorer-Builder gathers browser-observable structure, resources, and interaction outcomes, and an independent verifier checks the frozen candidate and triggers local repair or targeted recapture. The pipeline yielded 244 site artifacts spanning 14 domains with 12,984 accepted tasks, and in a blind audit it beat the human-assisted `WebHarbor` on three fidelity metrics with no losses. Fine-tuning `Qwen3.5-9B` on 5,856 trajectories from these environments improved success on `WebArena-Verified` by **13.33 percentage points**, with gains of 6 to 10 points on `REAL` and `Odysseys-Easy`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Web agents need diverse, executable, and resettable website environments, but existing routes trade off automation (human-assisted mirrors), source fidelity (generative construction), and interaction coverage (capture-and-replay). `WebAnything` automatically reconstructs real URLs into local, resettable environments grounded in browser-observable evidence, with an independent verifier that routes each discrepancy to either local repair or targeted recapture of the source.

- An Explorer-Builder records page structures, resources, and before/after interaction outcomes for each visited state and implements them as local routes and state transitions, after which an Independent Verifier re-renders and re-operates the frozen candidate in a separate context, returning evidence-supported failures for local repair and turning unresolved evidence gaps into bounded recapture requests.
- The pipeline produced **244 website artifacts** across 14 domains and 53 categories supporting **12,984 executed and accepted tasks**, with no recorded per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization on an 85-site historical subset and a recorded model-call cost of **$220.62** across 84 sites (median **$1.60** per site), stated as a lower bound.
- Against the human-assisted `WebHarbor` on five matched sites and 14 historical states, `WebAnything` scores higher on Pixel Similarity (**0.924 vs 0.808**) and SSIM (**0.790 vs 0.626**) and takes **12 wins, two ties, and no losses** in a blind fidelity audit, but `WebHarbor` retains broader tested interaction coverage at 80% vs 75% capability coverage and 76.7% vs 63.3% all-test pass.
- Fine-tuning `Qwen3.5-9B` on 5,856 interaction trajectories lifts `REAL` success from 24.2 to 34.1 (**+9.9pp**), `Odysseys-Easy` Rubric and Task averages by **+6.25pp** and **+6.32pp**, and `WebArena-Verified` Overall from 16.41 to 29.74 (**+13.33pp**), driven by Navigate (+18.49pp) and Mutate (+31.50pp) while Retrieve falls 8.75pp under strict scoring.
- Training utility is validated only at the 9B scale, mirrors freeze a site at capture time with no study of staleness or maintenance as live sources change, the fidelity and interaction comparisons rest on five-site subsets, and copyright and terms-of-service constraints limit redistribution of the reconstructed mirrors.

papers.title: Locating Sycophancy Across Training Stages in Open Language Models
papers.abstract: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.
papers.summary: Sycophancy, where an assistant abandons a correct answer after the user suggests a wrong one, is usually blamed on preference-based post-training, yet it has also been observed in base models. To locate its origin, the study measures sycophancy at 13 open checkpoints across 5 model lineages, from base through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release, separating how far an injected claim shifts an answer from how firmly the answer was held, and varying who makes the claim and how reliable they are said to be. **Two distinct behaviors emerge: deference to claims in the prompt is already present in every base model, while capitulation in conversation is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint.** When an objection names an alternative, most post-trained models surrender firmly held answers as readily as loosely held ones.

papers.title: Spokes, not a Ring: Revisiting the Weekday Manifold in Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent work has hypothesised that large language models may represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds instead of single directions. Using these manifolds to interpret or steer representations often assumes that moving along them corresponds to a continuous change in the represented concept. In this work, we test this continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday manifold. Despite its striking circular geometry, we find that the weekday representations behave more like seven discrete states arranged in a circle than a continuous ring. First, we show that local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Second, we test whether any concepts are represented along the manifold outside the seven discrete states, and find neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populate the intermediate space. Together, these results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds correspond to meaningful changes in model representations and behaviour.
papers.summary: Recent interpretability work hypothesizes that language models represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds, and steering along such manifolds assumes that movement corresponds to continuous change in the represented concept. Using the circular weekday manifold as the test case, the authors measure local sensitivity along the ring and probe whether anything occupies the space between days. **Sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behavior under on-manifold steering**, so the representation behaves like seven discrete states arranged in a circle rather than a continuous ring. Neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populates the intermediate space, which casts doubt on the continuous reading and motivates testing other claimed manifolds the same way.

papers.title: What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: LLM agents that answer questions over Web knowledge graphs are increasingly wrapped in checks derived from the graph's ontology, on the assumption that a formal schema makes a reliable judge. Yet a checker can be wrong as well: it can miss errors, and it can flag correct answers and push the agent into "fixing" them. Whether a curated ontology is worth its cost as such a judge, and how it compares with an ontology an LLM writes or a schema mined from the data, is unknown. We make the checker itself the object of study. Across curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies, used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, and across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of nearly $10^{9}$ triples, we account for what ontology-derived checks catch and what they wrongly flag. We show how each source trades caught errors against false alarms, how a curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, which errors structural checks miss, and whether combining sources or giving the agent the checker's specific feedback pays off. On UniProt, the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either an ontology derived from the data or one an LLM derives from a summary of the data with masked identifiers. On real agent answers, its flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.
papers.summary: Agents that answer questions over Web knowledge graphs are often wrapped in checkers derived from the graph's ontology, on the assumption that a formal schema is a reliable judge, yet a checker can miss real errors or flag correct answers and push the agent into breaking them. The study treats the checker itself as the object of evaluation, comparing curated, LLM-generated, and data-derived ontologies used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, with open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of roughly a billion triples. Each source trades caught errors against false alarms, a curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, and structural checks miss whole classes of errors. On `UniProt`, **the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either alternative, and its flags on real agent answers are only marginally more precise than random ones.**

papers.title: Responsible Quantum Machine Learning for Medical Imaging: A Fairness Audit Across Sensitive Subgroups
papers.abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) is increasingly explored for medical classification, yet its behaviour under subgroup-aware fairness criteria remains understudied. We present an empirical fairness audit of classical and quantum classifiers for medical imaging, assuming QML is not inherently fair. Two scenarios are evaluated: dermatological lesions on DDI (sensitive attribute: Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays on CheXpert-derived data (sensitive attribute: age group). Using ResNet-18 embeddings, we train SVM, MLP, QSVM and QCNN under a baseline and three mitigation settings: differentiable Equalized Odds (EO) regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning (GRL), and both combined. Foundation models (PanDerm, EVA-X) serve as external references. Quantum classifiers may achieve competitive aggregate performance while still exhibiting subgroup disparities. Since a smaller subgroup AUC gap may stem from degrading the best group rather than improving the worst, each mitigation is also tested against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin relative to its baseline. Under this criterion, several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, are not clinically acceptable due to loss of global discrimination. On DDI, QSVM with GRL+EO performed best and approached PanDerm in the performance/fairness trade-off; on CheXpert, QCNN with GRL achieved the highest aggregate performance but increased disparity, and EVA-X remained stronger. Fairness effects are model- and dataset-dependent, so QML requires empirical subgroup-aware evaluation. All quantum models run in classical simulation; we claim no quantum advantage.
papers.summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) is being tried for medical image classification, but how quantum classifiers behave under subgroup fairness criteria has not been examined. The audit trains SVM, MLP, QSVM, and QCNN classifiers on `ResNet-18` embeddings for skin lesions in `DDI` (grouped by Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays derived from `CheXpert` (grouped by age), under a baseline and three mitigations: differentiable Equalized Odds (EO) regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning (GRL), and both combined, with the `PanDerm` and `EVA-X` foundation models as external references. Because a smaller subgroup gap can come from degrading the best group rather than helping the worst, each mitigation is also held to a pre-specified non-inferiority margin, and **several of the lowest-disparity configurations fail that margin through loss of global discrimination**, notably QCNN with GRL on `DDI`. Fairness effects turn out to be model- and dataset-dependent, all quantum models run in classical simulation, and the authors claim no quantum advantage.

papers.title: Learning Without Clocks: Partition-Invariant Neural Network
papers.abstract: Event cameras, spiking cochleas and similar sensors emit asynchronous events, yet most learning systems first bin them into frames or packets, so the output depends on how the stream was sliced. Networks whose state is updated exactly at every event and evolves in closed form between events are invariant to this slicing. We ask what more makes the output (i) independent of the processing order of simultaneous events and (ii) continuous in the time stamps, even when two events cross in time, while (iii) staying sensitive to temporal order. For arbitrary nonlinear event models we prove that (i) and (ii) are each equivalent to pairwise commutation of the event updates, and that once updates commute, all order dependence comes from their non-commutation with the inter-event dynamics and vanishes linearly in the time lag. This identifies a class of time-mediated non-commutative (TM) models and yields a resolution-robustness bound for any model. We construct the minimal TM layer, a learnable, provably Lipschitz generalization of the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator; prove that no single additive layer can uniformly represent ordered pair interactions, whereas a three-dimensional TM state can; show that each TM layer adds two levels of temporal nesting versus one for additive layers; and give a single-layer higher-order construction (TM-k) and a stacking rule preserving all three properties. We instantiate these results as the Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer, linear in the number of events, give a topology-free variant for temporal point processes with closed-form likelihoods, and specify a preregistered clock-robustness protocol with a physical-time threat model for spike-retiming attacks. In preliminary development-set experiments, the TM state beats an otherwise identical additive state by 3.5-9.1 points on DVS128 Gesture and by 24.5 and 30.6 points on SHD and Speech Commands.
papers.summary: Event cameras and spiking cochleas emit asynchronous events, but most learning systems bin them into frames, so the output depends on how the stream was sliced. The authors ask what makes an event-driven network's output independent of the processing order of simultaneous events and continuous in the timestamps while remaining sensitive to temporal order, and prove that the first two properties are each equivalent to pairwise commutation of the event updates, with any remaining order dependence arising from non-commutation with the inter-event dynamics and vanishing linearly in the time lag. This defines a class of time-mediated non-commutative models, from which they build a minimal learnable layer generalizing the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator, show that no single additive layer can uniformly represent ordered pair interactions whereas a three-dimensional state can, and instantiate the result as the Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer with cost linear in the number of events. In preliminary experiments **the time-mediated state beats an otherwise identical additive state by 3.5 to 9.1 points** on `DVS128 Gesture` and by 24.5 and 30.6 points on `SHD` and `Speech Commands`.

papers.title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer from retrieved passages, but multi-hop questions require chaining facts across documents through entities the question never names, and graph-based methods retrieve only once while iterative methods overload the LLM with planning, dependency tracking, and rewriting. `DeFT-RAG` generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the question-answer (QA) pairs resolved so far, with each sub-question naming every entity it asks about, and offloads the bookkeeping to rule-based updates of a QA table plus a fine-tuned lightweight yes/no decision model. It also caches QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks something with the same meaning. **It achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines** on `MuSiQue`, `2WikiMultiHopQA`, and `HotpotQA` with both `gpt-4o-mini` and `Qwen3.6` backbones while feeding the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method, and a cache shared across 1,000 `MuSiQue` questions answers 23.1% of sub-questions without an LLM call, cutting calls by 12.9% at no accuracy cost.

papers.title: Learning Lotteries with Minimal Stakeholder Violations from Membership Queries
papers.abstract: An AI developer often has several candidate versions of a system and can deploy a mixture of them, sending each request to a randomly chosen version, as in A/B testing. Each stakeholder (e.g., a safety team, a regulator, or a customer with private test data) accepts a mixture exactly when its expected performance (e.g., its rate of harmful replies) meets the stakeholder's own standard, which the developer can learn only by asking whether a proposed mixture is acceptable. We model this as choosing a lottery over $m$ alternatives for $n$ agents, each of whom accepts exactly the lotteries in an unknown halfspace and answers such binary membership queries. While Choo et al. (ICML 2026) sought a lottery that every agent accepts, none may exist when, say, safety and helpfulness requirements conflict, so we minimize the number of rejecting agents. We show that this problem is APX-hard even when all halfspaces are known and all utilities are $0$ or $1$. We then give exact algorithms that run in polynomial time when $m$ is constant, and in quasi-polynomial time when, for a constant $\eta$, some optimal lottery has no accepting agent within $\eta$ of its threshold. When only some agents can be queried, optimizing over a uniform sample of agents gives additive and relative guarantees for the whole population, with a sample size that does not depend on $n$, and a linear program gives a polynomial-time method for any $m$. On the other hand, for $m\ge 3$, a deterministic algorithm that queries only $K$ distinct agents cannot guarantee fewer than $n-K$ extra rejections, and this is achievable; in other words, it can guarantee nothing for the agents it does not ask. Small synthetic experiments indicate that our worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.
papers.summary: A developer with several candidate versions of an AI system can deploy a randomized mixture of them, and each stakeholder (a safety team, a regulator, a customer with private tests) accepts a mixture only if its expected performance meets a private threshold that can be learned solely by asking whether a proposed mixture is acceptable. Modeled as choosing a lottery over m alternatives for n agents whose acceptance regions are unknown halfspaces, the goal is to minimize the number of rejecting agents, since a lottery everyone accepts may not exist when requirements conflict. **The problem is APX-hard even with known halfspaces and 0/1 utilities**, yet exact algorithms run in polynomial time for constant m and in quasi-polynomial time when some optimal lottery keeps every accepting agent a fixed margin from its threshold. Querying a uniform sample of agents gives population-wide additive and relative guarantees with sample size independent of n, while any deterministic algorithm that queries only K agents can guarantee nothing for the agents it skips, and small synthetic experiments suggest the worst-case bounds are conservative.

papers.title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
papers.abstract:
AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost.
  We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines.
  We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.
papers.summary: Agents can write smart contracts from plain-English descriptions, but code that runs is not code that does what was asked, and contracts cannot be patched once deployed. The evaluation replays identical transactions on the AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measures agreement, with every grading tool stress-tested on planted mistakes and the scorer audited until known wrong answers cannot pass, which revealed that AI judges and standard analysis tools miss obvious errors and that scoring only the functions every system implemented hid about half the difference between pipelines. The proposed elicitation-first architecture has the agent ask the client a short checklist of questions before coding, check the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and return disagreements to the client rather than silently rewriting. **Asking first mattered far more than reviewing or patching afterwards across three models**, automated security fixes often broke requested behavior, and the authors release their tools, 600 tasks, and all results.

papers.title: Depth through Recurrence: Towards Ultra-Efficient On-Device ASR
papers.abstract: Modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have achieved remarkable accuracy by scaling model depth and capacity, but at the cost of increased memory, energy, and computational demands. On edge devices where ASR is often most needed, such as watches and glasses, deploying such large models is infeasible due to extremely constrained resources. This raises a fundamental question: can we achieve high representational power in deep ASR models without scaling up parameterization? In this work, we revisit the role of depth and identify layer wise representational dynamics, in which most layers learn functionally similar transformations. Motivated by this insight, we propose a block-recurrent ASR architecture that replaces parameterized depth with a small set of recurrent blocks, each consisting of weight-shared layers, thereby preserving effective depth while drastically reducing model size. Through representation-guided grouping and knowledge distillation, block-recurrent models retain the accuracy of large reference models while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Across Open ASR Leaderboard benchmarks, a model with only two shared blocks recovers 97.4% of the accuracy of large models on average. The compact backbone further enables efficient on-device personalization through lightweight MoE-LoRA adaptation, allowing user-specific models to match or surpass the accuracy of general-purpose ASR systems with significantly lower inference cost. By reusing weights across recurrent steps, the proposed architecture reduces memory-access overhead and inference energy consumption. Together, these results show that high quality ASR can be achieved without large parameterization, and that structured recurrence provides a principled path towards ultra-compressed, energy-efficient, and personalized speech recognition on the edge.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) accuracy has come from scaling depth, which puts strong models out of reach for watches and glasses. Observing that most layers in deep ASR models learn functionally similar transformations, the authors replace parameterized depth with a small set of recurrent blocks of weight-shared layers, grouped by representation similarity and trained with knowledge distillation, so effective depth is preserved while parameter count drops by an order of magnitude. **A model with only two shared blocks recovers 97.4% of large-model accuracy on average** across `Open ASR Leaderboard` benchmarks. The compact backbone also supports on-device personalization through lightweight MoE-LoRA adapters that match or beat general-purpose systems at lower inference cost, and weight reuse across recurrent steps cuts memory-access overhead and energy.

papers.title: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks learn data-dependent features, a capacity widely credited for their empirical success. However, explicitly characterizing what features emerge -- and when they improve generalization -- is challenging, since training is nonlinear and non-convex and the data is often anisotropic. Here, we give a closed-form account of feature learning for a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization, trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional (spiked) signal. In the infinite-width mean-field limit, one step updates each layer's feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike, amplified by both the learning rate and the layer depth. We next assess how these features impact prediction through kernel ridge regression (KRR), finding that KRR on the learned feature kernel yields scalar inflation of the KRR estimator at initialization -- an "anti-shrinkage" mechanism that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by ridge, while also amplifying noise. To study when this inflation improves generalization, in the overparameterized proportional limit we derive closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization errors of these estimators in terms of key macroscopic parameters -- notably the spike strength and spike-target alignment. Crucially, we find that a one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when both the spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, demonstrating that a successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure.
papers.summary: Deep networks are credited with learning data-dependent features, but characterizing which features emerge and when they help generalization is hard because training is nonlinear and data is anisotropic. The authors analyze a deep linear network in mean-field parameterization after one gradient step on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional spiked signal, and show that in the infinite-width limit the step adds a target-aligned rank-one spike to each layer's feature kernel, amplified by learning rate and depth. Kernel ridge regression (KRR) on the learned kernel amounts to a scalar inflation of the initial KRR estimator, an anti-shrinkage effect that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by the ridge while also amplifying noise, and closed-form bias and variance expressions in the proportional limit tie generalization to spike strength and spike-target alignment. **The one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs** and appears only when both spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are large enough.

papers.title: Improving Data-Constrained Scaling with Hyperparameter Transfer and Ensembling
papers.abstract: As growing compute budgets outpace the growth of high-quality training data, large language models must be trained with both compute and data constraints in mind. Unfortunately, existing prescriptions for data-constrained scaling suffer from two important limitations. First, past works hold key hyperparameters such as weight decay fixed with scale, despite the fact that optimal hyperparameters vary wildly with model size and number of epochs. Second, past works neglect ensembling, a promising axis for scaling under data constraints. As a surprising consequence, prior prescriptions can lead to loss that increases with compute budget. We address both limitations by fitting power laws that prescribe how to transfer hyperparameters with scale and scaling laws that prescribe how to allocate compute with ensembling. Training on 100M tokens from FineWeb, our recipe reduces validation loss by over 0.15 nats compared to prior recipes, a 14% decrease in perplexity, and achieves monotonic improvements with compute through ensembling. These gains are achieved using prescriptions fit to smaller runs and validated at up to 12$\times$ larger compute budgets.
papers.summary: As compute budgets outgrow the supply of high-quality text, language models must be trained under both compute and data constraints, yet existing data-constrained scaling prescriptions hold hyperparameters such as weight decay fixed across scale and ignore ensembling, which can make loss increase with compute. The authors fit power laws for transferring hyperparameters with model size and epoch count, plus scaling laws for allocating compute across ensemble members. Training on 100M tokens from `FineWeb`, **the recipe lowers validation loss by over 0.15 nats versus prior recipes, a 14% drop in perplexity**, and loss improves monotonically with compute through ensembling. The prescriptions were fit on small runs and validated at up to 12x larger compute budgets.

papers.title: Where the Error Lives: Spectral Representations of Learned Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians
papers.abstract: Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) is the standard method for computing the electronic structure of molecules and materials, but its self-consistent-field (SCF) iterations make it expensive for large systems and high-throughput screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonian models offer a shortcut: an equivariant network predicts the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian matrix in one forward pass, and diagonalizing the prediction yields orbital energies, the HOMO-LUMO gap, molecular orbitals and the electron density. These models are trained to match the reference matrix entry by entry, yet a small entry-wise error does not guarantee accurate eigenvalues or eigenvectors. Two physics-informed alternatives go partway: a recently proposed wavefunction-alignment loss adds a spectral penalty without diagonalizing the prediction, and matching the electron density of the diagonalized prediction supervises it directly. Neither is complete: by representing the prediction error in the eigenbasis of the reference Hamiltonian, we show that each sees only part of the error, and that shifting the predicted orbital energies leaves the electron density exactly unchanged. The same analysis identifies a complete training signal: the cumulative local density of states (cumulative LDOS), the number of electrons at each point in space with energy below a given threshold. The cumulative LDOS is a single physical observable that contains the electron density as a special case, responds to every component of the error, determines the Hamiltonian uniquely, and yields gradients that do not vanish for large orbitalenergy errors. Fine-tuning three Hamiltonian networks on QH9 in this way, which we call FermiScope, reduces the HOMO-LUMO gap error without increasing the element-wise error. The gains carry over to out-of-distribution and molecular-dynamics splits, where the wavefunction-alignment loss helps less.
papers.summary: Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) is the standard route to electronic structure, but its self-consistent-field (SCF) iterations are expensive, so equivariant networks are trained to predict the Hamiltonian matrix directly, usually by matching the reference entry by entry even though small entry-wise error does not guarantee accurate eigenvalues or eigenvectors. By expressing the prediction error in the eigenbasis of the reference Hamiltonian, the authors show that both a wavefunction-alignment loss and an electron-density loss see only part of the error, and that shifting predicted orbital energies leaves the density exactly unchanged. The same analysis identifies the cumulative local density of states (cumulative LDOS), the number of electrons at each point in space below an energy threshold, as a single observable that responds to every error component, determines the Hamiltonian uniquely, and gives non-vanishing gradients for large orbital-energy errors. Fine-tuning three Hamiltonian networks on `QH9` with this signal, a method called `FermiScope`, **reduces HOMO-LUMO gap error without raising element-wise error**, with gains carrying over to out-of-distribution and molecular-dynamics splits.

papers.title: An $\Omega(T^{3/4})$ lower bound for projection-free online learning with linear minimization oracles
papers.abstract:
This work considers projection-free online learning algorithms with linear minimization oracles for handling the decision set. For Online Frank--Wolfe (OFW), regret upper bounds were already known for specific OFW tunings [Hazan and Kale, 2012, Hazan, 2016] which scaled as $T^{3/4}$ (where $T$ is the horizon length). However, it remained an open question whether the regret of all OFW tunings scaled as $T^{3/4}$.
  We answer that question, proving a universal worst-case regret lower bound $\Omega(T^{3/4} m^{-1/4})$ for any projection-free algorithm that makes at most $m$ linear minimization oracle calls per round. The analysis suggests an extended OFW to resort to multiple linear optimizations per round, for which we prove a regret upper bound $O(\max \{ T^{3/4} m^{-1/4}, \sqrt{T} \})$.
papers.summary: Projection-free online learning replaces costly projections onto the decision set with calls to a linear minimization oracle, and Online Frank-Wolfe (OFW) was known to achieve regret of order T to the three-quarters for specific tunings over a horizon of T rounds, leaving open whether any tuning could do better. **The authors prove a universal worst-case regret lower bound of order T to the three-quarters divided by the fourth root of m for any projection-free algorithm making at most m oracle calls per round**, which settles the question for standard OFW. The analysis motivates an extended OFW that performs multiple linear optimizations per round, for which they prove a matching upper bound of order the maximum of that quantity and the square root of T.

papers.title: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening
papers.abstract: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss them. We propose a behavioural test: a partner that uses a code reacts to the exact wording of a message, whereas an uninvolved agent placed in its seat does not. Partner--Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) is the difference between the two agents in how much their action changes when the message is reworded with its meaning kept, and it is computed after the fact by replaying logged prompts. In a simulated market with five conditions (no collusion, a joint reward with neutral messages, the same with an openly stated intention, a covert first-letter code, and the code with a stated intention), PoPLi is between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever the code is present (95% intervals all above 0.29) and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it. Message-only monitors did not separate the conditions: one reading the speaker's messages answered "no" in all 50 markets, and one reading every seller's messages flagged 9 of 10 markets with no collusion. PoPLi detects the use of a private channel, not collusion as such, and it cannot detect collusion through incentives alone or codes carried by meaning.
papers.summary: Agents sharing a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so monitors that only read the messages can miss collusion. The proposed behavioural test, Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (`PoPLi`), rewords a logged message while preserving its meaning and measures how much more the intended partner's action changes than that of an uninvolved agent placed in its seat, computed after the fact by replaying prompts. **In a simulated market the score sits between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever a covert first-letter code is in use and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it**, while one message-reading monitor never flagged the speaker and another flagged 9 of 10 non-colluding markets. The test detects use of a private channel rather than collusion itself, and cannot catch coordination through incentives alone or codes carried by meaning.

papers.title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding
papers.abstract: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.
papers.summary: Scientific-agent benchmarks rarely test whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows that sequencing protocols specify, a skill needed to analyze customized assays. `LibStructBench` is a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows from protocol text. **Frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction**, especially for molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity, and swapping the underlying language model changed scores more than swapping the agent harness, significantly so only for molecular-state reconstruction. Supplying extra knowledge improved recovery of oligo families in a small pilot without raising mean workflow scores, and letting agents autonomously accumulate procedural rules and cross-protocol examples gave non-monotonic validation performance and no held-out improvement.

papers.title: Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback
papers.abstract: Language-model agents differ fundamentally from prior intelligent systems in their ability to learn from natural language in context. This capability enables agents to iteratively refine their answers in response to feedback, a prevalent mode of operation in modern agentic workflows. However, the community primarily ranks models by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they utilize feedback on prior attempts.
