We introduce Seq@K, a natural evaluation protocol that measures whether a model can solve a problem within K sequential attempts, provided feedback after each previous failure. Unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that examine long-horizon planning, Seq@K isolates and formalizes the core capability of refinement from feedback. We evaluate Seq@K on a suite of 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models, and show that Seq@K reveals a materially different model-selection landscape: under Seq@K, (1) model rankings often differ, (2) the Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations and (3) the gains from choosing the optimal model configuration can widen or shrink relative to those of Pass@K. We further show that analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behavior, such as the rate at which models address issues raised in feedback, or how rigidly they hold onto their own answers. Finally, we study how the nature of feedback affects models' iterative refinement, showing that practitioners must carefully design and benchmark the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems. Together, these results establish how Seq@K offers a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that typically operate in such feedback loop, and the necessity to consider Seq@K in evaluating models for these systems.
papers.summary: Standard metrics such as Pass@1 and Pass@K rank language models on independent attempts, so they say nothing about how well a model refines an answer after being told it was wrong, even though that feedback loop sits at the center of most agentic workflows. The authors propose `Seq@K`, which measures whether a model solves a problem within K sequential attempts when it receives feedback after each failure, and evaluate it across 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models. **Model rankings under `Seq@K` often differ from those under Pass@K**, Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations, and trajectory analysis exposes behaviors such as how quickly models address issues raised in feedback or how rigidly they cling to prior answers. The form of the feedback itself materially changes refinement, so the authors argue that practitioners must design and benchmark the feedback loops of their iterative systems rather than rely on single-shot scores.

papers.title: Echo: Scaling Visual Reinforcement Learning with Off-policy Experience
papers.abstract: Scaling visual reinforcement learning (RL) with GPU-accelerated simulation is computationally expensive due to rendering and visual-policy inference costs. Consequently, two-stage teacher--student distillation is commonly used to train visual policies, but introduces an imitation gap. In this preliminary study, we introduce \echomethod{}, \textbf{a single-stage off-policy RL framework that scales experience collection without proportionally increasing visual computation}. Through \textbf{inverse distillation}, a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy and collects inexpensive, unrendered experience. Echo leverages this experience for off-policy value learning, directly improving the visual policy through a shared privileged critic. We instantiate \echomethod{} with FastTD3 and evaluate it on three visual control tasks and two dexterous manipulation tasks in Genesis. Relative to \sdpgmethod{} under the evaluated configurations, Echo reduces time to reference returns by an average of \textbf{60\% across the three locomotion tasks} and \textbf{56\% across both hand tasks}, while improving peak mean returns by \textbf{62\% and 12\%}, respectively. Both hand tasks also achieve higher mean returns at matched simulator-transition budgets. These initial results suggest that scaling off-policy experience is a promising approach to efficient direct visual RL.
papers.summary: Training visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies in GPU-accelerated simulators is costly because every environment step requires rendering and visual-policy inference, which is why practitioners usually distill a state-based teacher into a visual student at the price of an imitation gap. `Echo` is a single-stage off-policy framework in which a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy through inverse distillation and gathers cheap unrendered experience, which a shared privileged critic then uses to improve the visual policy directly. Instantiated with `FastTD3` on three visual locomotion tasks and two dexterous manipulation tasks in `Genesis`, **`Echo` cuts time to reference returns by an average of 60% on locomotion and 56% on the hand tasks** relative to the two-stage distillation baseline, while also raising peak mean returns by 62% and 12% respectively. The authors frame this as a preliminary study suggesting that scaling off-policy experience is a viable route to direct visual RL.

papers.title: Finite-Sample Optimal Conformal Prediction Sets under Covariate Shift
papers.abstract:
We study conformal prediction under covariate shift with a known covariate density ratio, seeking prediction sets with minimum expected length under the target distribution. For every calibration sample size, we prove that the rule combining the inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration minimizes this expected length among all rules valid over the full weighted-exchangeability class.
  We approximate the oracle using quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, and select estimators and tuning parameters by resampling to estimate calibrated target length. On a bounded response domain, we bound excess length linearly in $L^1$ density error at fixed calibration size, without requiring a uniform positive lower bound on the true density. We also bound selection-pool and resampling errors. Under explicit growth conditions, the selected procedure approaches the same oracle while the calibration size remains fixed.
  Experiments on 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets compare coverage, prediction-set length, and runtime with existing methods.
  In targeted low-coverage and strong-shift comparisons, inverse-density selection yields shorter mean sets in most cases and lower mean runtime than the evaluated weighted baselines, with some differences in achieved coverage.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction under covariate shift with a known density ratio can produce valid prediction sets in many ways, and the open question is which rule yields the shortest sets on the target distribution for a fixed calibration sample size. The authors prove that combining the inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration **minimizes expected set length among all rules valid over the full weighted-exchangeability class, for every finite calibration size**. They approximate this oracle with quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, select estimators and tuning parameters by resampling, and bound the excess length linearly in the L1 density error without assuming the true density is bounded away from zero. Experiments on 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets show shorter mean sets and lower runtime than the weighted baselines in low-coverage and strong-shift settings, with some differences in achieved coverage.

papers.title: What Constitutes Food Similarity? Visual Representations and Retrieval in Indian Cuisine
papers.abstract: Food similarity underlies retrieval, recommendation, substitution, and other food computing tasks, yet food representations are typically evaluated by identity preservation. We ask what happens to food similarity beyond identity: how different visual representations organize foods into relational neighborhoods, what culinary relationships these neighborhoods reveal or obscure, and how consistently these structures emerge across representations. Indian cuisine provides a challenging setting in which visually similar foods may have different culinary identities, while foods within a culinary family can vary substantially in appearance. Using an expanded Khana dataset and seven pretrained visual representations spanning convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, we evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, examining culinary-family structure, contrast cases, and cross-representation agreement. We also aggregate image representations to compare dish-level visual similarity across models and against recipe-derived similarity for the same dishes. Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations, including similarities across culinary-family boundaries. At the dish level, aggregation reveals common visual structure despite local variation, but this structure corresponds less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These findings show that recognition performance alone cannot characterize relational structure: food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the food collection. Understanding these structures is therefore a prerequisite to combining multiple food information modalities into a coherent notion of similarity.
papers.summary: Food image representations are usually judged by how well they preserve dish identity, which says little about how they organize foods into neighborhoods of related dishes for retrieval, recommendation, or substitution. Using an expanded `Khana` dataset of Indian cuisine and seven pretrained visual encoders spanning convolutional, transformer, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, the authors compare image-to-image and image-to-dish neighborhoods, culinary-family structure, and cross-model agreement, and contrast aggregated dish-level visual similarity with recipe-derived similarity for the same dishes. **Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations and often cross culinary-family boundaries**, while dish-level aggregation reveals shared visual structure that nonetheless aligns only weakly with recipe similarity. The authors conclude that food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the collection, so these structures must be understood before combining modalities into a single notion of similarity.

papers.title: Human-Residual Steering: Aligning Frozen LLM Judges with Human Judgment Distributions
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as automated judges, yet most alignment methods target aggregated human judgments and overlook variation among individual annotators. Existing approaches to matching the full distribution of human ratings mainly rely on output-level calibration or parameter fine-tuning. We propose Human-Residual Steering (HRS), to our knowledge the first method to align frozen LLM judges with human judgment distributions through learned hidden-state interventions. An oracle analysis shows that low-rank corrections at a single layer remove most of the discrepancy between judge and human distributions. HRS learns to predict such corrections from the judge's hidden representation and rating logits, training on individual annotations with proper scoring rules for ordinal and nominal judgments and optimising through the frozen downstream layers. Across 14 benchmarks and four judges from three model families, HRS outperforms all evaluated frozen-weight baselines. With Qwen2.5-7B, it achieves the lowest Jensen-Shannon distance on 13 of 14 benchmarks, reducing the mean from 0.565 to 0.352 versus 0.377 for the strongest calibrator. HRS also raises mean Spearman correlation with aggregate human scores from 0.449 to 0.579, improves population-level estimation under limited annotation budgets, and trains about 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning at a modest cost in alignment.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) used as judges are usually aligned to averaged human ratings, ignoring the spread of opinions across individual annotators, and existing distribution-matching methods rely on output-level calibration or weight fine-tuning. Human-Residual Steering (`HRS`) instead learns a low-rank correction to a frozen judge's hidden state at a single layer, predicted from that representation and the rating logits, trained on individual annotations with proper scoring rules for ordinal and nominal judgments and optimized through the frozen downstream layers. Across 14 benchmarks and four judges from three model families, `HRS` beats every frozen-weight baseline; **with `Qwen2.5-7B` it lowers the mean Jensen-Shannon distance to human rating distributions from 0.565 to 0.352**, versus 0.377 for the strongest calibrator. It also lifts mean Spearman correlation with aggregate human scores from 0.449 to 0.579, improves population-level estimates under small annotation budgets, and trains roughly 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning at a modest cost in alignment.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Global Climate Policy Cooperation
papers.abstract: International climate policy requires coordination among countries whose mitigation decisions impose local costs but generate global benefits. Classical game-theoretic and integrated assessment approaches can study these incentives, but typically rely on prescribed behavioural assumptions or equilibrium concepts. Recent work has therefore explored Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning as a way to model climate-policy cooperation as an emergent outcome of repeated strategic interaction. We extend an existing MARL climate framework with a multi-stage negotiation mechanism in which agents propose agreements, accept or reject commitments, and face penalties for non-compliance. This allows us to study how agreement design affects learned mitigation behaviour, compliance, and climate outcomes. In an idealized setting with four homogeneous agents, we find that non-binding agreements do little to overcome free-riding, while moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation and reduce warming. However, excessively strong penalties discourage ambitious commitments, revealing a trade-off between enforcement and participation. We position the framework as a methodological contribution for testing agreement design rather than a predictive model of real negotiations.
papers.summary: Climate mitigation is a collective-action problem in which each country bears local costs for global benefits, and classical game-theoretic or integrated assessment models impose fixed behavioral assumptions or equilibrium concepts. The authors extend an existing Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) climate framework with a multi-stage negotiation mechanism in which agents propose agreements, accept or reject commitments, and face penalties for non-compliance, so that cooperation emerges from repeated learned interaction. In an idealized setting with four homogeneous agents, non-binding agreements barely reduce free-riding, while **moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation and reduce warming but excessively strong penalties discourage ambitious commitments**, exposing a trade-off between enforcement and participation. The framework is positioned as a tool for testing agreement design rather than a predictive model of real negotiations.

papers.title: PairCLIP-SWA: Similarity-Guided Balancing and Stochastic Weight Averaging for Generalized Deepfake Image Detection with OpenCLIP
papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors are almost always deployed as the single checkpoint that scored best on a validation split, yet the reliability of that choice is rarely measured. We measure it with PairCLIP-SWA, a single-backbone detector that adapts an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 visual tower by progressive block unfreezing on a class-balanced corpus built by CLIP-similarity-guided one-to-one subsampling, and averages the fine-tuning trajectory in weight space. Trained in-domain on the IEEE SP Cup 2025 (DF-Wild-Cup) benchmark under the same protocol as the strongest published three-backbone ensemble, the weight-averaged detector reaches 97.04% accuracy, 98.64% AU-ROC and a 4.07% equal error rate, against 94.46%, 97.60% and 5.00%. Its training log shows why averaging matters: over the averaged epochs the non-averaged checkpoint swings across 5.34 points of validation accuracy while its validation loss more than doubles, whereas the average is never worse and is up to 5.99 points better. On an OpenForensics-derived benchmark the same instability becomes a misranking: the checkpoint that validation accuracy selects (98.43%) scores 88.85% on a disjoint 10,905-image test partition, rejecting 21.1% of genuine photographs, while the terminal average, ranked last on validation, scores 94.76%. A study of twenty-two in-house configurations on the identical DF-Wild-Cup split, including preprocessing ablations, shows that CLIP pre-training rather than ensembling drives accuracy, that secondary face cropping costs about 34 points, and that frequency-domain inputs transfer poorly. We recommend per-class selection criteria measured off the early-stopping split.
papers.summary: Deepfake detectors are typically shipped as whichever checkpoint scored best on a validation split, and the authors set out to measure how unreliable that selection is. `PairCLIP-SWA` fine-tunes a single `OpenCLIP` ViT-L/14 visual tower through progressive block unfreezing on a class-balanced corpus built by CLIP-similarity-guided one-to-one subsampling, then averages the fine-tuning trajectory in weight space. On the `DF-Wild-Cup` benchmark from the IEEE SP Cup 2025, the weight-averaged single model reaches **97.04% accuracy and a 4.07% equal error rate, beating the strongest published three-backbone ensemble** at 94.46% and 5.00%, and on an `OpenForensics`-derived benchmark the validation-selected checkpoint falls from 98.43% to 88.85% on a disjoint test partition while the last-ranked terminal average scores 94.76%. A study of twenty-two configurations indicates that CLIP pre-training rather than ensembling drives accuracy, that secondary face cropping costs about 34 points, and that frequency-domain inputs transfer poorly.

papers.title: Verification Learning Theory: A Process Model of Checking and Retention in AI-Assisted Judgment
papers.abstract: Accurate AI assistance can improve immediate judgments while reducing opportunities to practise the operations needed for independent performance. Verification Learning Theory (VLT) formalises this possibility for claim-evaluation practice followed by correct, independent, rule-specific feedback. The model links perceived assistant reliability to evidence checking and links the history of those checks to retained rule use. Its strict form assumes that task demands and perceived reliability influence learning only through checking, with equal learning per genuine check. It therefore predicts that perceived fallibility can improve delayed unaided judgment even without observed assistant errors, and that this advantage disappears when checking is already required and performed. Rule-specific gains and forecasts from checking histories provide further tests. Simulations examine the consequences and parameter dependence of these commitments; they do not constitute empirical validation. Comparisons with depth-of-processing and feedback-encoding accounts identify where predictions diverge and where the accounts remain observationally equivalent. The framework specifies experiments that can test the proposed mechanism and separates retention of practised rules from the broader problem of recognising which rule applies to a new claim.
papers.summary: Reliable AI assistance can improve the judgment a person makes in the moment while removing the practice needed to perform the same task unaided later. Verification Learning Theory (VLT) formalizes this for claim-evaluation practice followed by correct, independent, rule-specific feedback, linking perceived assistant reliability to how much evidence a person checks and linking the history of those checks to which rules they retain. In its strict form the model predicts that **perceiving the assistant as fallible can improve delayed unaided judgment even when the assistant never makes an observed error**, and that this advantage vanishes when checking is already required and performed. Simulations explore the consequences and parameter dependence of these commitments but are not empirical validation, and the paper lays out experiments that could separate VLT from depth-of-processing and feedback-encoding accounts.

papers.title: Interpretable neural equation learning for high-dimensional materials data
papers.abstract: Equation learning seeks to discover compact, interpretable equations from data using various machine-learning techniques. However, few workflows discover and interpret learned equations in sparse, high-dimensional materials datasets. We present nn-EQL, an equation-learning framework that generates candidate equations through iterative training, pruning, and retraining of a neural network with customizable, user-specified neuron-level activation functions. Candidate equations are ranked using a minimum description length (MDL)-inspired score, balancing error and sparsity, and diagnosed to assess term-wise contributions, input-scaled sensitivities, and uncertainties. We demonstrate nn-EQL on standard AI-Feynman benchmarks as well as multiscale high-dimensional materials datasets such as finite-element simulations of heterogeneous materials, and high-throughput experimental thin-film deposition data. nn-EQL integrates with tabular data and high-dimensional data via standard encoder models, learning equations and providing insight into learned terms. Looking forward, integrating physically interpretable representations, multimodal and multi-fidelity data, and adaptive data acquisition could enable equation learning to formulate and test mechanistic hypotheses.
papers.summary: Equation learning aims to recover compact, interpretable formulas from data, but few workflows handle the sparse, high-dimensional datasets common in materials science. `nn-EQL` generates candidate equations by iteratively training, pruning, and retraining a neural network whose neurons use user-specified activation functions, ranks the candidates with a minimum description length (MDL)-inspired score that balances error against sparsity, and diagnoses each with term-wise contributions, input-scaled sensitivities, and uncertainties. The framework is **demonstrated on `AI-Feynman` benchmarks as well as finite-element simulations of heterogeneous materials and high-throughput thin-film deposition experiments**, and it connects to high-dimensional inputs through standard encoder models. The authors point to physically interpretable representations, multi-fidelity data, and adaptive data acquisition as the path toward using equation learning to formulate and test mechanistic hypotheses.

papers.title: When More Planning Hurts: Learned Planners for World Models
papers.abstract: On PushT, our fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solves 8 of 16 scenes reserved from our configuration selection. The comparison planners perform as follows: Selected Adam (7 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 218.440s), adapted iCEM (2 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 49.309s), released LePlanner (16 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 5.652s). The total planning and encoding time for our action updater is 59.079s. Note that our action updater does not satisfy the task-cost criterion we fixed before evaluation. We also conduct another matched experiment where we only replay the first ten commands in each context and then allow the next solve 4, 8 or 12 updates (subsequent solves all get 8 updates). Among all 16 contexts (8 scene clusters), the 3 budgets get 9, 8 and 7 successes, respectively. Interestingly, the extra updates did not rescue any failing task in this experiment. All the changes in success/failure happen in one scene cluster, where we observe that the extra updates decrease the costs of the selected latent world-model trajectories for our updater, while the tasks that used to be successes become failures. The code, weights, evaluators, execution traces and cost accounting accompany the paper.
papers.summary: The question is whether a small learned action updater can stand in for optimization-based planners inside a latent world model, and whether granting it more planning updates helps. On `PushT`, a fixed action updater with only 1,505 parameters solves 8 of 16 scenes held out from configuration selection, against 7 for a selected Adam planner, 2 for an adapted `iCEM`, and 16 for the released `LePlanner`, with the updater spending about 59 seconds of planning and encoding time versus 218 seconds for Adam and under 6 seconds for `LePlanner`; the updater also fails the task-cost criterion the authors fixed before evaluation. In a matched experiment that replays the first ten commands and then allows 4, 8, or 12 updates on the next solve, success counts across 16 contexts were 9, 8, and 7, so **extra planning updates rescued no failing task and turned some successes into failures** in a single scene cluster where lower latent trajectory costs coincided with worse outcomes. Code, weights, evaluators, execution traces, and cost accounting are released.

papers.title: The Anatomy of Socio-Demographics in Pluralistic Offensiveness Modeling: When and Where It Helps, and the Role of Reasoning
papers.abstract: Subjective judgments such as offensiveness often vary substantially across individuals, motivating pluralistic modeling approaches that incorporate annotators' socio-demographic information to capture this variation. However, prior findings on the benefits of socio-demographic information for pluralistic modeling are mixed, calling for a systematic analysis of both its effectiveness and the mechanisms through which it improves prediction. In this work, we study $\textbf{when}$ and $\textbf{where}$ socio-demographics benefit pluralistic offensiveness modeling, as well as $\textbf{the role of explicit reasoning}$ in leveraging this information. Across three multi-annotator datasets with prompted and trained LLMs, we first show that demographic gains are small and inconsistent for individual predictions but become clearer at the group and population levels, because aggregation attenuates the idiosyncratic variation that masks small but systematic demographic signals. Second, using a reasoning and prediction format that explicitly decomposes individual judgment into an overall baseline and a demographic-specific deviation, we show that the gains arise from both components: demographic information improves baseline estimation and enables meaningful demographic-specific shifts, and interventions show that better component estimates improve final predictions. Finally, comparing direct demographic conditioning with explicit reasoning about how the text interacts with annotator demographics, we find that reasoning yields more accurate baseline and shift estimates as well as final predictions, whereas conditioning alone rarely produces informative shifts. These results suggest that the mixed evidence in prior work may partly stem from individual-level evaluation, and that the value of socio-demographic information depends on both how it is evaluated and how models are guided to use it.
papers.summary: Judgments of offensiveness vary widely between people, and prior evidence on whether feeding annotators' socio-demographic attributes to models actually improves pluralistic prediction has been mixed. Across three multi-annotator datasets with prompted and trained large language models (LLMs), the authors find that demographic gains are small and inconsistent for individual predictions but **become clear at the group and population level, because aggregation washes out the idiosyncratic noise that masks small systematic demographic signals**. Using a format that decomposes each judgment into an overall baseline plus a demographic-specific deviation, they show the gains come from both components, and that asking the model to reason explicitly about how a text interacts with annotator demographics yields better baselines, shifts, and final predictions than direct conditioning, which rarely produces informative shifts. They argue the mixed prior findings partly reflect individual-level evaluation and the way models are guided to use the information.

papers.title: SAC-GCL: Structure-Aware Compression for Graph Contrastive Learning
papers.abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has achieved remarkable success in self-supervised representation learning by maximizing agreement between augmented views of a graph. Although augmented view generation is the central step in GCL, existing models rely on stochastic augmentation of the input graph, such as edge perturbation and node masking, which lack structural awareness and frequently destroy critical topology or introduce semantically inconsistent views. While recent adaptive methods improve upon random perturbations, they primarily operate on localized node or edge neighborhoods and fail to capture higher-order, macro-level structural organization crucial for graph classification. To address this limitation, we propose Structure-aware Compression for Graph Contrastive Learning (SAC-GCL), a novel framework that employs structural decomposition and graph compression as a principled view generation strategy. Moving beyond random augmentations, SAC-GCL leverages structural decomposition techniques to extract cohesive subgraphs and condense them into supernodes, constructing coarsened graph views that preserve local density and capture higher-level structural patterns while reducing noise and redundancy. We leverage multiple cohesive subgraph models to derive complementary views of the graph, each capturing distinct structural properties. To capture multi-resolution information, a hierarchical view encoder processes these compressed views by initializing super-node features with shared-weight cohesive subgraph embeddings. Our results from extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that structure-aware compression provides a powerful alternative to random perturbations, yielding more robust and discriminative graph representations for graph classification tasks.
papers.summary: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) depends on generating augmented views of a graph, but standard stochastic augmentations such as edge perturbation and node masking ignore structure and can destroy critical topology, while adaptive alternatives act only on local neighborhoods and miss macro-level organization. Structure-aware Compression for Graph Contrastive Learning (`SAC-GCL`) instead builds views by extracting cohesive subgraphs with several structural decomposition models, condensing each into supernodes to form coarsened graphs that preserve local density and expose higher-order patterns, and encoding these multi-resolution views with a hierarchical encoder whose supernode features are initialized from shared-weight subgraph embeddings. **On six benchmark datasets the compressed views yield more robust and discriminative representations for graph classification than random perturbations**, which the authors present as evidence that structure-aware compression is a viable alternative to stochastic augmentation.

papers.title: Scan Before You Install: Detecting and Mitigating Local and Composite Vulnerabilities in Skills
papers.abstract: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.
papers.summary: Agent skills bundle natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM agent loads and runs with access to the file system, shell, and network, so unintended weaknesses in otherwise benign public skills can lead to unsafe execution, yet existing scanners focus on malicious skills examined one at a time. The authors build a six-module scanner covering content extraction, local analysis, composite analysis of interactions among skills, validation, reporting, and mitigation. Local analysis reaches 95.90% recall at a 4.22% false positive rate on a 556-case subset of `SkillTrustBench` and an F1 of 0.947 on 1,000 `MalSkillBench` skills, ahead of Cisco's `Skill Scanner`, NVIDIA's `SkillSpector`, `AgentSkillsScanner`, and `SkillSieve`, while composite analysis scores an F1 of 0.991 on `SCR-Bench` against 0.816 to 0.858 for `SkillsGuard`. **Scanning 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories produced 53 analyst-confirmed vulnerabilities across 23 repositories**, each backed by a proof-of-concept attack, with 10 medium- and high-severity cases disclosed to maintainers and the recommended mitigations blocking the attacks for 47 of 55 findings without breaking tested functionality.

papers.title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report
papers.abstract: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.
papers.summary: Metis is a one-person effort to test whether better data, training methods, and architecture can substitute for parameter count at a fraction of the usual cost. `Metis-1.6` comprises two from-scratch models, `Praxis` at 2.94B parameters with 0.46B active and `Logos` at 10.23B parameters with 1.18B active, each a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack that runs twice per token, trained on 1.02T tokens including context extension to 131,072 tokens and 200B tokens of supervised fine-tuning. Across 40 post-trained benchmarks `Logos` averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models and within a point of `Qwen3-4B`, but it gets there **on roughly a twelfth of the median disclosed training data and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it**, ranking second of 30 on mathematics with 67.50% on `AIME 2025` while remaining weak at code, instruction following, and long context. Much of the report covers what went wrong, including an optimizer configuration that never ran, a 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory that learned to switch itself off, and a group-mean-normalized length reward that penalized correct long solutions once a group's pass rate exceeded two thirds, which the author proves and fixes with a one-line clamp before closing with the ablations behind the Mixture of Recursive Experts (MoRE) architecture planned for Metis-1.7.

papers.title: FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision
papers.abstract: Public disclosure repositories such as SEC EDGAR support informed investment through web access to corporate filings. Supporting their review with language model agents requires discovering unstated deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts, and verifying that requested revisions satisfy evidence-backed requirements. Existing financial question-answering evaluations provide limited evidence of these interactive capabilities. We introduce \textbf{FilingLoop}, an interactive benchmark and a self-evolving agent framework for corporate disclosure review and revision. Grounded in historical U.S.\ Securities and Exchange Commission correspondence, FilingLoop reconstructs 380 predominantly IPO review tasks from 96 companies under distinct information constraints. An evaluator separate from the acting agents scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Our framework couples iterative review and revision within each case with procedural learning across cases, converting requirement-level evaluation feedback into role-specific guidance without updating model weights. Updates affect only subsequent cases, allowing procedural adaptation to be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the evaluated stream, evolution increases requirement fulfillment from 24.28\% to 27.96\% and full comment resolution from 16.90\% to 20.75\%, with a 5.8\% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant. FilingLoop connects the concerns an agent discovers with the company facts it obtains and the revisions it commits, providing requirement-level feedback for procedures used in later review tasks.
papers.summary: Reviewing corporate filings with language-model agents requires spotting unstated deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts, and verifying that revisions satisfy evidence-backed requirements, capabilities that existing financial question-answering benchmarks do not test. `FilingLoop` is an interactive benchmark that reconstructs 380 mostly IPO review tasks from 96 companies out of historical U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) correspondence, scoring final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements with a separate evaluator that also audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. The accompanying agent framework couples iterative review and revision within a case with procedural learning across cases, turning requirement-level feedback into role-specific guidance without weight updates, applied only to subsequent cases so that adaptation can be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the evaluated stream this evolution **raises requirement fulfillment from 24.28% to 27.96% and full comment resolution from 16.90% to 20.75%**, at a 5.8% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant.

papers.title: Beyond Low-Pass Dynamics: Frequency-Selective Spiking Reservoirs with Resonant Neurons
papers.abstract: Spiking reservoir computing combines the training efficiency of fixed recurrent reservoirs with the energy efficiency of event-driven inference, where computation is triggered by sparse spikes rather than executed densely at every timestep. However, existing spiking reservoirs almost exclusively rely on Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, whose low-pass dynamics limit their ability to distinguish information encoded at different temporal frequencies. We introduce HRF-Res, a liquid state machine in which LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire (HRF) neurons. These neurons exhibit intrinsic oscillatory dynamics and selectively respond to input frequencies, enabling the reservoir to capture frequency-specific temporal patterns. The result is more discriminative representations and higher classification accuracy than LIF-based reservoirs, achieved without sacrificing the energy efficiency of spiking computation, with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir. Evaluated on ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods. These results demonstrate that introducing frequency-selective dynamics into spiking reservoirs improves representational quality and classification performance while preserving their inherent energy efficiency.
papers.summary: Spiking reservoir computing pairs the cheap training of fixed recurrent reservoirs with event-driven inference, but nearly all such reservoirs use Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, whose low-pass dynamics blur information carried at different temporal frequencies. `HRF-Res` is a liquid state machine that swaps LIF units for a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire (HRF) neurons with intrinsic oscillations, so that different neurons respond selectively to different input frequencies and the reservoir can capture frequency-specific temporal patterns. Across ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, the model achieves **state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir**.

papers.title: TERRA: Task-Oriented Edge AI for Regional Fire Detection with Identity-Free Reporting
papers.abstract: Distributed fire-monitoring systems may involve many sensing devices reporting over a shared uplink, even though the operational objective is often to identify regions exhibiting evidence of fire rather than to recover device-specific measurements. We introduce TERRA (Task-Oriented Edge Representation and Regional Aggregation), an edge-AI framework that combines task-oriented local inference, identity-free region-tagged reporting, and permutation-invariant regional evidence aggregation. TERRA supports two reporting modes: TERRA-Score, in which each device communicates a quantized local fire probability, and TERRA-Feature, in which it communicates a compact learned representation for receiver-side aggregation using a permutation-invariant DeepSets model. Using all 15 numerical sensing modalities of the distributed indoor EN54 fire-alarm dataset as a proof-of-concept testbed, we evaluate regional inference for an episode-level fire-scenario target under repetition-disjoint three-fold cross-validation. We study representation size, task-payload quantization, report availability, and robustness to missed and false recovered messages. With nine reports and perfect message recovery, TERRA-Feature achieves mean AUPRC 0.990 using a 24-bit task payload, while TERRA-Score achieves 0.987 using only 6 bits; both attain an MDR of 1.81% at FAR $\leq$1%. TERRA-Feature achieves slightly higher AUPRC under reliable recovery, whereas the more compact TERRA-Score is less sensitive to increasing false-message contamination.
papers.summary: Distributed fire-monitoring deployments have many sensing devices sharing one uplink, yet the goal is usually to flag which regions show evidence of fire rather than to reconstruct each device's measurements. Task-Oriented Edge Representation and Regional Aggregation (`TERRA`) combines task-oriented local inference, identity-free region-tagged reporting, and permutation-invariant aggregation at the receiver, in either a `TERRA-Score` mode that sends a quantized local fire probability or a `TERRA-Feature` mode that sends a compact learned representation aggregated by a DeepSets model. On the indoor `EN54` fire-alarm dataset with all 15 numerical sensing modalities and nine reports per region, **`TERRA-Feature` reaches a mean area under the precision-recall curve of 0.990 with a 24-bit payload while `TERRA-Score` reaches 0.987 with only 6 bits**, both at a 1.81% missed detection rate with false alarms held at or below 1%. The more compact score mode degrades less as false recovered messages increase, while the feature mode is slightly more accurate under reliable recovery.

papers.title: Generative modeling for fusion: a large-scale benchmark of stellarator fast-ion simulations
papers.abstract: Stellarators offer a promising magnetic confinement approach for achieving controlled nuclear fusion. However, stellarator design remains challenging, as evaluating configuration performance requires computationally expensive, high-fidelity simulations. In particular, key performance metrics derived from guiding center simulations are costly to include directly in the design optimization loop, and are almost exclusively used as diagnostics. Machine learning has the potential to advance fusion research by enabling rapid generation and evaluation of new stellarator configurations. Effectively applying ML for fusion demands large-scale datasets that capture both design diversity and high-fidelity simulation outputs. In this work, we introduce the Benchmark of Stellarator Simulations (BoSS), a dataset of stellarator designs paired with guiding center simulation results and trajectories. The BoSS is the first large-scale dataset of guiding center simulations, containing simulation data for 180,000 distinct magnetohydrodynamic equilibria spanning a wide range of magnetic geometries and confinement properties. To exemplify the utility of ML to accelerate stellarator design, we formulate and address two sets of modeling tasks: generative modeling for designing stellarators with good particle confinement, and surrogate modeling for predicting stellarator heat deposition patterns and particle trajectories. The tasks reveal the potential impact ML can have in the stellarator field and important opportunities to improve the applicability of ML models in the sciences. Our baselines generate diverse, performant stellarators and provide useful surrogate predictions, and point to long-horizon trajectory forecasting and out-of-distribution generation as key directions for future work. The BoSS can be accessed through https://boss.flatironinstitute.org/.
papers.summary: Stellarator design for magnetic confinement fusion is bottlenecked by expensive high-fidelity simulations, and fast-ion confinement metrics from guiding center simulations are so costly that they serve only as diagnostics rather than optimization targets. The Benchmark of Stellarator Simulations (`BoSS`) pairs **180,000 distinct magnetohydrodynamic equilibria with guiding center simulation results and particle trajectories**, which the authors describe as the first large-scale dataset of its kind, spanning a wide range of magnetic geometries and confinement properties. They define two task families, generative modeling of stellarators with good particle confinement and surrogate modeling of heat deposition patterns and particle trajectories, and report baselines that produce diverse, performant designs and useful surrogate predictions while identifying long-horizon trajectory forecasting and out-of-distribution generation as open problems.

papers.title: Beyond Utterance-Level Speaker Similarity: Perception-Aligned Segmental Evaluation of Accent in Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Utterance-level similarity ratings do not reveal where perceived accent differences occur in generated speech. We introduce a segmental evaluation protocol combining speaker and accent similarity ratings with subword annotations of perceived accent differences provided by listeners from target accent regions. Using newly collected recordings, 47 retained listeners evaluate 200 content-matched reference--candidate pairs spanning four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot TTS systems, and an articulation-based voice conversion system. Subword annotations locate salient pronunciation differences and sometimes yield different system rankings from similarity ratings. Speaker and accent ratings remain strongly associated ($\rho = 0.71$), highlighting the value of examining local perceptual evidence beyond these scores. Evaluation of seven objective distances reveals weak correspondence with subword selections, with correlations reaching at most $\rho = 0.22$. We release code, data, and an interactive demo to support the development of perceptually grounded segmental accent evaluation.
papers.summary: Utterance-level speaker similarity ratings cannot show where in a generated utterance listeners perceive an accent mismatch. The authors introduce a segmental evaluation protocol that pairs speaker and accent similarity ratings with subword-level annotations of perceived accent differences from listeners native to the target accent region, applied by 47 retained listeners to 200 content-matched reference and candidate pairs across four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot text-to-speech systems, and one articulation-based voice conversion system. Subword annotations localize salient pronunciation differences and sometimes rank systems differently from similarity ratings, speaker and accent ratings remain strongly correlated at rho 0.71, and **seven objective distance measures correlate with the subword selections at no better than rho 0.22**. Code, data, and an interactive demo are released.

papers.title: Grounding Long Financial Text with Semantically-Enriched Tables via Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: We propose a multimodal transformer framework for efficiently modeling long1 financial documents that combine structured tabular data with noisy, unstructured2 textual disclosures. The framework represents financial tables as semantically3 enriched token sequences and integrates them with long-form text through a cross-4 attention mechanism that explicitly captures cross-modal dependencies. In par-5 ticular, we augment each numerical variable with a semantic embedding derived6 from its textual definition, enabling the model to encode both numerical magnitude7 and economic meaning. This design yields a more expressive and parameter-8 efficient representation of tabular data compared to value-only embeddings. Using9 a large-scale dataset of financial statements and MD&A disclosures, we show that10 structured numerical features remain the dominant source of predictive signal;11 however, textual information provides consistent incremental gains when incor-12 porated via cross-attention rather than simple concatenation. Our results further13 demonstrate that noisy textual disclosures are most useful when conditioned on a14 stable, semantically structured tabular representation. In particular, using frozen15 variable-level tabular representations as cross-attention queries enables the model16 to weight MD&A chunks differently for each financial variable and observation.17 These findings suggest that cross-attention provides an efficient mechanism for18 table-conditioned aggregation of long-form narrative evidence.
papers.summary: Long financial documents mix structured statement tables with noisy, unstructured narrative such as management discussion and analysis (MD&A), and the question is how to model both efficiently in one transformer. The proposed framework represents each financial table as a token sequence in which every numerical variable is augmented with a semantic embedding derived from its textual definition, then fuses these with long-form text through cross-attention that uses frozen variable-level tabular representations as queries over text chunks. On a large dataset of financial statements and MD&A disclosures, **structured numerical features remain the dominant predictive signal, but text adds consistent incremental gains when integrated via cross-attention rather than concatenation**, and the narrative is most useful when conditioned on a stable, semantically structured tabular representation that lets the model weight disclosure chunks differently for each variable and observation.

papers.title: Muon Makes the First Mixture-of-Experts Layer Harder to Balance
papers.abstract: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.
papers.summary: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models now train with the `Muon` optimizer rather than `AdamW`, and most balance expert load with a per-expert routing bias adjusted after each step, but recipes disagree on whether Muon should also update the router. The authors measure the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest within a layer, as a proxy for how hard a layer is to balance, in models with 55M and 108M active parameters. **Muon roughly doubled the span of the first MoE layer at every seed**, driven by Muon on the non-router weights regardless of which optimizer trained the router, with the first router's inputs sharing a common direction and its busiest expert drawing four to seven times its fair share soon after warmup. Subtracting the batch mean from router inputs or halving Muon's learning rate removed the overload with little change in loss, while moving only the router to `AdamW` made loads shift more during warmup and slightly raised the loss, so the results favor keeping the router on Muon at this scale.

papers.title: What Actually Matters? A Paired Evaluation of Inference Settings for $\pi_{0.5}$ on BEHAVIOR-1K
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for general-purpose household robotics. However, inference and data-collection strategies that have been deployed in smaller-scale settings do not necessarily generalize to large-scale, diverse task suites. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic, paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks. Our evaluation uses a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, which achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. These results show that proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks. Project page, videos, and detailed analysis: https://rubenhammele.github.io/behavior2026
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are a promising route to general-purpose household robots, but inference and data-collection tricks validated on small task suites may not carry over to large, diverse ones. The authors run a systematic paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks in `BEHAVIOR-1K`, using a fine-tuned `π0.5` model derived from the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner that reaches a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. **The proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks**, with gains seen in one setting failing to appear in others.

papers.title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks for large language model agents doing scientific discovery conflate law inference with programming, score data fitting rather than prediction on unseen inputs, and cannot separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. `SciGame` converts scientific literature into structured cards, each yielding an Original environment and a dimensionally consistent Counterfactual one with the same task interface, spanning a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection built from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs; agents are tested in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive experimentation protocols. Across five frontier models, **familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered**, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets, and plausible explanations can mask quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form of a law remains the main bottleneck even when agents interpret the evidence correctly.

papers.title: FAD-KV: Adaptive Dictionary KV Caching for Efficient Reasoning Decoding
papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is a core mechanism in large language models, where intermediate key and value representations are stored to accelerate autoregressive decoding. As generation length increases, KV cache memory and computation grow linearly, making compression critical for efficient long-output reasoning. Dictionary-based sparse KV compression is appealing because it represents each token's KV states as a sparse combination of learned basis elements (atoms) in a dictionary, preserving token-level structure without enforcing a global low-rank constraint. However, existing dictionary-based methods face two practical limitations during decoding: iterative sparse coding methods such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit add decoding-time overhead, and static dictionaries may mismatch evolving KV distributions under test-time generation. While adaptive dictionary updates can reduce this mismatch, naive append-only strategies lead to dictionary growth during generation. We propose FAD-KV, a \textbf{F}ast \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{D}ictionary KV caching framework for efficient reasoning decoding. FAD-KV integrates (i) a screening-based sparse coding scheme, where a one-shot Top-\(n\) selection identifies a small candidate pool followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, and (ii) a fixed-size dictionary adaptation mechanism that reuses inactive atoms instead of expanding the dictionary. By controlling both sparse coding cost and adaptive dictionary growth, FAD-KV provides a memory-bounded and computation-efficient KV compression framework for long reasoning workloads. Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show that FAD-KV achieves a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while avoiding unbounded dictionary growth during decoding.
papers.summary: Key-value (KV) caches grow linearly with generation length, making compression important for long-output reasoning, and dictionary-based sparse compression, which represents each token's KV states as a sparse combination of learned atoms, avoids a global low-rank constraint but suffers from slow iterative sparse coding such as `Orthogonal Matching Pursuit` and from static dictionaries that drift away from the KV distribution during generation. `FAD-KV` (Fast Adaptive Dictionary KV caching) pairs a screening-based sparse coder, which performs a one-shot Top-n atom selection followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, with a fixed-size dictionary adaptation scheme that recycles inactive atoms instead of appending new ones. On reasoning and long-context benchmarks, **the method achieves a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while keeping dictionary size bounded throughout decoding**.

papers.title: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns
papers.abstract: Across human history, knowledge has undergone several transitions, from orality to writing and then to digital archives. At each transition, humans established new conventions to preserve knowledge for the new era. Nowadays, as research agents are increasingly deployed for laboratory experiments, knowledge is crossing another boundary: from records written for humans to those for machines. In this work, we introduce VerifiedLab, a multi-agent harness framework for this human-to-machine transition of knowledge. VerifiedLab transforms research output from passive artifacts into active systems that accelerate downstream use, adoption and prediction of future trends. In VerifiedLab, a team of AI scientists with distinct roles reasons over records verified field by field: a principal investigator plans, a librarian computes the evidence directly from the records, specialists draft, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its data before the harness decides whether to release or withhold it. We demonstrate the efficacy of VerifiedLab through extensive experiments on perovskite solar cells: VerifiedLab recovers known physical trends, anticipates devices reported a year later, and lets AI scientists inherit the literature together with a measure of how far it can be trusted. By scaling the inference-time verification compute, VerifiedLab introduces a new pathway for knowledge dissemination and machine harness for AI co-scientists.
papers.summary: As research agents take over laboratory work, scientific records written for humans need to become records that machines can reason over and trust. `VerifiedLab` is a multi-agent harness in which a principal investigator agent plans, a librarian computes evidence directly from field-by-field verified records, specialists draft claims, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its underlying data before the system decides whether to release or withhold it. In experiments on perovskite solar cell literature, **the system recovers known physical trends and anticipates devices that were reported a year later**, and the authors frame scaling inference-time verification compute as a way to hand literature to AI co-scientists together with a measure of how far it can be trusted.

papers.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.
papers.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) depends heavily on hand-designed intermediate rewards that must be rebuilt whenever the environment or team changes, and although large language models (LLMs) can write reward code, such rewards are usually designed and tested in a single setting. `GARDEN` (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) has an LLM reward engineer inspect environment code, training records, and agent behavior to develop one reward program for a family of related scenarios, testing drafts in trial training runs while the learning algorithm and final-selection rule stay fixed, then transfers that program unchanged to scenarios unseen during design. On held-out `Overcooked` layouts, task returns rose 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards, and on two `SMAX` combat scenarios **the mean win rate climbed from 51.0% to 89.9%**, beating the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and `Eureka`-style reward reflection under matched candidate and probe budgets.

papers.title: Machine learning applications in the heliosphere
papers.abstract: Space weather is the study of the near-Earth impact of the processes on the Sun. In a this era of technology, space weather emerges as a crucial area of study wherein the state of the near-Earth conditions need to be modeled and forecasted. Crucially, the advent of machine learning provides us with opportunities to study this subject in a rather comprehensive manner. In this chapter, we treat the the processes arising from Sun to the impact on the ground as a set of coupled systems, which can be studied in isolation or in a coupled manner. We define these individual systems in terms of their state vector $\vec{S}$, which provides us with an opportunity to define the physical variables determining the system. This also allows us to consider the systems in terms of their observables, obtained through the action of operators as $\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$. In such a formalism, the machine learning algorithms serve as {\it learned operators}, defined generally as inference ($\mathcal{I}$), propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and emulation ($\mathcal{E}$). Through such a formalism, we present how machine learning helps advance our understanding of the physical systems under study, while also accelerating the development of operational models for space weather forecasting.
papers.summary: Space weather, the near-Earth impact of processes on the Sun, needs to be modeled and forecast as society grows more technology-dependent, and this chapter surveys how machine learning contributes. The chain from Sun to ground is treated as a set of coupled systems, each described by a physical state vector and observed through operators acting on that state, so that **machine learning algorithms become learned operators of three kinds: inference, propagation, and emulation**. Within this formalism, the chapter reviews how machine learning advances physical understanding of each system while accelerating operational space weather forecasting models.

papers.title: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential tools for numerical optimization. Despite promising results, their intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions. This paper investigates the ability of LLMs to exploit mathematical problem structures and generate feasible, near-optimal solutions. We develop an evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from execution failures, including numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations, and output-format errors. Using representative problems from convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection, we assess LLM performance against deterministic reference solvers across different dimensions. Our results reveal that LLMs can capture useful optimization structures and produce near-optimal solutions, even when their outputs fail to satisfy numerical or formatting requirements. However, reliability deteriorates with increasing problem dimension and depends strongly on the underlying optimization structure. To further investigate the limitations, we deploy an iterative refinement mechanism that provides targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the range of problem dimensions over which LLMs produce valid solutions. Nevertheless, persistent numerical and structural errors limit their applicability as standalone optimizers. These findings provide insights into the capacity and limits of LLM-based optimization and motivate hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as numerical optimizers, but how well they exploit mathematical problem structure, especially in high dimensions, is poorly understood. The authors build an evaluation framework that separates solution quality from execution failures such as numerical inaccuracy, constraint violations, and malformed output, and test LLMs against deterministic reference solvers on convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection problems of varying dimension. LLMs often capture the right structure and produce near-optimal solutions even when their outputs break numerical or formatting requirements, but **reliability degrades sharply as problem dimension grows** and depends strongly on the optimization structure. An iterative refinement loop with targeted feasibility and quality feedback substantially extends the range of dimensions where valid solutions appear, though persistent errors argue for hybrid pipelines that pair LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

papers.title: NLP-based Message Prioritisation for Opportunistic Routing: A Case Study of Nepal Earthquake Emergency Communication
papers.abstract: This dissertation investigates whether Natural Language Processing (NLP) based semantic message prioritisation can improve the treatment of urgent disaster messages in opportunistic emergency communication, using the 2015 Nepal earthquake as a case study. TF IDF with Logistic Regression and BERT are used to classify social media messages into nine humanitarian categories, which are mapped to four routing priorities from P1 to P4. These priorities are integrated into the ONE simulator within a controlled Kathmandu earthquake scenario using a modified Binary Spray and Wait router. BERT achieves higher priority accuracy and P1 recall than Logistic Regression, while reducing under prioritisation and severe priority errors. However, improved NLP performance does not produce uniform network gains. P1 delivery probability remains high and similar across routing conditions, and no consistent latency reduction is observed. The clearest difference appears under buffer pressure, where the BERT condition shows fewer observed ground truth P1 buffer losses than Logistic Regression. The results indicate that semantic prioritisation is most valuable when limited transmission and storage resources are contested, although it cannot overcome mobility and contact constraints in opportunistic networks.
papers.summary: Disaster-time opportunistic networks must decide which messages to forward and store when contacts and buffers are scarce, and this dissertation asks whether Natural Language Processing (NLP) based semantic prioritisation helps, using the 2015 Nepal earthquake as a case study. `TF-IDF` with logistic regression and `BERT` classify social media messages into nine humanitarian categories mapped to four routing priorities, which then drive a modified Binary Spray and Wait router inside the `ONE` simulator in a Kathmandu earthquake scenario. `BERT` achieves higher priority accuracy and top-priority recall with fewer severe misprioritisations, yet **better classification does not translate into uniform network gains**: top-priority delivery probability stays high across conditions and latency does not consistently drop, with the clearest benefit being fewer top-priority buffer losses under storage pressure.

papers.title: Bi-Phase Training: Learning Efficiently From Scratch
papers.abstract: Pre-training foundational models is computationally expensive as models scale. In this work, we introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pre-training method that preserves the high-rank learning dynamics observed in full-parameter optimization with substantially reduced trainable parameters. BPT parameterizes each weight update as a composition of constrained high-rank left/right transformations via trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters whose updates are periodically merged into the frozen base weights, resulting in a compounding expansion of accessible directions during training. Across language-model pre-training from scratch (Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B) on FineWeb-Edu (10B and 100B tokens), BPT achieves validation perplexity close to full-parameter baselines while using far fewer trainable parameters; e.g., at the 1.5B scale, BPT uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with only a small validation-perplexity gap. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation across diverse downstream tasks shows that BPT preserves much of the full-parameterized model's downstream performance.
papers.summary: Pre-training foundation models is expensive, and parameter-efficient alternatives typically sacrifice the high-rank update dynamics of full-parameter optimization. Bi-Phase Training (`BPT`) parameterizes each weight update as a composition of constrained high-rank left and right transformations built from trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters, periodically merging the adapter updates into the frozen base weights so the set of reachable directions compounds over training. Pre-training `Qwen2.5` architectures from 100M to 1.5B parameters and `OLMo-2-1B` from scratch on 10B and 100B tokens of `FineWeb-Edu`, **BPT at the 1.5B scale uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with only a small validation-perplexity gap** relative to full-parameter training, and a broad downstream evaluation shows it retains much of the full model's task performance.

papers.title: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning
