papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.
papers.summary: Latent multi-agent systems cut inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent messages in continuous representations, but reusable skills are still supplied as text or stored as per-layer key-value states or skill-specific parameters, adding repeated processing or heavy per-skill storage. `SkillMem` encodes each skill as a small external latent memory read through a role-conditioned cross-attention module, so the same memory can guide different agents according to their role and hidden state, and both the memories and the shared reader are trained by behavioral distillation to reproduce the shift in token predictions that the textual skill would induce, with the backbone frozen. Across six benchmarks and `Qwen3` models from 4B to 14B parameters, a fixed 8×256 memory costing 9.6 KB per skill delivers strong gains for smaller backbones, and **for a 100-skill library it cuts storage by more than 38× and speeds end-to-end inference by up to 4.23×** compared with alternative skill representations.

papers.title: Finite-Step Geometry of Marginal-Preserving Velocity Fields in Generative Flows
papers.abstract: Generative flows can admit different velocity fields that induce the same continuous marginal evolution but behave differently after numerical discretization. We study this finite-step non-equivalence while keeping the marginal path and numerical method fixed. Projected modified equations characterize the component of local integration error that changes the marginal law and give sufficient conditions for higher marginal convergence order. For affine fixed-shape distributions, we characterize exact finite-step reachability and derive spectral obstructions and sharp nearest-reachable Wasserstein errors. For diffusion probability-flow ODEs, we construct skew-score perturbations that preserve the exact marginal path under exact scores and quantify their leakage under score error. Controlled Gaussian and mixture experiments recover the predicted order, reachability, and obstruction phenomena.
papers.summary: Different velocity fields can induce the same continuous marginal evolution in a generative flow yet behave differently once the ordinary differential equation is discretized, and the authors study this finite-step non-equivalence with the marginal path and numerical integrator held fixed. Projected modified equations isolate the component of local integration error that actually changes the marginal law and yield sufficient conditions for higher marginal convergence order, and for affine fixed-shape distributions the paper characterizes exact finite-step reachability with spectral obstructions and sharp nearest-reachable Wasserstein errors. For diffusion probability-flow ODEs, **skew-score perturbations preserve the exact marginal path under exact scores**, and their leakage under score error is quantified, with controlled Gaussian and mixture experiments recovering the predicted order, reachability, and obstruction behavior.

papers.title: You Don't Need Aligned Representations: Knowledge Distillation via Random Prototype Spaces
papers.abstract: A widely held assumption in knowledge distillation is that teacher and student representations must occupy a compatible or explicitly aligned feature space. We propose RPKD (Random Prototype Knowledge Distillation), which discards this assumption by comparing both networks against a shared bank of randomly initialized, frozen prototype vectors. Alignment is therefore carried out in an external reference space rather than in the teacher's native feature coordinates: the teacher side is projected by fixed random maps that carry no trainable parameters, and only the student adapts. Two branches handle the transfer: a logit branch aligning global prototype similarity distributions and a feature branch matching spatially-resolved prototype activation maps. Both operate within the same fixed prototype space, which can be interpreted as a random feature embedding that approximately preserves inter-sample similarity structure, so the prototype bank and the distillation objective stay unchanged across teacher-student pairs while only the input projections are instantiated per architecture. In low-category settings, decoupling the prototype vocabulary from the task label space yields richer supervision than the label space alone, an advantage absent from logit-based methods, whose supervisory signal collapses as class count shrinks. This advantage is especially relevant in real-world scenarios where the label space is typically constrained. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RPKD, achieving a maximum gain of +7.98% over OFA on CIFAR-100, +12.44% on ImageNet-100, and +1.28% on ImageNet-1K. Source code is available at https://github.com/HamzaEtcibasi/RPKD
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation is usually assumed to require teacher and student features to live in a compatible or explicitly aligned space. Random Prototype Knowledge Distillation (`RPKD`) drops that assumption by comparing both networks against a shared bank of randomly initialized, frozen prototype vectors: the teacher is projected by fixed random maps with no trainable parameters, only the student adapts, and two branches transfer knowledge, one aligning global prototype similarity distributions and one matching spatially resolved prototype activation maps. Because the prototype vocabulary is decoupled from the label space, supervision stays rich even with few classes, where logit-based methods collapse, and the method gains **up to +7.98% over `OFA` on `CIFAR-100`**, +12.44% on `ImageNet-100`, and +1.28% on `ImageNet-1K`.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Semantic Communications over Multiple Access Channels
papers.abstract: This paper presents a federated learning (FL) framework for semantic communication (SemCom) over the multiple access channel (MAC), where multiple distributed transmitters simultaneously convey semantic information to a common receiver using end-to-end learned semantic representations. Semantic feature extraction, compression, wireless transmission, and semantic inference are jointly optimized through FL-based SemCom. Unlike conventional SemCom systems that train users independently, simultaneous semantic transmissions over the MAC enable concurrent training of multiple transmitters within the same transmission interval, thereby reducing training overhead and channel usage. Federated semantic aggregation is incorporated with shared and personalized encoder components, allowing transmitters with limited local training data to benefit from semantic representations learned from transmitters possessing larger datasets while preserving local adaptation. Evaluated using the CIFAR-10 dataset over fading channels, the proposed approach maintains high semantic inference accuracy under shared wireless access and significantly improves performance under severe data imbalance. In the meantime, simultaneous semantic transmissions can significantly reduce training overhead while preserving robust semantic performance across distributed transmitters with heterogeneous local datasets. These results highlight the potential of combining FL and SemCom to support scalable and communication-efficient edge intelligence in future wireless networks.
papers.summary: Semantic communication (SemCom) systems learn end-to-end representations for transmitting task-relevant information, but conventional designs train each user independently. The authors propose a federated learning (FL) framework for SemCom over a multiple access channel (MAC), in which several transmitters send learned semantic features to a common receiver simultaneously, so feature extraction, compression, wireless transmission, and inference are jointly optimized and multiple transmitters train concurrently within the same transmission interval; aggregation uses shared and personalized encoder components so data-poor transmitters can borrow representations from data-rich ones while keeping local adaptation. On `CIFAR-10` over fading channels, the approach maintains high semantic inference accuracy under shared access and **significantly improves performance under severe data imbalance** while reducing training overhead.

papers.title: SAG-Sep: Sparse Augmented Graphs and Onion-Guided Search for Rounded Capacity Cut Separation
papers.abstract: Rounded capacity cuts (RCCs) are among the most effective cuts for capacitated vehicle-routing relaxations, but exact separation is computationally prohibitive at scale. Existing heuristic and neural separators can be fast, but often fail to produce sufficiently many effective cuts within practical separation budgets. We introduce SAG-Sep, a separator that scores node membership in RCC-inducing subsets across vehicle-count levels from a fractional LP solution in a single encoder forward pass, avoiding the iterative predict-and-coarsen inference used by NeuralSEP-style separators. SAG-Sep encodes the LP solution as a Sparse Augmented Graph (SAG), adding flow-informed multi-hop edges that expose long-range routing structure without densifying attention. Beyond LP-aware sparse encoding, we observe that high-value exact RCCs are typically nested, organizing into onion-like subset families, and SAG-Sep's node scores track subset nesting depth. This motivates Onion-Sweep (OS), a training-free decoder that ranks customers by their scores, evaluates the RCC violation of every prefix of the ranking in one vectorized pass, and emits the most violated prefix of each replica together with a cross-replica family of nested proposals, converting independent node scores into structurally coordinated RCC candidates without a tuned threshold or probing band. On the NeuralSEP benchmark with N=1000 customer instances, SAG-Sep with OS reduces the average root gap by 17.7% relative to the strongest NeuralSEP baseline, while the single-pass SAG-Sep separator achieves a roughly 30-fold per-iteration neural separation speedup. Our findings suggest that LP-aware sparse encoding and the nested structure of high-value cuts are structural patterns worth leveraging in neural separation more broadly.
papers.summary: Rounded capacity cuts (RCCs) are among the strongest cuts for capacitated vehicle routing relaxations, but exact separation is too slow at scale and existing heuristic or neural separators often produce too few effective cuts within a practical budget. `SAG-Sep` encodes the fractional linear programming solution as a Sparse Augmented Graph with flow-informed multi-hop edges that expose long-range routing structure without dense attention, and scores node membership in RCC-inducing subsets across vehicle-count levels in a single encoder pass, avoiding the iterative predict-and-coarsen loop of `NeuralSEP`-style separators. Observing that high-value exact RCCs nest like onion layers, the authors add Onion-Sweep, a training-free decoder that ranks customers by score and evaluates every prefix's violation in one vectorized pass; on `NeuralSEP` benchmark instances with 1000 customers, **the combination reduces the average root gap by 17.7% relative to the strongest NeuralSEP baseline** with a roughly 30-fold per-iteration speedup in neural separation.

papers.title: Statistical Detection of Positional Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems: Methodologies and Empirical Evidence
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as recommendation generators in conversational recommender systems (RS) via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This flexible design introduces new sources of structural bias. This paper studies positional bias in top-1 and single-turn LLM-based RS: systematic dependence of the recommended item on the order in which candidates are presented in the prompt. We propose two complementary detection methodologies: (i) POB-ICM, based on contingency matrix analysis and Chi-square independence testing, and (ii) POB-UNBP, a sample-efficient approach derived from a uniformity null model under permutation-based evaluation, enabling stochastic decoding with formal statistical guarantees. Using a controlled RAG testbed for product recommendation, built on a real product catalog, a fixed prompt template and 2000 template-generated user queries with 20 permutations each (40,000 instances), both methodologies reject the null hypothesis of positional independence and uniformity in all evaluated state-of-the-art models. We introduce three complementary metrics -- permutation sensitivity, positional bias, and strong positional bias -- to quantify this effect, the latter targeting cases where the position displaces the recommendation towards clearly less relevant items rather than only choosing among comparably relevant ones. A robustness analysis across candidate-set size and decoding temperature shows that the bias is structural and model-dependent, not an artifact of deterministic decoding or candidate-set size. These results establish positional bias as a measurable, reproducible property of prompt-mediated recommendation pipelines in the evaluated setting and motivate routine auditing and governance controls (e.g., order randomization, standardized prompting) for deployed LLM-based RS. Source code is publicly released.
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) used as recommendation generators inside retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines may systematically favor candidates based on where they appear in the prompt. The authors propose two detection methods, `POB-ICM`, which applies contingency-matrix analysis with Chi-square independence testing, and `POB-UNBP`, a sample-efficient test derived from a uniformity null model under permutation-based evaluation that supports stochastic decoding with formal guarantees, plus three metrics for permutation sensitivity, positional bias, and strong positional bias where position pushes the pick toward clearly less relevant items. In a controlled RAG testbed over a real product catalog with 2000 template-generated queries and 20 candidate permutations each, **every evaluated state-of-the-art model rejects the null hypothesis of positional independence**, and the bias persists across candidate-set sizes and decoding temperatures, motivating routine auditing and controls such as order randomization.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Latent Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
papers.abstract: Time-series data play an important role in various tasks, such as weather forecasting, web traffic analysis, and speech recognition. Recently, pioneering studies have increasingly adopted Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) based encoders to learn time-series representations through latent-space prediction. However, they often overlook the underlying factors governing transitions between time-series observations. In this work, we hypothesize that explicitly modeling the information behind changes in time series can facilitate time-series modeling. Building on this hypothesis, we propose ACTS-WM, a self-supervised latent action-conditioned world model framework for time-series analysis. First, we introduce a latent action modeling approach that infers the underlying information behind time-series transitions as latent actions, without requiring explicit action annotations. We then develop a JEPA-based encoder and an action-conditioned world model to predict target time-series representations conditioned on the learned latent actions and task information. We evaluate ACTS-WM across 4 representative tasks on 22 datasets from diverse domains, covering univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ACTS-WM can improve downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders by learning complementary representations.
papers.summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) encoders have become popular for learning time-series representations via latent-space prediction, but they ignore the underlying factors that drive transitions between observations. `ACTS-WM` infers these factors as latent actions without any action annotations, then trains a JEPA-based encoder together with an action-conditioned world model that predicts target representations given the inferred latent action and task information. Across four tasks on 22 datasets spanning univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification, **the learned representations improve downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders** by capturing complementary information.

papers.title: Meta-Initialization of Implicit Neural Representations to Accelerate Deformable Medical Image Registration
papers.abstract: Implicit neural representation (INR) methods for deformable medical image registration require the network parameters to be optimized for each new image pair, making adaptation speed a practical limitation. This work investigates whether early adaptation can be accelerated using an initialization learned from a collection of previously solved registration tasks. We examine two schemes: Reptile meta-initialization and STRAINER transfer of the shared component of a coordinate network. KAN-IDIR is used as the base INR displacement-field model. Experiments are conducted on OASIS-1, with 364 consecutive pairs used for training and 49 pairs for test-time adaptation. Registration quality is evaluated using mean Dice and HD95, together with the fraction of voxels with a negative Jacobian determinant at iteration 1500. In the configurations studied, both schemes yield higher Dice and lower HD95 at early iterations than random initialization. Reptile numerically outperforms STRAINER under a small iteration budget, although their pretraining budgets are not matched. As the number of iterations increases, the differences between the schemes shrink. STRAINER pretraining takes 39-40 minutes, compared with 44.98 hours for Reptile.
papers.summary: Implicit neural representation (INR) methods for deformable medical image registration must optimize network parameters anew for every image pair, so adaptation speed is a practical bottleneck. The authors test whether initializations learned from previously solved registration tasks accelerate early adaptation, comparing `Reptile` meta-initialization against `STRAINER` transfer of the shared component of a coordinate network, with `KAN-IDIR` as the base displacement-field model on 364 training and 49 test pairs from `OASIS-1`. Both schemes give higher Dice and lower HD95 than random initialization in early iterations, with **Reptile ahead under a small iteration budget though at a pretraining cost of about 45 hours versus 40 minutes for STRAINER**, and the gap between them narrows as iterations increase.

papers.title: Application of PDE emulators for a multi-material, multi-physics simulation problem
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) architectures are being developed for fast emulation of numerical simulators to accelerate both scientific discovery and engineering design. While these approaches are well-tested on popular PDE (partial differential equation) benchmarks, it is necessary to evaluate their performance on datasets that more accurately reflect industrial and engineering applications. We evaluate several computer vision-based architectures trained as surrogate models on a challenging computational physics task involving multiple materials, revealing significant implementation challenges for adapting certain pre-trained models, including transformer-based architectures. For such multi-physics multi-material datasets, our results underscore the importance of learning algorithms designed for sparse and imbalanced data, techniques for adapting spatial encodings and physical consistency metrics, in addition to methods for reducing the cost of generating sufficient training data.
papers.summary: Machine learning surrogates for numerical simulators are usually benchmarked on clean partial differential equation (PDE) datasets that do not reflect the messiness of industrial and engineering problems. The authors evaluate several computer-vision-based architectures as surrogate models on a multi-material, multi-physics computational physics task and find **significant implementation challenges in adapting certain pre-trained models, including transformer-based architectures**, to this setting. The results point to the need for learning algorithms suited to sparse and imbalanced data, adapted spatial encodings and physical consistency metrics, and cheaper ways to generate enough training data.

papers.title: Merge and Branch: Efficient Tree-Structured Supervised Fine-Tuning of LLMs for Recommendation
papers.abstract: LLM-based generative recommendation reads long, text-rich interaction histories but generates only short semantic identifiers (SIDs). This asymmetry makes supervised fine-tuning inefficient: encoding the history is expensive, yet each history usually provides supervision for only one target. We present Merge and Branch (M&B) to reduce input cost and learn more from each encoded history. Merge compresses each historical item's SID and text into a small number of learned tokens. Branch uses the compressed history to predict multiple target SIDs. To share history computation while keeping these targets independent, M&B organizes each example as a shallow, wide tree. We develop tree FlashAttention to execute this layout efficiently, processing the shared history once and propagating gradients from every branch for end-to-end training. A tree-structured key/value cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding. Experiments on public benchmarks show that M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines while substantially improving training and decoding efficiency.
papers.summary: LLM-based generative recommenders read long, text-rich interaction histories but emit only short semantic identifiers (SIDs), so supervised fine-tuning spends most of its compute encoding a history that supervises just one target. Merge and Branch (`M&B`) compresses each historical item's SID and text into a few learned tokens and then predicts multiple target SIDs from the shared compressed history, laying each example out as a shallow, wide tree; a custom tree `FlashAttention` kernel processes the shared history once while propagating gradients from every branch, and a tree-structured key/value cache carries the same sharing into constrained decoding. On public benchmarks, **M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines while substantially cutting training and decoding cost**.

papers.title: FORGE: Feasible Online Reduced-Order Reference Generation and Whole-Body Execution for Agile Humanoid Locomotion
papers.abstract: This paper presents a two-stage learning framework for versatile and agile humanoid locomotion that couples online reduced-order model (ROM) reference generation with whole-body tracking control. In the first stage, we train a command-conditioned whole-body reference generator using single rigid body dynamics combined with full humanoid kinematics. In the second stage, the frozen ROM policy is rolled out online to generate references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics model. Learning a kino-dynamically consistent reference generator in the simplified ROM space enables us to generate references over a broad command space and over multiple locomotion strategies using a single unified framework. We demonstrate the approach on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, achieving longitudinal velocities from -2.0 m/s to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to +-1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to +-3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and continuous transitions across the commands, all using one unified reference policy and one whole-body tracking policy.
papers.summary: Agile humanoid locomotion over a wide command range usually requires separate controllers or hand-designed references for each gait. The authors propose a two-stage learning framework: a command-conditioned reference generator is first trained in a reduced-order model (ROM) space that combines single-rigid-body dynamics with full humanoid kinematics, and that frozen policy is then rolled out online to supply references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics. On a `Unitree G1` humanoid, one reference policy and one tracking policy together achieve **longitudinal velocities from -2.0 to 2.8 m/s**, lateral velocities up to 1.0 m/s, turning rates up to 3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and continuous transitions between these commands.

papers.title: Sometimes less is more: Investigating inductive biases of MLPs and Transformers on noisy k-parity features
papers.abstract: We empirically investigate how MLPs and Transformers differ when trained on data sets containing one or more features encoded by noisy k-parity. Noisy k-parity gives us hard synthetic data sets in which we can control the predictivity and availability of every feature. Across a range of data distributions, data scales and model sizes, we find large differences in the training dynamics and inductive biases of the two architectures: Transformers are more robust to noisy features but struggle to learn complex, low-availability features, whereas MLPs show the opposite trend and improve steadily with more data. We also find that, under a fixed training budget, increasing the number of unique training examples can slow Transformer optimisation enough to reduce final accuracy, so that a smaller data set performs better. Training-accuracy results show this is an optimisation-speed effect; it shrinks, but does not vanish, when the budget is scaled with the data set size. By giving precise control over feature predictivity and availability, this testbed offers a clear starting point for understanding when and why Transformers and MLPs learn differently, and for designing data and training budgets that exploit those differences.
papers.summary: How do multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and Transformers differ in what they learn from the same data? The authors build synthetic datasets from noisy k-parity features, which let them control exactly how predictive and how available each feature is, and train both architectures across many data distributions, data scales, and model sizes. Transformers prove more robust to noisy features but struggle to pick up complex, low-availability features, while MLPs show the reverse trend and improve steadily with more data. **Under a fixed training budget, adding more unique training examples can slow Transformer optimisation enough that a smaller dataset yields higher final accuracy**, an effect that shrinks but does not vanish when the budget scales with dataset size.

papers.title: Separability Is Not Alignability: Representations for Spectrum-to-Molecule Retrieval
papers.abstract: Identifying a small molecule from its tandem mass spectrum is limited by paired data. Foundation models offer a way around this scarcity: pretrain a spectrum encoder on unlabeled spectra and a molecule encoder on a large corpus of structures, then align the two frozen representations, as in vision-language and as the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests. We audit this route on MassSpecGym with spectrum encoders retrained free of test-fold contamination. Alignment needs a metric relating distinct molecules, but the objectives that produce spectrum encoders never see molecular structure: we prove that some predictive objectives fix molecular identity without fixing that metric. Moreover, we find that a candidate-based objective rewards a spectrum-independent prior over the benchmark's decoys, which we isolate. What ultimately addresses data scarcity is not architectural: simulated spectra surpass frozen geometry.
papers.summary: Identifying a small molecule from its tandem mass spectrum is bottlenecked by scarce paired data, and one proposed workaround is to pretrain separate spectrum and molecule encoders and then align their frozen representations, as in vision-language models. The authors audit this route on `MassSpecGym` with spectrum encoders retrained to avoid test-fold contamination. They prove that some predictive pretraining objectives fix molecular identity without fixing the metric between distinct molecules that alignment requires, and they isolate a candidate-based objective that rewards a spectrum-independent prior over the benchmark's decoys. **Simulated spectra end up outperforming alignment of frozen pretrained geometry**, suggesting the remedy for data scarcity is not architectural.

papers.title: Predicting Sparse Observables in Parameterized Unsteady Flows Using Coarse-Mesh Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Full-order surrogates for high-dimensional nonlinear flows are often unnecessary when applications require only selected degrees of freedom. We propose reduced-order models that bypass full-state reconstruction by deploying graph neural networks (GNNs) directly on coarse meshes. Applied to parameterized 2D/3D confined cylinder flows and an unevenly heated cavity over Reynolds/Rayleigh-number ranges, the models generalize to unseen conditions and accurately predict sparse probe locations and integrated quantities. Coarse-mesh GNNs match or outperform finer-mesh surrogates while reducing training time and memory, even for 3D chaotic dynamics. A dynamics-informed adaptive sampling strategy guided by frequency-spectrum variations reduces maximum errors by an order of magnitude versus uniform sampling at negligible cost. Coarse-mesh training also makes noise-augmented multi-step unrolling practical, improving long-horizon autoregressive predictions. The approach outperforms parametric DMD, sparse MLPs, U-Nets, and Fourier neural operators at lower cost, and enables system identification and state estimation from sparse observations. These results show that coarse-mesh representations, adaptive sampling, and noise-augmented unrolled training form an efficient framework for reduced-order modeling of parameterized unsteady flows without solver-resolution reconstruction.
papers.summary: Many engineering applications need only a few probe values or integrated quantities from an unsteady flow, yet surrogate models typically reconstruct the full high-dimensional state. The authors instead train graph neural networks (GNNs) directly on coarse meshes to predict sparse observables for parameterized 2D and 3D confined cylinder flows and an unevenly heated cavity across Reynolds and Rayleigh number ranges. The coarse-mesh models generalize to unseen conditions, match or beat finer-mesh surrogates at lower training time and memory, and outperform parametric dynamic mode decomposition, sparse MLPs, U-Nets, and Fourier neural operators. **A dynamics-informed adaptive sampling strategy guided by frequency-spectrum variation cuts maximum errors by an order of magnitude** relative to uniform sampling, and coarse meshes make noise-augmented multi-step unrolled training practical for long-horizon autoregressive prediction.

papers.title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.
papers.summary: Operators provisioning large language model (LLM) inference fleets must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs), but a single throughput figure cannot capture how the prefill and decode phases, continuous batching, and queueing interact to shape tail latency. `GAUSS` is a workload-aware simulator that pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence queueing model under stochastic arrivals, then uses ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling to predict **full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT) together with the sustainable request rate** for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. Because it does not replay a single trace, it can evaluate workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed and captures latency tails that trace-driven simulators under-sample. The authors show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and capacity questions about shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling.

papers.title: Deep learning for non-transvenous ICD screening: tailored neural network architectures, extended experiments, and explainability
papers.abstract: This paper studies two non-transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs), namely the Subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) and the Extravascular ICD (EV-ICD). Both avoid the complications of transvenous leads but are prone to oversensing, which can trigger inappropriate shocks associated with increased mortality. Oversensing risk is predicted by the ratio of T- or P-wave amplitude to R-wave amplitude (T:R, P:R), and these ratios vary over a 24-hour period. Yet S-ICD screening uses a single 10-second electrocardiogram (ECG) segment, and the EV-ICD has no formal screening protocol whatsoever. We present a 24-hour ambulatory screening framework for both devices which includes the first T:R analysis in an EV-ICD cohort and the first full evaluation of P:R prediction. We introduce AmpRatioNet, a family of 1D convolutional neural network architectures operating directly on the ECG signal, and benchmark it against the best existing approach - based on 2D phase space reconstruction images. Evaluation uses 4,605 clinician-annotated 10-second segments from 89 patients, with patient-level 10-fold cross-validation and bootstrap confidence intervals. AmpRatioNet-SE demonstrates superior performance on every metric in each setting with no device- or ratio-specific redesign. An explainability analysis against interpretable classical peak labelling algorithms shows that AmpRatioNet-SE's increase in error on oversensing-prone segments is up to 14 times smaller than theirs. Segment-level predictions are aggregated into a 24-hour timeline, extending S-ICD screening beyond 10 seconds and offering a plausible EV-ICD screening pathway pending device-level validation.
papers.summary: Subcutaneous and extravascular implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (S-ICD and EV-ICD) avoid transvenous leads but are prone to oversensing, where large T- or P-waves relative to the R-wave trigger inappropriate shocks; current S-ICD screening uses a single 10-second electrocardiogram (ECG), and the EV-ICD has no formal screening protocol. The authors propose 24-hour ambulatory screening for both devices and introduce `AmpRatioNet`, a family of 1D convolutional networks that predict T:R and P:R amplitude ratios directly from the ECG signal, benchmarked against the prior best approach based on 2D phase-space reconstruction images. On 4,605 clinician-annotated segments from 89 patients with patient-level 10-fold cross-validation, `AmpRatioNet-SE` outperforms the baseline on every metric in every setting without device- or ratio-specific redesign, and **its error increase on oversensing-prone segments is up to 14 times smaller than that of classical peak-labelling algorithms**. Segment-level predictions are aggregated into a 24-hour timeline, offering a plausible EV-ICD screening pathway pending device-level validation.

papers.title: Towards Generalizing Pretrained All-Atom Representations to Unified Binder Design
papers.abstract: PairFormer-based all-atom models demonstrate strong capabilities in biomolecular binder design. However, existing methods often use all-atom representations for modality-specific binder design, such as protein and peptide design. In contrast, recent geometric latent diffusion models pursue unified binder design by representing molecular blocks from different modalities in a shared latent space. These complementary strengths motivate us to investigate how to generalize the use of pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design. We introduce PairFuse, a parameter-efficient method that enables this generalization through representation fusion. Specifically, we use lightweight layerwise adapters to integrate pretrained all-atom representations into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model. Our adapters integrate pretrained all-atom representations through two mechanisms: enriching the diffusion model's molecular block features and incorporating pairwise structural information into the geometric diffusion model's denoiser. Theoretically, we prove that the augmented denoiser preserves geometry and pairwise attention fusion provides additional attention expressivity beyond feature-only fusion. Experimentally, across antibody, peptide, and small molecule binder-design benchmarks, PairFuse achieves stronger performance than the pretrained diffusion model and existing representation-fusion baselines.
papers.summary: All-atom models built on the PairFormer architecture excel at designing biomolecular binders but are usually specialized to a single modality such as proteins or peptides, whereas geometric latent diffusion models handle multiple modalities by representing molecular blocks in a shared latent space. `PairFuse` bridges the two with lightweight layerwise adapters that inject pretrained all-atom representations into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model, both enriching block features and feeding pairwise structural information into the denoiser's attention. The authors prove that the augmented denoiser preserves geometry and that pairwise attention fusion adds expressivity beyond feature-only fusion. **Across antibody, peptide, and small-molecule binder-design benchmarks it outperforms both the base diffusion model and existing representation-fusion baselines**.

papers.title: QMUL_AK at AISA-ArabicFC: Schema-Constrained Function Calling with ALLaM
papers.abstract: We describe the QMUL_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.
papers.summary: The QMUL_AK team adapted the Arabic-English `ALLaM-7B-Instruct` model to function calling for the `AISA-ArabicFC 2026` shared task using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), training only on the official task data. The system combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, resampling of dialectal and no-call examples, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema, with one output format serving both the plain function-calling track and the reasoning-augmented track. On the blind test set it ranks 3rd on both submission tracks and **1st of 21 teams on the dialect-robustness diagnostic with the smallest dialect gap in the task (0.077)**. Function selection is nearly saturated, so argument extraction remains the main source of error.

papers.title: Preserving Safety During Sequential Fine-Tuning: A Factorial and Geometric Analysis of Replay
papers.abstract: Benign fine-tuning can erode safety alignment in large language models, and sequential adaptation substantially compounds this risk. Prior work mitigates this erosion by replaying harmful-prompt refusals and benign-compliance examples, while other work instead matches base-model logits via distillation. However, the individual contributions of supervised exposure and distillation to safety behavior and refusal geometry during sequential adaptation remain unclear. We factor these two strategies apart and study their behavioral and geometric effects during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B across diverse task sequences (code generation, German-language summarization, and science question-answering). Behaviorally, supervised replay exposure yields the largest reduction in HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) on Mistral, averaging 51.1 points below base, but at a substantial over-refusal cost, averaging 53.4 points above base on OR-Bench-hard. Logit distillation, without any supervised replay loss, largely prevents safety erosion at a fraction of this cost: an average 5.4-point ASR reduction against only a 5.1-point rise in over-refusal. Llama shows the same asymmetry between the two strategies. Combining exposure and distillation moderates exposure's over-refusal while leaving downstream task scores largely unaffected. Geometrically, the two models diverge: on Mistral, distillation preserves the base refusal direction more closely than exposure does, whereas on Llama, refusal behavior after exposure largely survives ablation of the extracted refusal direction. This dissociation between models indicates that preserving the base refusal direction is not a reliable proxy for behavioral safety.
papers.summary: Benign fine-tuning erodes safety alignment in large language models, and sequential adaptation across several tasks compounds the damage; prior fixes either replay refusal and benign-compliance examples or distill the base model's logits, but their separate contributions were unclear. The authors factor these two strategies apart during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of `Mistral-7B` and `Llama-3-8B` on code generation, German summarization, and science question answering, measuring attack success rate (ASR) on `HarmBench`, over-refusal on `OR-Bench-hard`, and the geometry of each model's refusal direction. Supervised replay exposure cuts ASR the most on Mistral but raises over-refusal by a comparable amount, whereas **logit distillation alone largely prevents safety erosion at a fraction of the over-refusal cost (a 5.4-point ASR reduction against a 5.1-point over-refusal rise)**, and combining the two moderates exposure's over-refusal without hurting task scores. Geometrically the models diverge, with refusal behavior on Llama largely surviving ablation of the extracted refusal direction, so preserving the base refusal direction is not a reliable proxy for behavioral safety.

papers.title: New Multiple Descent Phenomena Induced by Heterogeneous Data
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models are often trained on large datasets assembled from many different sources, whose statistical properties can differ substantially. Understanding how this heterogeneity affects generalization performance is therefore important for explaining how model performance changes as model size increases. In this work, we study this question in linear random-feature models and show that mixtures of datasets with different covariance structures can give rise to a range of multiple-descent phenomena. We derive exact asymptotic expressions for the test error of each data source in the high-dimensional regime, and show how heterogeneity in covariance scale and spectral structure can introduce additional, group-dependent interpolation thresholds as model size increases. These phenomena arise even with noiseless labels and linear activations, showing that neither label noise nor activation nonlinearity is necessary for multiple-descent. Our results therefore provide a different perspective from classical explanations of multiple descent. More broadly, our results have potential implications for algorithmic fairness by showing that model scaling can affect different data groups unevenly, amplifying disparities in their generalization errors. We validate our theoretical results on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and real-world datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10.
papers.summary: Training sets are increasingly assembled from many sources with different statistics, and the authors ask how this heterogeneity shapes generalization as model size grows. Working in linear random-feature models, they derive exact high-dimensional asymptotics for the test error of each data source when sources differ in covariance scale and spectral structure. **Heterogeneity alone introduces additional, group-dependent interpolation thresholds, producing multiple-descent curves even with noiseless labels and linear activations**, so neither label noise nor nonlinearity is necessary for the phenomenon. Because scaling can shift error unevenly across groups, the results bear on algorithmic fairness, and they are validated on synthetic Gaussian mixtures as well as `MNIST` and `CIFAR-10`.

papers.title: Are Seismic Foundation Models More Than Glorified Feature Extractors?
papers.abstract: Earthquake sequences are stochastic on two separated timescales: the seismic waves of any individual earthquake propagate over seconds to minutes, while the earthquakes themselves arrive as a sparse, self-exciting occurrence process, with inter-event intervals from seconds to months. Respecting both scales in one training objective is the open challenge. Foundation models (FMs) for seismic waveforms instead import their learning targets from audio and vision, where every target is computed from a single fixed-length window. Such a window holds one realization of the wave propagation (an earthquake trace), never the occurrence process that decides when earthquakes happen. We develop nine model designs sharing one Mamba encoder-decoder, trained on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer; the two key comparisons are architecture-matched, varying the objective alone. Each checkpoint is evaluated frozen on three downstream tasks. Varying the target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it, and no checkpoint wins everywhere. Adding masking pressure to our strongest classifier re-specializes it rather than making it a generalist: it gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision and loses 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. By the standard imported from language and vision, these models are feature extractors rather than FMs. Controls on capacity, architecture, and domain proximity do not explain why skill moves rather than rises. Against task-specific baselines the advantage is regime-dependent: our checkpoints beat them few-shot on classification and ground-motion prediction, and trail them on full data. We argue the binding constraint is the target, and that settling the question requires a learning target defined across events, the timescale that makes seismicity stochastic in the first place.
papers.summary: Earthquake data are stochastic on two separated timescales, the seconds-to-minutes propagation of individual waveforms and the sparse, self-exciting process that governs when events occur, yet seismic foundation models (FMs) borrow single-window pretraining targets from audio and vision that can only see the first. The authors train nine designs sharing one `Mamba` encoder-decoder on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck, and mixer, and evaluate each frozen checkpoint on three downstream tasks. **Changing the pretraining target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it, and no checkpoint wins everywhere**; adding masking pressure to the strongest classifier gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision while losing 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. Against task-specific baselines the models win few-shot but trail with full data, and the authors argue the binding constraint is the lack of a learning target defined across events.

papers.title: "It Would Make a Geordie Feel at Home": Regional Accent Perceptions and Speech Accommodation in Voice AI
papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often perform less accurately for speakers of regional dialects, but less is known about how users respond to these limitations and how regional voices produced by voice assistants (VAs) are evaluated through a sociolinguistic lens. This study investigates these issues among speakers of Newcastle English (Geordies), examining both linguistic accommodation to voice technologies and perceptions of regional versus mainstream-accented VA voices. Participants interacted with a simulated VA that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE). They subsequently completed semi-structured interviews about their experiences with the experimental VA and voice technologies, language use, accent attitudes, and place orientation. The findings reveal a two-way process of sociolinguistic bias. The Geordie VA was associated with familiarity, warmth, personality, and local belonging, but also with concerns about professionalism and authority, whereas the SSBE voice was perceived as more neutral, clear, and credible. Participants also reported adapting their speech when voice technologies failed to recognise them, most commonly by shifting to a more mainstream accent, enunciating more clearly, and speaking more slowly. These strategies are similar to accommodation in human-human interaction and reflect users' perceptions of what technologies can recognise, also known as perceived intelligibility pressures. Overall, the findings demonstrate that voice technologies can reproduce existing accent biases both by encouraging users to suppress regional features and by activating established social stereotypes through synthetic voices. The study positions sociolinguistics as a bridge between understanding human-AI interaction and designing inclusive technologies around users' own linguistic priorities.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) performs worse on regional dialects, but little is known about how speakers respond to these failures or how they judge regionally accented synthetic voices. Speakers of Newcastle English interacted with a simulated voice assistant that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE), then completed semi-structured interviews on their experiences, language use, accent attitudes, and sense of place. The Geordie voice evoked familiarity, warmth, and local belonging alongside doubts about professionalism and authority, while the SSBE voice was heard as more neutral, clear, and credible. **Participants reported shifting toward a more mainstream accent, enunciating more, and slowing down when voice technologies failed to recognise them**, mirroring accommodation in human conversation and showing how voice systems can reinforce accent bias both by suppressing regional features and by activating stereotypes through synthetic voices.

papers.title: Algorithmic Bias from the Perspectives of Healthcare Professionals
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on algorithmic bias of machine learning and artificial intelligence applications in healthcare information systems. Based on the quantitative data and qualitative comments from a survey and interviews with healthcare professionals, who have different job roles (e.g., clinical vs. administrative), this study provides findings about the relationships between algorithmic bias, perceived fairness, and the intended acceptance and adoption of ML algorithms and algorithm generated outcomes. The results suggest that the opinions of healthcare professionals toward the causes of algorithmic bias, the criteria of algorithm assessment, the perceived fairness, and bias mitigation approaches may vary depending on their job roles, perspectives, tasks, and the algorithm characteristics. More research is needed to investigate algorithmic bias to ensure fairness and equality in healthcare.
papers.summary: How do healthcare professionals perceive algorithmic bias in machine learning tools embedded in healthcare information systems? Drawing on quantitative survey data and qualitative interview comments from staff in clinical and administrative roles, the authors examine relationships between perceived algorithmic bias, perceived fairness, and willingness to accept and adopt algorithms and their outputs. **Views on the causes of bias, the criteria for assessing algorithms, perceived fairness, and preferred mitigation approaches vary with job role, perspective, task, and algorithm characteristics.** The authors call for further research on algorithmic bias to support fairness and equality in healthcare.

papers.title: Making Smart Homes Fit for Autistic Children: Family Work and Monitored Independence
papers.abstract: General-purpose smart-home technologies are increasingly present in family life, yet how they support or disrupt autistic children and families with autistic children remains underexamined. We conducted a multi-source qualitative study drawing on five caregiver interviews, Xiaohongshu (also known internationally as RedNote) posts explicitly situated in autism contexts, and contextual posts from Xiaohongshu and Weibo. We find that families create support for autistic children by adapting environmental outputs, prompts, and interaction channels, while sensory intensity, communicative rules, and opaque operating states can turn the same technologies into barriers. Support also depends on continuing family work, including translation, configuration, modification, maintenance, and boundary-setting. Remote monitoring enables conditional independence while generating tensions among safety, privacy, and control. We contribute three concepts, including relational fit, family work as support infrastructure, and monitored independence, for understanding accessible domestic technology. We derive design implications for adjustable interaction, legible and recoverable failure, lower-burden configuration, and negotiable monitoring.
papers.summary: General-purpose smart-home devices are common in family life, but how they help or hinder autistic children has received little attention. The authors conducted a multi-source qualitative study combining five caregiver interviews with Xiaohongshu (RedNote) posts explicitly situated in autism contexts and contextual posts from Xiaohongshu and Weibo. Families build support by adapting environmental outputs, prompts, and interaction channels, yet **sensory intensity, rigid communicative rules, and opaque operating states can turn the same devices into barriers**, and support depends on ongoing family work such as translation, configuration, maintenance, and boundary-setting, while remote monitoring enables conditional independence at the cost of tensions among safety, privacy, and control. The paper contributes the concepts of relational fit, family work as support infrastructure, and monitored independence, with design implications for adjustable interaction, legible and recoverable failure, lower-burden configuration, and negotiable monitoring.

papers.title: Large Language Models for Accurate Medical Chart Abstraction: Enabling Scalable and Secure Artificial Intelligence Deployment in Stroke
papers.abstract: Medical chart abstraction transforms unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring. We evaluated a prompting-based large language model (LLM) framework for extracting eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals. Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs were evaluated across architectures, model sizes, and biomedical adaptations using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard. Evaluation was restricted to report-variable pairs with a valid LLaMA3.3-70B CoT prediction and a corresponding reference label. Performance measures included extraction accuracy, inference latency, and agreement with expert adjudication. Twenty discordant cases per variable underwent review by two senior physicians and four medical students. LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved performance on inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication showed that AI predictions were more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge. Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.
papers.summary: Medical chart abstraction turns free-text clinical notes into structured variables for research and quality monitoring, and the authors test whether locally deployed open-source large language models (LLMs) can do it reliably. They evaluated 22 instruction-tuned models across architectures, sizes, and biomedical adaptations on extracting eight variables from 2,416 neurointerventional stroke reports from three hospitals, comparing a direct Quick Response prompt with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting against non-expert staff annotations, with discordant cases adjudicated by senior physicians and medical students. **`LLaMA3.3-70B` reached the highest overall accuracy at 94.8%**, CoT helped on inference-dependent variables such as occlusion site while Quick Response was best for directly stated procedural fields, and on most variables the model's predictions aligned more closely with expert adjudication than the non-expert reference labels did. Intracranial angioplasty remained difficult, so the authors recommend expert oversight for ambiguous cases.

papers.title: Finite-step statistical mechanics of scale-invariant learning: spectral equations of state and curvature transport
papers.abstract: Stationary learning admits an ideal-gas description under restrictive noise assumptions. In neural networks whose gradient noise departs from these assumptions, however, an entropy-scaling relation resembling a Maxwell relation remains approximately valid. We ask which thermodynamic-looking relations follow from scale symmetry rather than equilibrium, and how departures from the ideal-gas description can be quantified, for discrete stochastic gradient dynamics with memory. An exact rescaling of trajectories explains the entropy relation without assuming thermal equilibrium. Within a local harmonic approximation, self-adjusting weight norms yield a spectral equation of state whose virial coefficients are set by moments of the curvature spectrum, and coupled parameter groups can sustain stationary probability currents. Our central result beyond this approximation is an exact curvature-transport identity. Together with a finite-step loss balance, it decomposes corrections to the harmonic fluctuation relation into measurable curvature changes, finite-step remainders, gradient-memory correlations and finite-window drift terms. A related displacement-weighted curvature change provides a diagnostic of the arrow of time; its mean and second moment give a lower bound on the relative entropy between forward and reversed state pairs. We also calculate the activation-boundary contribution to curvature for rectified teacher-student networks with Gaussian inputs. Tests in sphere models, teacher-student networks and convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support the transport description and identify limits of the harmonic and cubic-remainder approximations. These results separate symmetry-based relations from equilibrium assumptions and provide quantitative diagnostics of nonideal fluctuations in learning dynamics.
papers.summary: Stationary stochastic gradient dynamics in scale-invariant networks have been described as an ideal gas, but that picture relies on restrictive noise assumptions that real gradient noise violates, even though an entropy-scaling relation resembling a Maxwell relation still approximately holds. The authors ask which thermodynamic-looking relations follow from scale symmetry alone rather than equilibrium, showing that an exact rescaling of trajectories explains the entropy relation without assuming thermal equilibrium and, within a local harmonic approximation, that self-adjusting weight norms obey a spectral equation of state whose virial coefficients are moments of the curvature spectrum. **Their central result is an exact curvature-transport identity that, with a finite-step loss balance, decomposes deviations from the harmonic fluctuation relation into measurable curvature changes, finite-step remainders, gradient-memory correlations, and drift terms**, and a related displacement-weighted curvature change bounds the relative entropy between forward and reversed dynamics. Experiments on sphere models, teacher-student networks, and convolutional networks on `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100` support the transport description and mark the limits of the harmonic and cubic-remainder approximations.

papers.title: Measured or Real? When Model-Derived Measurements Can Be Corrected or Compared
papers.abstract: Numbers computed from trained models, such as an example's difficulty or a model's benchmark lead, change with seed and prompt. We ask when such measurements can be corrected or compared. Noise shrinks correlations, and the textbook correction divides by the square root of two estimated reliabilities. On two CIFAR-100 difficulty scores, it returned correlations above one in 70 of 100 classes. We prove that its mean squared error is infinite even when the correlation and the reliabilities use separate seeds. Our rule corrects only when both reliabilities pass a significance test, then divides by their upper confidence bounds. Its output is always bounded, and its coverage guarantees assume Gaussian noise. It helps once reliability is well estimated, more than halving the error with 500 simulated units. Prompt settings can reverse rankings. On ARC, Qwen2-1.5B trails Llama-3.2-3B by 3.8 points with no examples in the prompt and leads by 16.6 with two. Across four benchmarks, averaging the two settings names one winner for 15 of 16 such reversals. We compare models within each setting, controlling family-wise error asymptotically in the number of items for a fixed prompt grid. Aligning embedding coordinates across seeds raises held-out per-dimension reliability from 0.003 to 0.813.
papers.summary: Quantities computed from trained models, such as per-example difficulty scores or one model's lead over another on a benchmark, shift with random seed and prompt format, so the authors ask when such measurements can be corrected for noise or compared at all. The textbook attenuation correction, dividing a correlation by the square root of two estimated reliabilities, returned correlations above one in 70 of 100 `CIFAR-100` classes, and the authors prove its mean squared error is infinite even with separate seeds; their replacement corrects only when both reliabilities pass a significance test and then divides by their upper confidence bounds, giving bounded output with Gaussian coverage guarantees and more than halving error at 500 simulated units. On model comparison, **`Qwen2-1.5B` trails `Llama-3.2-3B` by 3.8 points on `ARC` with no in-context examples but leads by 16.6 points with two**, and across four benchmarks averaging the two settings resolves 15 of 16 such reversals, motivating within-setting comparisons that control family-wise error. Aligning embedding coordinates across seeds raises held-out per-dimension reliability from 0.003 to 0.813.

papers.title: Beyond Aggregate WER: In-domain Adaptation, Learner Speech, Code-Switching, and Speaker Attribution in Online Spanish Learning Classrooms
papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly supplies transcripts for educational NLP, but aggregate word error rate (WER) can conceal errors concentrated in learner speech, multilingual turns, and speaker attribution. We compare platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted, and commercial ASR configurations on held-out sessions of online L2 Spanish interaction between L1 English learners and their instructors and tutors. Because English is the learner's shared first language, the interactions contain Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns. Evaluation combines overall WER and character error rate (CER), WER disaggregated by speaker role and language context, and diarization error rate (DER). We also adapt Whisper large-v3 and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize with LoRA using human-corrected in-domain classroom data. MOSS adaptation produced consistent improvements across speaker roles and language contexts, whereas Whisper showed smaller gains. Domain match proved more important than data volume: Larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora did not outperform the smaller classroom corpus, where learner speech and code-switching are embedded in instructor--learner interaction. The open-weight MOSS adapter was competitive with commercial Muse Voice Transcribe on WER and CER and achieved lower system-provided DER on the recordings eligible for each system. Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech. The findings demonstrate the value of condition-aware evaluation and interactionally matched data for bilingual educational ASR.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly feeds educational language-processing pipelines, but aggregate word error rate (WER) can hide errors concentrated in learner speech, code-switched turns, and speaker attribution. The authors compare platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted, and commercial ASR systems on held-out online Spanish lessons between first-language-English learners and their instructors, disaggregating WER and character error rate (CER) by speaker role and language context and measuring diarization error rate (DER), and they adapt `Whisper large-v3` and `MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize` with LoRA on human-corrected classroom transcripts. Adapting MOSS yielded consistent gains across roles and language contexts, and **the small in-domain classroom corpus outperformed larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora**, with the adapted open-weight model competitive with commercial `Muse Voice Transcribe` on WER and CER and lower on DER. Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained harder than instructor and Spanish-only speech.

papers.title: Detecting Brain Cancer Progression Through Signatures of Wearable Accelerometry Data
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma and other high-grade gliomas (HGG) have a poor prognosis and are associated with progressive functional decline. The standard of care to assess progressive disease is contrast-enhanced MRI, which is expensive, claustrophobic, and performed only once every 2-3 months. Wearable accelerometers offer a non-invasive alternative for continuously monitoring patient function between clinic visits. However, accelerometry data streams are typically noisy and highly patient-specific, making conventional time series methods and summary statistics poorly suited to detecting clinically meaningful change. This work aims to classify stable versus progressive disease states by applying rough path signatures for feature extraction from wrist-worn accelerometer data. We convert accelerometer recordings from HGG patients enrolled in the BrainWear study into walking-path segments and use signature kernel maximum mean discrepancy (SigMMD) to quantify change in patients' walking behaviour. We overcome the challenge of inter-patient heterogeneity by adjusting for the natural variation in a patient's walking during stable tumour periods. This patient-specific normalisation substantially improves separation, yielding a candidate biomarker of tumour progression. Our results provide proof-of-concept evidence that signature-based analysis of wearable accelerometry can distinguish stable from progressive disease states, motivating larger longitudinal studies of continuous wearable monitoring as a digital biomarker in neuro-oncology.
papers.summary: High-grade gliomas (HGG) carry a poor prognosis and progressive functional decline, yet progression is tracked with contrast-enhanced MRI performed only every two to three months. The authors ask whether wrist-worn accelerometer data from HGG patients in the `BrainWear` study can distinguish stable from progressive disease, converting recordings into walking-path segments and applying rough path signatures with a signature kernel maximum mean discrepancy (`SigMMD`) to quantify changes in walking behaviour. Because accelerometry is noisy and highly patient-specific, they normalise each patient against the natural variation of their own walking during stable periods, which **substantially improves separation between stable and progressive states** and yields a candidate digital biomarker of tumour progression. The results are proof-of-concept and motivate larger longitudinal studies of continuous wearable monitoring.

papers.title: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case
papers.abstract: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.
papers.summary: Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, the authors build an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation, scored with deterministic numerical and symbolic checks plus language-model judges. They compare a range of closed- and open-source large language models against `Prospero`, a model specialized for ICF through domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, and run initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. **`Prospero` improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model with gains on every question type, yet frontier models still scored highest**, though critical physics errors persisted, especially in numerical calculations, and retrieval helped a smaller model but gave no significant gain for a frontier one. Two stress tests underscore the need for expert review of physical assumptions, and the authors recommend assessing existing capabilities and retrieval benefits before investing in heavy specialization.

papers.title: Making Sense of Audience Change: Causal Attribution and Boundary Management on Xiaohongshu
papers.abstract: Recommendation-driven platforms can reshape not only what users see, but also who becomes visible and how community boundaries are negotiated. We examine Xiaohongshu discussions surrounding a perceived World Cup-related audience influx to understand how users attributed community change and how those explanations related to boundary-management strategies. We analyzed 262 comments from eight high-engagement threads using researcher-led thematic analysis, structured coding, and permutation-based association analysis. Users described personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, interpreted platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define community membership. Among 70 comments with explicit attributions and strategies, attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V = .583): algorithmic attributions concentrated in technical boundary management, while social-actor attributions more often aligned with social enforcement or normative socialization. These findings connect causal sensemaking with boundary management and show how audience restructuring can create governance consequences on recommendation-driven platforms.
papers.summary: Recommendation-driven platforms reshape who becomes visible in a community, and the study asks how users explain such shifts and respond to them. Using thematic analysis, structured coding, and permutation-based association tests on 262 comments from eight high-engagement Xiaohongshu threads about a perceived World Cup audience influx, the authors examine how causal attributions relate to boundary-management strategies. Users framed personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, read platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define membership. **Among 70 comments with explicit attributions and strategies, attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V of 0.583)**, with algorithmic explanations concentrating in technical boundary management and social-actor explanations aligning with social enforcement or normative socialization.

papers.title: METATRON: A Promptable Whole-Body Execution Layer for Humanoids
papers.abstract: Humanoid controllers often require task-specific training despite sharing the need for balance and whole-body coordination. We present Metatron, a promptable whole-body execution layer combining a generative base policy with a programmable skill layer. The base policy receives partial goals, collectively called a prompt, that can combine timed body-part targets, velocity commands, and style cues. It produces diverse whole-body motions consistent with these goals. Training combines motion capture, synthetic recovery trajectories, and retargeted scene-interaction motions. After training, the policy is frozen. Stateful programs called skills express task intent as prompts at each control step, drawing rough geometric sketches that the policy turns into coordinated movement. Skills are ordinary code, refined by coding agents that analyze motion data and fit compact rules without task-specific policy training. On the physical Unitree G1, one frozen checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup, and sitting on furniture. Comparative evaluations show higher reaching success and push robustness than the tested reference-tracking pipelines. The same recipe produces climbing and acrobatics on a simulated character. Metatron enables coding agents to turn learned motor capabilities into new skills through code, without further policy training.
