We audit both benchmarks with 18 public checkpoints of eight methods under one metric implementation that reproduces every published number to within 0.09 dB, and find that their test labels differ from their training labels. (i) The 15 LOL-v1 test labels are rendered differently: the same captures appear in LOLv2 with labels of identical luminance but 1.48x lower saturation, and LOL-v1's own training labels match the LOLv2 rendering; we confirm this on the official release. (ii) The LOLv2-Real test set is the contiguous block of images 690-789, whose labels are 14% darker than the training labels (Cliff's delta = -0.45, p < 1e-12) with no comparable shift in the input statistics we examined; methods trained without any labels score up to 5.5 dB higher on test than on train. (iii) All 15 LOL-v1 test inputs reappear in LOLv2-Real, 12 in its training set. The released test-time settings are consistent with compensating for these shifts. Separating what can be calibrated on training data from what only test-set tuning finds, the test-only residual has median 0.00 dB on LOLv2-Syn, which has no shift, but 0.37 dB on LOL-v1 and 0.92 dB on LOLv2-Real (up to 3.9 dB). Under the shift, test-set checkpoint selection inflates a from-scratch model by 0.9-2.0 dB, and removing the released settings changes which method ranks first. We give concrete reporting recommendations.
papers.summary: `LOL-v1` and `LOLv2-Real`, the standard supervised low-light image enhancement benchmarks, are audited with 18 public checkpoints from eight methods under one metric implementation that reproduces every published number to within 0.09 dB. The audit finds test labels that differ from training labels: `LOL-v1` test labels have 1.48x lower saturation than the same captures in `LOLv2`, `LOLv2-Real` test labels are 14% darker than its training labels with no comparable input shift, and all 15 `LOL-v1` test inputs reappear in `LOLv2-Real`, 12 of them in its training set. The hand-set test-time adjustments shipped with leading methods are consistent with compensating for these shifts, with a test-only residual of 0.92 dB on `LOLv2-Real` versus 0.00 dB on the shift-free `LOLv2-Syn`, and **test-set checkpoint selection inflates a from-scratch model by 0.9 to 2.0 dB while removing the released settings changes which method ranks first**.

papers.title: MiniMMD: Minimization of MMD for Sampling, Inference and Integration
papers.abstract: Many problems in computational statistics and machine learning can be formulated as approximating a target distribution by minimizing a discrepancy over a restricted class of candidate distributions. This minimum-discrepancy viewpoint appears, for example, in numerical integration, sampling, generative modelling, and statistical inference, but these instances are often studied separately in the literature. This thesis develops the first unified treatment of these many problems through the minimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a kernel-based discrepancy between probability measures. The central theme is that MMD is not only a statistically meaningful distance between probability distributions, but also a tractable optimization objective to design practical and efficient algorithms. This thesis summarizes the recent theoretical and empirical advancements of such minimum-MMD based algorithms.
papers.summary: Numerical integration, sampling, generative modelling, and statistical inference can all be cast as approximating a target distribution by minimizing a discrepancy over a restricted class of candidate distributions, yet these instances are usually studied in isolation. This thesis gives a unified treatment through minimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a kernel-based distance between probability measures, on the premise that **MMD is both a statistically meaningful distance and a tractable optimization objective for practical, efficient algorithms**, and it summarizes recent theoretical and empirical advances in minimum-MMD methods across these settings.

papers.title: Answer-Only Disclosure: Private-Context LLM Assistance over Web APIs with a Leakage Ledger
papers.abstract: Web assistants increasingly answer questions about a user's private documents by pairing a small on-device model with a cloud LLM behind a Web API. In collaborative decoding, the document stays on the client, and the cloud receives only a public view that the user approves, such as the question alone, but the two models exchange messages while the answer is generated. We show that the message transcript can disclose private content that neither the public view nor the answer contains. In a planted-secret audit, speculative decoding with private drafts did not include the secret code in its answers, yet sent the code to the cloud in rejected drafts. We present ADLER, a decoding protocol for streaming LLM APIs in which every message to the cloud depends only on the public view and the answer the user sees, regardless of how the client combines the two models or how the cloud behaves. A client-side leakage ledger then bounds how much the answer itself reveals relative to a public reference process built from the cloud's replies. In the audit, no ADLER configuration exposed the secret beyond the answer. On GSM8K math problems with numerical values masked in the cloud's input, ADLER with an unlimited leakage budget raises the exact-match accuracy of a 0.5B client from 0.41 to 0.83 and of a 1.5B client from 0.67 to 0.85 under lenient answer parsing, close to the 0.92 achieved by uploading the full problem. It also exceeds a zero-leakage program baseline (0.69) by 0.14 and 0.16, respectively. In this baseline, the cloud writes a program that the client runs offline using the private numbers. The ledger records the disclosure charge associated with this gain; budgets of 16 nats or less leave accuracy near the cloud-only baseline on GSM8K.
papers.summary: Web assistants that pair a small on-device model with a cloud large language model (LLM) keep private documents on the client and send only a user-approved public view, but the two models exchange messages during collaborative decoding, and a planted-secret audit shows speculative decoding with private drafts sent a secret code to the cloud in rejected drafts even though it never appeared in the answer. `ADLER` is a decoding protocol for streaming LLM APIs in which every message to the cloud depends only on the public view and the answer the user sees, regardless of how the client combines the models or how the cloud behaves, paired with a client-side leakage ledger that bounds how much the answer itself reveals relative to a public reference process built from the cloud's replies. No `ADLER` configuration exposed the secret beyond the answer, and on `GSM8K` with numerical values masked from the cloud, **an unlimited leakage budget raises a 0.5B client from 0.41 to 0.83 exact-match accuracy** and a 1.5B client from 0.67 to 0.85, close to the 0.92 from uploading the full problem and above a zero-leakage program baseline of 0.69, while budgets of 16 nats or less stay near the cloud-only baseline.

papers.title: A Separation Principle for Adversarial Attacks and Defense of Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Adversarial attacks on graph neural networks (GNNs) have been studied as a model-centric optimization problem driven by gradients, learned policies, or meta-learning, with the graph treated as a passive substrate. This view overlooks a defining feature of GNNs: their predictions are produced by structured message passing along the graph, so their adversarial vulnerabilities are encoded as much in the geometry of the graph as in the learned weights. We develop a structure-driven framework for feature attacks in which the attack is derived from the spectral properties of the normalized adjacency operator. Its central result is a separation principle: under a natural relaxation of the attack objective, the optimal feature perturbation is rank one and factorizes into a graph-dependent component (degree-proportional spatial allocation, depending only on the graph) and a weight-dependent component (top singular vector of the composed weights, depending only on the weights). Node degree thus emerges as the fundamental graph quantity governing adversarial vulnerability to feature perturbations. The resulting attack, which we call SepAttack, requires no gradient computation, carries analytical guarantees, achieves competitive or superior performance against established baselines such as Nettack and IG-Attack with up to ${\sim}70\times$ speedup in the targeted setting, and transfers near-perfectly across architectures on continuous-feature graphs because its graph-dependent component is architecture-invariant by construction. We further derive a separation-principle adversarial training procedure (SepAT) directly from the closed-form worst-case attack and report robustness gains on binary-feature benchmarks.
papers.summary: Adversarial attacks on graph neural networks (GNNs) are usually framed as model-centric optimization over gradients, learned policies, or meta-learning, treating the graph as a passive substrate even though predictions arise from message passing along its structure. Deriving feature attacks from the spectral properties of the normalized adjacency operator yields a separation principle: **under a natural relaxation of the attack objective, the optimal feature perturbation is rank one and factorizes into a degree-proportional graph-only component and a weight-only component given by the top singular vector of the composed weights**, making node degree the governing quantity for vulnerability. The resulting gradient-free `SepAttack` matches or beats `Nettack` and `IG-Attack` with up to about 70x speedup in the targeted setting and transfers near-perfectly across architectures on continuous-feature graphs, and a derived adversarial training procedure `SepAT` improves robustness on binary-feature benchmarks.

papers.title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.
papers.summary: Graph-based nearest neighbor search methods such as `HNSW`, `DiskANN`, and `NSG` outperform space-partitioning approaches like inverted file (IVF) indexes and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) in practice, but unlike LSH they have resisted strong worst-case theoretical guarantees. The authors prove that **no standard graph-based method running greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor**. Allowing Steiner points in the search graph restores sublinear time with LSH-comparable bounds, such as query time of roughly n^(1/(c-1)) for c-approximate search, and initial experiments explore incorporating Steiner points into practical graph-based methods.

papers.title: Decompose, Don't Expand: Capability-Independent AI Systems by Construction
papers.abstract: A recurring design choice in building AI systems is whether, when a task is too hard for a model, to expand the model (make it larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned), or to decompose the task (extract the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host, leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue). We make three claims. First, that many tasks commonly delegated whole to a model are in fact deterministic tasks with a small generative core. Second, and our central empirical result, that decomposing such a task yields a measurable and desirable property we call parity by construction: on the extracted sub-tasks the model-size performance curve becomes flat, because no model performs them at all. We measure this across nine models spanning a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model, a thirty-fold parameter range on the local family alone: once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine, while the one task that does not decompose, labelling, remains sloped across the same range. Because the task leaves the model, a stock checkpoint suffices: no task-specific training and no fine-tuning. Third, that this is a general design discipline, not a domain trick: we show the same move recurring across physics setup, motion retargeting, and object-model editing, and in a Web-CLI tool family (same author, so not an independent replication). We give a method for locating the cut, the construction that makes a cut exist (a deterministic surface and a closed grammar over it), and a way to make the residue safe (resolve the deterministic context; verify the generative output), position the work against neuro-symbolic AI, tool-augmented language models, and generate-and-verify approaches, and are explicit about what is measured (one domain) versus illustrative (the rest).
papers.summary: When a task is too hard for a model, builders can expand the model (larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned) or decompose the task by extracting the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host and leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue. The authors argue that many tasks delegated whole to a model are mostly deterministic with a small generative core, and measure a property they call "parity by construction" across nine models from a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model: **once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine**, while labelling, the one task that does not decompose, remains sloped with model size, and a stock checkpoint suffices with no fine-tuning. They give a method for locating the cut (a deterministic surface with a closed grammar over it), a way to make the residue safe by resolving context deterministically and verifying generative output, and illustrative recurrences in physics setup, motion retargeting, object-model editing, and a Web-CLI tool family, while stating that only one domain is actually measured.

papers.title: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment
papers.abstract: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories. However, existing skill benchmarks primarily focus on downstream task execution, insufficiently assessing specification quality, behavioral robustness, semantic alignment, and responsibility boundaries. Their reliance on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated executions limits scalability and pre-deployment assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillCT, a benchmark that broadens skill assessment from downstream utility to a multidimensional characterization of skill quality. SkillCT evaluates skills across nine complementary dimensions spanning three aspects: Static Assessment, which captures intrinsic properties of the skill specification; Dynamic Assessment, which measures whether the induced behavior remains stable across backbone models and request variations; and Human-Assisted Assessment, which examines behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. These dimensions provide a broader view of skill quality than execution success. Applying SkillCT to a public skill corpus establishes a reference benchmark for analyzing quality weaknesses and relationships across dimensions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an execution-free quality evaluation baseline that predicts the multidimensional quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving and leveraging similar reference skills, without executing the skills under evaluation. This reduces token consumption and evaluation time, while preserving consistency with the full assessment. Furthermore, SkillCT-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency, demonstrating its value for skill refinement. These findings highlight the effectiveness of SkillCT in supporting scalable skill assessment, optimization, and repository maintenance.
papers.summary: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories, but existing skill benchmarks judge them mainly by downstream task execution and depend on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated runs. `SkillCT` evaluates skills across nine dimensions grouped into static assessment of the specification itself, dynamic assessment of whether induced behavior stays stable across backbone models and request variations, and human-assisted assessment of behavior-chain consistency and task granularity, and applies this to a public skill corpus to establish a reference benchmark. An execution-free baseline predicts a skill's multidimensional quality profile by retrieving similar reference skills without running it, **reducing token consumption and evaluation time while staying consistent with the full assessment**, and `SkillCT`-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency.

papers.title: Estimating Implicit Expected Log Density Ratios
papers.abstract: When exact probabilities cannot be computed, \emph{density ratio estimation (DRE)} is a key subroutine in the wide range of applications where density ratios appear, from experimental design to generative modelling and reinforcement learning. In this paper, we introduce the concept of an \emph{expected log density ratio (ELDR)}: log density ratios that are integrated under some third, possibly distinct measure. We show many problems with implicit densities where DRE is na\"ively used are actually ELDR estimation tasks, and prove fundamental limitations on finite-sample ELDR estimation. Based on these results, we argue that the typical DRE-based approaches are unsuitable for ELDR estimation, and provide some foundational motivation towards bespoke ELDR estimators. To demonstrate, we propose a simple modification to some DRE methods that allows samples convergent to the integral distribution to appear in training data. We show through benchmarks that this can improve ELDR estimation error.
papers.summary: Density ratio estimation (DRE) is a standard subroutine when exact probabilities are unavailable, but many problems with implicit densities actually call for an expected log density ratio (ELDR), a log ratio integrated under a third, possibly distinct, measure. The authors formalize this distinction, show that several tasks where DRE is used naively are really ELDR estimation problems, and **prove fundamental finite-sample limitations on ELDR estimation** that argue against reusing standard DRE approaches. As a first step toward bespoke estimators, they modify some DRE methods so that samples converging to the integrating distribution appear in the training data, and report lower ELDR estimation error on benchmarks.

papers.title: BridgeRouter: Gain-Aware Instance Routing over Cross-Modal Bridge Portfolios
papers.abstract: Lightweight representation bridges make pretrained, task-adapted EEG foundation models executable on other biosignal modalities without retraining their backbones. However, selecting a single bridge pathway globally assigns every instance to the same transfer route and ignores complementary errors across routes. We therefore formulate multi-bridge transfer as an instance-level algorithm-selection problem and introduce BridgeRouter, a gain-aware router over a portfolio of frozen cross-modal pathways. A validation-selected Single Best Solver (SBS) serves as a protected default route. During training, task labels are used to compute the reduction in negative log-likelihood provided by each alternative route relative to the SBS, and a lightweight MLP predicts these route-specific gains from a target-modality representation extracted by a frozen encoder. At inference, BridgeRouter observes only the target modality, requires neither EEG, task labels, nor predictions from all candidate routes, and executes exactly one bridge pathway: the route with the largest predicted gain when that gain exceeds a validation-calibrated threshold, and the SBS otherwise. We evaluate seven EEG foundation-model bridge pathways for EMG-based freezing-of-gait detection on FOG and ECG-based sleep classification on ISRUC. Across five seeds, BridgeRouter achieves $81.38\pm1.11\%$ balanced accuracy on FOG, improving over the BIOT SBS by $11.49$ percentage points, and $62.92\pm2.17\%$ on ISRUC, improving over the CBraMod SBS by $3.83$ points. Per-instance bridge oracles reach $99.96\%$ and $78.61\%$, respectively, revealing substantial remaining portfolio headroom. These results show that anchor-relative gain prediction can convert complementary cross-modal bridge behavior into deployable instance-level routing improvements while retaining single-route inference.
papers.summary: Lightweight representation bridges let pretrained EEG foundation models run on other biosignals such as EMG or ECG without retraining their backbones, but choosing one bridge globally sends every instance down the same route and ignores complementary errors across routes. `BridgeRouter` treats multi-bridge transfer as instance-level algorithm selection: a validation-chosen Single Best Solver (SBS) is the protected default, and a small multilayer perceptron predicts each alternative route's reduction in negative log-likelihood relative to the SBS from a frozen encoder's target-modality representation, executing exactly one route per input and only switching when the predicted gain clears a calibrated threshold. Across seven EEG foundation-model bridges, it reaches **81.38% balanced accuracy for EMG freezing-of-gait detection on `FOG`, 11.49 points above the `BIOT` single best route**, and 62.92% for ECG sleep classification on `ISRUC`, 3.83 points above the `CBraMod` route, while per-instance oracles of 99.96% and 78.61% show substantial remaining headroom.

papers.title: MASS: Multi-mask Selective Self-Distillation for Leakage-Resilient Reasoning
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation enables the same model to act as student and teacher, with dense token-level supervision obtained by the teacher being given access to privileged information. However, conditioning the teacher on a single reference can concentrate its predictions on one reasoning trajectory and limit transfer to the student. We propose Multi-Mask Selective Self-Distillation (MASS), which approximates the unavailable marginal over diverse reference realizations using multiple independently masked views of one verified solution. MASS aggregates these complementary teacher predictions, selectively transfers reliable token-level corrections, and adaptively focuses masking on influential reference spans. Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks and model families, MASS consistently outperforms strong self-distillation baselines.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation lets one model act as both student and teacher, with the teacher given privileged information such as a reference solution, but conditioning on a single reference can concentrate the teacher on one reasoning trajectory and limit what transfers to the student. Multi-Mask Selective Self-Distillation (`MASS`) approximates the unavailable marginal over diverse references by giving the teacher multiple independently masked views of one verified solution, aggregating their complementary token-level predictions, selectively transferring only reliable corrections, and adaptively focusing masking on influential reference spans. **Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks and multiple model families, `MASS` consistently outperforms strong self-distillation baselines.**

papers.title: Floor It, Then Fill It: Simulating Creator Ecosystems for Fair Video-Content Recommendation Systems at Billion User Scale
papers.abstract: Engagement-optimized content recommendation systems exhibit a well-documented rich-get-richer dynamic that structurally disadvantages emerging creators on large-scale platforms. Evaluating debiasing interventions at scale demands faithful simulation of creator-viewer ecosystems, yet the fidelity, diversity, and validity of such simulators remain underexplored. We present a grounded user-simulation framework that models a heterogeneous population of ${\sim}42$K creators and their coupled viewer interactions over 12~weeks, and use it to evaluate equitable view-allocation policies formulated as a budgeted multi-armed bandit (MAB). The simulator captures three behavioral dimensions: (i)~\textbf{creator diversity}, modeled via a clustering approach grounded in real platform creator-level distributions; (ii)~\textbf{behavioral fidelity}, captured through coupled creator-content state machines that represent growth trajectories, engagement accumulation, and graduation dynamics; and (iii)~\textbf{population-level validity}, measured by calibration against observed platform metrics. We evaluate simulative-configurations that vary content-viewership target definitions, reward functions, and a small-creator reserve lever to maximize creator-content recommendation equity. A floor-protected per content-view-target with a view-parity-gap reward guarantees 90\% of view targets being met by creators every week, grows small-creator organic reach ${\sim}{+}33\%$ per week, and achieves high distribution stability (set of creators with funded-views Jaccard $= 0.819$). We analyze the Sim2Real gap and propose validation protocols, contributing evidence for when simulation-derived fairness conclusions can be trusted.
papers.summary: Engagement-optimized recommenders exhibit rich-get-richer dynamics that disadvantage emerging creators, and testing debiasing interventions at platform scale requires simulators whose fidelity and validity are rarely examined. The authors build a grounded simulation of roughly 42,000 creators and their coupled viewer interactions over 12 weeks, with creator diversity derived by clustering real platform distributions, coupled creator-content state machines for growth and graduation dynamics, and calibration against observed platform metrics, then use it to evaluate equitable view-allocation policies framed as a budgeted multi-armed bandit (MAB). **A floor-protected per-content view target with a view-parity-gap reward meets 90% of creator view targets every week and grows small-creator organic reach by about 33% per week**, with a stable set of funded creators (Jaccard 0.819). They also analyze the simulation-to-reality gap and propose validation protocols for deciding when simulation-derived fairness conclusions can be trusted.

papers.title: ATI-OPD: Adaptive Teacher Intervention for Stable Long-Sequence On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level teacher feedback, but as responses grow longer the student's prefix drifts from the teacher's reasoning, weakening feedback on later tokens and destabilizing training, and prior fixes such as length control, loss reweighting, or fixed cutoffs either leave the prefix unchanged or discard later reasoning. Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (`ATI-OPD`) replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text, and excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful continuations. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses, and **across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, `ATI-OPD` improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD**.

papers.title: Replaying the Same Gradients at a Different $\varepsilon$: A Registered Test of the Fixed-Trajectory Account of Adam's $\varepsilon$ for One Rare Row
papers.abstract:
Adam divides every update by the square root of a running average of squared gradients plus a small constant, epsilon. For an output-embedding row whose token is rare, which we call the probe row, raising epsilon can be read as shrinking that row's steps by arithmetic alone. We test that reading directly. While a training run proceeds, we also divide the probe row's update by a different epsilon, using the run's own moment estimates; this replay is exact arithmetic on the gradients the run actually saw, so it holds the run's trajectory fixed. A rule for when the replay counts as wrong was written down before the runs.
  We train a small causal transformer in a standard configuration. When epsilon rises by four orders of magnitude, the replay counts as wrong on each of the three seeds registered for the test: the probe row keeps 8.9--11.4 times more of its displacement than predicted with the main, sampled-negative head, and 5.0--7.7 times more with a full-softmax head scored as a second instrument. At three orders of magnitude, tested with the main head only, it does not, by narrow margins; a further two seeds, registered after this result had been committed and scored on their own, follow the same pattern. In separate real runs, raising epsilon on the probe row alone is enough to reproduce the row's change and raising it on every other parameter alone also moves the row part of the way --- readings about the runs that do not rescue the replay; scaling the row's learning rate instead, with the denominator untouched, is mispredicted by the replay in the same direction.
  This is one embedding row of one model family on one corpus; we make no claim about rates, about rows in general (other rows were read only as a panel on one trajectory) or about how the effect changes with model size.
papers.summary: `Adam` divides each update by the square root of a running average of squared gradients plus a small constant epsilon, so for a rarely updated output-embedding row one might expect that raising epsilon shrinks that row's steps by arithmetic alone. The authors test this fixed-trajectory reading by replaying the probe row's updates at a different epsilon using the run's own moment estimates, which holds the trajectory fixed, with a rule for when the replay counts as wrong written down before the runs. On a small causal transformer, **raising epsilon by four orders of magnitude leaves the probe row with 8.9 to 11.4 times more displacement than the replay predicts on all three registered seeds**, while a three-order change narrowly passes and two later-registered seeds follow the same pattern. Separate real runs show that raising epsilon on the probe row alone reproduces its change while raising it on all other parameters also moves the row part of the way, and the authors restrict their claim to one embedding row of one model family on one corpus, with no claims about rates or model-size scaling.

papers.title: B2P-Corr: Batch-to-Population Gradient Estimators for Non-Decomposable Correlation Losses
papers.abstract: Correlation metrics such as the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) and Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) are standard regression metrics and learning objectives, but their non-decomposable nature poses a challenge for stochastic optimization. Since these metrics depend on dataset-level moments (mean, variance, covariance), naive mini-batch training with local statistics yields biased, high-variance gradients whose expectation does not align with the population gradient. To bridge this ``batch-to-population'' (B2P) gap, we propose \textbf{B2P-Corr}, a novel framework that transforms correlation objectives into decomposable pseudo-losses driven by lightweight global ``moment sketches''. We introduce two efficient variants: \textbf{B2P-EMA}, which utilizes exponential moving averages and stop-gradient operators to ensure asymptotic gradient tracking with $O(B)$ cost ($B$ is batch size); and \textbf{B2P-U}, which uses sampled cross-batch U-statistic estimators and a reservoir-based stabilization with an $O(B)$ implementation. Theoretically, we quantify the $O(B^{-1})$ bias of naive mini-batch optimization, prove a moving-target tracking result for B2P-EMA under a fast-sketch / slow-parameter regime, and provide an idealized control-variate analysis for B2P-U. Experiments on two synthetic and three real-world datasets demonstrate B2P-Corr achieves stable optimization and higher correlation than naive mini-batch optimization with negligible overhead.
papers.summary: The Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) and Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) are common regression objectives, but because they depend on dataset-level means, variances, and covariances, naive mini-batch training yields biased, high-variance gradients whose expectation does not match the population gradient. `B2P-Corr` closes this batch-to-population gap by turning correlation objectives into decomposable pseudo-losses driven by lightweight global moment sketches, with an exponential-moving-average variant (`B2P-EMA`) that uses stop-gradient operators and a cross-batch U-statistic variant (`B2P-U`) with reservoir-based stabilization, both at cost linear in batch size. The authors quantify the **O(1/B) bias of naive mini-batch optimization**, prove a moving-target tracking result for `B2P-EMA` under a fast-sketch, slow-parameter regime, give an idealized control-variate analysis for `B2P-U`, and show on two synthetic and three real-world datasets that the method optimizes more stably and reaches higher correlation with negligible overhead.

papers.title: Data Amount Heterogeneity Improves Performance in Federated Learning for Neuroimaging
papers.abstract:
Federated Learning (FL) allows for secure analysis of distributed data without data sharing. We and others have successfully applied FL to neuroimaging tasks, such as Alzheimer's disease classification from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). FL trains a deep learning model locally at each site, encrypts the local model parameters and sends them to a federation controller that aggregates the local models under homomorphic encryption, the resulting community model is sent back to the sites for further training, and the process repeats for a number of rounds. FL often achieves learning performance (e.g., accuracy) close to centralized training, but no data leaves the sites and model parameters are protected through encryption and other measures.
  In this paper, we show that federations composed of sites with heterogeneous amounts of data (1 large site plus small sites) perform better than homogeneous (same data per site) federations, particularly in low data regimes, while reaching performance close to centralized training. Having a big site often results in faster convergence and higher final accuracy. Heterogeneous federations better exploit sites with small amounts of data, a common situation in large consortia such as ENIGMA.
papers.summary: Federated Learning (FL) lets consortia analyze distributed neuroimaging data without sharing it, by training locally at each site and aggregating encrypted model parameters at a federation controller over repeated rounds. Applying FL to Alzheimer's disease classification from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), the authors compare federations where every site holds the same amount of data against ones composed of one large site plus several small sites. **Heterogeneous federations converge faster and reach higher final accuracy than homogeneous ones, particularly in low-data regimes**, while approaching centralized training performance, suggesting that large consortia such as ENIGMA can better exploit sites with little data.

papers.title: A Gradient based Adversarial Augmentation Framework for Mitigating Unlearnable Datasets
papers.abstract: Unlearnable data methods (ULD) protect public data from unauthorized model training by adding imperceptible perturbations that create a learning shortcut. A deep neural network can exploit the shortcut learning path to minimize training loss without learning generalizable features. Intuitively, finding adversarial versions of perturbed images that can substantially increase the model's loss can force the model to learn generalizable features. Existing data augmentation based attacks rely on heuristic search strategies/random sampling over a curated augmentation set to identify adversarial augmentation operations, an approach that often does not scale when the number of candidate operations is large. To address the challenge of a large search space, we propose {\techname}, a gradient based adversarial augmentation framework that learns an augmentation policy via stochastic gradient ascent. {\techname} leverages a differentiable data augmentation pipeline to efficiently search a set of up to 18 augmentation techniques, from which a grid search selects a protection-specific subset. The augmentation subset is trained to maximize a surrogate model's classification loss. We introduce a perceptual-plus-pixel regularization to learn operation parameters that preserve image semantics. Under a controlled ablation, {\techname} consistently outperforms an equivalent random sampling baseline (80.0\% vs. 77.29\% clean test accuracy on EMIN-protected CIFAR-10 for ResNet-18 and 83.28\% vs. 66.45\% on NTGA-protected CIFAR-10 for MobileNet-V2), demonstrating that gradient guidance drives the clean test accuracy recoverability rather than the expanded search space. {\techname} offers an effective and scalable adversarial augmentation framework for stress-testing ULD methods, a critical tool for developing robust ULD methods.
papers.summary: Unlearnable data methods (ULD) add imperceptible perturbations to public images that create a learning shortcut, letting a network minimize training loss without learning generalizable features, and existing augmentation-based countermeasures rely on heuristic search or random sampling over a curated operation set that scales poorly. The proposed framework instead learns an augmentation policy by stochastic gradient ascent through a differentiable augmentation pipeline of up to 18 operations, with a grid search selecting a protection-specific subset, maximizing a surrogate model's classification loss while a perceptual-plus-pixel regularizer preserves image semantics. In a controlled ablation it consistently beats an equivalent random-sampling baseline, **recovering 83.28% versus 66.45% clean test accuracy on `NTGA`-protected `CIFAR-10` with `MobileNet-V2`** and 80.0% versus 77.29% on `EMIN`-protected `CIFAR-10` with `ResNet-18`, which the authors read as evidence that gradient guidance rather than the larger search space drives recoverability.

papers.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
papers.abstract: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.
papers.summary: `EasyProver` is a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service, driven by an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training. **It proves 669 of 672 `PutnamBench` problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations**, and resolves 597 of 600 `NTP4VC` verification conditions and all 189 `VERINA` tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, the authors also introduce `Aegis`, a pipeline that writes safe Rust solutions to competitive programming problems, translates them to Lean with `Aeneas`, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation, yielding 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications that carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, loops, casts, and mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 such statements, `EasyProver` proves 52.7% within a 30-minute budget per statement, and the tasks can also benchmark other provers or serve as reinforcement learning rewards.

papers.title: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms
papers.abstract: Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the solver's code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108 attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimalif, occurs 96 times, 92 of them in one model.Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defecective gaps. Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.
papers.summary: Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. `DecompGym` provides 81 instances from nine problem families in which a coding agent must write a solver for a prescribed method that runs within 60 seconds, passes a numerical feasibility check plus an LLM-judged audit of whether the code follows the method, and lands within 1% of the stored optimum. Evaluating 12 `GPT`, `Claude`, and `Gemini` models inside coding-agent tools, two models solve every instance on the first attempt and seven exceed 90%, yet output checks alone would have accepted 93 of the 108 attempts that failed the method audit, and the most common rejection type occurred 96 times with 92 coming from a single model. **Reflection that first diagnoses the failure turns 66% of retries into successes, versus 39% for independent regeneration**, and is what repairs method-audit failures, leading the authors to argue that such agents need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error.

papers.title: In-Context Learning for Multi-Fidelity Multiscale Model Closure and Cross-Operator Out-Of-Distribution Generalization
papers.abstract: Multi-fidelity learning uses low-fidelity information (coarse-scale PDE models) together with limited high-fidelity data (fine-scale solutions) to obtain high-accuracy PDE solutions. It is a data-driven approach to downscale reduced-order models to solve PDEs efficiently and accurately. Standard multi-fidelity learning focuses on one operator or PDE; given a new PDE, retraining using additional coarse-fine solution pairs may be required, which is costly. In this work, we propose an in-context multi-fidelity learning framework for learning multiple multi-fidelity operators with one shared model. The model is trained using paired low- and high-fidelity examples as demonstrations from multiple operators, together with a new coarse-scale solution query, to predict the corresponding fine-scale solution. Once trained, given a new PDE operator, a few (fewer than five) coarse-fine demonstration pairs, and a low-cost coarse query, the model predicts the corresponding fine-scale solution without fine-tuning. When the target operator appears in the training dataset but has a different prediction goal, such as predicting beyond the training time interval, no additional demonstrations are needed. Instead, the model uses training coarse-fine pairs from that PDE and information from other training operators. Testing then only requires generating a low-cost coarse-scale solution query, without fine-tuning. Notably, our smallest model contains only 255,364 trainable parameters, corresponding to approximately 456 parameters per training operator for 560 operators.
papers.summary: Multi-fidelity learning combines cheap coarse-scale partial differential equation (PDE) solutions with scarce fine-scale data to obtain accurate solutions efficiently, but standard approaches handle one operator at a time and need costly retraining on new coarse-fine pairs for each new PDE. The proposed in-context framework trains one shared model on paired low- and high-fidelity demonstrations from many operators together with a coarse-scale query, so that at test time a new PDE operator needs **fewer than five coarse-fine demonstration pairs and no fine-tuning** to predict the fine-scale solution from a low-cost coarse query. For operators seen in training but with a different prediction goal, such as extrapolating beyond the training time interval, no new demonstrations are needed at all, and the smallest model has only 255,364 trainable parameters, roughly 456 per operator across 560 training operators.

papers.title: Component Translation and Judge-Labelled Refusal: A Multilingual Safety Evaluation
papers.abstract: Whole-prompt translation evaluates a request in different languages but does not compare which component carries a language. We introduce a paired reversal: translate the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language, holding behaviour, English frame and translated-span count fixed. Component identity and non-English text quantity change together. Assigning English, Chinese and Spanish independently to the two components yields nine configurations on 190 of 300 sampled harmful behaviours retained after consensus annotation and automatic gating. Refusal scored by language-model judges is the primary outcome; unsafe compliance is reported separately. On Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, three refusal swaps are about 5.3 percentage points and the fourth is -0.5; none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction. In an exploratory extension, Mistral Small 4 has a 13.7-point Spanish swap (95% interval [8.4, 18.9]), which survives the twelve-test Holm sensitivity correction under the primary judge, and 12.1 points under a second judge. GPT-5.4-mini estimates are within 2 points of zero. Component assignment supplies an additional evaluation dimension. Evaluations should record component languages and translated text quantity, comparing matched behaviours at equal translated-span count while interpreting refusal and unsafe compliance separately.
papers.summary: Whole-prompt translation measures how refusal changes across languages but cannot tell which part of a harmful request carries the effect. The authors introduce a paired reversal that translates either the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language while holding the behaviour, English frame, and translated-span count fixed, assigning English, Chinese, and Spanish independently to the two components for nine configurations over 190 harmful behaviours retained after consensus annotation and automatic gating, with refusal scored by language-model judges and unsafe compliance reported separately. On `Gemini 2.5 Flash` and `DeepSeek`, three component swaps shift refusal by about 5.3 percentage points and one by -0.5, and **none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction**, while an exploratory extension finds a 13.7-point Spanish swap on `Mistral Small 4` that survives a twelve-test correction under both judges and effects within 2 points of zero on `GPT-5.4-mini`. They recommend that multilingual safety evaluations record component languages and translated text quantity and compare matched behaviours at equal translated-span count.

papers.title: Barren Plateaus in Quantum Linear Combinations: Interference and Lie-Algebraic Control
papers.abstract: A coherent sum of quantum circuits introduces interference that can alter the training signal. We distinguish a single linear combination of unitaries (LCU) from a circuit that repeatedly alternates branch operations and ancilla mixing. For a single-pass LCU, independent branches with zero matrix means cannot erase the differentiated branch's gradient variance: the total variance is at least the branch variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude. This bound holds at any gate position and does not require the circuit unitaries to be Haar-random. Beyond this lower bound, we derive exact loss and gradient formulas that quantify the additional contributions from interference between branches. One of these terms depends on relative coefficient phases and vanishes when the branch ensemble is invariant under multiplication by $i \mathbb{I}$; a four-qubit matchgate example shows that it can be nonzero. For repeated interleaving with full special-unitary ancilla control, we determine the generated Lie algebra from the associative algebra of the branches, including the available central phase directions. This control result predicts concentration only with additional assumptions on circuit sampling. Matchgate examples exhibit polynomial single-pass LCU variances and exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling. We also derive coefficient-selection rules and bounds for postselection, measurement error, and approximate moments.
papers.summary: Coherently summing quantum circuits introduces interference that can alter the gradient signal used to train variational models, raising the question of whether linear combinations of unitaries (LCU) suffer from barren plateaus. For a single-pass LCU with independent zero-matrix-mean branches, the authors prove that **the total gradient variance is bounded below by the differentiated branch's variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude**, at any gate position and without assuming Haar-random unitaries, and they derive exact loss and gradient formulas that quantify inter-branch interference, including a term depending on relative coefficient phases that a four-qubit matchgate example shows can be nonzero. For circuits that repeatedly interleave branch operations with full special-unitary ancilla mixing, they determine the generated Lie algebra from the associative algebra of the branches, which predicts concentration only under additional circuit-sampling assumptions, and matchgate examples exhibit polynomial single-pass variances but exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling. The paper also gives coefficient-selection rules and bounds for postselection, measurement error, and approximate moments.

papers.title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection
papers.abstract: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection.
papers.summary: Shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs) whose geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions change how the same defect appears, yet existing industrial datasets rarely pair instance-level defect annotations with product-variant identities. `Bottle-SKU` is a benchmark of **13,119 images with 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes across seven defect categories and 48 bottle SKUs**, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To handle that variation, Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (`ProDMM`) builds a visual prototype per SKU from training images, predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input, and uses the prototype-conditioned representation to generate low-rank query/value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention while preserving the pretrained `Grounding DINO` detection pathway, trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on `Bottle-SKU` and the public `GC10-DET-SKU` metallic-surface dataset support the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning.

papers.title: GearUp: DAG-aware Acceleration for Serverless Inference Serving via Slack-guided Pre-loading
papers.abstract: Serverless platforms increasingly host machine learning (ML) inference workflows, modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of interdependent functions. Beyond container startup, each ML node must load libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels before it can run. These costs accumulate along dependent DAG paths and place initialization on the end-to-end critical path. Existing systems optimize one half of this problem. DAG-agnostic pre-loading prepares nodes the request may never reach, wasting host and GPU memory. DAG-aware serving routes and scales whole functions, leaving the loading stages inside a node untouched. This paper presents GearUp, a serverless DAG inference serving system that removes ML-node loading from the end-to-end critical path at low resource cost. GearUp profiles the loading stages of each node and schedules them inside the slack time the DAG exposes, hiding initialization behind upstream execution. It reuses initialized instances within and across requests to avoid redundant cold starts. A probabilistic, traffic-adaptive keep-alive policy sets how long idle instances are retained, balancing memory cost against cold-start risk under bursty load. On the AMBER Alert and FINRA-ML workflows with NVIDIA L40S GPUs, GearUp reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% against SMIless, for median speedups of 3.1x and 10.0x over cold execution. Integrated GPU and host memory allocation fall by up to 83.9% and 94.6% against eager pre-loading in InstaInfer. GearUp achieves 4.2x strong scaling on four workers.
papers.summary: Serverless platforms increasingly host machine learning inference workflows as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of functions, where each node must load libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels before it can run, so initialization accumulates along dependent paths onto the end-to-end critical path; DAG-agnostic pre-loading wastes host and GPU memory on nodes a request may never reach, while DAG-aware serving leaves the loading stages inside a node untouched. `GearUp` profiles each node's loading stages and schedules them inside the slack time the DAG exposes, hiding initialization behind upstream execution, reuses initialized instances within and across requests, and sets idle keep-alive durations with a probabilistic, traffic-adaptive policy that balances memory cost against cold-start risk under bursty load. On the `AMBER Alert` and `FINRA-ML` workflows with NVIDIA L40S GPUs, **it reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% versus `SMIless`**, for median speedups of 3.1x and 10.0x over cold execution, cuts integrated GPU and host memory by up to 83.9% and 94.6% versus eager pre-loading in `InstaInfer`, and achieves 4.2x strong scaling on four workers.

papers.title: Convex-SKM-Net: Low-Latency Block Halfspace Corrections for Neural Convex Constraint Satisfaction
papers.abstract: Fast inference and strict constraint satisfaction are essential for learning-based decision-making. Existing methods often rely on constraint-specific projections or feasible-set parameterizations, while iterative repair can be costly. We introduce Convex-SKM-Net, a convex constraint-satisfaction layer that forms linearization halfspaces from residual and (sub)gradient oracles without constraint-specific inequality projectors. It applies fixed-depth dual projected-gradient descent (dual PGD) to minimum-displacement block problems using GPU-friendly matrix operations. We jointly learn the predictor and a positive-definite mobility, adapting the correction geometry to improve objective quality. We prove convergence of the outer iterates at fixed dual depth and linear convergence in distance under Slater's condition and bounded subgradients. All our test outputs on three second-order-cone model-predictive control (SOC-MPC) horizons and six power-system convex relaxations satisfy a $10^{-3}$ feasibility tolerance. Comparisons with the latest constraint-satisfaction methods show inference speedups of up to $144.3\times$ on SOC-MPC and $7.7\times$ on a convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) benchmark with joint training. On QCQP, the mean objective gap is $0.012\%$, with full test feasibility at $10^{-4}$. Learning mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by $22.4\%$ and improves gaps in matched power-system comparisons.
papers.summary: Learning-based decision-making needs fast inference together with strict constraint satisfaction, but existing methods rely on constraint-specific projections or feasible-set parameterizations, and iterative repair can be costly. `Convex-SKM-Net` is a convex constraint-satisfaction layer that forms linearization halfspaces from residual and subgradient oracles without constraint-specific projectors, applies fixed-depth dual projected-gradient descent to minimum-displacement block problems using GPU-friendly matrix operations, and jointly learns the predictor and a positive-definite mobility that adapts the correction geometry. The authors prove convergence of the outer iterates at fixed dual depth and linear convergence in distance under Slater's condition with bounded subgradients, and report that every test output on three second-order-cone model-predictive control (SOC-MPC) horizons and six power-system convex relaxations meets a 1e-3 feasibility tolerance, with **inference speedups of up to 144.3x on SOC-MPC** and 7.7x on a convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) benchmark, where the mean objective gap is 0.012% with full feasibility at 1e-4. Learning the mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by 22.4%.

papers.title: Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation
papers.abstract: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.
papers.summary: Behavior cloning generalizes well for robotic manipulation on land, but marine visual distortion and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that has kept generalist architectures from working in underwater field manipulation. The authors collected 1,616 episodes of underwater manipulation in calm and turbulent water and trained 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (`DynamicVLA`) with varying proprioception configurations, finding across three tasks and 1,260 graded pool rollouts that 10 models beat the baseline and the best reached a 93.3% overall success rate including partial successes. In a field case study on grasping and mooring tasks for marine archaeology and conservation, conducted on an ROV around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at a marina in Malta, **a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (`ACT`) policy substantially outperformed the generalist `SmolVLA` at 47.9% versus 7.9% pooled success** over 508 rollouts, reaching 66.7% on its best task at the wreck site. The `BLUEMBODIED KIT` used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV is open sourced.

papers.title: From Natural Language to Real Schematics: An Automated Workflow for Power Electronics Schematic Synthesis
papers.abstract: Designing power electronics converters traditionally requires intensive human expertise across topology sizing, commercial component selection, circuit simulation verification, and schematic drafting. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in electronic design automation (EDA), applying standalone LLMs directly to board-level power electronics schematic synthesis suffers from severe engineering hallucinations, including inaccurate analytical sizing, fabricated or mismatched component part numbers, violated voltage derating margins, and broken topological connectivity. In this paper, we propose a Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework that translates natural language specifications into verified, editable KiCad schematics and manufacturing deliverables. Our workflow integrates six stages across three functional columns: (1) requirement parsing and knowledge-driven power stage synthesis covering non-isolated (Buck, Boost) and isolated/resonant (Flyback, DAB, half-bridge LLC) topologies; (2) contract- and evidence-coordinated component selection grounded in distributor APIs and OEM datasheets, coupled with closed-loop ngspice transient verification and stress feedback; and (3) modular control hardware integration and multi-format deliverable generation featuring native KiCad netlist round-trip verification. End-to-end case studies on a 24-36V to 12V,2A Buck converter (29 positions, 83 verified terminals) and an isolated 48V to 24V, 0.5A, Dual-Active Bridge (DAB) converter (87 positions, 341 verified terminals), alongside comparative evaluations against a Vanilla LLM baseline, demonstrate that our framework improves component verification coverage from 22.2 to 98.6, nominal value consistency from 0 to 97.7, and SPICE simulation pass rates from 0 to 100.
papers.summary: Designing power electronics converters requires expertise in topology sizing, commercial component selection, simulation verification, and schematic drafting, and standalone Large Language Models (LLMs) applied to board-level schematic synthesis produce engineering hallucinations such as inaccurate sizing, fabricated part numbers, violated voltage derating margins, and broken connectivity. The Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework translates natural-language specifications into verified, editable `KiCad` schematics through six stages: requirement parsing and knowledge-driven power-stage synthesis covering Buck, Boost, Flyback, dual-active-bridge, and half-bridge LLC topologies; component selection grounded in distributor APIs and OEM datasheets with closed-loop `ngspice` transient verification and stress feedback; and modular control hardware integration with native `KiCad` netlist round-trip verification and multi-format deliverables. On a 24-36V to 12V, 2A Buck converter and an isolated 48V to 24V, 0.5A dual-active-bridge converter, compared against a vanilla LLM baseline, **component verification coverage rises from 22.2 to 98.6 and the SPICE simulation pass rate from 0 to 100**, with nominal value consistency improving from 0 to 97.7.

papers.title: Two Birds with One Stone: Skill-Augmented Generation via Unified Retrieval and Utilization
papers.abstract: Skills, as reusable external knowledge, have demonstrated substantial potential to enhance the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks. However, existing skill-augmented generation methods typically rely on separate models for skill retrieval and skill utilization, resulting in disconnected optimization of these two processes. To address this gap, we propose Skill-Uni, a unified reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes skill retrieval and utilization. Specifically, we adopt a generative skill retrieval paradigm that enables a single model to both learn how to retrieve relevant skills and leverage them for task solving. To effectively train this unified framework, we introduce a two-stage training strategy consisting of warm-up instruction tuning and GRPO, allowing the model to progressively improve its skill retrieval and utilization capabilities. Extensive experiments on five skill-related benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Skill-Uni, yielding average performance gains of 66.59% and 34.82% over the base Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.1-8B models, respectively. Besides, Skill-Uni is compatible with various skill retrieval engines, demonstrating its flexibility and generalizability. Additional in-depth analyses also provide insights into the effectiveness of Skill-Uni.
papers.summary: Skills, meaning reusable external knowledge that Large Language Models (LLMs) can draw on for complex tasks, are typically retrieved by one model and used by another, so the two processes are optimized in isolation. `Skill-Uni` is a unified reinforcement learning framework in which a single model both generatively retrieves relevant skills and leverages them to solve the task, trained in two stages of warm-up instruction tuning followed by `GRPO`. On five skill-related benchmarks it delivers **average performance gains of 66.59% over base `Qwen3-4B` and 34.82% over `LLaMA3.1-8B`**, remains compatible with various skill retrieval engines, and comes with analyses of where the gains arise.

papers.title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part II: Langevin Dynamics
papers.abstract: We consider the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem on the sphere, in which we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\mathcal{S}_N=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\lVert x\rVert^2=N\}$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. Continuing the program initiated in Part I [arXiv:2610.16705], we show that spherical Langevin dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Together with Part I, our results demonstrate that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.
papers.summary: Tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) asks for recovery of an unknown vector on the sphere from a noisy observation of its k-th tensor power, and it exhibits a well-studied gap between what is information-theoretically possible and what global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares can achieve in polynomial time. Local algorithms like Markov chains were previously known to succeed from a random initialization only at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio and were believed to be inferior to global methods. Continuing the program begun in Part I, the authors show that spherical `Langevin dynamics`, supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, **achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization**. Together with Part I, this establishes that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.

papers.title: Progressive Coupling Method for Diffusion Posterior Sampling in Ptychography
papers.abstract: Ptychography is a computational imaging method that reconstructs a sample from overlapping diffraction measurements. This technique relies on these overlapping measurements to provide the redundancy information needed for robust reconstruction, but dense scanning increases acquisition time and data volume. Reducing scan overlaps can improve measurement efficiency but weakens the physical constraints available for reconstruction. Diffusion models provide strong learned prior information, offering a promising approach to compensate for the loss of measurement redundancy. However, effectively utilizing this prior information under weak measurement constraints remains a challenge. We propose a progressive coupling posterior sampling (PCPS) method, which allows for a broader exploration of the solution space under high uncertainty while maintaining stronger diffusion-guided consistency as the reconstruction becomes more refined. Experiments on real X-ray ptychographic data at various scan overlaps demonstrate that PCPS consistently improves reconstruction accuracy compared to traditional iterative methods and existing diffusion posterior samplers, especially at low overlaps. These results show that diffusion priors can reduce the measurement redundancy required for accurate ptychography reconstruction.
papers.summary: Ptychography reconstructs a sample from overlapping diffraction measurements, but dense scan overlap drives up acquisition time and data volume, and reducing overlap weakens the physical constraints available to the reconstruction. The authors propose progressive coupling posterior sampling (`PCPS`), a diffusion-based posterior sampler that explores the solution space broadly while uncertainty is high and enforces stronger diffusion-guided consistency as the reconstruction refines. On real X-ray ptychographic data at a range of scan overlaps, **`PCPS` consistently improves reconstruction accuracy over traditional iterative methods and existing diffusion posterior samplers, with the largest gains at low overlap**, indicating that learned diffusion priors can substitute for part of the measurement redundancy.

papers.title: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents that share experiences on social platforms and store new preferences in memory are vulnerable to a role-to-principal attribution flaw the authors call Role Grounding Misattribution. They formalize the Role Grounding Attack (`RGA`): an attacker publishes an experience-sharing post that quotes a nested conversation between the attacker's agent and its user, and when the victim agent extracts preferences from that post it loses the context binding and records the attacker's preference as belonging to the victim's own user. The misattributed memory persists and steers later decisions; instantiated as tool-selection manipulation and privacy leakage, the attack pushes the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool and into placing sensitive information in tool arguments. **Across five mainstream memory systems and six language models, both attack variants achieve high success rates**, and the authors call for stronger role grounding in memory formation.
