papers.title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
papers.abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.
papers.summary: Weight-only quantization shrinks model storage, but the key-value (KV) cache remains the memory and bandwidth bottleneck for long-context large language model (LLM) inference on personal devices. Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (`GAAC`) is a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits redundancy in BF16 exponents, encoding them with calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes whose widths adapt across small groups, while a fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly so the cache is never fully decompressed. **Across five models it reaches 1.405 to 1.407 times lossless BF16 KV compression**, with smaller ratios on FP8 caches, and on NVIDIA DGX Spark it speeds up decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19 to 1.27 times, cuts resident KV memory by roughly 26%, and raises serving throughput by 13 to 29% under matched memory budgets. Attention speedups of up to 1.25 times on Apple M4 show portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

papers.title: RainCheck: Harnessing Historical Weather Data with Machine Learning for Rainfall Forecasting in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Machine-learning rainfall forecasts are often evaluated by shuffling station records into random training and test sets. For rainfall, this lets a model see what happened at neighbouring stations on the very day it is asked to forecast, and it hides the fact that a seasonal lookup table already explains most of the variance. We quantify both effects on 618,650 station-days from 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations (1948-2014). We compare random, temporal (train <=1999, test 2005-2014) and spatio-temporal (unseen stations and unseen years) evaluation, calendar-only versus antecedent-rainfall features, and six learners against climatology, persistence and SARIMA. Three findings stand out. First, a station-month climatology alone classifies high-rainfall months with 88.4% accuracy (AUC 0.950), and no learner improved on it by more than 0.8 points under temporal evaluation. Second, a calendar-only random forest reached a next-day wet-day AUC of 0.889 under a random split, higher than any model with real predictors under temporal evaluation, yet fell to 0.835, below climatology (0.859), on future years. Third, models with lagged rainfall add genuine but modest skill for next-day forecasts: a Brier skill score of 0.074 (95% CI 0.064-0.088) over climatology, rising to 0.091 when station and year inputs are removed and to 0.131 when other stations' same-day observations are added. A GRU sequence model matches but does not exceed gradient boosting, and skill disappears beyond a two-day lead. For monthly totals, no learner beat climatology significantly. We release a leakage-aware protocol and code so that future station-based studies report skill against climatology on held-out years.
papers.summary: Machine-learning rainfall forecasts are commonly evaluated with random train/test splits of station records, which lets a model see what happened at neighbouring stations on the very day it is forecasting and hides how much a seasonal lookup table already explains. The authors quantify both effects on 618,650 station-days from 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations spanning 1948 to 2014, comparing random, temporal, and spatio-temporal splits, calendar-only versus antecedent-rainfall features, and six learners against climatology, persistence, and `SARIMA`. **A station-month climatology alone classifies high-rainfall months with 88.4% accuracy, and no learner beat it by more than 0.8 points under temporal evaluation**, while a calendar-only random forest that looked strong under a random split fell below climatology on future years. Lagged rainfall adds modest genuine next-day skill that vanishes beyond a two-day lead, a `GRU` sequence model matches but does not beat gradient boosting, and the authors release a leakage-aware protocol and code so future station-based studies report skill against climatology on held-out years.

papers.title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as a Specification for Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input--output examples. How many such specifications must a developer provide, and which ones, for the agent to produce the developer's intended program? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, for it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure---a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions---which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another badly underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, developers cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering it from thousands of lines of generated code. To resolve this, we introduce Skeleton Coding, in which developers jointly specify the structure---in high-level, code-like format---alongside behavioral specifications. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests developers must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27.0%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15--26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.
papers.summary: Coding agents are usually steered with end-to-end behavioral specifications such as tests and input-output examples, but how many such specifications suffice depends on the program structure the agent itself chooses, so a test set that pins down one decomposition can leave another badly underdetermined. The authors introduce `Skeleton Coding`, in which developers supply a high-level, code-like skeleton of data types, modules, and functions alongside behavioral specifications, and they model AI-assisted coding as a control problem to show that skeletons can exponentially reduce the number of tests needed to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. **Across four models and three benchmarks, the best skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications**, and still cut error by up to 27.0% when the agent can query a complete reference implementation. Skeletons also narrow the gap between small and large models by about 52.4%, lower implementation cost by 15 to 26 times, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.

papers.title: Disparity Laundering: Consensus Without Fairness in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Clinical large language models are increasingly fielded as multi-agent teams, on the assumption that deliberation averages out individual error. It does not average out bias. Across a full factorial of five model families and four aggregation topologies on 120 real MIMIC-IV emergency cases under counterfactual demographic swaps, no configuration neutralizes the disparity: all 20 cells commit the direction of their agents' independent answers, giving Black patients more acute triage. Every model has a topology that amplifies its baseline gap, but which one varies by model, so no design is reliably safe or reliably amplifying: the disparity is relocated, never removed. Late-stage fixes fail: fairness instructions and demographic masking leave the gap untouched, and per-agent self-debiasing widens it, because the bias is already encoded in the agents' ordinary clinical numbers. We call this disparity laundering; the audits now applied to clinical AI, per model, per output, per version, can certify the parts but never the committed decision. Interventions close the gap exactly when they make counterfactual versions visible inside the system and pool them, through deliberation, into the committed decision. A diverse-perspective ensemble does both while keeping the team, with no retraining or architectural change: the disparity falls by 67 to 94% where all five perspectives pool at every round, and the one topology that never pools them is the one it cannot reliably repair. Medical multi-agent systems do not filter demographic bias; they launder it into plausible decisions no single-version audit can catch, and the only defense is to make the bias visible.
papers.summary: Clinical large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as multi-agent teams on the assumption that deliberation averages out individual error, and the authors test whether it also averages out demographic bias. In a full factorial of five model families and four aggregation topologies on 120 real `MIMIC-IV` emergency cases with counterfactual demographic swaps, **none of the 20 configurations neutralizes the disparity: every one commits the direction of its agents' independent answers, giving Black patients more acute triage**, and each model has some topology that amplifies its baseline gap. Late-stage fixes such as fairness instructions and demographic masking leave the gap untouched and per-agent self-debiasing widens it, because the bias is already encoded in the agents' ordinary clinical numbers. The authors call this disparity laundering and find that only interventions which make counterfactual versions visible inside the system and pool them through deliberation close the gap, with a diverse-perspective ensemble cutting the disparity by 67 to 94% where all five perspectives pool at every round.

papers.title: HotPOT: Operator Transformer with Heterogeneous Physics Experts for Large-Scale PDE Pre-training
papers.abstract: Large-scale PDE pre-training trains a single model on the data from multiple partial differential equations (PDEs). However, adding heterogeneous PDEs with different governing equations, physical variables, and variable interactions does not always improve predictive performance across tasks. Existing PDE mixture-of-experts models mitigate cross-task interference through learned routing, but typically use homogeneous expert architectures, making it difficult to directly reflect differences in state evolution across equations. We introduce HotPOT, an operator transformer with heterogeneous physics experts for large-scale PDE pre-training. HotPOT uses a shared encoder to capture information common across PDEs, while each PDE family uses a neural-numerical expert that pairs a learnable predictor with a fixed numerical update containing no trainable parameters. Each predictor outputs the quantities required by its paired numerical update, which then computes the next state. This design allows different PDEs to share a common encoder while retaining their own learnable predictors and numerical updates. Experiments across five PDE families and six settings show that HotPOT outperforms MoE-POT in all 24 matched-scale comparisons before and after fine-tuning, reducing rollout error by 50.7% on average. Notably, the 17M model also surpasses substantially larger MoE-POT models, and the performance gains extend to zero-shot prediction under unseen physical conditions. Code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/HotPOT-code.
papers.summary: Pre-training a single model on data from many partial differential equations (PDEs) does not reliably help when the equations differ in governing dynamics, physical variables, and variable interactions, and existing PDE mixture-of-experts models route between homogeneous experts that cannot directly reflect those differences. `HotPOT` is an operator transformer with heterogeneous physics experts: a shared encoder captures information common across PDEs, while each PDE family gets a neural-numerical expert that pairs a learnable predictor with a fixed, parameter-free numerical update that computes the next state from the predictor's outputs. **Across five PDE families and six settings, `HotPOT` beats `MoE-POT` in all 24 matched-scale comparisons before and after fine-tuning, reducing rollout error by 50.7% on average**, and a 17M-parameter version surpasses substantially larger `MoE-POT` models, with gains that carry over to zero-shot prediction under unseen physical conditions.

papers.title: Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training
papers.abstract: Rubrics enable reward assignment on tasks without verifiable answers, but are expensive to manually produce from scratch. We present Rubricon, a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics without requiring human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator-model training. Using any LLM, Rubricon samples multiple rubrics, selects the most discriminative candidate, adds criteria to capture overlooked requirements or response flaws, and prunes criteria that are misaligned or shallow. Alongside LLM self-critique and test-time scaling, Rubricon uses observed criterion pass rates on example model responses to guide refinement. Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and general-use LLM benchmarks, Rubricon produces rubrics whose scores of frontier LLM responses exhibit 9% greater alignment with labor-intensive expert-authored rubrics, compared to the best alternative synthetic rubric generation method among RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, and agentic generation via harnesses like Codex. On HealthBench, post-training a Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from the strongest alternative synthetic rubric generator, RRD.
papers.summary: Rubrics make it possible to assign rewards on tasks without verifiable answers, but writing them from scratch by hand is expensive. `Rubricon` is a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics with any LLM and no human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator training: it samples multiple candidate rubrics, keeps the most discriminative one, adds criteria for overlooked requirements or response flaws, prunes misaligned or shallow criteria, and uses observed criterion pass rates on example responses to guide refinement alongside self-critique and test-time scaling. **Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and general-use benchmarks, `Rubricon` rubrics score frontier-model responses with 9% greater alignment to expert-authored rubrics than the best alternative synthetic generator** among `RRD`, `QSRG`, `OpenRubrics`, and agentic generation via harnesses like `Codex`. Post-training a `Qwen3.5-9B` model on `HealthBench` with `Rubricon` rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from `RRD`.

papers.title: CuraEval: Evaluating Demonstration Curation on Mixed-Skill Robot Data
papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning uses demonstrations from operators of varying skill, but selecting training data remains challenging. Existing methods score demonstrations using smoothness, diversity, or estimated influence on policy performance, but differences in selection and evaluation protocols make it difficult to determine whether they outperform simple baselines. We introduce \textbf{CuraEval}, a framework combining mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled comparisons against fixed size-matched random subsets and full-data training on mixed-skill robomimic data using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN. We show that the evaluated PSD score depends only on episode length and squared position magnitudes, and produces nearly the same ranking as episode length on \textit{square} ($\rho=0.999$). With Diffusion Policy, selecting the shortest 50\% of demonstrations improves \textit{square} success from 70.7\% under random selection to 76.5\%. Compared with random selection, our adapted geometric-entropy LOO selector reduces success at 25\% retention from 94.7\% to 74.0\% on \textit{can} and achieves 41.7\% on \textit{square}, below the mean success rates of all three independently sampled random subsets (59.8--62.5\%). On the same 3 \textit{square} Diffusion Policy training seeds, length-based selection at 75\% retention improves success over full-data training from 76.7\% to 86.7\% under the original protocol, but lowers it from 80.5\% to 79.5\% after checkpoint reporting, rollout count, and evaluation seed change jointly. No evaluated curated condition significantly outperforms full-data training after Holm correction, although confidence intervals still permit useful gains. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CuraEval.
papers.summary: Robot imitation learning draws on demonstrations from operators of varying skill, and existing curation methods score demonstrations by smoothness, diversity, or estimated influence on policy performance, but inconsistent selection and evaluation protocols make it unclear whether they beat simple baselines. `CuraEval` combines mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled comparisons against size-matched random subsets and full-data training on mixed-skill `robomimic` data using `Diffusion Policy` and `BC-RNN`. The analysis shows the evaluated `PSD` score depends only on episode length and squared position magnitudes and ranks demonstrations nearly identically to episode length, while an adapted geometric-entropy leave-one-out selector falls well below random selection at 25% retention. **No evaluated curated condition significantly outperforms full-data training after Holm correction**, and a seemingly strong length-based gain on the `square` task reverses once checkpoint reporting, rollout count, and evaluation seed are changed together, although confidence intervals still permit useful gains.

papers.title: FACTS-MAS: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Adaptive Forecasting from Heterogeneous Evidence
papers.abstract: Real-world forecasting often requires integrating heterogeneous evidence whose predictive value varies across horizons, operating regimes, and domains. We introduce FACTS-MAS, a domain-agnostic multi-agent forecasting framework that decomposes evidence into specialized channels for temporal dynamics, exogenous context, seasonality, structural information, and discrete events. Each agent generates an independently testable forecast through a common interface, while leakage-safe historical validation measures its predictive skill relative to a naive reference. These skill estimates are used to weight and combine agent forecasts, so that uninformative evidence is either removed or downweighted rather than forced to participate. A calibration procedure selects domain-specific constant means based on historical validation folds. We evaluate FACTS-MAS on weekly for-sale housing inventory from Zillow and weekly unemployment insurance claims from FRED, for 15 U.S. metropolitan areas at 4-, 8-, and 13-week forecasting horizons. Our method outperforms both a naive last-value forecast method and the TimesFM foundation model. However, a factor-adjusted exponential smoothing model performs as well as the fused forecast. The evidence therefore supports FACTS-MAS as a systematic protocol for testing, calibrating, and recomposing evidence channels before assembling them into the strongest single model for a specific application domain. Code, data, and results are available at https://github.com/Madumita24/FACTS-MAS.
papers.summary: Real-world forecasting must integrate heterogeneous evidence whose predictive value shifts across horizons, operating regimes, and domains. `FACTS-MAS` is a domain-agnostic multi-agent forecasting framework that routes evidence into specialized channels for temporal dynamics, exogenous context, seasonality, structural information, and discrete events; each agent produces an independently testable forecast, leakage-safe historical validation measures its skill against a naive reference, and those skill estimates weight the combination so uninformative channels are downweighted or dropped. On weekly `Zillow` for-sale housing inventory and weekly `FRED` unemployment insurance claims for 15 U.S. metropolitan areas at 4-, 8-, and 13-week horizons, the method beats a naive last-value forecast and the `TimesFM` foundation model, **but a factor-adjusted exponential smoothing model performs as well as the fused forecast**. The authors therefore position the framework as a protocol for testing, calibrating, and recomposing evidence channels before assembling the strongest single model for a given domain.

papers.title: The Endgame of FSDP Communication: Layout-Aware Collectives on Copy Engines, RDMA, and NVSwitch
papers.abstract: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP2) maintains parameters and gradients as per-parameter tensors, whereas its collective path operates on flat, rank-major buffers. Converting between these layouts copies all-gather outputs into parameter storage and packs gradients into full-group fp32 buffers. Layout conversion alone accounts for 6.4% of step time in Llama-3.1 70B training at 8K tokens per GPU. Communication kernels impose a second cost: a default NCCL reduce-scatter can slow a concurrent GEMM that would otherwise complete in a single wave by 69%. We present TIDE, a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs. TIDE preserves FSDP2's per-parameter storage and compute kernels while folding layout placement into collective addressing. TIDE-AG delivers shards directly to parameter storage using NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA, with no SMs used for transport or placement. TIDE-RS consumes per-parameter bf16 gradients directly and reduces them into fp32 shards (a mixed-precision mode that NCCL does not provide) using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks (CTAs) for node-local accumulation and NVSwitch for cross-node reduction. A two-phase pipeline separates gradient reads from network progress; Slot-Reuse optionally stages gradients in vacated all-gather slots. On 64 GPUs, TIDE reduces step time by up to 27.1% relative to Stock FSDP2 and 6.0% relative to FSDP2+SymmMem across Llama-3.1 70B, Wan2.2, and Qwen3-30B-A3B. It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by factors of 12.5-14.5 and cuts interference with concurrent compute by up to an order of magnitude. Its reduce-scatter buffer remains nearly constant from 16 to 64 GPUs at a fixed per-GPU output size, and its peak memory is up to 4.7 GiB below FSDP2+SymmMem's and, with Slot-Reuse on Wan2.2, below Stock FSDP2's.
papers.summary: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (`FSDP2`) stores parameters and gradients as per-parameter tensors while its collectives operate on flat rank-major buffers, and converting between the two layouts accounts for 6.4% of step time when training `Llama-3.1 70B` at 8K tokens per GPU; a default NCCL reduce-scatter can also slow a concurrent GEMM by 69%. `TIDE` is a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs that fold layout placement into collective addressing: `TIDE-AG` delivers shards directly into parameter storage via NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA without using streaming multiprocessors for transport, and `TIDE-RS` consumes per-parameter bf16 gradients and reduces them into fp32 shards using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks, a mixed-precision mode NCCL does not provide. **On 64 GPUs, `TIDE` cuts step time by up to 27.1% versus stock `FSDP2` and 6.0% versus `FSDP2` with symmetric memory** across `Llama-3.1 70B`, `Wan2.2`, and `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, reduces reduce-scatter SM time by 12.5 to 14.5 times, and lowers peak memory by up to 4.7 GiB.

papers.title: 3DCodeEdit: Benchmarking Instruction-Guided 3D Program Editing
papers.abstract: Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.
papers.summary: Language models increasingly produce 3D content as code, and practical workflows edit existing programs rather than regenerating them, which requires understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it. `3DCodeEdit` is a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 `Blender` programs that construct objects entirely in code, spanning parameter tweaks, structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. **Across 17 models the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits**, with failures in more capable models shifting toward geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. Feedback from a separate reviewer model describing how renders differ from the request helps more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and lets a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.

papers.title: Variational Consequence-Driven Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically mitigates distribution shift by imposing divergence constraints on the action distributions of the learned and behavior policies. However, this paradigm cannot ensure the underlying dynamic consistency structure: even minor action deviations can lead to drastically different transitions, inadvertently driving the agent away from the offline dataset. To address this, we explore policy constraints through their induced state-consequence distributions rather than relying on pure action-distribution matching. Nevertheless, directly enforcing such consequence-aware constraints is computationally intractable without access to the true underlying dynamics model. To bypass this issue, we propose Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), which replaces the intractable objective with a closed-form latent divergence. Structuring this latent space to reflect transition dynamics renders the latent divergence a theoretically bounded surrogate for the true consequence-distribution divergence. By regularizing the learned policy with this latent divergence, StBR adaptively tightens the behavior constraint in dynamics-sensitive regions, effectively preventing deviations outside the offline dataset. Empirically, we demonstrate that StBR achieves superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.
papers.summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically guards against distribution shift by constraining the divergence between the learned and behavior policies' action distributions, but small action deviations can still produce very different transitions and push the agent away from the dataset. The authors instead constrain policies through the state-consequence distributions they induce, and since that is intractable without the true dynamics, they propose Structural Behavior Regularization (`StBR`), which replaces the objective with a closed-form divergence in a latent space structured to reflect transition dynamics. **This latent divergence is a theoretically bounded surrogate for the true consequence-distribution divergence**, and regularizing with it adaptively tightens the behavior constraint in dynamics-sensitive regions; empirically `StBR` outperforms baselines across diverse offline RL benchmarks.

papers.title: The Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) Dataset : Auditing Socioeconomic and Demographic Disparities in LLM-Generated Financial Advice in India
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice shifts with social identity in Global South settings. The Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (`IFAAB`) benchmark is a counterfactual audit of 31,734 `GPT-4o` financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district, evaluated on implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments while holding the request fixed. **In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1% higher initial and 46.8% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles**, the gap remains 49.4% in the caste-augmented audit and shrinks to 7.9% once district information is added, and OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice resources than General-category profiles. Qualitatively, women are steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy while men receive growth-oriented advice on investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation.

papers.title: MEV: A Multi-Event Video Dataset for Long-Take Generation
papers.abstract: Current datasets for text-to-video generation are largely limited to short clips depicting a single event or coarse-grained captions. As a result, they provide limited supervision for modeling long-take temporal dependencies, often leading to temporally inconsistent generations when describing multiple events. In this paper, we introduce MEV, a multi-event video dataset designed for long-take video generation. MEV provides high-quality real-world videos where subjects can perform a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping events, featuring precise temporal boundaries and fine-grained procedural annotations. This event-centric discretization reduces confounding factors and enables models to support temporally localized conditioning and build long-take videos from atomic event units. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive annotation pipeline that segments videos into temporally grounded events, and generates structured captions at both the global level and the event level. In addition, under an event-centric evaluation protocol, we conduct multi-event generation experiments by fine-tuning on MEV with temporally grounded event conditioning, leading to improved long-take event transitions and more coherent content. We believe this work provides a publicly available resource for multi-event fine-tuning and event-centric evaluation, together with practical insights into learning from temporally structured video-text data.
papers.summary: Text-to-video datasets mostly contain short single-event clips or coarse captions, which gives models little supervision for long-take temporal dependencies and leads to inconsistent generations when a prompt describes several events. `MEV` is a multi-event video dataset of high-quality real-world videos in which subjects perform sequences of distinct, non-overlapping events, with precise temporal boundaries and fine-grained procedural annotations, built by an annotation pipeline that segments videos into temporally grounded events and writes structured captions at both the global and event level. **Fine-tuning on `MEV` with temporally grounded event conditioning improves long-take event transitions and content coherence** under an event-centric evaluation protocol, and the dataset is released as a public resource for multi-event fine-tuning and evaluation.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax Optimal Regret for Adversarial Linear Bandits with Strong Corruptions
papers.abstract: We study adversarial linear bandits with strong corruption, in which an adaptive adversary chooses the reward vectors and a strong adversary corrupts each observed reward after seeing the learner's action, subject to a known total corruption budget $C$. Strong corruption breaks the importance-weighted reward estimates used by adversarial bandit algorithms: by corrupting only the rounds in which a rarely sampled action is drawn, the adversary amplifies each unit of corruption by the inverse of its sampling probability. The best known bound for this problem, $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3T} + dC)$ by Liu et al. (2024), is a factor $\sqrt{d}$ above the corruption-free rate in its leading term, and whether $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T} + dC)$ regret is achievable was left open. We propose CRW-FTRL, which runs follow-the-regularized-leader with a radius-weighted entropy regularizer and estimates rewards with a normalized kernel estimator whose sensitivity to corruption is governed by per-action radii instead of inverse sampling probabilities. The radii are nondecreasing and are chosen jointly with the sampling distribution through a monotone log-determinant barrier problem, so that a negative linear term in the regularizer cancels both the corruption bias and the estimation error of every comparator. For $K$ actions in $\mathbb{R}^d$, CRW-FTRL achieves $\tilde O(\sqrt{dT\log K} + dC)$ regret with high probability against an adaptive adversary, which matches the best known corruption-free rate and the $\Omega(dC)$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Applied to a discretization of a general compact action set, it yields $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T} + dC)$ regret, which settles the statistical rate of corrupted adversarial linear bandits under strong corruption.
papers.summary: In adversarial linear bandits with strong corruption, an adaptive adversary picks the reward vectors and a second adversary corrupts each observed reward after seeing the learner's action, under a known total budget C; this breaks the importance-weighted estimates used by standard algorithms, since corrupting only rarely sampled actions amplifies each unit of corruption by the inverse sampling probability. The best previous bound carried an extra square-root-of-d factor in its leading term, leaving open whether the corruption-free rate was attainable. `CRW-FTRL` runs follow-the-regularized-leader with a radius-weighted entropy regularizer and a normalized kernel reward estimator whose corruption sensitivity is governed by per-action radii chosen jointly with the sampling distribution through a monotone log-determinant barrier problem. **It achieves Õ(√(dT log K) + dC) regret with high probability against an adaptive adversary, matching the best known corruption-free rate and the Ω(dC) lower bound up to logarithmic factors**, and applied to a discretization of a general compact action set it yields Õ(d√T + dC), settling the statistical rate for this problem.

papers.title: Precedent or Intent? What Coding Agents Follow When Evolving Existing Code
papers.abstract: Existing code reveals past implementation decisions but rarely explains the reasoning behind them. When coding agents implement new features or modify existing functionality, past decisions may conflict with new task instructions. This raises a fundamental question for agentic software evolution: when multiple implementations satisfy the same functional requirements, how do coding agents decide whether to follow existing code or new task instructions? We investigate this question through bidirectional, controlled experiments in purpose-built repositories, followed by validation in real-world open-source repositories. Our approach isolates three competing sources of guidance: (1) agents' default preferences, (2) repository precedents, and (3) explicit task instructions. We conduct 5,625 trials across four coding agents and six implementation pairs, with validation in four open-source repositories spanning three programming languages. We find that agents share the same default implementation choices, yet overwhelmingly follow repository precedent when it conflicts with those defaults (359/360 trials). Crucially, not all precedents carry equal influence: three supporting local files yield 96% adoption, compared with only 4% for sibling-resource files, and changing file placement alone can shift adoption from 0% to 100% at a fixed example count. When new task intent conflicts with existing code, written priority rules achieve substantially higher success than code examples alone (59/60 versus 38/60 joint successes for two agents on two implementation pairs). The effectiveness of explicit rules also extends to open-source repositories, where a harness-loaded rule raises joint success from 0/120 to 117/120. These findings motivate design-decision traceability that preserves not only implementation choices but also the rationale and priorities that should guide future changes.
papers.summary: Existing code records past implementation decisions without the reasoning behind them, so when coding agents evolve a codebase, repository precedent can conflict with new task instructions. The authors run bidirectional controlled experiments in purpose-built repositories and then validate in real open-source projects, isolating three sources of guidance: agents' default preferences, repository precedents, and explicit task instructions, across 5,625 trials with four coding agents and six implementation pairs, plus four open-source repositories in three languages. Agents share the same default choices yet **follow repository precedent over those defaults in 359 of 360 trials**, though influence depends heavily on placement: three supporting local files yield 96% adoption versus 4% for sibling-resource files, and changing file placement alone can shift adoption from 0% to 100%. When task intent conflicts with existing code, written priority rules beat code examples alone (59/60 versus 38/60 joint successes), and a harness-loaded rule raises joint success in open-source repositories from 0/120 to 117/120, motivating traceability of design rationale and priorities alongside implementation choices.

papers.title: Verification-Guided Retrosynthesis: Reaction Feedback and Evidence Timing
papers.abstract: Retrosynthesis planning seeks synthesis routes from purchasable starting materials to a target molecule. Search over predicted reactions can connect a target to available materials, yet an infeasible reaction can invalidate the resulting route. Evaluating route quality only after search has finished cannot correct errors made during search. We introduce Verification-Guided Reflow (VGR), incorporating reaction verification as a decision action in AND/OR search. Verification results are represented as binary verdicts; queries are scheduled from the search structure, and acquired verdicts exclude reactions or adjust search priorities. We define verified solvability as the fraction of targets for which a complete route accepted stepwise by the verifier is found. On Retro190, feeding verification results into search increases verified solvability from 51.1% to 62.6% relative to route evaluation without feedback. Further controlled experiments show that earlier verification and immediate prioritization of accepted reactions each improve route discovery, yet combining them performs worse than either change alone. We therefore propose early pruning and delayed guidance: rejected reactions are pruned immediately, while accepted reactions gain search priority when processed as part of a complete candidate route. In a separate comparison with the verification scheduling rule fixed, this strategy increases verified solvability from 61.1% with immediate guidance to 71.1%, using fewer proposal calls and unique verifier queries.
papers.summary: Retrosynthesis planning searches for routes from purchasable starting materials to a target molecule, but a single infeasible predicted reaction can invalidate a route, and evaluating routes only after search finishes cannot correct errors made during it. Verification-Guided Reflow (`VGR`) makes reaction verification a decision action inside AND/OR search: verifier queries are scheduled from the search structure, and the resulting binary verdicts either exclude reactions or adjust search priorities. **On `Retro190`, feeding verification results back into search raises verified solvability from 51.1% to 62.6%** compared with post-hoc route evaluation. Earlier verification and immediate prioritization of accepted reactions each help on their own but hurt when combined, so the authors propose early pruning with delayed guidance, which lifts verified solvability from 61.1% to 71.1% while using fewer proposal calls and unique verifier queries.

papers.title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health
papers.abstract: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace.ai is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace.ai outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.ai.
papers.summary: Sports-and-health guidance from large language models (LLMs) promises safe, scientifically grounded, personalized exercise advice at scale, but the domain lacks curated training corpora and rigorous benchmarks. `Keepace.ai` is a domain-specialized model post-trained from `Qwen3.5-27B` and currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge question answering, and personal sports data analysis. **In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, it outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines**, with the largest gains in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy; the report covers the design, data pipeline, and safety-first evaluation framework.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Generative Models for Music Audio
papers.abstract: Music audio generation spans instrumental clips, full songs with vocals, edits of existing recordings, and systems that play alongside a musician in real time. This monograph explains the methods behind these systems for readers familiar with neural-network training who are new to music generation. It introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration, and preference optimization in a shared notation. Worked examples connect training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. The application sections relate the musical requirements of instrumental generation, songs, editing, and live performance to model design. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks, and release information documented in papers and official sources. Symbolic composition, speech, and sound effects are included where they connect to music audio. We explain how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, design and report listening tests, and assess evidence about data provenance, memorization, attribution, and output detection. Selected legal decisions and disputes illustrate the implications for training and release. The reviewed systems combine established generative paradigms with new representations, planning stages, and post-training procedures. Differences in data, scale, and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.
papers.summary: Written as a monograph for readers who know neural-network training but are new to music generation, it covers the methods behind instrumental clips, full songs with vocals, edits of existing recordings, and systems that play alongside a musician in real time. It introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration, and preference optimization in a shared notation, with worked examples tying training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks, and release information, and later sections explain how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, design and report listening tests, and assess evidence about data provenance, memorization, attribution, and output detection, with selected legal disputes illustrating implications for training and release. **Differences in data, scale, and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.**

papers.title: Transportable Offline Reinforcement Learning in Presence of Unmeasured Confounding
papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning seeks to learn decision policies from previously collected data, but deployment environments may differ from the domains in which the data were collected, and logged variables may omit confounders that affected both historical actions and outcomes. We study offline policy learning under the joint challenges of domain discrepancy and unmeasured confounding, where multiple heterogeneous source datasets provide complementary information about a target domain. We develop a causally adjusted transportability framework combining transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls, and proxies to identify target-domain causal quantities. For confounded contextual bandits, identification reduces to systems of bridge-function integral equations, enabling minimax estimation from finite samples. Confidence sets for the identified quantities are then used for pessimistic policy optimization, yielding CAT-CCB. We extend the framework to episodic confounded Markov decision processes, where complementary sources identify target reward and transition mechanisms under structural and completeness conditions. Under Gaussian dynamics and linear function approximation, this yields CAT-CMDP. We establish high-probability finite-sample suboptimality guarantees that quantify the effects of approximation, estimation, source-to-target shift, offline coverage, and sample size. For bounded finite-dimensional linear classes, the contextual-bandit guarantee recovers the standard $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N^{-1/2})$ rate. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of the framework for learning target-domain policies from heterogeneous confounded data. Together, the results provide a principled approach when no single source dataset suffices for causal identification and policy optimization.
papers.summary: Offline reinforcement learning learns policies from logged data, but the deployment domain may differ from the domains where data were collected, and the logs may omit confounders that influenced both historical actions and outcomes. The authors combine transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls, and proxies so that several heterogeneous source datasets can jointly identify target-domain causal quantities, reducing identification to bridge-function integral equations for confounded contextual bandits and extending it to episodic confounded Markov decision processes under Gaussian dynamics and linear function approximation. Confidence sets for the identified quantities feed pessimistic policy optimization in two algorithms, `CAT-CCB` and `CAT-CMDP`, with high-probability finite-sample suboptimality bounds that separate the effects of approximation, estimation, source-to-target shift, offline coverage, and sample size. **For bounded finite-dimensional linear classes, the contextual-bandit guarantee recovers the standard Õ(N^-1/2) rate**, and numerical experiments support the framework for learning target-domain policies when no single source dataset suffices.

papers.title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Moreover, their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, while decoding requires no refinement iterations. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. In practice, two iterations suffice. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.
papers.summary: Test-time training (TTT) layers give recurrent architectures a small neural network as memory, trained online by gradient descent, which is more expressive than the linear memories of `Gated DeltaNet` and `Mamba-2` but hard to parallelize: implementations such as `TTT-MLP` rely on sequential block-wise weight updates that only approximate the token-by-token recurrence and run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. `ParaTTT` (`PTTT`) parallelizes arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining an estimate of the inner-loop gradient trajectory, where each refinement is three chunkwise-parallel passes (a forward pass over the feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass for the readout and its feature gradients, and a backward pass), the exact online recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, and decoding needs no refinement at all. The authors prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under contraction conditions and find that two iterations suffice in practice. **With two refinement steps at 4K context, the inner-loop trajectory is evaluated 32× faster than `TTT-MLP` at matched error and the full 340M model trains 4.9× faster**, while models at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed `Gated DeltaNet` and `Mamba-2`, stay competitive with same-size Transformers on perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, and show better recall than the linear recurrences.

papers.title: Cross Lingual Abstractive Summarization for Marathi
papers.abstract: Text summarization is an important task for advancing natural language processing (NLP) research and applications in Indic languages. Despite progress in extractive and abstractive summarization, both monolingual summarization (MS) and cross-lingual summarization (CLS) remain relatively underexplored for these languages. Recent advances in Transformer architectures, pretrained language models (PLMs), and dataset availability offer new opportunities to address this gap. In this work, we construct cross-lingual training data from the monolingual Marathi MahaSum corpus and combine it with the smaller cross-lingual PMIndiaSum dataset to fine-tune IndicTrans2, an Indic neural machine translation model. We evaluate the resulting models using ROUGE, chrF and chrF++ metrics, focusing primarily on Marathi-to-English summarization due to computational constraints. We also discuss the applicability of our approach to the English-to-Marathi direction. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging a pretrained translation model yields substantially better summarization performance than the IndicBART and mBART-50 based baselines reported in previous work on cross-lingual summarization.
papers.summary: Both monolingual summarization (MS) and cross-lingual summarization (CLS) remain underexplored for Indic languages despite advances in Transformer architectures and pretrained language models (PLMs). The authors build cross-lingual training data from the monolingual Marathi `MahaSum` corpus, combine it with the smaller cross-lingual `PMIndiaSum` dataset, and fine-tune `IndicTrans2`, an Indic neural machine translation model, evaluating with `ROUGE`, `chrF`, and `chrF++` and focusing on Marathi-to-English because of computational constraints while discussing the English-to-Marathi direction. **Starting from a pretrained translation model yields substantially better summarization than the `IndicBART` and `mBART-50` baselines reported in previous cross-lingual summarization work.**

papers.title: A Hybrid Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks Method
papers.abstract: Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks (PIHNNs) exploit complex-analytic representations to satisfy homogeneous PDEs by construction, but their extension to nonhomogeneous problems is nontrivial. We propose a hybrid physics-informed holomorphic neural network (HPIHNN) framework based on a decomposition of the solution into particular and homogeneous components. The particular component is computed by a spectral method on a simple extended domain, while the homogeneous component is approximated by a PIHNN trained only on the boundary with modified boundary data. The resulting formulation avoids meshing complex geometries and retains the dimensionality-reduction advantage of holomorphic representations. The method is applied to nonhomogeneous Poisson, Stokes, biharmonic, linear elasticity, and Helmholtz equations. Numerical experiments covering complex geometries, corner singularities, and nearly incompressible regimes demonstrate that the proposed method accurately resolves the corresponding solutions and, in the considered tests, generally achieves lower errors and shorter training times than standard PINNs. The results indicate that coupling spectral particular solutions with holomorphic neural approximations provides an efficient approach to nonhomogeneous PDEs on complex domains.
papers.summary: Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks (PIHNNs) use complex-analytic representations to satisfy homogeneous partial differential equations by construction, but extending them to nonhomogeneous problems is not straightforward. The hybrid PIHNN (`HPIHNN`) framework splits the solution into a particular component, computed by a spectral method on a simple extended domain, and a homogeneous component approximated by a PIHNN trained only on the boundary with modified boundary data, which avoids meshing complex geometries while keeping the dimensionality-reduction advantage of holomorphic representations. Applied to nonhomogeneous Poisson, Stokes, biharmonic, linear elasticity, and Helmholtz equations across complex geometries, corner singularities, and nearly incompressible regimes, **the method generally achieves lower errors and shorter training times than standard physics-informed neural networks (PINNs)** in the considered tests.

papers.title: NAGO: Noise-Aware Generative Operator via Flow Matching
papers.abstract: We introduce NAGO, a noise-aware generative operator for efficient sampling from invariant measures of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) in function space. Our central idea is to treat the source measure as a design variable rather than a fixed Gaussian default. We establish admissibility conditions for well-defined infinite-dimensional flows and show that the finite-band source--target covariance ratio controls the spectral stiffness of the marginal velocity field. This analysis yields an admissibility-constrained spectral-matching rule: choose a source that is sufficiently rough for well-posedness, then minimize covariance mismatch over the resolved Fourier modes. On three representative stochastic-field benchmarks, this source design improves few-step spectral accuracy and several complementary distributional and physical statistics. In a controlled Matern-field ablation, it reduces the accurate RK4 budget from about 30 steps for Gaussian functional flow matching to 3--5 steps, a $6$--$10\times$ reduction in neural ODE evaluations. These gains are strongest for stationary multiscale fields and depend on the metric, resolution, and guidance protocol.
papers.summary: Sampling from the invariant measures of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) in function space with flow matching normally starts from a fixed Gaussian source, which `NAGO`, a noise-aware generative operator, instead treats as a design variable. The authors establish admissibility conditions for well-defined infinite-dimensional flows, show that the finite-band ratio of source to target covariance controls the spectral stiffness of the marginal velocity field, and derive a rule from this: choose a source rough enough for well-posedness, then minimize covariance mismatch over the resolved Fourier modes. On three stochastic-field benchmarks the source design improves few-step spectral accuracy and several distributional and physical statistics, and **in a controlled Matérn-field ablation it reduces the accurate `RK4` budget from about 30 steps for Gaussian functional flow matching to 3–5 steps, a 6–10× reduction in neural ODE evaluations**, with gains strongest for stationary multiscale fields and dependent on the metric, resolution, and guidance protocol.

papers.title: The Role of Quantization in Loss Spikes
papers.abstract: Loss spikes in language model pretraining can waste substantial compute and derail otherwise healthy training runs. A primary driver of these instabilities is the growth and divergence of output logits in the final language modeling (LM) head. In this work, we study a particularly costly form of this instability associated with output logit growth: delayed, terminal divergences that emerge only after prolonged training, which we call time-bomb spikes. We find that these instabilities are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head, which eventually culminates in a loss spike. Crucially, reducing numerical precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while increasing precision improves stability. We then propose a simple yet effective mitigation that replaces AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum, suppressing logit growth and improving stability over long training horizons. Finally, we find that existing mitigation techniques from the literature (along with our own) all reduce quantization error, suggesting a shared numerical mechanism behind their effectiveness. Together, our results identify finite precision error as a hidden driver of time-bomb spikes and show that suppressing this error is key to stable long-horizon pretraining.
papers.summary: Loss spikes during language model pretraining waste compute and can derail otherwise healthy runs, and a primary driver is growth and divergence of the output logits in the final language modeling (LM) head. The authors study delayed, terminal divergences that emerge only after prolonged training, which they call time-bomb spikes, and find they are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head; **reducing numerical precision accelerates these spikes, while increasing precision improves stability**. Replacing `AdamW` with `SGD` with momentum on the LM head suppresses logit growth and improves stability over long horizons, and existing mitigations from the literature, along with this one, all turn out to reduce quantization error, pointing to a shared numerical mechanism behind their effectiveness.

papers.title: A Witnessing Duality for ReLU Network Depth
papers.abstract: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks asserts that every shallower network errs on some input; we ask when a weak theory can prove such a bound so that an error can be computed. For the exact computation of $\max(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, recent work shows two hidden layers suffice with unrestricted rational weights. By contrast, Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023) proved that integer weights require depth logarithmic in $n$, and Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025) extended the bound to nonbias weights whose denominators are powers of a fixed integer not divisible by a prime $q$. With integer weights the bound is sharp: the classical balanced construction has depth $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. For each fixed $q$ and depth cap $K$, we prove this known bound in $\mathbf{VTC}^0$, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation, together with a refuter that is itself such a computation and whose correctness the theory proves. Given a network with at most $K$ hidden layers, nonbias weights whose reduced denominators avoid $q$, arbitrary rational biases and $n>q^K$ inputs, the refuter returns a rational input of polynomial length on which the network errs. The proof makes the obstruction finite: an iterated intersection product of piecewise-linear functions is divisible by $q$ for the network but not for the maximum, so one of finitely many test points exposes the error. By witnessing, provable refutation corresponds to a provably correct refuter, and provable existence of a certified network to a provably correct constructor. On the construction side, we introduce certificates that label each maximum gadget by the inputs it aggregates; with them the theory verifies the balanced construction, which meets the refuter at the sharp threshold $n\le2^K$, and a rational family of polynomial description length and depth $O(\log n/\log\log n)$ built from known depth-two blocks.
papers.summary: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks states that every shallower network errs on some input, and the question here is when a weak formal theory can prove such a bound so that an erring input can actually be computed. For exact computation of the maximum of n inputs, prior work showed that integer weights need depth logarithmic in n, later extended to nonbias weights whose denominators avoid a prime q, and the classical balanced construction of depth ⌈log₂ n⌉ makes the integer bound sharp. For each fixed q and depth cap K, the authors prove this bound in `VTC⁰`, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation, **together with a refuter that is itself a constant-depth threshold computation and provably returns a polynomial-length rational input on which any such network with more than q^K inputs errs**, using an iterated intersection product of piecewise-linear functions that is divisible by q for the network but not for the maximum. On the construction side, certificates that label each maximum gadget by the inputs it aggregates let the theory verify the balanced construction, which meets the refuter at the sharp threshold n ≤ 2^K, as well as a rational family of polynomial description length and depth O(log n / log log n) built from known depth-two blocks.

papers.title: Human Evaluation with Automatic Scores: Separating Sampling and Estimation Gains
papers.abstract: Automatic judges offer inexpensive information about model outputs, but an evaluation team must decide how to turn that information into fewer human annotations. Scores can guide sampling, correct an estimate, or support adaptive acquisition, and these uses may capture overlapping gains. We compare their incremental value on fixed evaluation pools from three preference datasets, and 19 attributed-question-answering systems. Matched comparisons use the same scores, account for pilot labels and budget rules, and separate acquisition from estimation. Score stratification is a strong reference: after ten-bin stratification, the best fixed local linear correction offers only 1.00--5.27% further MSE reduction in the primary configurations. Unequal allocation offers larger gains in some pools, but can increase error when confident scores conceal variable human outcomes. Comparison on AttributedQA, shrinking learned quotas toward score-only quotas lowers pooled MSE for 17 of 19 systems relative to the score-only procedure, but ordinary pooled 95% intervals cover only 88.09--93.54%. The same shrinkage improves on the score-only reference in only one of eight preference configurations. Ranking experiments further show that lower individual MSE need not improve system selection. These findings support a simple starting procedure, proportional sampling within score strata followed by a stratified human mean, and identify what additional evidence is needed to justify correction or adaptation for the intended evaluation output.
papers.summary: Automatic judges provide cheap information about model outputs, and an evaluation team must decide whether to use those scores to guide sampling, correct an estimate, or drive adaptive acquisition, three uses whose gains may overlap. The authors compare the incremental value of each on fixed evaluation pools from three preference datasets and 19 attributed question-answering systems, with matched scores, pilot labels, and budget rules so that acquisition and estimation effects are separated. **After ten-bin score stratification, the best fixed local linear correction reduces mean squared error by only a further 1.00–5.27% in the primary configurations**; unequal allocation helps in some pools but can increase error when confident scores conceal variable human outcomes, shrinking learned quotas toward score-only quotas lowers pooled error for 17 of 19 `AttributedQA` systems but leaves ordinary 95% intervals covering only 88.09–93.54%, and lower individual error does not necessarily improve system ranking. The recommended starting procedure is proportional sampling within score strata followed by a stratified human mean, with correction or adaptation justified only by additional evidence tied to the intended evaluation output.

papers.title: Vendster: An Evaluation Arena to Investigate How Forecasting Tool Quality Affects LLM Agent Behaviors in Buyer-Vendor Negotiation
papers.abstract: Time-series forecasters are ranked almost entirely by accuracy metrics, but a forecast's decision value, its effect on the downstream decision, need not track accuracy and is rarely measured. This problem compounds as large language model (LLM) agents increasingly consume forecasters as tools, mediating them through stochastic, opaque policies. We present Vendster, an evaluation arena measuring how a forecaster's bias and prediction-interval width change the outcome of a buyer--vendor discount negotiation between two LLM agents. In the reference instance Vendster-M5, sampling base demand patterns from the M5 dataset, we evaluate two frontier-closed LLM families (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.6 Sol) and two open ones (DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-235B-A22B). Model-generated forecasts raise sales target attainment by up to +17 percentage points (p<0.001), yet standard forecast evaluation metrics such as relWQL and MASE do not predict negotiation outcomes at a statistically significant level. To isolate the causal structure, we substitute in synthetic forecasts with controlled bias and interval width. Under-prediction bias significantly improves outcomes for agents that react more to the forecasts---dose-response slopes -0.387 and -0.416 (p<0.001). Interval width has no statistically significant effect at zero bias. These findings indicate that the direction of forecast bias and agent forecast-reactivity are more strongly associated with downstream outcomes than forecast accuracy. Vendster is fully customizable and released under CC BY-NC 4.0 at https://github.com/amazon-science/Vendster.
papers.summary: Time-series forecasters are ranked almost entirely by accuracy, yet a forecast's decision value need not track accuracy, and the gap widens when large language model (LLM) agents consume forecasts as tools through stochastic, opaque policies. `Vendster` is an evaluation arena that measures how a forecaster's bias and prediction-interval width change the outcome of a buyer–vendor discount negotiation between two LLM agents; the reference instance `Vendster-M5` samples base demand patterns from the `M5` dataset and evaluates `Claude Opus 4.6`, `GPT-5.6 Sol`, `DeepSeek-V3.2`, and `Qwen3-235B-A22B`. Model-generated forecasts raise sales target attainment by up to 17 percentage points, but standard forecast metrics such as `relWQL` and `MASE` do not predict negotiation outcomes at a statistically significant level, and substituting synthetic forecasts with controlled bias and width shows that **under-prediction bias significantly improves outcomes for agents that react more to forecasts, while interval width has no significant effect at zero bias**. The arena is fully customizable and released under a non-commercial license.

papers.title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting
papers.abstract: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires an agent to connect financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce a company's reported earnings. We introduce EPSBench, a benchmark for studying this ability across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies. Agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts, and news, then estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence. A shared accounting calculator converts these estimates into GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS), providing a common basis for comparing forecast assumptions. We evaluate six models under a common harness, assessing point forecast error relative to date-matched analyst consensus and checking whether their prediction intervals achieve the stated coverage. Three models show no detectable paired difference in point forecast error from consensus, and three have higher error. Across all six models, nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37--70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because the forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.
papers.summary: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires connecting financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce a company's reported earnings. `EPSBench` covers 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies: agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts, and news, estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence, and a shared accounting calculator converts those estimates into GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS) so that forecast assumptions are comparable. Six models evaluated under a common harness are scored on point error against date-matched analyst consensus and on prediction-interval coverage; three show no detectable paired difference from consensus and three have higher error, and **nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37–70% of runs that return an interval**, with most misses above the upper bound because the forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.

papers.title: Inner-Learning: From Hand-Coded Beliefs to Declarative Knowledge in Trick-Taking Games
papers.abstract: We present a declarative approach to belief-state modeling in trick-taking card games. Starting from a state-of-the-art Skat player, we automatically extract its hand-coded inference rules into a domain-specific language built on the primitive $\neg\mathsf{holds}(P,C)$, denoting that player $P$ cannot hold any card in set $C$. Round-trip code generation verifies that the extracted rules reproduce the original engine's intended behavior, up to three audited bugs in the original that the declarative engine corrects. We then grow the rule base through symmetric derivation and annotation of an expert strategy document---unifying code, symmetry, and expertise in one representation. We extend the knowledge representation with \emph{cardinality constraints}: at-most-$k$ and at-least-$k$ bounds on the cards a player holds from a named group, expressed in the same declarative language and enforced at world-generation time. Confidence parameters connect symbolic rules to probabilistic belief updates. Self-play evaluation shows the declarative engine measurably improving winning percentage and score over the original hand-coded engine, with the extracted rules, the human-annotated rules, and the cardinality constraints each contributing to the effect.
papers.summary: Belief-state modeling in trick-taking card games is usually hand-coded, so starting from a state-of-the-art Skat player, the authors automatically extract its inference rules into a domain-specific language built on a single primitive stating that a given player cannot hold any card from a given set. Round-trip code generation verifies that the extracted rules reproduce the original engine's intended behavior, up to three audited bugs in the original that the declarative engine corrects, and the rule base is then grown through symmetric derivation and by annotating an expert strategy document, unifying code, symmetry, and human expertise in one representation. Cardinality constraints, at-most-k and at-least-k bounds on the cards a player holds from a named group, are expressed in the same language and enforced at world-generation time, with confidence parameters connecting symbolic rules to probabilistic belief updates. **In self-play, the declarative engine measurably improves winning percentage and score over the original hand-coded engine**, with the extracted rules, the human-annotated rules, and the cardinality constraints each contributing.

papers.title: Does 3D Pose Improve Action Valuation in Football? An Empirical Study of Pose Representations and Learning Objectives
papers.abstract: Football action valuation estimates players' contributions to future scoring. Existing multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) models use 2D positions and velocities, omitting posture information relevant to imminent actions. We investigate whether adding 3D pose to a SARSA-based model improves observed-action values relative to attack returns: goals, conceded goals or final expected possession value. Using UEFA Champions League 2022/23 event, tracking and 3D pose data, we compare six representations (no pose, raw joints, torso and head orientation, and spatial-temporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) embeddings) across five learning settings and three seeds. The settings vary temporal-difference targets and action-prediction loss, with Monte Carlo return regression as a reference.
