Across 50 on-ball and off-ball comparisons, pose robustly improved return prediction in only three, all using torso and head orientation, while worsening it in twelve, mostly with ST-GCN. Training choices had greater effects: removing the action-prediction loss raised on-ball skill of position-only values from 0.003 to 0.040 and their correlation with expected goals from 0.23 to 0.60; the improvement in return prediction persisted at matched training length. Separately, pose improved prediction of the on-ball action 0.2 s ahead (macro AUC 0.914 to 0.934 with raw joints), while the passer's pose during execution improved pass-success prediction (AUC 0.844 to 0.856). Within this training protocol, pose informed imminent actions but rarely improved observed-action values.
papers.summary: Football action valuation estimates players' contributions to future scoring, and existing multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) models use only 2D positions and velocities, omitting posture that is relevant to imminent actions. Using UEFA Champions League 2022/23 event, tracking, and 3D pose data, the authors add pose to a `SARSA`-based model and compare six representations (no pose, raw joints, torso and head orientation, and spatial-temporal graph convolutional network (`ST-GCN`) embeddings) across five learning settings that vary temporal-difference targets and an action-prediction loss, with Monte Carlo return regression as a reference. **Across 50 on-ball and off-ball comparisons, pose robustly improved return prediction in only three, all using torso and head orientation, and worsened it in twelve**, mostly with `ST-GCN`; training choices mattered more, since removing the action-prediction loss raised the on-ball skill of position-only values from 0.003 to 0.040 and their correlation with expected goals from 0.23 to 0.60. Pose did help predict the on-ball action 0.2 seconds ahead (macro AUC 0.914 to 0.934 with raw joints) and pass success from the passer's pose during execution (AUC 0.844 to 0.856), so within this protocol pose informed imminent actions but rarely improved observed-action values.

papers.title: Robust LLM-Generated Text Detection through Matched Conditional-Response Probing
papers.abstract: Reliable detection of large language model (LLM)-generated text must remain effective under meaning-preserving text revisions, such as rewriting, polishing, and expansion. In practice, LLM outputs are often rewritten, polished, expanded, translated, or lightly edited before publication, weakening the lexical, syntactic, and local discourse cues used by many existing detectors. We introduce \textbf{M}atched \textbf{C}onditional-\textbf{R}esponse \textbf{P}robing (\textbf{MCRP}), a frozen-LLM probing framework that measures how a candidate text responds when a semantically matched condition is introduced, removed, or replaced. For each candidate, the frozen probe LLM first generates a short semantic condition and then compares token-level losses and prompt--target attention measurements under matched, null, and control conditions. It aggregates bidirectional conditioned alignment, counterfactual sensitivity, and internal attention coupling into a probe representation, on which it trains a lightweight supervised random-forest classifier while keeping the probe LLM frozen. Across standard detection, robustness to meaning-preserving text revisions, multilingual, and multidomain evaluations, MCRP achieves consistently strong performance. Under rewriting, polishing, and expansion, it reaches 93.97\% F1 and 96.24\% ROC-AUC, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 19.50 and 25.77 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations show that the response feature groups make complementary contributions to predictive performance. In the condition-control study, matched conditions consistently outperform random, mismatched, and corrupted alternatives, demonstrating a measurable incremental benefit from semantic matching.
papers.summary: Detectors of large language model (LLM)-generated text must stay effective under meaning-preserving revisions such as rewriting, polishing, and expansion, which weaken the lexical, syntactic, and local discourse cues that many existing detectors rely on. Matched Conditional-Response Probing (`MCRP`) uses a frozen probe LLM that first generates a short semantic condition for each candidate text and then compares token-level losses and prompt–target attention measurements under matched, null, and control conditions, aggregating bidirectional conditioned alignment, counterfactual sensitivity, and internal attention coupling into a representation for a lightweight random-forest classifier. **Under rewriting, polishing, and expansion it reaches 93.97% F1 and 96.24% ROC-AUC, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 19.50 and 25.77 percentage points respectively**, performs consistently across standard, multilingual, and multidomain evaluations, and a condition-control study shows matched conditions beat random, mismatched, and corrupted alternatives.

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
papers.abstract: Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $\gamma=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.
papers.summary: Bisimulation metrics give a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions are largely confined to discounted Markov decision processes, where contraction arguments guarantee well-defined fixed points. The authors reinterpret prior metric operators as Bellman–Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define the metrics as the corresponding game value functions, **which yields unique definitions for total-reward and average-reward problems even when the discount factor equals 1** and lets dynamic-programming theory and algorithms transfer. The game view also characterizes when metric finiteness follows from structural properties of the underlying MDP, motivates directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs, and supports an abstract framework over transition coupling sets that recovers many existing metrics and guides new ones. The metrics are shown to bound total-reward differences and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences, with error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in both settings.

papers.title: CHORD: Cross-Model Hallucination Detection via Relational Graph Discrimination
papers.abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. Due to strong empirical performance, internal representation-based methods have emerged as the prevailing direction for detecting hallucinations, yet they remain largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs. In this paper, we study an important yet underexplored problem, termed cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD), which aims to train hallucination detectors on source LLMs while ensuring performance on unseen target LLMs. The core challenge of CMHD lies in cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits the transferability of classical representation-based detectors. Through analysis and empirical validation, we show that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features capture transferable detection signals despite semantic inconsistency. Based on this observation, we propose cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (CHORD), a relational graph discrimination framework that represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features. It feeds these graphs into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. Extensive experiments show that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/MiracleworkerD/CHORD.
papers.summary: Hallucination detectors built on a large language model's (LLM's) internal representations perform well but are largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs, because hidden states from different models are semantically inconsistent. The authors frame this as cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD) and show, through analysis and experiments, that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features carry transferable detection signals despite that heterogeneity. Cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (`CHORD`) represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features, applies relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape those features toward transferable detection signals; **in extensive experiments it outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization**. Code is released.

papers.title: LLM-PowerTrace: A Dataset of Time-Resolved GPU Power Traces for AI Compute
papers.abstract: AI compute is becoming large and fast-changing electrical loads. Its impacts on data center infrastructure and power grids depend not only on total energy consumption, but also on how their power draw moves over sub-second to minute timescales, including peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations across accelerators. Existing energy benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) report aggregate quantities such as joules per token and rarely release the underlying time-series measurements, leaving these power dynamics poorly characterized and difficult to model. We introduce LLM-PowerTrace, an open dataset of time-resolved, per-GPU power traces for LLM fine-tuning and inference, sampled every 100\,ms on varying NVIDIA platforms paired with complete workload and system metadata. For fine-tuning, LLM-PowerTrace profiles open model families spanning a wide range of model sizes and fine-tuning methods, together with controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing. For inference, it covers variations in concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request-arrival patterns. LLM-PowerTrace profiles a set of open model families across a wide range of model sizes, and controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing for fine-tuning, and it sweeps concurrency, GPU frequency, KV cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request arrival patterns for inference. Built upon power traces, we define power-grid-facing metrics as well as AI-compute power\&energy scaling law for extrapolating beyond the measured settings. Together, LLM-PowerTrace provides a dataset foundation for modeling, forecasting, and managing the fast-changing electrical behavior of AI compute.
papers.summary: AI compute is becoming a large and fast-changing electrical load whose impact on data centers and power grids depends on sub-second to minute-scale peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations across accelerators, yet existing large language model (LLM) energy benchmarks report aggregates such as joules per token and rarely release the underlying time series. `LLM-PowerTrace` is an open dataset of per-GPU power traces sampled every 100 ms on varying NVIDIA platforms with complete workload and system metadata, covering fine-tuning across open model families, sizes, and methods with controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing, and inference sweeps over concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request-arrival patterns. **Built on the traces, the authors define power-grid-facing metrics and an AI-compute power and energy scaling law for extrapolating beyond the measured settings**, positioning the dataset as a foundation for modeling, forecasting, and managing the electrical behavior of AI workloads.

papers.title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.
papers.summary: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training, and the question here is what an 8B-scale system should retain and how that information should be organized for later decisions. The agent keeps complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories holding instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry, with an 8B observer summarizing observations, an 8B reasoner using the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, and a geometric controller executing the selected targets. On `R2R-CE` val-unseen the complete system scores highest among the evaluated `Qwen3`-based zero-shot baselines, and **removing temporal memory reduces success rate and raises average path length from 16.9 m to 39.1 m**, while removing the spatial-map and planning component also lowers success. On a `Unitree Go2` robot the zero-shot method achieves higher success than a post-trained baseline in corridor and office environments, and a complementary `LAW2` evaluation uses paired instruction interventions to examine instruction following beyond endpoint success.

papers.title: Extremely Sparse-View Computed Tomography from 2D Projections via Pose-Aware Diffusion Priors
papers.abstract: Extremely sparse-view computed tomography (xSV-CT) is critical when scanning time, motion, or radiation tolerance limits each scan to only a few projections. In many such scenarios, the same acquisition limits also constrain dataset construction, making pre-reconstructed 3D volumes from dense scans unavailable. This exposes a gap in current sparse-view approaches: Optimization-based methods, which use the sparse measurements directly but lack data-driven priors to suppress artifacts, and learning-based methods, which use strong priors but usually require densely scanned training volumes acquired outside the xSV-CT regime. We study this train-sparse / infer-sparse setting by learning a pose-aware diffusion prior from one 2D projection per training sample, then guiding diffusion sampling with measured-view fidelity, shared-volume reprojection, and projection-physics consistency for tomographic reconstruction. On two public CT datasets across 1-, 4-, and 8-view settings, the proposed method achieves the best novel-view synthesis scores and best or competitive reconstruction quality compared with baselines that use dense-volume supervision.
papers.summary: Extremely sparse-view computed tomography (xSV-CT) matters when scanning time, motion, or radiation tolerance limit each scan to a few projections, and the same constraints often prevent building the densely scanned 3D training volumes that learning-based methods usually require. In this train-sparse / infer-sparse setting, the authors learn a pose-aware diffusion prior from one 2D projection per training sample, then guide diffusion sampling with measured-view fidelity, shared-volume reprojection, and projection-physics consistency to reconstruct the volume. **On two public CT datasets at 1, 4, and 8 views, the method achieves the best novel-view synthesis scores and best or competitive reconstruction quality against baselines that use dense-volume supervision.**

papers.title: Can LLMs Faithfully Solve Ontology Engineering Tasks? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study
papers.abstract: Ontological knowledge underpins large language model (LLM) performance on knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing evaluations of LLMs' ontological understanding largely rely on behavioral correctness, leaving the underlying mechanisms unexplained. Existing mechanistic interpretability work has largely focused on instance-level factual knowledge, leaving ontological knowledge under-explored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MIOE, a causal-abstraction benchmark that evaluates interchange interventions for two ontology engineering tasks: entity typing and subsumption prediction. MIOE tests whether learned internal intervention targets can change an ontology-level target answer while preserving class-specific auxiliary information. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, we evaluate SAE-, DBM-, and DAS-based methods, including multi-task and multi-layer variants. Distributed subspace methods give the strongest results and generalize across prompt settings, but the induced changes remain only partially separated from auxiliary class-specific information. Multi-task objectives and contiguous layer-window interventions improve this balance, while class-level analyses reveal substantial variation across ontology classes. These results suggest that ontological predictions are mechanistically accessible in LLMs, although current methods do not yet isolate a cleanly disentangled causal mechanism for ontological knowledge.
papers.summary: Evaluations of large language models' (LLMs') ontological understanding rely on behavioral correctness, and mechanistic interpretability work has concentrated on instance-level factual knowledge rather than ontological knowledge. `MIOE` is a causal-abstraction benchmark that applies interchange interventions to two ontology engineering tasks, entity typing and subsumption prediction, testing whether learned internal intervention targets can change an ontology-level answer while preserving class-specific auxiliary information. Across `Qwen3-8B` and `Qwen3-4B`, comparing `SAE`-, `DBM`-, and `DAS`-based methods including multi-task and multi-layer variants, **distributed subspace methods give the strongest results and generalize across prompt settings, but the induced changes remain only partially separated from auxiliary class-specific information**; multi-task objectives and contiguous layer-window interventions improve this balance, and results vary substantially across ontology classes. The authors conclude that ontological predictions are mechanistically accessible but that current methods do not yet isolate a cleanly disentangled causal mechanism.

papers.title: A Case Study of a Multi-Agent Kernel-Optimization Loop That Learns a New AI Accelerator
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models write correct CUDA kernels for most single-operator benchmark tasks, yet their accuracy collapses on accelerators whose architecture and programming language they have rarely seen. We present a case study of an LLM agent loop built for such accelerators. Our example is the FuriosaAI RNGD NPU, programmed in a recent, sparsely documented Rust DSL, where the loop optimized three Gemma-4-12B decode kernels over 12 days on a shared, scarce device. The loop builds its own target knowledge: it writes and checks a summary of the DSL documentation, measures the chip with microbenchmarks, records compiler-derived legality rules, and revisits this knowledge when the toolchain changes, rechecking rules and measurements where it can. A role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees explores whole-kernel designs and accumulates small accepted changes in the best version of each kernel. Because device time is scarce and readings are noisy, cheap checks screen new designs before any device run, and late in the run a change was accepted only after repeated comparisons with the best kernel on the device. The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline, each within 1.25x of the cycles needed just to move its weights. Our prompts, profiler and acceptance test are available at https://github.com/bgchun-fs/multi-agent-kernel-gen-loop.
papers.summary: Frontier large language models write correct CUDA kernels for most single-operator tasks, but their accuracy collapses on accelerators whose architecture and programming language they have rarely seen. The case study runs an LLM agent loop that optimizes three `Gemma-4-12B` decode kernels for the FuriosaAI `RNGD` NPU, programmed in a recent and sparsely documented Rust domain-specific language, over 12 days on a shared device. The loop builds its own target knowledge by summarizing and checking the DSL documentation, running microbenchmarks on the chip, and recording compiler-derived legality rules, then runs a role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees with cheap checks screening every design before a scarce device run. **The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline**, each within 1.25x of the cycles needed just to move its weights.

papers.title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
papers.abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.
papers.summary: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, but its standard training objective carries a flaw that grows with scale. The MTP cross-entropy gradient decomposes exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and a low signal-to-noise residual that buries that useful signal. A KL gradient-recovery trick recovers the KL gradient exactly by routing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy gradients straight-through, which needs no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and works with fused cross-entropy kernels, giving `Soft-MTP`, a one-line change that supports both DeepSeek-style and Meta-style MTP with no added parameters or measurable overhead. **From 167M to 1.2B parameters, `Soft-MTP` beats standard MTP on NTP perplexity, speculative decoding speed, and zero-shot accuracy at every scale**, with stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B, and it matches or exceeds direct KL minimization on most metrics.
papers.highlight_summary:
Standard multi-token prediction (MTP) heads are trained with cross-entropy against the data, but the gradient of that loss decomposes exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each head toward the model's own next-token distribution and a noisy residual equal to the next-token cross-entropy gradient. The paper shows the residual has low signal-to-noise ratio and interferes with learning, then removes it with a one-line change that recovers the KL gradient without ever materializing vocabulary-sized logits.

- The KL gradient-recovery trick adds a zero-valued straight-through term to the NTP hidden states so that the NTP loss backpropagates the negative residual into each MTP head, which combined with the ordinary MTP cross-entropy gradient leaves exactly the KL gradient reaching the MTP heads and shared trunk while the shared output head still sees cross-entropy.
- The residual carries roughly **80%** of the MTP gradient reaching the trunk yet has about **4x lower SNR** than the KL component, with the gap widening from **4.1x at 167M to 4.6x at 1.2B**, and a step along it consistently increases NTP loss.
- On `LLaMA`-style models from 167M to 1.2B trained on 31.5B `FineWeb-Edu` tokens with `DeepSeek`-style MTP, `Soft-MTP` beats standard MTP on NTP perplexity, speculative-decoding acceptance length (**+1.8 to 2.2%**) and speedup at every scale, raises average zero-shot accuracy by about **0.5 points** at 689M and 1.2B where it also surpasses the NTP baseline, and after NTP-only fine-tuning at 1.2B leads MTP in seven of eight math and code cells, including **+3.1 points** on `HumanEval` pass@64 and **+1.8** on `MATH-500`.
- It matches or exceeds explicit `KL-MTP` on most metrics at identical FLOPs, MFU and fused-cross-entropy peak memory to standard MTP, whereas `KL-MTP` lowers throughput by **5.6%** and adds **21 GB** of peak memory; keeping cross-entropy at the output head also preserves the readout's effective rank (**437 vs. 131** for standard MTP and 496 for NTP).
- Limitations are that the KL gradient is biased toward the NTP distribution rather than the data, the largest model is only 1.2B so frontier-scale gains are extrapolated, sequence-sharded parallelism needs a small extra backward-pass exchange, and the trick delivers the exact KL gradient only to the heads and trunk, not the shared output head.

papers.title: MUSE: Multi-Level Memory with Selective Runtime Injection for Scientific Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Historical experience can guide scientific coding at multiple levels, but task-level retrieval may miss implementation lessons that become relevant during execution. We introduce MUSE, a memory management framework combining multi-level memory with selective runtime injection for scientific coding agents. MUSE builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories. At initialization, the agent receives global memory and problem-matched approach-level memory. During execution, current interactions are used to retrieve implementation-level memory. An LLM gate selects relevant experience and generates specific review advice, or skips injection. Across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics. Ablations support the multi-level design and gated injection, while transfer experiments show that memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks. These results show that multi-level memory and selective runtime injection enable effective reuse of experience in scientific coding. Code is available at https://github.com/hr-jin/MUSE.
papers.summary: Historical experience can guide scientific coding agents at several levels, but retrieving memory only at the task level misses implementation lessons that become relevant during execution. `MUSE` builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from past trajectories, gives the agent global and problem-matched approach-level memory at initialization, and retrieves implementation-level memory from the current interactions during execution, with an LLM gate that either selects relevant experience and writes specific review advice or skips injection. **Across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, `MUSE` outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on every evaluation metric**, and ablations plus transfer experiments between kernel benchmarks support the multi-level design and gated injection.

papers.title: Fu-TCM: a multimodal large language model that learns traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.
papers.summary: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to locate and characterize disease, differentiate syndromes, and guide treatment, a complete chain of reasoning. `Fu-TCM` is a multimodal large language model trained on data retained after cleaning roughly 7.12 million examples from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases, and public datasets, then optimized with Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (`BGPO`), which rewards response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields, and the final syndrome prediction. **`Fu-TCM-27B` led all six TCM reasoning, text, and vision benchmarks with a macro-average accuracy of 81.01%**, 7.13 points above the strongest reference model with complete results, with its largest margin of 11.90 points on `Fu-bianzheng`. Case-level analysis found a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome selection in most evaluated models.

papers.title: Optimal Regret for Communication-Efficient Decentralized Online Learning
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, where $n$ learners over a network jointly minimize a sequence of global loss functions based only on their local losses and compressed messages from their neighbors. The best known regret bounds for this problem are $O(\omega^{-1/2}n\rho^{-1}\sqrt{T\ln n})$ and $O(\omega^{-1}n\rho^{-2}\ln n\ln T)$ for convex and strongly convex loss functions, respectively, where $\rho\in(0,1)$ is the spectral gap of the communication matrix and $\omega\in(0,1]$ is the compression quality factor. Compared with the corresponding lower bounds of $\Omega(\omega^{-1/2}n\rho^{-1/4}\sqrt{T})$ and $\Omega(\omega^{-1}n\rho^{-1/2}\ln T)$, these upper bounds exhibit polynomial gaps in their dependence on $\rho^{-1}$. To close these gaps, we first develop Ascent-gossip, which combines an online compression strategy with a Chebyshev recursion and attains a faster consensus rate than existing compressed gossip methods. Furthermore, by adopting Ascent-gossip, we propose an online algorithm that achieves optimal regret bounds of $\widetilde O(\omega^{-1/2}n\rho^{-1/4}\sqrt{T})$ and $\widetilde O(\omega^{-1}n\rho^{-1/2}\ln T)$ for convex and strongly convex loss functions, respectively. Up to logarithmic factors in $n$ and $\rho^{-1}$, these results match the lower bounds in terms of $T$, $n$, $\rho$, and $\omega$.
papers.summary: In decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, n learners on a network jointly minimize a sequence of global losses using only local losses and compressed messages from neighbors, and the best known regret bounds have polynomial gaps in the spectral gap ρ of the communication matrix relative to the lower bounds. `Ascent-gossip` combines an online compression strategy with a Chebyshev recursion to reach consensus faster than existing compressed gossip methods, and an online algorithm built on it closes the gaps. **The resulting regret bounds of Õ(ω^(-1/2) n ρ^(-1/4) √T) for convex and Õ(ω^(-1) n ρ^(-1/2) ln T) for strongly convex losses match the lower bounds** in T, n, ρ, and the compression quality factor ω up to logarithmic factors in n and 1/ρ.

papers.title: Learning a Prior-Data Fitted Network for Graph Foundation Models via Structural Causal Model Priors
papers.abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for learning transferable representations across different graphs and domains. However, existing GFMs face notable limitations, including limited pre-training scale or reliance on aligning with textual information in Large Language Models (LLMs). To overcome these limitations, recent studies have drawn inspiration from prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), which learn from large synthetic datasets and support multi-domain prediction backed by causal learning. However, existing graph PFNs encounter severe difficulties in modeling causal relationships within and across node and edge sets, generating diverse graph structures, and designing suitable architectures that can learn from complex synthetic datasets. To address these challenges, we propose **GSCM-PFN** (Graph SCM-based Prior-Data Fitted Network), a graph PFN pre-trained on synthetic data generated from an SCM-based prior that jointly models nodes and graph topology. Specifically, we (1) design a joint feature-edge-label structural causal model (SCM) to guide synthetic graph generation and capture causal relationships within and across node and edge sets; (2) introduce prior-guided node-edge dependency modeling to instantiate diverse graph generation strategies, and prove that our SCM-based generation prior is more expressive than existing priors; and (3) propose a feature-permutation-invariant dual-path graph network with theoretical guarantees for learning from diverse synthetic graphs. Experiments on 23 real-world benchmarks show that GSCM-PFN outperforms both conventional GFMs and PFN-based GFMs, without utilizing real-world graph data for pre-training. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GSCM-PFN-A3A3/
papers.summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) promise transferable representations across graphs and domains, but existing ones have limited pre-training scale or depend on aligning with text in large language models, and prior graph prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) struggle to model causal relationships within and across node and edge sets, to generate diverse structures, and to learn from complex synthetic data. `GSCM-PFN` is pre-trained only on synthetic graphs generated from a joint feature-edge-label structural causal model (SCM) that models nodes and topology together, uses prior-guided node-edge dependency modeling to instantiate diverse generation strategies, and learns with a feature-permutation-invariant dual-path graph network; the authors prove the SCM prior is more expressive than existing priors. **On 23 real-world benchmarks, `GSCM-PFN` outperforms both conventional GFMs and PFN-based GFMs without using any real-world graph data for pre-training.**

papers.title: Statutory Article Retrieval from Arabic Judicial Narratives: Family Law and Law of Evidence in Saudi Arabia
papers.abstract: Reliable legal information retrieval must ground legal reasoning in authoritative statutory sources. In Arabic judicial settings, long factual narratives must be mapped to concise articles that express abstract legal rules, creating a narrative-to-legal-rule abstraction gap. Using a benchmark of 200 synthetic Saudi Arabic judicial cases and 381 articles from the Family Law and the Law of Evidence, we compare word-level and char-4 BM25, zero-shot dense encoders, per-law retrieval, dense-sparse reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), and a proposed Decompose-and-Refine (DaR) pipeline. In DaR, a large language model splits each narrative into disputed legal issues and generates, for each issue, three retrieval channels: a statute-style paraphrase, legal keywords, and a candidate taxonomy chapter. On the whole corpus, the instructed Qwen3-Embedding-8B dense encoder reaches an MRR@10 of 0.849, the best result of any non-decomposed system. Under per-law scoring, this advantage reflects Family Law only: restricted to Evidence articles, the same encoder drops to an MRR@10 of 0.087, and fusion with BM25 raises it only to 0.207. DaR changes this picture, raising Evidence MRR@10 to 0.696 and Family MRR@10 to 0.864. Without decomposition, the two laws favor different strategies; under DaR, the same retriever achieves the best MRR@10 on both.
papers.summary: Legal retrieval in Arabic judicial settings must map long factual narratives onto concise statutory articles that express abstract rules, creating a narrative-to-legal-rule abstraction gap. On a benchmark of 200 synthetic Saudi judicial cases and 381 articles from the Family Law and the Law of Evidence, the study compares word-level and character 4-gram `BM25`, zero-shot dense encoders, per-law retrieval, dense-sparse reciprocal rank fusion, and a Decompose-and-Refine (`DaR`) pipeline in which a large language model splits each narrative into disputed legal issues and generates a statute-style paraphrase, legal keywords, and a candidate taxonomy chapter for each. The instructed `Qwen3-Embedding-8B` encoder reaches a mean reciprocal rank at 10 (MRR@10) of 0.849 on the whole corpus, the best non-decomposed result, but drops to 0.087 on Evidence articles alone, and fusion with `BM25` lifts that only to 0.207. **`DaR` raises Evidence MRR@10 to 0.696 and Family MRR@10 to 0.864**, so the same retriever is best on both laws.

papers.title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?
papers.abstract: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, with predictions evaluated against subsequent outcomes. Existing benchmarks assess financial knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting, but evaluating the full research process requires a strictly frozen information set and professional evaluation criteria. We introduce Investor's Last Exam (ILE), an equity-research benchmark led by experienced buy-side investors and fund managers. Its three components are a versioned financial database spanning 3.43 million document versions and nine source categories, supplemented by structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation; a task taxonomy organized around professional analyst deliverables; and an expert-led framework linking scoring criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Evaluation spans 86 assignments and jointly assesses research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead overall at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet even Astra scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Our results show that even state-of-the-art models fail to translate overall research capability into predictive performance. ILE shifts the evaluation unit from isolated capabilities to the evidence--assumption--judgment chain, allowing researchers to locate where analytical advantages fail to translate into forecasts and investment judgments, and providing a traceable, diagnostic foundation for training and evaluating financial agents.
papers.summary: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, yet existing benchmarks test knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting in isolation rather than the full research process under a strictly frozen information set. Investor's Last Exam (`ILE`), led by buy-side investors and fund managers, combines a versioned financial database of 3.43 million document versions across nine source categories plus structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation, a task taxonomy built around professional analyst deliverables, and an expert-led scoring framework linking criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Across 86 assignments scored on research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance, **`GPT-6 Astra` and `Claude Opus 5.5` lead at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet `Astra` scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model**, showing that overall research capability does not translate into predictive performance.
papers.highlight_summary:
Existing finance benchmarks filter retrieval by publication date only, so post-cutoff information still leaks into retrieval, computation, and scoring, and they test isolated skills rather than the full analyst chain from evidence to forecast to decision. `ILE` is a buy-side-expert-authored equity research benchmark built on a versioned corpus where every document version carries a validated availability timestamp enforced across the entire toolchain, with rubrics tied to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs, and it scores research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment returns jointly.

- The corpus holds **3.43 million document versions** across nine source categories (1.52 TB), the cutoff applies to search, read, download, and table tools with retrieved results frozen against later revisions, and 86 expert-authored tasks span seven deliverable categories, graded by deterministic checks for numeric criteria and `GPT-6 Astra` for semantic ones.
- `GPT-6 Astra` leads overall at **68.1** and `Claude Opus 5.5` follows at **66.9**, but Astra's 78.9 on Research & Evidence and 77.6 on Evaluate & Decide fall to **52.5** on Forecast & Model, with Opus essentially tied at 52.6, so forecast construction is the shared weak point.
- Predictive criteria reorder the field: `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash` leads forecast-outcome scoring at 40.3 versus 37.7 for Astra and 37.6 for Opus, and in the March to August 2026 trading simulation `Hunyuan 4 Preview` returns **8.50%**, Flash 7.98%, Astra 7.18%, and `Kimi K3` 7.15%, ahead of Opus at 6.39% and an always-long baseline of 1.18%, while Flash costs $0.36 per task against $7.96 for Opus.
- Astra scores 68.3 on public-web search versus 68.1 on the versioned database, yet **57%** of its public-web trajectories contain post-cutoff sources such as realized Microsoft revenue and Tesla deliveries despite dated queries, so comparable scores do not certify that the information boundary held.
- The top-scoring model also serves as the semantic grader, which the authors acknowledge invites self-enhancement bias, pretraining memorization of historical outcomes remains uncontrolled since only retrieval leakage is blocked, the trading sample covers just 20 assignments and 11 companies, and strict submission mode drops some systems sharply, with `Step 5 Preview` falling from 55.1 to 34.5.

papers.title: Aligning Misaligned Benchmarks for Single-View Novel View Synthesis
papers.abstract: While single-view novel view synthesis methods have been dramatically enhanced recently, how to quantify their performance has yet to be standardized. In this work, we demonstrate that an important factor lies in how each method's own reference frame is aligned with the so-called ground-truth pose. Existing methods often rely on test-time optimization of target poses for this alignment, which inherently is ill-posed due to the complexity of the optimization landscape of camera poses vs render accuracy, leading to methods being evaluated at an arbitrary local optimum. Some recognize this limitation and thus rely on 3D reconstructions of entire scenes using training and test views to align poses, which may be infeasible. In this work, instead, we propose to use traditional 2D-to-2D and 2D-to-3D image matching techniques to align 3D reconstructions. We also evaluate only within co-visible regions, between different views, which is the only place where a `correct' ground truth can be defined. Our evaluations show that with proper coordinate alignment, novel-view synthesis methods that use explicit 3D Gaussians achieve the state of the art, despite being previously reported in the literature to be outperformed by pure image-based 2D methods. We further provide a simple baseline that directly utilizes an off-the-shelf video generator and a feed-forward geometry estimator. Our simple baseline is already comparable to state-of-the-art methods specifically trained for novel-view synthesis, without any task-specific training.
papers.summary: Single-view novel view synthesis has improved rapidly, but its evaluation is not standardized because each method's own reference frame must be aligned with the ground-truth pose, and the usual test-time optimization of target poses is ill-posed and lands at arbitrary local optima. The proposed protocol instead aligns 3D reconstructions with classical 2D-to-2D and 2D-to-3D image matching and evaluates only co-visible regions between views, the only place where a correct ground truth exists. **With proper coordinate alignment, methods using explicit 3D Gaussians achieve the state of the art despite being reported in prior literature as outperformed by pure image-based 2D methods.** A simple baseline that pairs an off-the-shelf video generator with a feed-forward geometry estimator is already comparable to methods trained specifically for novel-view synthesis.

papers.title: WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent From Narration to Long-Form Video
papers.abstract: Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear. We address this gap with WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions and repairs. Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos, this pipeline yields over 130K training examples. We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates production and recovers from failures within the same harness. Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing quality and delivery reliability. Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33x fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.
papers.summary: Producing a long-form video from narration requires interdependent editing decisions that must stay coherent across shots, and existing agentic editors use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving unclear how compact task-adapted policies trade quality against cost. `WeVisCut` pairs an agent harness that maintains shared production state, so tool feedback informs later decisions and repairs, with a four-stage data pipeline that uses editing inversion and verified replay to recover editing intent from 3,750 finished videos into over 130K executable training examples for a single 9B policy. On a new 100-task benchmark with five metrics for editing quality and delivery reliability, under a shared tool environment, **the 9B policy performs comparably to `Claude Opus 5` while using nearly 33x fewer generated tokens per successful output minute**, and it outperforms task-matched native editors on the proposed metrics.
papers.highlight_summary:
Turning a fixed narration script into a long-form video requires interdependent decisions across planning, retrieval, speech synthesis, and timeline assembly, and prior agentic editors drive multi-stage workflows with general-purpose models without showing whether a compact, task-trained policy can match that quality at a fraction of the token cost. WeVisCut answers this with a single 9B policy that serves as orchestrator, generator, and critic inside a stateful tool harness, trained on executable trajectories reconstructed from finished videos rather than on final-video preferences alone.

- Because finished videos expose only narration and shot structure, a four-stage pipeline recovers script-to-shot intent through editing inversion, re-executes it with real production tools under verified replay, applies bounded observe-reflect-repair, and materializes the recorded calls, returns, and failures into **134,771 role-specific examples** from 3,750 Bilibili projects.
- Training proceeds in three phases on a `Qwen3.5-9B` backbone with LoRA: supervised fine-tuning plus runtime-verified rejection sampling, then `Guided-OPD` distillation with teacher intervention phased out to zero, then `RCF-DAPO`, a variant of `DAPO` that compares rewards only within the same role and production context.
- In a shared tool environment on the authors' 100-task benchmark, the policy raises the Overall Score from 74.5 to **90.5**, a **16.0-point gain** over its base, and matches `Claude Opus 5` at 89.9 while generating **2,377 versus 78,763 tokens per successful output minute**, roughly **33× fewer**, though Opus still edges it on visual-narration alignment at 74.8 versus 74.6.
- Against native end-to-end editors on the same tasks, it scores 90.5 versus 84.9 for `Crayotter` and 82.5 for `VideoAgent`, costs an estimated **$0.09 per output minute** versus $0.97 and $0.58, and wins a blinded three-rater human preference at 4.56 versus 3.48 and 3.46.
- The benchmark, metrics, and source videos are all the authors' own and share a single platform with the training data, the comparison models receive no task-specific tuning, the human ratings carry no significance test, the stage ablation is cumulative rather than factorial, and the authors name limited template coverage and retrieval robustness as open gaps.

papers.title: Encode Once, Answer Many: Internalizing Context via Parametric Flow
papers.abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.
papers.summary: Adapting a large language model to a task means either placing knowledge in the input context, which is re-encoded on every call, or fine-tuning, which internalizes it but costs a round of optimization per task. `CLIK` is a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a context to LoRA parameters in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, so the generated adapter is inserted into a frozen base model and reused for every query on the same document, with no test-time gradient updates and no context in the prompt. **On document question answering, `CLIK` outperforms the no-context base model and existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly**, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without multi-turn training. Analysis shows the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.

papers.title: CSO: Refining Robotic Policies via Skill Distribution Alignment and Skill-Grained Optimization
papers.abstract: Discretizing continuous actions into discrete skills using methods like VQ-VAE has emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation. However, quantization errors yield a suboptimal distribution for the skill prior, degrading its performance. While reinforcement learning offers a path for refinement, its direct application faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling. To address these challenges, we introduce Cascaded Skills Optimization (CSO), a two-stage post-training framework. First, Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning aligns the model's observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories via supervised fine-tuning. Second, with the observation encoder frozen, Skills Policy Optimization computes an independent, clipped importance ratio for each complete skill, enabling stable and efficient updates. With a lightweight QueST-style policy, CSO raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves performance on RoboTwin2.0, and achieves 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks. Additional comparisons with FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL further validate the effectiveness of our two-stage post-training strategy.
papers.summary: Discretizing continuous robot actions into skills with methods like the vector-quantized variational autoencoder (`VQ-VAE`) works well for manipulation, but quantization error leaves the skill prior suboptimal, and refining it with reinforcement learning faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling. Cascaded Skills Optimization (`CSO`) first runs Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning to align the observation-to-skill mapping with successful online trajectories, then freezes the observation encoder and applies Skills Policy Optimization, which computes an independent clipped importance ratio for each complete skill. **With a lightweight `QueST`-style policy, `CSO` raises overall `LIBERO` success from 80.1% to 97.5%**, improves `RoboTwin2.0`, and reaches 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks, with further comparisons against `FAST`, discrete `BEAST`, and fixed-buffer `IQL`.

papers.title: SparseTokenGS: Gaussian-based Sparse-View CBCT Reconstruction via Reusable Token Pool
papers.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography is widely used for fast, low-dose volumetric imaging and lesion localization in dentistry and image-guided interventions, but it introduces severe artifacts. Feed-forward Gaussian methods transfer the reconstruction cost to training and decode each coordinate from projection-aligned features and neighboring anchors. However, information from the whole scan is written only when the field is constructed and cannot be retrieved during coordinate decoding, leaving the volume inconsistent within the scan. This is a common limitation of such methods: once the field is fixed, decoding uses only local features and reconstruction quality drops substantially. We propose SparseTokenGS, a Gaussian-based method for sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography reconstruction via a reusable token pool. Anchor Token Fusion and Point-Token Attention query this shared pool at the anchors and at the query coordinates, respectively. The local Gaussian prior is retained, and the volume is reconstructed in one forward pass, without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss. On three public chest and dental datasets, SparseTokenGS achieves the highest reconstruction performance among the compared methods. On clinical dental scans, reconstruction from only six projections reaches 29.51 decibels in peak signal-to-noise ratio and a structural similarity of 0.842 against the full-view reference, and off-the-shelf tooth-and-pulp segmentation keeps these structures separable for root-canal localization. Experiments on volcanic rock and chicken show performance after same-object adaptation. A reusable token pool gives feed-forward reconstruction a mechanism that keeps scan-wide context available through decoding and can benefit future rapid clinical lesion localization and analysis. The code is available at: https://github.com/FrankDengAI/SparseTokenGS.
papers.summary: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) gives fast, low-dose volumetric imaging for dentistry and image-guided interventions but suffers severe artifacts, and feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction methods lose scan-wide information once the field is built because each coordinate is then decoded only from local projection-aligned features and neighboring anchors. `SparseTokenGS` keeps a reusable token pool that Anchor Token Fusion queries at the anchors and Point-Token Attention queries at the coordinates being decoded, retaining the local Gaussian prior while reconstructing the volume in one forward pass without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss. It reaches the highest reconstruction quality among compared methods on three public chest and dental datasets, and **on clinical dental scans from only six projections it achieves 29.51 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio and 0.842 structural similarity** against the full-view reference, keeping teeth and pulp separable for off-the-shelf segmentation and root-canal localization.

papers.title: Manifest-Assisted Retrieval in Artificial Intelligence Search: Evidence Gaps and a Security Evaluation
papers.abstract: The external sources retained in our non-systematic audit did not isolate the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary retrieval remained fixed. The initial audit covered 39 sources through August 16, 2026, with later targeted updates through October 14. A purposive 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint; a non-probability log study found that 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests in May 2026. We separate publication, fetch, model use, and action; define five operational threat paths and paired security-utility estimands; and exercise deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. We also execute a reduced pilot: 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions, and 120 real model responses, with ordinary evidence held fixed. Frozen automatic scoring identifies attacker-target adoption in $21/24$ raw adversarial responses, with one further response unresolved; the adversarial URLs-only condition has no known adoptions and one unresolved response. The pilot measures output changes conditional on supplied evidence, without live retrieval or external actions. Together, the framework and pilot distinguish manifest-content effects from publication, discovery, and downstream execution, while leaving full retrieval and agent evaluation open.
papers.summary: Websites can publish an /llms.txt manifest intended for consumption by AI search and retrieval tools, but the sources retained in a non-systematic audit of 39 sources through August 2026 did not isolate what that manifest adds to security or utility when ordinary retrieval is held fixed. A 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint, and a log study found that 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests in May 2026. The framework separates publication, fetch, model use, and action, defines five operational threat paths with paired security-utility estimands, and exercises deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. In a reduced pilot of 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions, and 120 real model responses, with ordinary evidence fixed and no live retrieval or external actions, **frozen automatic scoring found that 21 of 24 raw adversarial responses adopted the attacker's target**, while the adversarial URLs-only condition produced no known adoptions; full retrieval and agent evaluation are left open.

papers.title: TCC-RAG: Temporal Causal Chain-Guided RAG for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred growing interest in temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA). Most existing methods rely on semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which suffers from fundamental limitations in complex temporal reasoning. On the one hand, semantic-based RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge required for complex temporal reasoning. On the other hand, these methods introduce excessive redundant knowledge, trapping LLMs in spurious reasoning chains that potentially result in erroneous answers. To address these problems, we propose a Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (TCC-RAG) to retrieve a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge to support complex temporal reasoning. Specifically, we reformulate the temporal knowledge graph into a multi-view causal cue graph, with causal cues inducing connections that explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics. Based on the causal cue graph, we construct a query-specific temporal causal chain to guide the retrieval process, enabling the model to focus on a concise set of causally relevant knowledge. Finally, we introduce a causal evidence filter to refine the retrieved knowledge, ensuring its causal consistency with the underlying temporal logic of the query. Experiments show that TCC-RAG achieves substantial performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, and delivers a remarkable 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.
papers.summary: Temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA) with semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG) struggles to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge that complex temporal reasoning needs and retrieves so much redundant knowledge that large language models fall into spurious reasoning chains. Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (`TCC-RAG`) reformulates the temporal knowledge graph as a multi-view causal cue graph whose cues explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics, builds a query-specific temporal causal chain to steer retrieval toward a concise but sufficient set of causally relevant facts, and applies a causal evidence filter to keep retrieved knowledge consistent with the query's temporal logic. **`TCC-RAG` improves performance by 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks and by 62.97% on multi-step temporal reasoning.**

papers.title: Towards Reliable, Scalable, and Value-Aligned Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale Advertising
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) reformulates item retrieval as autoregressive generation of discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs), offering a unified paradigm for personalized recommendation. GR4AD, as an industrial generative recommendation framework, has greatly improved advertising revenue while enabling efficient real-time serving in Kuaishou.However, continued deployment has exposed three limitations: deterministic SID assignment remains sensitive to semantic boundaries; conventional backbone scaling provides diminishing revenue gains under strict serving constraints; and sequence-level value optimization provides limited credit assignment to intermediate SID decisions, causing likelihood-based beam search to prematurely prune potentially high-value candidates. We present GR4AD-X, which addresses these limitations through reliable SID construction, serving-efficient capacity scaling, and unified value alignment. Specifically, GR4AD-X improves SID reliability through Multi-Path assignment. It expands model capacity along multiple complementary dimensions rather than relying solely on wider or deeper backbones, achieving a better effectiveness-efficiency trade-off under strict serving constraints. Finally, Unified Value-Guided Generation and Discrimination (UniVGD) aligns generation with commercial value through prefix-level reward optimization, value-guided beam pruning, and discriminative reranking within a unified model. Large-scale online A/B tests on the Kuaishou advertising platform demonstrate that GR4AD-X achieves a cumulative revenue improvement of 3.07% over the deployed GR4AD baseline while satisfying strict latency and throughput constraints.
papers.summary: Generative recommendation (GR) reformulates item retrieval as autoregressive generation of discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs), and continued deployment of the `GR4AD` framework in Kuaishou advertising exposed three limits: deterministic SID assignment is sensitive to semantic boundaries, scaling the backbone yields diminishing revenue under strict serving constraints, and sequence-level value optimization assigns little credit to intermediate SID decisions, so likelihood-based beam search prunes high-value candidates early. `GR4AD-X` responds with Multi-Path SID assignment, capacity scaling along multiple complementary dimensions rather than only wider or deeper backbones, and Unified Value-Guided Generation and Discrimination (`UniVGD`), which combines prefix-level reward optimization, value-guided beam pruning, and discriminative reranking in one model. **Large-scale online A/B tests on the Kuaishou advertising platform show a cumulative revenue improvement of 3.07% over the deployed `GR4AD` baseline** while meeting latency and throughput constraints.

papers.title: Compute Has Shape: Self-Morphing the Internal Computation of Frozen LLMs
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves large language models through additional computation, but how to adapt the topology of internal computation to individual inputs remains underexplored. Existing approaches largely fix recurrent or parallel architectures during training, or reconfigure frozen models along a single structural axis. We introduce SelfMorph, which makes computational shape an input-dependent inference-time decision. It unifies the original forward path (BASE), serial reuse of a layer span (REPEAT), and local branching and merging of perturbed hidden states (BRANCH) in a unified space parameterized by type, location, and intensity. Since they offer complementary benefits rather than uniform dominance, we use a lightweight selector that reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden state trajectory on the prompt to choose a morphology before response generation. We train the selector by distilling utility-based distribution from offline morphing that jointly account for task performance and computational cost. Evaluated on three LLMs spanning 4B-27B, SelfMorph achieves a 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks. It achieves the strongest performance in 24 of 27 settings. These findings identify input-adaptive computational topology as a complementary axis of test-time scaling beyond generating more tokens. Our code is available at https://github.com/creator-xi/SelfMorph.
papers.summary: Test-time scaling adds computation to large language models, but adapting the topology of a model's internal computation to each input is underexplored, since prior work fixes recurrent or parallel architectures during training or reconfigures frozen models along a single structural axis. `SelfMorph` makes computational shape an input-dependent inference-time decision by unifying the original forward path, serial reuse of a layer span, and local branching and merging of perturbed hidden states in one space parameterized by type, location, and intensity; a lightweight selector reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden-state trajectory on the prompt and chooses a morphology before generation, trained by distilling a utility distribution from offline morphing that accounts for both task performance and compute cost. **Across three LLMs from 4B to 27B parameters, `SelfMorph` delivers an 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks**, with the strongest result in 24 of 27 settings.

papers.title: How Much Do Teacher Bridges Matter in Interleaved On-Policy Distillation?
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student using teacher predictions on student-generated responses. Some methods insert teacher-written segments, or bridges, but disagree on how to train on those tokens. We compare no loss, forward KL and reverse KL on identical trajectories using Qwen3-1.7B as student and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher. We separate gradients by which model wrote each token. Under our short training runs and BF16 inference, pre-specified tests detected no added accuracy benefit from teacher text as context or as a training target. A one-paragraph bridge after the student's first paragraph is only 2.7% of the tokens and contributes a small gradient nearly orthogonal to the student-token gradient. In this main comparison, the three loss treatments gave similar gradient directions and were statistically equivalent in accuracy within a +/-5 percentage-point margin. An exploratory pilot placing the bridge where failed responses disagreed most with the teacher suggested a benefit from teacher-token loss. A pre-specified replication did not confirm this, and fourfold weighting showed no significant accuracy benefit. Two limitations bound these findings. Among the tested amounts of training on fixed responses, gains peaked after four updates before the student increasingly failed to stop generating. None of the tested online training variants met the criteria for stable stopping and improved accuracy. Our evaluations used BF16 inference, which rounds away most of the small weight changes. When evaluated in exact FP32, the tested replication models frequently reached the response-length limit. Our accuracy findings therefore concern BF16 inference; they do not establish that teacher-token supervision is generally unnecessary.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on teacher predictions over student-generated responses, and some methods insert teacher-written segments, or bridges, without agreement on how to train on those tokens. Using `Qwen3-1.7B` as student and `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` as teacher, the study compares no loss, forward KL, and reverse KL on identical trajectories, separating gradients by which model wrote each token. **Under short training runs and BF16 inference, pre-specified tests detected no added accuracy benefit from teacher text as context or as a training target, with the three loss treatments statistically equivalent within a plus or minus 5 percentage-point margin**; a one-paragraph bridge after the student's first paragraph is only 2.7% of tokens and contributes a small gradient nearly orthogonal to the student-token gradient. An exploratory pilot placing the bridge where failed responses most disagreed with the teacher suggested a benefit that a pre-specified replication did not confirm, and because BF16 rounds away most small weight changes, the findings are scoped to BF16 inference and do not establish that teacher-token supervision is generally unnecessary.

papers.title: Pronunciation-Supervised Text-to-Speech for Irish (Gaeilge)
papers.abstract: Speech technology for Irish must be built from very little transcribed speech, yet the language's pronunciation is thoroughly documented in dictionaries and dialect descriptions. We ask whether that documentation can supervise the adaptation of a large pretrained text-to-speech model to a language it was never trained on. We adapt Qwen3-TTS to Irish using 12.8 hours of crowdsourced Common Voice speech, correcting two defects in the vendor fine-tuning script that training loss does not reveal (Appendix A), and reach character error rate (CER) 0.225 on held-out cross-corpus text, against 0.397 for an exhaustively tuned from-scratch system and 0.437 for zero-shot cloning. We then compile the Wiktionary pronunciation record into a lexicon and a phoneme critic, and use that critic as the verifier in one round of rejection fine-tuning: CER 0.159 cross-corpus and 0.067 in-domain, with the voice still anonymous across all 202 training speakers. The same critic explains why the voice cannot yet be steered to a minority dialect: 229 of 12,311 training clips lean Ulster against 8,451 Munster. Pronunciation documentation, converted into a verifier, is a practical lever for low-resource speech synthesis, and a way to measure what the available data cannot support.
papers.summary: Irish has very little transcribed speech, but its pronunciation is thoroughly documented in dictionaries and dialect descriptions, raising the question of whether that documentation can supervise adapting a large pretrained text-to-speech model to a language it never saw. Adapting `Qwen3-TTS` on 12.8 hours of crowdsourced `Common Voice` Irish, after correcting two defects in the vendor fine-tuning script that training loss does not reveal, reaches a character error rate (CER) of 0.225 on held-out cross-corpus text, against 0.397 for an exhaustively tuned from-scratch system and 0.437 for zero-shot cloning. Compiling the Wiktionary pronunciation record into a lexicon and a phoneme critic and using the critic as the verifier in one round of rejection fine-tuning **lowers CER to 0.159 cross-corpus and 0.067 in-domain** while the voice remains anonymous across all 202 training speakers. The same critic explains why the voice cannot yet be steered to a minority dialect: only 229 of 12,311 training clips lean Ulster against 8,451 Munster.

papers.title: Revisiting Temporal Link Prediction through Structural Proximity
papers.abstract: Existing temporal link prediction methods typically rely on learned temporal representations to capture evolving interaction patterns. In this paper, we show that a classical structural proximity measure can match or outperform these methods without training or learned temporal sequence modeling. We revisit Personalized PageRank (PPR) on historical interaction graphs, using simple sliding-window retention or exponential time decay. Surprisingly, across 14 datasets, Time-decay PPR ranks first on nine and second on four among the compared methods, including datasets with few repeated edges. To understand this result, we examine the historical paths connecting source nodes to previously unseen destinations. We find that such paths contain useful predictive information, and that PPR outperforms a strong neural baseline on queries where historical structure clearly distinguishes the true destination from negative candidates. These results show that strong performance on current benchmarks does not necessarily require complex temporal models. More fundamentally, they raise the question of how much predictive value learned temporal modeling adds beyond historical structural proximity. Our findings motivate reassessing progress in temporal link prediction with strong classical baselines.
papers.summary: Temporal link prediction methods typically learn temporal representations to capture evolving interaction patterns, but a classical structural proximity measure can match or beat them without training or learned sequence modeling.
