Revisiting Personalized PageRank (`PPR`) on historical interaction graphs with simple sliding-window retention or exponential time decay, **time-decay `PPR` ranks first on nine of 14 datasets and second on four among the compared methods**, including datasets with few repeated edges. Examining historical paths from source nodes to previously unseen destinations shows these paths carry useful predictive information, and `PPR` beats a strong neural baseline on queries where historical structure clearly separates the true destination from negative candidates. The results raise the question of how much learned temporal modeling adds beyond structural proximity and motivate reassessing progress against strong classical baselines.

papers.title: SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides coarse supervision for long-horizon LLM agents: failed trajectories may contain correct steps, while successful trajectories can contain errors. Trajectory-level skills can also shift teacher preferences at unrelated steps, introducing off-target distillation signals. We introduce SCOPE, a framework for Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation. After a supervised warm-up, the policy analyzes its own trajectories, generates step-specific hindsight skills, and distills their guidance only at selected error steps. A bounded signed teacher-student coefficient stabilizes auxiliary updates while preserving positive reinforcement and negative correction. A success-relative pairwise length reward further encourages efficient task completion. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple model backbones. With Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% success on ALFWorld and 85.2% on WebShop, outperforming SEED by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE reaches 89.6% success, improving over GRPO by 23.2 percentage points with 46.7% fewer interactions. Scaling to Qwen3-32B, SCOPE achieves 99.2% success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 94.0% on unseen tasks.
papers.summary: Outcome-based reinforcement learning gives long-horizon LLM agents only coarse credit: failed trajectories often contain correct steps, successful ones contain errors, and trajectory-level skill hints can shift the teacher at unrelated steps. `SCOPE` has the policy, after a supervised warm-up, analyze its own rollouts, write step-specific hindsight skills, and distill that guidance only at selected error steps, using a bounded signed teacher-student coefficient to stabilize the auxiliary update and a success-relative pairwise length reward to favor efficient completion. With `Qwen2.5-3B` it reaches 97.7% success on `ALFWorld` and 85.2% on `WebShop`, beating `SEED` by 5.9 and 6.3 points, and **on unseen `ALFWorld` tasks it reaches 89.6% success, 23.2 points above `GRPO` with 46.7% fewer environment interactions**. Scaling to `Qwen3-32B` yields 99.2% on seen and 94.0% on unseen tasks.

papers.title: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents
papers.abstract: Self-improving LLM agents edit their own harness, the prompts and rules around a fixed model, and keep an edit only if an acceptance gate scores it higher on a batch of tasks. Such a gate sees what the harness does under the current model, not what it would still prevent if one safeguard failed. When safeguards overlap, deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen. We measure harm for every subset of four written safeguards in two agent environments and run 411 improvement loops under ten gate rules, mostly as controlled deletion experiments, plus three runs of the GEPA optimizer. A deletion behind another working safeguard adds almost no observable harm. A paired significance test blocks deletions that pass by chance but not deletions that genuinely raise task success, and a larger evaluation batch lets it delete cheaper safeguards: at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six. Large harm audits prevent exposure but not the loss of depth, which turns into harm when the harness is reused with a weaker model. GEPA kept every safety rule verbatim, yet two of its three final harnesses misused credentials under a weaker model. A statistical model frozen before the runs predicts where each gate's protection breaks as safeguard cost and batch size change, and freezing safety text or auditing one-layer ablations preserves depth.
papers.summary: Self-improving agents edit their own harness, the prompts and rules around a fixed model, and keep an edit only if an acceptance gate scores it higher on a batch of tasks; because overlapping safeguards mask one another, deleting one costs nothing observable and redundancy erodes unseen. The authors measure harm for every subset of four written safeguards in two agent environments, run 411 improvement loops under ten gate rules, mostly controlled deletion experiments, and add three runs of the `GEPA` optimizer. A deletion behind another working safeguard adds almost no observable harm, a paired significance test blocks deletions that pass by chance but not those that genuinely raise task success, and **at equal cost, 20-task evaluation batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six**. `GEPA` kept every safety rule verbatim, yet two of its three final harnesses misused credentials when reused with a weaker model, and a statistical model frozen before the runs predicts where each gate breaks as safeguard cost and batch size change, with freezing safety text or auditing one-layer ablations shown to preserve depth.

papers.title: Agent Transfer Protocol: Server-Mediated Agent-to-Agent Communication Architecture for the Agentic Web
papers.abstract: The Agentic Web needs to support continuous collaboration among agents from different organizations. These collaborative relationships may span multiple tasks, network connections and execution instances. Such interactions require stable communication entries, message reception when instances are offline, and source verification after delayed reading. How to organize these responsibilities so that cross domain communication does not depend on specific execution instances being continuously online is a key issue for building long term agent interaction infrastructure. We propose ATP (Agent Transfer Protocol), a cross organization agent communication protocol adopting a domain mediated architecture. In this architecture, administrative domains maintain stable addresses and receiving entries for logical agents. The domain servers of both parties continuously undertake cross domain transmission. The receiving domain verifies and saves messages for execution instances to read later. The sending domain signs the complete message envelope. This allows the receiving instance to independently reverify the domain source and content integrity after the original connection ends, provided the original verification public key is still trusted and obtainable. We implemented an ATP prototype and evaluated it through a controlled cross organization LLM agent workflow, mechanism checks and latency measurements. The workflow completed subsequent business processing after instances went offline or were replaced. The independent verifier successfully verified the domain source and content integrity of saved messages. Latency measurements further quantified the communication and processing overhead introduced by the continuous mediation of domain servers.
papers.summary: Agents from different organizations need to collaborate across tasks, connections, and execution instances, which requires stable addresses, message delivery while an instance is offline, and verification of a message's origin long after the original connection has closed. The Agent Transfer Protocol (`ATP`) adopts a domain-mediated architecture in which administrative domains maintain stable addresses and inboxes for logical agents, domain servers relay messages across organizations, the receiving domain verifies and stores messages for later reading, and the sending domain signs the full envelope so a receiver can independently re-verify source and integrity afterward. In a prototype driven by a cross-organization LLM agent workflow, **business processing continued after agent instances went offline or were replaced**, an independent verifier confirmed the origin and integrity of stored messages, and latency measurements quantify the overhead of continuous server mediation.

papers.title: LLMs as Judges and Examinees for Medical Item Difficulty Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting medical item difficulty from item text alone remains challenging. Prior work has largely relied on linguistic features or text representations derived from general-purpose and domain-specific language models, but predictive performance has remained modest. This study takes a different approach by using difficulty-related signals that emerge when open-weight large language models (LLMs) interact with test items. Using USMLE and PANCE medical licensure examination items, we examined LLMs in two roles. As judges, the models provided absolute difficulty ratings and pairwise difficulty comparisons. As simulated examinees, they generated response-based signals including correctness, keyed-option probability, response entropy, and the probability margin between the top two options. We then combined the strongest judgment and response signals with baseline item features in downstream prediction models. Pairwise difficulty judgment was the most consistent individual LLM signal across both datasets, while simulated-examinee signals and absolute judgments provided complementary information in some feature combinations. The best configurations reached a Spearman correlation of $\rho$ = .447 on USMLE, exceeding the best system in the 2024 BEA shared task ($\rho$ = .25), and $\rho$ = .494 on PANCE. These results were comparable to direct absolute judgments from the proprietary frontier model Claude Opus 5 ($\rho$ = .443 and .488, respectively). Overall, judgment and response signals from open-weight LLMs captured difficulty-related information beyond text representations. Because these models can be deployed locally, the approach offers a practical option for predicting the difficulty of unreleased or high-security test items.
papers.summary: Predicting how hard a medical exam item is from its text alone has remained difficult, with linguistic features and text embeddings giving only modest accuracy. Using `USMLE` and `PANCE` licensure items, open-weight large language models are put in two roles: as judges giving absolute difficulty ratings and pairwise comparisons, and as simulated examinees whose correctness, keyed-option probability, response entropy, and top-two probability margin serve as signals, which are then combined with baseline item features in downstream predictors. Pairwise judgments were the most consistent single signal, and **the best configurations reached a Spearman correlation of 0.447 on `USMLE`, against 0.25 for the best system in the 2024 `BEA` shared task**, and 0.494 on `PANCE`, comparable to direct ratings from `Claude Opus 5` at 0.443 and 0.488. Because the models run locally, the approach suits unreleased or high-security items.

papers.title: SpaceAct: Benchmarking 3D Spatial and Temporal Reasoning via Closed-Loop Action and Active Perception
papers.abstract: To solve problems in 3D space rather than merely describe images, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) need 3D spatiotemporal reasoning: reconstructing 3D geometry from occluded 2D views, anticipating physical dynamics, and executing precise, closed-loop actions. Prior studies test passive VQA on static images or symbolic planning, requiring no execution or supplying privileged coordinates while ignoring collision, statics, and timing. We introduce SpaceAct, an interactive benchmark evaluating 3D spatiotemporal reasoning via closed-loop physical action and active perception, with SAPA, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework. Built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, it has 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, without privileged coordinates, and diagnostic modes (+plan, +state, no-camera, blind, L7 levers). In brick-bridging or aperture-threading, models rotate the camera to resolve occlusion, read in-scene rulers, output 6-DoF poses under swept-collision and statics checks, and self-correct via split-screen rollback feedback (dynamic tasks freeze time during deliberation and give five strobe frames). Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8-79.1 (seven solve at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks); for the top three, a reference plan (+plan) closes 44% of the gap while leaving collisions at 5.2 per episode, whereas adding exact 3D state (+state) closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5; for four others, +plan lifts the mean score from 10.9 to 35.3 and +state to 81.8; and 46% of failures are collision or observation loops. SpaceAct and SAPA advance evaluation to closed-loop physical interaction, showing that even with a valid plan, MLLMs remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, while offering a testbed for active multi-view exploration and explicit 3D grounding.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that must act in 3D space need to reconstruct geometry from occluded 2D views, anticipate physical dynamics, and execute precise closed-loop actions, but existing tests use passive visual question answering or symbolic planning with privileged coordinates and no collision or timing checks. `SpaceAct` is an interactive benchmark built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, with 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, paired with `SAPA`, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework in which models rotate the camera, read in-scene rulers, output six-degree-of-freedom poses under swept-collision and statics checks, and self-correct from split-screen rollback feedback. Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances scores span 4.8 to 79.1, and **seven of the ten solve at most 27.3% of the six-degree-of-freedom tasks**. Supplying a reference plan closes 44% of the gap for the top three models while leaving 5.2 collisions per episode, whereas supplying exact 3D state closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5, pointing to 3D visual grounding and action refinement rather than planning as the bottleneck.

papers.title: Holistic Diversity Management in LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search
papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search iteratively selects existing programs, uses LLMs as mutation operators to generate a new program, and evaluates it to guide subsequent search. To preserve diversity and reduce the risk of premature convergence, it often adopts the island model, in which groups of programs, called islands, evolve separately. However, this structure alone does not guarantee distinct search directions, as islands may start from similar programs or converge toward similar solutions during evolution. This suggests that diversity must be considered throughout the search process, from initializing islands with distinct programs to developing island trajectories and sharing discoveries across islands. To this end, we propose HoliDivEvolve , a holistic approach to establishing and effectively utilizing island diversity throughout evolutionary search. Specifically, we introduce diverse initialization to establish different initial programs, trajectory adaptive island selection to allocate computation based on current score, recent growth, and the remaining search budget, and growth adaptive migration to share alternative ideas across islands. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show that HoliDivEvolve achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks. We further conduct controlled analyses to examine how our design choices affect search behavior and final performance.
papers.summary: LLM-guided evolutionary search repeatedly picks existing programs, uses an LLM as a mutation operator, and evaluates the result, commonly using an island model to preserve diversity, but islands can start from similar programs or drift toward the same solutions. `HoliDivEvolve` manages diversity across the whole search: diverse initialization seeds islands with distinct programs, trajectory-adaptive island selection allocates compute based on current score, recent growth, and remaining budget, and growth-adaptive migration shares alternative ideas between islands. **Across diverse benchmarks the method achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks**, and controlled ablations examine how each component changes search behavior and final results.

papers.title: Governance-Aware Federated Learning for Multi-Agent AI Systems: A Policy-Driven Framework for Trustworthy Collaborative AI
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exchanging raw data, but conventional FL provides limited runtime governance, evidence verification, fairness assessment, explainability monitoring, and auditability. This paper proposes Governance-Aware Federated Learning (GAFL), which combines independent governance-evidence verification, temporal trust, fairness and explanation assessment, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, normalized aggregation, and tamper-evident audit logging. Client-reported governance values are authenticated, bound to their submitted model updates, and independently recomputed before aggregation. A cross-silo prototype with 10 participants was evaluated on the Adult Income dataset under honest, benign non-IID, biased-data, malicious-update, non-compliant, falsified-evidence, and mixed-threat scenarios. Four methods were compared across five random seeds: FedAvg, FedAvg with anomaly filtering, GAFL without independent verification, and complete GAFL. Complete GAFL intervened on all affected participants at the final round across the evaluated risk scenarios, including identifying 100% of falsified-evidence participants, whereas GAFL without verification identified none of the falsified-evidence participants. Final macro-F1 ranged from 0.7520 to 0.7733 across GAFL scenarios. Complete GAFL required 173.67 plus or minus 26.94 ms of governance processing per round, compared with 3.82 plus or minus 0.79 ms for FedAvg. A strict demographic-parity threshold also caused frequent interventions for honest participants, demonstrating a significant fairness-policy and utility trade-off.
papers.summary: Federated Learning (FL) trains models collaboratively without sharing raw data but offers little runtime governance, evidence verification, fairness or explainability monitoring, or auditability. Governance-Aware Federated Learning (`GAFL`) adds independent verification of client-reported governance evidence, which is authenticated, bound to each submitted update, and recomputed before aggregation, alongside temporal trust scoring, fairness and explanation checks, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, normalized aggregation, and tamper-evident audit logs. In a ten-participant cross-silo prototype on the `Adult Income` dataset under honest, non-IID, biased, malicious, non-compliant, falsified-evidence, and mixed scenarios, **complete `GAFL` flagged 100% of falsified-evidence participants, while the variant without independent verification flagged none**. Macro-F1 stayed between 0.7520 and 0.7733, governance processing cost about 174 ms per round versus about 4 ms for `FedAvg`, and a strict demographic-parity threshold triggered frequent interventions on honest participants.

papers.title: Deeper Backpropagation or More Updates? Training Looped Language Models Across Budgets
papers.abstract: Repeating transformer layers can improve language model performance without adding parameters. However, the added computational depth increases both forward and backward computation costs during training. Training such models requires choosing a backward window that controls how many final layer repetitions retain gradients during backpropagation. Longer windows improve per-token learning efficiency but increase per-update cost, while shorter windows reduce per-update cost but sacrifice per-token efficiency. Understanding which window performs better requires examining different training budgets. Prior work compares backward windows across computational budgets. When training budgets increase, it remains unclear whether the same window continues to perform best. We measure how the relative performance of two windows shifts as training budgets grow. Our method isolates per-token efficiency by training both windows on identical data, and compares complete training recipes at approximately equal training time at each budget. Results show that shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow. Controlled experiments show that both benefits decrease at larger budgets, with a greater decline in the benefit of extended training. Backward window comparisons depend on the available budget, and the preferred window among the tested candidates can change as the budget grows.
papers.summary: Looping transformer layers improves language models without adding parameters but raises training cost, and practitioners must choose a backward window, the number of final loop repetitions that keep gradients, trading per-token learning efficiency against per-update cost. The study trains two windows on identical data to isolate per-token efficiency and compares complete recipes at roughly equal training time across increasing budgets. **Shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow**, both benefits shrink at larger budgets with the gain from extended training declining fastest, and the preferred window among the tested candidates can change as the budget increases.

papers.title: The Code Behind the Layout: AI Agents for Analog Layout Generators
papers.abstract: Analog layout remains largely manual and hard to automate. Generator frameworks such as gLayout express layouts as programs, producing layouts from parameterized, design-rule-aware generators; however, writing such generators still takes expert effort. Large language models (LLMs) could now write generator code, and frontier models can even draw layout geometry from design intent. This raises a practical question: if a model can draw the layout itself, what does a generator framework still contribute, and is applying these models to a generator framework better than having them draw a layout from scratch? Through controlled experiments on gLayout in SKY130, we find that the main obstacle to drawing a layout directly is its time and token cost, and that the main advantage of a model building on a generator framework is reusability. Its verified primitives keep each model edit small enough to check, and its parameters allow a single edit to be evaluated across an entire family of layouts. Accordingly, a model is most effective when it develops the layout from the generator source of the family that the design intent belongs to, and tests each edit on the family members most likely to fail, so that one verified change improves every layout the generator produces. The results of these family tests can then serve as supervision for a local model, which learns edits that hold across the family at a fraction of the inference cost.
papers.summary: Analog chip layout is still mostly manual; generator frameworks such as `gLayout` express a layout as a parameterized, design-rule-aware program, but writing those generators takes expert effort, and frontier LLMs can now draw layout geometry directly from design intent, which raises the question of what a generator framework still contributes. Controlled experiments on `gLayout` in the `SKY130` process compare models drawing layouts from scratch with models editing generator code. **Drawing a layout directly is limited mainly by time and token cost, while building on a generator framework pays off through reusability**, since verified primitives keep each edit small enough to check and parameters let one edit be evaluated across a whole family of layouts. A model works best when it edits the generator source for the family the design belongs to and tests on the family members most likely to fail, and those family test results can supervise a local model that learns the same edits at a fraction of the inference cost.

papers.title: DecisionUnlearn-Bench: Unlearning Probabilistic Decisions under Changing Schemas
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to reproduce the behavior of a model trained without designated data. For probabilistic decision models, this target also depends on the candidate options supplied at inference. We introduce DecisionUnlearn-Bench, an empirical framework that compares full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities, label renderings, and candidate sets. Across 20 eligible model configurations on the BANKING77 dataset, full-to-oracle displacement increases consistently from example to association to class deletion. Replacing semantic option labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes, even with successful acquisition of the full model, whereas changing the candidate set alters both the oracle and the measured unlearning progress. SimNPO satisfies the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations, but its gains vary substantially across seeds and deletion targets. Development tuning on the CLINC150 dataset does not establish a positive pooled effect across 48 intents. At approximately matched suppression, methods can differ markedly in oracle fidelity. Recovery experiments further distinguish initial forgetting from subsequent adaptation and show conclusions that depend on both architecture and metric. These results show that evaluating decision-model unlearning relative to a schema-specific retraining target, with separate reporting of effect size, utility, robustness, and recoverability.
papers.summary: Machine unlearning aims to reproduce a model trained without certain data, but for probabilistic decision models the target also depends on which candidate options are presented at inference. `DecisionUnlearn-Bench` compares full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities, label renderings, and candidate sets, using 20 model configurations on `BANKING77` with development tuning on `CLINC150`. Displacement between the full model and the retrained oracle grows from example to association to class deletion, and **replacing semantic option labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes**, while changing the candidate set shifts both the oracle and the measured unlearning progress. `SimNPO` passes the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations but its gains vary widely across seeds and targets, and recovery experiments show conclusions depend on both architecture and metric, arguing for evaluation against a schema-specific retraining target with separate reporting of effect size, utility, robustness, and recoverability.

papers.title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training
papers.abstract: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring only helps safety if the final answer actually depends on the written steps, and prior measurements used natural tasks where the true reasoning is unknown. On a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known, one step inside a model's own chain is replaced with a wrong but valid state and the test is whether the answer follows the edit, across 25 open-weight models including `Qwen3` from 0.6B to 14B in base and post-trained form, `Gemma 3`, `Llama 3`, and eight `OLMo 2` checkpoints on 7,200 items each. **Reliance rises with scale and saturates, going from 16 to 18% at 0.6B to 97 to 100% at 14B in `Qwen3`**, with a logistic fit in log parameter count at R-squared 0.89; reliance correlates with step accuracy at r of 0.99 across families, size still matters at matched correctness, and post-training changes reliance by at most 0.03 from 4B upward. No model up to 14B solves the task internally, performing at chance without written steps once a problem has four or more swaps, so in this regime scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing.

papers.title: Continual Adaptation Across Modalities: Learning and Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Models
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs), which can process and generate diverse modalities within a single framework, have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm. However, when these models undergo continual learning on multiple tasks across different modalities, their learning and forgetting dynamics remain poorly understood. In this paper, we systematically investigate how architectural design and adaptation method shape intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides. Specifically, we report three findings. First, the severity of cross-modal interference decreases with the degree of modality-specific parameter isolation. Second, a within-model asymmetry: the generation side of a UMM is markedly more fragile than its understanding side. Third, what post-training adds is the first to be forgotten: purely post-training capabilities such as personalized generation collapse by 84\% to 90\%, while pretraining capabilities remain stable. Together, these results clarify how parameter isolation and post-training fragility shape UMMs' learning and forgetting dynamics, offering a starting point for developing continually evolving UMMs.
papers.summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) can both understand and generate several modalities in one network, but how they learn and forget when trained continually on tasks across modalities is poorly understood. The study systematically varies architectural design and adaptation method and measures intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides. Cross-modal interference falls as modality-specific parameter isolation increases, the generation side is markedly more fragile than the understanding side, and **capabilities added in post-training are forgotten first, with personalized generation collapsing by 84 to 90% while pretraining capabilities remain stable**.

papers.title: Capacity of the Hopfield-Hebbian dynamics with correlated patterns
papers.abstract:
Allowing for small fraction of errors in retrieved stored binary patterns, Hopfield-Hebbian neural network (NN) associative memory dynamics [14] achieves linearly scaled capacity. The famous proportionality constant $\alpha_c\approx 0.14$ is obtained in a large dimensional scenario as the ratio of the number of reliably stored patterns $m$ and the patterns' length $n$ under the assumption that uniformly randomly chosen binary patterns are \emph{independent} among themselves.
  While such an idealized scenario is now well understood, more practical scenarios with correlated/noisy datasets remaining challenging even for classical statistical mechanics replica approaches. We consider precisely such practical settings where each \emph{archetype} pattern is replaced with $M$ correlated \emph{examples} with parameter $r$ governing the quality of correlation. We develop a powerful Random Duality Theory (RDT) based framework to analyze correlated data and already on the first level of RDT lifting obtain capacity characterizations that remarkably well match behavior exhibited through simulated dynamics. Moreover, characterizations explicitly feature correlation parameters $M$ and $r$, which allows to precisely determine their effects on phase-transitioning behavior of the underlying dynamics.
  Our results are also a well-fitting complement to the existing literature. Namely, to circumvent challenging statistical mechanics analyses, an alternative combination of spectral and replica methods is considered in [4]. We confirm that [4]'s elegant spectral characterizations are excellent approximations in the low correlated regime. At the same time, we also close the gap in the regimes with higher correlation levels where spectral methods deviate from the practical dynamics performance.
papers.summary: Hopfield networks with Hebbian learning store a number of random binary patterns proportional to pattern length, with the classic constant of about 0.14, but that result assumes independent patterns, and correlated or noisy data has resisted even replica-based statistical mechanics. Each archetype pattern is replaced by M correlated examples with a parameter r controlling correlation strength, and a Random Duality Theory (RDT) framework is developed to analyze the resulting dynamics. **Already at the first level of RDT lifting, the capacity characterizations closely match simulated retrieval dynamics** and expose explicitly how M and r shift the phase transition. The results confirm that earlier spectral approximations hold well at low correlation and close the gap at higher correlation where those methods diverge from observed behavior.

papers.title: RoleFUZZER: User-Behaviour Fuzzing for Role-Specification Adherence in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often conditioned into specific roles such as tutors, interviewers, or agents acting for an organisation, through system prompts that specify how they should behave. The extent to which they can actually adhere to these role specifications under multi-turn interactions with realistic and potentially problematic users is understudied. To address this, we propose user behaviour fuzzing, a guided search over plausible user behaviours that can lead a model to violate its role specification, and introduce RoleFUZZER, a framework that adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing to operationalise the search. RoleFUZZER constructs scenarios guided by a user-behaviour coverage grid that crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types and the role specification of the model under test i.e. what is under pressure. With RoleFUZZER, we evaluate LLMs across five role specifications, including tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent under organisational policies. Across simulated and validated conversations in 15 campaigns, the framework reaches >= 89% coverage of the 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role tested, and surfaces specification-grounded failure patterns. At an equal budget of conversations, removing the RoleFUZZER grid and asking an LLM to generate specification targeting users free-form lowers coverage to 39-69% with fewer kinds of violations. The same specification can also fail in opposite directions. For e.g., on the antagonist, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead. RoleFUZZER offers a tractable way to uncover vulnerabilities in LLMs across role specifications by testing diverse user behaviours that are likely to violate them.
papers.summary: System prompts cast LLMs as tutors, interviewers, or organizational agents, yet how well models hold to such role specifications across multi-turn interaction with realistic and difficult users is understudied. `RoleFUZZER` adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing into user-behaviour fuzzing: a coverage grid crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types with the role specification under test, and a guided search constructs scenarios to fill the grid. Across 15 campaigns spanning tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and policy-bound web agent roles, **the framework reaches at least 89% coverage of the 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role, versus 39 to 69% when an LLM generates adversarial users free-form at equal budget**, surfacing more kinds of specification-grounded violations. The same specification can fail in opposite directions: on the antagonist role, open-weight models override the player's safety signals while `Claude Haiku 4.5` breaks character instead.

papers.title: Predict the Reward, Not the World: World Reward Models for ML Agents
papers.abstract: Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards. Recent agents try to save these runs by letting a large language model act as a world model that predicts how each program would perform. However, a wrong prediction feeds the search false information. We argue that an agent does not need to predict the outcome of execution, only the decision that execution would support. We propose World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to choose directly which candidate will perform better, without predicting any intermediate outcome. We prove that a selector which predicts execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add an error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum. Our WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs. On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, it picks the better program 79.4% of the time, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53--62%, and its probabilities are calibrated. Inside AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4--7.5 times while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.
papers.summary: Search-based machine-learning agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best, but runs can take hours and most are discarded, and using an LLM as a world model to predict outcomes risks feeding the search false information. World Reward Models (`WRMs`) instead learn from real execution results to pick directly which of two candidates will perform better, backed by proofs that a selector predicting execution cannot beat the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add error that can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM to the optimum. The instantiation `ForeCritic`, a 9B typed decision model adapted on 5k executed program pairs, **picks the better program 79.4% of the time on 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, where general-purpose LLM judges reach 53 to 62%**, with calibrated probabilities. Plugged into `AIDE`, `ML-Master`, and `ForeAgent`, it cuts mean task time by 4.4 to 7.5 times while keeping mean scores within 0.01 or improving them.

papers.title: DES-JEPA: Learning a Shared Vocabulary for High-Dimensional Discrete Event Sequences
papers.abstract: Temporal foundation models such as Chronos and TimesFM generalize across domains through a shared numerical observation space. In contrast, discrete event sequences (DESs), including operational event logs or patient clinical-event trajectories, have domain-specific event vocabularies whose labels lack a consistent correspondence across domains. Beyond this lack of consistency, the number of distinct events in real-world settings is high enough to challenge both classical temporal point process modeling and current in-context foundation inference models such as FIM-PP. Critically, current foundation models for DESs are limited to a small, fixed number of event types, restricting their applicability to realistic, high-dimensional event streams. To address this, we propose two complementary modules: (i) DES-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that learns a shared discrete vocabulary from synthetic stochastic processes with unaligned event vocabularies; and (ii) DES-PFN, a discrete event sequence prior-fitted network that reuses the learned vocabulary for in-context next-event prediction. Without task-specific fine-tuning, this framework achieves competitive zero-shot performance on eight unseen real-world datasets and scales up to 700 distinct event types.
papers.summary: Temporal foundation models such as `Chronos` and `TimesFM` transfer across domains through a shared numerical observation space, but discrete event sequences (DESs) like operational logs or clinical event trajectories have domain-specific vocabularies with no consistent correspondence, and existing in-context models such as `FIM-PP` handle only a small fixed number of event types. `DES-JEPA`, a joint-embedding predictive architecture, learns a shared discrete vocabulary from synthetic stochastic processes with unaligned event vocabularies, and `DES-PFN`, a prior-fitted network, reuses that vocabulary for in-context next-event prediction. **Without task-specific fine-tuning the framework achieves competitive zero-shot performance on eight unseen real-world datasets and scales to 700 distinct event types.**

papers.title: Benchmarking decision models against generative large language models on medical multiple-choice questions
papers.abstract: Medical workflows often require selecting among predefined options. We compared 13 decision models with 15 generative large language model configurations, including different reasoning settings, using 1,273 four-option MedQA questions under text-only conditions. Accuracy ranged from 67.71% to 89.08% for decision models and from 78.32% to 96.86% for generative configurations. Among the tested configurations, Mercury Decide had the lowest mean final-attempt cost (USD 0.0069 per 1,000 questions), while Clef Omni had the shortest median request duration (0.291 seconds). Decision-model probabilities distinguished correct from incorrect answers, but error rates among answers assigned probabilities of at least 0.90 ranged from 1.71% to 12.77%. Answer agreement across three runs ranged from 92.30% to 100%, while probability repeatability varied. Decision models offered resource advantages alongside lower peak accuracy; selecting models for medical workflows requires considering probability quality and repeatability together with accuracy and the resources needed to detect and correct errors.
papers.summary: Medical workflows often reduce to choosing among predefined options, so the comparison pits 13 decision models, which return probabilities over fixed choices, against 15 generative large language model configurations with varied reasoning settings on 1,273 four-option `MedQA` questions in text-only form. **Accuracy ranged from 67.71% to 89.08% for decision models and from 78.32% to 96.86% for generative configurations**, with `Mercury Decide` cheapest at USD 0.0069 per 1,000 questions and `Clef Omni` fastest at a 0.291-second median request. Decision-model probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers, yet error rates among answers assigned at least 0.90 probability ran from 1.71% to 12.77%, and answer agreement across three runs ranged from 92.30% to 100% while probability repeatability varied, so model choice must weigh probability quality and repeatability alongside accuracy and the cost of catching errors.

papers.title: CoSTA: Co-Evolving Self-Play Timeline Agents for Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
papers.abstract: Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) involves more than retrieving facts: the timestamp or validity interval of one fact can constrain the search for another, while multiple intervals may jointly determine the answer. Existing single-agent TKGQA methods typically investigate these facts within a single reasoning context, where evidence from different event histories can become interleaved and distractors can misdirect subsequent retrieval. Distributing investigations across agents can separate event-specific evidence into distinct contexts, but effective collaboration must still be learned because question decomposition, subtask investigation, and evidence synthesis are interdependent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving \textbf{S}elf-Play \textbf{T}imeline \textbf{A}gents (CoSTA), which organizes facts into navigable timelines, delegates investigations to workers, and uses a coordinator to synthesize their original timestamped observations. CoSTA initializes a shared policy through role-conditioned distillation and jointly optimizes both roles through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards. Across three benchmarks, CoSTA achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-fact questions, while its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.
papers.summary: Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires chaining facts whose timestamps or validity intervals constrain each other, and single-agent methods that investigate everything in one reasoning context let evidence from different event histories interleave and distractors derail later retrieval. Co-Evolving Self-Play Timeline Agents (`CoSTA`) organizes facts into navigable timelines, delegates sub-investigations to worker agents with separate contexts, and has a coordinator synthesize their original timestamped observations; a shared policy is initialized by role-conditioned distillation and both roles are then jointly optimized through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards. **Across three benchmarks `CoSTA` reaches state-of-the-art overall performance with the largest gains on complex multi-fact questions**, and its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.

papers.title: When Support Crosses the Line: Evaluating Ethical Boundaries in LLM-Based Mental Health Support in the Chinese Context
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for mental health support, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on supportive capabilities rather than whether models consistently adhere to professional ethical boundaries. This issue is particularly important in multi-turn interactions, where users may introduce new information or exert emotional pressure over time. We introduce MindEth-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating ethical boundary adherence in multi-turn mental health interactions. Grounded in professional ethical standards for mental health services in China, MindEth-Bench covers multiple dimensions of ethical conduct and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to systematically explore interaction trajectories that stress-test model boundaries. Experiments across nine LLMs show that models that initially respond appropriately can shift toward ethical violations over extended interactions, with substantial variation across models and ethical dimensions. These results show that single-turn evaluations may overestimate the ethical reliability of LLM-based mental health support systems and highlight the need to evaluate ethical behavior throughout multi-turn interaction.
papers.summary: LLMs are increasingly tried for mental health support, but existing benchmarks measure how supportive they are rather than whether they keep to professional ethical boundaries, especially over multi-turn conversations where users add information or apply emotional pressure. `MindEth-Bench` grounds its ethical dimensions in Chinese professional standards for mental health services and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore conversation trajectories that stress-test those boundaries. **Across nine LLMs, models that respond appropriately at first drift into ethical violations as interactions extend**, with large variation across models and dimensions, so single-turn evaluation overstates ethical reliability.

papers.title: Tracekit Box: Running AI Agents in Micro-VMs Where Every Way Out Is Decided and Signed
papers.abstract: AI agents now install packages, call model APIs with their operators' keys and change code in repositories that deploy to production. The network, credentials and write access they need are also how they can leak data, steal a key or change a system nobody approved. Sandboxes contain an agent but leave little evidence of what crossed their boundary; tracing records what happened but contains nothing. We present Tracekit Box, an open-source system (MIT, v0) that does both. Each job runs in its own Firecracker micro-VM with no network card. The only ways out are doors on the host, served over vsock: commands, outbound connections, secrets, model calls and the workspace patch. At every door a Tracekit signer the agent cannot reach decides what passes and signs it into one run per box. Names are resolved on the host; private and cloud-metadata addresses are always refused; secrets never enter the VM, which sees placeholders the host proxy swaps for real values only in one header for bound hosts; and changes come back as a patch applied file by file after the signer decides each file. Box fails closed, and each job ends as a .tkb bundle anyone can verify offline. All 13 end-to-end checks pass on a real KVM runner (the test that runs them takes 28.5 s, including image pull and boot); 15 fuzz targets on the trust boundary produced nine findings, all fixed; and the demo run's 102 signed records verify. Box does not yet run Firecracker's jailer, needs a co-located signer, and records processes inside the VM only where they cross a door.
papers.summary: Coding agents now install packages, call model APIs with their operators' keys, and change repositories that deploy to production, and the network, credentials, and write access they need are the same channels through which they can leak data or alter unapproved systems; sandboxes contain without leaving evidence, while tracing records without containing. `Tracekit Box` runs each job in a `Firecracker` micro-VM with no network card, so the only exits are host-side doors served over vsock for commands, outbound connections, secrets, model calls, and the workspace patch, and at every door a signer the agent cannot reach decides what passes and signs it into a single per-run record. Names resolve on the host, private and cloud-metadata addresses are always refused, secrets never enter the VM but are swapped in by a host proxy for bound hosts only, code changes return as a patch applied file by file after per-file approval, the system fails closed, and each job ends as a bundle anyone can verify offline. **All 13 end-to-end checks pass on a real KVM runner in 28.5 seconds including image pull and boot**, 15 fuzz targets on the trust boundary yielded nine findings that were all fixed, and the demo run's 102 signed records verify, though the system does not yet use Firecracker's jailer, needs a co-located signer, and records in-VM processes only where they cross a door.

papers.title: Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Networks for QC-MDPC Error Decoding in McEliece Cryptosystems
papers.abstract: As the advent of large-scale quantum computing threatens classical encryption, Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes have emerged as a foundational element of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). However, decoding these relatively dense codes using classical Belief Propagation algorithms often leads to failures caused by short graph cycles that stall the decoder. In cryptographic applications, these failures are severe security vulnerabilities that leak secret key information. To address this, this paper proposes a Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network (R-BGNN) as proof of concept. By integrating Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) into the message-passing framework and employing a multi-topology curriculum training strategy, the R-BGNN actively learns to break limit-cycle oscillations. Evaluated across 20 unseen matrix topologies, the proposed architecture significantly outperforms classical Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum baselines, reducing the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) by 63.7\% at moderate noise levels ($t=10$) while converging in fewer iterations.
papers.summary: Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes underpin several post-quantum McEliece-style cryptosystems, but classical belief-propagation decoders stall on short graph cycles, and in a cryptographic setting those decoding failures leak information about the secret key. The authors propose a Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network (`R-BGNN`) that inserts Gated Recurrent Units into the message-passing steps and is trained with a multi-topology curriculum so it learns to escape limit-cycle oscillations. Tested on 20 parity-check matrix topologies not seen in training, it outperforms `Bit-Flipping` and `Min-Sum` baselines, **cutting the decoding failure rate by 63.7% at moderate noise (t=10)** while converging in fewer iterations.

papers.title: Beyond Reachability: When Edit Order Preserves Couplings in Graph Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Shortest-path optimality does not guarantee that a memoryless graph generator preserves a prescribed source-target correspondence. We study whether reordering legal shortest edits can retain this correspondence without changing the pairing, mandatory edits, or sampling budget. Under a common Poisson clock, we establish an exact criterion for endpoint coupling recoverability: the source-blind Markov projection attains the unavoidable clock-error floor if and only if routes to distinct targets do not share graph states. Routes to the same target may merge without sacrificing endpoint fidelity. This characterization leads to an exact finite-state routing formulation and a legality-preserving scheduling procedure with recovery certificates. A marker-free construction demonstrates how shared edge structure can retain source distinctions, while a capacity-constrained family exhibits a sharp separation in paired error between edit orders with identical marginal error. Finally, a target-conditioned aliasing bound connects structural route design to the terminal fidelity of a learned graph-only generator. These results characterize when legal edit ordering can preserve a prescribed coupling under fixed operational costs.
papers.summary: In graph generation by flow matching, a memoryless generator that follows shortest edit paths can still lose track of which source graph should map to which target. The authors ask when reordering legal shortest edits preserves this source-target coupling without changing the pairing, the mandatory edits, or the sampling budget. Under a common Poisson clock they prove that **the source-blind Markov projection reaches the unavoidable clock-error floor exactly when routes to distinct targets share no intermediate graph states**, while routes to the same target may merge freely. This yields a finite-state routing formulation with recovery certificates, a capacity-constrained family where edit orders with identical marginal error differ sharply in paired error, and an aliasing bound that links route design to the terminal fidelity of a learned graph-only generator.

papers.title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
papers.abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.
papers.summary: Behavior cloning of a nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) expert is hard for multiscale systems because slow states, fast stiff states, and predictable exogenous inputs interact nonlinearly in ways a single shared latent space represents poorly. Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (`SRLBC`) gives each timescale group its own embedding and is evaluated on a pressurized water reactor load-following benchmark over 500 long-horizon rollouts and 20 training seeds. Separated embeddings beat shared-embedding baselines on cost, imitation accuracy, and constraint satisfaction, and **standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at 15x lower compute**; wrapping them in a safety-augmented scheme that only invokes the optimizer when a predicted input sequence is not certified safe keeps a 6.8x speedup with at least 99.8% feasibility and the best robustness under distribution shift. Jacobian sensitivity analysis shows the learned controller relies on sparse latent features that each map to one group of physical variables.

papers.title: SaiVLA-JEPA: Evaluating Future Latent Prediction in JEPA-Conditioned VLA Control
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn to predict representations rather than pixels, offering a compact way to model how visual scenes evolve. We ask whether this predictive objective improves closed-loop control when a vision-language-action (VLA) policy already uses V-JEPA features. We call our JEPA-conditioned flow policy family SaiVLA-JEPA. It combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and receives features from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference, leaving the action sampler unchanged. We compare policies without JEPA features, with current JEPA conditioning, and with additional future supervision on 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes. Current JEPA conditioning reaches about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA, while future supervision provides no detectable aggregate gain at the evaluated training budget. We separately evaluate SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA, which adapts latent context, and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA, which adapts selected parameters. The context-retry gain is a system-level result under a larger attempt budget; parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls. These results motivate assessing latent-prediction objectives through paired closed-loop rollouts rather than latent loss alone.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict future representations rather than pixels, and the authors test whether that predictive objective helps a vision-language-action (VLA) policy that already consumes frozen `V-JEPA` features. The `SaiVLA-JEPA` family pairs a vision-language model with a diffusion-transformer action expert and adds two lightweight heads that predict future latents during training only, leaving the action sampler unchanged at inference. On 10,030 paired `LIBERO-Plus` episodes, conditioning on current JEPA features lifts success from 71.6% to about 82.5%, but **adding future-latent supervision gives no detectable aggregate gain** at the training budget studied. A context-adaptation variant improves only under a larger retry budget, parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy, and the authors argue latent-prediction objectives should be judged by paired closed-loop rollouts rather than latent loss alone.

papers.title: Leaving the Cave by Breaking the Symmetry: Identifiable Structure Can Enable Cross-Lingual Generalization
papers.abstract: Why do multilingual language models generalize across languages even without shared vocabulary? The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different data, objectives, and modalities converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. Extending this intuition to representations inside a single multilingual model, we propose the Relational Identifiability Hypothesis: relations in a shared world can promote entity alignment by ruling out alternative cross-lingual correspondences, making corresponding entities more likely to become directly readable without an additional transformation. We test this hypothesis in a controlled bilingual Transformer whose two token-disjoint languages describe the same modular-arithmetic world. We find that the languages can develop a shared answer subspace without aligning corresponding numbers. Cross-lingual alignment emerges selectively when the available relations constrain number correspondences: subtraction makes zero task-level identifiable, inducing selective alignment, while an order-sensitive operation produces broad alignment across numbers. These patterns predict success in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. Together, our results show that relational structure in a shared world can promote entity alignment and enable transfer.
papers.summary: Why multilingual language models transfer across languages without shared vocabulary is examined through the proposed Relational Identifiability Hypothesis: relations in a shared world rule out alternative cross-lingual correspondences, making matching entities directly readable without an extra transformation. The authors train a controlled bilingual Transformer on two token-disjoint languages that describe the same modular-arithmetic world. The two languages can develop a shared answer subspace without aligning corresponding numbers, and **alignment emerges only when the available relations constrain number correspondences**: subtraction makes zero identifiable and induces selective alignment, while an order-sensitive operation produces broad alignment across numbers. These alignment patterns predict success in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.

papers.title: Similar Scores, Opposite Failures: Human Correction as an Instrument for Video Caption Evaluation
papers.abstract: Video captioning models are increasingly evaluated with metrics designed for single-sentence image captions. We test whether those metrics recover human judgement on dense, multi-window video description, and find that they do not. Six frontier models captioned 196 short clips. Trained annotators post-edited every caption against a failure taxonomy fixed before annotation, once as a whole-clip overview and once window by window, and a quality-control reviewer checked each annotation, yielding 1,144 overview verdicts and 4,672 window verdicts. Reference-overlap metrics do not separate the captions reviewers accepted from those they rejected: BLEU-4 reaches an AUC of 0.510 and a CIDEr-style tf-idf cosine 0.528, and restricting references to reviewer corrections leaves BLEU-4 at 0.479 (95% CI 0.431-0.529), indistinguishable from chance. Review granularity changes what is detected. The same annotators record camera and shot errors on 2.7% of captions when reading the overview and on 12.8% when reading window by window, a 4.7x gap that holds across every robustness check we ran, on the mode most likely to need a near-total rewrite. Correct-overview rates span 54.1-72.7%, but only 4 of 15 pairwise gaps survive Bonferroni correction (5 after adjusting for reviewer and clip effects), and accuracy and derived severity order the models differently. Models with statistically indistinguishable accuracy have sharply different failure profiles, which no single scalar shows. We argue that caption evaluation should record what was wrong rather than only how often, and we report the taxonomy, the per-model profiles, the corpus properties that predict difficulty, and the code that regenerates every number in the paper.
papers.summary: Metrics built for single-sentence image captions are routinely applied to dense, multi-window video descriptions, and the authors test whether they track human judgment. Six frontier models captioned 196 clips; trained annotators post-edited each caption against a failure taxonomy fixed before annotation, both as a whole-clip overview and window by window, producing 1,144 overview and 4,672 window verdicts. Reference-overlap metrics fail to separate accepted from rejected captions, with **`BLEU-4` reaching an AUC of 0.510** and a `CIDEr`-style tf-idf cosine 0.528, and scoring against reviewer corrections stays indistinguishable from chance. Window-level review surfaces camera and shot errors 4.7 times more often than overview review, and models with statistically indistinguishable accuracy show sharply different failure profiles, leading the authors to argue evaluation should record what went wrong rather than only how often.

papers.title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery in crystal structure prediction. AtomSteer improves molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity. For protein-ligand complexes, AtomSteer reduces ligand E/Z errors relative to experimental reference structures while achieving competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity. Our method provides a unified framework for adding chemical and crystallographic control to existing atomistic generative models without retraining or architectural changes.
papers.summary: Diffusion and flow-matching models for crystals, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes often violate crystallographic symmetry, geometric, and stereochemical constraints. `AtomSteer` is a test-time steering framework that corrects intermediate predictions during sampling using bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections onto periodic symmetries, accepting an update only when it improves constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. Applied to the pretrained `FlowMM`, `ET-Flow`, and `Boltz-2` backbones, it improves space-group coverage and target space-group recovery for crystals, **raises molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while preserving conformer ensemble fidelity**, and reduces ligand E/Z errors in protein-ligand complexes with competitive docking success and `PoseBusters` validity, all without retraining or architectural changes.

papers.title: What Hallucinations Have We Measured? Semantic Illusion, Confabulation, and Expressed Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Hallucination remains one of the most critical challenges in deploying large language models (LLMs) reliably and safely. Yet the term is used inconsistently across the research community. We argue for a strict definition of hallucinations in LLMs. First, hallucinations should be confident incorrectness, kept separate from expressed uncertainty (UNK)1. UNK reveals that the model may be wrong, whereas a hallucination does not reveal it and is therefore more dangerous in practice. Conflating the two obscures their distinct behaviors and makes them hard to study. Second, hallucinations should be split by a simple re-elicitation test: does any semantically equivalent prompt recover the correct response? This test probes whether the relevant knowledge2 is accessible. If none does, the knowledge is likely absent or inaccessible, and the error type is a confabulation (CF) that likely requires external knowledge or retraining; if some does, the knowledge is accessible from the model but applied inconsistently, and the error type is a semantic illusion (SI) that simple prompt or decoding changes can mitigate3. Re-evaluating 14 recent hallucination methods under this taxonomy yields three findings. (1) Detection methods flag UNK more often than hallucinated responses (i.e., SI and CF). (2) Mitigation methods are far more effective for SI than for CF. (3) Latent signals are more informative than output-level signals for CF. An audit of recent hallucination papers shows that most conflate these categories. We recommend reporting CF, SI, and UNK separately, and introduce a practical labeling protocol that needs only a modest number of semantically equivalent prompts.
papers.summary: The term hallucination is used inconsistently across large language model (LLM) research, so the authors propose a strict taxonomy. Confident incorrectness is separated from expressed uncertainty (UNK), and hallucinations are further split by a re-elicitation test: if some semantically equivalent prompt recovers the correct answer, the error is a semantic illusion (SI) that prompt or decoding changes can fix, and if none does, it is a confabulation (CF) that likely needs external knowledge or retraining. Re-evaluating 14 recent hallucination methods under this scheme shows that detection methods flag UNK more often than actual hallucinations, **mitigation methods work far better on SI than on CF**, and latent signals beat output-level signals for CF. An audit finds most recent papers conflate these categories, and the authors provide a labeling protocol that needs only a modest number of semantically equivalent prompts.

papers.title: Value Probes: Learned Value Functions for Beam-Search Red Teaming
papers.abstract: Automated red-team auditing of language models is an important way to evaluate safety-relevant behaviors. These audits implicitly search a tree of possible conversation pathways: at each turn an auditor model decides which conversation to continue, and an LLM judge scores the dialogue. We emphasize that this auditing procedure is a Markov decision process, where states are the conversation history, actions are candidate responses, and rewards are judge scores for the target behavior. By adopting this perspective, we introduce two major improvements to auditing. First, we propose adopting beam search for the audit rather than relying on the auditor alone. We then interpret the problem of finding states that are likely to lead to problematic behavior as value estimation. Surprisingly, we show that this value function can be estimated by linear probing from the target model's activations to predict discounted future rewards - a method we term "Value Probes." By using Value Probes as a heuristic in our beam-search audit, we are able to substantially improve auditing success. Across 18 target behaviors and 3 scales of models, our approach raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% compared to (token-matched) standard auditing approaches. Furthermore, we show that Value Probes can be fit using off-policy data from smaller models. We also ablate individual components, and show that our method offers a comparably-performant and more efficient alternative to more expensive language model follow-ups. We hope these methods will improve language model auditing and lead to safer models.
papers.summary: Automated red-team audits of language models implicitly search a tree of conversations, with an auditor choosing which dialogue to extend and an LLM judge scoring the result. The authors frame this as a Markov decision process, replace the auditor's greedy choice with beam search, and treat the question of which conversation states lead to problematic behavior as value estimation. They find that **a linear probe on the target model's activations can predict discounted future judge scores**, and using these `Value Probes` as a beam-search heuristic raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% over token-matched standard auditing across 18 target behaviors and three model scales. The probes can be fit on off-policy data from smaller models and match more expensive language-model follow-ups at lower cost.

papers.title: From Leniency to Suspicion: How an Open Post-Training Recipe Changes Whom LLM Fact-Checkers Believe
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly fact-check online content with the poster's identity in view. However, it remains unclear which post-training changes how much a model's truth judgement depends on the poster's social class, and how such a change happens inside the model. This paper investigates job-based doubt, i.e., judging a claim false more often when the poster has a lower-status job, using fact-checked claims with randomised poster profiles in base and post-trained checkpoints of six model families. Our results reveal that: 1) post-training creates such doubt only with the open T\"ulu-3 recipe (OLMo-2 32B, T\"ulu-3 70B), not with Meta's, Alibaba's or Mistral's; the effect is under one percentage point but statistically reliable, exceeding training drift and replicating on independent claim sets; 2) in OLMo-2 32B, the model does not start noticing the poster's job more, but starts interpreting it differently: a lower-status job pushes the base model toward "true" and the post-trained model toward "false"; and 3) this flip is carried by a single residual-stream direction and happens at supervised fine-tuning. The mechanism was confirmed on 400 new claims with pre-specified predictions. None of seven deployed commercial models doubts lower-status posters more. Our work underscores the need to audit speaker bias per training recipe.
papers.summary: LLMs increasingly fact-check posts with the author's identity visible, raising the question of whether post-training makes truth judgments depend on the poster's social class. Using fact-checked claims paired with randomized poster profiles, the authors measure job-based doubt, judging a claim false more often when the poster holds a lower-status job, across base and post-trained checkpoints from six model families. **Only the open `Tülu-3` recipe (`OLMo-2 32B`, `Tülu-3 70B`) introduces such doubt**, with an effect under one percentage point that is nonetheless statistically reliable and replicates on independent claim sets, while the Meta, Alibaba, and Mistral recipes and seven deployed commercial models do not. In `OLMo-2 32B` the model does not attend to the job more but interprets it differently, a flip carried by a single residual-stream direction that appears at the supervised fine-tuning stage and was confirmed on 400 new claims with pre-specified predictions.

papers.title: An Alignment Benchmark for Enterprise Agents on Era by Eon
papers.abstract: AI agents are widely used in enterprises to access business systems and act on them in pursuit of a goal. However, fulfilling a user's request can cause harm. Era by Eon is a product that creates a digital twin of a company by simulating its business systems and data. Its simulators implement the programming interfaces of real products. Our benchmark uses ten of these systems, including Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira and Slack. We tested whether agents would carry out harmful business requests or trust misleading information in company records. We ran 19 models on 41 tasks three times, for 2,337 runs. Of the 2,304 runs that produced an answer, 918 (40%) contained a violation. The most common were false claims about actions or records (290 runs), following planted instructions (266) and disclosing sensitive data to the wrong audience (249). Every attempted change was recorded and blocked before it took effect. Misleading Slack messages caused 16 models to report an incorrect ticket status in 47 of 57 runs. No model was free of violations. The four best models violated in 22 to 24% of their runs. Yet one of them, Nova Pro, did the task correctly in only 30 runs.
