papers.summary: Enterprise AI agents act on business systems to fulfill user requests, and those requests can themselves be harmful or rest on misleading records. The benchmark uses ten simulated business systems from `Era by Eon`, a digital-twin product that implements the programming interfaces of real tools such as Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira, and Slack, and tests whether agents carry out harmful requests or trust planted misinformation. Across 19 models, 41 tasks, and 2,337 runs, **40% of answered runs contained a violation**, most commonly false claims about actions or records, following planted instructions, and disclosing sensitive data to the wrong audience, with every attempted change blocked before it took effect. No model was violation-free; the four best violated in 22 to 24% of runs, and misleading Slack messages led 16 models to report a wrong ticket status in 47 of 57 runs.

papers.title: Implicit Minor Detection from Multi-Turn Dialogue in High-Risk AI Interactions: A Constrained Self-Evolving LLM Harness
papers.abstract: In high-risk text interactions, a system may need to estimate whether the current speaker is likely to be a minor before applying age-conditioned safeguards. Many text-based dialogue systems lack strong identity signals such as account information, verified identity, facial data, or device data, and must rely on weak cues that emerge across multiple turns. We formulate implicit minor detection under weak identity information as a high-risk user-attribute inference task and propose a constrained framework comprising a large language model, a Harness, and a Maker-Checker protocol. The framework controls when inference is invoked, requires structured dialogue-linked evidence, and subjects validation-selected Harness revisions to version-level review. On a controlled Chinese benchmark comprising 8,328 multi-turn dialogues, our method improves average precision and minor-class F1 by 7.60 and 6.37 percentage points, respectively, over direct inference using the same LLM family.
papers.summary: Text-only dialogue systems in high-risk settings may need to estimate whether a speaker is a minor before applying age-conditioned safeguards, yet they usually lack account, identity, facial, or device signals and must rely on weak cues spread across turns. The authors cast this as a high-risk user-attribute inference task and propose a constrained framework combining a large language model, a Harness that controls when inference is invoked and requires structured dialogue-linked evidence, and a Maker-Checker protocol that subjects validation-selected Harness revisions to version-level review. On a controlled Chinese benchmark of 8,328 multi-turn dialogues, **the method improves average precision by 7.60 and minor-class F1 by 6.37 percentage points** over direct inference with the same LLM family.

papers.title: PT$^3$: Prototype-Guided Self-Supervised Pretraining for Generalizable mmWave Human Point Cloud Representation
papers.abstract: Multi-source millimeter-wave (mmWave) observations offer an opportunity to learn human representations reusable across sensing tasks. However, sparse detections and multipath effects make these observations unstable, challenging existing point cloud pretraining methods. We propose PT$^3$, a prototype-guided self-supervised pretraining framework for mmWave human point clouds. PT$^3$ represents local states in spatial regions as sparse compositions of shared prototypes and learns their temporal evolution through autoregressive prediction. Observation consistency further stabilizes representations under radar perturbations. After pretraining on unlabeled sequences from multiple sources, the same frozen encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction on datasets not used for pretraining. Across these tasks, PT$^3$ outperforms the compared pretraining baselines and achieves competitive or superior performance to task-specific models.
papers.summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar produces sparse, multipath-corrupted human point clouds that destabilize existing point cloud pretraining methods. `PT³` is a prototype-guided self-supervised framework that represents local states in spatial regions as sparse compositions of shared prototypes, learns their temporal evolution through autoregressive prediction, and adds an observation-consistency objective to stabilize representations under radar perturbations. After pretraining on unlabeled multi-source sequences, **a single frozen encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction on datasets excluded from pretraining**, outperforming the compared pretraining baselines and matching or exceeding task-specific models.

papers.title: REVBRAIN: Real-time Probabilistic EEG Forecasting Using Residual Vector Quantization
papers.abstract:
Real-time forecasting of resting-state EEG signals is required by applications like brain-state-dependent stimulation, where computer generated actions are coupled with ongoing neural oscillations. Recently, the deep learning model WaveNet was proposed for the forecasting task. It shows superior accuracy compared to the prevailing method, the linear autoregressive (AR) model, and provides a built-in uncertainty measure due to its probabilistic modeling framework. However, inference using WaveNet is too slow for real-time use due to its sample-by-sample autoregressive operation: a single forecast requires evaluating the model tens or hundreds of times depending on the length of the prediction window.
  In this paper, we present REVBRAIN, a probabilistic deep learning method that produces forecasts in real time by generating the forecast over the whole prediction horizon at once. This is achieved by tokenizing the output space using residual vector quantization (RVQ) and generating forecasts over the items in the tokenized space.
  We tested REVBRAIN for forecasting 200 ms of EEG time series in the alpha-frequency band (8-13 Hz) and compared our results against WaveNet model. We found that REVBRAIN achieved real-time inference on a laptop GPU and an over $50\times$ speedup compared to WaveNet, while reaching superior prediction accuracy.
  By achieving real-time inference speed, REVBRAIN enables incorporating accurate and probabilistic EEG forecasting into BCI applications, opening up new ways for investigating the functioning of the human brain.
papers.summary: Brain-state-dependent stimulation needs real-time forecasts of resting-state electroencephalography (EEG), and while `WaveNet` beats the standard linear autoregressive (AR) model on accuracy and provides built-in uncertainty estimates, its sample-by-sample autoregressive inference is too slow for real-time use. `REVBRAIN` tokenizes the output space with residual vector quantization (RVQ) and generates the forecast over the whole prediction horizon at once in the tokenized space. Forecasting 200 ms of alpha-band (8-13 Hz) EEG, it runs in real time on a laptop GPU with **over a 50x speedup compared with `WaveNet`** while also reaching higher prediction accuracy, which the authors say makes probabilistic EEG forecasting usable in brain-computer interface (BCI) applications.

papers.title: A goodness of fit approach to select the optimal visit sequence for nonparametric data synthesis
papers.abstract: Synthetic data are a promising way to maintain privacy while disseminating research data, thereby enabling compliance with the open science principles. Popular methods for generating synthetic data include sequential synthesis, where each variable is generated conditionally on the preceding ones in a given order. This order, also called the visit sequence of the synthesizer, is known to affect the quality of synthetic data. This raises the question of the criteria that should guide its choice. In this work, we present a novel method to perform such selection based on a goodness of fit criterion, and show that it outperforms alternative structure-based methods, both in terms of synthesis quality and time complexity. The proposed method also has the advantage of being applicable to any type of data and any class of conditional distribution models.
papers.summary: Sequential synthesis generates synthetic research data one variable at a time, each conditioned on those before it, and the chosen variable order, known as the visit sequence, is known to affect data quality. The authors propose selecting the visit sequence with a goodness-of-fit criterion rather than structure-based heuristics. **The goodness-of-fit approach outperforms structure-based alternatives in both synthesis quality and time complexity**, and it applies to any data type and any class of conditional distribution model.

papers.title: Persona Learning from Feedback for Personalized AI Assistants
papers.abstract: Personalizing AI assistants requires adapting their behavior to users' preferences and task contexts. Existing work elicits assistant personas through persona prompting or finetuning on persona-conditioned generations. However, persona descriptions alone do not identify what to change or preserve in a particular response, or which behaviors suit the current request. We introduce $\textit{Persona Learning from Feedback (PLF)}$, a framework that learns reusable, preference-grounded assistant personas as independent LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone. During training, a frozen self-teacher conditions on persona specifications and response-specific feedback to provide token-level supervision on each adapter's own generated prefixes. A feedback gate focuses corrective updates on responses judged to need improvement. At deployment, a supervised router uses the request or dialogue to select a single adapter or a fixed composition, without user-specific finetuning. We evaluate PLF on single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and multi-turn tutoring with simulated students' reactions. Across both settings, PLF improves model-judged preference fit over fixed-persona policies and strong baselines including persona prompting and persona distillation, demonstrating how feedback-trained behaviors can be reused for adaptive assistant personalization without degrading general capabilities.
papers.summary: Persona prompting and persona-conditioned finetuning describe how an assistant should behave but do not identify what to change or preserve in a specific response, or which behaviors suit the current request. Persona Learning from Feedback (`PLF`) trains reusable personas as independent `LoRA` adapters on a shared frozen backbone, where a frozen self-teacher conditioned on the persona specification and response-specific feedback supplies token-level supervision on each adapter's own generated prefixes, and a feedback gate concentrates updates on responses judged to need improvement. At deployment a supervised router picks a single adapter or a fixed composition from the request or dialogue, with no user-specific finetuning. On single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and multi-turn tutoring with simulated students, **`PLF` improves model-judged preference fit over persona prompting, persona distillation, and fixed-persona policies** without degrading general capabilities.

papers.title: Co-Evolving Policy and Rubric via Capability Awareness for Open-Ended Generation
papers.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers interpretable, fine-grained supervision for aligning large language models (LLMs) on open-ended generation tasks. However, static rubric criteria may become saturated or remain beyond the policy's exploration, rendering the reward signals insufficiently discriminative. While recent efforts seek to guide sampling exploration or evolve rubrics, they fail to explicitly factor in how rubric difficulty should track the evolving policy's capabilities, resulting in a persistent mismatch between the optimization objective and the policy's current capability frontier. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving Policy and Rubric via \textbf{C}apability \textbf{A}wareness (\textbf{CoCA}), a closed-loop framework that jointly adapts the rubric and policy through criterion-level diagnosis. Specifically, CoCA contrasts query-only and rubric-guided rollouts to characterize each criterion relative to the current policy, recalibrates criteria with mismatched difficulty, and identifies guidance-revealed capability gaps for frontier-based learning. Based on this insight, CoCA either expands rubric-conditioned frontiers through guided optimization or transfers qualified gains through on-policy self-distillation. As the policy updates, CoCA improves the capability diagnosis and enables more reliable distillation, thereby completing the co-evolution loop. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and LLMs demonstrate that CoCA consistently improves performance over rubric-based RL methods. Moreover, CoCA promotes the internalization of guidance-revealed capabilities into query-only behavior while mitigating capability degradation.
papers.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) gives interpretable, fine-grained rewards for open-ended generation, but static rubric criteria can become saturated or sit beyond what the policy can reach, so the reward stops discriminating. Co-Evolving Policy and Rubric via Capability Awareness (`CoCA`) contrasts query-only and rubric-guided rollouts to diagnose each criterion relative to the current policy, recalibrates criteria whose difficulty is mismatched, and identifies capability gaps that only appear under guidance. It then either expands the rubric-conditioned frontier through guided optimization or transfers qualified gains back into query-only behavior through on-policy self-distillation, and the improved policy in turn sharpens the diagnosis. **Across diverse benchmarks and LLMs, `CoCA` consistently outperforms rubric-based RL methods**, internalizing guidance-revealed capabilities while mitigating capability degradation.

papers.title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement requires a model to decide not only what training experience to generate but also when its current experience has stopped being useful, and many methods additionally derive training targets from majority voting over the model's own uncertain predictions. `A-RSI` separates the two: it monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh the task pool when the learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores, while a static library of model-authored programs generates multimodal questions with independently checkable reference answers. The task-generation contract is specified explicitly, chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules are verified automatically, and generated answers are audited separately, with no external training examples or human-written labels used. **On an eleven-benchmark suite, the average score rises from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.**
papers.highlight_summary:
Zero-data recursive self-improvement loops tend to keep spending updates on a self-generated task pool after it stops yielding useful gradient, and when training targets come from majority voting the model's own errors become its next labels. `A-RSI` separates the two problems: it decides *when* to swap the pool purely from training logs, never from validation or test scores, and it gets answer correctness from a frozen library of model-written programs that render the image, question, and reference answer from one shared configuration.

- The Solver trains with `GRPO` in windows of 100 updates on a 400-task pool, using a reward of correctness plus a format bonus and a truncation penalty, and after at least three windows the controller replaces the whole pool with 400 unused random tasks under fixed family quotas (geometry, charts, tables, counting) if the count of distinct prompts with nonzero within-group advantage drops to **at most 85%** of its value two windows earlier or training accuracy rises by **at least 10 points**, carrying the model weights forward.
- On an eleven-benchmark suite (`MathVision`, `MathVerse`, `MMMU-Pro`, `ChartQA`, `PhyX`, and others), `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` improves from **57.77 to 61.05** macro average over eight continuation windows with only **800 fresh tasks** (the public base scores 56.65 before initialization), while `MiMo-VL-7B-SFT` goes from **59.08 to 60.71**.
- At matched update budgets, refreshing every window reaches 60.64 using **3,200** new tasks, periodic refresh reaches 59.89 with 1,200, and never refreshing scores 58.35 at window 6 versus **60.40** for `A-RSI` before its training health gate fails and halts the run.
- Difficulty-aware replacement strategies (frontier, failure-prioritized, learnable-band, ladder controllers) all trail plain random draws by 0.05 to 2.63 points, and the gain over base retains **80%** when the output limit doubles from 4096 to 8192 tokens, compared with 59% for `MM-Zero` v5 (3.25 versus 2.45 points above base).
- Each arm is a single run with no replications, the detector is not shown to beat a fixed three-window schedule (with frontier selection held fixed, log-triggered refresh trails periodic refresh by 0.30 points and the first two triggers coincided with a three-window cadence), and the +2.05-point edge over no-refresh decomposes into **+2.66 from responses that now finish within the token budget and −0.60 on answers both arms completed**, so most of the gain comes from completing rather than correcting answers.

papers.title: Do Audio LLMs HEAR Pain? Tracing Acoustic Evidence from Speech to Language Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.
papers.summary: Large audio language models (LALMs) take speech as input, but it is unclear how much they use the non-lexical acoustic information it carries. Using `TAME-Pain`, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels, the authors introduce `HEAR`, a four-stage diagnostic that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. **On Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, every model performs at chance**, with same-speaker references or few-shot examples adding at most six points of balanced accuracy, while the same models reach 87.5-99.7% on spoken ratings whose words reveal the answer. Layer-wise probing shows pain is decodable from early audio representations but fades in deeper layers, and reinjecting recovered acoustic cues as structured text into the prompt improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points.

papers.title: CALM: Conflict-Aware Lifecycle Memory Governance for Long-Horizon Language Agents
papers.abstract: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet indispensable for reconstructing the past. Relevance-based retrieval overlooks this tension: semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility are distinct. We propose CALM, a conflict-aware lifecycle memory governance framework that decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission. CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits query-appropriate evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the best overall accuracy. Compared with simple filtering and reranking, query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection. Conflict-blocking and robustness analyses show CALM suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence. Historical-reconstruction experiments demonstrate that preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.
papers.summary: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet essential for reconstructing the past, and relevance-based retrieval conflates semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility. `CALM` decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission: it converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates their validity and lifecycle states from support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. **On `LongMemEval-S` and `LoCoMo` with `Qwen` and `GPT` backbones, `CALM` achieves the best overall accuracy against state-of-the-art baselines**, and query-conditioned admission beats simple filtering and reranking at evidence selection. Conflict-blocking analyses show it suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while keeping useful ones, and preserving superseded records enables accurate earlier-state reasoning without hurting current-state answers.

papers.title: Episodic looking - using reinforcement learning to bias perception enhances few-shot and continual learning with protection from forgetting
papers.abstract:
There is a fundamental contradiction between the desire for models that can generalize, and models that can continuously adapt to recent input with changing statistics. These conditions, captured in few-shot and continual learning settings, can bias or disrupt learned representations. This harms generalization to a broader context, leaving the model unable to overcome input variance.
  This paper proposes a solution based on the Complementary Learning System architecture (CLS), in which a Short-Term Memory (STM) delegates generalization to a slow, statistical Long-Term Memory (LTM). Delegation is achieved by working in a space of robust, generalized perceptions produced by the LTM. With this separation, the STM can focus on memorizing recent input and avoiding interference between memories.
  We show that on an image classification task, the resulting CLS model is more resistant to forgetting in a domain-incremental continual learning setting than a baseline ResNet LTM, and generalizes more effectively in a few-shot setting than other continual learners.
  In the continual setting, overall accuracy is slightly worse than existing continual learning models, but with a different mix of performance characteristics. Results analysis suggests that the model is limited by the representations and representational plasticity of the LTM. In future work, we will seek to address this by replaying STM memories to the LTM.
papers.summary: Models that generalize broadly and models that adapt quickly to recent, shifting input pull in opposite directions, and few-shot and continual learning settings expose that tension as disrupted representations and forgetting. The authors build on the Complementary Learning System (CLS) architecture: a slow, statistical Long-Term Memory (LTM) produces robust generalized perceptions, and a Short-Term Memory (STM) operating in that perceptual space memorizes recent inputs while avoiding interference between memories. On image classification, the `CLS` model **forgets less in a domain-incremental continual learning setting than a baseline `ResNet` LTM** and generalizes better in few-shot settings than other continual learners, though its overall continual-learning accuracy is slightly below existing methods; the authors attribute the gap to the LTM's limited representational plasticity and plan to address it by replaying STM memories into the LTM.

papers.title: Dual DeltaNet: Value-Side Memory Reorganization for Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. Code: https://github.com/ReichtumQian/DualDeltaNet
papers.summary: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) keep a fixed-size recurrent state in place of softmax attention, and the delta rule reduces interference in that state by correcting the value stored for each key, but it ignores how related value features are spread across the state. Viewing the state matrix as a bank of addresses storing values, where reading with a value-feature selector aggregates the addresses whose stored values match it, the authors extend `Kimi Delta Attention` (`KDA`) with a two-sided delta rule: the key-side rule corrects the value associated with the current key while a value-side rule reorganizes the addresses occupied by selected features of the current value. They derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that raises arithmetic intensity at inference, and report that **`Dual DeltaNet` (`DDN`) achieves the strongest overall results against `KDA`, `GDN-2`, and `Mamba-3` across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval** with modest training and inference overhead relative to `KDA`.

papers.title: Structural Pattern Mining in Inka Khipus: A KFG Re-Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper reports a methodological pivot from the Open Khipu Repository to the Khipu Field Guide (KFG) database, prompted by stalled progress on the OKR, and a full re-analysis of the resulting 650-khipu sample. Three findings recur across every analysis attempted. First, khipu size confounds nearly every derived structural count, explaining 42-70% of its variance; all subsequent models control for it. Second, the two-letter name prefix (AS, UR, HP, QU, JC, MM, KH) identifies the original cataloger, not a site or period, which turns documentation completeness into a second confound that must be modeled explicitly. Controlling for both, khipus cataloged by Hugo Pereyra's Proyecto Quipu (HP) show significantly fewer Ascher sum-relation types than Gary Urton's (UR) khipus (p = 0.044), while the Ascher-cataloged (AS) khipus are too collinear with their own near-total lack of side/direction documentation to assess (VIF = 5.0). Third, generic structural clustering (UMAP+HDBSCAN) does not separate the pooled 650-khipu sample from two independent null models (permutation and Gaussian), corroborating an independent conclusion already reached by the KFG itself; the same test restricted to a single cataloger (UR) proved not reproducible across runtime environments and is reported here as a methodological caveat rather than evidence of structure. A targeted replication of the KFG's own S/Z-knot spatial-block heuristic for calendar/astronomical khipus recovers 8 of 10 published candidates and proposes 34 additional ones under the same criterion.
papers.summary: After progress on the Open Khipu Repository stalled, the authors switched to the Khipu Field Guide (KFG) database and re-analyzed a sample of 650 Inka khipus for structural patterns. Khipu size explains 42-70% of the variance in nearly every derived structural count, and the two-letter name prefix identifies the original cataloger rather than a site or period, which makes documentation completeness a second confound that must be modeled explicitly. Controlling for both, khipus cataloged by Hugo Pereyra's Proyecto Quipu show significantly fewer Ascher sum-relation types than Gary Urton's (p = 0.044), **generic structural clustering with `UMAP` and `HDBSCAN` fails to separate the pooled sample from permutation and Gaussian null models**, and a replication of the KFG's S/Z-knot spatial-block heuristic for calendar or astronomical khipus recovers 8 of 10 published candidates and proposes 34 more under the same criterion.

papers.title: Robust Active Learning for More Efficient and Reliable Paths to Optimal Design
papers.abstract: Simulation-driven design optimization requires active learning strategies that efficiently combine models with different computational costs and levels of fidelity. We introduce Multifidelity Cost-Aware Screening (MF-CAS), which enables the joint selection of sampling location and fidelity using a surrogate that provides decomposed uncertainty intervals rather than a complete predictive probability distribution. MF-CAS exploits the contribution of each fidelity to the high-fidelity uncertainty together with its computational cost to determine whether a candidate should first be evaluated at low fidelity or directly progressed towards high fidelity. The method is assessed on the constrained 14-dimensional hydrodynamic optimization of the DTMB 5415 hull under a deliberately limited computational budget. MF-CAS achieves an approximately 9.0% resistance reduction, compared with 6.7% for the best baseline optimisation method, demonstrating that incorporating fidelity-resolved uncertainty directly into the joint location-fidelity decision can substantially improve multifidelity active learning efficiency.
papers.summary: Simulation-driven design optimization has to combine simulators of different fidelity and cost, so an active learning strategy must decide jointly where to sample and at which fidelity. Multifidelity Cost-Aware Screening (`MF-CAS`) uses a surrogate that provides decomposed uncertainty intervals rather than a full predictive distribution, weighs each fidelity's contribution to the high-fidelity uncertainty against its computational cost, and decides whether a candidate should first be screened at low fidelity or sent directly toward high fidelity. On the constrained 14-dimensional hydrodynamic optimization of the `DTMB 5415` hull under a deliberately limited compute budget, **`MF-CAS` reduces resistance by approximately 9.0%, versus 6.7% for the best baseline optimizer**.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM Jailbreak Evaluation: Continuous Risk Landscapes Beyond Binary Outcomes
papers.abstract: A binary success indicator is a natural representation for discriminative tasks such as image classification under adversarial perturbations, where each input is mapped to a single prediction. However, generative tasks are fundamentally different: an LLM jailbreak prompt induces a distribution over open-ended trajectories, while a sampled response reveals only one path. Yet LLM jailbreak evaluation typically retains the binary response indicator underlying attack success rate, obscuring the surrounding structure of possible generations. We introduce a continuous, context-conditioned risk landscape over first-token branches, estimated by fixing candidate openings and repeatedly sampling their continuations. This continuous risk-landscape perspective reveals two complementary properties: current decoder exposure and safe rerouting capacity, which have been obscured by binary-indicator-based ASR. The resulting representation also provides a common basis for comparing clean prompts, attacked variants, and attack strength against a known adaptive defense. Across multiple target models and jailbreak attacks, we uncover risky branches beneath apparently safe outputs, identify qualitatively different ways attacks reshape the model's opening distribution, and show that attacks strongest before a defense do not necessarily remain the strongest after the adaptive defense reacts. These findings recast jailbreaks as deformations of the surrounding continuation-risk landscape, establishing a more informative foundation for understanding jailbreak behavior and developing safer language models.
papers.summary: Jailbreak evaluation for large language models (LLMs) usually inherits the binary success indicator used for adversarial image classification, but a jailbreak prompt induces a distribution over open-ended generations of which any sampled response reveals only one path, so attack success rate (ASR) hides the structure of what the model might have produced. The authors instead estimate a continuous, context-conditioned risk landscape over first-token branches by fixing candidate openings and repeatedly sampling their continuations, exposing two properties, current decoder exposure and safe rerouting capacity, and giving a common basis for comparing clean prompts, attacked variants, and attack strength against a known adaptive defense. Across multiple target models and attacks they **uncover risky branches beneath apparently safe outputs**, identify qualitatively different ways attacks reshape the model's opening distribution, and show that the attacks strongest before a defense reacts are not necessarily the strongest afterward.

papers.title: Two-Stage Clipping: Linear-Time Approximate and Exact Mixed-Norm Projections for Transformers
papers.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable performance across artificial intelligence tasks, but their computational cost remains a major bottleneck. Structured sparsification provides a promising approach to reducing this cost. In particular, $\ell_{1,\infty}$ projections can induce column-wise sparsity in model matrices, but existing proximal methods (Prox) typically require $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(nm))$ operations for matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, limiting their computational and energy efficiency.
  In this paper, we introduce Two-Stage Clipping (TSC), an efficient structured sparsification operator inspired by bilevel optimization. Rather than solving a bilevel optimization problem in the strict sense, TSC decomposes the computation into two successive stages. First, group-level quantities are projected to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups. Second, the resulting values are used as group-wise clipping thresholds for the matrix coefficients. For square attention matrices ($n \times n$), the complexity of our TSC method is $O(n^2)$, which is linear in the number of matrix coefficients.
  We establish a theoretical bound on the discrepancy between TSC and the exact proximal projection and show on synthetic data that the additional Euclidean approximation cost remains small in practice. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines and validate the theoretical norm identities underlying the proposed construction.
papers.summary: Column-wise structured sparsity in Transformer matrices can be induced with ℓ1,∞ projections, but existing proximal methods cost O(nm log(nm)) operations for an n-by-m matrix, which limits their computational and energy efficiency. Two-Stage Clipping (`TSC`), inspired by bilevel optimization without solving a bilevel problem in the strict sense, first projects group-level quantities to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups, then uses the resulting values as group-wise clipping thresholds for the individual matrix coefficients, giving **O(n^2) complexity for square attention matrices, linear in the number of coefficients**. The authors bound the discrepancy between `TSC` and the exact proximal projection, show on synthetic data that the extra Euclidean approximation cost stays small in practice, and report substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines in benchmarks that also validate the norm identities behind the construction.

papers.title: The Artificial Personality Model: Theory, Implementation, Measurement and Experimental Validation in Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: Artificial personality shapes user experience (UX) in human-machine interaction, yet coherent theoretical frameworks and validated measurement instruments remain limited. This paper refines and empirically evaluates the Artificial Personality Model (APM), a hybrid framework integrating human-centred and machine-specific personality dimensions. Across three experiments (N = 395), the model was operationalised and evaluated using the Artificial Personality Questionnaire (APQ). Factor analyses revealed that some human personality dimensions (e.g., agreeableness, conscientiousness) are partially transferable, whereas others (e.g., extraversion) did not emerge as distinct dimensions. Additional machine-specific dimensions were identified. The APQ provided encouraging initial psychometric evidence, while the human-centred BFI-2 showed poor reliability and an uninterpretable factor structure in Experiment 3. Experimental manipulations demonstrated significant effects of artificial personality on user satisfaction, continuous use intention, and social presence. The findings contribute an empirically refined framework and a novel instrument for measuring perceived artificial personality, offering practical guidance for designing conversational agents.
papers.summary: Artificial personality shapes user experience (UX) in human-machine interaction, yet coherent theory and validated measurement instruments for it remain scarce. The authors refine the Artificial Personality Model (`APM`), a hybrid framework combining human-centred and machine-specific personality dimensions, and evaluate it across three experiments with 395 participants using the new Artificial Personality Questionnaire (`APQ`). Factor analyses show that **agreeableness and conscientiousness partially transfer to machines while extraversion does not emerge as a distinct dimension**, additional machine-specific dimensions appear, the human-centred `BFI-2` showed poor reliability and an uninterpretable factor structure in the third experiment, and manipulating artificial personality significantly affected user satisfaction, continuous use intention, and social presence.

papers.title: Repairs for Whom? Evaluator-Executor Mismatch in Selecting Repairs for Failed LLM Agents
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent fails, repair methods choose which action to replace and what to put in its place. They often score candidate repairs with greedy replay, a stronger model, an environment oracle, or a judge that reads the failed log. We ask whether these evaluators pick repairs that help the agent that will actually execute them. Holding failed trajectories and candidate single-step repairs fixed, we label every candidate with independent rollouts of the deployed policy and measure how much deployment value each evaluator's choice loses. On failures not screened for repair value, pre-specified tests show that greedy replay loses 0.08-0.13 in expected net success gain in ALFWorld and 0.06-0.13 in net reward in WebShop, relative to selection with the deployed agent's own rollouts. At an equal rollout budget, selecting repairs for Qwen2.5-7B with Qwen2.5-14B rollouts loses 0.25 in ALFWorld and 0.07 in WebShop, twenty 14B rollouts per candidate are worth no more than two of the 7B agent's own, and fresh rollouts confirm that the two models prefer opposite repairs on selected disagreement cases. Between similar-sized models from different families, the losses appear in both directions in both environments (0.07-0.17). The scoring executor also changes repair-location labels and method rankings. Repairs should be verified with the executor that will run them, and repair labels should name their executor.
papers.summary: When a large language model (LLM) agent fails, repair methods choose which action to replace and what to put in its place, scoring candidates with greedy replay, a stronger model, an environment oracle, or a judge that reads the failed log; the authors ask whether those evaluators pick repairs that help the agent that will actually execute them. Holding failed trajectories and candidate single-step repairs fixed, they label every candidate with independent rollouts of the deployed policy and measure how much deployment value each evaluator's choice loses. In `ALFWorld` and `WebShop`, greedy replay loses 0.08-0.13 in expected net success gain and 0.06-0.13 in net reward relative to selection with the deployed agent's own rollouts, and **selecting repairs for `Qwen2.5-7B` with `Qwen2.5-14B` rollouts loses 0.25 in `ALFWorld`, with twenty 14B rollouts per candidate worth no more than two of the 7B agent's own**. Fresh rollouts confirm that the two models prefer opposite repairs on disagreement cases, losses of 0.07-0.17 appear in both directions between similar-sized models from different families, and the scoring executor also changes repair-location labels and method rankings, so repairs should be verified with the executor that will run them.

papers.title: How Deterministic SAST and AI Security Agents Divide the Work: Coverage, Harness Policy and Cost in Snyk VulnBench 2.0
papers.abstract: We ask what AI coding agents and AI security harnesses find that deterministic static application security testing (SAST) does not, and what they miss that SAST catches. VulnBench 2.0 is a benchmark of 108 hand-curated, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source web applications in Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Java; 62 flow across more than one file. A finding is credited only if it locates the vulnerability's attacker-controlled source and its dangerous sink, each within two lines. We evaluate nine productized configurations under one blind protocol: the Snyk Code static analyzer, Claude Code's /security-review with three model and effort settings (one with the Snyk MCP server), Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra and Sol, and the DeepSec scanner with two model backends. Snyk Code reached 82.4% macro recall (89 of 108) and Claude Code with Opus 5 at xhigh effort 79.3% (85 of 108); they disagree on 28 vulnerabilities, split 16 to 12, too few to tell them apart. Neither engine was sufficient alone: together they reached 101 of 108, the ceiling of all seven comparable configurations combined, and the AI configurations also reported at least seven real vulnerabilities that the reference set did not contain and Snyk Code did not report. What an AI engine misses depends on its harness as much as on its model: without Claude Code's built-in review policy, the same model matched 16 instead of 9 of the 20 vulnerabilities in the classes that policy excludes or restricts (supplementary run on 19 of 20 applications); Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Sol located 80 vulnerabilities at file level but 34 at line level; DeepSec's model-free file selection kept a file from only 56 of the 108 flows. Coverage and cost were only loosely related. The harness, fixtures, reference sets and all run data are public.
papers.summary: To learn what AI coding agents and AI security harnesses find in web applications that deterministic static application security testing (SAST) misses, and what they miss that SAST catches, the authors built `VulnBench 2.0`, a benchmark of 108 hand-curated, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, and Java applications, 62 of them flowing across more than one file, which credits a finding only if it locates both the attacker-controlled source and the dangerous sink within two lines. Nine productized configurations are evaluated under one blind protocol: `Snyk Code`, `Claude Code`'s `/security-review` at three model and effort settings (one with the Snyk MCP server), `Codex Security` with `GPT-5.6 Luna`, `Terra` and `Sol`, and the `DeepSec` scanner with two model backends. `Snyk Code` reached 82.4% macro recall (89 of 108) and `Claude Code` with `Opus 5` at xhigh effort 79.3% (85 of 108), disagreeing on 28 vulnerabilities, but **neither engine was sufficient alone: together they reached 101 of 108, the ceiling of all seven comparable configurations combined**, and the AI configurations also reported at least seven real vulnerabilities missing from the reference set. What an AI engine misses depends on its harness as much as its model: without `Claude Code`'s built-in review policy the same model matched 16 instead of 9 of the 20 vulnerabilities in classes that policy excludes or restricts, `Codex Security` with `GPT-5.6 Sol` located 80 vulnerabilities at file level but only 34 at line level, and coverage and cost were only loosely related.

papers.title: Think Before You Act: Decision Gate for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly perform consequential actions through external tools, yet their proposed actions are often executed without independent verification of policy compliance or task completion. We introduce JevAct, a runtime verification framework that intercepts selected agent actions before execution and enables feedback-driven correction. JevAct compiles domain policies into executable state checks and structured questions evaluated by a prefill-only decision model, which produces probability-based judgments without relying on LLM generation. By combining deterministic verification of tool-state facts with probabilistic assessment of conversational context, the framework identifies potentially invalid actions and premature task termination, providing targeted feedback for bounded revision. JevAct operates independently of the underlying agent model and requires no modifications to its parameters or tools. We evaluate JevAct across eleven LLM agents on $\tau^2$-bench Airline and Telecom tasks and BFCL. Results show improvements in agent reliability across multiple models and benchmarks, with particularly consistent gains on Telecom and BFCL, while performance on Airline is more mixed. Overall, these findings suggest that combining structured decision models with executable verification can improve the reliability of tool-using LLM agents.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents take consequential actions through external tools, yet their proposed actions are usually executed without any independent check of policy compliance or whether the task is actually complete. `JevAct` is a runtime verification framework that intercepts selected actions before execution, compiles domain policies into executable state checks and structured questions evaluated by a prefill-only decision model that yields probability-based judgments without LLM generation, and combines deterministic verification of tool-state facts with probabilistic assessment of conversational context to flag invalid actions and premature termination and feed targeted feedback back for bounded revision; it requires no changes to the agent's parameters or tools. Evaluated on eleven LLM agents across `τ²-bench` Airline and Telecom tasks and `BFCL`, it improves reliability across multiple models, with **particularly consistent gains on Telecom and `BFCL`** while results on Airline are more mixed.

papers.title: Cross-Primitive Consistency in Jev
papers.abstract: Jev enables efficient decision-making with large language models (LLMs) through typed querying primitives, allowing the same semantic state to be expressed in different formats, such as binary and multiple-choice queries. However, the consistency of decisions across primitives has not been systematically evaluated. This work introduces PrimaCons, a four-axis benchmark for assessing cross-primitive consistency while preserving the semantics of the query. Evaluations across three Jev sizes reveal consistency violations across all four axes. Our analysis shows that these violations follow systematic patterns and that cross-primitive discrepancies predict decision failure with a ROC-AUC of 0.91. To mitigate these inconsistencies, we propose the Cross-Primitive Residual Calibrator (CPRC), which attaches a lightweight residual network to a frozen backbone and jointly optimizes predictive accuracy and cross-primitive consistency. Under a leave-one-domain-out protocol, CPRC reduces cross-primitive inconsistency by 58.57% and improves accuracy by +2.97%., demonstrating its effectiveness in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Our findings establish cross-primitive consistency as a key dimension for evaluating Jev and provide a practical approach to improving the reliability of its decisions. Code and benchmark is available at https://github.com/67L1/PrimaCons-CRPR.
papers.summary: `Jev` lets large language models (LLMs) make decisions efficiently through typed querying primitives, so the same semantic state can be posed as, for instance, a binary or a multiple-choice query, but whether decisions stay consistent across those primitives had not been systematically evaluated. `PrimaCons` is a four-axis benchmark for cross-primitive consistency under semantics-preserving reformulations; evaluations across three `Jev` sizes find violations on all four axes that follow systematic patterns, and **cross-primitive discrepancies predict decision failure with a ROC-AUC of 0.91**. The proposed Cross-Primitive Residual Calibrator (`CPRC`) attaches a lightweight residual network to a frozen backbone and jointly optimizes accuracy and consistency, cutting inconsistency by 58.57% and raising accuracy by 2.97% under a leave-one-domain-out protocol.

papers.title: Right Numbers, Wrong Questions: Evaluating LLMs on Underspecified Financial Queries
papers.abstract: Financial assistants answer questions that sound factual but depend on what the user leaves unsaid: what a data figure measures, which product variant is meant, and the investor's situation and the rules that apply. An assistant that ignores these can still answer with a real number from its data, one that answers a different question. We call this frame collapse. We study it in Indian mutual funds, where product variants and tax rules are formally defined, so the correct answer can be computed for every reading. One study tests each challenge. Given an ambiguously labelled figure, models used it, often under the user's label. Given every alternative labelled, they listed them all, but the layout decided which came first. Missing a fact about the investor, weaker agents assumed a default or an outdated tax rule; requiring the fact did not guarantee its use. Because such answers match their data, checks against the data pass them. An AI judge caught mislabelled figures only when told what each field means, and still passed answers that silently chose another reading. We show how these failures arise, not how often, and propose controls for financial assistants.
papers.summary: Financial assistants field questions that sound factual but hinge on what the user leaves unsaid: what a figure measures, which product variant is meant, and the investor's situation and applicable rules, so a model can return a real number from its data that answers a different question, which the authors call frame collapse. They study it in Indian mutual funds, where product variants and tax rules are formally defined so the correct answer can be computed for every reading, with one study per challenge. Models used ambiguously labelled figures under the user's label, listed every alternative when each was labelled but let layout decide which came first, and weaker agents assumed a default or an outdated tax rule when a fact about the investor was missing; **because such answers match the underlying data, checks against the data pass them, and an AI judge caught mislabelled figures only when told what each field means** while still passing answers that silently chose another reading. The work shows how these failures arise rather than how often, and proposes controls for financial assistants.

papers.title: "Close enough?" An investigation into multiplication errors in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently fail at multi-digit arithmetic, but the underlying mechanisms governing these failures remain poorly understood. While recent work demonstrates that addition errors follow a "noisy quantisation" model localised around carry boundaries, whether this framework generalises to multiplication remains an open question. In this work, we evaluate multiplication capabilities across several small base LLMs on a dataset of 16,991 problems spanning varied operand lengths. We show that multiplication errors do not conform to the addition-style noisy quantisation model. Instead, we uncover a novel error regime in small Qwen models: errors in lower-order columns predominantly preserve parity. Conversely, higher-order digit errors shift toward off-by-one carry failures. Our findings suggest that arithmetic computation in LLMs relies on distinct, multi-periodic internal representations where parity is tracked more robustly than exact digit identity, providing new mechanistic insights into numerical reasoning in transformers.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often fail at multi-digit arithmetic, and prior work showed that addition errors follow a noisy quantisation pattern concentrated around carry boundaries, leaving open whether multiplication behaves the same way. Evaluating several small base LLMs on a dataset of 16,991 multiplication problems with varied operand lengths, the authors find that multiplication errors do not conform to the addition-style noisy quantisation model. Instead, in small `Qwen` models **errors in lower-order columns predominantly preserve parity**, while higher-order digit errors shift toward off-by-one carry failures, which the authors read as evidence for distinct multi-periodic internal representations in which parity is tracked more robustly than exact digit identity.

papers.title: Curriculum-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Robust Autonomous Rocket Landing under Atmospheric Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Autonomous far-range rocket landing is a challenging control problem because navigation, descent-rate regulation, attitude management, and fuel use must be coordinated in the presence of uncertain atmospheric and vehicle dynamics. This paper presents a curriculum-driven proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework for three-dimensional rocket landing in a stochastic environment incorporating altitude-dependent aerodynamic drag, wind shear, temporally correlated turbulence, discrete gusts, uncertain propulsion and aerodynamic parameters, thrust-vector misalignment, engine lag, actuator-gain variation, noisy observations, and command latency. Learning is organised into far-range approach, soft descent, and integrated landing stages. Policy transfer, critic warm-up after reward changes, rehearsal of earlier tasks, and progressive expansion of weather severity are used to support learning across these coupled phases. Across 100,000 evaluation episodes, the policy achieves 96,656 successful landings, corresponding to a success rate of 96.656\% and a 95\% Wilson confidence interval of 96.543--96.766\%. Success decreases from 98.84\% under zero-disturbance conditions to 88.07\% in the highest weather-severity band. Successful touchdowns exhibit small miss distances and low residual horizontal and vertical velocities. An exploratory logistic-regression analysis identifies mean wind speed as the strongest measured correlate of success, with initial distance, initial altitude, initial vertical velocity, and wind-shear exponent also associated with outcomes. The results quantify both the effectiveness of the learned policy over the evaluated disturbance distribution and the degradation that occurs under severe compound atmospheric conditions.
papers.summary: Autonomous far-range rocket landing requires coordinating navigation, descent-rate regulation, attitude management, and fuel use under uncertain atmospheric and vehicle dynamics. The authors train a proximal policy optimization (`PPO`) policy for three-dimensional landing in a stochastic simulator with altitude-dependent drag, wind shear, temporally correlated turbulence, discrete gusts, uncertain propulsion and aerodynamic parameters, thrust-vector misalignment, engine lag, actuator-gain variation, noisy observations, and command latency, organizing learning into far-range approach, soft descent, and integrated landing stages supported by policy transfer, critic warm-up after reward changes, rehearsal of earlier tasks, and progressively harsher weather. Over 100,000 evaluation episodes the policy **achieves 96,656 successful landings, a 96.656% success rate**, falling from 98.84% with no disturbances to 88.07% in the most severe weather band, and an exploratory logistic regression identifies mean wind speed as the strongest measured correlate of success.

papers.title: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Teacher Evolution
papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), which aligns a student model's token-level distribution with that of its self-teacher prompted by privileged context, has emerged as a promising direction to mitigate reward sparsity in sequence-level post-training paradigms. However, OPSD often fails to achieve continuous performance gains during training. In this paper, we find that the model's limited self-teaching capability underlies this phenomenon by generating unreliable guidance on certain samples. To address this problem, we propose Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD), which enables the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive environmental feedback based on task correctness and context independence. First, using these rewards as training objectives, we perform teacher-oriented optimization to continuously enhance the model's self-teaching capability during distillation. Second, by estimating teacher guidance reliability from these rewards, we apply adaptive student-oriented optimization to down-weight samples with unreliable guidance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show that TESD consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods, highlighting the necessity of improving supervision quality in OPSD.
papers.summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (`OPSD`) trains a student to match the token-level distribution of its own self-teacher, the same model prompted with privileged context, as a way around sparse sequence-level rewards in post-training, but it often fails to keep improving during training. The authors trace the stall to the model's limited self-teaching capability, which produces unreliable guidance on certain samples, and propose Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (`TESD`): the self-teacher generates rollouts and receives environmental feedback on task correctness and context independence, those rewards drive teacher-oriented optimization that strengthens self-teaching throughout distillation, and estimated guidance reliability down-weights student updates on unreliable samples. Across multiple datasets and model scales, **`TESD` consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods**, pointing to supervision quality as the bottleneck in `OPSD`.

papers.title: Enhanced image forensics through partial C2PA-based provenance information
papers.abstract: Cryptographically verifiable C2PA-based Content Credentials (CCs) can be attached to freshly acquired or generated digital images but also to already existing ones with no previous provenance information, for instance after processing through trusted C2PA-enabled software tools. The latter case leads to images with so-called partial CCs, which capture only the last operations applied, while prior provenance remains unknown and can be investigated through signal forensics. This paper addresses the forensic analysis of such images, highlighting the opportunity to leverage the partial CCs as additional trusted knowledge to adapt forensic detectors towards the statistical characteristics of the image under analysis and mitigate potential distribution shifts. To this end, a two-step strategy is envisioned: (i) reconstructing the operations applied by the last signer through a structural analysis of the partial CCs; (ii) exploiting the obtained reconstruction to enhance the forensic detector of the analyst through an adaptation process. An empirical analysis on partial CCs produced by commercial C2PA-enabled software tools through different editing operations is carried out, providing evidence on the feasibility of the reconstruction in practical cases. An experimental case study on the forensic task of synthetic image detection is then presented, showing that the proposed strategy can significantly enhance the performance of state-of-the-art detectors on test images that are postprocessed via C2PA-enabled software tools after being generated/acquired.
papers.summary: C2PA-based Content Credentials (CCs) can be attached not only to freshly acquired or generated images but also to pre-existing ones processed through trusted C2PA-enabled software, yielding partial credentials that record only the last operations applied while earlier provenance stays unknown and must be investigated through signal forensics. The authors propose treating those partial credentials as additional trusted knowledge: first reconstruct the operations applied by the last signer through a structural analysis of the credentials, then use that reconstruction to adapt the analyst's forensic detector to the statistical characteristics of the image under analysis and mitigate distribution shift. An empirical analysis of partial credentials produced by commercial C2PA-enabled tools under different editing operations shows reconstruction is feasible in practice, and a synthetic image detection case study shows the strategy **significantly improves state-of-the-art detectors on images post-processed through C2PA-enabled software after being generated or acquired**.

papers.title: CFKS: Continuum-Feature Kernel PDE Solvers
papers.abstract: Neural-network-based PDE solvers require architectural choices, particularly the number of layers and neurons per layer. Fixing a single Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) feature layer and taking the number of features to the continuum limit removes the need to prescribe a finite feature count or select individual feature centers, thereby reducing representation arbitrariness. Motivated by this principle, we introduce Continuum-Feature Kernel Solver (CFKS), a deterministic framework for PDEs obtained by analytically marginalizing a bounded continuum of Gaussian RBF features. CFKS works directly with the resulting continuum-feature mean kernel and its operator-applied counterparts, parameterized by prescribed Gaussian widths and bounded center distributions. For linear PDEs, CFKS leads to symmetric operator-kernel collocation systems with null-space enforcement of physical constraints. Nonlinear PDEs are addressed through linearized initialization and nonlinear least-squares residual minimization using analytical kernel derivatives and Jacobians. Residual-guided collocation enrichment and sequential space--time-slab marching provide additional resolution strategies, while prescribed multiscale kernel refinement helps resolve localized nonlinear structures. Finite-feature experiments confirm convergence of empirical value and operator Gram matrices toward their continuum counterparts. Numerical studies include oscillatory and multiscale ODEs, irregular-domain Poisson and biharmonic problems, singular perturbations, transient transport equations, and viscous Burgers' equation. The results establish CFKS as a direct computational connection between finite Gaussian-RBF representations and continuum-feature kernel PDE solvers. Codes: https://github.com/vikas-dwivedi-2022/CFKS_Codes
papers.summary: Neural-network PDE solvers require architectural choices such as the number of layers and neurons per layer; fixing a single Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) feature layer and taking the number of features to the continuum limit removes the need to prescribe a feature count or pick individual centers. The Continuum-Feature Kernel Solver (`CFKS`) analytically marginalizes a bounded continuum of Gaussian RBF features into a mean kernel and its operator-applied counterparts, parameterized by prescribed Gaussian widths and bounded center distributions; linear PDEs become symmetric operator-kernel collocation systems with null-space enforcement of physical constraints, while nonlinear PDEs use linearized initialization followed by nonlinear least-squares residual minimization with analytical kernel derivatives and Jacobians, supplemented by residual-guided collocation enrichment, sequential space-time-slab marching, and prescribed multiscale kernel refinement. Finite-feature experiments **confirm that empirical value and operator Gram matrices converge toward their continuum counterparts**, and numerical studies cover oscillatory and multiscale ODEs, irregular-domain Poisson and biharmonic problems, singular perturbations, transient transport equations, and viscous Burgers' equation.

papers.title: When AI performs, what remains? An integrative review of generative AI and cognitive capital in individuals and organizations
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enables an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.
papers.summary: Generative AI's short-term productivity benefits in knowledge work are increasingly documented, but much less is known about what happens over time to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. The integrative narrative review frames this through cognitive capital, the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that lets an individual or organization learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt, and separates it from the capability of the human-AI system so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, it proposes four mechanisms, substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation, and distills seven principles, including that **assisted performance differs from retained competence** and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity, along with testable propositions per mechanism and five organizational design levers offered as proposals to be validated rather than established practice.

papers.title: Logical Guidance of Stochastic Interpolants
papers.abstract: Guidance and composition of generative models have applications in visual design, chemistry, and biology. Logical guidance composes conditional scores exactly for diffusion models. However, Flow Matching (FM) and Stochastic Interpolants (SI) learn velocity fields. We show that negation and exclusive disjunction admit exact conditional velocity composition on any interpolant, whereas conjunction, and therefore any formula containing one, is exact on Gaussian paths but in general incurs a drift-interaction error, so composed velocities need not sample the logical target. LOGSI solves this by using score-based re-equilibration as our principled mechanism and falling back to the Gaussian-path velocity rule as an approximate transport predictor. In non-Gaussian bridge problems, generation alternates transport steps with score re-equilibration steps. On image trans fer (EMNIST to CMNIST, CelebA) and QM9 source-to-target molecular editing with logical attribute constraints, LOGSI improves rule conformity at the same network-evaluation budget over composed-velocity baselines, while also improving fidelity on the image tasks. More broadly, LOGSI applies wherever stochastic interpolants need guidance and logical combinations of constraints are natural.
papers.summary: Logical guidance composes conditional scores exactly for diffusion models, but Flow Matching (FM) and Stochastic Interpolants (SI) learn velocity fields rather than scores. The authors show that negation and exclusive disjunction admit exact conditional velocity composition on any interpolant, whereas **conjunction, and therefore any formula containing one, is exact only on Gaussian paths and in general incurs a drift-interaction error**, so composed velocities need not sample the intended logical target. `LOGSI` addresses this by using score-based re-equilibration as the principled mechanism and the Gaussian-path velocity rule as an approximate transport predictor, alternating transport steps with re-equilibration steps in non-Gaussian bridge problems; on image transfer (`EMNIST` to `CMNIST`, `CelebA`) and `QM9` source-to-target molecular editing under logical attribute constraints, it improves rule conformity over composed-velocity baselines at the same network-evaluation budget while also improving fidelity on the image tasks.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Reliability--Safety Bounds and Finite-Alignment Dynamics in AI Knowledge Distillation
papers.abstract: The reliability and safety of artificial intelligence (AI), together with their transfer and evolution through knowledge distillation, have attracted growing attention. We establish an information-theoretic bound on the reliability--safety trade-off and characterize the dynamics of this trade-off under knowledge distillation. We first prove a universal trade-off inequality that is independent of the specific model form. Its boundary is determined solely by a single parameter Kh, which quantifies the hidden layer's ability to distinguish benign from hazardous inputs. We then develop a canonical Boltzmann-machine model of AI response behavior and derive two exact relations between reliability and safety. The trade-off curve is determined by the hazard discrimination capacity K, while the overall answer tendency controls the operating point along the curve. These relations agree well with existing experimental data. In knowledge distillation, we find that teacher responses induce a renormalization of the student model's trade-off parameters. We further use a renormalization-group approach to study multigenerational distillation, deriving exact recursion relations and the associated renormalization-group-like flows for two representative direct intergenerational distillation protocols at arbitrary teacher--student alignment strength. These flows reveal fixed-point structures, long-term dynamics, and critical behavior, yielding testable predictions for the critical transition between capability loss and stable transmission.
papers.summary: The reliability and safety of artificial intelligence (AI) systems trade off against each other, and knowledge distillation transfers and reshapes that trade-off across model generations. The authors prove a universal trade-off inequality independent of model form whose boundary is set solely by a single parameter Kh, the hidden layer's ability to distinguish benign from hazardous inputs, then develop a canonical Boltzmann-machine model of AI response behavior that yields **two exact reliability-safety relations in which the hazard discrimination capacity K determines the trade-off curve and the overall answer tendency sets the operating point along it**, reported to agree well with existing experimental data. For knowledge distillation, teacher responses are shown to renormalize the student's trade-off parameters, and a renormalization-group treatment of multigenerational distillation derives exact recursion relations and flows for two direct intergenerational protocols at arbitrary teacher-student alignment strength, revealing fixed points, long-term dynamics, and a predicted critical transition between capability loss and stable transmission.

papers.title: Explore Where It Matters: Targeted Exploration for Efficient Rover Adaptation
papers.abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io
papers.summary: Planetary rovers face slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation on steep soft ground that simulators only partly capture, and deployment leaves little room for trial-and-error adaptation. `TERRA` (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation) adapts a simulation-trained world model online with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor that estimates where performance-relevant model errors are likely, using that estimate to steer exploration during model predictive control (MPC). In simulation it reaches **about 90% slope-climbing success within five trials** under severely out-of-distribution pretraining, beating exploration baselines on reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the `ERNEST` rover it recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials.

papers.title: ExplainCC: Explaining Correlated Clusters by Node Labels
papers.abstract: An increasingly important requirement for clustering algorithms is that decisions and outcomes need to be clearly understandable for human users. We address this requirement for the Correlation Clustering (CC) problem, in case the objects to be clustered are accompanied by labels. In CC one seeks to partition a set of objects into clusters based on pairwise similarity and dissimilarity information.
