We conducted two Visual Turing Test (VTT) experiments with a total of 90 participants on videos generated by latest generative models, in which participants watched each video twice and then gave their feedback. Across the experiments, we collected 4,286 valid eye-tracking trials on 438 videos. Our analysis indicates that gaze patterns offer informative evaluation signals that align with explicit human feedback. Building on the findings, we propose the first computational method GazeEval to predict the perceived visual realism of AI-generated videos from eye-tracking data. It achieves 71.3% accuracy in prediction, providing evidence that eye tracking data carries informative signals about how people evaluate a video. We release the study data to support further research on eye tracking for evaluating AI-generated video.
papers.summary: Human evaluation of generated video has relied on ratings and judgments, which capture the conclusion a viewer reaches but not the perception behind it. Two Visual Turing Test experiments with 90 participants, who watched each video twice before giving feedback, yielded 4,286 valid eye-tracking trials over 438 videos from recent generative models. Gaze patterns turned out to align with explicit feedback, and the authors build `GazeEval` to predict perceived visual realism from eye-tracking alone, reaching **71.3% prediction accuracy**. The study data is released for further work on gaze-based evaluation.

papers.title: Discovering Jailbreaks via Curriculum of Models
papers.abstract:
Automated jailbreak discovery aims to find prompts that elicit prohibited behaviors from safety-trained language models, helping developers identify vulnerabilities before deployment. One class of approaches uses reinforcement learning to train an investigator model to generate prompts that elicit a specified behavior from a target model. However, training directly against a safety-trained target is difficult because nearly all prompts are refused, leaving the investigator with a sparse reward signal. Prior work addresses this with the propensity bound (PRBO), a proxy reward estimated by sampling responses from a more compliant target, and then adjusting for how likely those responses would have been under the original target.
  We introduce Curriculum of Models (CoM), an alternative method that trains the investigator against a sequence of modified versions of the target, progressing gradually from a version that readily exhibits the specified behavior to the original target. For jailbreak discovery, training begins against a target version that rarely refuses harmful requests, and advances to the next, harder version once the investigator reliably elicits the behavior from the current one.
  We evaluate CoM on elicitation tasks involving CBRN materials, explosives, and illicit drugs, using two open-weight targets, gemma-4-31b-it and gpt-oss-120b. We compare against PRBO and direct training on the original target without a curriculum. When the investigator is trained to elicit a single behavior, CoM finds successful jailbreaks more reliably than either baseline. When trained on multiple behaviors simultaneously, the CoM-trained investigator can elicit held-out behaviors, though PRBO-trained investigators achieve higher success rates. Our results suggest that a simple curriculum over target models offers a promising approach for addressing sparse rewards in rare-behavior elicitation.
papers.summary: Training an investigator model with reinforcement learning to elicit prohibited behavior is hard against a safety-trained target, because nearly every prompt is refused and the reward signal is sparse. `Curriculum of Models` trains the investigator against a sequence of modified targets, beginning with a version that rarely refuses harmful requests and advancing only once the current one is reliably broken, as an alternative to the propensity bound (`PRBO`) proxy reward estimated from a more compliant target. On elicitation tasks covering chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear materials, explosives and illicit drugs against `gemma-4-31b-it` and `gpt-oss-120b`, **the curriculum found successful jailbreaks more reliably than `PRBO` or direct training when targeting a single behavior**. Trained on multiple behaviors at once it generalized to held-out behaviors, though `PRBO`-trained investigators still achieved higher success rates there.

papers.title: What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
papers.abstract: Chemical language models can struggle to generate new molecules when trained on small datasets, where a model may reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution. Randomized SMILES augmentation varies atom traversal, whereas Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) also allows the order of fragment blocks to vary. How these distinct sources of representational variation affect low-data molecular generation has not been clearly studied. Here, using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, we compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora. Three findings emerge. First, randomization of SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold, turning a model that merely reproduces its training set into a practical molecular generator. Second, the two axes of randomization act jointly rather than additively: atom order alone reaches a tenth, and fragment order alone a seventh, of the genuine yield obtained when both vary, which is four times their combined contribution. Third, at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES. Welch tests with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons resolve every difference on the primary outcomes. In the low-data regime, thus, what one randomizes rather than only how much determines whether augmentation produces new molecules or merely new spellings of the training set.
papers.summary: Chemical language models trained on small datasets often reproduce their training molecules instead of learning a usable generative distribution, and it has been unclear which kind of representational randomization fixes that. Using 1,000 seed molecules and an autoregressive sequence model, the authors compare canonical with randomized Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) at growing corpus sizes, isolate its atom-order and fragment-order axes, and match corpora against randomized SMILES. Randomizing SAFE **raised the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold**, the two axes act jointly rather than additively, and at matched corpus size and compute randomized SAFE gave 2.8 times the yield of randomized SMILES. In the low-data regime, what gets randomized matters more than how much.

papers.title: Discovery of Diverse and Realistic Financial Tail-Risk Using Generative Flow Networks
papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of rare, high-impact financial events is essential for robust risk management. Sampling-based techniques such as Sequential Markov Chain Monte Carlo (SMCMC) generate diverse scenarios but inefficiently explore high-risk regions, while Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) converges on narrow sets of scenarios, limiting diversity. We present GRID, which uses Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) -- samplers that draw objects in proportion to a reward -- to systematically generate diverse and realistic financial tail-risk scenarios. Building on continuous GFlowNets, GRID introduces a flexible mixture-policy architecture with variable-specific distribution families for high-dimensional, sequential macro-financial data, together with plausibility constraints that keep generated trajectories realistic. A central practical advantage is robustness to reward-proxy imperfection: because GFlowNets sample proportionally rather than maximize, they remain broadly exploratory even when the oracle's out-of-sample accuracy is low -- an unavoidable reality in financial forecasting. On three real-world crises, GRID improves scenario diversity, realism, and tail-risk coverage over RL and MCMC baselines, and ablations over oracle architectures and distribution families yield practical insights into continuous GFlowNet behavior under noisy rewards.
papers.summary: Risk management needs generators of rare, high-impact financial scenarios, but sequential Markov chain Monte Carlo explores high-risk regions inefficiently and deep reinforcement learning collapses onto a narrow set of scenarios. `GRID` builds on continuous Generative Flow Networks (`GFlowNets`), samplers that draw objects in proportion to reward rather than maximizing it, adding a mixture-policy architecture with variable-specific distribution families for high-dimensional sequential macro-financial data plus plausibility constraints on trajectories. Because sampling is proportional, **the method stays broadly exploratory even when the reward oracle has low out-of-sample accuracy**, and across three real crises it improves scenario diversity, realism and tail-risk coverage over both baseline families. Ablations over oracle architectures and distribution families report practical behavior of continuous GFlowNets under noisy rewards.

papers.title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI
papers.abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.
papers.summary: Characterizing quantum materials takes iterative decisions and accumulated lab know-how that is hard to document or transfer. `QUANTA` is an agentic framework driving a commercial Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS), pairing retrieval over literature, protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experiment planning, troubleshooting and data interpretation, while a separate deterministic control layer validates every instrument action. Guided by incoming data, it judges measurement quality, revises plans and chooses what to measure next, demonstrated on **transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP and nonlinear responses in the magnetic material Co2MnGa**. The authors present it as a generalizable pattern for safeguarded closed-loop materials characterization.

papers.title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) only covers tasks where correctness can be checked automatically, leaving out domains where good answers are recognizable but hard to score. Reinforced Adversarial Learning (`RAL`) co-trains a language model judge so that reference answers alone become the sole reward for on-policy post-training, needing no reference reasoning traces or external critic signal. On three verifiable tasks, integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic expression synthesis and SMILES-to-formula translation, **a sufficiently capable judge plus enough training let the method match direct RLVR while verifiers were used only for evaluation**. Applied to scientific abstract generation, including abstracts conditioned on U.S. National Institutes of Health grant titles, human scientists and an ensemble of judges found its output harder to distinguish from real abstracts than frontier-model baselines.

papers.title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
papers.abstract:
Contextual embeddings represent chunks of a document with respect to the document's global context. These models are typically trained and evaluated under the assumption that a relevant document contains only a single relevant chunk. In this work, we argue that in real-world use cases a retriever should not only find answers spread over several chunks but also surface the evidence needed to verify them. To address this, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-context, a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model. This removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of the chunking. We utilize a vision-language backbone for training and release pplx-embed-v2-context in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces. On the evaluation side, we introduce two benchmarks that label both the chunks that answer a query and the evidence needed to verify the answer. Context-bench is a controlled diagnostic, and Q2D-Chunk is built from real-world search queries. To encourage further research, we also publish Q2D-Chunk as a public leaderboard. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art on both benchmarks and ConTEB.
  We find that the visual retrieval capabilities of our 9B model transfer from its vision-language base model and propose to extend chunking to image inputs. We demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3 and that performance improves with granular image chunking.
papers.summary: Contextual embedding models are usually trained and scored as if a relevant document holds exactly one relevant chunk, which ignores answers spread over several chunks and the extra evidence a user needs to verify them. `pplx-embed-v2-context` is trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model, which removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes training targets independent of the chunking, released at 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces on a vision-language backbone. Two new benchmarks label both answering and verifying chunks, `Context-bench` as a controlled diagnostic and `Q2D-Chunk` from real search queries with a public leaderboard, and **the 9B model sets a new state of the art on both plus `ConTEB`**. Visual retrieval ability carries over from the base model, giving the best dense-retriever scores on `ViDoRe-V3` and improving with finer image chunking.

papers.title: Where You Inject Matters: The Trust Region Effect in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly adopted in long-horizon tasks and interact with diverse external environments. Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.
papers.summary: Indirect prompt injection hides malicious instructions in the external content that language model agents read, and risk assessments so far have studied the injection text rather than its location. Three agentic testbeds covering tool use, coding and daily workflows hold the injection content fixed while varying where it appears, across both coarse environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. Agents turn out to trust some regions of their environment more than others, a pattern the authors name the trust region effect: a `GPT-5.4` agent **followed an unsafe instruction placed in repository documentation such as a README or TODO file 2.6 times more often than the same instruction in a code or data file**. Learning-based attackers that pick both content and placement confirm location contributes to attack strength alongside wording, which the authors argue should inform defenses.

papers.title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
papers.summary: As language model systems become multimodal, tool-using and multi-agent, safety failures arise not only from individual harmful outputs but from how agents update, store and propagate evidence-based commitments across retrieval, memory, tools and peer messages. Treating belief as an engineering abstraction, the authors propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (`EB-MAS`), which **externalizes belief state into a structured substrate where update operators propose changes and a Cognitive Firewall bounds or rejects updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues**. They also lay out group-level risks including manufactured consensus, collusion and cascading misinformation, plus integration problems around grounding, false positives, scalability and ethical misuse. The position is that scalable agent safety needs runtime interfaces for tracing and constraining belief revision, not just output filtering or stronger base models.

papers.title: Aligning Autoresearch: Co-Improvement between Agents and Humans
papers.abstract: Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end, i.e., self-improvement. However, best results are still obtained by research agents interacting with human researchers, and improving AI's ability to perform this co-research will only reinforce this effect---a process termed co-improvement (Weston and Foerster, 2025). Further, aligning with human expectations is likely a safer path for research agents, especially given recent agent reward hacking phenomena (OpenAI, 2026b). In this work we address these issues in four ways: (i) we empirically study the role of humans in directing autoresearch agents, focusing on the domain of benchmark creation, and find humans still play a pivotal role particularly in the ideation phase; (ii) we also develop a benchmark, HackBench, that shows current autoresearch agents are not aligned and are unable to achieve hack localization sufficiently; (iii) we present a method to train agents for improved human interaction by using human simulators as a proxy during reinforcement learning (RL); and finally (iv) we develop a method to improve model text generation, and hence agent communication, by RL with rubrics aligned with human experts. Together, our training and evaluation recipes provide a path toward more capable and aligned (co-)research agents.
papers.summary: Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research on their own, but the best results still come from agents working alongside human researchers, and recent reward-hacking incidents make alignment with human expectations a safety concern for such agents. The work studies the human role in directing agents on benchmark creation, introduces `HackBench` to test whether agents can localize reward hacks, trains agents for better human interaction using simulated humans as proxies during reinforcement learning (RL), and improves agent communication with RL against rubrics aligned with human experts. **Humans remain pivotal in the ideation phase**, and current autoresearch agents fail to localize hacks sufficiently on `HackBench`, indicating they are not yet aligned.

papers.title: FlipJev: Fast Black-Box Red Teaming Finds Universal Adversarial Suffixes for Typed Decision Models
papers.abstract: Typed decision models are an emerging class of language models that make decisions instead of generating free-text responses. They answer in a single fast and cheap query and are increasingly used, including in security-sensitive tasks. However, red teaming of these models leaves two gaps: existing adaptive attacks do not use their speed, and few studies have searched for universal adversarial examples. We fill both gaps on Jev, the representative typed decision model, with a quick black-box query-based attack that calls no attacker language model. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 datasets with different data types and application scenarios. The results show that Jev resists common prompt injections: no strategy changes a correct answer in 10,240 paired tests. In contrast, our attack finds short suffixes that flip confident answers within minutes. These suffixes are universal: one suffix per dataset flips 43% of unseen documents. Because typed decision models, unlike classic NLP models, can serve many tasks, we test whether these suffixes transfer across tasks. We find that one suffix generated from one task can flip 90-100% of the samples in other tasks. We therefore believe the evaluation of typed decision models must include strict adaptive attacks to fully reveal their robustness.
papers.summary: Typed decision models answer with a decision rather than free text in a single fast and cheap query and are increasingly used in security-sensitive settings, but existing red teaming neither exploits their speed nor searches for universal adversarial examples. A fast black-box query-based attack that needs no attacker language model is run against `Jev`, a representative typed decision model, across 12 datasets spanning different data types and scenarios. `Jev` resists common prompt injections, with no correct answer changed in 10,240 paired tests, yet the attack finds short suffixes within minutes that flip confident answers, one suffix per dataset flips 43% of unseen documents, and **a single suffix generated from one task flips 90-100% of samples in other tasks**. The results motivate including strict adaptive attacks whenever the robustness of such models is evaluated.

papers.title: Geometric Time Score Estimators: Bridging Self-Predictive Representations and Generative Occupancy Models For Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning (RL), estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure is central to temporal reasoning, but self-predictive representations turn out to give surprisingly poor density estimates while generative occupancy models produce accurate samples yet cannot easily recover densities. `GTSE` (Geometric Time Score Estimators) bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths, with an analysis of how this induces better representation learning and a way to extract self-predictive representations directly from the framework. On locomotion and manipulation tasks, **goal-conditioned RL performance improves by 2x to 6x over state-of-the-art methods**, and the learned representations transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks.

papers.title: HEDGE: Gated Hypergraph Memory for Scalable Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate systems require agents to retain and revisit arguments across multiple rounds, yet limited context windows and unstructured memories make relevant information increasingly difficult to recover. Existing flat and pairwise-graph memories also struggle to capture higher-order relations, including multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus. We introduce HEDGE, a selective memory framework that represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs. Hyperedges connect related claims across agents, while intra-hyperedge relational graphs preserve fine-grained argumentative structure. A learned memory selection module (MSM), trained through supervised learning and reinforcement learning, routes each memory candidate to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT, retaining useful information while limiting redundancy. Across seven diverse benchmarks, HEDGE consistently outperforms strong single-agent, multi-agent, and memory baselines, improving accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent system with GPT-4o-mini. The gains reach 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while HEDGE reduces memory usage by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%.
papers.summary: Multi-agent debate requires agents to retain and revisit arguments across rounds, but limited context windows and flat or pairwise-graph memories struggle to capture higher-order relations such as multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus. `HEDGE` represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs, with hyperedges linking related claims across agents and intra-hyperedge graphs preserving fine-grained argumentative structure, while a memory selection module (MSM) trained with supervised and reinforcement learning routes each candidate to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT. Across seven benchmarks using `GPT-4o-mini`, **accuracy improves by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent baseline**, reaching 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while memory use drops by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%.

papers.title: Structural-Test Geometry as an Inductive Bias for Partially Observable World Models
papers.abstract: Predictive world-model objectives need not organize latent histories according to distinctions required for later control. With privileged simulator access during training, should response-derived structural information be predicted, decoded, or imposed directly on latent geometry--and how do these choices compare with structured belief distillation? We define posterior-marginalized structural tests whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, then train quotient-preserving (QP) world models by aligning shared latent Euclidean distances to that metric. Across a fixed six-task diagnostic suite, the largest differences appear under held-out structural variation: QP improves planning success by 26.1 points $[21.5,30.7]$ over metric decoding and 6.4 points $[3.8,9.0]$ over structured belief distillation. On GridWorld, metric decoding accurately recovers held-out structural distances ($\rho=.91$) while its native latent geometry remains more distorted than QP's (paired IQD difference $.22$ $[.20,.24]$), showing that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.
papers.summary: Predictive world-model objectives do not necessarily organize latent histories according to the distinctions that later control requires, raising the question of whether structural information available from a simulator during training should be predicted, decoded, or imposed directly on latent geometry. Posterior-marginalized structural tests are defined whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, and quotient-preserving (QP) world models are trained by aligning latent Euclidean distances to that metric, then compared against metric decoding and structured belief distillation. On a six-task diagnostic suite the differences are largest under held-out structural variation, where **QP improves planning success by 26.1 points over metric decoding** and 6.4 points over structured belief distillation; on `GridWorld`, metric decoding recovers held-out structural distances accurately (rho of 0.91) yet its native latent geometry stays more distorted than QP's, showing that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.

papers.title: Interventional Training Reduces Causal Bypass in In-Context Introspection
papers.abstract: Introspection, the ability of a system to access and reason about its internal signals, is crucial for language model (LM) self-consistency and scalable interpretability. Prior work argues that LMs possess introspective capabilities, and that training (SFT) could enhance such behavior. However, most setups leave open the possibility of "causal bypass," in which the self-report relies on signals that are correlated with the self-report's subject, while being causally unrelated to it. Although high-level concepts are difficult to intervene on, lower-level signals (such as a single neuron activation) allow precise interventions. Understanding such signals can serve as a minimal prerequisite before understanding more complex introspection. In this study, we train hundreds of introspectors across three low-level signal types and eight LMs. We find that straightforward SFT training leads to causal bypass, and propose interventional training, an alternative where we train the model to report on counterfactually perturbed values. This method enables more accurate introspection of endogenous $\textit{and}$ injected signals, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) data. The mechanism generalizes across token positions and scales with more data. Our results demonstrate that while causally grounded introspection is possible, it is not guaranteed -- emphasizing the need to train on mechanisms, rather than behaviors alone.
papers.summary: Introspection, the ability of a language model (LM) to access and reason about its own internal signals, matters for self-consistency and scalable interpretability, but prior setups leave open causal bypass, where a self-report relies on signals merely correlated with its subject rather than causally tied to it. Hundreds of introspectors are trained across three low-level signal types, such as single neuron activations, and eight LMs, comparing standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) against interventional training, in which the model learns to report counterfactually perturbed values. **Straightforward SFT leads to causal bypass, while interventional training yields more accurate introspection of both endogenous and injected signals**, particularly on out-of-distribution (OOD) data, with the mechanism generalizing across token positions and scaling with more data, so causally grounded introspection is possible but not guaranteed.

papers.title: Lev-3B: A Data Recipe for Compact Probabilistic Log Decision Models
papers.abstract: Many log-analysis tasks involve choosing among known options, such as detecting anomalous sessions or identifying attack techniques, and benefit from calibrated probabilities. We present Lev-3B, an open 3B-parameter decision model built on Granite-4.1-3B-Base with a shared pointer readout, and study its training recipe. The recipe has two key parts. First, training follows a curriculum: the model learns bounded natural-language decisions, using no log data, before it sees any logs. Second, the log stage mixes the target tasks with general log data spanning 35 auxiliary tasks unrelated to either evaluation task. We evaluate one shared checkpoint on sources seen in training and on sources excluded from training, calibration and model selection. The two-stage recipe transfers substantially better than training on log data alone. Adding general log data improves performance on excluded sources. At a fraction of their serving cost, Lev-3B outperforms prompted frontier models on anomaly detection, including on an excluded logging system, but trails them on attack-technique classification. Its probabilities are well calibrated on familiar sources, but on the excluded logging system it confidently misses anomalies. We release the checkpoint, recipe, data manifests, and prediction-level artifacts.
papers.summary: Many log-analysis tasks, such as detecting anomalous sessions or identifying attack techniques, amount to choosing among known options and benefit from calibrated probabilities. `Lev-3B` is an open 3B-parameter decision model built on `Granite-4.1-3B-Base` with a shared pointer readout, trained with a two-stage curriculum: bounded natural-language decisions with no log data first, then a log stage mixing the target tasks with general log data spanning 35 unrelated auxiliary tasks. The curriculum transfers substantially better than training on logs alone, and **at a fraction of the serving cost the model outperforms prompted frontier models on anomaly detection**, including on a logging system excluded from training, though it trails them on attack-technique classification and confidently misses anomalies on the excluded system. The checkpoint, recipe, data manifests, and prediction-level artifacts are released.

papers.title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become a default source of help for students in science and engineering courses. In foundational engineering mechanics courses such as statics, students routinely use these tools to check answers, work through partial solutions, and ask for explanations. Effective tutoring in this setting requires more than a correct final answer. A model must also confirm correct work when a student doubts it, and identify errors in flawed work. Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs primarily on final-answer accuracy, so it is unclear whether models that can solve mechanics problems also have the other technical capabilities that tutoring depends on. Here we introduce TrussTutor-Bench, a benchmark of 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, and use it to evaluate thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Every model detected nearly all injected errors in synthetic flawed student work (90.4% to 100%), so error detection did not distinguish models under these clean conditions. Sycophancy did. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions to problems they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases. These results show that performance varies widely across models: the leading models solve, check, and defend student work nearly perfectly, while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work. TrussTutor-Bench provides a verified, extensible standard for determining which models are technically reliable enough to put in front of students. Follow-up work must now focus on teaching rather than technical capability, drawing on learning science to determine whether LLM help leads students to understand the material or simply to reach the right answer.
papers.summary: Students in engineering mechanics courses routinely use large language models (LLMs) to check answers and work through solutions, but effective tutoring also requires confirming correct work when a student doubts it and spotting errors in flawed work, which final-answer benchmarks do not measure. `TrussTutor-Bench` pairs 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems with automatically generated student solutions and evaluates thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0% and every model caught nearly all injected errors, but sycophancy separated them: **when a student insisted correct work was wrong, models rejected solutions they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases**, so the leading models are near-perfect at solving, checking, and defending work while others are far less reliable.

papers.title: TreasuryQA Bench: Can AI Agents Work an Archive of Scanned Financial Records?
papers.abstract: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.
papers.summary: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives that AI agents can now reach through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet existing benchmarks either hand agents the relevant documents or provide pre-extracted text, skipping the search or the reading. `TreasuryQA Bench` poses 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications held in a high-fidelity Dropbox twin, requiring each agent to find the right file through Dropbox's MCP server, read the needed pages with a hosted OCR server or its own tools, and return one exact figure that a Python grader checks against an accepted range. Among ten agents, **the best solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst 16.7%**, with `Claude Opus 5.5` in Claude Code leading and `GPT-5.6 Terra` in Codex trailing; every agent does worse on the blurriest scans, and most failures return a wrong number, most often from a misread digit.

papers.title: Memorization Capacity of Invariant Convolutional Neural Nets
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful memorizers which are often able to interpolate their training data even when the labels have been randomized. While there exists an extensive literature on the memorization capacity of fully connected networks, in practice more specific architectures with problem-dependent properties are preferred, such as convolutional networks for image classification. In this paper we consider convolutional networks which are invariant with respect to a given arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, which may include translations, reflections, and/or rotations of images and invariances of higher order tensors. We prove upper bounds on the size of an invariant convolutional neural network with threshold activations that is required to interpolate a given dataset with two classes. Our bounds are formulated in terms of a complexity measure that takes the invariant structure into account and is instance-specific, i.e., it is related to the mutual arrangement of the classes in the given dataset and their geometric properties rather than the number of samples. Our proof is constructive: for given input data, instances of an interpolating network can be computed via a randomized algorithm with high probability. In numerical experiments we investigate the practical effectiveness of this algorithm.
papers.summary: Neural networks readily interpolate training data even with randomized labels, and while memorization capacity is well studied for fully connected networks, practical architectures such as convolutional networks carry problem-specific structure. The work considers convolutional networks invariant under an arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, covering translations, reflections, and rotations of images as well as invariances of higher-order tensors, and proves upper bounds on the size of an invariant network with threshold activations needed to interpolate a two-class dataset. **The bounds depend on an instance-specific complexity measure reflecting the geometric arrangement of the classes rather than the number of samples**, the proof is constructive via a randomized algorithm that builds an interpolating network with high probability, and numerical experiments examine the algorithm's practical effectiveness.

papers.title: Optimization-based lane-changing trajectory planning in mixed traffic with embedded input convex neural networks
papers.abstract: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a B\'ezier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.
papers.summary: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic are hard to plan because surrounding-vehicle behavior is uncertain and realistic prediction models are expensive to embed inside an optimizer. The approach embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a Bezier-curve trajectory planner, composed of input convex recurrent, fully input convex, and partially input convex networks, and formulates them as linear programs (LP) that avoid the binary variables of conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP), with exactness at optimality established theoretically. On a hybrid real-world and simulated dataset, surrogate accuracy matches unconstrained baselines while **optimization efficiency improves substantially over MIP formulations**, and closed-loop simulations show the planners reduce weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.

papers.title: MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design seeks to learn reusable orchestration policies, yet prevailing approaches remain largely one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system but only observes and learns from its terminal outcome. This paradigm discards execution trajectories that expose system-level failures and contain fine-grained information beyond the terminal outcome, leaving no direct basis for revising the source MAS, evaluating the updated MAS, or learning from the resulting contrast. To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that closes this feedback loop by coupling an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. For each task, the Orchestrator constructs and executes a source MAS to obtain an outcome score and an intermediate trajectory. Conditioned on the trajectory, the Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the agents, information flow, or execution configuration. The executable updated MAS is re-executed on the same task to measure its realized outcome under stochastic execution. This pair-MAS comparison provides complementary learning signals: the Orchestrator learns to generate strong systems with fewer recoverable failures, whereas the Refiner learns to expose and repair observed weaknesses, thereby driving policy-level co-evolution across training iterations. Experiments show that MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines, with consistent gains from refinement across all evaluated benchmarks. The co-evolution process also yields MAS-JudgeCorpus, a dataset of execution-grounded source-updated pairs with orchestration- and trajectory-level supervision, which can provide the community with support for MAS reward modeling and trajectory-aware investigation.
papers.summary: Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design aims to learn reusable orchestration policies, but prevailing approaches are one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system and learns only from its terminal outcome, discarding execution trajectories that reveal system-level failures. `MAS-Loop` pairs the Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner that localizes an actionable failure, forms a trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the agents, information flow, or execution configuration; the patched system is re-executed on the same task, and the pairwise comparison supplies learning signals to both components so they co-evolve across training iterations. **The framework achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines, with consistent gains from refinement on every benchmark**, and the process yields `MAS-JudgeCorpus`, a dataset of source-updated MAS pairs with orchestration- and trajectory-level supervision for reward modeling.

papers.title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets
papers.abstract:
We study episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, with independent arms. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from unknown recurring priors. Observations arrive after known delays, and plays obey hard per-episode caps and total budgets. A play earns reward and informs both the current quality and the recurring prior: the learner must explore, use, and generalize.
  We formulate a common planning optimization over learning trajectories. Its LP relaxation values experiments through current reward, resource consumption and continuation: the value of future decisions from the learning state produced. Dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling. Execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss. The framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options.
  Delayed reports create planned restlessness: an arm's information changes while it is not played, through reports of its own earlier plays arriving on a known calendar. For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by $O(\sqrt{N})$ over $N$ episodes, with other parameters fixed. For one undelayed $T$-step episode with arms capped at $T/X$ plays each, we obtain the LP-relative approximation factor $1+(2\pi X)^{-1/2}+O(X^{-1})$, improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.
papers.summary: Episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, draw fresh arm qualities each episode from unknown recurring priors, with observations arriving after known delays and plays subject to hard per-episode caps and total budgets, so a learner must explore, use, and generalize at once. A planning optimization over learning trajectories is formulated whose linear programming relaxation values experiments by current reward, resource consumption, and continuation value, with dual prices separating arms into local programs and certifying any admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling, while also covering risk-sensitive objectives and purchased observations. Delayed reports create planned restlessness, where an arm's information changes while it is not played; under stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded lag, and nonbinding budgets, **posterior sampling bounds the price of not knowing the priors by O(sqrt(N)) over N episodes**, and for one undelayed T-step episode with arms capped at T/X plays the LP-relative approximation factor 1 + (2 pi X)^(-1/2) + O(1/X) improves earlier factors with a matching lower bound for the leading term.

papers.title: Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
papers.abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.
papers.summary: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires resolving cross-modal correspondences and temporal grounding from sparse evidence, and omni-modal agents that orchestrate perception tools do well, but it is unclear whether they need broad modality-specific toolsets, which lengthen trajectories and raise inference cost. Starting from the specialized-tool `OmniAgent`, staged controlled experiments prune the toolset and progressively consolidate audio- and vision-specific tools into omni-modal ones, arriving at a two-tool agent with only omni-modal captioning and omni-modal QA. Across three AVQA benchmarks, **the compact agent matches or beats the specialized-tool agent while cutting inference cost by around 70%**.

papers.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length shrinks as the batch grows, and although `vLLM` lets operators map batch size to draft length with a hand-written table, nothing measures or corrects it. `TableTune` has a tuner that times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on `vLLM`'s own serving path and computes a throughput-maximizing table in minutes, plus a controller plugin that tracks live acceptance rates and rebuilds the table while serving. On an H100 the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the best fixed draft length's throughput at every load in four of five drafter settings, its worst-case loss never exceeds that of reimplemented TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style controllers, and **starting from mistuned tables the controller raises throughput by up to 58%**; in an llm-d deployment of two `Qwen3-32B` replicas on four GPUs the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 at high load.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Clustered Federated Learning in Non-IID Wireless Networks
papers.abstract:
Current and emerging mobile networks face increasing privacy, scalability, and performance challenges as distributed learning becomes essential for advanced 6G services. These challenges are amplified by the presence of non-IID data, naturally arising in heterogeneous wireless environments, that degrade the performance of standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches. To address non-IID data across clients, we propose a Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that assigns clients to specialized models during training. Data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering, enabling identification and exploitation of client similarities without sharing raw data while reducing communication cost.
  Motivated by mmWave beam selection, we evaluate our methods on a wireless simulation dataset (DeepMIMO) and complement it with two non-IID benchmarks (FEMNIST, Rotated CIFAR-10) to isolate different non-IID characteristics. Our best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 pp on DeepMIMO and 10.6 pp on FEMNIST while reducing downlink data volume by 83.1 % on FEMNIST compared to IFCA.
  We demonstrate that different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics. These results show that our CFL methods enable resource-efficient, and high-performance distributed learning in future 6G networks.
papers.summary: Distributed learning for 6G mobile services faces privacy, scalability, and performance pressures that non-IID data across heterogeneous wireless clients makes worse, degrading standard Federated Learning (FL). A Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework assigns clients to specialized models during training, using data-domain clustering to initialize model-based clustering so client similarities can be exploited without sharing raw data and at lower communication cost. Motivated by mmWave beam selection, evaluation on the `DeepMIMO` wireless simulation dataset plus `FEMNIST` and Rotated `CIFAR-10` shows the best configurations improve accuracy over `IFCA` by **4.8 and 10.6 percentage points** on `DeepMIMO` and `FEMNIST` respectively while cutting downlink data volume by 83.1% on `FEMNIST`, with different clustering strategies suiting different non-IID characteristics.

papers.title: Dungeons & Dragons Encounter Analysis with Semi-Random Simulation in Foundry VTT
papers.abstract: Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) is a tabletop roleplaying game (TTRPG) in which a group of players, guided by a Game Master, roleplay a fantasy adventure with simulated combat and improvisational narrative. In D&D, an encounter is a single instance of simulated combat, where the players must use their characters to attempt to defeat a selection of enemy characters that the GM controls. D&D has multiple systems that approximate encounter difficulty by summing individual difficulty values that designers predefine for each enemy. However, since players and enemies can have a wide variety of capabilities, encounter difficulty depends on more than just the estimated difficulty of each monster. For example, these metrics do not account for positioning and dungeon layout, the synergies between monster abilities, and player party composition. We have created a tool, Mage-Hand, that can simulate D&D encounters semi-randomly using Foundry Virtual Tabletop, a virtual tabletop (VTT) system. In this paper, we show that our tool's simulated winrates have a strong correlation with D&D's published difficulty evaluation metrics, while also better aligning with some players' reported experiences.
papers.summary: Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) is a tabletop roleplaying game (TTRPG) whose published encounter-difficulty systems sum predefined per-monster values and therefore ignore positioning, dungeon layout, synergies between monster abilities, and party composition. `Mage-Hand` is a tool that simulates encounters semi-randomly inside Foundry Virtual Tabletop, a virtual tabletop (VTT) system, so difficulty can be estimated from simulated outcomes rather than static sums. **Simulated winrates correlate strongly with D&D's published difficulty metrics** while also aligning better with some players' reported experiences.

papers.title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting
papers.abstract: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) and hybrid modeling have attracted significant attention as approaches for combining physical knowledge with the flexibility of deep learning. In this work, we investigate whether these approaches deliver their commonly claimed benefits for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting. We develop two hybrid forecasting architectures that integrate the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer neural forecasting architecture through feature augmentation and residual learning. The proposed models are evaluated on a dataset comprising over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries. We assess convergence speed, forecasting accuracy, transferability across geographical regions, and data efficiency. Although the physics-informed models seem to exhibit slightly faster convergence during training, they do not achieve consistent improvements in test-set accuracy, generalization, or performance under limited training data compared to the purely data-driven baseline. These findings suggest that, for modern deep forecasting architectures trained on large datasets, explicitly incorporating the ADR physical model provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead PV forecasting.
papers.summary: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) and hybrid modeling are widely claimed to improve deep learning by injecting physical knowledge, and the work tests whether that holds for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting. Two hybrid architectures combine the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the `TSMixer` neural forecaster through feature augmentation and residual learning, evaluated on over 3 million samples from 3,713 installations across 33 European countries for convergence speed, accuracy, cross-region transfer, and data efficiency. **The physics-informed models converge slightly faster but show no consistent gains in test accuracy, generalization, or low-data performance over the purely data-driven baseline**, suggesting the explicit physical model offers limited practical benefit for day-ahead forecasting with modern architectures on large datasets.

papers.title: Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether their code is readable, efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities, yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026), with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute, variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks, extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B. At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs. In the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal.
papers.summary: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether generated code is readable, efficient, or secure, and techniques claiming to improve those qualities are rarely compared at equal compute budgets. A systematic review of 628 primary studies from July 2021 to October 2026 organizes techniques by stage, signal source, and quality target, finding that most measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals get gamed, and compute, variance, and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets, extends to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on `Gemma 4 31B`: best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent, and retrieval, and **only 1 of 66 techniques beats it on its primary target beyond the 95% interval**, a rate consistent with chance. Large correctness losses on `HumanEval+`, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs, so gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline on measures independent of the technique's own signal.

papers.title: Context Compaction for World Models
papers.abstract: World models let observers explore and interact with generated worlds. Recent work shows that when observers revisit a region, current models often fail to regenerate it consistently. We view this as a context retrieval problem. LLM agents manage context retrieval at two layers of their stack. At the model layer, the KV cache design determines how much context fits in memory. At the agent harness layer, harnesses such as Claude Code pick the context sent to the LLM. Prior work on world models has mostly focused only on the model layer. In this paper, we make three contributions. First, we build a benchmark to measure world model context retrieval. It generates new worlds for every episode, preventing a model from recalling rooms using training data. It also separates context retrieval from guesses based on nearby frames. Second, we build an agent harness that performs context compaction for world models, which to our knowledge no prior work has studied. Third, we use our benchmark to study four world model designs. Context compaction lets our world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining. However, world models with sliding-window attention lose most of their context retrieval when dreaming. Therefore, a dreaming world agent benefits more from extending the reach of its world model using context compaction than switching to sliding window attention at the model layer.
papers.summary: World models let observers explore generated worlds, but when an observer revisits a region current models often fail to regenerate it consistently, which can be framed as a context retrieval problem spanning both the model layer, where KV cache design sets how much context fits, and the agent harness layer that picks what context the model sees, as Claude Code does for LLM agents. Three contributions follow: a benchmark that generates a new world every episode so rooms cannot be recalled from training data and that separates true retrieval from guesses based on nearby frames, an agent harness that performs context compaction for world models, and a study of four world model designs on the benchmark. **Context compaction lets the world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining**, whereas models with sliding-window attention lose most of their retrieval ability when dreaming, so a dreaming world agent gains more from compaction than from switching to sliding-window attention at the model layer.

papers.title: Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive inference by leveraging the memory bound nature of decoding, verifying multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch size relationship, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation. We evaluate this across 10 sparse MoE models (30B--1T parameters, 8--512 experts) and find recent fine-grained models break this trend, showing higher speedup at low batch size. We find verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes, but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics. At low batch size, MoE layers in fine-grained models account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights; on H100, kernel profiling attributes this mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts. Across draft tokens, routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification relative to independence assumptions. We model this effect using a maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4\% error, and substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the qualitative low-batch trend from synthetic routing.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up autoregressive inference by verifying several draft tokens in one forward pass, and prior analyses predicted that for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models the speedup would peak at intermediate batch sizes because more experts become active. Evaluating ten sparse MoE models from 30B to 1T parameters with 8 to 512 experts, the authors find that recent fine-grained MoE models instead show **the highest speedup at low batch sizes**. Kernel profiling on H100 attributes this to MoE kernels achieving higher bandwidth utilization than attention, to L2 cache absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts, and to routing overlap across draft tokens that activates fewer unique experts than an independence assumption predicts. A maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting (`IPF`) model predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with under 4% error and closes much of the gap between predicted and measured speedup curves.

papers.title: Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks for AC Power Flow: The Role of Inductive Biases and Physical Constraints
papers.abstract:
Fast and accurate models for AC power flow (ACPF) are increasingly important as modern electrical grids require more frequent system analyses. Graph neural networks (GNNs) naturally exploit electrical grid topology, yet the effects of architectural design choices on predictive performance remain poorly understood given differences in graph representations and evaluation settings across studies.
  We present a unified benchmark of representative GNN architectures for ACPF prediction under a common experimental framework. All models use identical preprocessing and training procedures and comparable parameter budgets, isolating the impact of message-passing mechanisms and inductive biases. We also analyze errors by distance from the slack bus and systematically ablate key design components. We evaluate predictive accuracy and physical consistency on the IEEE 14-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems.
  Results indicate that anisotropic message-passing architectures offer the most favorable trade-off between predictive accuracy and physical consistency under the studied parameter and topology constraints. Explicit edge features encoding line impedances and global context aggregation are particularly important for representing electrical interactions and system-wide dependencies, especially for voltage-angle predictions on the topologically bottlenecked IEEE-118 grid. Under a budget with approximately fixed parameters, two or three message-passing layers generally provide the best balance between depth and representation width, while additional depth offers no consistent improvement. Ablations also show that standard residual and root connections are not necessarily beneficial in shallow models, and that aggregation operators involve trade-offs between statistical accuracy and physical consistency. These results provide practical guidelines for designing graph-based power system models.
papers.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a natural fit for predicting alternating-current power flow (ACPF) on electrical grids, but studies use different graph representations and evaluation setups, so it has been unclear which architectural choices actually matter. The authors benchmark representative GNN architectures under identical preprocessing, training, and parameter budgets on the `IEEE 14-bus` and `IEEE 118-bus` systems, measuring predictive accuracy and physical consistency and ablating individual design components. **Anisotropic message-passing architectures give the best trade-off between accuracy and physical consistency**, and explicit edge features encoding line impedances plus global context aggregation matter most for voltage-angle predictions on the bottlenecked 118-bus grid. Two or three message-passing layers suffice under a fixed parameter budget, while extra depth, residual connections, and root connections offer no consistent benefit in shallow models.

papers.title: Syntactic Segmentation and Collage Generation for Videogame Levels with Perceptual Distance
papers.abstract: In procedural videogame level design, many existing techniques combine hand-authored level chunks. Some existing analysis techniques also rely on a higher-level graph structure which abstracts the level design. In this paper, we explore techniques for computing both of these things automatically from an existing design. We introduce the concept of perceptual distance, based on analysis techniques from the architecture subfield of Space Syntax. We use this perceptual distance to segment level designs with hierarchical clustering. We compare with past work on StarCraft analysis, show results on rooms from Super Metroid, and also demonstrate a proof-of-concept level generation algorithm based on this segmentation method.
papers.summary: Procedural level generation often stitches together hand-authored chunks, and level analysis often relies on a high-level graph abstracting the design, yet both the chunks and the graph are usually produced by hand. The authors introduce a perceptual distance measure derived from Space Syntax, an analysis tradition from architecture, and use it with hierarchical clustering to segment existing level designs into chunks and an abstract graph automatically. They compare against prior `StarCraft` map analysis, show segmentations of rooms from `Super Metroid`, and demonstrate a **proof-of-concept collage generator** that assembles new levels from the extracted segments.

papers.title: Rethinking GFlowNet Training: Negative Reinforce Dynamics
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are models that learn to sample discrete objects proportional to a target reward.
