papers.summary: Robot dexterous manipulation policies and world models need naturalistic human demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose, but no existing wearable provides calibrated fingertip force sensing together with occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation. `Tactus` is a textile-integrated sensing glove with a thin conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup), capacitive tactile sensors placed at manipulation-relevant regions identified from empirical contact studies, and IMU-fused pose tracking that holds up through hand-object occlusions, plus a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session subject correction. Using newly introduced standardized protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation applied to `Tactus` and two commercial tactile gloves, **`Tactus` resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 to 2.7 times lower than the commercial baselines**, with 0.87 cross-participant consistency and 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during heavily occluded manipulation. The combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction.

papers.title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents
papers.abstract: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.
papers.summary: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request, but existing evaluations rely on automated scores or binary verdicts that offer little human diagnosis of evidence use or intervention quality. `HALO` (Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents) introduces `HALO-Arena`, which spans four proactive need types (Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity) across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments where agents must retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether help is warranted and choosing its scope, and `HALO-8K`, 8,000 responses from 10 models on 400 scenarios annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and diagnosed timing, intensity, and other issues. The best proprietary and open-source models reach 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, and **over-proactivity is the dominant failure mode, with premature timing or excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses**. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds support further analyses of the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.

papers.title: PALATE: Pretrained Autoregressive LATent Embeddings
papers.abstract: Local-commerce and food-delivery marketplaces run large ads businesses: across hundreds of thousands of stores, merchants pay to be surfaced on browse and search surfaces, and a ranker decides which ads each consumer sees. Ranking well demands strong per-consumer personalization, yet a consumer's raw interaction history is sparse and high-cardinality. Our production ranker had personalized only through hand-engineered signals: aggregate engagement counts, categorical embeddings, and order-agnostic pooled history, with no learned per-consumer sequence representation. We learn one by training a GPT-style generative model of the consumer's engagement sequence to predict their next few engagements, and read its last-token hidden state as the consumer embedding. That single frozen vector becomes one shared personalization input for every ad surface: a daily job refreshes it, and each ranker consumes it as an ordinary dense feature. Offline it is the largest single-feature gain in our ranking-AUC ladder, a relative Eval-AUC gain of +0.59% on a browse-driven feed and +0.57% on a query-driven search surface. Online, it shipped as one component of bundled ranker retrains on both surfaces: Discovery (revenue +0.79%, conversion rate +1.17%) and Search (revenue +0.94%, conversion rate +1.50%). Three design choices adapt the generative objective to a repurchase-heavy marketplace, and are the core of our contribution: an exploration-weighted loss that up-weights businesses new to the consumer over ones already engaged; a two-stage curriculum: a click pretrain that keeps the representation broad and exploratory, then a conversion fine-tune that sharpens purchase intent; and a designed negative set that pairs a fixed popular-business pool and businesses shown but not ordered with random and in-batch negatives.
papers.summary: Ad rankers on local-commerce and food-delivery marketplaces need strong per-consumer personalization, but raw interaction histories are sparse and high-cardinality, and the authors' production ranker had personalized only through hand-engineered signals such as aggregate engagement counts, categorical embeddings, and order-agnostic pooled history. `PALATE` (Pretrained Autoregressive LATent Embeddings) trains a GPT-style generative model of each consumer's engagement sequence to predict their next few engagements and reads the last-token hidden state as a single frozen consumer embedding, refreshed by a daily job and consumed by every ad surface's ranker as an ordinary dense feature. Three adaptations to a repurchase-heavy marketplace form the core contribution: an exploration-weighted loss that up-weights businesses new to the consumer, a two-stage curriculum of broad click pretraining followed by conversion fine-tuning, and a designed negative set that pairs a fixed popular-business pool and shown-but-not-ordered businesses with random and in-batch negatives. Offline the embedding is the largest single-feature gain in the ranking-AUC ladder (+0.59% relative Eval-AUC on a browse feed, +0.57% on search), and **online, as part of bundled ranker retrains, Discovery revenue rose 0.79% and Search revenue rose 0.94%**, with conversion rate up 1.17% and 1.50% respectively.

papers.title: Generating Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. World models offer an alternative way to generate new experience through a learned dynamics model, yet learning policies in latent space is limited due to compounding errors in imagined rollouts. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.
papers.summary: Learning from offline datasets is hard to scale because collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe, and while world models can generate experience from a learned dynamics model, compounding errors make policy learning over long imagined rollouts in latent space unreliable. Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (`CGSE`) instead treats a frozen latent world model as a local transition generator: it samples candidate actions from an offline policy, refines each to maximize a first-order approximation of the Q-function within a trust region, imagines the next state for every refined action, lets the critic select the best, and appends that synthetic transition to the replay buffer. The procedure needs no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, and **on three `OGBench` manipulation tasks it improves an offline policy's average success rate by a relative 7.1%**.

papers.title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
papers.abstract: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.
papers.summary: When one AI agent tells another that tests passed or that a person approved a refund, the receiver has only the sender's word, and because `A2A` and `MCP` authenticate the channel rather than the sender's claims, a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. Proof-Carrying Messages (`PCM`) makes each claim carry evidence in the form of records from an append-only Merkle log the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control, so receivers check messages offline and label each claim proven, unproven, or failed, a claim resting only on the agent's own report is never proven, and authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval that can only narrow. The protocol specifies four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, with proofs of the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies across 16 classes, **`PCM` accepts 10 lies, all stale evidence (1.4%), whereas plain `A2A` accepts all 712** and models of six deployed protocols accept 504 to 712; two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts and verification takes about 1 ms.

papers.title: From Local Recovery to Unified Generation: Discovering Triple Set in Knowledge Graphs via Observation-Anchored Latent Diffusion
papers.abstract: Triple set prediction (TSP) is to recover missing relational triples in a knowledge graph by predicting the triple set instead of isolated links. Existing approaches predominantly rely on the subgraph-based completion paradigm, where the original graph is first partitioned into local subgraphs which are then independently completed. Such a paradigm suffers from fragmented structural reasoning, limited cross subgraph dependency modeling, and missing predictions across subgraphs. This paper proposes LatentDiff, a novel unified latent generative framework for TSP, which reformulates knowledge graph completion as latent space graph generation. LatentDiff first learns a compact latent representation using a relation-aware residual-quantized knowledge graph autoencoder, which encodes the whole graph into relation-aware latent embeddings, quantizes them with chunked residual codebooks, and reconstructs triples through a factorized decoder. On top of this latent space, we introduce an observation-anchored latent graph diffusion model, where the target latent graph representation is perturbed toward the observed latent. The reverse process recovers missing triples through progressive latent denoising. Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that LatentDiff outperforms the SOTA in terms of F_{tsp} by 5.4 percentage points on average. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LKGDiff-44A5.
papers.summary: Triple set prediction (TSP) recovers the missing relational triples of a knowledge graph as a set rather than as isolated links, but existing methods partition the graph into local subgraphs that are completed independently, which fragments structural reasoning, misses cross-subgraph dependencies, and loses predictions that span subgraphs. `LatentDiff` reformulates knowledge graph completion as latent-space graph generation: a relation-aware residual-quantized autoencoder encodes the whole graph into relation-aware latent embeddings, quantizes them with chunked residual codebooks, and reconstructs triples through a factorized decoder, while an observation-anchored latent diffusion model perturbs the target latent graph toward the observed latent so that reverse denoising progressively recovers the missing triples. **On three benchmark datasets `LatentDiff` outperforms the state of the art in F_tsp by 5.4 percentage points on average.**

papers.title: Uncertainty-Guided Cross-Modal Alignment for Diffusion-Based IoT Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Diffusion models evolve noisy states toward a learned data distribution, so their sampling behavior depends on the geometry of the representation in which denoising occurs. This dependence is especially important for multimodal data: independently trained encoders can map synchronized views to incompatible latent regions, while uniform alignment can let an uncertain view distort the shared geometry. To address this gap, we introduce a novel reliability-guided alignment rule that uses normalized VAE posterior variance to control directional cross-modal influence before diffusion training. We study this issue in minority-attack generation for imbalanced Internet-of-Things intrusion detection. Tabular flow attributes, a DeepInsight image, and a packet sequence are encoded by modality-specific variational autoencoders. Per-modality normalized VAE posterior variances provide bounded, sample-specific weighting signals in an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective. We use these quantities as heuristic encoder-derived reliability proxies rather than calibrated probabilistic uncertainties. The full modality-specific latent means obtained after alignment fine-tuning are standardized and modeled jointly by a class-conditional EDM; a second-order sampler then generates paired attack-conditioned latent blocks for the three decoders. In controlled experiments on TON-IoT, uncertainty-aware alignment obtains the highest mean precision, recall, density, and coverage among three diffusion variants. Augmenting only the training split yields ROC-AUC 0.9515, PR-AUC 0.8954, balanced accuracy 0.8395, and attack-class F1 0.7940 on an untouched real test set. Among the two variants with matched alignment fine-tuning, posterior-variance-based weighting improves both tabular generative fidelity and downstream detection relative to uniform weighting.
papers.summary: Diffusion models move noisy states toward a learned distribution, so their sampling behavior depends on the geometry of the latent representation, and for multimodal data independently trained encoders can map synchronized views to incompatible latent regions while uniform alignment lets an uncertain view distort the shared geometry. In the setting of generating minority attack samples for imbalanced Internet-of-Things intrusion detection, tabular flow attributes, a `DeepInsight` image, and a packet sequence are each encoded by a modality-specific variational autoencoder (VAE), and normalized VAE posterior variances serve as heuristic encoder-derived reliability proxies that weight an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective before the aligned latent means are modeled jointly by a class-conditional `EDM` with a second-order sampler. On `TON-IoT`, the uncertainty-aware alignment achieves the highest mean precision, recall, density, and coverage among three diffusion variants, and **augmenting only the training split yields ROC-AUC 0.9515, PR-AUC 0.8954, balanced accuracy 0.8395, and attack-class F1 0.7940 on an untouched real test set**, with posterior-variance weighting beating uniform weighting on both tabular generative fidelity and downstream detection.

papers.title: Appreciation Teaches Unauthorized Execution: Self-Evolution Degrades the Robustness of Personal Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Self-evolving personal agents act for users and learn from user feedback. However, if an agent obeys an instruction that an untrusted third party hides in content, the third party gains control of the agent. Such indirect prompt injection (IPI) poses severe risks. We investigate whether self-evolution degrades the robustness of personal agents to IPI. To study this question, we design a controlled two-phase methodology. In the adaptation phase, the user asks the agent to read external content and complete the task described in it, a common request in daily use. The agent then learns from the user's feedback and improves itself as designed. In the test phase, a third party writes a similar task into new external content, but the user's test request does not authorize the injected task. Using this methodology, we build multiple tasks with diverse test instances in different domains for a real personal agent. Our extensive experiments reveal that self-evolution substantially degrades robustness to IPI. Specifically, compared with the base agent, which does not evolve from user feedback, the average attack success rate rises by 14.0--48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0--39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning, posing safety risks. The code is available at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/Evolve-IPI
papers.summary: Self-evolving personal agents act on a user's behalf and learn from user feedback, but if an agent obeys an instruction that an untrusted third party hides in content, the third party gains control of the agent, a threat known as indirect prompt injection (IPI). The authors design a controlled two-phase methodology: in an adaptation phase the user asks the agent to read external content and complete the task it describes, a common everyday request, and the agent improves from the resulting feedback as designed; in a test phase a third party writes a similar task into new external content that the user's request does not authorize. Across multiple tasks with diverse instances in different domains on a real personal agent, **self-evolution raises the average attack success rate over the non-evolving base agent by 14.0 to 48.8 percentage points under skill evolution** and by 3.0 to 39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning, indicating that feedback rewarding content-driven task completion carries over to instructions the user never authorized.

papers.title: Clean Sheets and Checkpoints: Evidence Complexity for Certifying Sequential Agent Risk
papers.abstract: Dangerous-capability evaluations often test an AI agent from prepared states at ordered milestones. A clean sheet records no successes. What it certifies about a campaign of $B$ attempts depends on what a failed attempt erases. We model the task as a chain of $k$ milestones divided into checkpoint segments and ask how many zero audit responses certify, at level $\alpha$, a completion probability of at most $\epsilon$. For segments chosen before the audit, counting possible completion windows gives a certificate for any specified budget. The bound also covers adaptive deployment processes that follow the chain's transitions, provided their success probabilities after every complete history are capped by the corresponding audit success probabilities. The audit does not test this transport assumption. In rare-risk phase interiors, each segment is either rarely completed within the budget (active) or nearly always completed (free). The minimum expected number of zero responses is asymptotic to $\log(1/\alpha)\,(B^a/(a!\,\epsilon))^{1/K_A}$, where the $a$ active segments contain $K_A$ milestones and are those at least as long as a budget-dependent threshold. The certificate attains this constant. Every asymptotically optimal evaluator must divide its expected response count equally among active milestones in the limit, with a vanishing share elsewhere. Where a single segment passes from active to free, each of its milestones receives a smaller limiting share than an active milestone; a crossover-aware certificate attains the optimal constant. For selected segments with known or unqueried prefix steps, counting failed cycles can sharpen the certificate.
papers.summary: Dangerous-capability evaluations often probe an AI agent from prepared states at a chain of ordered milestones, and a clean audit with no successes is taken as evidence that a real campaign of B attempts would also fail. The work models the task as k milestones split into checkpoint segments and asks how many zero-success audit responses are needed to certify, at a given confidence level, that completion probability stays below a target epsilon, including for adaptive deployers whose per-step success rates are capped by the audited ones. **The minimum expected number of zero responses grows asymptotically as log(1/alpha) multiplied by the K_A-th root of B^a over a-factorial times epsilon**, where the a active segments hold K_A milestones, and any asymptotically optimal evaluator must spread its queries equally over active milestones. A proposed certificate attains this constant, with a sharper variant for segments whose prefix steps are known or unqueried.

papers.title: DICE: Decentralized Incentive-driven Federated Learning for Efficient & Scalable Customization of Pretrained Models in Web3
papers.abstract: Customizing Pretrained Models (PMs) for downstream tasks demands task-specific data, which burgeoning Web3 applications provide abundantly. Blockchain-powered federated learning (BCFL) offers a secure and privacy-preserving paradigm to customize PMs among self-interested and untrusted Web3 participants. Yet, existing BCFL algorithms face severe efficiency and scalability challenges when applied to large PMs, due to their substantial computational and memory requirements and the hardware constraints of many participants. This paper introduces DICE, a novel BCFL algorithm that addresses the efficiency and scalability challenges of customizing large PMs in Web3 via two sets of synergistic techniques: (i) a dynamic progressive learning scheme and a model slice verification scheme to enable a wider range of honest participants, including those unable to deploy the full model, to engage in customizing PMs, while preserving model utility; (ii) a tree-structured committee consensus protocol and an efficiency-driven incentive scheme to address the dominant bottleneck that hinders existing BCFL algorithms from scaling to a larger number of data holders for customizing data-hungry large PMs, while maintaining security. Theoretical analysis and extensive experimental results on customizing vision and language PMs demonstrate DICE's efficiency, effectiveness, and security.
papers.summary: Customizing pretrained models for downstream tasks needs task-specific data that Web3 applications generate in abundance, and blockchain-powered federated learning (BCFL) lets self-interested, untrusted participants contribute without sharing raw data, but existing BCFL methods do not scale to large pretrained models given most participants' hardware limits. `DICE` combines a dynamic progressive learning scheme with model-slice verification so that honest participants who cannot host the full model can still contribute, and pairs a tree-structured committee consensus protocol with an efficiency-driven incentive scheme to handle many more data holders securely. **Theoretical analysis and experiments on customizing both vision and language pretrained models support the method's efficiency, effectiveness, and security.**

papers.title: REALM: Identifying Minimal Task Assets for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often receive access to more files, accounts, and services than a task requires. Prompt injection turns this excess access into an opportunity to redirect execution toward unrelated resources. Applying least privilege therefore requires identifying the assets needed by a task, including assets whose identities emerge only during execution. We present REALM (Required Execution Assets Linked to a Mission), an approach to identifying and maintaining a task's required assets and their permitted uses. The approach represents required assets as Dependency Graph nodes, resolves prerequisite relationships, and admits newly discovered assets through source-scoped selection. It separates discovering an asset from authorizing its use, while preserving the agent's freedom to choose its computation. The REALM Builder maintains the selected grants and projects Asset Files; the Partial API Manager exposes resource-bound Partial APIs to the Agent inside a Task Container. Across 60 clean tasks and 560 injected cases in AgentDyn, it completes 40.0% and 36.4% of tasks and decreases ASR from 16.6% to 0.2% with qwen3.5-flash as the base model.
papers.summary: Large language model agents are usually granted far more files, accounts, and services than a task needs, and prompt injection exploits that excess to redirect execution toward unrelated resources, so enforcing least privilege requires identifying a task's required assets, including ones whose identities only emerge mid-execution. `REALM` (Required Execution Assets Linked to a Mission) represents required assets as nodes in a dependency graph, resolves prerequisite relations, admits newly discovered assets through source-scoped selection, and separates discovering an asset from authorizing its use; a builder component maintains grants and projects asset files, while a partial API manager exposes resource-bound APIs to the agent inside a task container. **On 60 clean tasks and 560 injected cases in `AgentDyn`, it completes 40.0% and 36.4% of tasks while cutting attack success rate from 16.6% to 0.2%** with `qwen3.5-flash` as the base model.

papers.title: Learning Erasing Equal-Length Relational Pattern Languages in the Limit from Positive Data over Binary Alphabets
papers.abstract: Relational pattern languages generalize Angluin's pattern languages by requiring the strings substituted for repeated occurrences of a variable to stand in a given relation, rather than to be identical. We study erasing pattern languages under the equal-length relation, where all occurrences of a variable must be replaced by strings of the same length. Over alphabets with at least three letters, this class is known to be learnable in the limit from positive data. We show that over a binary alphabet it is not, which resolves an open question from earlier work. Our proof reveals that non-learnability already holds for the restricted subclass of languages generated by patterns that have exactly three maximal substrings of variables. We then show that patterns with at most two maximal substrings of variables are learnable in the limit from positive data for every alphabet of size at least two. If the target pattern is known to have at most one maximal substring of variables, this can even be achieved by an iterative learner, which updates its hypothesis using only the current example and its previous hypothesis.
papers.summary: Relational pattern languages extend Angluin's pattern languages by requiring repeated occurrences of a variable to be replaced by strings standing in a given relation rather than identical strings; here the relation is equal length and variables may be erased. Over alphabets of at least three letters this class was known to be learnable in the limit from positive data, and the open question was whether the same holds for binary alphabets. **The answer is no: over a binary alphabet the class is not learnable in the limit, and non-learnability already arises for patterns with exactly three maximal variable substrings.** Patterns with at most two maximal variable substrings remain learnable for every alphabet of size at least two, and with at most one such substring an iterative learner that uses only the current example and its previous hypothesis suffices.

papers.title: A Novel Approach to Evaluating Evaluation Metrics for Multi-Output Structured Prediction
papers.abstract: In multi-output structured prediction tasks, while only one ground truth label may be provided in the training data, multiple equally valid outputs may be possible, making reliable evaluation a persistent challenge. We postulate that human evaluators implicitly use task-specific invariants, e.g., object boundaries in colorized images or named entities in translations, to judge if an output is acceptable. Under this assumption, we introduce a notion of approximate task-specific invariants and use them as diagnostic tools to evaluate a variety of existing metrics for vision and language tasks. We use these task invariants as part of a framework to systematically test metric reliability by encouraging domain-relevant invariants in model outputs via an augmented loss function. In our experiments, we observe that enforcing invariants with an augmented loss yields substantial improvements in popular distributional metrics while more traditional metrics change only marginally. Through this invariants-driven evaluation, we expose where standard metrics fail to detect meaningful differences, and we highlight the conditions under which distributional metrics succeed or still fall short.
papers.summary: In structured prediction tasks such as image colorization or translation, many outputs can be equally valid even though training data supplies a single ground truth, which makes metric reliability hard to assess. The authors hypothesize that human judges implicitly rely on task-specific invariants, such as object boundaries or named entities, and formalize approximate invariants as diagnostic tools; they then encourage those invariants in model outputs through an augmented loss and check which metrics register the resulting change. **Enforcing invariants produced substantial improvements in distributional metrics while traditional metrics barely moved**, exposing cases where standard metrics miss meaningful differences and identifying conditions under which distributional metrics succeed or still fall short across vision and language tasks.

papers.title: Reading-Level Verification of Kanji Words in Japanese Financial Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Few-shot voice cloning makes it cheap to produce daily Japanese financial commentary with several synthetic speakers, but kanji words with more than one reading, such as the word for "market" (shijo vs. ichiba) or "overall trend" (taisei vs. oze), are still misread. A common quality gate transcribes each synthesized sentence with automatic speech recognition (ASR), converts both the input and the transcript to kana, and regenerates on mismatch. We show that this gate is unreliable in both directions: when the audio contains a misreading, the ASR language model frequently writes the expected kanji back, hiding the error, and when the audio is correct, ordinary recognition errors trigger needless regeneration. We propose a reading-level check that scores the expected reading and its confusable alternatives with a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) hiragana recognizer and flags a word when an alternative explains the audio better. On 540 utterances from three voice-cloned production voices covering 30 financial terms, with misreadings injected under controlled conditions, the transcript-based gate detected 78.9% of misreadings at a 44.4% false-alarm rate, whereas the proposed check detected 91.7% at 5.0% (AUC 0.990). On natural kanji input, it caught a front-end error that the transcript-based gate missed for one voice, and reduced regeneration requests from 38.9% to 6.1% of sentences.
papers.summary: Few-shot voice cloning makes it cheap to produce daily Japanese financial commentary with several synthetic speakers, but kanji words with multiple readings, such as the word for market read as shijo or ichiba, are still misread, and the usual quality gate of transcribing the audio with automatic speech recognition (ASR) and comparing kana fails in both directions: the ASR language model often rewrites a misreading back to the expected kanji, and ordinary recognition errors trigger needless regeneration. The proposed reading-level check scores the expected reading against its confusable alternatives using a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) hiragana recognizer and flags a word when an alternative explains the audio better. **On 540 utterances from three production voices covering 30 financial terms, the new check detected 91.7% of injected misreadings at a 5.0% false-alarm rate, versus 78.9% at 44.4% for the transcript-based gate**, and on natural input it cut regeneration requests from 38.9% to 6.1% of sentences.

papers.title: ACAM-J-MARS: Multi-Atlas Riemannian Spectral Representations for Decoding Advanced Meditation States from fMRI
papers.abstract: Inferring jhana-type advanced concentration absorption meditation (ACAM-J) states from fMRI data is challenging due to the spatially distributed nature of meditation-related effects, substantial inter-individual variability that can exceed within-subject state differences, and limited sample sizes. Conventional machine-learning approaches often formulate this problem as unimodal, Euclidean, atlas-based classification, thereby neglecting the non-Euclidean geometry of functional connectivity matrices and underrepresenting temporal information in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI); these limitations can lead to suboptimal classification performance. We propose ACAM-J-MARS (\textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{A}tlas \textbf{R}iemannian \textbf{S}pectral representation), which computes functional connectivity using multiple atlases, represents symmetric positive definite (SPD) connectivity matrices on a Riemannian manifold, projects them into a log-Euclidean tangent space, and augments connectivity-derived features with low-frequency BOLD spectral energy to better resolve subtle state differences under heterogeneous variability. Evaluated on 204 segments from 22 practitioners, ACAM-J-MARS improves performance across multiple backbone models, achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.757 for early versus late ACAM-J classification and 0.545 for three-class classification, corresponding to a 10.8-point absolute improvement over the strongest baseline. These findings suggest that the proposed representation improves the decoding of advanced meditative brain states and may enable downstream applications such as closed-loop neurofeedback and real-time psychophysiological brain-computer interfaces.
papers.summary: Decoding jhana-type advanced concentration absorption meditation (ACAM-J) states from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is hard because meditation effects are spatially distributed, between-subject variability can exceed within-subject state differences, and samples are small, while conventional classifiers treat connectivity matrices as flat Euclidean vectors from a single atlas. `ACAM-J-MARS` computes functional connectivity from multiple atlases, treats the symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices as points on a Riemannian manifold projected into a log-Euclidean tangent space, and adds low-frequency blood-oxygen spectral energy features. **On 204 segments from 22 practitioners it reaches 0.757 balanced accuracy for early-versus-late state classification and 0.545 for three-class classification, a 10.8-point absolute gain over the strongest baseline**, with improvements holding across several backbone models.

papers.title: PRISM: Personalized Item Representations in User History
papers.abstract:
Sequential recommenders typically construct history inputs from item identifiers or content features using an embedding map shared across users. The same item therefore yields the same initial embedding representation, even when users have different relationships to the item. We propose personalized item representations in user history, where each item's embedding expresses its relationship to the user. Personalization becomes a property of the history inputs themselves, supplying richer evidence for later sequence modeling.
  We instantiate this idea with PRISM, which reuses upstream ranking computation to generate personalized item embeddings. An autoencoder jointly compresses all layer states from a user tower, a user--item tower, and same-request candidate mixing into one embedding per scored pair for downstream replay. Offline evaluation on Surface 1, a major recommendation surface at billion scale, reports an average downstream normalized entropy (NE) change of $-0.15\%$, compared with $-0.07\%$ for VISTA at similar history lengths. We further identify an empirical sequence-length scaling law: over history lengths of 26--240 events, NE gain follows a fitted power law with exponent 0.468, increasing from 0.06\% to 0.17\%. Therefore, personalized item representations in user history provide a new scaling dimension for improving recommendation quality.
papers.summary: Sequential recommenders build history inputs from item identifiers or content features through an embedding map shared by all users, so the same item gets the same initial representation regardless of a given user's relationship to it. `PRISM` instead reuses upstream ranking computation to produce personalized item embeddings: an autoencoder jointly compresses all layer states from a user tower, a user-item tower, and same-request candidate mixing into one embedding per scored pair, which is replayed as the history input for downstream sequence modeling. **On a billion-scale recommendation surface, it improves downstream normalized entropy (NE) by an average of 0.15%, compared with 0.07% for `VISTA` at similar history lengths**, and the gain follows a fitted power law in history length with exponent 0.468 over 26 to 240 events, suggesting personalized history representations as a new scaling dimension.

papers.title: EmbodiExp: Compositional Experience Transfer for Embodied Agents
papers.abstract: Experience can help embodied agents turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring it across tasks remains challenging: previously effective strategies may be inapplicable to the current state or fail to produce their intended outcomes. We present EmbodiExp, a framework for constructing transferable experiences and composing them online during embodied task execution. Our key observation is that tasks often share subgoals whose completion can be assessed independently of overall task success. We therefore introduce an outcome-grounded subgoal experience that specifies a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome. During execution, applicable experiences guide action generation, while verified outcomes can establish the conditions required by subsequent experiences, enabling online composition. Subgoal-level outcome attribution further enables failure utilization: failed trajectories can still contribute verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid. Experiments on multiple embodied benchmarks under a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks demonstrate the effectiveness of EmbodiExp.
papers.summary: Embodied agents can use prior experience to turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring experience across tasks is hard because a strategy that worked before may not apply to the current state or may fail to produce its intended effect. `EmbodiExp` builds on the observation that tasks share subgoals whose completion can be checked independently of overall success, and packages each experience as a subgoal, its applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome; at execution time, applicable experiences guide action generation and verified outcomes unlock the conditions for subsequent experiences, allowing online composition. **Subgoal-level outcome attribution lets failed trajectories still contribute verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid**, and experiments on several embodied benchmarks under a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks show the approach is effective.

papers.title: Reasoning or Pattern Exploitation? Mechanistic Insights from RL-Trained Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly described as acquiring "reasoning" skills after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, whether these gains reflect genuine reasoning or more superficial adaptations remains underexplored. In this work, we probe LLMs trained in a finite and exhaustively analyzable logical domain, namely Tic-Tac-Toe, and trace how internal representations evolve across reinforcement learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quantitatively, RL yields high accuracy and robustness across prompt variations, suggesting the emergence of game reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability, however, paints a different picture: features extracted with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that models primarily adapt to rely more heavily on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression and board occupancy. In comparison, high-level concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented, raising concerns that reasoning benchmarks overestimate model abilities. This suggests that RL-driven "reasoning" may conflate task-specific adaptations to input information with reasoning ability. We provide, for the first time: (i) a systematic interpretability pipeline tracing representation dynamics across RL training in small-scale LLMs; (ii) an extension of SAE-based feature discovery to hypothesis-driven testing in a finite logical domain; and (iii) an interpretability-based demonstration that RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate the representation, with causal interventions locating the decision downstream of it, in the late-layer state.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are said to acquire reasoning after reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards, but it is unclear whether the gains reflect genuine reasoning or shallower adaptations. The authors train small LLMs on Tic-Tac-Toe, a finite and fully analyzable domain, with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`), and trace internal representations across training using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) extended to hypothesis-driven testing of game concepts, plus causal interventions. Although RL yields high accuracy and robustness to prompt variations, **the models mainly learn to lean harder on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression, and board occupancy, while concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks stay weakly represented.** RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate, with the decision located downstream in the late-layer state, suggesting reasoning benchmarks may overestimate model abilities.

papers.title: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.
papers.summary: LLM-based agents working on long-horizon tasks must switch among duties such as planning and verification, and **a preliminary study finds that verification is the duty most strongly associated with task success yet tends to happen late, leaving little room for correction**, while duty-relevant information gets diluted as records from different duties pile up in a shared context. Splitting duties across agents with separate contexts does not fix this on its own, since agents lose sight of the overall goal, repeat earlier investigations, and receive irrelevant information while lacking needed background. Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (`GAD`) organizes subtasks and dependencies in a growing execution graph, keeps the original instruction plus each assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions in every agent's context, and lets agents split tasks and declare dependencies based on execution evidence. Dependencies determine when agents run and which results they see, and verification and recovery steps check subtask and whole-task results against their goals to trigger repair when checks fail.

papers.title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes
papers.abstract: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). Under such rank-deficient rarity ($n_1 < p$), maximum likelihood estimators suffer from quasi-complete separation, penalized likelihood methods exhibit severe intercept bias, and convex minority oversampling techniques such as SMOTE collapse into an $(n_1 - 1)$-dimensional affine subspace. In this paper, we propose a novel \textit{Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement} estimator that shifts the paradigm from minority interpolation to majority fringe extrapolation. Grounded in Stein's Lemma, we prove that the conditional expectation shift of the abundant majority class ($Y=0$) induced by logistic truncation uniquely identifies the true hyperplane normal $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ after Mahalanobis whitening. We further establish that extrapolating synthetic minority instances outward from the high-quantile density fringe of the majority distribution along the conjugate direction preserves full-rank covariance regularity ($\mathrm{rank} = p$). To accommodate both semi-supervised environments (with an unlabeled background mean) and strictly supervised subsamples, we introduce a hybrid estimator incorporating the intrinsic third-moment skewness of the majority class alongside a location-shift-invariant zero-boundary intercept calibration. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and real-world benchmark applications (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer and Banknote Authentication) under extreme rarity ($n_1 \in \{3, 5\}$) demonstrate that our approach prevents parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane with high fidelity, and substantially outperforms Firth's regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability.
papers.summary: Binary logistic regression breaks down when the minority class has fewer observations than there are features: maximum likelihood suffers quasi-complete separation, penalized methods show heavy intercept bias, and oversampling techniques like `SMOTE` collapse into a low-dimensional affine subspace. The proposed `Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement` estimator flips the usual strategy from interpolating among minority points to extrapolating outward from the high-quantile fringe of the abundant majority class, using Stein's Lemma to show that the truncation-induced shift in the majority class's conditional mean identifies the true hyperplane normal after Mahalanobis whitening, and that the synthetic minority points preserve full-rank covariance. A hybrid variant incorporates majority-class skewness and a location-shift-invariant intercept calibration to cover both semi-supervised and strictly supervised settings. **With only three or five minority examples on the `Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer` and `Banknote Authentication` benchmarks, the method avoids parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane closely, and substantially beats `Firth` regression and `SMOTE` in F1-score and estimation stability.**

papers.title: Analyzing Condensation on Patterned Surfaces via Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Dropwise condensation is key to power and water systems. State-of-the-art condensation surfaces are often inhomogeneous, either patterned by design or random defects. Inhomogeneous surface features dictate the rates of each stage of dropwise condensation-nucleation, growth, coalescence, and shedding. Characterizing these rates requires the precise detection of thousands of droplets. Yet, existing segmentation methods are unable to detect droplets on inhomogeneous surfaces. We developed TileSAM3, a universal droplet segmentation tool built on the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3). Hierarchical tiling with per-tile inference followed by post-processing extended SAM3's detection cap and raised the effective resolution of small droplets. We created two datasets: High Quality Droplet Dataset (N=365,826; HQDD) with homogeneous surfaces and Low Quality Droplet Dataset (N=63,577; LQDD) with patterned, defect-laden surfaces under adverse lighting. TileSAM3 closely reproduced thresholding annotations on HQDD, surpassed it over sixfold on LQDD (Average Precision 0.57 versus 0.088), and outperformed other deep learning models on all metrics evaluated. Combined with KD-tree tracking, TileSAM3 identified localized nucleation and coalescence in narrow active bands on a stiffness-patterned surface. TileSAM3 enables analysis of understudied inhomogeneous substrates with poor lighting and videography which facilitates faster, lower cost research of condensation materials.
papers.summary: Dropwise condensation underpins power and water systems, and modern condensation surfaces are typically inhomogeneous by design or through defects, so characterizing nucleation, growth, coalescence, and shedding rates requires detecting thousands of droplets that existing segmentation methods miss on patterned surfaces. `TileSAM3` wraps the Segment Anything Model 3 (`SAM3`) in hierarchical tiling with per-tile inference and post-processing to lift its detection cap and effective resolution for small droplets, and the authors release two datasets: the `High Quality Droplet Dataset` of 365,826 droplets on homogeneous surfaces and the `Low Quality Droplet Dataset` of 63,577 droplets on patterned, defect-laden surfaces under poor lighting. **On the low-quality dataset it reached an average precision of 0.57 versus 0.088 for thresholding, more than a sixfold gain**, outperformed other deep learning models on all metrics, and when combined with KD-tree tracking revealed localized nucleation and coalescence bands on a stiffness-patterned surface.

papers.title: Pair-Dependent Judge Errors Change the Minimax Rate of Semantic Entropy
papers.abstract: Semantic entropy, the entropy of the meanings among a language model's sampled answers, is estimated from the verdicts of a judge that declares pairs of answers equivalent or not, and automatic judges err in ways that depend on the answers they compare. The existing minimax theory covers only judges whose false-equivalence probability is the same for all pairs. We model a known judge that declares two answers with meanings $a$ and $b$ equivalent with probability $q+\Delta M_{ab}$, for a symmetric matrix $M$ and $q$ bounded away from $0$ and $1$, and show that for three meanings the rate is set by tree statistics on four answers, while on an open set of channels the consistency threshold is set by trees on five. For every channel in an explicit open class, the minimax squared risk is of order $N^{-1/3}$ with $N=n^4\Delta^6$ on polynomial weak windows on which $n^5\Delta^8$ exceeds a multiple of $\log n$, and of order $\min\{1,N^{-1/3}\}$ on every polynomial weak window when the tree functions on at most four vertices are injective. The exponent comes from a cubic degeneracy at the equitable point. On an open set of channels in the class, the four-vertex tree functions take equal values at two distributions with different entropies. For such a channel, on every polynomial weak window, the minimax risk is of the order of the sum of $\min\{1,N^{-1/3}\}$ and a term that decays exponentially in $n^5\Delta^8$, so no estimator is consistent while $n^5\Delta^8$ stays bounded, even as $N\to\infty$. For $\Delta=n^{-\beta}$ with $\beta>1/2$, channels of the class with injective four-vertex tree functions allow consistent estimation exactly for $\beta<2/3$, and the channels of this open set exactly for $\beta<5/8$, at which the risk exponent drops from $1/12$ to $0$. Computer-assisted certificates show that both kinds of channels occur on open sets.
papers.summary: Semantic entropy, which measures uncertainty as the entropy over meanings among a language model's sampled answers, relies on a judge that declares pairs of answers equivalent or not, and existing minimax theory assumes the judge's false-equivalence probability is identical for every pair. The work models a known judge whose equivalence probability for meanings a and b is a base rate q plus a pair-dependent perturbation of size Delta, and derives minimax rates for estimating entropy over three meanings. **For an explicit open class of judge channels the minimax squared risk scales as N to the power of minus one third, with N equal to n to the fourth times Delta to the sixth, driven by a cubic degeneracy at the equitable point**, and on an open subset of channels where four-answer tree statistics cannot distinguish two distributions with different entropies, no estimator is consistent until a five-answer quantity grows, so for Delta equal to n to the minus beta the consistency threshold drops from beta below 2/3 to beta below 5/8. Computer-assisted certificates confirm both kinds of channels occupy open sets.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders as Implicit Diversification Regularisers for Cross-Sectional Cryptocurrency Returns
papers.abstract: Factor models are central to asset pricing and portfolio construction, but neural factors are often difficult to interpret, and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) may address both concerns by describing daily returns across many assets with only a few active features. We ask whether this sparse representation produces stable financial factors and better-diversified portfolios. We study cryptocurrency returns, use equities as a secondary test, and compare the SAE with common benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation. We find consistently lower volatility in SAE portfolios and link this result to lower correlations among the selected assets. However, the SAE does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return, and its factor identities are not stable across training runs. Our contribution is to show that sparse coding can support portfolio diversification, while clearly separating this risk effect from claims about alpha or stable factor identities.
papers.summary: Neural factor models for asset pricing are hard to interpret and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear, so the authors test whether a sparse autoencoder (SAE), which describes daily returns across many assets with only a few active features, yields stable financial factors and better-diversified portfolios. They study cryptocurrency returns with equities as a secondary test, comparing SAE-based portfolios to standard benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation. **SAE portfolios show consistently lower volatility, traced to lower correlations among the selected assets, but the SAE does not beat a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return and its factor identities are not stable across training runs.** The contribution is to separate the diversification effect of sparse coding from any claim about alpha or stable factors.

papers.title: Event2Reward: Learning Robotic Rewards from Progress Relations
papers.abstract: Learning task progress from robot demonstrations provides a practical way to construct dense shaping rewards for robotic reinforcement learning. A common approach uses normalized demonstration time as progress labels, implicitly assuming monotonically increasing task progress. During policy exploration, however, actual task progress can stall or even regress. Such models may mistake regressions for progress, assigning positive shaping rewards to actions that cause progress loss. Real suboptimal and failed executions offer corrective experience, but assigning absolute progress values to their states is difficult. Our key observation is that stalls, regressions, and recoveries establish local relative progress relations even when absolute progress is unknown. We introduce Event2Reward, which uses normalized temporal labels to anchor the progress scale and these within-trajectory relations to constrain local changes, combining absolute and relative progress supervision. Its progress predictions serve as potentials for reward shaping. We curate an event-annotated dataset from approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records, covering successful, suboptimal, and failed executions, without requiring framewise absolute progress labels. Under the same training budgets, Event2Reward improves average policy success by 18.16 percentage points over a baseline using only sparse task rewards across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites. On real robots, average success after 30 minutes of wall-clock training reaches 60.0% on three precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three object manipulation tasks, exceeding the sparse-reward baseline under the same budget by 36.7 and 23.3 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further show that absolute progress supervision and relative progress relations are complementary, with joint supervision yielding better downstream policy learning.
papers.summary: Dense shaping rewards for robotic reinforcement learning are often learned from demonstrations by using normalized time as a progress label, which assumes progress only increases; during exploration, however, progress can stall or regress, and such models may reward actions that lose progress. `Event2Reward` keeps normalized temporal labels to anchor the absolute progress scale but adds within-trajectory relations drawn from annotated stalls, regressions, and recoveries in real suboptimal and failed executions, so local progress changes are constrained without requiring framewise absolute labels; the learned progress predictor then serves as a potential for reward shaping. The authors curate an event-annotated dataset from roughly 100K raw real-robot execution records. **Under matched training budgets it lifts average policy success by 18.16 percentage points over a sparse-reward baseline across 40 tasks in four `LIBERO` suites**, and on real robots after 30 minutes of training reaches 60.0% on three precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three manipulation tasks, with ablations showing absolute and relative supervision are complementary.

papers.title: Where Position Matters: Profiling-Guided Layer-Wise RoPE Allocation in Transformers
papers.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) typically uses uniform coverage across Transformer layers despite heterogeneous positional requirements. Phase-off interventions reveal non-uniform, model-specific rotary-phase dependence, while coverage interventions relate it to coverage-upgrade benefits. We propose profiling-guided layer-wise RoPE allocation, assigning high/low coverage under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles. The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within model families, enabling small-model measurements to guide larger-model allocations before pretraining. A brief analysis relates selection and transfer to score calibration and inter-layer interactions. From-scratch experiments demonstrate validation-loss improvements over available budget-matched baselines, while analytical resource accounting identifies favorable quality--storage--compute trade-offs for physical MLA. These results connect positional demand to transferable, efficient architecture design.
papers.summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is normally applied with the same coverage in every Transformer layer even though layers differ in how much they depend on position. Phase-off interventions show that rotary-phase dependence is non-uniform and model-specific, and coverage interventions tie that dependence to the benefit of upgrading coverage, motivating profiling-guided layer-wise allocation that assigns high or low RoPE coverage per layer under a fixed budget based on early coverage-benefit profiles. The scheme supports fixed-width query and key representations as well as physical allocation of rotary dimensions in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and **normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within a model family so that measurements on a small model can set the allocation for a larger one before pretraining.** From-scratch experiments show validation-loss gains over budget-matched baselines, and resource accounting points to favorable quality, storage, and compute trade-offs for the MLA variant.

papers.title: XLaw-JP-27B: A Lightweight Open Model Specialized for Japanese Law
papers.abstract: We present XLaw-JP-27B, an open-weight model specialized for Japanese law that runs on a single 48\,GB GPU under the Apache~2.0 licence. It adapts Qwen3.8-27B with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions (self-distillation), a contract-specific LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting. We evaluate it on eight Japanese legal tasks---the multiple-choice section of the bar examination in 2024, 2025 and 2026, statement-level bar questions (JBE-QA), statute questions (LawQA-JP), the patent attorney exam, and contract review and drafting built from government model contracts---against open models of 12--33B under identical prompts and retrieval. XLaw-JP-27B ranks first on six tasks, ties on one and is third on one (mean rank 1.3 against 2.8--3.1 for the baselines). It is the only system that passes the bar exam in all three years (129, 120 and 130 of 175, meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used in training), while open Japanese 32--33B models fail at least one year. A controlled study of each component shows that retrieval, voting and self-distillation help, and that thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification, per-statement decomposition and more self-distillation do not. The largest remaining gaps to frontier models are in contract review and patent law. The model is available as a free web service at https://x-law.jp/ with the weights available at https://huggingface.co/X-LawJapan/xlaw-jp-27b under Apache~2.0.
papers.summary: `XLaw-JP-27B` is an Apache 2.0 open-weight model for Japanese law that runs on a single 48 GB GPU, built by adapting `Qwen3.8-27B` with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions (self-distillation), a contract-specific LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting. Evaluated against 12B to 33B open models under identical prompts and retrieval on eight tasks, including the 2024 to 2026 bar exam multiple-choice sections, `JBE-QA`, `LawQA-JP`, the patent attorney exam, and contract review and drafting, it ranks first on six tasks, ties on one, and places third on one. **It is the only system to pass the bar exam in all three years, scoring 129, 120, and 130 of 175 while meeting every subject minimum, whereas open Japanese 32B to 33B models fail at least one year.** Component ablations show retrieval, voting, and self-distillation help while thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification, per-statement decomposition, and additional self-distillation do not, with the largest remaining gaps to frontier models in contract review and patent law.

papers.title: Beyond LLM Wrappers: Context Engineering and the Three-Engine Architecture for Reliable Financial AI
papers.abstract:
Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants.
  Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks.
  We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.
papers.summary: Financial AI must answer decision-bearing questions about payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance with numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability, which large language models alone cannot guarantee. The proposed production architecture combines a financial knowledge graph holding enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, orchestration, explanation, and claim validation, coordinated by a context engineering layer that selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, tools, and tenants. **Across 15 deployments over about 11 months, single-agent pipelines hallucinated on roughly 7 to 9% of queries, including invented invoices, while graph-backed multi-agent validation brought observed rates below 1%**, though the authors stress these findings are observational rather than causal. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with deployment time falling from about six weeks to two, and ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained the main obstacles.

papers.title: AgentHeal: Evaluating Goal-Preserving Resource Recovery of Web Agents under Access Barriers
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating complex information-seeking and transactional tasks across the open web. However, their real-world reliability remains limited by access barriers, such as dead links, authentication walls, rate limits, and anti-scraping defenses. These barriers block the primary execution path, causing agents to abort prematurely, loop indefinitely, or quietly compromise the user's original constraints. Existing evaluations either implicitly assume that target resources are freely accessible or focus on transient perturbations that simple retries can resolve, failing to capture scenarios where agents must actively reroute around impassable bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces AgentHeal, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating goal-preserving resource recovery, defined as the ability of web agents to detect non-transient access barriers, pivot to legitimate alternative sources, and fulfill the user's exact original objective. Spanning nine barrier families across a counterfactual sandbox and real-website replay, our experiments on leading LLM backbones show that average task success drops sharply from 89.4% to 43.7% under access barriers. Further analysis reveals that agents frequently fall for deceptive look-alikes, fail to escalate to users when necessary, violate access policies, or waste computation on futile retries, providing actionable diagnostics for developing resilient web agents.
papers.summary: Web agents built on large language models can handle complex information-seeking and transactional tasks, but real deployments hit dead links, authentication walls, rate limits, and anti-scraping defenses that make agents abort, loop, or quietly drop the user's constraints, and existing evaluations either assume free access or only test transient failures a retry would fix. `AgentHeal` is a benchmark for goal-preserving resource recovery: detecting a non-transient barrier, pivoting to a legitimate alternative source, and still satisfying the user's exact original objective, spanning nine barrier families across a counterfactual sandbox and real-website replay. **Across leading LLM backbones, average task success falls from 89.4% without barriers to 43.7% with them.** Failure analysis shows agents fall for deceptive look-alike sources, fail to escalate to the user when they should, violate access policies, or burn computation on futile retries.

papers.title: Grounding Multimodal Reasoning with Evidence-Ablated Negatives
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful tool for improving multimodal reasoning. However, standard outcome supervision suffers from credit assignment ambiguity, as a model may receive positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than grounding its reasoning in the requisite visual evidence. This makes high-quality negative responses critical, since effective negatives should remain plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut that should be suppressed. In this paper, we propose EVAN, a multimodal reinforcement learning framework utilizing EVidence-Ablated Negatives to train LMMs against their own language-prior failures. EVAN first identifies highly visually dependent examples using a scaled image information gain metric and preserves data diversity with a mixed-ranking strategy. It then constructs evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative image patches, eliciting plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy. During policy optimization, these negative responses are incorporated as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability. Experiments across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/DawnLIU35/EVAN.git.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can reward a multimodal model for answers that lean on language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than the image, which makes credit assignment ambiguous and calls for negative responses that stay plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut. `EVAN` selects highly image-dependent training examples with a scaled image information gain metric and a mixed-ranking strategy that preserves data diversity, then masks the most discriminative image patches to elicit plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the policy. During policy optimization those responses are added as bounded auxiliary negatives under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while keeping training stable. **Across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks, `EVAN` mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines.**

papers.title: IMRouter: Imbalance-aware Temporal Pattern Routing for LLM-based Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate time series forecasting (TSF) is essential for Web applications, such as traffic monitoring and online resource management. Recent advances in leveraging pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have shown promising performance in TSF. However, existing LLM-based TSF methods largely optimize the overall forecasting objective while overlooking temporal pattern imbalance (TPI), where different temporal patterns occur at highly unequal frequencies. Our empirical analysis reveals that TPI is prevalent across widely used TSF benchmarks, with substantially higher forecasting errors on less frequent patterns. To address this issue, we propose IMRouter (Imbalance-aware Temporal Pattern Routing), a novel framework that mitigates TPI-induced biases in both temporal representation learning and cross-modal alignment. Specifically, IMRouter introduces Pattern-Adaptive Temporal Representation Learning (PATR), which leverages gradient conflict and local gradient density to guide expert specialization. By penalizing incompatible expert assignments with density-aware weighting, PATR reduces the dominance of frequent optimization signals in router training. Furthermore, Routing-Guided Semantic Alignment (RGSA) transfers the pattern-specific knowledge learned by the router to cross-modal alignment through mutual information maximization, preserving distinctive temporal information across different patterns. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of IMRouter, particularly in improving forecasting performance on less frequent temporal patterns.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) based time series forecasting (TSF) methods optimize an overall forecasting objective and overlook temporal pattern imbalance (TPI), where different temporal patterns occur at highly unequal frequencies. An empirical analysis shows **TPI is prevalent across widely used TSF benchmarks, with substantially higher forecasting errors on less frequent patterns**. `IMRouter` counters this with Pattern-Adaptive Temporal Representation Learning (PATR), which uses gradient conflict and local gradient density to guide expert specialization and down-weight the dominant optimization signals in router training, and Routing-Guided Semantic Alignment (RGSA), which transfers the router's pattern-specific knowledge into cross-modal alignment through mutual information maximization. Experiments on benchmark datasets show gains concentrated on the less frequent temporal patterns.

papers.title: SocialArena: Evaluating Social Intelligence in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions.
