(2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest $132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially interactive settings such as counseling, companionship, and tutoring, yet existing evaluations of their social intelligence test isolated capabilities or single scenarios and rarely verify their own reliability. `SocialArena` defines social intelligence along three dimensions, role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning, and assesses all three at once through a role-playing dialogue paradigm in which characters think explicitly before they respond. A context-synthesis framework called `U-TRIMF` generates social scenarios with broad coverage so conclusions are not confined to particular settings. For reliable judgments the authors use a human-annotated arena protocol, **investing $132.4K to recruit and train annotators** who compare model responses and provide preference labels alongside natural-language critiques.

papers.title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.
papers.summary: Trajectory-level `GRPO` is the common way to train multi-step graphical user interface (GUI) agents, but rolling out full trajectories from the task root is wasteful: task-level rewards say little about which intermediate decisions need improvement, and already-mastered prefixes are re-executed before reaching the hard states. The proposed two-stage framework builds reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and picks informative pivot states by action disagreement, an uncertainty measure computed directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage one applies one-step reinforcement learning at those pivots to improve uncertain local decisions, and stage two progressively widens the policy's responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training as task progress grows, with recoverable checkpoints allowing repeated training from intermediate states without replaying what came before. **On `MobileGym` and `CUA-Gym-Hub`, the method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to vanilla `GRPO` while improving task performance.**

papers.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
papers.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
papers.summary: Frontier vision-language models navigate user interfaces (UIs) well but cost too much for everyday use, while smaller models trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning memorize static trajectories and cannot recover from errors. The proposed framework trains UI agents with online reinforcement learning directly on live iOS applications, splitting the agent into a planning agent and a UI grounding model, scoring intermediate steps and final task completion with an LLM-as-a-Judge, and optimizing with Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`) using step-level advantages plus a neighbor-conditioned value estimator called `GiGPPO` that stabilizes the critic by pooling reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent rollouts. An accompanying infrastructure orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices to make this training practical at scale. On `UINavBench`, `iOSWorld`, and `AndroidWorld` the online-trained agents beat SFT and terminal-only RL baselines, and **the 8B agents outperform `Gemini-3.5-Flash` and tie `Gemini-3.1-Pro` on real iOS applications** while generalizing nearly sevenfold better than SFT to unseen Android environments.
papers.highlight_summary:
Small vision-language models trained for UI navigation with supervised fine-tuning tend to memorize trajectories and cannot recover from errors, while frontier models that navigate well cost dollars per task. The authors train an 8B planner with online reinforcement learning directly on hundreds of live iOS devices, pairing it with a frozen grounding model and rewarding every step with an LLM judge in addition to a terminal task-completion reward.

- The planner is warm-started from `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` and trained with `PPO` using step-level advantages, where a `Gemini-3.5-Flash` judge scores each step as success, fail, or overcomplete and a `Gemini-3.1-Pro` judge scores the final outcome, with dense rewards discounted at γ=0.5 and the terminal reward left undiscounted to stop the agent from padding trajectories for step credit.
- `GiGPPO` stabilizes the critic by pairing each state with the closest screen by 64-bit perceptual hash among sibling rollouts and feeding that neighbor's return and Hamming distance into the value estimate, which on `UINavBench` lets training at steps 75 and 168 match standard `PPO` at steps 168 and 336, while dense rewards alone let `PPO` at one epoch match terminal-only `PPO` at two.
- On `UINavBench`, a benchmark of 116 tasks across 36 real iOS apps, `PPO` at step 336 reaches **32.4%** versus **16.7%** for the SFT baseline, tying `Gemini-3.1-Pro` and beating `Gemini-3.5-Flash` at 28.4% and `Qwen3.8-27B` at 19.6%, and on the out-of-distribution `AndroidWorld` it scores **32.8% versus 4.7%** for SFT, the paper's "nearly sevenfold" claim.
- The infrastructure runs **512 concurrent trajectories** on cloud-hosted iOS virtual machines, with episodes reset by snapshot rollback in roughly 10 seconds rather than by tearing down sessions.
- Gains on the synthetic-app `iOSWorld` benchmark are small and noisy, with the best RL checkpoint at **9.8%** against 39.5% for `Gemini-3.1-Pro` and one `PPO` checkpoint dropping below the SFT baseline, frontier planners still lead on `AndroidWorld` by roughly 25 to 28 points, and the comparison carries caveats since frontier models were evaluated only as planners inside the authors' own harness, two of three benchmarks use `Gemini-3.5-Flash` as the grounder, and the training signal itself depends on Gemini judges.

papers.title: DeCoRL: Decomposed Consistency Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Image Composition
papers.abstract: Multi-image composition (MICo) is a critical yet challenging capability for large-scale image editing models, where consistency degrades rapidly as the number of reference images increases. While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip models with basic MICo ability, it provides only implicit supervision on the composed image and often fails to learn reliable object-level correspondence across multiple references. We propose DeCoRL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that improves MICo consistency by decomposing holistic MICo consistency into object-level consistency. DeCoRL first establishes instruction-relevant object correspondences across reference images and localizes the corresponding regions in the generated image. It then uses a VLM-based reward model trained on single-object consistency annotations to produce fine-grained, object-wise feedback, which is aggregated into a multi-object consistency reward to guide RL post-training. We further introduce DeCo-Bench, a benchmark covering compositions from 2 to 6 reference images. Experiments on DeCo-Bench and the public MICo-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in MICo consistency.
papers.summary: Multi-image composition (MICo), in which an image editing model combines content from several reference images, loses consistency rapidly as the number of references grows, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) supervises only the composed image and fails to learn reliable object-level correspondence across references. `DeCoRL` is a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that decomposes holistic MICo consistency into object-level consistency: it first establishes instruction-relevant object correspondences across the references and localizes the matching regions in the generated image, then scores each object with a vision-language-model reward model trained on single-object consistency annotations and aggregates those scores into a multi-object consistency reward for RL post-training. The authors also introduce `DeCo-Bench`, which covers compositions from 2 to 6 reference images. **On `DeCo-Bench` and the public `MICo-Bench`, `DeCoRL` consistently improves composition consistency.**

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign
papers.abstract: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.
papers.summary: Engineering redesign adapts a prior solution to changed conditions such as material prices or new requirements, often relying on simulators too costly for numerical solvers that lack domain knowledge about the system. The study builds an integrated large language model (LLM) plus optimization approach and compares three ways of using the LLM (warm start, variable fixing, and `ReAct`) with four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search, and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case across four kinds of redesign scenarios. **The integrated approach matches the solvers' feasible-design discovery with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions.** The best integration strategy depends on how the design requirements changed, and larger LLMs help more as the LLM takes more control of the search.

papers.title: MemSteer: Turning User Histories into Supervision for Agent Memory Optimization
papers.abstract: An effective agent memory system should adapt to a user's history and task requirements. Human-annotated supervision can guide this adaptation by providing feedback for evaluating and improving memory designs. Yet suitable labels are rarely available for new user histories, and manually constructing QA pairs and supporting evidence is costly. We introduce MemSteer, which turns unlabeled user histories into question-answer (QA) supervision with supporting evidence for memory-design optimization. MemSteer constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer. The plan guides question generation, while source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery check the resulting annotations. To study the utility of this supervision, we develop MemSteer-Opt, which combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory store, retrieval, and context construction without updating model parameters. Experiments on ATM-Bench and RHELM show that this supervision is competitive with official-QA-guided optimization. Relative to Base-BM25, MemSteer-Opt improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points and RHELM accuracy by 4.1 and 6.6 points without and with external data, respectively. The supervision also benefits two existing optimizers on ATM-Bench, while new-user experiments demonstrate continued design optimization using supervision generated from the target histories.
papers.summary: An agent memory system should adapt to each user's history and task, but the labeled question-answer (QA) pairs and supporting evidence needed to evaluate and improve a memory design are rarely available for new users and costly to build by hand. `MemSteer` turns unlabeled user histories into QA supervision by constructing an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer, generating questions from that plan, and checking the results with source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery. A companion optimizer, `MemSteer-Opt`, combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory storage, retrieval, and context construction without updating model parameters. **On `ATM-Bench` and `RHELM` the generated supervision is competitive with optimization guided by the official QA sets**, with `MemSteer-Opt` improving `ATM-Bench` Question Score by 13.4 points over a `BM25` baseline and `RHELM` accuracy by 4.1 to 6.6 points, and the supervision also helps two existing optimizers and keeps improving designs for new users.

papers.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
papers.abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://worldflow-rbs.github.io/.
papers.summary: Video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-conditioned models are tied to particular robot configurations, and 3D motion predictors trained only on flow receive a weak learning signal about physics. `WorldFlow` is a generative world model that predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories jointly, encoding 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned to the video grid and denoising both modalities with one Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone under a rectified-flow objective. It is trained on 1.44 million object-level samples from simulated and real-world sources and evaluated on the new `WorldFlowBench`, 1,678 samples from 11 data sources including spatial reasoning tasks. `WorldFlow` achieves the lowest average and final displacement error among learning-based methods on all three evaluation sets, and **on the `SpatialCog` set it reaches an average displacement error of 0.060 m, a 54.2% reduction over the strongest external baseline**, with joint prediction cutting errors sharply relative to a flow-only variant.

papers.title: What Does "Now" Mean to Your Computer-Use Agent? Stale Screenshots, Page Loads, and Which Check to Run Before a Click
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents plan on a screenshot for several seconds and then click at a position on the screen; if the page has changed in the meantime, the click lands on an unintended element. Prior work treats the planning interval as the source of this risk. Measuring planned clicks on 31 public web pages, we find that the risk lies in page loading: 0.4% of clicks planned on fully loaded pages became stale within 30 seconds, against 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened. On these pages, waiting about one second for network activity to stop removes most of this risk, yet the wait rules of eight of ten widely used open-source agents leave more than 1% of clicks stale. Commercial pages keep loading for longer: in the HTTP Archive's public crawl, 15% of 65 desktop booking and buying home pages went 500 ms without network requests within 3 seconds of their HTML being parsed, against 63% of 3,028 .gov pages, and 52% shifted their layout within 6.5 seconds of a network-idle wait capped at 3 seconds, against 8% (61% against 26% among pages recorded in full). Where a check before the click is needed, as before irreversible actions and on pages that are still loading, a pixel comparison verifies the target's position as accurately as a frontier vision-language model at one eighth of the latency, and a 4B model matches the frontier model in verifying whether the previous action succeeded. We release a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a check pays, and three rules for agent developers: https://github.com/multimodal-ai-engineering/preflight-bench
papers.summary: Computer-use agents plan on a screenshot for several seconds and then click, so if the page changed in the meantime the click lands on the wrong element. Measuring planned clicks on 31 public web pages, the authors find the risk lies in page loading rather than planning time: **0.4% of clicks planned on fully loaded pages went stale within 30 seconds, against 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened**, and waiting about one second for network activity to stop removes most of the risk, yet the wait rules of eight of ten widely used open-source agents still leave more than 1% of clicks stale. Commercial booking and shopping pages in the HTTP Archive crawl keep loading much longer than .gov pages and frequently shift layout after a capped network-idle wait. Where a check before the click is warranted, such as before irreversible actions, a pixel comparison verifies the target position as accurately as a frontier vision-language model at one eighth of the latency, a 4B model matches the frontier model at verifying whether the previous action succeeded, and the release includes a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a check pays off, and three rules for agent developers.

papers.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning Achieves Uniform Discounted Regret
papers.abstract: Discounted regret measures the performance of an online learner by assigning exponentially decaying weights to past losses, reflecting the greater importance of recent losses in non-stationary online learning. While previous work obtains uniform discounted regret bounds over a continuous range of discount factors using a specialized meta-algorithm, its results are limited to convex functions. In this paper, we demonstrate that strongly adaptive regret bounds can directly imply uniform discounted regret guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and exp-concave loss functions. Our key observation is that discounted regret against a fixed comparator admits an exact decomposition into a convex combination of interval regrets. For convex functions, this reduction yields an $O(\sqrt{\log T/(1-\lambda)})$ discounted regret bound for all discount factors $\lambda\in(0,1)$, matching the previous rate over a broader range of discount factors. For strongly convex and exp-concave functions, we provide regret bounds of $O\left(\log T\left(1+\log\frac{1}{1-\lambda}\right)\right)$.
papers.summary: Discounted regret weights past losses by exponentially decaying factors to reflect the greater importance of recent losses in non-stationary online learning, but earlier uniform guarantees over a continuous range of discount factors relied on a specialized meta-algorithm and covered only convex losses. The key observation is that discounted regret against a fixed comparator decomposes exactly into a convex combination of interval regrets, so any strongly adaptive regret bound directly implies a uniform discounted regret guarantee for convex, strongly convex, and exp-concave losses. **For convex functions this gives an O(sqrt(log T/(1-λ))) discounted regret bound for every discount factor λ in (0,1)**, matching the previous rate over a broader range, and for strongly convex and exp-concave functions it gives bounds of O(log T (1 + log(1/(1-λ)))).

papers.title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models
papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) image generators are powerful in principle but inflexible in practice: training with a fixed raster-scan order hardcodes a single factorization of the image distribution into the model, leaving it unable to inpaint, outpaint, or edit at inference time. Existing solutions, including the modern discrete-diffusion family, train from scratch on a mixture of token orderings, paying roughly 3x the compute of standard raster-scan training; discrete diffusion further sacrifices compatibility with the AR inference ecosystem (KV caching, vLLM) by construction. We argue that this cost is unnecessary. A pretrained raster-scan AR model has already learned the joint distribution over image tokens; what it lacks is not knowledge but the ability to express that knowledge through non-sequential conditional pathways. We propose a recipe for adapting pretrained raster-scan models into any-order generators using two components: future-aware positional embeddings that resolve a target-position identifiability problem at negligible overhead, and an ordering curriculum that traces a stable optimization path from the pretrained solution to a good any-order basin. Applied to four base models across two architectures and two scales (LlamaGen-L/XL, RAR-L/XL), the recipe substantially outperforms MaskGIT on ImageNet inpainting (FID 6.21 vs. 10.44) and outpainting, is competitive with MAR-L, trades a 1.2-1.9 increase in class-conditional FID for this flexibility, and costs 13-33% additional compute beyond pretraining, while leaving the standard AR inference stack untouched. Inpainting, outpainting, and editing, our results suggest, need not be added to autoregressive image models. They can be unlocked from the ones that exist. Code is available at https://github.com/Ordered-AR/unlockedadaptation.
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) image generators trained in a fixed raster-scan order cannot inpaint, outpaint, or edit at inference time, and existing fixes such as discrete diffusion train from scratch on mixed token orderings at roughly three times the compute while giving up compatibility with KV caching and serving stacks like `vLLM`. The authors argue that a pretrained raster-scan model already knows the joint distribution over image tokens and only lacks non-sequential conditional pathways, so they adapt it with future-aware positional embeddings that resolve a target-position identifiability problem and an ordering curriculum that traces a stable optimization path from the pretrained solution to an any-order basin. Applied to `LlamaGen-L/XL` and `RAR-L/XL`, **the recipe reaches FID 6.21 on `ImageNet` inpainting versus 10.44 for `MaskGIT`**, is competitive with `MAR-L`, costs 13-33% extra compute beyond pretraining, and trades a 1.2-1.9 increase in class-conditional FID for the added flexibility while leaving the standard AR inference stack untouched.

papers.title: There Is No Free Lunch in RLVR: Every pass@1 Gain Has a pass@k Price
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) makes a language model solve more problems on the first try and fewer when given many tries: it raises pass@1 while the base model overtakes it at large sampling budget k. Is this a failure of RL to add reasoning, or a transient that more training removes? We settle the question with a theorem. The reversal is a price, and we compute its exact rate. Modeling RLVR as an exponential tilt of a base policy over strategies shared across prompts, we prove that under exclusive specialization every update that raises pass@1 strictly lowers the success of some prompt; a strictly positive price on prompts (Stiemke duality) is the exact condition, and being merely the best strategy on a prompt is provably not enough. When the loss reaches the hardest prompts, it forces a pass@k crossover, and the number of crossings is at most the sign variation of the shift in per-prompt success, a totally positive bound that is tight and that recovers the known single-crossover result as its order-preserving case. The crossover is not a bug to patch: a constrained update traces the exact pass@1 versus pass@k frontier, and removing the crossover entirely costs the entire pass@1 gain. The same tilt identity yields entropy collapse and the entropy-performance law with an identifiable exponent, unifying two literatures under one mechanism. Reinforcement cannot widen the reasoning frontier; it can only move along it, at a price we make measurable by a diagnostic that reads the bound, the order-preserving test, and the price from any evaluation log. There is no free lunch, only a price.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) raises a language model's pass@1 while the base model overtakes it at large sampling budgets k, and the question is whether this reversal reflects a failure to add reasoning or a transient that more training removes. Modeling RLVR as an exponential tilt of the base policy over strategies shared across prompts, the authors prove that under exclusive specialization **every update that raises pass@1 strictly lowers success on some prompt**, with a strictly positive price on prompts via Stiemke duality as the exact condition, and that once the loss reaches the hardest prompts a pass@k crossover is forced, with the number of crossings bounded by the sign variation of the per-prompt success shift. A constrained update traces the exact pass@1 versus pass@k frontier, and removing the crossover entirely costs the whole pass@1 gain. The same tilt identity also yields entropy collapse and an entropy-performance law with an identifiable exponent, and the paper offers a diagnostic that reads the bound, the order-preserving test, and the price from any evaluation log.

papers.title: Multi-Solution Inverse Design of Pixelated Patch Antennas Using an Autoregressive Transformer
papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based inverse design has emerged as a promising framework for pixelated patch antenna synthesis by enabling broader exploration of discrete geometry spaces and reducing design time compared with conventional template-based methods. Existing methods, including surrogate-assisted metaheuristic optimization, tandem inverse networks, and diffusion models, have advanced the field but still face practical limitations. Metaheuristic methods such as binary particle swarm optimization (BPSO) are sensitive to initialization and search hyperparameters and are often time-consuming, tandem networks have difficulty capturing the one-to-many nature of inverse antenna design, and diffusion models may require excessive complexity and data for moderate-scale binary layout synthesis. In this paper, an autoregressive (AR) transformer is presented for the inverse design of 10 x 10 pixelated patch antennas. Its sequential discrete generation process enables the synthesis of multiple feasible structures for a given target response. The pretrained model is further fine-tuned for dual-band design using step-shaped target responses with sharp spectral transitions, allowing intuitive band specification without manually constructing detailed S11 curves. Compared with BPSO, our proposed method generates valid and diverse antenna candidates more efficiently. Fabricated and measured examples confirm that distinct pixelated layouts can realize the desired antenna responses, thereby demonstrating the multi-solution capability of the proposed framework.
papers.summary: Inverse design of pixelated patch antennas has used surrogate-assisted metaheuristics, tandem inverse networks, and diffusion models, but binary particle swarm optimization (`BPSO`) is sensitive to initialization and slow, tandem networks struggle with the one-to-many nature of the problem, and diffusion models demand more complexity and data than moderate-scale binary layouts justify. An autoregressive (AR) transformer generates 10 x 10 pixelated layouts token by token, so a single target response can yield multiple feasible structures. The pretrained model is fine-tuned for dual-band design using step-shaped target responses with sharp spectral transitions, letting a designer specify bands without hand-constructing detailed S11 curves. **Compared with `BPSO`, the method generates valid and diverse antenna candidates more efficiently**, and fabricated, measured examples confirm that distinct layouts realize the desired responses.

papers.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
papers.abstract: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations.
papers.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. The authors prove a Platonic Representation Theorem: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to a rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene, which they call good views, and they show next-token prediction is a JEPA with bad views, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Experiments from 145k captions up to the texts of 940M web images yield a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise, and **a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with the `DINOv2` and `CLIP` image encoders better than every language model evaluated up to 72B parameters**, with good views needing 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction to reach the same alignment. A single rotation turns the separately trained encoders into an image captioner scoring CIDEr .838 on `COCO`, and on a pair-free benchmark the text JEPA reaches 64% top-5 accuracy on `ImageNet-100` against at most 56% for language models up to 8B.

papers.title: Learning to Bound: Monotonic, Calibrated Neural Upper Bounds for MPE Inference
papers.abstract: Probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) compactly encode structured joint distributions, but Most Probable Explanation (MPE), which finds the highest-probability assignment to unobserved variables, remains computationally intractable in large, densely structured models. Anytime systematic search, such as branch-and-bound (B&B), is a popular approach, but its efficiency depends on tight admissible upper bounds that are often prohibitively expensive to compute using classical methods like Mini-Bucket Elimination (MBE). We introduce Learning to Bound (L2B), a data-driven framework that amortizes bound computation cost by training a neural predictor. L2B targets two key properties required for effective search bounds: admissibility, which is achieved via statistical calibration techniques, and progressive tightening as evidence accumulates, which is enforced through structural architectural constraints that ensure monotonicity by construction. Across challenging benchmarks, L2B delivers tighter, monotonic bounds at orders-of-magnitude lower cost on every PGM family, and yields measurable improvements when integrated with branch-and-bound on high-treewidth instances.
papers.summary: Most Probable Explanation (MPE) inference in probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) finds the highest-probability assignment to unobserved variables, and branch-and-bound search for it depends on tight admissible upper bounds that classical methods like Mini-Bucket Elimination (`MBE`) compute at prohibitive cost. `L2B` (Learning to Bound) trains a neural predictor to amortize that cost, achieving admissibility through statistical calibration and guaranteeing that bounds tighten as evidence accumulates through architectural constraints that make the predictor monotonic by construction. **Across benchmark PGM families, `L2B` delivers tighter, monotonic bounds at orders-of-magnitude lower cost**, and integrating it into branch-and-bound gives measurable improvements on high-treewidth instances.

papers.title: Unlimited OCR Works 2
papers.abstract: Unlimited OCR ushers the era of long-horizon parsing, substantially mitigating the growth of working memory as document lengthens. However, as document length scales to hundreds of pages, the visual context grows substantially, sharply increasing the computational cost of each decoding step and limiting the scalability of ultra-long document parsing. Inspired by human book transcription via localized focus without re-scanning preceding pages, we introduce Unlimited OCR 2, a document parsing model that looks only at what it transcribes. Building on Unlimited OCR, we upgrade all the decoder attention modules to Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), bounding active reference tokens to a fixed capacity and thus sustaining constant computational costs across arbitrarily long documents. By combining SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm, Unlimited OCR 2 enables document parsing over virtually unlimited lengths without prohibitive memory overhead. At the hundred-page scale, Unlimited OCR 2 achieves 7.0$\times$ and 5.6$\times$ per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA, respectively. Furthermore, it delivers state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on both MPDocBench and MarathonDocBench, our newly proposed benchmark targeting hundred-page document parsing. Ultimately, the capacity for uninterrupted, one-shot document parsing signifies a fundamental paradigm shift into the OCR 3.0 era.
papers.summary: `Unlimited OCR` made long-horizon document parsing feasible by limiting working-memory growth, but at hundreds of pages the visual context still grows enough to make each decoding step expensive. `Unlimited OCR 2` replaces every decoder attention module with Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), which caps the active reference tokens at a fixed capacity so per-step compute stays constant regardless of document length, and pairs it with the Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm to parse arbitrarily long documents in a single pass. **At the hundred-page scale it achieves 7.0x and 5.6x per-step speedups over full attention and R-SWA**, and it reports state-of-the-art end-to-end results on `MPDocBench` and on `MarathonDocBench`, a new benchmark for hundred-page document parsing.

papers.title: TaxoMFM: A Taxonomy-Aware Foundation Model for the Human Gut Microbiome
papers.abstract: Existing gut microbiome foundation models typically use flat taxon representations, limiting their ability to exploit known taxonomic hierarchies. We introduce TaxoMFM, a microbiome foundation model that integrates taxonomic structure into self-supervised learning. TaxoMFM jointly learns abundance patterns across taxonomic ranks and relative proportions within groups through taxonomy-aware encoding and hierarchical compositional reconstruction. We further construct TaxoGut-HPP, comprising 100,806 gut microbiome profiles from 231 source cohorts and covering 40 classification and 8 regression tasks. TaxoMFM achieves competitive performance across disease, gut health, host trait, and liver ultrasound phenotype prediction. In cross-cohort zero-shot transfer, where target cohorts are excluded from both pretraining and downstream adaptation, TaxoMFM achieves AUROCs of 0.838, 0.736, and 0.722 for colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease, respectively. Further analyses show that TaxoMFM recovers community changes across taxonomic scales, while preserving community information and producing consistent representations under database updates and species-vocabulary shifts. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TaxoMFM-F16D/.
papers.summary: Gut microbiome foundation models usually treat taxa as a flat vocabulary and cannot exploit known taxonomic hierarchies. `TaxoMFM` builds taxonomic structure into self-supervised pretraining, jointly learning abundance patterns across taxonomic ranks and relative proportions within groups through taxonomy-aware encoding and hierarchical compositional reconstruction. The authors also assemble `TaxoGut-HPP`, 100,806 gut microbiome profiles from 231 source cohorts covering 40 classification and 8 regression tasks, on which the model is competitive for disease, gut health, host trait, and liver ultrasound phenotype prediction. **In cross-cohort zero-shot transfer it reaches AUROCs of 0.838 for colorectal cancer, 0.736 for type 2 diabetes, and 0.722 for inflammatory bowel disease**, and its representations stay consistent under database updates and species-vocabulary shifts.

papers.title: BEVLight: Generalizable Traffic Signal Control from UAV Bird's-Eye Views
papers.abstract: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) has achieved promising performance, but most methods rely on structured traffic states that must be estimated from sensor observations in real deployments. Visual TSC learns signal decisions directly from images, yet existing methods depend on fixed roadside cameras and remain tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains. UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye-view (BEV) observations that jointly capture intersection topology and traffic dynamics, making them a promising sensing platform for visual TSC. We present BEVLight, a generalizable TSC framework that directly maps BEV observations to signal actions. BEVLight grounds visual features onto individual lanes and composes them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, allowing a shared policy to score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. To train the policy, we develop a web-based virtual teleoperation platform and collect over 5K human control decisions together with their underlying traffic states. Simulator-provided traffic states first supervise lane- and movement-level representations, after which human phase selections and rankings supervise the phase scorer. Re-rendering the recorded trajectories under diverse appearances preserves both forms of supervision and encourages robustness to visual changes. Closed-loop experiments demonstrate zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections: BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7--9\% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or outperforms structured-state RL controllers that receive ground-truth traffic states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study further shows that BEVLight transfers to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.
papers.summary: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) typically consumes structured traffic states that real deployments must estimate from sensors, and existing visual TSC methods rely on fixed roadside cameras tied to specific intersections and visual domains. `BEVLight` maps bird's-eye-view (BEV) images from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) directly to signal actions by grounding visual features onto individual lanes and composing them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, so one shared policy can score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. Training draws on over 5K human control decisions collected through a web-based teleoperation platform, with simulator states supervising lane and movement representations, human phase selections supervising the phase scorer, and re-rendering under varied appearances for visual robustness. **In closed-loop zero-shot tests it cuts average waiting time by 7-9% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or beats structured-state RL controllers given ground-truth states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios**, and an offline study shows transfer to real UAV observations without adaptation.

papers.title: Satisficing Regret Minimization in Bandits with Knapsacks
papers.abstract: We study satisficing regret minimization in bandits with knapsacks (BwK), where a learner sequentially selects randomized policies, i.e., distributions over arms, to obtain mean rewards above a satisficing threshold as frequently as possible while respecting finite resource budgets. The performance is measured by satisficing regret, the cumulative deficits of the selected policies' mean rewards below this threshold. Resource constraints introduce two difficulties: an algorithm can incur linear satisficing regret even with small standard regret as deficits to the threshold cannot be compensated, and random consumption can cause early resource depletion even when policies are feasible in expectation. To address these challenges, we propose SELECTwK, a general algorithmic template that uses a BwK learning oracle algorithm with sub-linear expected (standard) regret upper bound to search for and test candidate satisficing policies (i.e., policies whose mean rewards exceed satisficing threshold and whose expected resource consumption is feasible over the time horizon). Our regret analysis, supported by an LP-duality argument, establishes that SELECTwK attains constant expected satisficing regret when a satisficing policy exists. We further introduce a stronger regret condition that bounds the expected sum of positive reward deficits to the optimal one at each time step, under which SELECTwK achieves a sharper constant bound together with a sub-linear bound in the time horizon. As a complement, SELECTwK still preserves the oracle's sub-linear expected standard regret bound if the satisficing threshold is unattainable. Finally, we establish the oracle conditions and corresponding satisficing regret bound for existing finite-armed BwK and dynamic pricing algorithms, and conduct numerical experiments on dynamic pricing with limited inventory to demonstrate the empirical performance of SELECTwK.
papers.summary: Satisficing regret minimization in bandits with knapsacks (BwK) asks a learner to choose distributions over arms whose mean rewards clear a threshold as often as possible under finite resource budgets, measuring performance by the cumulative shortfall below that threshold. Resource constraints make this hard because small standard regret can still mean linear satisficing regret, since shortfalls cannot be compensated, and random consumption can deplete resources early even for policies that are feasible in expectation. `SELECTwK` is a general template that uses any BwK oracle with sub-linear expected standard regret to search for and test candidate satisficing policies, and an LP-duality analysis shows **it attains constant expected satisficing regret whenever a satisficing policy exists**, with a sharper bound under a stronger per-step condition and the oracle's sub-linear standard regret preserved when the threshold is unattainable. The authors verify the oracle conditions for existing finite-armed BwK and dynamic pricing algorithms and run experiments on dynamic pricing with limited inventory.

papers.title: Class-aware Latent Attention Replay (CLAR): Class Incremental Hazard Diagnosis for Resilient AI in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems provide critical computation services in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet (MII), and their resilience depends on timely diagnosis of hazards across the data, AI pipeline, and cyber-physical layers. During operation, new hazard types keep emerging with only a few samples each, hazards co-occur, and the diagnosis model runs on memory-constrained computation nodes. Replay-based class-incremental learning (CIL) can learn new hazard classes while revisiting a small memory of past samples, but existing methods assume single-label, balanced streams, store high-dimensional raw samples, and select them independently of the classifier. We propose Class-aware Latent Attention Replay (CLAR), which combines a dual buffer that stores mostly compact latent representations with a few raw samples, an Attention Leverage Score (ALS) that upper-bounds the classifier logit and guides class-balanced reservoir sampling, and an exponential-moving-average teacher that slows latent-space drift. For an idealized buffer model, we prove that the buffer is class-balanced and follows an ALS-weighted class distribution, and that below a critical per-class capacity, ALS-guided replay has a lower replay-gradient error than class-balanced uniform replay. In the case study, On hazard diagnosis data from an MII testbed, CLAR achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 score among the evaluated replay methods with the same buffer size
papers.summary: Hazard diagnosis models in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet (MII) must keep learning new hazard types that arrive with only a few samples each, often co-occur, and run on memory-constrained nodes, while existing replay-based class-incremental learning (CIL) methods assume single-label balanced streams and store raw samples chosen independently of the classifier. `CLAR` pairs a dual buffer holding mostly compact latent representations with a few raw samples, an Attention Leverage Score that upper-bounds the classifier logit and guides class-balanced reservoir sampling, and an exponential-moving-average teacher that slows latent-space drift. Under an idealized buffer model the authors prove the buffer stays class-balanced and that, below a critical per-class capacity, score-guided replay has lower replay-gradient error than uniform class-balanced replay. **On hazard data from an MII testbed, `CLAR` achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 among the compared replay methods at equal buffer size.**

papers.title: Telling Is Not Seeing: Textual Personas Rarely Make Vision-Language Models Answer Like the People They Describe
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly prompted with personas, such as "You have low vision", to stand in for people in user studies. We ask whether a persona makes a model see like the person it describes. We compare persona answers with measured people with low vision, color blindness or hearing loss, and with simple rules that use only the facts the persona states. The persona never beats these rules, and it erases the real differences between groups and individuals. Describing blur leaves recognition unchanged in all 14 models we test, while blurring the photo lowers it as it does for people. Inside open models, the description changes neither the image information nor the answer probabilities. Yet the models know the effects they fail to show: they can estimate how blur and illusions affect people. Telling is not seeing: a persona makes a model say what it knows about people, not see what they see.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly given textual personas, such as a user with low vision, to stand in for real participants in user studies, so this study compares persona answers against measured responses from people with low vision, color blindness, or hearing loss, and against simple rules that use only the facts the persona states. **The persona never beats the simple rules, and it erases the real differences between groups and individuals.** Describing blur leaves recognition unchanged in all 14 models tested, while actually blurring the photo lowers it as it does for people, and inside open models the description changes neither the image information nor the answer probabilities. The models can nonetheless estimate how blur and illusions affect people, so a persona makes a model say what it knows about people rather than see what they see.

papers.title: Does the Citation Matter? Quality, Grounding, and Physician-Rubric Accuracy of Google's AI Overviews for Medical Information
papers.abstract: Google's AI Overviews (AIOs) are the first result users encounter when searching the web, shifting the work of selecting and evaluating sources from the user to Gemini. This may be especially consequential for health information, given that Google's traditional algorithm was designed to prioritize quality sources, and inaccurate information carries health risks. We evaluated 3,611 benchmark health questions, comparing each AIO against that question's top five traditional results on source selection and quality. We also evaluated the AIOs' statement grounding in their cited sources and how accurate AIOs were against physician-written rubrics. Overviews appeared for 96.4% of questions but drew on substantially different evidence than traditional search: only 44.4% of the top five results were cited by the corresponding AIO, which instead overrepresented commercial health publishers (e.g., WebMD, Healthline) at the expense of academic and government sources (e.g., Cleveland Clinic, National Health Service). AIO-cited pages scored lower than traditional results on four of six well-established credibility criteria. The grounding of AIO statements to their sources was poor: after correcting for classifier error, an estimated 56.7% of cited statements were supported by their cited page, and a further 20.8% of all statements were factual claims with no citation at all. When AIOs were graded against physicians' rubrics, they earned 38.2% of all available points (e.g., accuracy 54.2%, completeness 21.6%), and among the subset of AIOs whose physician rubric anticipated a specific inaccurate or potentially harmful claim, 22.2% of AIOs contained the harmful content. Notably, the accuracy of AIOs was unrelated to the grounding of their statements. We recommend AIO literacy interventions for users and holding AIOs at least to Google's own health-ranking standards.
papers.summary: Google's AI Overviews (AIOs) now sit above traditional search results and shift the work of choosing and vetting sources to `Gemini`, which matters for health queries where inaccurate information carries real risk. Across 3,611 benchmark health questions, the study compares each overview with the question's top five traditional results on source selection and credibility, measures how well overview statements are grounded in the pages they cite, and grades the overviews against physician-written rubrics. Overviews cited fewer than half of the top traditional results, leaned on commercial health publishers over academic and government sources, and scored lower on four of six credibility criteria, and **after correcting for classifier error only an estimated 56.7% of cited statements were supported by their cited page, with a further 20.8% of statements being uncited factual claims.** Against physician rubrics the overviews earned 38.2% of available points, 22.2% of overviews contained a harmful claim the rubric had anticipated, and accuracy turned out to be unrelated to how well statements were grounded.

papers.title: RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories
papers.abstract: Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples.
papers.summary: Frontier language models have contributed to research mathematics, yet they still fail at reasoning tasks governed by explicit rules, and retrograde chess, where a solver must reconstruct legal game histories and separate possible events from forced ones, offers a clean test of this. `RetroChessBench` is a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with reference solutions, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. **In two trials per task, `GPT 6 Astra High` fails to produce the required final answer in 22 of 24 attempts without tools and 18 of 24 with code execution**, with mean terminal rewards of 14.75% and 27.19%, and failed responses tend to reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. The authors hypothesize that online puzzle archives rarely include detailed derivations, so web-derived training data gives little exposure to the needed reasoning, and argue that claims of general intelligence need evidence of transfer to areas with few worked examples.

papers.title: MulClip: A table-free activation function with monotonic and folding regimes for reservoir computing on microcontrollers
papers.abstract: This letter proposes MulClip, a lightweight activation function for reservoir computing (RC) on microcontrollers (MCUs). In a ring reservoir, a representative sparse RC topology, multiply-accumulate operations are few, and evaluating tanh accounted for 75% of the state-update time on a Cortex-M4. MulClip introduces curvature into the response using only comparison, absolute value, multiplication, and subtraction, and places its clipping threshold not at the extremum but at the point where the response returns to zero after passing the extremum. As a result, a single function has both a monotonic regime and a nonmonotonic folding regime that increases the expressiveness of a single unit. Which regime is used is determined by the usual hyperparameter search, e.g., over the input scale, so no task-specific threshold tuning is required. The state-update time measured on hardware was 0.34 times that of tanh and shorter than that of any of the 11 evaluated tanh approximations. In PC-based evaluation, third-order MulClip achieved a 22% lower NMSE than tanh on NARMA-20, where the pre-activations remained in the monotonic regime, and on 8-bit parity it raised the accuracy from 0.76-0.78 for the monotonic-clip variant without folding to 0.97-0.98. For these two tasks, on-device inference yielded nearly the same values as on the PC.
papers.summary: Reservoir computing (RC) on microcontrollers (MCUs) is dominated not by multiply-accumulate work but by the activation function: in a sparse ring reservoir, evaluating tanh took 75% of the state-update time on a Cortex-M4. `MulClip` builds curvature from only comparison, absolute value, multiplication, and subtraction, and places its clipping threshold past the extremum where the response returns to zero, so a single unit has both a monotonic regime and a nonmonotonic folding regime, with the regime chosen implicitly by the usual hyperparameter search over input scale. **On hardware the state update ran in 0.34 times the tanh time, faster than all 11 tanh approximations evaluated.** Third-order `MulClip` cut normalized mean squared error by 22% versus tanh on `NARMA-20` and lifted 8-bit parity accuracy from roughly 0.77 to 0.97 relative to a clip variant without folding, with on-device results matching the PC.

papers.title: CoToan: Executable Rules and a Representation Contract for Reproducible Game AI Evaluation
papers.abstract: Game AI results are comparable only when different implementations expose the same decision problem. Yet seemingly minor representation choices can silently change that problem by altering action probabilities or collapsing states with different outcomes. We study this issue through CoToan, an executable specification and representation contract for Vietnamese Mathematical Chess connecting the Game Description Language (GDL) with OpenSpiel. The game provides a useful case because a single capture may have multiple arithmetic justifications, while outcomes can depend on scoring rules and a finite playing horizon. CoToan therefore represents actions by their state transitions rather than by arithmetic witnesses, and treats time and victory configuration as part of task identity. Cross-representation tests show agreement in legal actions, successor states, and terminal outcomes across hundreds of sampled and constructed positions, complemented by exhaustive checks of all 32 operator masks and 512 opposing-material subsets. Controlled diagnostics further show that uniform witness-level sampling alters endpoint-action probabilities, while omitting remaining time or victory settings can merge states with different terminal behavior. These results show that action semantics, time, and victory configuration are not merely implementation details. They are part of the experimental task itself and must be represented explicitly for reproducible game AI.
papers.summary: Game AI results are only comparable when different implementations expose the same decision problem, yet small representation choices can silently change that problem by altering action probabilities or merging states with different outcomes. `CoToan` is an executable specification and representation contract for Vietnamese Mathematical Chess that connects the Game Description Language (GDL) with `OpenSpiel`, representing actions by their state transitions rather than by the arithmetic justifications of a capture, and treating remaining time and victory configuration as part of task identity. Cross-representation tests show agreement in legal actions, successor states, and terminal outcomes across hundreds of positions, plus exhaustive checks of all 32 operator masks and 512 opposing-material subsets. **Controlled diagnostics show that uniform sampling at the witness level changes endpoint-action probabilities, and that omitting remaining time or victory settings merges states with different terminal behavior**, so these choices are part of the experimental task rather than implementation details.

papers.title: Semantic Mismapping in Generalized Category Discovery: Evaluation and Mitigation
papers.abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to perform old-category recognition and novel-category discovery in the same unlabeled set. Early methods address both objectives through clustering and evaluate the exchangeable predicted indices with global Hungarian (GH) matching. Recent methods adopt trainable parametric heads, using supervision for old-category recognition and discovery-oriented objectives for new categories. In this way, the output space becomes partially exchangeable: old indices are semantically anchored, while new indices remain exchangeable. However, these methods still apply global matching, which can reassign anchored old indices to other categories and hide some prediction errors. Empirically, we are surprised to observe that this reassignment can induce an overestimation of new-category accuracy by up to 25.63 points. We term this phenomenon semantic mismapping and further derive a permutation-cycle condition that characterizes when semantic mismapping can increase the global matching score. To fix this issue, we propose Semantics-Preserving Evaluation (SPE), which preserves the supervised semantics of old indices and restricts Hungarian matching to the new region. Furthermore, we propose Mismapping-Mitigating Optimization (MMO) to alleviate the prediction errors that can give rise to semantic mismapping, combining a region-balance loss (RBL) for old/new routing with a novel-diversity loss (NDL) that encourages orthogonality among new prototypes. Theoretically, we show that minimizing the two losses can tighten an upper bound on spurious accuracy gains from semantic mismapping, with controllable residual terms. Empirical results under both GH and SPE demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.
papers.summary: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) asks a model to recognize old categories and discover new ones within the same unlabeled set, and recent parametric methods anchor old-class output indices to supervised semantics while leaving new indices exchangeable. Evaluating such methods with global Hungarian matching can reassign anchored old indices to other categories and hide prediction errors, a phenomenon the authors call semantic mismapping, and **they find it can inflate reported new-category accuracy by up to 25.63 points.** They derive a permutation-cycle condition for when mismapping raises the matching score, propose Semantics-Preserving Evaluation (`SPE`) that fixes old indices and restricts Hungarian matching to the new region, and add Mismapping-Mitigating Optimization (`MMO`), which combines a region-balance loss for old/new routing with a novel-diversity loss encouraging orthogonal new prototypes. The two losses provably tighten an upper bound on spurious accuracy gains, and results under both evaluation protocols support the method.

papers.title: Before the Next Rollout: Diagnosing Skill Utility Shifts from Policy Updates
papers.abstract: Skill-evolution methods typically analyze execution trajectories to guide agent skill refinement. However, policy updates can change the behavioral effects and marginal utility of an unchanged skill. Attribution based on earlier trajectories may therefore no longer reflect the skill's contribution under the updated policy. Moreover, trajectory failures can arise from multiple factors, making individual skill contributions difficult to isolate. We evaluate whether policy-update signals contain predictive information about changes in skill marginal utility. At fixed contexts from pre-update training rollouts, we measure how policy updates change the contrast in token preferences between skill and control conditions. Combining these interaction shifts with advantage estimates yields reward-directed readouts for diagnosing utility changes. The readouts reuse existing training rollouts and require only forward passes for single-step action scoring, without additional post-update rollout evaluation. Our experiments show that policy updates can alter skill marginal utility and that policy-update readouts carry diagnostic information for identifying skills with declining utility. Integrating readout-guided prioritization into skill evolution improves downstream performance while reducing policy and editor token consumption.
papers.summary: Methods that evolve an agent's skill library usually attribute credit from execution trajectories, but once the underlying policy is updated an unchanged skill can have a different behavioral effect and marginal utility, so attributions from earlier rollouts may no longer hold, and multiple failure causes make a single skill's contribution hard to isolate. The authors test whether policy-update signals predict changes in skill utility: at fixed contexts drawn from pre-update rollouts, they measure how the update shifts the contrast in token preferences between skill and control conditions, and combine these interaction shifts with advantage estimates into reward-directed readouts. The readouts reuse existing training rollouts and need only forward passes for single-step action scoring, with no post-update rollout evaluation. **Experiments show policy updates do alter skill marginal utility, the readouts identify skills with declining utility, and prioritizing skill evolution by them improves downstream performance while cutting policy and editor token consumption.**

papers.title: More Is Better? Exploring Latent Correspondence in Federated Hypergraph Learning
papers.abstract: Federated hypergraph learning with latent cross-client hyperedge correspondence poses fundamental identifiability and computational challenges, as the same local release can correspond to multiple global hypergraph structures. We characterize the tractability of recovering these latent correspondences, showing tractable pairwise assignment but generally intractable multi-client hyperedge matching. Building on this characterization, we derive a cross-entropy decomposition that reveals when local prediction can outperform predictors fitted with additional cross-client information. Motivated by this principle, we introduce Federated Adaptive Spectral Training with Representation Alignment (FedASTRA), which learns correspondence-invariant diffusion representations through adaptive heat diffusion and masked latent prediction while communicating model parameters only. We establish its asymptotic optimality with respect to the permitted local information and prove global population-risk convergence under explicit conditions on recovery, representation, and update alignment. Experiments on eight real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedASTRA against identifier-free federated graph and hypergraph methods. On ogbn-papers100M, FedASTRA reaches the performance-communication Pareto frontier, achieving 50.07 Accuracy and 29.73 Macro-F1 while communicating only 59.60 MiB per round.
papers.summary: In federated hypergraph learning, hyperedges that span clients are only latently matched, so the same local data release can correspond to many global hypergraph structures, raising identifiability and computational problems. The authors show that pairwise correspondence assignment is tractable while general multi-client hyperedge matching is intractable, and derive a cross-entropy decomposition that characterizes when purely local prediction can beat predictors fitted with additional cross-client information. Building on this, Federated Adaptive Spectral Training with Representation Alignment (`FedASTRA`) learns correspondence-invariant diffusion representations through adaptive heat diffusion and masked latent prediction while communicating only model parameters, with proofs of asymptotic optimality relative to the permitted local information and of global population-risk convergence. **On eight real-world datasets it outperforms identifier-free federated graph and hypergraph baselines, and on `ogbn-papers100M` it sits on the performance-communication Pareto frontier at 59.60 MiB per round.**

papers.title: Cord: Confidence-Anchored Order Residual Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: The decoding order of masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) can substantially affect generation quality, yet common decoders typically apply the same reveal rule throughout generation. Confidence provides a strong default, but it measures how decisively a position can be predicted now, not how useful revealing that position will be for subsequent decoding. We propose Cord, a lightweight prompt-conditioned policy that retains confidence decoding as a stable reference and learns when and how to depart from it through geometric residuals over generation direction, proximity to revealed context, and two-sided infilling. The residuals adapt to both the prompt and the evolving partial response. Rather than sampling a new policy action at every decoding step, Cord samples a single low-dimensional coefficient matrix per rollout, which induces an entire state-dependent reveal trajectory. This yields a contextual-bandit formulation trained directly from sequence-level rewards, without step-level credit assignment or backbone updates. Across three dLLMs and five reasoning, code, and constraint-satisfaction benchmarks, Cord improves average task success from 32.0% under confidence decoding to 48.2%, and further improves over the best per-domain fixed residual. Behavioral audits show that the learned residuals induce substantial, task-dependent changes in reveal locality and two-sided infilling. Cord adds only $0.53$M trainable parameters, requires no additional backbone forward passes, and incurs only 5.39% inference latency overhead.
papers.summary: The order in which a masked diffusion language model (dLLM) reveals tokens strongly affects output quality, but standard decoders apply one fixed reveal rule, usually confidence, which measures how decisively a position can be predicted now rather than how useful revealing it will be later. `Cord` keeps confidence decoding as a stable reference and learns a lightweight prompt-conditioned policy for when and how to depart from it, through geometric residuals over generation direction, proximity to already revealed context, and two-sided infilling. Instead of acting at every step, it samples a single low-dimensional coefficient matrix per rollout that induces a whole state-dependent reveal trajectory, which turns training into a contextual bandit over sequence-level rewards with no step-level credit assignment or backbone updates. **Across three dLLMs and five reasoning, code, and constraint-satisfaction benchmarks, average task success rises from 32.0% under confidence decoding to 48.2%**, with only 0.53M trainable parameters, no extra backbone forward passes, and 5.39% latency overhead.

papers.title: What Makes Medical Examination Items Difficult? Using Large Language Models to Explore Patterns Associated With Empirical Item Difficulty
papers.abstract: Research on medical item difficulty has largely focused on prediction rather than on identifying interpretable patterns associated with empirical difficulty. This study used empirical difficulty labels to guide large language models (LLMs) in inducing difficulty rubrics and examined how rubric guidance affected LLM difficulty judgments. Using training items and their empirical difficulty estimates from the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) and the Physician Assistant National Certifying Examination (PANCE), Claude Opus 5 induced separate rubrics for absolute and pairwise difficulty judgment. None of the induced rubrics treated surface features, such as stem length, option count, or images, as major sources of difficulty. Several patterns emerged across both examinations, including cue convergence, misleading cues, and option competition, although their specific forms differed. Retrieval of knowledge that could not be derived from the stem was particularly prominent in the PANCE rubrics, whereas the USMLE rubrics placed greater emphasis on integrating multiple clinical cues. We compared commercial and open-weight LLMs on held-out items under unguided and rubric-guided conditions. Rubric guidance changed how models used the difficulty scale but did not consistently improve performance. In absolute judgments, guidance encouraged broader use of the scale and generally improved coarse-grained agreement, without consistently improving rank ordering. In pairwise comparisons, its effects varied across models and examinations, and judgments became more sensitive to presentation order. These findings suggest that the value of label-guided rubric induction may lie more in generating interpretable, testable hypotheses from empirical difficulty data than in reliably improving difficulty judgments.
papers.summary: Work on the difficulty of medical exam items has mostly aimed at prediction rather than at interpretable patterns behind empirical difficulty. Using items and empirical difficulty estimates from the `USMLE` and `PANCE` licensing exams, `Claude Opus 5` was prompted to induce rubrics for absolute and pairwise difficulty judgments, and commercial and open-weight LLMs were then compared on held-out items with and without rubric guidance. **None of the induced rubrics treated surface features such as stem length, option count, or images as major sources of difficulty**, instead surfacing patterns like cue convergence, misleading cues, option competition, and, especially for `PANCE`, recall of knowledge not derivable from the stem. Rubric guidance changed how models used the difficulty scale and generally improved coarse-grained agreement for absolute judgments, but it did not consistently improve rank ordering and made pairwise judgments more sensitive to presentation order, suggesting its main value lies in generating testable hypotheses rather than better difficulty judgments.

papers.title: AgentDecept: Benchmarking Deceptive Behavior in Tool-Using LLM Agents under Pressure
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly carry out multi-turn tasks across everyday applications, yet users often see only the agent's report rather than the observations, API calls, and state changes behind it.
