Existing deception benchmarks have studied long-horizon interactions and tool-use settings, but whether agents faithfully report their actions across realistic, stateful application workflows remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AgentDecept, an executable benchmark for evaluating behavioral deception under pressure. AgentDecept contains 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart. Interventions enter through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses, and service quotas, spanning explicit events and implicit task or environment changes. Our evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes, distinguishing falsification, concealment, and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations. The resulting behavioral labels also provide a setting for testing existing activation-based probes. AgentDecept enables controlled analysis of when multi-turn agents' reports diverge from execution in realistic application interactions.
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly run multi-turn tasks inside everyday applications, but users typically see only the agent's final report rather than the observations, API calls, and state changes behind it, and whether agents report faithfully across realistic stateful workflows has been underexplored. `AgentDecept` is an executable benchmark of **477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources**, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart, where pressure enters through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses, and service quotas. An evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes, distinguishing falsification, concealment, and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations. The resulting behavioral labels also serve as a testbed for existing activation-based deception probes.

papers.title: Learning to Formulate: Agentic Hardware-Software Co-Design of AI Infrastructure through Progressive Optimization and Verification
papers.abstract: AI infrastructure, the chips and software that train and serve AI models, is designed in layers. Layers make the system manageable, but they also fix which choices an optimizer can consider. Gains that need the chip and its software to change together are excluded before optimization begins: the formulation leaves them out. Language-model agents make it possible to revisit these boundaries, but an agent's proposal cannot show by itself that a design is correct or optimal. We present Formulaic, a flow that divides the work. The agent writes the formulation, a mathematical solver optimizes within it, and verification and measurement check its assumptions and results. The agent refines the problem step by step, from the computation graph toward the chip. Each step is a template: a family of programs with the conditions under which they are correct. Wall relaxation searches the chip by pricing the hardware limits that bind the software. This paper takes a first step, through separate studies rather than one end-to-end run. On NVIDIA GB10, templates the agent wrote run complete Qwen3-8B layers $1.075\times$ faster than SGLang. In a simulated Ventus GPU study, joint design cuts the worst-scenario cycles of Qwen2.5-0.5B to 0.428 of the reference, against 0.934 for software alone. On a five-step GEMM refinement chain, reusing proofs makes checking $2.51\times$ faster.
papers.summary: AI infrastructure is designed in layers, and that layering fixes which choices an optimizer can consider, so gains that need the chip and its software to change together are excluded before optimization begins. `Formulaic` divides the work: a language-model agent writes the mathematical formulation, a solver optimizes within it, and verification and measurement check its assumptions and results, with the agent refining the problem step by step from the computation graph toward the chip using templates, each a family of programs with the conditions under which it is correct, plus a wall-relaxation search that prices the hardware limits binding the software. The paper reports separate studies rather than one end-to-end run. **On an NVIDIA `GB10`, agent-written templates run complete `Qwen3-8B` layers 1.075 times faster than `SGLang`**, in a simulated `Ventus` GPU study joint hardware-software design cuts worst-scenario cycles for `Qwen2.5-0.5B` to 0.428 of the reference versus 0.934 for software alone, and on a five-step GEMM refinement chain reusing proofs makes checking 2.51 times faster.

papers.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.
papers.summary: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices let human experts demonstrate manipulation tasks for robot learning without teleoperating a robot, but turning those demonstrations into training data still demands consistent hardware, calibration, and data processing. `UMI-Live` is a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild collection, with custom hardware that integrates camera and LiDAR-inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power so that no external tracking or in-environment calibration is needed, plus a simple recording interface and an asynchronous pipeline that runs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. The release also includes software for dual-YAM teleoperation and vision-language-action (VLA) policy training and inference. **Fine-tuning `pi0.5` and `MolmoAct2` on the collected data reached 10/10 and 8/10 success on a bimanual pick-and-place task**, and 40 hours of data across three tasks are released along with hardware designs and reproduction guides.

papers.title: OPERA: OPamp Design by an Expert-Taught Reasoning Agent, from Specifications to Layout
papers.abstract: Analog flows from specifications to a signed-off layout rarely run without manual iteration. Recent large language model (LLM) agents size circuits with optimizer loops over the device dimensions and stop at the schematic. We present OPERA (OPamp design by an Expert-taught Reasoning Agent), in which a general-purpose LLM agent designs CMOS opamps from specifications to post-layout sign-off with open-source tools. First, the designer teaches the agent the gm/ID method: map the specifications to transconductances and minimum currents, choose gm/ID per device role from characterized lookup tables, and size from equations, leaving a few knobs to search and an explainable design. Second, the agent learns the gLayout framework and taught layout practice, and writes a reusable layout generator that closes the layout and extraction loop at designer-approved gates. In SKY130, the agent designed a shared constant-gm bias and six opamps (5T, folded-cascode and telescopic OTAs; Miller, folded-cascode and telescopic two-stage) for fun >= 50 MHz, PM >= 60 degrees, SR 25 V/{\mu}s into 1 pF and a minimum dc gain of 30 to 60 dB. All six layouts are DRC-clean and LVS-matched, and their extracted netlists meet every target at all 15 PVT corners ( fun >= 53.7 MHz, PM >= 62.1 degrees, SR >= 27.9 V/{\mu}s). The benchmark netlists are released at https://github.com/AMPICLab/AMPICBench.
papers.summary: Analog design flows from specifications to a signed-off layout rarely run without manual iteration, and recent LLM agents for circuit sizing stop at the schematic. `OPERA` has a general-purpose LLM agent design CMOS operational amplifiers end to end with open-source tools: a designer first teaches it the gm/ID method, mapping specifications to transconductances and minimum currents, choosing gm/ID per device role from characterized lookup tables, and sizing from equations, then teaches it the `gLayout` framework and layout practice so it writes a reusable layout generator that closes the layout and extraction loop at designer-approved gates. In the `SKY130` process the agent designed a shared constant-gm bias and six opamp topologies against targets of at least 50 MHz unity-gain frequency, 60 degrees phase margin, and 25 V/us slew rate into 1 pF. **All six layouts are DRC-clean and LVS-matched, and their extracted netlists meet every target at all 15 process-voltage-temperature corners.**

papers.title: Robustness of Chatbot LLM Judgments of Presidential Actions and Hypothetical Reforms
papers.abstract: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their judgments of policies are useful only if they are robust. We measure this robustness in the setting of an ordinary user, through consumer chat interfaces. For 30 days, five chatbot configurations (Mistral, Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Opus at two effort settings) were asked twice a day to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions of the last four presidential administrations and of 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment. The judgments are robust: all configurations agree on the sign and the ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two different configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in about 4% of cases. Responses from different days differ more than same-day responses, but the difference grows slowly over the month, except where the service itself changed. We identify three such changes, which shifted the judgments while leaving little or no trace in the interface. Treating the comments as a retrieval task, we find them specific to each item and consistent across runs and chatbots, with lexical and embedding similarities agreeing. We release the dataset of 16,500 judgments.
papers.summary: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their policy judgments are only useful if they are stable, so this study measures robustness the way an ordinary user would experience it, through consumer chat interfaces. For 30 days, five configurations, namely `Mistral`, `Gemini Flash`, `Claude Sonnet`, and `Claude Opus` at two effort settings, were asked twice daily to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions by the last four presidential administrations and 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment. **All configurations agree on the sign and ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in only about 4% of cases.** Responses drift more across days than within a day, but the drift grows slowly over the month except around three service-side changes that shifted judgments while leaving little trace in the interface, and the dataset of 16,500 judgments is released.

papers.title: SymKL: A Unified Representation-Space Measure of Signal Degradation
papers.abstract: Quantifying degradation between a pristine signal and its degraded observation is fundamental to signal processing, yet existing full-reference measures are inherently modality-specific. We introduce SymKL, a unified full-reference degradation measure based on implicit neural representations (INRs). An INR is fitted once to the pristine reference and characterized by its diagonal Fisher information, which captures the local information geometry of the learned representation. Evaluating the Fisher information with the pristine reference and a degraded observation yields two parameter-sensitivity profiles whose symmetric KL divergence defines the degradation score. The proposed formulation requires only the reference and degraded observation, without knowledge of the corruption process or degradation severity, making it applicable across images, audio, and 3D data. We further derive an exact closed-form expression for the diagonal Fisher of SIREN, enabling efficient computation. Experiments on image, speech, and volumetric 3D benchmarks demonstrate that SymKL accurately tracks degradation severity, remains monotonic where conventional metrics saturate or fail, and provides a unified modality-agnostic measure of signal degradation. Code will be made publicly available after the review process.
papers.summary: Full-reference measures of how much a signal has degraded relative to a pristine original are typically tied to a single modality. `SymKL` fits an implicit neural representation (INR) once to the pristine reference and characterizes it by its diagonal Fisher information, then evaluates that Fisher information under both the reference and the degraded observation to obtain two parameter-sensitivity profiles whose symmetric KL divergence is the degradation score. The measure needs only the reference and the observation, with no knowledge of the corruption process or its severity, and a closed-form expression for the diagonal Fisher of `SIREN` networks makes it cheap to compute. **On image, speech, and volumetric 3D benchmarks it tracks degradation severity and stays monotonic where conventional metrics saturate or fail**, giving one modality-agnostic measure.

papers.title: Safe Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning: Zero Constraint Violation and Primal-Averaging Convergence
papers.abstract: Many applications of multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) require policies that balance conflicting objectives while satisfying safety constraints. We study safe MORL with zero constraint violation throughout learning, covering both cumulative and stepwise constraints. A key challenge is to explore sufficiently under unknown dynamics and constraint costs without violating the constraints. For a given preference over objectives, we develop an algorithm to learn a safe Pareto optimal policy by combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds. With high probability, every policy executed over $T$ episodes incurs zero constraint violation. The algorithm returns a safe Markov policy induced by the averaged occupancy measure and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization. We further develop a preference-free algorithm that first explores safely without a prespecified preference and then computes a safe policy for any given preference without further interaction. Over $T$ exploration episodes and $K$ planning iterations, it retains the same safety guarantee and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T}+1/\sqrt{K})$ suboptimality gap. Both algorithms require knowledge of a policy that strictly satisfies the constraints and its costs. We then relax these requirements, incurring at most constant cumulative violation. To our knowledge, we provide the first sample-efficient MORL algorithms that guarantee safety for every executed policy.
papers.summary: Many multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) problems need policies that trade off conflicting objectives while never violating safety constraints, which means exploring under unknown dynamics and costs without ever stepping outside the constraints. For a given preference over objectives, the authors combine optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds to learn a safe Pareto optimal policy, and a preference-free variant first explores safely and then computes a safe policy for any preference afterwards without further interaction. **With high probability every policy executed during T episodes incurs zero constraint violation, with a suboptimality gap of order 1/sqrt(T) under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization**, and the preference-free version adds a 1/sqrt(K) term after K planning iterations. Both algorithms assume access to a strictly feasible policy and its costs, relaxing that assumption costs at most constant cumulative violation, and the authors describe these as the first sample-efficient MORL algorithms that guarantee safety for every executed policy.

papers.title: Retaining Repair Hypotheses for Cost-Aware Execution
papers.abstract: Several corrections of an executable model can fit the same observations while predicting different execution outcomes. We study a repair-to-execution interface that retains compatible finite guard repairs, conditions their weights on diagnostic and ordinary-execution observations, and uses their predictions to choose routes, priced tests, or a backup. On 24 synthetic two-stage devices, an equal mixture of a language-model-generated repair and a uniform belief over compatible repairs (the AI-weighted belief) lowers no-test cost by 2.14 percent relative to committing to the generated repair. Access charges can erase the benefit of diagnosis on isolated tasks, while repeated work can recover it under the AI-weighted belief. With normal-execution learning in every repeated-work arm, workload-valued testing costs 3.33 percent less than same-budget random selection under the AI-weighted belief. Weighting changes the comparison: uniform normal learning costs 540.75 less than AI-weighted normal learning on this cohort, with a device-paired interval excluding zero. Testing recovers part of that gap, but uniform normal learning still has a lower aggregate cost than AI-weighted workload-valued selection. Under uniform beliefs, information-gain selection has the lowest total among the compared selectors, while workload-valued testing costs more than normal learning. These results support retaining alternatives to a generated repair and evaluating diagnostic selection together with repair weighting and learning from execution.
papers.summary: When an executable model of a device is corrected to fit observations, several different repairs can match the same data yet predict different execution outcomes. The authors study a repair-to-execution interface that keeps all compatible finite guard repairs, updates their weights from diagnostic and ordinary-execution observations, and uses their predictions to choose routes, priced tests, or a backup option. **On 24 synthetic two-stage devices, mixing a language-model-generated repair equally with a uniform belief over compatible repairs lowers no-test cost by 2.14 percent compared with committing to the generated repair alone.** Further comparisons show that access charges can erase the value of diagnosis on isolated tasks while repeated work recovers it, that uniform beliefs with learning from normal execution can beat the AI-weighted belief in aggregate cost, and that diagnostic test selection should be evaluated jointly with repair weighting and learning from execution.

papers.title: Dobb: Shard-Local Preconditioning in Block-Diagonal Eigenbases
papers.abstract: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node's memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.
papers.summary: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed one node's memory requires sharding across devices, and under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as `Muon` must communicate across shards to perform global matrix operations. `Dobb` (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases) approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks, tracks a complete basis within each block, projects momentum into those bases, sign-normalizes the coefficients, and reconstructs the update, so when each block lies within one shard the matrix update is computed locally with no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the second moments. **On `GPT-2 XL` with 1.56B parameters, `Dobb` with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476 versus 2.511 for `Dion` at rank fraction 1/16.** Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs it cuts amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for `Dion` to 9.2 ms.

papers.title: How Specific Do I Need to Be? Effects of User Query Underspecification on Deep Research Agents
papers.abstract: Deep research agents (DRAs) conduct long-horizon reasoning, search, and literature synthesis to provide long-form answers to complex, domain-specific questions. These agents are typically trained and evaluated on fully specified user queries. However, real-world user queries can often be underspecified. We introduce UNDERSPEC-DR, a framework for systematically evaluating how underspecified queries affect agents' final answer quality and intermediate search behavior. Across three DRAs we evaluated, underspecification substantially reduces how well DRA's answers fulfill users' information needs, even though they remain grounded in cited evidence. Our analysis of intermediate search behavior suggests a possible explanation: DRAs conduct broader searches that draw less on the original user query but rely more on their learned prior during training, which can be misaligned with users' intent. Our findings reveal the vulnerability of current DRAs to underspecified user queries and inform future efforts to build DRAs that proactively recognize when additional user input is needed to reliably complete deep research tasks.
papers.summary: Deep research agents (DRAs) are usually trained and evaluated on fully specified queries, but real users often leave out details the agent needs. `UNDERSPEC-DR` is a framework that systematically varies how underspecified a query is and measures both final answer quality and the agent's intermediate search behavior across three agents. **Underspecified queries substantially reduce how well answers meet the user's information need, even though the answers stay grounded in cited evidence.** The search traces point to a cause: agents respond by searching more broadly, leaning on priors learned during training rather than the user's wording, which can diverge from what the user actually wanted.

papers.title: Accuracy is not compatibility: two Evo 2 checkpoints hinge on one FP8 matrix multiplication
papers.abstract: FP8 formats specify how values are stored, not how products are summed; this gap can break checkpoints. Evo 2, a DNA language model, documents a Hopper FP8 requirement for its 1B and 40B checkpoints. On two Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs both fail the developers' forward test (the 7B passes); on an RTX 5070 Ti the 40B's next-base accuracy is 25.7%, near guessing. Greater accuracy breaks them, as BioNeMo saw for the 40B on Hopper: natively, 99.996% of one projection's outputs are correctly rounded (H100: about 30%), and fp32 accumulation of the same operands fails. Our H100 FP8 GEMM emulator, mmaemu (bit-exact on captured 1B projections), localises the dependence to the 1B's first projection (of 21), where exact sums fail but pass when shrunk by the H100's 1.4% (measured in-sample), not 2.1%. The 40B fails with only its first projection native. Emulating only that projection, weights unchanged, raises 40B BRCA1 variant-classification AUROC from 0.434 to 0.869 (H100: 0.868) on the RTX 5070 Ti, despite a narrow forward-test miss, and 0.481 to 0.867 on an RTX PRO 6000. We tested one model family but not training origin; releases should specify reference arithmetic.
papers.summary: FP8 number formats define how values are stored but not how products are accumulated, and the DNA language model `Evo 2` turns out to depend on the specific accumulation behavior of Hopper GPUs. On Blackwell cards the 1B and 40B checkpoints fail the developers' forward test, and the 40B model's next-base accuracy on an RTX 5070 Ti drops to near chance, while more accurate fp32 accumulation of the same operands also fails. Using `mmaemu`, a bit-exact emulator of H100 FP8 matrix multiplication, the authors trace the dependence to a single first projection layer where exact sums fail but H100-style slightly shrunken sums pass. **Emulating only that one projection, with weights unchanged, restores the 40B model's BRCA1 variant-classification AUROC on the RTX 5070 Ti from 0.434 to 0.869**, matching the H100, and the authors argue model releases should specify their reference arithmetic.

papers.title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering (SE) tasks, driving the need for high-quality datasets for reliable training and evaluation. SWE-bench-style datasets (SWE datasets) are widely used to evaluate LLM-based coding agents on real-world software issues, where task clarity and test coverage directly affect whether instances are solvable and verifiable. However, quality issues persist in existing SWE datasets, and manual annotation is costly and labor-intensive, motivating LLM-based annotation. Existing approaches typically rely on static, overly general rubrics, limiting their ability to handle diverse and nuanced scenarios and often yielding high false positive rates. In contrast, human annotators draw on accumulated experience to make context-aware judgments. Inspired by this, we propose ExLabel, an LLM-based, self-evolving, experience-guided assistant for task clarity and test coverage assessment in SWE datasets. ExLabel maintains an evolving experience bank that distills cross-instance knowledge into stable yet adaptive judgment criteria and reuses relevant experience to guide the assessment of new instances. For systematic evaluation, we construct SWE-TQ, a new benchmark spanning eight programming languages, by cleaning human annotations from SWE-bench and Multi-SWE-bench. Experiments with three backbone LLMs show that ExLabel achieves the best F1 across all settings, with relative improvements of 44.2%/49.9% and 24.0%/18.4% over the best baseline for task clarity and test coverage assessment on the Python/Multilingual subsets, respectively. Moreover, a coding model fine-tuned on SWE-rebench data filtered by ExLabel resolves 66.2% of issues on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the model trained on data filtered by the best baseline by 14.5%.
papers.summary: SWE-bench-style datasets are the standard way to evaluate large language model (LLM) coding agents on real repository issues, but instance quality depends on whether the task is clearly described and the tests actually cover the fix, and existing LLM annotators rely on static rubrics that produce many false positives. `ExLabel` is a self-evolving annotation assistant that maintains an experience bank distilled from previously judged instances and retrieves relevant experience to guide the assessment of new ones. To evaluate it the authors build `SWE-TQ`, a benchmark across eight programming languages cleaned from human annotations in `SWE-bench` and `Multi-SWE-bench`, where `ExLabel` achieves the best F1 with all three backbone models and improves on the strongest baseline by up to roughly 50 percent relative on task clarity. **A coding model fine-tuned on `SWE-rebench` data filtered by `ExLabel` resolves 66.2% of `SWE-bench Verified` issues, 14.5% more than one trained on data filtered by the best baseline.**

papers.title: LinQuant: Functional Invariances for Low-Precision Linear Recurrences
papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. Finally, we translate this framework to production by augmenting SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances. LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B and Nemotron-H 8B, demonstrating the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.
papers.summary: Linear recurrences such as those in `Mamba-2` are increasingly used in place of or alongside softmax attention, but low-precision inference for them lags well behind what exists for attention, and naively quantizing the dense matrix multiplications in chunkwise-parallel prefill is fragile. `LinQuant` identifies seven functional invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of the recurrent decay and write factors, that leave the full-precision computation unchanged while making the operands easier to quantize, and derives when each is valid across linear, gated, and delta-rule recurrences. Added on top of `SSDi8`, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline, **the invariances improve perplexity at matched latency on `Mamba-2` at 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B parameters and on `Nemotron-H` 8B**.

papers.title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models can recognize objects in an image yet still fail at multi-step reasoning over them, for example losing track of which objects have already been counted. The authors argue these failures reflect a reference gap, meaning a failure to bind language to specific visual entities, regions, or locations, rather than a perception deficit, and test whether external scaffolds such as numbering the objects can close it. `ReGap-Bench` pairs five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are held fixed and only the reference overlay varies. **Task-matched references raise accuracy by up to 25 percent, while mismatched references help little or hurt**, suggesting that constructing appropriate visual references is a training-free skill for improving multimodal reasoning.

papers.title: FDSML: Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning with Parameter-Aware Triplet Loss
papers.abstract: Formula-Driven Supervised Learning (FDSL) enables vision pre-training without real images, but existing methods cast pre-training as classification on discretized labels, discarding continuity in the generative process. We propose Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning (FDSML), which derives relational supervision from image-generation parameters beyond discrete class labels. FDSML combines FineFractalDB, our refined fractal dataset with higher intra-class variation and more stable structures, with a Parameter-Aware Triplet (PA-Triplet) Loss that assigns positives and negatives according to distances in the underlying Iterated Function System parameter space. This objective trains embeddings to respect parameter-derived relative similarity orderings. Experiments show that FDSML improves transferability to image retrieval while remaining competitive on downstream classification and improving robustness under several corruption settings. On ResNet-50, Recall@1 improves from 65.6% to 74.0% on Stanford Online Products and from 56.2% to 78.4% on Stanford Cars over FDSL pre-training. These results suggest that parameter-derived relational supervision provides a stronger synthetic pre-training signal than label-based classification for transfer beyond recognition.
papers.summary: Formula-Driven Supervised Learning (FDSL) pretrains vision models on synthetic fractal images without any real data, but existing methods frame it as classification over discretized labels and discard the continuous structure of the generative process. Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning (`FDSML`) instead derives relational supervision from the image-generation parameters themselves, pairing a refined fractal dataset, `FineFractalDB`, with a Parameter-Aware Triplet loss that chooses positives and negatives by distance in Iterated Function System parameter space. **On `ResNet-50`, Recall@1 rises from 65.6% to 74.0% on `Stanford Online Products` and from 56.2% to 78.4% on `Stanford Cars` compared with standard FDSL pretraining**, while classification transfer stays competitive and robustness under several corruption settings improves.

papers.title: ARBITRA: Robust Document-Level ATT&CK Extraction via Multi-Expert Argumentation
papers.abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports describe adversary behavior in natural language, but converting them into structured MITRE ATT&CK mappings remains difficult: existing methods decompose reports to sentence-level granularity for extraction, while modern LLMs can work with full reports in a single pass but with noticeable performance degradation. We present ARBITRA, which orchestrates multiple role-specialized LLM experts that propose candidate ATT&CK entities from the full report, which are then verified through a per-candidate quantitative bipolar argumentation framework (QBAF) grounded in document evidence and rationales. We additionally construct reasoning-specialized corpora for fine-tuning so experts can act as effective participants during this verification process. Across ATT&CK extraction benchmarks, ARBITRA reaches a stronger precision-oriented operating point than sentence-level pipelines, recent LLM-based extraction systems, and frontier models including GPT-5.5. Under adversarial perturbations simulating conflicting TTP statements, cross-report contamination, and semantic poisoning, ARBITRA limits mean precision degradation to roughly half that of frontier-model baselines for a more robust extraction.
papers.summary: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports describe attacker behavior in prose, and mapping them to structured MITRE ATT&CK techniques is hard because sentence-level pipelines lose document context while single-pass large language model (LLM) extraction over a full report degrades in accuracy. `ARBITRA` orchestrates several role-specialized LLM experts that propose candidate ATT&CK entities from the whole report, then verifies each candidate through a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework (QBAF) grounded in document evidence and rationales, with the experts fine-tuned on reasoning-specialized corpora so they argue effectively. Across ATT&CK extraction benchmarks it reaches a stronger precision-oriented operating point than sentence-level pipelines, recent LLM extractors, and frontier models including `GPT-5.5`. **Under adversarial perturbations such as conflicting technique statements, cross-report contamination, and semantic poisoning, it limits mean precision degradation to roughly half that of frontier-model baselines.**

papers.title: Verifiable LLM-Guided Focal SMT Solving for Quantified Arrays
papers.abstract: Large language models can often identify useful semantic structure in formal artifacts, but their outputs cannot be trusted as proofs or solver decisions. We study whether LLMs can instead guide formal reasoning systems through a narrow, solver-verifiable interface. We instantiate this idea in quantified array SMT solving, where modern instantiation-based techniques can fail when key ground terms and equalities are hidden by auxiliary variables, axiom guards, and nested array terms. We observe that many instances are largely driven by a small set of focal ground terms or constraints, similar to the backdoor sets in SAT solving. Building on this, we present LinguaArray, a framework where an LLM proposes a small Semantic Focus Set (ground terms/constraints), while a conventional SMT solver remains the sole proof engine and certifies all results. LinguaArray uses these LLM-suggested, solver-validated finite sets to significantly enhance solver capability, solving additional satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances that the backend alone fails to solve. It interacts within a finite time and then falls back to the backend solver to mitigate potential regressions. Evaluation on 1015 SMT-LIB instances across five logics under 1200s timeout (including LLM latency) shows that LinguaArray solves up to 69.1% of instances and increases solved-instance counts by 105%--397% over the corresponding backends.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can often spot useful semantic structure in formal problems, but their outputs cannot be trusted as proofs, so the question is whether they can guide a solver through a narrow interface in which the solver still certifies everything. In quantified array Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solving, instantiation-based methods often stall because the key ground terms are hidden behind auxiliary variables, axiom guards, and nested array terms, yet many instances hinge on a small set of focal terms much like backdoor sets in SAT solving. `LinguaArray` has an LLM propose a small Semantic Focus Set of ground terms and constraints that the SMT solver validates and exploits, with a bounded interaction time and a fallback to the plain backend to avoid regressions. **On 1,015 `SMT-LIB` instances across five logics under a 1200-second timeout that includes LLM latency, it solves up to 69.1% of instances and raises solved counts by 105% to 397% over the corresponding backends.**

papers.title: ATLAS-Bench: An Agentic Tool-Use Benchmark for Local Area Search
papers.abstract: Reliable local search is essential for LLM agents to support everyday decisions and longer plans by finding places that meet users' needs at given times and locations. Yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of whether search results satisfy mandatory requirements, account for preferences, and ground factual and experiential judgments in place attributes and reviews. We introduce ATLAS-Bench, a benchmark of 1,200 queries across three regions, expanded from real search events using place attributes, reviews, and existing user profiles from the platform. Each query distinguishes mandatory requirements from preferences and factual conditions from subjective judgments, with supporting evidence and criteria for checking each requirement. Queries are validated through iterative assertion checks and cross-model review. We also introduce ATLASBox, a standardized evaluation environment with search tools and a fixed point-of-interest (POI) knowledge base. Given a query, timestamp, and location, an agent searches place attributes and reviews to recommend evidence-supported options or report that no place meets all mandatory requirements. We evaluate answer quality, trajectory quality, and execution cost. Across 14 configurations of 11 models, GPT-6-Luna achieves the highest constraint satisfaction rate among returned recommendations (71.5%) and factual accuracy (95.6%). However, it returns at least one acceptable recommendation for fewer satisfiable queries than GLM-5.3 (67.3% versus 85.3%). These results highlight the challenge of satisfying individual requirements while providing usable recommendations across queries.
papers.summary: Local search, meaning finding places that satisfy a user's needs at a given time and location, is a common job for LLM agents, but existing benchmarks rarely check whether results meet hard requirements, respect preferences, and ground judgments in place attributes and reviews. `ATLAS-Bench` contains 1,200 queries across three regions expanded from real search events, each separating mandatory requirements from preferences and factual conditions from subjective ones, with evidence and checking criteria per requirement, and `ATLASBox` provides a standardized environment with search tools over a fixed point-of-interest (POI) knowledge base. Agents must recommend evidence-backed options or report that nothing satisfies all mandatory requirements, and are scored on answer quality, trajectory quality, and execution cost. Across 14 configurations of 11 models, `GPT-6-Luna` has the highest constraint satisfaction rate among returned recommendations and the highest factual accuracy, **yet it returns at least one acceptable recommendation for only 67.3% of satisfiable queries versus 85.3% for `GLM-5.3`**.

papers.title: Timbre: Reliability-aware harmonic consensus for label-free multimodal test-time rexinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Label-free test-time reinforcement learning adapts vision--language models using rewards derived from their own predictions. However, misinterpreted visual evidence and sensitivity to textual formulation can produce a consistent but incorrect consensus that majority voting reinforces. Cross-view aggregation can expose such errors, but image and text transformations may themselves degrade task-relevant evidence to different extents. We introduce \method, a reliability-aware harmonic consensus framework for multimodal test-time reinforcement learning. \method constructs a $2\times2$ grid combining original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing modes, selects pseudo-labels through weighted harmonic aggregation, and adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a heuristic reliability signal. We formulate consensus as a weighted $\chi^2$-barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized weighted harmonic aggregate, without requiring correct-answer invariance. An exact support--dispersion decomposition characterizes when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings, while a sensitivity analysis establishes how modality reweighting changes pairwise ranking margins, informing interpretation of the heuristic updates. Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, \method outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark--model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances under matched estimation and optimization rollout counts. These results demonstrate improved target-task adaptation and transfer to unseen instances without further updates.
papers.summary: Label-free test-time reinforcement learning adapts vision-language models using rewards derived from their own predictions, but majority voting can reinforce a consensus that is consistent yet wrong when the model misreads the image or is sensitive to how the question is phrased. `Timbre` builds a two-by-two grid combining original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing prompt modes, selects pseudo-labels by weighted harmonic aggregation across these views, and adapts per-modality weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a reliability signal. The consensus step is formulated as a weighted chi-squared barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized harmonic aggregate, with supporting analysis of when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic-mean rankings. **Across six benchmarks and three `Qwen3-VL` model scales, it beats `TTRV` in 16 of 18 settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 on held-out instances** at matched rollout counts.

papers.title: Softmax Routing Dynamics in Mixture-of-Experts Models: Collapse and Recovery
papers.abstract: Softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models can concentrate probability on a subset of experts, suppressing access to the others. We study how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed probabilities recover. For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with freely trainable expert outputs, slow adaptation tracks fixed-expert dynamics on finite horizons, while every fixed positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit. An exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage. Under positive two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, uniform over initial masses, the resulting coefficient's order of vanishing gives logarithmic or power-law recovery times. Integrations of constructed fields reproduce these orders. An exact discrete log-odds identity relates neural updates to threshold crossing. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, both with and without capacity constraints.
papers.summary: Softmax routers in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can collapse, concentrating probability on a few experts and starving the rest. The analysis studies how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed experts recover, using a stationary-loss barrier for fixed experts, a square-loss model with trainable expert outputs in which any positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit, and an exact decomposition of routing velocity into complementary-expert covariance and relative gradient advantage. **Under two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, the theory predicts logarithmic or power-law recovery times**, which numerical integrations of constructed fields reproduce. In paired Transformer-MoE training runs, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, with and without capacity constraints.

papers.title: End-to-End Guarantees for Masked Diffusion Models under Conditional Mixing
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models train a denoiser on masked cross-entropy and generate by unmasking many positions in parallel. Existing MDM sampling bounds assume an exact denoiser or leave its error uncontrolled while training bounds cover only the masking distribution on which the model was trained. We present an end-to-end guarantee for a learned denoiser under conditional mixing (CM): stationary sources (e.g. floored order-$r$ Markov and two-sided-Doeblin hidden-Markov sources) for which revealing distant visible tokens moves a masked token's posterior on average exponentially little in the distance with correlation length $\tau_c$. We show the empirical risk minimizer trained under any masking distribution attains per-token excess $\varepsilon'$ on that distribution from $\varepsilon'^{-\mathcal{O}(\tau_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)}$ training sequences, independent of sequence length $N$ -- one sample budget serves every decoding schedule when each schedule's denoiser is trained under its own weighting. We further show that the exponent's order $\Theta(\tau_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)$ is minimax-optimal up to constants; more efficient rates require added structure. With this, we bound the end-to-end KL as $\mathrm{KL}(\pi\Vert p_{\mathrm{alg}})\leq \varepsilon+N\varepsilon'$ under a dilated schedule of $T=\mathcal{O}(\tau_c\log(N|\mathcal{V}|/\varepsilon))$ denoising steps versus $\Omega(N)$ steps for a fixed random order on an explicit CM source. Finally, we show that block-autoregressive samplers chain across blocks with no added error and that a $\Lambda$-looped order-$r$ message-passing class on order-$r$ sources achieves polynomial sample complexity, with approximation error improving per loop until saturation at $\Lambda r\approx \tau_c\log(1/\varepsilon')$. Experiments on released and retrained models support our results' qualitative predictions.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) train a denoiser with masked cross-entropy and generate by unmasking many positions in parallel, but existing sampling guarantees assume an exact denoiser and existing training bounds cover only the masking distribution used in training. The authors give an end-to-end guarantee under a conditional mixing assumption, meaning stationary sources such as floored order-r Markov chains where revealing distant visible tokens shifts a masked token's posterior exponentially little in distance, with correlation length tau_c. **The empirical risk minimizer reaches per-token excess error epsilon' from a number of training sequences exponential in tau_c times log of the vocabulary size but independent of sequence length, and this exponent is minimax-optimal up to constants.** With a dilated unmasking schedule this yields an end-to-end KL bound using a number of denoising steps logarithmic rather than linear in sequence length, block-autoregressive samplers chain across blocks with no added error, and experiments on released and retrained models match the qualitative predictions.

papers.title: Smooth Action Chunking Via Movement-Primitive Representations for Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Imitation learning has become a widely adopted approach for vision-based robot policies, owing to its conceptual simplicity, scalability, and ability to leverage large-scale datasets. As these policies have grown more capable, action chunking has become their standard interface. At each decision step the policy outputs several future actions at once. Backbones from diffusion policies to large vision-language-action models all share it. Whatever backbone produces the chunk, its temporal structure is learned only implicitly. The commanded trajectory is therefore jerky both within a chunk and between successive chunks. On real hardware this appears as visible vibration and as repeated saturation of the follower's velocity limit. We address this issue by incorporating a movement-primitive-based trajectory representation into action chunking. Specifically, a trajectory segment is represented as a linear combination of smooth basis functions, yielding smooth trajectories by construction while leaving the policy architecture, training objective, and inference procedure unchanged. The same representation also yields a closed-form, inference-time correction for the second source of jerk. We condition the predicted coefficients so that the new chunk passes through a via-point at the previous chunk's last commanded action. This correction needs no retraining and, unlike asynchronous Real-Time Chunking, applies to policies queried in one shot. We instantiate it on a one-shot (ACT) and an iterative (DiT) backbone and evaluate in simulation and on a real bimanual ALOHA platform. The representation lowers within-chunk jerk by an order of magnitude on the one-shot backbone and by 2.4 times on the iterative one, with task success statistically non-inferior. The conditioning then removes 73-84% of the boundary discontinuity, at negligible per-step cost.
papers.summary: Action chunking, where a policy emits several future actions at once, has become the standard interface for imitation-learned robot policies from diffusion policies to vision-language-action models, but each chunk's temporal structure is learned only implicitly, producing jerky motion within chunks and discontinuities between them that show up on hardware as vibration and velocity saturation. The authors represent each chunk as a linear combination of smooth movement-primitive basis functions, which guarantees smooth trajectories by construction without changing the policy architecture, training objective, or inference procedure. The same representation gives a closed-form inference-time correction that conditions the new chunk to pass through the previous chunk's last commanded action, needing no retraining and working for one-shot policies where asynchronous real-time chunking does not apply. On `ACT` and `DiT` backbones in simulation and on a real bimanual `ALOHA` platform, **within-chunk jerk drops by an order of magnitude on the one-shot backbone and by 2.4 times on the iterative one with statistically non-inferior task success**, and the via-point conditioning removes 73 to 84 percent of the boundary discontinuity at negligible cost.

papers.title: Kairos: Semantics-Aware Orchestration of Planning Engines across Classical, Numeric, Temporal and Hybrid PDDL
papers.abstract: Planning at run time, as in robots that re-plan while they act, needs a planner that reads the PDDL its users write (durative actions, numeric resources, time windows, continuous change), answers quickly, and delivers only validated plans. Specialised planners are strong on individual fragments of PDDL, but they differ in coverage, latency and in what their failures mean. We study whether selecting heterogeneous engines from the semantics of each task can give broad coverage of PDDL, from STRIPS to PDDL+, while remaining competitive with specialised planners and making explicit what each answer guarantees. Kairos profiles each task to decide which of five engines apply (ground heuristic search, compressed and snap-action temporal search, time steps for hybrid dynamics, lifted search) and schedules them under one budget of time and memory. Every candidate plan is checked by a validator independent of the planner's transformations, and "unsolvable" is reported only when a search whose exhaustion is a proof exhausts its space. On 1,756 tasks from nine comparative suites, Kairos solves more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite, with the largest differences on numeric, temporal, PDDL3 and PDDL+ planning, and it also solves the most tasks at 100 ms and 1 s. Resampling over domains, the gain is above zero in six of the nine suites, while on classical planning against LAMA it is within the noise. A further 450 feature-oriented tasks and 26 one-feature probes show that Kairos handles all seventeen features probed, where no other planner evaluated handles more than eight. Ablations identify compressed temporal search and the novelty fallback as major contributors, and a comparison with VAL traces every disagreement to a PDDL+ convention or to a documented VAL defect. Planner and benchmark are open source.
papers.summary: Robots that re-plan while acting need a planner that accepts the full range of PDDL their users write, including durative actions, numeric resources, time windows, and continuous change, answers quickly, and returns only validated plans, but specialized planners cover different fragments with different latencies and failure semantics. `Kairos` profiles each task to decide which of five engines apply, spanning ground heuristic search, compressed and snap-action temporal search, time-stepped search for hybrid dynamics, and lifted search, schedules them under one time and memory budget, checks every candidate plan with a validator independent of the planners' transformations, and reports unsolvable only when an exhaustive search proves it. **On 1,756 tasks from nine comparative suites it solves more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite**, with the largest gains on numeric, temporal, PDDL3, and PDDL+ planning and a result within noise of `LAMA` on classical planning. On 450 feature-oriented tasks and 26 single-feature probes it handles all seventeen features probed where no other evaluated planner handles more than eight, and both planner and benchmark are open source.

papers.title: Sparse Fine-Tuning for Parameter-Efficient Adversarial Training
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks achieve strong performance across many tasks but remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Adversarial training (AT) is one of the most effective defenses, yet it suffers from high memory cost on large models and the persistent clean-robust accuracy trade-off. Recent work introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning, such as LoRA, into AT, but this constraint induces a notable robustness gap relative to full-parameter AT. In this work, we revisit parameter-efficient adversarial fine-tuning from a parameter space perspective. Through gradient analysis, we find that adversarial optimization is highly concentrated on a small subset of parameters, which we call Robustness-Critical Parameters (RCPs), suggesting that robustness is encoded in a sparse subspace. Building on this observation, we propose Sparse Adversarial Fine-Tuning (SAFT), which identifies RCPs via adversarial gradient saliency and performs AT by updating only these parameters while freezing the rest. Across architectures and datasets, SAFT outperforms LoRA-based methods in both clean and robust accuracy with fewer trainable parameters, and approaches or surpasses full parameter AT in robustness while updating only about 5\% of parameters.
papers.summary: Adversarial training (AT) is among the most effective defenses against adversarial perturbations, but it is memory-hungry on large models, and parameter-efficient variants built on `LoRA` leave a sizable robustness gap relative to full-parameter training. A gradient analysis shows that adversarial optimization concentrates on a small subset of weights the authors call Robustness-Critical Parameters, suggesting robustness is encoded in a sparse subspace. Sparse Adversarial Fine-Tuning (`SAFT`) selects these parameters by adversarial gradient saliency and updates only them while freezing the rest. **Across architectures and datasets it beats `LoRA`-based adversarial fine-tuning in both clean and robust accuracy with fewer trainable parameters, and approaches or surpasses full-parameter adversarial training while updating about 5% of weights.**

papers.title: Achieving Minimax-Optimal First-Order and Best-of-Both-Worlds Regret Simultaneously in Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.abstract: We study first-order and best-of-both-worlds regret guarantees in multi-armed bandits. Pogodin and Lattimore (2019) proposed an algorithm that combines minimax-optimal worst-case regret with a first-order guarantee whose loss-dependent term is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{K L^\star}\log T)$, where $T$ denotes the horizon, $L^\star$ denotes the smallest expected cumulative loss among fixed arms, and $K$ denotes the number of arms. However, a logarithmic gap remains between this loss-dependent term and the optimal first-order scale. In this paper, we remove this logarithmic factor by proposing an efficient and parameter-free algorithm that achieves the minimax optimal first-order regret guarantee $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{K L^\star})$. Technically, our algorithm is built upon FTRL with a Tsallis entropy regularizer (Zimmert and Seldin,2021), with a learning rate adapted to the learner's cumulative loss and a sampling distribution determined by a scalar fixed point. This construction controls the combined estimation and stability cost in terms of the learner's loss. Moreover, we show that the same algorithm achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee, with $\mathcal{O}(\sum_{i\ne i^\star}\frac{\log T}{\Delta_i})$ regret for i.i.d. losses with a unique best arm $i^\star$, where $\Delta_i$ denotes the suboptimality gap of arm $i$.
papers.summary: In multi-armed bandits, first-order regret bounds scale with the smallest cumulative loss L* of any fixed arm rather than with the horizon, and the prior algorithm of Pogodin and Lattimore combined minimax worst-case regret with a first-order term of order sqrt(K L*) log T, leaving a logarithmic gap to the optimal scale. The proposed algorithm builds on follow-the-regularized-leader with a Tsallis entropy regularizer, adapts its learning rate to the learner's own cumulative loss, and sets its sampling distribution through a scalar fixed point, which controls the combined estimation and stability cost in terms of the learner's loss. **It is efficient and parameter-free and achieves the minimax-optimal first-order regret of order sqrt(K L*) with no logarithmic factor.** The same algorithm also gives a best-of-both-worlds guarantee, with logarithmic gap-dependent regret for i.i.d. losses with a unique best arm.

papers.title: Integrating Heterogeneous Echocardiography AI Outputs in Language Space: Learnable Late Fusion with a Supervised LLM
papers.abstract: View- and target-specific echocardiography AI models capture useful but complementary information and may not achieve sufficient predictive performance in isolation. A learned ensemble is a natural way to combine these outputs, but heterogeneous models typically require each output to be converted into a binary decision, probability, confidence score, or fixed-length feature vector. We developed a supervised large language model (LLM)-based late-fusion module that directly aggregates view-specific predicted finding statements and predicted measurements in language space and learns a case-level fusion function. In patient-level three-fold cross-validation of 859 examinations from 646 patients, the proposed method integrated heterogeneous outputs within a single framework, performed comparably to the best-performing reference strategy evaluated, and outperformed a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training. These results suggest that a supervised LLM can combine multiple upstream models without model-specific output conversion or feature engineering that requires medical knowledge.
papers.summary: View-specific and target-specific echocardiography AI models each capture complementary information but may not be accurate enough alone, and combining them in a learned ensemble normally requires converting every output into a common form such as a probability, confidence score, or fixed-length feature vector. The authors train a supervised large language model (LLM) as a late-fusion module that directly consumes the predicted finding statements and measurements from each upstream model as text and learns a case-level fusion function. **In patient-level three-fold cross-validation on 859 examinations from 646 patients, the fused model performed comparably to the best reference ensembling strategy and outperformed a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training**, suggesting that fusion in language space can skip model-specific output conversion and medically informed feature engineering.

papers.title: CBE: A Complexity-adaptive Boundary-aware Ensemble Method for Imbalanced Data
papers.abstract: In many real-world classification tasks, datasets exhibit class imbalance, which can degrade the generalization performance of conventional learning algorithms. Data complexity has recently been recognized as a more objective indicator of learning difficulty than the imbalance ratio alone, because class overlap and complex decision boundaries often impair classifiers more severely than imbalance itself. Samples near the decision boundary are inherently difficult to classify, which has motivated many researchers to focus on such instances to improve classifier performance. However, most under-sampling approaches fail to differentiate their sampling of boundary samples across datasets of varying complexity. To overcome this limitation, we propose a complexity-adaptive boundary-aware ensemble (CBE) framework that links the sampling weight distribution to data complexity and dynamically adjusts the boundary preference of under-sampling accordingly. We also introduce an overall complexity measure that combines metrics at multiple levels and use it to divide imbalanced datasets into three categories. Extensive experiments on 24 benchmark datasets from UCI and KEEL show that the proposed method outperforms many existing methods in terms of F-measure and G-mean on Easy and Median datasets, without degrading performance on hard cases.
papers.summary: Class imbalance degrades conventional classifiers, but data complexity, meaning class overlap and convoluted decision boundaries, is often a better indicator of difficulty than the imbalance ratio alone, and most under-sampling methods treat boundary samples the same way regardless of how complex the dataset is. The complexity-adaptive boundary-aware ensemble (`CBE`) ties the sampling weight distribution to a new overall complexity measure that combines metrics at multiple levels, dynamically adjusting how strongly under-sampling favors boundary samples and sorting datasets into easy, median, and hard categories. **On 24 benchmark datasets from `UCI` and `KEEL`, it outperforms many existing methods on F-measure and G-mean for easy and median datasets without degrading performance on hard ones.**

papers.title: Soei: Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent for Multi-Agent AI Software Engineering
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now do long, multi-step and multi-session software work with little supervision. When a developer comes back to that work, the useful question is not what the model said but what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished. We study this in three parts. First, we verify Agenttrail, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, against its source at commit e4ba2da: nine documented constants and mechanisms hold at file-and-line level, two event pipelines are never unified, and its Map service has an unauthenticated local mutation surface. Second, we run a prototype of our system on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes). With a blind-audited classifier (precision 83.3% and 96.7%) we estimate that 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete after editing had no proof in between. A 10-minute timing heuristic for session hand-offs recovers 6 of the 24 session pairs that content lineage links. 42% of sessions run longer than 24 hours, 48.1% of transcript bytes lie past a 2 MiB replay bound, and 1,326 records in 16 sessions contain credential-like strings. Third, we propose Soei (Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent): an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer that keeps a claim of completion apart from proof. On the same corpus the ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s, detects tampering and replays deterministically. We position the work against concurrent 2026 proposals and define autonomy levels with evidence gates and harness metrics baselined on our data.
papers.summary: When a developer returns to work that AI coding agents carried out over long, multi-session runs, the useful question is what was actually done, by whom, and whether it was verified, not what the model said. The authors first audit `Agenttrail`, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, confirming nine documented mechanisms at file-and-line level while finding two event pipelines that are never unified and an unauthenticated local mutation surface. They then analyze 45 real coding-agent sessions with a blind-audited classifier, **estimating that 23.4% of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete had no proof in between**, alongside findings that many sessions run past 24 hours and that over a thousand records contain credential-like strings. Finally they propose `Soei`, an acknowledgement-aware event schema with a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned provenance graph, calibrated attribution and lineage inference, and a verification layer that keeps claims of completion apart from proof, which on the same corpus is a fifth of the raw size, stores no content or credentials, detects tampering, and replays deterministically.

papers.title: Topology Survives Shuffling: Robust Long-Context Memory Access Prediction for Graph Analytics
papers.abstract: Graph analytics generates irregular, topology-dependent memory-access streams via indirect traversals, limiting data prefetching. Accurate prediction enables timely prefetches that hide memory latency. However, ML predictors couple short histories with fixed horizons, fitting the training trace's node layout rather than learning transferable graph patterns. We propose LoCoMAP, a long-context representation-learning framework for memory-access prediction with independently controlled observation history and prediction horizon. We evaluate Connected Components (CC), PageRank (PR), and Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) on six synthetic graph families, with Erdos-Renyi (ER) and Grid as random and deterministic controls. We test two interventions: same-family regeneration changes connectivity, while node shuffling disrupts layout but preserves connectivity. Across 18 graph-workload pairs, extending history from 8 to 128 accesses improves F1 by 7.8%, while extending prediction horizon from 8 to 512 improves F1 by 88.3%. For CC, regeneration is less disruptive than shuffling: without retraining, long context retains 95.4% of original F1 and outperforms short context in six families. Under full shuffle, long context improves CC F1 by 33.6% across ER, Barabasi-Albert, Copying Model, and Stochastic Block Model (SBM), with a 2.06x gain on SBM, but not on Watts-Strogatz or Grid, where near-zero delta mass shifts into heavy tails beyond the predictor's range. Long context outperforms short context on six real-world CC graphs. At full shuffle, long-context PR retains 57.6% of original F1 and averages 11.0% above short context. Both SSSP models retain about 30% of original F1 under full shuffle as distance updates access vertex data in a new order. Within these bounds, long-context predictors are robust across related graphs and layouts without retraining, enabling a generalizable graph prefetcher.
papers.summary: Graph analytics workloads produce irregular, topology-dependent memory-access streams through indirect traversals, which defeats hardware prefetchers, and existing machine-learned predictors couple short histories to fixed horizons and end up fitting the training trace's node layout rather than learning transferable graph patterns. `LoCoMAP` is a long-context representation-learning framework for memory-access prediction with independently controlled observation history and prediction horizon, evaluated on Connected Components, PageRank, and Single-Source Shortest Paths across six synthetic graph families plus real-world graphs, using same-family regeneration, which changes connectivity, and node shuffling, which changes layout but not connectivity, as controlled interventions. **Across 18 graph-workload pairs, extending the prediction horizon from 8 to 512 accesses improves F1 by 88.3%, versus 7.8% from extending history from 8 to 128.** Under full node shuffling without retraining, long context retains most of its accuracy on Connected Components and PageRank and improves Connected Components F1 by 33.6% over short context on four random graph families, though not on Watts-Strogatz or grid graphs where the access deltas shift into heavy tails beyond the predictor's range.

papers.title: Does Federated Training Degrade Explainability? A Comparative Analysis of Grad-CAM Faithfulness in Centralized vs. Federated Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Automated detection has become the essential safeguard against realistic synthetic media, but deploying it at scale requires training on sensitive data from multiple organizations, putting privacy and the transparency demanded by forensic review in direct conflict. Federated learning resolves the privacy side by sharing only model updates rather than raw data, but whether this comes at the cost of trustworthy gradient-based explanations, which analysts rely on to decide whether or not to trust a flagged clip, has not been studied. We present the systematic study of Grad-CAM explanation faithfulness under federated deepfake detection, evaluating an EfficientNet-B4 detector on FaceForensics++ across five federated clients under varying degrees of data heterogeneity. We find that the relationship between federation and explanation quality is non-monotonic: at near-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed Data) and moderate heterogeneity, federated models match or exceed the faithfulness of a centralized baseline, but at extreme heterogeneity, explanations break down entirely, becoming spatially incoherent and, on average, causally misleading. This degradation is not a general cost of federated training but a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity, and we offer practical guidance for identifying when privacy-preserving deepfake detection can be deployed safely and when its explanations can no longer be trusted. Code and data partitions are available for reproducibility.
papers.summary: Deepfake detectors increasingly need to be trained across organizations without sharing raw data, but whether federated learning preserves the gradient-based explanations forensic analysts rely on had not been tested. The authors train an `EfficientNet-B4` detector on `FaceForensics++` across five federated clients with varying data heterogeneity and measure the faithfulness of `Grad-CAM` explanations against a centralized baseline. **At near-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed) and moderate heterogeneity, federated models match or exceed centralized explanation faithfulness, but at extreme heterogeneity explanations become spatially incoherent and causally misleading.** They characterize this as a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity rather than a general cost of federation, and offer guidance on when such explanations can still be trusted.

papers.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study \textit{conditional interaction}, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.
papers.summary: Scaling toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has mostly meant scaling a costly System-2 executive through bigger models, longer reasoning, and more agents. The authors instead propose `conditional interaction`, a predict-gate-execute-update loop in which a lightweight System-1 predictor estimates each candidate interaction's utility, System-2 executes only those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and outcomes feed back to the predictor, with applications spanning training, test-time reasoning, decision-making, and agentic tool use. **Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching one over the density of utility-relevant interactions**, with prediction error, exploration, and distribution shift eroding the saving, and selection regret bounded by predictor error and the utility margin. They argue this density is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and that informative compute describes scaling better than total compute.

papers.title: Integrated Feature Selection for classification and Representation Learning with Group-Lasso Siamese Networks
papers.abstract: The Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso) has been widely employed for feature selection in linear models and has also been extended to multi-layer perceptron (MLP) networks for both feature and group feature selection. Group-Lasso has also been used in feature selection using feed-forward neural networks.
