To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to incorporate the Group-Lasso principle into a Siamese network architecture for feature selection. Unlike existing approaches that primarily optimize classification accuracy, the proposed method aims to identify a compact subset of features that simultaneously preserves the intrinsic representation of the input data (the goal of Siamese network) and is expected to achieve high classification performance. Two variants of the proposed framework are developed: one based on the Euclidean distance and the other on a modified Jaccard similarity measure for real-valued vectors. The latter is specifically designed to improve feature selection for high?dimensional sparse data. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated on 12 benchmark datasets with feature dimensions ranging from 6 to 7070 using eight different classifiers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Siamese Lasso framework consistently identifies compact and discriminative feature subsets maintaining competitive or superior classification performance, although the loss function used explicitly did not consider any regularizer to learn classification. In addition, the quality of the embeddings produced by these networks is assessed using manifold learning techniques such as UMAP and t-SNE.
papers.summary: Feature selection with the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso) and its group variant has been applied to linear models and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), but not to Siamese networks, whose objective is to preserve the input's intrinsic representation rather than classification accuracy. The proposed `Siamese Lasso` framework applies a Group-Lasso penalty inside a Siamese architecture, in a Euclidean-distance variant and a modified Jaccard-similarity variant aimed at high-dimensional sparse data. **Across 12 benchmark datasets with 6 to 7070 features and eight downstream classifiers, the selected subsets are compact and give competitive or superior classification accuracy** despite the loss containing no classification term, and embedding quality is checked with `UMAP` and `t-SNE`.

papers.title: What Breaks When Facts Become Stories? The Distortions Source-Agreement Metrics Miss When Models Retell Real Events
papers.abstract: Language models are now widely used to turn recorded facts into media for public consumption, yet evaluation of such output still assumes agreement with the source as its measure of success. In reconstruction, where departing from the source can itself be the goal, this criterion measures the wrong construct: applied as is, it counts intended departures as errors; withheld, it lets real distortion through. We had three model families rewrite 2,000 news articles as summaries and as stories, measured what changed on every axis of the five Ws and how, and asked of each detected distortion whether the assigned perspective warranted it, which set a third of them aside. Time and manner were not lost but replaced, while place and causation lost the expressions that carry them. Accountability distortion behaved otherwise. Barely present in summaries, it rose up to sevenfold in stories, and of those whose direction could be determined, two in three lightened the perpetrator's responsibility. Such distortions survive claim-level fact checking and leave the retelling grammatically cleaner than its source. Where our judges disagreed, three authors relabeling the same cases converged on whether a distortion had occurred but not on whether it was warranted, a boundary contested rather than merely hard to detect. To support work on detecting and reducing them, we release ReTold-2k, a reconstructable corpus with the scoring protocol and per-judge baselines kept unaggregated.(https://github.com/Retold2K/retold2k).
papers.summary: When language models retell recorded facts as summaries or stories, judging output by agreement with the source either counts intended departures as errors or, if dropped, lets genuine distortion through. The authors had three model families rewrite 2,000 news articles as summaries and as stories, tracked changes along each of the five Ws (who, what, when, where, and why), and asked whether the assigned perspective warranted each detected distortion, which set aside about a third of them. Time and manner were replaced rather than lost, place and causation lost the expressions that carry them, and **accountability distortion, barely present in summaries, rose up to sevenfold in stories, with two in three directional cases lightening the perpetrator's responsibility**. Such distortions survive claim-level fact checking, and the `ReTold-2k` corpus is released with the scoring protocol and unaggregated per-judge baselines.

papers.title: Agent-Wise Test-Time Normalization for Camera-Based Cooperative Perception with Corrupted Collaborators
papers.abstract: Intermediate-fusion cooperative perception lets a vehicle detect objects beyond its own field of view by fusing features shared by nearby agents. When only a collaborator's cameras are degraded by fog, motion blur or exposure errors, the features it shares drift away from the training distribution while the ego input stays clean, and cooperation can become worse than not cooperating at all. Test-time batch-normalization adaptation, the standard training-free remedy, estimates statistics over the pooled batch of all agents and therefore normalizes both the clean ego and the corrupted collaborator with a mixture of two distributions. We show that this mixing harms even the clean ego: when the ego shares BN statistics with a corrupted collaborator, its detection from its own features drops by 3.58 to 6.68 AP@0.5 points although its cameras are untouched. We propose AgentNorm, an agent-wise test-time normalization that i) estimates the normalization statistics of every collaborator from its own current observation and ii) anchors the ego to its source statistics, so that the ego path remains exactly the original model. AgentNorm has no learnable parameters, needs no gradients or labels, is independent of the order of test frames, and runs locally on each agent without changing the transmitted features. On camera-based OPV2V with four fusion checkpoints and collaborator-only corruptions, AgentNorm raises AP@0.5 under severity-5 fog from 29.42-37.25 to 43.32-58.86 and outperforms pooled normalization by 5.53-12.94 points under fog and motion blur, at an extra latency of 2.3 ms per frame. On the real-world DAIR-V2X-C dataset, it outperforms pooled normalization in all ten infrastructure-corruption settings. We also report the cases it does not fix: occlusion, which removes image content rather than shifting feature statistics, and the case in which all agents share the same shift.
papers.summary: In camera-based cooperative perception, a vehicle fuses intermediate features shared by nearby agents, but when only a collaborator's cameras are degraded by fog, blur, or exposure errors, its shared features drift from the training distribution and cooperation can hurt. Standard test-time batch-normalization adaptation pools statistics across all agents, and the authors show this mixing lowers even the clean ego vehicle's own detection by 3.58 to 6.68 AP@0.5 points. `AgentNorm` instead estimates normalization statistics per collaborator from its own current observation and anchors the ego to its source statistics, with no learnable parameters, gradients, or labels and about 2.3 ms of added latency per frame. **On `OPV2V` under severity-5 fog it raises AP@0.5 from 29.42-37.25 to 43.32-58.86** and beats pooled normalization in all ten infrastructure-corruption settings on `DAIR-V2X-C`, while leaving occlusion and shifts shared by all agents unaddressed.

papers.title: Interpretable by Design Tabular Prediction via In-Context Local Linear Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets tabular foundation models make predictions without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. These models achieve strong predictive accuracy, but interpreting how individual features contribute to the prediction remains difficult. In biology, for example, feature contributions can help identify biomarkers or risk genes. Post-hoc interpretability methods assign feature importance scores, but these scores do not indicate what the model actually uses and can lead to explanation errors. We introduce TICL$^3$ (Tabular In-Context Local Linear Learning), an interpretable-by-design predictor that uses a tabular foundation model to guide a simple linear prediction rule. TICL$^3$ first learns a shared linear model to capture dataset-level feature effects. Then, for each query, it retrieves similar training samples using representations from the foundation model and fits a second linear model to the residuals in that neighborhood. The shared model captures broad effects, while the local model corrects errors among similar samples. Their combined coefficients determine each feature contribution to the final query-specific linear score, so the same model makes and explains the prediction. Across 386 classification benchmark-dataset evaluations, TICL$^3$ trails TabICLv2 by 1.1 percentage points and outperforms CatBoost in 266 evaluations. It improves average support F1 over MAPLE by 4.7 points and achieves the best performance on both real-data selected-feature utility metrics.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models predict well via in-context learning (ICL) but make it hard to see how individual features drive a prediction, and post-hoc importance scores need not reflect what the model actually uses. `TICL^3` (Tabular In-Context Local Linear Learning) fits a shared linear model for dataset-level feature effects, then for each query retrieves similar training samples using foundation-model representations and fits a second linear model to the residuals in that neighborhood, so the combined coefficients both produce and explain the prediction. **Across 386 classification evaluations it trails `TabICLv2` by 1.1 percentage points while beating `CatBoost` in 266 of them**, improves average support F1 over `MAPLE` by 4.7 points, and scores best on both real-data selected-feature utility metrics.

papers.title: Compile Away Uncertainty: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Programmatic Compilation
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agent skills let agents accumulate procedural knowledge without parameter updates, but because skills are stored as text and re-interpreted by a large language model (LLM) on every run, even well-learned procedures carry execution uncertainty. `SkillCompiler` decomposes each skill into fine-grained operations, analyzes which are well-specified enough to execute deterministically, and builds hybrid skill skeletons that compile those into validated programs while leaving context-dependent steps to LLM reasoning. A program asset reuse mechanism stores validated programs for retrieval across evolving skills, synthesizing and verifying new ones only when nothing applicable exists. **On five benchmarks and six model families it consistently outperforms prior self-evolving skill methods, with gains of up to 32.33% in task performance.**

papers.title: DEG: Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet for Solving Vehicle Routing Problems
papers.abstract: Traditional neural solvers for solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs) often suffer from limited solution diversity, motivating the development of Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet)-based models. However, the effectiveness of these models is frequently constrained by insufficient flow expansion in high-reward regions, limiting their ability to distribute probability across promising solution routes. Deeper exploration could yield superior results. Diffusion models, in contrast, provide stronger structural guidance for exploration. These two paradigms are naturally complementary: GFlowNet can supply edge-level signals for diffusion to embed, while diffusion can guide broader exploration. Leveraging this synergy, we propose Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet (DEG), a novel framework that integrates GFlowNet with a diffusion model to encourage richer flow expansion toward high-reward regions and derive higher-quality solutions. Specifically, DEG exploits GFlowNet's inherent diversity to generate edge-specific backward signals, applies the stochastic noise schedule of diffusion to perturb these signals, and then denoises them within the GFlowNet paradigm. To further improve scalability, we introduce a specialized decoder capable of dynamically adapting to diverse problem scales. Extensive experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, including instances with up to 10,000 nodes, demonstrate that DEG consistently achieves favorable performance compared to baseline methods.
papers.summary: Neural solvers for vehicle routing problems (VRPs) often produce low-diversity solutions, and Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet) solvers that address this still expand flow too weakly into high-reward regions. `DEG` (Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet) uses the GFlowNet's diverse samples to produce edge-level backward signals, perturbs them with a diffusion noise schedule, and denoises them within the GFlowNet framework so that diffusion guides broader exploration, with a scale-adaptive decoder for larger instances. **On synthetic and real-world instances with up to 10,000 nodes, the authors report consistently favorable performance against baseline neural solvers.**

papers.title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.
papers.summary: Predicting transport properties of liquid electrolytes for battery design needs force fields with near-quantum accuracy that are also fast enough for long molecular dynamics runs, and large pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are accurate but too slow. The authors distill a large teacher MLIP into small, system-specific student models without any new ab initio data. **The students run about 40 times faster, reproduce the teacher's structural observables, and complete stable 20 ns trajectories in days rather than months.** Across sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and beat classical force fields, which the authors present as a practical route to high-throughput electrolyte screening.

papers.title: Category-Anchored Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation
papers.abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination from spatio-temporal check-in data, and serves as the foundation for many location-based services. Recent advances incorporate large language models (LLMs) into this task by textualizing user trajectories to exploit their semantic reasoning ability. However, directly generating POI identifiers with such models is unreliable: POIs are sparse, localized, and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose ANCHOR, a category-anchored framework for semantic-to-entity grounding in next POI recommendation. Specifically, ANCHOR first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact and stable semantic space, rather than predicting concrete POI entities directly. The inferred intent is then grounded into a candidate set by integrating three complementary sources of mobility evidence: category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences. Finally, a history-aware reranker selects the target POI by matching each candidate with the user's historical mobility patterns and current context. Experiments on three real-world check-in datasets show that ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of semantic-to-entity grounding and show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.
papers.summary: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation predicts a user's next destination from check-in trajectories, and large language model (LLM) approaches that textualize these trajectories struggle to emit POI identifiers directly because POIs are sparse, long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics. `ANCHOR` first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact semantic space, grounds that intent into a candidate set using category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences, and then applies a history-aware reranker to pick the target POI. **On three real-world check-in datasets it outperforms traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics**, with analyses showing favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.

papers.title: Lost in the Latent Space: How Code Embeddings Represent Functional Intent and Implementation Fidelity
papers.abstract: Code embedding models have become a key building block for many software engineering applications, yet their internal representations remain poorly understood. Existing evaluations tend to focus on downstream task performance, offering limited insight into whether a single embedding can support both functional abstraction and implementation-sensitive analysis. To address this gap, we present a large-scale empirical study of 14 state-of-the-art code embedding models. We evaluate their representational behavior through three complementary analyses: supervised probing for functional abstraction and implementation fidelity, zero-shot retrieval experiments to assess geometric similarity, and controlled perturbation experiments that measure embedding responses to semantics-preserving code transformations. The results reveal a consistent abstraction-fidelity tension: models that better preserve stylistic and structural signals tend to do so at the expense of semantic generalization, while models with similar retrieval performance can nevertheless respond very differently to the same implementation changes. Overall, our findings suggest that a single universal code representation remains out of reach, motivating more representation-aware evaluation, selection, and deployment of code embedding models in software engineering.
papers.summary: Code embedding models underpin many software engineering tools, yet evaluations focus on downstream task scores and say little about whether one embedding can serve both functional abstraction and implementation-sensitive analysis. The authors study 14 state-of-the-art code embedding models with supervised probing for functional intent and implementation fidelity, zero-shot retrieval to assess embedding geometry, and controlled semantics-preserving code transformations to measure embedding sensitivity. **They find a consistent abstraction-fidelity tension: models that preserve stylistic and structural signals generalize worse semantically, and models with similar retrieval scores can react very differently to the same implementation change.** They conclude a single universal code representation remains out of reach and argue for representation-aware selection and deployment of embedding models.

papers.title: Last-Iterate Convergence for Constrained MDPs: From Dual Descent to Primal-Dual
papers.abstract: We study policy optimization for infinite-horizon, discounted constrained Markov decision processes. While primal-dual ($\texttt{PD}$) methods are widely used in practice, their theoretical guarantees typically hold for an impractical mixture policy. In contrast, dual descent ($\texttt{DD}$) methods output a single policy ("last iterate") with guarantees on its performance. However, such methods require iteratively solving entropy-regularized MDPs in an inner-loop, limiting their practical effectiveness. Moreover, existing analyses rely on strong coverage assumptions that are difficult to satisfy in practice. Consequently, we first provide a new analysis of $\texttt{DD}$ methods that does not require coverage assumptions. We then employ entropy-regularized natural policy gradient and dual regularization to eliminate the inner loop, resulting in an efficient $\texttt{PD}$ algorithm. We develop a novel tracking analysis which shows that, compared to existing methods, the proposed algorithm achieves improved last-iterate convergence guarantees. Furthermore, our theoretical framework allows us to analyze a truncated bilevel method that interpolates between $\texttt{DD}$ and $\texttt{PD}$ methods. Finally, we generalize our analysis to handle linear function approximation. Compared to prior last-iterate methods, we prove stronger guarantees under less restrictive assumptions.
papers.summary: Primal-dual (PD) methods for infinite-horizon discounted constrained Markov decision processes are widely used, but their guarantees typically apply to an impractical mixture of iterates, while dual descent (DD) methods give last-iterate guarantees at the cost of repeatedly solving entropy-regularized MDPs in an inner loop and strong coverage assumptions. The authors first reanalyze DD without coverage assumptions, then remove the inner loop using entropy-regularized natural policy gradient with dual regularization to obtain an efficient PD algorithm. **A new tracking analysis yields improved last-iterate convergence guarantees under less restrictive assumptions than prior last-iterate methods**, and the framework also covers a truncated bilevel method interpolating between DD and PD and extends to linear function approximation.

papers.title: Conic-Lifting for Learning-rate-free Convex Optimization
papers.abstract: A central topic in online and stochastic optimization is to design algorithms that do not require tuning of hyperparameters. Successful strategies in online learning include AdaGrad-style learning rates, Conic Blackwell algorithms, and parameter-free algorithms. However, these classes require different, often difficult, analyses. We develop a unifying family of Online Convex Optimization (OCO) algorithms that require no user-tuned learning rate on convex domains that may be unbounded. The construction lifts the domain to a cone by adding one scalar coordinate, an idea going back to Blackwell (1954). The lifted subgradients are orthogonal to the corresponding lifted decisions, leaving the comparator scale free to optimize in the regret analysis. Applying Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) and Online Mirror Descent (OMD) on the cone recovers Conic Blackwell Algorithm (CBA) and Conic Blackwell Algorithm Plus (CBA$^+$) on bounded domains in Hilbert spaces and extends them to finite-dimensional normed spaces with a strongly convex squared norm. For arbitrary nonempty closed convex domains in these spaces, a known gradient bound yields parameter-free regret guarantees. Surprisingly, on an unconstrained Hilbert space, the construction recovers the Krichevsky--Trofimov (KT) coin-betting algorithm exactly. We also give a parameter-free algorithm for unconstrained domains that requires no gradient bound.
papers.summary: Learning-rate-free methods in online and stochastic optimization, such as AdaGrad-style rates, Conic Blackwell algorithms, and parameter-free algorithms, each require their own often-difficult analysis. The authors unify them for Online Convex Optimization (OCO) by lifting the decision domain to a cone with one extra scalar coordinate, an idea traced to Blackwell (1954), so that lifted subgradients are orthogonal to lifted decisions and the comparator scale is free in the regret analysis. Running Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (`FTRL`) and Online Mirror Descent (`OMD`) on the cone recovers the Conic Blackwell Algorithm (`CBA`) and `CBA+` on bounded Hilbert domains and extends them to finite-dimensional normed spaces, and **on an unconstrained Hilbert space the construction recovers the Krichevsky-Trofimov (KT) coin-betting algorithm exactly**. They also give a parameter-free algorithm for unconstrained domains that needs no gradient bound.

papers.title: Judging Before Propagation: Task-Graph Contextual Integrity for Multi-Agent Privacy
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on persistent memory and inter-agent communication. These capabilities create privacy risks that extend beyond individual interactions: a release appropriate in isolation may become inappropriate when combined with information previously disclosed to a recipient or propagated to downstream agents along the planned workflow. Existing Contextual Integrity (CI) mechanisms for agentic systems typically rely on local judgments that assess each disclosure in isolation, with or without regard to the recipient's history, but do not account for how information propagates downstream. However, compliance at the current boundary does not guarantee appropriateness across the workflow. We introduce Task-Graph Contextual Integrity (TG-CI), to our knowledge the first task-graph-native formalization of Contextual Integrity for multi-agent systems. TG-CI represents a workflow as a Multi-Agent Task Graph (MATG) and extends CI from atomic transfers to stateful, graph-level information flows by jointly considering an item's intended propagation scope and recipients' evolving disclosure states. We operationalize TG-CI through propagation-scoped authorization under two complementary policies: Full-Scope, which requires admissibility across the complete downstream scope, and Auto-Region, which confines each item to its maximal admissible region using lightweight frontier gates. We further introduce MAPLE-Bench, a benchmark of 144 cases across four scenarios that jointly vary MATG topology, disclosure history, compromised-agent placement, and item-level privacy policies. In our primary experimental configuration, TG-CI reduces the mean unauthorized disclosure count by 85.8-94.1% relative to the Local-History CI baseline, while retaining 93.6-96.1% of the baseline's task accuracy, with the two enforcement policies providing complementary privacy--cost--utility trade-offs.
papers.summary: Multi-agent large language model systems with persistent memory and inter-agent messaging can leak private information even when each individual disclosure looks acceptable, because a release can become inappropriate once combined with a recipient's prior knowledge or propagated downstream. Task-Graph Contextual Integrity (`TG-CI`) models the workflow as a Multi-Agent Task Graph (MATG) and extends Contextual Integrity (CI) from single transfers to graph-level flows that track each item's intended propagation scope and recipients' evolving disclosure states, enforced either by a Full-Scope policy requiring admissibility across the whole downstream scope or an Auto-Region policy that confines items to their maximal admissible region via frontier gates. The authors also release `MAPLE-Bench`, 144 cases varying graph topology, disclosure history, compromised-agent placement, and item-level policies. **`TG-CI` cuts mean unauthorized disclosures by 85.8 to 94.1% relative to a local-history CI baseline while keeping 93.6 to 96.1% of its task accuracy.**

papers.title: ROAD: Modern Adversarial Training for Simple One-Step Distillation at Scale
papers.abstract: One-step distillation turns pretrained diffusion models into fast generators, but strong results often require substantial training machinery and compute. Pure adversarial distillation offers a simpler route, yet has struggled at modern text-to-image scale. To address this limitation, we propose ROAD (Representation-grounded One-step Adversarial Distillation), a one-stage framework that distills text-to-image models with one adversarial objective and a lightweight representation-space critic. First, we replace the classical convolutional head with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head with token-level text conditioning, which matches the semantic tokens of modern visual encoders. Second, we observed a fixed random feature mixing leads to long-horizon degradation. We attribute it to generator-critic co-adaptation around one realization-specific view, and periodically re-draw the mixing to keep the randomization effective. Third, for our dense and vector-valued logits, we introduce Jacobian R1 which penalizes the full input-logit Jacobian, overcoming pooled R1's limitation of neglecting most of logit sensitivities. A single adversarial objective then suffices: in one step, ROAD reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, surpassing the multi-step teachers at a fraction of distribution matching's training compute.
papers.summary: One-step distillation makes diffusion text-to-image models fast, but strong results usually need heavy training machinery, and purely adversarial distillation has struggled at modern scale. `ROAD` (Representation-grounded One-step Adversarial Distillation) uses a single adversarial objective with a lightweight critic in representation space, replacing the convolutional head with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head with token-level text conditioning, periodically re-drawing the random feature mixing to avoid generator-critic co-adaptation, and adding a Jacobian R1 penalty over the full input-logit Jacobian. **In one step it reaches 11.03 FID on `SDXL` and 13.73 on `SD3.5-M` on `COCO-10K`, surpassing the multi-step teachers** at a fraction of the training compute of distribution-matching methods.

papers.title: The Cost of Working Memory in Streaming Mean Estimation
papers.abstract: A streaming estimator must compute from the evidence that fits in memory. We determine when storing an accurate mean is easier than computing it. For Gaussian mean estimation over the Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we establish the minimax rate under squared error with $K$ persistent states, a known horizon, and a public time index: $\min\{1, K^{-2/d}+\frac{d}{n} (1+\frac{\log(ed)}{1+(\log K)/d})\}$. Unrestricted computation followed by $K$-level encoding has rate $\min\{1,d/n+K^{-2/d}\}$. At a fixed sufficiently small error, statistically optimal sample size therefore requires order $d\log d$ working bits, while order $d$ bits suffice to store the answer. The lower bound tracks repeated state compression through an entropy potential obtained by Gaussian smoothing. A matching construction combines a multiscale modular counter with workspace reused across coordinate groups. In one dimension, it attains the terminal rate $n^{-1}+K^{-2}$. Any fixed confidence requirement that the realized loss not exceed the zero baseline preserves these rates. Increasing confidence creates a further memory requirement: at fixed nontrivial risk in every fixed dimension, failure probability $e^{-\gamma n}$ requires and permits order $\log n$ working states for sufficiently small fixed $\gamma>0$. In the scalar problem, a fixed terminal alphabet suffices under the same protection. These bounds separate the memory needed to represent an answer from the memory needed to accumulate evidence and validate a decision.
papers.summary: A streaming estimator can only use the evidence it keeps in memory, raising the question of when storing an accurate mean is easier than computing one. For Gaussian mean estimation over the Euclidean unit ball in d dimensions with K persistent states, a known horizon, and a public time index, the authors establish the minimax squared-error rate and compare it with unrestricted computation followed by K-level encoding. **At a fixed small error, statistically optimal sample complexity requires on the order of d log d working bits, whereas on the order of d bits suffice to store the answer.** The lower bound uses an entropy potential from Gaussian smoothing, the matching construction combines a multiscale modular counter with workspace reused across coordinate groups, and they further show that exponentially small failure probability demands on the order of log n working states.

papers.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation of feature extractors in computer vision
papers.abstract: Feature detection and matching are fundamental components in computer vision, underpinning a broad spectrum of applications. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of traditional feature detections and descriptors, analyzing methods such as Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF), Binary Robust Independent Elementary Features (BRIEF), Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB), Binary Robust Invariant Scalable Keypoints (BRISK), KAZE, Accelerated KAZE (AKAZE), Fast Retina Keypoint (FREAK), Dense and Accurate Invariant Scalable descriptor for Yale (DAISY), Features from Accelerated Segment Test (FAST), and STAR. Each feature extractor was assessed based on its architectural design and complexity, focusing on how these factors influence computational efficiency and robustness under various transformations. Utilizing the Image Matching Challenge Photo Tourism 2020 dataset, which includes over 1.5 million images, the study identifies the FAST algorithm as the most efficient detector when paired with the ORB descriptor and Brute-Force (BF) matcher, offering the fastest feature extraction and matching process. ORB is notably effective on affine transformed and brightened images, while AKAZE excels in conditions involving blurring, fisheye distortion, image rotation, and perspective distortions. Through more than 2 million comparisons, the study highlights the feature extractors that demonstrate superior resilience across various conditions, including rotation, scaling, blurring, brightening, affine transformations, perspective distortions, fisheye distortion, and salt-and-pepper noise
papers.summary: Classical keypoint detectors and descriptors remain fundamental building blocks for image matching, and this study benchmarks `SIFT` (Scale Invariant Feature Transform), `SURF` (Speeded-Up Robust Features), `BRIEF` (Binary Robust Independent Elementary Features), `ORB` (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF), `BRISK` (Binary Robust Invariant Scalable Keypoints), `KAZE`, `AKAZE` (Accelerated KAZE), `FREAK` (Fast Retina Keypoint), `DAISY`, `FAST` (Features from Accelerated Segment Test), and `STAR`. Using the `Image Matching Challenge Photo Tourism 2020` dataset of over 1.5 million images and more than 2 million comparisons, each extractor is assessed for computational efficiency and robustness under rotation, scaling, blur, brightening, affine and perspective transforms, fisheye distortion, and salt-and-pepper noise. **`FAST` paired with the `ORB` descriptor and a brute-force matcher is the fastest extraction-and-matching pipeline**, `ORB` holds up best on affine-transformed and brightened images, and `AKAZE` is strongest under blur, fisheye, rotation, and perspective distortion.

papers.title: Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.
papers.summary: Fraud detection in mobile financial services faces severe class imbalance and tight operational limits on how many alerts analysts can review. The authors build a framework combining chronological train-test splits, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, `SHAP` explanations, and an adaptive alert-prioritization policy, comparing `Logistic Regression`, `Random Forest`, `XGBoost`, and `LightGBM` on the synthetic `PaySim` mobile-money benchmark. **`XGBoost` performs best at a fixed threshold with a PR-AUC of 0.5658, and Platt calibration cuts the Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245**, while an adaptive top-1% alert policy reduces false positives from 192 to 117 at the cost of recall falling from 0.4236 to 0.2122. Because `PaySim` is synthetic, the authors frame the result as a reproducible methodology rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh.

papers.title: LatentWeave: Test-Time Latent Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/jins7/LatentWeave.
papers.summary: Test-time optimization can improve multimodal reasoning in large multimodal language models (MLLMs) without changing backbone weights, but existing methods act at the prompt or output level and leave the latent reasoning trajectory uncontrolled, so errors accumulate during autoregressive generation. `LatentWeave` treats reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory, refining intermediate hidden states segment by segment to correct emerging deviations and inserting lightweight `WEAVE` tokens as Reasoning Anchors that stabilize reasoning structure and steer answer-oriented generation, all with the MLLM backbone frozen. **Across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks the authors report improvements over the evaluated baselines**, with ablations separating the contributions of latent optimization, anchor training, and extra test-time compute.

papers.title: TabCUQ: Context-Uncertainty Quantification for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models use in-context learning to estimate conditional expected outcomes and average treatment effects for specific groups of individuals. Using these estimates to guide scientific decisions requires reliable uncertainty quantification. The challenge is to account simultaneously for two sources of uncertainty: limited-context bias and context variation arising from the small labeled sample supplied at inference. Predictive spread does not directly quantify both sources of uncertainty, and we observe that the ordinary bootstrap may substantially overestimate context variation, whereas subsampling may underestimate it. We introduce TabCUQ, a perturbation-based framework that injects noise into observed outcomes and applies the foundation model to the perturbed contexts. TabCUQ estimates context variation using wild-bootstrap dispersion and accounts for limited-context bias using the maximum deviation between perturbed and original estimates. For a kernel-regression analogue whose estimation error admits an exact decomposition into these two components, we show that our framework provides asymptotically valid pointwise coverage. In simulations, TabCUQ substantially improves coverage, with average interval widths typically about twice those of an oracle bias-aware benchmark. Across seven real-world tasks, it also improves coverage of reference functions learned from much larger samples.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models estimate conditional expected outcomes and average treatment effects for groups via in-context learning, but using them for scientific decisions needs uncertainty estimates that capture both limited-context bias and variation from the small labeled context supplied at inference. Predictive spread does not capture both, and the authors observe that the ordinary bootstrap can substantially overestimate context variation while subsampling underestimates it. `TabCUQ` injects noise into observed outcomes and re-applies the foundation model to the perturbed contexts, estimating context variation from wild-bootstrap dispersion and bias from the maximum deviation between perturbed and original estimates, with asymptotically valid pointwise coverage proven for a kernel-regression analogue. **In simulations it substantially improves coverage with interval widths about twice those of an oracle bias-aware benchmark**, and on seven real-world tasks it improves coverage of reference functions learned from much larger samples.

papers.title: Non-Zero Radius: The Missing Component of Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Inspired by the analogy between the all-or-none activation of biological neurons and the true-false of logic circuits, McCulloch and Pitts proposed a mathematical model of the biological neuron in 1943 with the aim of simulating logical reasoning. Although Norbert Wiener considered the model overly simplistic at the time, it later became a building block of modern neural networks, including large language models. Despite their remarkable empirical success, however, conventional neural networks remain largely black-box systems and struggle with reliable symbolic reasoning. Viewing vectors as spheres of zero radius, we relax the zero-radius constraint and represent concepts as spheres with non-zero radii. We argue that sphere-based representations can capture additional features of biological cognition, including representing spatial concepts as regions and reasoning through model construction and inspection. Building on sphere embeddings, we introduce Sphere Neural Networks (SphNNs), which use a transition map to achieve symbolic-level Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning without training data, thereby taking an initial step toward the original goal of McCulloch and Pitts. We suggest that the zero-radius constraint may reflect an aspect of the oversimplification identified by Wiener and may limit conventional neural networks' capacity for symbolic-level logical reasoning.
papers.summary: Conventional neural networks descend from the 1943 McCulloch-Pitts neuron yet remain black boxes that struggle with reliable symbolic reasoning. Treating ordinary vectors as spheres of zero radius, the authors relax that constraint and represent concepts as spheres with non-zero radii, arguing that region-based representations better capture spatial concepts and reasoning by constructing and inspecting models. Building on these embeddings, `Sphere Neural Networks` (`SphNNs`) use a transition map to perform **Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning at the symbolic level without any training data**. The authors suggest the zero-radius constraint may be part of the oversimplification Norbert Wiener identified in the original model and may limit conventional networks' capacity for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Quantifying the Relay-Coverage Trade-off in Mobile Multihop Flooding
papers.abstract: Network-wide flooding in mobile multihop networks selects relays from locally maintained topology information. Mobility makes this information outdated, leaving two basic responses: add redundant relays or refresh the topology and re-select relays more frequently. How these mechanisms trade reliability for overhead, however, is not well quantified. We quantify this trade-off on a public trace of 157 vehicles using Optimized Link State Routing version 2 (OLSRv2) and exact minimum-cost relay sets. Twofold coverage increases median relay-cover lifetime by only 2.3x, rather than about an order of magnitude as predicted by an independent-hazard model. The limitation is structural: 43.6 % of two-hop neighbours have only one possible relay, and newly appearing neighbours invalidate existing covers. Moreover, the delivery gain of a second relay falls from 0.061 to 0.016 when relay selection uses instantaneous link state, showing that redundancy mainly compensates for outdated topology information. Relay coverage and topology refresh therefore form a measurable redundancy-freshness trade-off rather than independent robustness mechanisms. In our trace, twofold coverage has lower overhead below about 100 bit/s of application flooding per node, whereas fresher topology information has lower overhead above it. This makes relay redundancy a load-dependent design choice rather than a fixed heuristic robustness setting.
papers.summary: Network-wide flooding in mobile multihop networks picks relays from locally maintained topology information that mobility quickly renders stale, leaving a choice between adding redundant relays or refreshing topology more often. The authors quantify this trade-off on a public trace of 157 vehicles using `Optimized Link State Routing version 2` (`OLSRv2`) and exact minimum-cost relay sets. **Twofold coverage extends median relay-cover lifetime by only 2.3x**, far short of the order-of-magnitude gain an independent-hazard model predicts, because 43.6% of two-hop neighbours have only one possible relay and newly appearing neighbours invalidate existing covers. Redundancy mainly compensates for outdated topology, so it is cheaper below roughly 100 bit/s of flooding per node while fresher topology wins above that, making relay redundancy a load-dependent design choice rather than a fixed heuristic.

papers.title: Raincheck: Deferred Multimodal Prefill for Efficient Multi-Turn MLLM Inference
papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).
papers.summary: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse long multimodal inputs, which inflates time to first token (TTFT), and query-aware hard pruning that cuts prefill tokens permanently discards information later questions may need. `Raincheck` decouples initial token selection from later availability: an existing pruning method picks tokens for the initial prefill, while the unselected tokens are preserved and progressively prefilled in source order using spare compute during decode and scheduling gaps after the answer returns, with attention visibility control and affine state mapping enabling context updates mid-generation in both full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. With 30% initial token retention on `Qwen3-VL-8B` and `Qwen3.5-9B` across four pruning methods, **`Raincheck` recovers on average 77.7% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on `MultiVerse`** and 60.4% on `ConvBench`. The `SGLang` implementation cuts mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill with under a 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).

papers.title: Trajeform: Embedding Crowd Data
papers.abstract: Crowd simulation aims to generate agent behaviours that are rich, natural, and appropriate to their surrounding environment. Recent advances in Machine Learning have enabled such behavioural patterns to be learned directly from trajectory data, allowing simulation models to capture increasingly complex crowd dynamics. However, the capabilities of these systems remain strongly dependent on the type and diversity of the data used during training. When evaluating how well crowd simulators generalise to real-world datasets, most existing metrics focus primarily on trajectory-level differences rather than behaviour-level similarity. In this paper, we present Trajeform, a framework that trains a reconstruction VAE (Variational Autoencoder) on real trajectory data to learn a meaningful continuous embedding that preserves behavioural characteristics of real crowds. The trained encoder can then be applied to synthetic trajectories generated by simulators and used to compare the resulting embedding distributions. Additionally, the learned embedding can be used to analyse supplementary data, such as trajectories corresponding to a simulator's principal behaviours or captured data from controlled environments (e.g., cycling), providing insight into their ability to span the real behavioural embedding space. The framework compares data from three simulators (CCP, modCCP, and RVO) against ground-truth datasets and is evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively using latent-space analysis, distributional metrics, and trajectory generation through sampling from the aggregated posterior distribution. The results indicate that the learned latent space captures meaningful trajectory dependencies found in the real data, making the framework useful both as an additional measure of synthetic data believability and as a tool for informing the training of future trajectory models.
papers.summary: Crowd simulators are increasingly trained on trajectory data, but existing metrics for judging how well they match real crowds compare trajectories rather than behaviours. `Trajeform` trains a reconstruction Variational Autoencoder (VAE) on real trajectory data to learn a continuous embedding that preserves behavioural characteristics, then applies the trained encoder to synthetic trajectories so the resulting embedding distributions can be compared. The framework compares the `CCP`, `modCCP`, and `RVO` simulators against ground-truth datasets through latent-space analysis, distributional metrics, and trajectory generation by sampling from the aggregated posterior. **The learned latent space captures meaningful trajectory dependencies present in the real data**, making it usable both as a measure of synthetic data believability and as a guide for training future trajectory models.

papers.title: Diffusion models for the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model
papers.abstract: A score-based diffusion model is trained on the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model, the lattice representation of the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model. Neural networks are trained on three different coarse-grainings of the same training set to implement a multiscale sampling scheme that modestly improves both the accuracy and computational cost of direct sampling on the finest lattice. Stein (or Schwinger-Dyson) diagnostics for the two-point correlation function are introduced to assess the quality of the learned score without relying on reverse diffusion sampling. These diagnostics are also incorporated into an additional training loss. We discuss several technical considerations relevant to implementing diffusion models on $S^2$. These include a consideration of lifting the network input to $S^3$, as in the $CP^1$ representation, and developing a boundary-layer approximation to the short-time spherical heat kernel that extends its usefulness to larger diffusion times.
papers.summary: Sampling configurations of the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model, the lattice form of the O(3) nonlinear sigma model, is tackled with a score-based diffusion model whose spins live on the sphere S^2. Networks are trained on three coarse-grainings of the same training set to build a multiscale sampling scheme that **modestly improves both accuracy and computational cost over direct sampling on the finest lattice**. Stein (or Schwinger-Dyson) diagnostics for the two-point correlation function assess the learned score without running reverse diffusion and are also folded into an additional training loss. The authors discuss lifting network inputs to S^3 as in the CP^1 representation and a boundary-layer approximation to the short-time spherical heat kernel that extends its usefulness to larger diffusion times.

papers.title: LLM Agent-Based Design of RISC-V CPUs with FPGA-in-the-Loop Evaluation
papers.abstract: Long-run RTL simulation of CPU candidates can take hours, while short diagnostic runs may miss performance degradation that emerges later in execution. This evaluation cost can delay design decisions in LLM-agent-based CPU development. We present a development environment in which LLM agents implement CPU candidates on an FPGA and use on-board performance measurements to guide design decisions. We applied it to the human-supervised development of a single-cycle RV32I core into a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core. The final design reaches 5.61 CoreMark/MHz at 130 MHz on a Artix-7 FPGA. For the same CPU candidate running 8,000 CoreMark iterations, FPGA evaluation, including implementation, was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation. In one case, board measurements revealed long-run performance degradation in a candidate that improved in a short diagnostic run. The result guided candidate selection and led to RTL-based root-cause analysis and a fix.
papers.summary: Evaluating CPU candidates with long register-transfer level (RTL) simulation can take hours, while short diagnostic runs can miss performance degradation that only appears late in execution, slowing LLM-agent-driven CPU development. The authors build an environment in which LLM agents implement candidate designs on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and use on-board performance measurements to guide design decisions, applied to the human-supervised evolution of a single-cycle RV32I core into a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core. The final design reaches 5.61 `CoreMark`/MHz at 130 MHz on an Artix-7 FPGA, and **FPGA evaluation including implementation was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation** for 8,000 CoreMark iterations. In one case board measurements exposed a long-run slowdown in a candidate that had looked better in a short diagnostic run, steering candidate selection and leading to an RTL root-cause analysis and fix.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence prompting strategies among Chinese university students across academic tasks
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.
papers.summary: Effective use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in university learning depends on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts, not just on access to the tools. Questionnaire data from 234 Chinese university students were analysed with descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of comments to examine perceived prompting capability and reported strategies. Students expressed confidence, especially in supplying context and refining prompts after initial outputs, but **their strategies showed limited sensitivity to task type**: specifying output format was endorsed more for a creative workshop scenario than for a research assignment, while other matched strategies did not differ. Fixed prompt templates drew lower endorsement than other strategies, perceived cognition had the clearest unique association with prompting capability, and open-ended responses flagged prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

papers.title: Hidden Phase Transition in Single-Polymer Stretching under Elongational Flow
papers.abstract: Using machine learning, we identify a second transition in polymer chain stretching driven by planar elongational flow, beyond the well-known coil-stretch transition. We achieve this by developing a conditional extension of Universal and Identifiable Dissipative Dynamics (UIDD) that jointly learns reduced stochastic dynamics from microscopic trajectories across flow strengths and yields the corresponding stationary nonequilibrium free energy landscapes. As the flow strength increases, the evolving landscape exhibits the expected coil-stretch transition, and then a previously unrecognized dynamical transition. In the latter, the stretched states persist, but the distribution along a folding coordinate becomes bimodal when conditioned on small end-to-end separation. Large-deviation analysis of a simplified analytical chain model reproduces both transitions and shows that they are phase transitions in the long-chain limit. Single-molecule DNA experiments provide qualitative support for the dynamical transition through the predicted reversal of the folding response.
papers.summary: Beyond the well-known coil-stretch transition, a second transition is identified in polymer chain stretching under planar elongational flow. A conditional extension of `Universal and Identifiable Dissipative Dynamics` (`UIDD`) jointly learns reduced stochastic dynamics from microscopic trajectories across flow strengths and yields the corresponding stationary nonequilibrium free energy landscapes. As flow strength increases, the landscape reproduces the coil-stretch transition and then **a previously unrecognised dynamical transition in which stretched states persist but the distribution along a folding coordinate becomes bimodal** when conditioned on small end-to-end separation. Large-deviation analysis of a simplified analytical chain model recovers both transitions as phase transitions in the long-chain limit, and single-molecule DNA experiments qualitatively support the predicted reversal of the folding response.

papers.title: Learning Kolmogorov Backward Operators for Spectral Analysis and Forecasting: A Data-Driven Variational Galerkin Framework
papers.abstract: For a time-homogeneous Markov process, the fixed-lag solution operator \( (T_\tau f)(x)=\mathbb E[f(X_{t+\tau})\mid X_t=x] \) of the Kolmogorov backward equation evolves observables linearly and deterministically, even when the dynamics are stochastic. We approximate this operator using a two-stage method where we first approximate this operator directly from data, without knowledge of the governing equation (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), and then compress the Galerkin projection onto a finite-dimensional observable space that is fixed in advance or selected variationally. The error analysis traces the learning error of the estimator, the sampling error of the Galerkin inner products, and the invariance and reconstruction properties of the observable space to the computed spectra and forecasts. The sampling error enters only through a multiplicative factor. Near an isolated spectral cluster, the invariance defect of a subspace controls its distance from the target invariant subspace. The forecast error is controlled by the one-step error of the reduced model and the projection error of the observable; when the measure is invariant and the reduced model preserves constants and is stable on mean-zero observables, the bound is uniform in the horizon. For deterministic dynamics, a learning rate for Fourier neural operators (FNOs) gives one explicit bound for the learning error. Numerical experiments illustrate spectral approximation and forecasting, including long-rollout stability and a comparison with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) when fewer transition pairs than basis functions are observed.
papers.summary: For a time-homogeneous Markov process, the fixed-lag solution operator of the Kolmogorov backward equation evolves observables linearly and deterministically even when the underlying dynamics are stochastic. The authors approximate it in two stages: first learning the operator directly from data without the governing equation, for example with a `Fourier Neural Operator` (`FNO`), then compressing it via Galerkin projection onto a finite-dimensional observable space that is fixed in advance or chosen variationally. The error analysis traces learning error, sampling error of the Galerkin inner products, and the invariance and reconstruction properties of the observable space through to the computed spectra and forecasts, and **the forecast error bound becomes uniform in the horizon when the measure is invariant and the reduced model preserves constants and is stable on mean-zero observables**. Numerical experiments show spectral approximation, long-rollout stability, and a comparison with `extended dynamic mode decomposition` (`EDMD`) when fewer transition pairs than basis functions are observed.

papers.title: Red-Teaming Large Language Models in Low-Resource African Languages: A Case Study of Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more widespread in Africa, their safety in low-resource languages remains largely untested since most red-teaming work focuses on English. This study evaluates six state-of-the-art LLMs using 400 explicit adversarial prompts in Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin, categorised into four harm categories. The responses were scored by native-speaker annotators and reliability was assessed using Cohen's $\kappa$. While models that rejected up to 69% of English prompts rejected as few as 0% in Yoruba, this was not because they were safer, but because they failed to understand the prompts. Attack success rates increased for most models in the Nigerian languages, with GPT-4o Mini demonstrating the most significant cross-lingual safety discrepancy (+0.23 in Yoruba). When models did engage with adversarial prompts, many of the responses were harmful, with rates of harmful content reaching 0.63 in English and 0.50 in Nigerian Pidgin. The most difficult harm category to detect was cultural stereotypes and discrimination (ASR = 0.44 in Nigerian Pidgin). Comprehension in Yoruba was low across most models, and this directly suppressed apparent attack success without indicating actual safety. Gemini 2.0 Flash was the most consistent model across languages. Despite its explicit training in African languages, Aya 101 had the highest attack success rate in English (0.60) and one of the lowest Yoruba comprehension rates (0.28). These results demonstrate that English-centric safety alignment does not transfer to Nigerian languages, highlighting the urgent need for language-specific safety evaluations.
papers.summary: Safety testing of large language models (LLMs) has concentrated on English, so how they respond to adversarial prompts in Yoruba or Nigerian Pidgin has gone largely unexamined. Six state-of-the-art models were evaluated on 400 explicit adversarial prompts in Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin across four harm categories, with responses scored by native-speaker annotators and agreement checked with Cohen's kappa. **Models that rejected up to 69% of English prompts rejected as few as 0% in Yoruba, not because they were safer but because they failed to understand the prompts**, so low Yoruba comprehension suppressed apparent attack success without indicating real safety. Attack success rose in the Nigerian languages for most models, with `GPT-4o Mini` showing the largest cross-lingual gap, and cultural stereotypes and discrimination proved the hardest category to detect, while `Gemini 2.0 Flash` was the most consistent across languages and `Aya 101` had the highest English attack success rate despite explicit African-language training.

papers.title: Improving the Intrinsic Interpretability of Differentiable Decision Trees through Euclidean Feature-Concentration Regularisation
papers.abstract: Differentiable decision trees (DDTs) support end-to-end optimisation and explicit decision paths, but dense oblique splits can obscure the role of individual input features. We propose the Euclidean-Concentrated Differentiable Decision Tree (EU-DDT), which regularises the relative absolute feature weights at each internal node using their normalised squared Euclidean distance from the uniform distribution. This encourages dominance by a small number of features while retaining probabilistic soft routing. Across five matched random seeds, EU-DDT reduces the mean effective number of features from 8.94 to 1.54 on Wine and from 45.28 to 9.06 on Digits. Mean test accuracy changes from 100.0% to 93.9% on Wine and from 92.3% to 94.6% on Digits, illustrating the dataset-dependent trade-off between concentration and predictive performance. We also use EU-DDT to parameterise a PPO actor with an MLP critic. Two random-seed runs per environment show a consistent qualitative increase in concentration while preserving effective task performance. In representative CartPole-v1 and MiniPacman runs, EU-DDT reaches 100% final evaluation success, while mean node concentration increases from 0.1272 to 0.7179 and from 0.0437 to 0.7237, respectively. These results support EU regularisation as a mechanism for reducing node-level feature complexity; the reinforcement-learning evidence remains preliminary because only two seeds are evaluated.
papers.summary: Differentiable decision trees (DDTs) allow end-to-end optimisation with explicit decision paths, but their dense oblique splits can obscure which input features drive each decision. The `Euclidean-Concentrated Differentiable Decision Tree` (`EU-DDT`) regularises the relative absolute feature weights at every internal node by their normalised squared Euclidean distance from the uniform distribution, encouraging a few dominant features while keeping probabilistic soft routing. Across five matched seeds, **the mean effective number of features drops from 8.94 to 1.54 on `Wine` and from 45.28 to 9.06 on `Digits`**, with test accuracy moving from 100.0% to 93.9% and from 92.3% to 94.6% respectively. Used to parameterise a `PPO` actor on `CartPole-v1` and `MiniPacman`, the tree reaches 100% final evaluation success in representative runs while node concentration rises sharply, though the authors note the reinforcement-learning evidence rests on only two seeds per environment.

papers.title: Evaluating Cultural Knowledge Editing in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently fail to recognize culture-specific concepts, especially from underrepresented regions. Effectively injecting this long-tail knowledge into existing models remains a challenge. In this work, we investigate knowledge editing as a targeted alternative by introducing CulturalBind, a benchmark comprising 3.2K images of 1K concepts from 6 domains, designed to evaluate culture-aware cross-modal knowledge as well as concept-level knowledge editing in VLMs. Pre-edit evaluation reveals that textual and visual knowledge is decoupled: models often demonstrate text-based knowledge of cultural concepts but fail to identify them from images. We then evaluate editing methods in single and sequential scenarios. Although current methods successfully correct individual visual recognition errors, they exhibit low cross-modal portability, failing to integrate edits into the model's broader parametric knowledge. Furthermore, performance degrades rapidly under sequential editing, highlighting the need for comprehensive adaptation approaches that better consolidate multimodal knowledge over time.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to recognise culture-specific concepts, especially from underrepresented regions, and injecting such long-tail knowledge into existing models remains difficult. `CulturalBind` is a benchmark of 3.2K images covering 1K concepts from six domains, built to evaluate culture-aware cross-modal knowledge and concept-level knowledge editing in VLMs. Pre-edit evaluation shows **textual and visual knowledge are decoupled: models often know a cultural concept in text but cannot identify it in images**. Existing editing methods fix individual visual recognition errors but show low cross-modal portability, failing to integrate edits into the broader parametric knowledge, and their performance degrades rapidly under sequential editing.

papers.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
papers.abstract: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.
papers.summary: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems often trace back to how their training data were generated, yet whether health AI education programs teach practitioners to examine data provenance has been unknown. A cross-sectional analysis coded the publicly advertised curricula of 36 U.S. university programs, identified through a structured multisource web search, for coverage of data provenance, ethics, sustainability, collaborative structure, technical prerequisites, and instructor background. **Ethics was covered by 80.6% of programs but data provenance by only 22.2%** and structural provenance by 16.7%, with none of the seven master's programs meeting the primary outcome and no program addressing the environmental cost of computation. Only 5 of the 18 programs with team-based work mixed clinical and technical backgrounds, and 76.1% of named instructors came from computational disciplines versus 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities.

papers.title: From Intent to Improvement: Agentic Dataset Search for Better Model Training
papers.abstract: Finding training data in million-scale machine learning repositories is a Web search problem where text relevance is not enough. A query couples a semantic training goal with constraints such as task, license, and training stage, and the metadata that would verify them are often missing. Text retrieval ranks dataset cards by similarity but cannot enforce hard constraints or follow the relations that reach a sparsely described dataset. Free-form tool-calling agents are more flexible, but the same model that picks a dataset also declares it a match, and nothing checks that the query's constraints are actually met. Neither approach establishes that the data it returns will improve model training. To address it, we propose AgenticDS, a contract-governed agentic framework in which every language model decision instantiates a typed object before deterministic code consumes it. The framework compiles a query into a typed search plan, executes it through admissible deterministic operators over hybrid retrieval and bounded graph expansion, and verifies the provenance-grounded evidence before accepting a ranking or emitting a typed diagnosis that permits only local repairs. On HuDS-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 queries with 24,908 graded judgments pooled over 15 systems, AgenticDS improves NDCG@10 by 25.7\% over the strongest dense--sparse hybrid and by 18.9\% over a commercial LLM agent. A controlled search-to-train study further shows that the datasets it retrieves give the best downstream accuracy in mathematics, code, and medicine. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/nju-websoft/AgenticDS.
