papers.summary: Finding training data in million-scale repositories couples a semantic training goal with hard constraints such as task, license, and training stage, which text retrieval cannot enforce and free-form tool-calling agents cannot verify, since the same model that picks a dataset also declares it a match. `AgenticDS` is a contract-governed agentic framework in which every language-model decision instantiates a typed object before deterministic code consumes it: a query is compiled into a typed search plan, executed through admissible operators over hybrid retrieval and bounded graph expansion, and its provenance-grounded evidence is verified before a ranking is accepted or a typed diagnosis permitting only local repairs is emitted. On `HuDS-Bench`, a new benchmark of 200 queries with 24,908 graded judgments pooled over 15 systems, **it improves NDCG@10 by 25.7% over the strongest dense-sparse hybrid and by 18.9% over a commercial LLM agent**. A controlled search-to-train study further shows the datasets it retrieves give the best downstream accuracy in mathematics, code, and medicine.

papers.title: Emergence of the transformer architecture as the score of entropic laws of random measures
papers.abstract: We show that the transformer architecture emerges as the score of last-token laws in a natural statistical model of language, where sentences are empirical measures of tokens, a language is a law on $P(S^d)$, and our prior belief is that sentences carry no structure at all. By the maximum-entropy principle, we select the law closest to this prior in relative entropy among those reproducing an observed sentence-level statistic. We discuss the relevance of the statistic in the posterior interaction between tokens and we build a statistic, able to capture that interaction, with Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order. This procedure gives the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter. The query--key matrix is then the Lagrange multiplier of a maximum-entropy problem inside each sentence, and the value matrix the multiplier of the constraint over the language, so that the two are untied. Under the optimal entropic law we then show that a transformer head appears in the score of the last-token law. For ordered sentences, causal masking follows from the masked reference choice rule, and with a next-token cross-moment the score equals one causally masked attention head. We also discuss multi-head attention, weight-tied unembedding, and a heuristic reading of residual blocks as projected Langevin steps.
papers.summary: The transformer architecture is derived as the score of last-token laws in a statistical model of language where sentences are empirical measures of tokens, a language is a law on the space of such measures, and the prior assumes sentences carry no structure at all. Applying the maximum-entropy principle to select the law closest to this prior among those reproducing an observed sentence-level statistic, with that statistic built from Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order, yields the softmax choice rule with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter. **The query-key matrix emerges as the Lagrange multiplier of a within-sentence maximum-entropy problem and the value matrix as the multiplier of the language-level constraint, so the two are naturally untied, and a transformer head appears in the score of the last-token law.** For ordered sentences, causal masking follows from a masked reference choice rule, and the authors extend the reading to multi-head attention, weight-tied unembedding, and a heuristic view of residual blocks as projected Langevin steps.

papers.title: Letting AI Formulate the Research Question: Autonomous Research Agents
papers.abstract: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.
papers.summary: Systems like `The AI Scientist` have shown agents can execute and write up research, but humans chose the research area and selected which outputs to show. Here an off-the-shelf coding agent receives an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the research question, which diverges from recent technologies into problems in other fields, screens candidates for known failure modes, and obtains a critique from a different model, and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. During 13 development runs, changing the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in the candidate questions and chosen papers, after which the system was frozen and every run reported: a pilot plus four pre-registered runs. **All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper using only local laptop computation and no human research input, and external AI reviewers judged them at or near workshop level**, with the system, the five papers, and the reproduction records released.

papers.title: The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.
papers.summary: Agentic architectures have sharply increased token consumption by large language models (LLMs), yet energy estimates for API-based models typically count only generated output tokens and ignore the large input contexts such workflows carry. The authors systematically profile compute time and energy across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths and fit generalized linear models to the measurements. **Decode time and energy scale linearly with output length, while prefill time and energy show both linear and quadratic scaling with input length**, making context size a material factor for large-context workloads. Compute time proves a reliable proxy for energy when direct measurement is unavailable, giving a mapping framework for estimating the energy footprint of agentic deployments.

papers.title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching
papers.abstract: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/IDM.
papers.summary: One-step and few-step text-to-image generators must render prompt details accurately with little room for refinement, and distribution matching distillation (DMD) narrows the gap to a reference distribution using score differences, estimated here with internal velocity branches rather than a separate fake-score network. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly, motivating `Intrinsic Distribution Matching` (`IDM`), which keeps the full DMD correction and additionally matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, with no external feature encoder. With full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on `Z-Image-Turbo 6B` and `Qwen-Image 20B`, **`IDM` reaches 94.25% on Chinese and 90.20% on English `LongText-Bench` at two network evaluations, the highest among compared methods at that budget**. Ablations attribute the gains to the added moment loss, and generator EMA features perform competitively with an external `DINOv2` encoder across the five reported metrics.
papers.highlight_summary:
One- and few-step text-to-image generators must reproduce fine prompt detail, with long legible text as the stress test, despite having almost no refinement steps. `IDM` keeps the APEX-style internal distribution matching distillation (DMD), which estimates the score difference from two velocity branches of the same generator rather than a separate fake-score network, and adds an explicit loss matching feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations in the generator's own exponential-moving-average (EMA) feature space, so neither a discriminator nor an external encoder is needed.

- Decomposing the reverse-KL score difference into a Gaussian moment component (means and covariances) plus a non-Gaussian residual motivates keeping the full `DMD` correction while adding a moment constraint, implemented as a diagonal-Gaussian 2-Wasserstein loss on mean-pooled last-layer EMA activations at high noise, compared against detached queues of 16,384 model and reference features, on top of an `RCGM` base loss with weights 1 for the score term and 0.5 for the moment term.
- On `Z-Image-Turbo` 6B at 2 network function evaluations (NFE), `IDM` reaches **94.25% LongText-CN** and **90.20% LongText-EN**, the best among compared methods at that budget, beating `Z-Image-Turbo++` by 2.63 and 0.32 points and `APEX` by 3.87 and 1.44 points, though the 8-NFE `Z-Image-Turbo` baseline still scores higher on LongText-EN at 91.74.
- On `Qwen-Image` 20B with full-parameter tuning at 2 NFE, `IDM` reaches **0.91 GenEval** and FID 6.34 versus `APEX` at 0.90 and 6.44 at essentially the same latency (0.44 vs 0.45 s per sample), while rank-64 LoRA training of only 0.4B parameters retains 0.90 `GenEval`.
- Controlled ablations show the moment loss lifts the internal-DMD control on all five aggregate metrics (`GenEval` 77.46 to 77.81, LongText-CN 93.87 to 94.25, LongText-EN 89.79 to 90.20), removing DMD costs more than removing the moment loss (0.91 vs 0.35 `GenEval` points), EMA features perform on par with an external `DINOv2` encoder (94.25 vs 94.13 LongText-CN) and better than teacher or live self-features, and equal-weight velocity-plus-endpoint regression beats either term alone.
- The objective's own contribution is small (tenths of a point), the larger system-level gaps over `APEX` are confounded by a far bigger text-rendering training set (5M synthesized samples versus APEX's 200K), `APEX` still leads on `DPG-Bench` (88.64 vs 86.82), the Z-Image results start from the already-distilled Turbo checkpoint rather than the base model, and the moment loss matches only pooled diagonal statistics across prompts rather than per-condition distributions.

papers.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
papers.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench
papers.summary: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right yet fail to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. `BedBench` is a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers, evaluated on twelve open-weight and four frontier models. **Per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans reach 93.3% accuracy versus 7.2% for the best model**, and while targeted fine-tuning lifts one model from 3.0% to 68.6%, its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own counts unless those counts are supplied as text. Probing `Qwen3.5-27B` shows exact per-color counts are still recoverable at the language model's input (65.0% for the probe versus 3.0% for the model), image-removal controls reveal some apparent successes need no visual evidence, and reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues improve individual judgments without making exact answers reliable.

papers.title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed
papers.abstract: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.
papers.summary: A field's open problems live in surveys, keynotes, and community reports written every few years, so nobody can ask who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. The authors make the problems data: a hand-curated problem layer is carried in unchanged beneath an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database, with a language model handling per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdicts, and idea generation, each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. On catalogs of 1,053 database-research and 1,000 AI-research problems, the rebuilt graph answers nearly every question the catalog-only graph could plus new ones about recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers, but **of 41 hand-checked solve and refute verdicts only 9 were correct, no refute verdict disproved an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closed the central question**. The design conclusion is that a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied automatically, making the human reviewer part of the architecture.

papers.title: Carbon-Aware Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Decision-Focused Learning
papers.abstract: Electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions, but charging them produces emissions that depend on the time-varying generation mix of the electricity consumed. We study an Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with a carbon-aware objective that accounts for charging-related emissions alongside conventional routing costs. The problem determines routing, charging, and waiting decisions, allowing charging demand to be shifted toward periods with lower grid carbon intensity. Because these decisions depend on forecasts of future carbon intensity, we propose a decision-focused learning approach so that the training of the model employed for predicting the carbon intensity of the grid over time is solver-aware. In particular, we train a linear predictor using approximate SPO+ directions and employ a time-limited Large Neighborhood Search followed by exact postprocessing as the underlying solver. Experiments on realistic Germany-based instances show that explicitly considering charging-related emissions reduces realized emissions by 28.76% on average relative to carbon-blind optimization, although at the expense of higher non-carbon operating cost. Moreover, decision-focused training reduces realized total cost by 2.30% on average relative to conventional prediction-focused learning and performs better on 75.5% of the test instances, despite substantially lower pointwise predictive accuracy. Finally, we show that its average advantage remains positive across varied solver configurations and carbon-cost weights.
papers.summary: Charging an electric vehicle produces emissions that vary with the grid's generation mix over the day, so routing and charging decisions can be timed to lower-carbon periods. The authors formulate an Electric Vehicle Routing Problem whose objective adds charging-related emissions to conventional routing costs and train the carbon-intensity forecaster in a decision-focused way: a linear predictor is fit with approximate `SPO+` directions while a time-limited Large Neighborhood Search followed by exact postprocessing serves as the solver. On realistic Germany-based instances, carbon-aware optimization **cuts realized emissions by 28.76% on average** relative to carbon-blind routing at the cost of higher non-carbon operating cost, and decision-focused training lowers realized total cost by 2.30% over prediction-focused training and wins on 75.5% of test instances despite worse pointwise forecast accuracy.

papers.title: A New AFIB Detection Method with Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Early detection of atrial fibrillation (AFIB), characterized by irregular heart rhythms, can potentially save thousands of lives annually [20]. Numerous studies have attempted to address this challenge using various algorithms and methodologies. This paper introduces a novel and robust method that enhances the precision of AFIB detection. Neural Networks (NN) are widely recognized for their ability to identify complex electrocardiogram (ECG) patterns, facilitating the accurate detection of irregular heart rhythms. This study explores multiple conventional machine learning algorithms alongside neural network approaches to develop a robust AFIB detection system. To evaluate the effective- ness and robustness of the proposed method, the MIT BIH arrhythmia database (MITDB) and the Long-term Atrial Fibrillation Database (LTAFDB), both available on the Physionet site. Our approach presents a novel feature engineering technique, employing specific features such as a time series of the differences in successive heart rates (dBPM) rather than traditional inter-beat intervals. The model analyzes inputs labeled into five distinct classes, using only clean intervals identified through a new labeling method for training while treating others as outliers. This strategy ensures a more accurate and reliable AFIB detection process. The best-performing model, a Deep Neural Network (DNN), achieved an F1 score of 95.18% for binary atrial fibrillation classification on a benchmark dataset distinct from the training set. Models trained using our approach have demonstrated superior performance than previously published models.
papers.summary: Atrial fibrillation (AFIB) detection from electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings is approached with a new feature-engineering scheme that feeds models a time series of differences in successive heart rates (dBPM) instead of traditional inter-beat intervals. Inputs are labeled into five classes, a new labeling method selects only clean intervals for training while treating the rest as outliers, and several conventional machine-learning algorithms are compared against neural networks using the `MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database` and the `Long-Term Atrial Fibrillation Database` from PhysioNet. The best model, a deep neural network, **reaches an F1 score of 95.18% for binary AFIB classification** on a benchmark dataset distinct from the training set, which the authors report as exceeding previously published models.

papers.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.
papers.summary: Solving problems in unfamiliar domains requires a model to acquire knowledge and reason with it at the same time, rather than only retrieving facts or learning from a preassembled context. The authors frame this as self-learning and test it with textbook-based mathematical problem solving: the model must navigate textbook exposition through a `BookNavigator` interface, learn the relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises whose reference solutions are withheld, with reinforcement learning (RL) and fine-grained rewards used to incentivize the study process. The method **raises `Intern-S2-Preview-35B`'s overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5%**, beats RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks, and transfers gains of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points to `BrowseComp-Plus` and `CL-bench`.

papers.title: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
papers.abstract: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $\Theta$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $\Theta$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $\Theta$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $\Theta$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.
papers.summary: The intrinsic dimension of an objective landscape, introduced by Li et al. (2018) as the size of a random subspace in which training still succeeds, is given a precise definition: for a set in parameter space, it is the minimal dimension at which a random plane intersects the set with probability one. The authors show this is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of the set, study its mathematical properties, and derive upper and lower bounds for the sets of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, covering finite and infinite samples with and without regularization. **The theory yields new kinds of generalization bounds, establishing intrinsic dimension as a measure of learning complexity**, and connects the classification of ReLU network symmetries with stochastic geometry.

papers.title: Event-SAMA: Language-Grounded Video Object Segmentation on Neuromorphic Event Streams
papers.abstract: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) lacks event-stream datasets and models. We introduce Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event conversion of the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus and all additional SAMA training data: 30,650 video clips and 392,162 images. Optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator preserves all mask, referring-expression and dialogue annotations. We also introduce Event-SAMA, adapting SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter. End-to-end training yields 24.37 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on the converted ReVOS valid subset, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline (RGB SAMA-4B: 55.4 on MeViS). Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions of the same events scores 13.23 and 15.94 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$. Without retraining, Event-SAMA works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches their event density. A seed-controlled ablation with a measured noise floor of 0.47 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ finds gains from diverse training sources over MeViS alone (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33), and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity are within noise at this budget. An earlier, partially converted corpus snapshot trained with the identical recipe scores 1.38 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ higher on MeViS and 1.12 higher on ReVOS. Both are single runs that also differ in schedule length, so we draw no conclusion about corpus scale.
papers.summary: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) has had no event-stream datasets or models. The authors build `Event-SAMA-239K`, a synthetic-event conversion of the `SAMA-239K` grounded video-chat corpus and additional SAMA training data covering 30,650 clips and 392,162 images, using optical-flow, FILM, or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator so that all mask, referring-expression, and dialogue annotations carry over. They adapt `SAMA-4B` with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialized from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialized event adapter, and end-to-end training **reaches 24.37 J&F on `MeViS` valid_u and 22.33 on the converted `ReVOS` subset, the first event-native RVOS baseline, versus 55.4 for RGB `SAMA-4B`** and 13.23 to 15.94 for a frozen RGB model fed pseudo-RGB renderings or `E2VID` reconstructions. A seed-controlled ablation with a 0.47 J&F noise floor finds gains from diverse training sources, RGB-mean event-stem initialization, and a trainable `SAM2` mask decoder, while the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing, and event polarity fall within noise.

papers.title: Can AI Agents Interface Clinicians and Complex Models?
papers.abstract:
Background: Contemporary healthcare institutions generate daily very large amounts of data, which contain highly useful information for the improvement of work organization, planning and overall efficiency. While models and techniques to extract these insights are well known and constantly developed in mathematical biology, complex systems physics and data science, the adoption of these techniques among Clinicians and Hospital Administrators remains limited, mainly due to language and methodological divides.
  Objective: In this article we implement an AI Multi Agent System (MAS) that allows Users to use predictive models and make statistical analyses via natural language conversations.
  Methods: We developed EpidemIA, a training-free MAS endowed with a modular suite of epidemiological models written by human experts, executable on a single-GPU workstation. To avoid relaying sensitive data to third parties, the system uses locally an open-weights LLM as backbone for its two subagents.
  Results: Using a dataset of Emergency Department visits provided to us by IRCCS Sant'Orsola (Bologna) we test the model on a few typical use cases, demonstrating the possibility of performing both simpler statistical analyses and visualizations as well as more complicated epidemiological predictions based on dynamical models, through simple queries made in natural language.
  Conclusions: While still being a proof-of-concept implementation, EpidemIA showcases the transformative capabilities of LLM based technologies as an enabling factor in the widespread adoption of complex dynamical models, which is at present hindered by their steep learning curve.
papers.summary: Hospitals generate large volumes of data that could inform planning and efficiency, but clinicians and administrators rarely use the epidemiological and complex-systems models that could extract those insights because of language and methodological barriers. `EpidemIA` is a training-free multi-agent system (MAS) that wraps a modular suite of expert-written epidemiological models behind natural-language conversation, using a locally run open-weights large language model as the backbone for its two subagents on a single-GPU workstation so that sensitive data never leaves the institution. Tested on Emergency Department visit data from IRCCS Sant'Orsola in Bologna, **the system handles both simple statistical analyses and visualizations and dynamical-model epidemiological predictions from plain-language queries**, though the authors describe it as a proof of concept.

papers.title: Heterogeneous Co-Evolution Learning for Tool-Efficient Search Agents with Zero Labels
papers.abstract: Deep search agents extend language models by interleaving reasoning with external retrieval. However, effective search-agent training requires addressing two challenges beyond final-answer optimization. First, the capability frontier of agents is largely determined by training questions, whereas fixed or labeled task collections cannot adapt as agents improve. Second, outcome-only reinforcement learning treats all successful trajectories equally, even when some correct answers rely on redundant searches, creating an inherent tension between answer accuracy and tool efficiency. To address these issues, we introduce \textsc{ZEST-Search}, a zero-label and tool-efficient framework for search-agent training via heterogeneous co-evolution. Starting from unlabeled reference questions, \textsc{ZEST-Search} constructs validated search tasks online through an answer-first and evidence-path-guided generation process. A heterogeneous proposer adaptively constructs training tasks around the solver's evolving capability boundary, while the solver learns search-augmented reasoning through reinforcement learning. To jointly optimize task difficulty and search efficiency, \textsc{ZEST-Search} employs an intermediate-difficulty reward for the proposer and a task-local tool-aware reward for the solver, encouraging informative tasks and correct answers with fewer redundant searches. Experiments on seven general-domain and multi-hop question answering benchmarks demonstrate that \textsc{ZEST-Search} consistently improves search-agent performance while achieving higher tool efficiency without labeled search-training data or expert search trajectories. Further analyses show that heterogeneous generation, adaptive difficulty control, and tool-aware optimization enable more effective search-agent training.
papers.summary: Training deep search agents, which interleave reasoning with external retrieval, runs into two problems: fixed or labeled question sets cannot keep pace with an improving agent, and outcome-only reinforcement learning rewards correct answers equally even when they relied on redundant searches. `ZEST-Search` addresses both through heterogeneous co-evolution: starting from unlabeled reference questions, a proposer constructs validated search tasks online via answer-first, evidence-path-guided generation and is rewarded for producing intermediate-difficulty tasks near the solver's capability boundary, while the solver learns search-augmented reasoning under a task-local, tool-aware reward that favors correct answers with fewer searches. Across seven general-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, **the framework consistently improves accuracy while raising tool efficiency, using no labeled search-training data or expert search trajectories**.

papers.title: Practical Assessment of Agentic Systems in Acoustics
papers.abstract: In engineering, applications of artificial intelligence have so far been largely limited to surrogate models and optimization tasks. Large language models changed this, as they can write software from a task given in words. Placed inside a harness, a system of components that lets it search for information and execute software, such a model becomes an agent that can take over recurring engineering tasks. This work measures how the model and the elements of the harness shape the performance and behavior of the agent in two common acoustic applications. In the first, the agent detects and locates faults in audio recordings from a vehicle interior with near-perfect accuracy. A benchmark on this task shows that a weak model sets a limit that no harness design can overcome, and that design choices take effect only once the model is capable enough to use them. In the second, a case study on the design of a metamaterial unit cell, the agent reliably finds designs that achieve a specified insertion loss over a given frequency range. The results aim to help the reader understand what each element of an agent contributes and how to design an agent for acoustic tasks.
papers.summary: Large language models placed in a harness that lets them search for information and execute software can take over recurring engineering tasks, and this work measures how the choice of model and each harness element shapes agent performance on two acoustic problems. In the first, detecting and locating faults in vehicle-interior audio recordings, the agent reaches near-perfect accuracy, and a benchmark shows that **a weak model sets a ceiling no harness design can overcome, with design choices only taking effect once the model is capable enough to use them**. In the second, a case study on designing a metamaterial unit cell, the agent reliably finds designs that meet a specified insertion loss over a given frequency range, and the authors use both to explain what each agent component contributes.

papers.title: Transformer-inspired architectures make machine-learned electron densities accurate and transferable enough to bypass self-consistency
papers.abstract: We introduce machine learning models that accurately predict the electron density, the central variable of density functional theory. They are built on Transformer-inspired architectures, which require little computation per parameter and can therefore be enlarged at low cost. The proposed models, SwinUNETR-V2 and its attention-free counterpart NeXtUNETR, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on QM9, with normalized mean absolute errors in the density averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.
papers.summary: Predicting the electron density, the central quantity in density functional theory, directly with machine learning would let simulations skip the expensive self-consistent iteration. The authors build two Transformer-inspired models, `SwinUNETR-V2` and its attention-free counterpart `NeXtUNETR`, which need little computation per parameter and can be scaled cheaply, and report state-of-the-art accuracy on `QM9` with normalized mean absolute density errors of 0.075% and 0.046%. **The predicted densities are accurate enough that a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure**, with `NeXtUNETR` giving median errors of 0.036 meV in total energy and 0.65 meV per angstrom in forces. Those forces recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization and drive ab initio molecular dynamics, and after fine-tuning on small datasets both networks transfer accurately to elements and molecule sizes absent from `QM9`.

papers.title: Smartphone Indoor Localization Enhanced by Hierarchical Multi-Sensor Context Recognition
papers.abstract: Smartphone indoor localization requires low-cost, robust positioning across scene transitions and phone-use variations. Pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) enables infrastructure-free deployment but accumulates errors from heading drift, structural transitions, and carrying-mode changes. Existing methods often treat contextual cues as a single event stream or local correction signal, limiting their ability to address distinct localization errors. This paper presents a framework enhanced by hierarchical multi-sensor context recognition. A jointly data- and model-driven recognition model predicts environment, scene, and activity probabilities, which are converted into scene-event and action-context segments. Scene-event segments guide scene-constrained PDR correction through corridor heading constraints, landmark attraction, fixed-lag backtracking, and vertical-transition handling. Action-context segments drive action-aware RoNIN-based position compensation for carrying-mode-dependent drift. Experiments on cross-floor and multi-action trajectories against LiDAR-SLAM references show that the proposed framework outperforms PDR and representative learned inertial odometry baselines, demonstrating that hierarchical semantics provide reliable, localization-specific correction cues.
papers.summary: Pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) lets smartphones localize indoors without infrastructure but accumulates error from heading drift, structural transitions, and changes in how the phone is carried, and prior methods treat contextual cues as a single event stream or a local correction signal. The proposed framework uses a jointly data- and model-driven recognition model to predict environment, scene, and activity probabilities, converts them into scene-event segments that drive corridor heading constraints, landmark attraction, fixed-lag backtracking, and vertical-transition handling, and into action-context segments that drive action-aware `RoNIN`-based position compensation for carrying-mode drift. On cross-floor and multi-action trajectories judged against LiDAR-SLAM references, **the framework outperforms plain PDR and learned inertial odometry baselines**.

papers.title: Bayes-Consistent Losses for Adaptive Inference in Classification
papers.abstract: Adaptive inference systems balance accuracy and inference cost by routing inputs to models with varying capabilities. Although jointly training models and routers is empirically more sample-efficient than training them separately, principled losses for joint training remain underexplored. We address this gap in a classification setting by proposing cost-sensitive hinge losses for jointly training classifiers with single-stage or cascade routers. Single-stage routers directly select a model per input, whereas cascade routers sequentially decide at each stage whether to predict with the current model or defer to the next stage, which uses a more accurate but more costly model. For both settings, we prove linear calibration bounds establishing Bayes consistency: minimizing the hinge risk recovers the Bayes-optimal risk under the target cost-sensitive zero-one loss. Moreover, since routers can require more labeled data to train than classifiers, we propose a novel post-training prediction-powered inference (PPI) procedure that uses unlabeled data to refine a trained single-stage router. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed hinge losses are effective for joint training and that PPI can correct routing errors when labeled data is scarce.
papers.summary: Adaptive inference routes each input to a model of appropriate cost and accuracy, and jointly training classifiers with their routers is known to be more sample-efficient than training them separately, but principled losses for that joint training have been lacking. The authors propose cost-sensitive hinge losses for classifiers paired with either single-stage routers, which pick a model per input, or cascade routers, which decide at each stage whether to predict or defer to a costlier model, and **prove linear calibration bounds showing that minimizing the hinge risk recovers the Bayes-optimal risk under the target cost-sensitive zero-one loss**. Because routers need more labeled data than classifiers, they add a post-training prediction-powered inference (PPI) procedure that uses unlabeled data to refine a single-stage router, and experiments on synthetic and real datasets show the losses work for joint training and PPI corrects routing errors when labels are scarce.

papers.title: Sandman: Building and Operating Sandboxes for Agentic Reinforcement Learning on Shared Kubernetes
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) often requires repeated tool calls in task-specific environments. A training job may create thousands of these environments in bursts while sharing a cluster with other jobs. We present Sandman, a sandbox service built and operated at Amazon for agent tool execution and evaluation. It serves multiple production agentic RL workloads on shared Kubernetes. A training framework supplies a task image and uses commands and file operations in the returned sandbox. Files and processes persist across calls until the framework releases the environment. Sandman manages creation, readiness and cleanup. Each sandbox is a Kubernetes pod with a small daemon mounted into the unmodified image. In a scale test, Sandman held 11,858 concurrent tiny sandboxes. Four production SWE-bench Verified training campaigns created 3.1 million sandboxes in October 2026. We report the design trade-offs and operational lessons from handling creation bursts, preparing task environments, reclaiming abandoned sandboxes, and running evaluation under controlled conditions. We will open-source Sandman's daemon, provider and pool.
papers.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning jobs create thousands of tool-execution environments in bursts while sharing a cluster with other workloads. `Sandman` is a sandbox service built and operated at Amazon on shared Kubernetes: a training framework supplies a task image, each sandbox runs as a pod with a small daemon mounted into the unmodified image, files and processes persist across command and file-operation calls until the framework releases the environment, and the service manages creation, readiness, and cleanup. In a scale test it **held 11,858 concurrent tiny sandboxes**, and four production `SWE-bench Verified` training campaigns created 3.1 million sandboxes in October 2026. The authors report design trade-offs and operational lessons on creation bursts, environment preparation, reclaiming abandoned sandboxes, and running evaluation under controlled conditions, and plan to open-source the daemon, provider, and pool.

papers.title: MoLRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery
papers.abstract: Molecular discovery requires navigating vast combinatorial search spaces while balancing competing biological objectives. AI agents can automate expert-defined molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MoLRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide subsequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workflows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MoLRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MoLRSI developed a screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design, MoLRSI developed workflows that jointly consider target binding and specificity, producing eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets while Claude Science completely failed. These findings demonstrate how experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives while improving the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.
papers.summary: Molecular discovery means searching huge combinatorial spaces while trading off competing biological objectives, and automating expert-designed protocols does not by itself tell an agent how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve with experience. `MoLRSI` combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory, so that workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide later searches and improve both the workflows and the strategy for building them. In antibiotic discovery the agent's screening workflow, which balances antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity, and structural novelty, **achieved an experimental hit rate of 15.9% versus 8.7% for a prior expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library**. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design it produced eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets, where `Claude Science` produced no validated hits.

papers.title: Adaptive Federated Optimization Across Smooth and Nonsmooth Regimes
papers.abstract: AdaGrad-style methods can simultaneously adapt to both the order and constants of smoothness in centralized optimization. However, existing extensions to federated optimization with heterogeneous client objectives and multiple local steps require the smoothness order to be specified in advance. We address this limitation with AdaFed, a federated method that adapts across several regimes under a single choice of parameters. In the deterministic setting, AdaFed achieves an $O(1/T)$ convergence rate for both smooth nonconvex and smooth convex objectives, and an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate for Lipschitz nonsmooth convex objectives up to logarithmic factors. Under a light-tailed stochastic-gradient noise assumption, these guarantees extend to the stochastic setting with additional logarithmic factors and noise-dependent terms. Experiments across the three problem classes further support our theoretical findings.
papers.summary: AdaGrad-style methods adapt to both the order and the constants of smoothness in centralized optimization, but existing federated extensions with heterogeneous client objectives and multiple local steps require the smoothness order to be specified in advance. `AdaFed` is a federated method that adapts across several regimes under a single choice of parameters, achieving in the deterministic setting **an O(1/T) rate for smooth nonconvex and smooth convex objectives and an O(1/sqrt(T)) rate for Lipschitz nonsmooth convex objectives** up to logarithmic factors. Under a light-tailed stochastic-gradient noise assumption these guarantees carry over to the stochastic setting with extra logarithmic and noise-dependent terms, and experiments on all three problem classes support the theory.

papers.title: Implicit Bias of (Stochastic) Gradient Descent on Deep Linear Diagonal Networks
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models are often overparameterized, i.e., have more parameters than training data. This typically implies that the loss function admits multiple minimizers so that training methods (and their hyperparameter choices) have significant influence on the computed solution. We study this so-called implicit bias phenomenon in the context of training deep linear diagonal networks. Previous work has shown that the gradient flow for learning such networks converges to (almost) sparse solutions when initialized small. For an arbitrary number of layers, we extend this analysis to the practically more realistic (stochastic) gradient descent iterations. Our approach identifies (stochastic) gradient descent as a perturbed (stochastic) mirror gradient descent. This allows us to establish convergence and characterize the limiting solution, relating it to weighted $\ell_1$-minimization. Moreover, we provide sufficient conditions on the step sizes and quantify the influence of the step sizes on the implicit bias.
papers.summary: Overparameterized models have many loss minimizers, so the training method and its hyperparameters determine which solution is found, a phenomenon known as implicit bias. For deep linear diagonal networks with an arbitrary number of layers, where gradient flow from small initialization is known to reach almost sparse solutions, the authors extend the analysis to the more realistic setting of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent by viewing the iterations as a perturbed (stochastic) mirror gradient descent. This **establishes convergence and characterizes the limiting solution as a weighted l1-minimization**, with sufficient conditions on step sizes and a quantification of how the step sizes shape the implicit bias.

papers.title: Grounding Predictive Reliability through Masked Observability
papers.abstract: An uncertainty estimate is meaningful only if its semantics can be tied to observable predictive behavior. Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) evidential regression provides a structured decomposition of predictive variability into data-scale and predictive-mean components, but marginal likelihood does not identify their allocation. We address this semantic ambiguity in masked representation learning. MORSE (Masked Observability for Reliable Structured Encoding) predicts the same hidden target under controlled changes in visible context and uses normalized cross-context variation to ground predictive-mean uncertainty, while a Gaussian objective learns the conditional mean and data scale. The normalized variation plays the role of the NIG factor $1/\nu$, which the marginal leaves unidentified; this yields a policy-relative observability variance that measures dependence on visible evidence, distinct from variation induced by resampling the training set. On a Gaussian-process benchmark with a contextual reference built from analytic Bayes conditional means, MORSE has the lowest log-variance error among compared evidential, ensemble, and dropout estimators in all nine tested settings, while the estimator closest to training-set variation perturbs the model rather than its context in every setting, so the two references separate the estimators empirically. MORSE amortizes observability estimation into one forward pass per observation state. On a heteroscedastic pulse benchmark, its predictor's cross-context variance approaches a large-sample reference as training data increase. MORSE also improves low-label transfer on PTB-XL and in-distribution trajectory prediction on IMPTC.
papers.summary: An uncertainty estimate is only meaningful if its semantics can be tied to observable predictive behavior, and Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) evidential regression splits predictive variability into data-scale and predictive-mean components without the marginal likelihood identifying how to allocate between them. `MORSE` (Masked Observability for Reliable Structured Encoding) resolves this in masked representation learning by predicting the same hidden target under controlled changes in visible context and using the normalized cross-context variation, which plays the role of the unidentified NIG factor, to ground predictive-mean uncertainty, while a Gaussian objective learns the conditional mean and data scale. On a Gaussian-process benchmark with an analytic Bayes-conditional-mean reference, **`MORSE` has the lowest log-variance error among the compared evidential, ensemble, and dropout estimators in all nine settings**, its cross-context variance approaches a large-sample reference on a heteroscedastic pulse benchmark as data grow, and it improves low-label transfer on `PTB-XL` and in-distribution trajectory prediction on `IMPTC`.

papers.title: Going deep, reaching further: What can Boltzmann machines efficiently represent?
papers.abstract: While universal approximation theorems theoretically underpin the representation capabilities of machine learning models, they have two shortcomings: They do not focus on efficient representations and they tend to be insensitive to depth and other heuristically important properties. In this work we show that these two shortcomings are intertwined. We prove that machine learning models which are deeper or have higher-order interactions can efficiently represent a larger set of functions, i.e. have larger efficient reach. It follows that deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) have maximal efficient reach, restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) sub-maximal, and k-body generalizations of RBMs form a hierarchy between the two, even though all are universal. More generally, (i) we provide a full characterization of machine learning models with maximal efficient reach; (ii) we derive separations between deep and shallow models for three representation tasks; and (iii) we prove that the efficient reach of shallow models constitutes an infinite hierarchy indexed by the interaction order. The proofs draw on different methodologies, namely on (i) a recent characterization of universal spin models; (ii) computational complexity bounds for spin models; and (iii) communication complexity bounds applied to shallow models. This work shows that universal machine learning models can strongly differ in their efficient representation capabilities, and provides a theoretical foundation for heuristic observations.
papers.summary: Universal approximation theorems say nothing about efficient representation and are insensitive to depth and interaction order, and this work shows the two gaps are linked by proving that deeper models or models with higher-order interactions can efficiently represent strictly more functions, a property the authors call efficient reach. **Deep Boltzmann machines have maximal efficient reach, restricted Boltzmann machines sub-maximal, and k-body generalizations form a hierarchy in between, even though all are universal.** The authors fully characterize models with maximal efficient reach, derive deep-versus-shallow separations for three representation tasks, and prove that the efficient reach of shallow models forms an infinite hierarchy indexed by interaction order, drawing on a characterization of universal spin models, computational complexity bounds, and communication complexity bounds.

papers.title: Bank-World: A Benchmark for Evaluating Agents on Banking Workflows
papers.abstract: Bank-World is a benchmark of 50 banking tasks across two simulated institutions. Completing banking work requires more than producing the right calculation: agents must reconcile records, obtain permission, execute transactions, and keep instructions and status reports consistent as circumstances change. Bank-World tests these requirements through single-turn assignments and multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions, and revise instructions. Grading combines executable checks of recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them. Across 1,600 attempts by four models, we find that correct decisions often fail to become completed work. Agents charge fees twice, distribute the correct total in incorrect amounts among the recipients, and execute payments while approval is pending. Their strengths also differ: Sol leads single-turn completion, Opus has the highest observed multi-turn completion rate, and Grok succeeds across more multi-turn tasks but less consistently. Bank-World makes these differences inspectable through task-level results and worked examples connecting source evidence, agent decisions, and simulated consequences. We retain the task environments, executable graders, and full trajectories privately to reduce contamination and preserve the benchmark for future evaluations.
papers.summary: `Bank-World` is a benchmark of 50 tasks across two simulated banking institutions that tests whether agents can reconcile records, obtain permission, execute transactions, and keep instructions and status reports consistent as circumstances change. Tasks include single-turn assignments and multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions, and revise instructions, and grading combines executable checks on recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them. Across 1,600 attempts by four models, **correct decisions often fail to become completed work**, with agents charging fees twice, splitting the right total into wrong per-recipient amounts, and executing payments while approval is pending. `Sol` leads single-turn completion, `Opus` has the highest observed multi-turn completion rate, and `Grok` succeeds across more multi-turn tasks but less consistently, and the environments, graders, and trajectories are kept private to limit contamination.

papers.title: From the Transformer to a Formal Semantics of Coordinated Transformations
papers.abstract: We develop a formal semantics for a general class of coordinated systems of parameterized transformations, taking the Transformer as a paradigmatic starting point but abstracting from its particular mathematical instantiation. Representational vectors receive both extensional reference and ordered intensional interpretations, while parameter structures acquire relative, second-level interpretations that determine how argument properties are preserved, replaced, or combined. This yields the notion of a transforming concept: a parameterized transformation whose numerical action is coordinated with a corresponding property-level map. We then distinguish the common algebraic-semantic core of these systems from their architecture-specific functional organization, allowing different mathematical instantiations and mechanical realizations of the same abstract system type. The framework is applied to attention heads and residual connections, providing semantic explanations that depend only on the shared algebraic-semantic core and their local functional organization and therefore generalize beyond the standard Transformer. These analyses also reveal the modularity of the framework: complex architectures can be decomposed into simpler semantically coordinated subsystems whose organization may recur across different abstract system types.
papers.summary: A formal semantics is developed for a general class of coordinated systems of parameterized transformations, taking the Transformer as the starting point but abstracting away from its particular mathematics. Representational vectors receive both extensional reference and ordered intensional interpretations, parameter structures receive second-level relative interpretations describing how argument properties are preserved, replaced, or combined, and the result is the notion of a transforming concept, a parameterized transformation whose numerical action is coordinated with a property-level map. **Separating the shared algebraic-semantic core from architecture-specific functional organization lets the same abstract system type admit different mathematical instantiations and mechanical realizations**, and the framework is applied to attention heads and residual connections to give semantic explanations that generalize beyond the standard Transformer and show how complex architectures decompose into semantically coordinated subsystems.

papers.title: The Importance of Speech Genre for End-of-Turn Detector Training
papers.abstract: End-of-turn (EoT) detection has been studied mostly through features, models, and modalities, while the speech genre of the training data has drawn far less attention. We isolate this factor. Using one reproducible annotation pipeline, we build a matched pair of corpora, multi-turn human-human conversational and single-turn human-machine, and train the same streaming ConvLSTM EoT detector on each. Across four test sets the conversational model reaches up to +0.45 higher F1, driven by fewer false alarms on the mid-turn pauses and hesitations that are rare in single-turn corpora. This conversational-training effect is not specific to frame-level decoding. Under a matched complete-or-not test it also appears at the utterance level, across two encoders, but only on conversational test data. Testing only on single-turn speech, as most prior work does, therefore hides the benefit of conversational training data. Against open-source baselines, our 1.8M-parameter model attains the highest F1 on every test set.
papers.summary: End-of-turn (EoT) detection research has focused on features, models, and modalities while largely ignoring the speech genre of the training data. Using one reproducible annotation pipeline, the authors build a matched pair of corpora, multi-turn human-human conversation and single-turn human-machine speech, and train the same streaming `ConvLSTM` EoT detector on each. Across four test sets **the conversationally trained model reaches up to 0.45 higher F1**, mainly from fewer false alarms on the mid-turn pauses and hesitations that are rare in single-turn corpora. The effect also appears at the utterance level across two encoders but only on conversational test data, so evaluating only on single-turn speech as most prior work does hides it, and the 1.8M-parameter model attains the highest F1 on every test set against open-source baselines.

papers.title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?
papers.abstract: Before AI can be trusted to discover new science, it should be able to reproduce what science already knows. Reproduction provides a rigorous checkpoint for an AI scientist: the target claim is known, yet recovering it still requires translating an incomplete scientific description into an executable experiment and producing evidence that can be independently verified. Existing research-reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, where experiments share relatively homogeneous software stacks. Extending this capability across scientific disciplines introduces a different challenge: agents must operate domain-specific scientific software, make physical and numerical choices, diagnose long-running computations, and distinguish valid evidence from merely plausible outputs. We introduce PAPERBENCHX, a benchmark of 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics. Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification, and a domain-native scientific environment involving specialized scientific software. Agents must reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow that supports the target scientific claim. To evaluate scientific validity rather than surface-level agreement, we replay every submission from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% tasks under the 90% threshold. Meanwhile, mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%, indicating that substantial partial progress rarely translates into complete scientific reproduction. These results reveal a large gap between paper understanding and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence.
papers.summary: AI systems that aim to discover science should first be able to reproduce it, yet existing reproduction benchmarks cover only AI and machine learning papers with relatively homogeneous software stacks. `PAPERBENCHX` supplies 93 expert-constructed reproduction tasks across 12 research areas in electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics, each pairing a source paper with a domain-native environment built on specialized scientific software; agents must rebuild a key experiment, run and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow, which is then replayed from scratch and scored only on regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, **the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% of tasks under the 90% threshold**, while mean rubric scores of 27.53% to 59.08% show that substantial partial progress rarely turns into complete reproduction.

papers.title: When the Top Answer Decides: Gender Bias in Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models are language models built to route, classify and triage: they return option probabilities from one forward pass, and an application acts on the top answer. They are offered off the shelf, trained for the decision format rather than for fairness or any one application, and we found no bias measurement in their cards. We test TypeSafe's closed Jev and five open decision models on gender-swapped yes/no decisions about people (Tamkin et al., 2023), BBQ, StereoSet and the gender-bias studies of Fulgu and Capraro (2024). Five of the six give women significantly more favourable answers than men (+0.05 to +0.10 in log-odds), and a gender swap changes 1-3.5% of top answers (Jev's partly through its call-to-call variation). The makers' recommended confidence gate removes many biased commitments but raises the stereotyped share of those it keeps in ambiguous BBQ gender questions (granite-switch 0.76 to 0.85, pplx 0.81 to 1.00). Probes show gender preferences in the same models: all six rate violence for a greater good as more acceptable against a man than against a woman, and two default to "girl" when forced to guess a child's gender without a cue. Decision-level and probability-level measures differ, so audits should read a model as its application does.
papers.summary: Decision models are language models built to route, classify, and triage by returning option probabilities from a single forward pass so an application can act on the top answer, and their model cards contain no bias measurements. The audit tests TypeSafe's closed `Jev` and five open decision models on gender-swapped yes/no decisions about people, `BBQ`, `StereoSet`, and earlier gender-bias studies. **Five of the six models give women significantly more favourable answers than men**, with log-odds shifts of 0.05 to 0.10, and a gender swap changes 1 to 3.5% of top answers; the makers' recommended confidence gate removes many biased commitments but raises the stereotyped share of the answers it keeps on ambiguous `BBQ` gender questions. Because decision-level and probability-level measures disagree, the authors argue audits should read a model the way its application does.

papers.title: Activation Probes Are Reliable With a Handful of Positive Examples
papers.abstract: Efforts to monitor advanced AI for rare misalignments face a data challenge: abundant aligned examples but only a handful of misaligned ones. We test activation probes in this "few vs. thousands" regime on spam and honesty detection tasks. For our tasks, training with many negative examples is on average more positive-sample-efficient than balanced training for small numbers (1-10) of positive samples. We also find that LLM upsampling can provide a performance boost equivalent to roughly doubling the number of real positive samples, though excessive upsampling hurts performance. Finally, we show a positive scaling trend, where larger models are more positive-sample-efficient to probe. Our findings suggest we should leverage the large number of negative samples available to amplify the signal from rare but critical misalignment examples.
papers.summary: Monitoring advanced AI for rare misalignment faces a data imbalance: aligned examples are abundant while misaligned ones number in the handful. The authors test activation probes in this few-versus-thousands regime on spam and honesty detection, varying the number of positive examples from 1 to 10 against thousands of negatives. **Training with many negative examples is on average more positive-sample-efficient than balanced training**, LLM upsampling of positives delivers a boost roughly equivalent to doubling the real positive samples before excessive upsampling starts to hurt, and larger models need fewer positives to probe reliably.

papers.title: Multi-output LSTM soft sensors for industrial anaerobic co-digestion using LSTM-beta-VAE generative data augmentation
papers.abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) requires close monitoring of key process variables, including pH, the ratio of volatile organic acids to alkaline buffer capacity and biogas production, to maintain biological stability and prevent process failure. While mechanistic frameworks such as the Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 are highly parameterised, computationally expensive, and difficult to calibrate for real-time applications, data-driven Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks offer a potentially more adaptable alternative. However, current data-driven approaches in AD are predominantly limited to single-output architectures that focus solely on production yields, as opposed to simultaneous prediction of vital stability indicators. Furthermore, industrial AD datasets are typically sparse and skewed toward steady-state operations. Baseline evaluations demonstrated this scarcity prevents standard algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost) and unaugmented LSTMs from recognising the transition to unstable operations, resulting in poor estimation of stability indicators. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a novel generative data augmentation framework using an LSTM-beta-Variational Autoencoder coupled with a multi-output LSTM (MO-LSTM) soft sensor. By synthesising physically valid sequences of these transitions to unstable operations from one year of full-scale plant data, the method safely populates sparse regions of the feature space. Trained on this augmented dataset, the MO-LSTM achieved robust simultaneous estimation across all targets. This approach mitigates data sparsity, providing a basis for hybrid mechanistic-data-driven modelling and early-warning soft sensors in industrial bioprocesses.
papers.summary: Anaerobic digestion (AD) plants must track pH, the ratio of volatile organic acids to alkaline buffer capacity, and biogas production to avoid process failure, but industrial datasets are sparse and skewed toward steady-state operation, so `Random Forest`, `XGBoost`, and unaugmented Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks fail to recognise transitions to unstable operation. The approach uses an `LSTM-beta-VAE` generative model to synthesise physically valid sequences of these transitions from one year of full-scale plant data, then trains a multi-output LSTM (`MO-LSTM`) soft sensor on the augmented dataset. **The augmented MO-LSTM achieves robust simultaneous estimation of all target stability indicators**, which the authors position as a basis for early-warning soft sensors and hybrid mechanistic-data-driven modelling in industrial bioprocesses.

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Convolutional Networks for High-Resolution Pseudo-Label Generation from Multimodal Earth Observation Data
papers.abstract: Accurate land-cover mapping from multimodal Earth observation (EO) data remains a challenge in regions where high-resolution annotations are scarce or costly to obtain. This work introduces a quantum convolutional encoder-decoder network for pseudo-label generation using Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, guided only by coarse MODIS-derived land-cover maps. The proposed framework uses quantum-inspired convolutional blocks to enhance feature extraction and cross-sensor fusion, enabling the model to infer a fine-scale semantic structure from heterogeneous inputs. Experiments were conducted on the DFC2020 dataset, which provides a quadruple of Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 multispectral, low-resolution MODIS labels and high-resolution reference land-cover maps. The proposed training framework first learns a robust representation of multimodal inputs through the reconstruction branch before any supervision from low-resolution labels is applied. This self-supervised stage enables the model to capture a fine-scale spectral-spatial structure, which is then used to generate high-resolution pseudo-labels. These pseudo-labels are subsequently evaluated through classification metrics on the test data, demonstrating that the proposed approach produces more spatially coherent and class-consistent compared to classical baselines. The results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired deep learning to improve label generation in low-annotation remote sensing scenarios, offering a scalable path towards high-quality land-cover products for EO applications.
