We introduce eCoMAE, an evidential masked pretraining method for multivariate time series that explicitly aligns predictive evidence with what is observed. eCoMAE combines block-wise time-step masking with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma decoder and three observability-aware mechanisms: uncertainty-weighted mean consistency on positions visible in both a masked view and a reference pass, evidence suppression on masked positions, and representation consistency across stochastic masks. On IMPTC benchmark for VRU intention prediction under leave-one-environment-out weather shift, eCoMAE improves the strongest baseline from 0.7971 to 0.8068 in OOD accuracy and from 0.0718 to 0.0648 in OOD AURC. Additional evaluation on pedestrian trajectory forecasting across IMPTC, Waymo, nuScenes, and inD further yields the best fine-tuning MSE on all four datasets. These results show that observability-aligned evidential pretraining improves reliability under shift and remains effective beyond the primary benchmark.
papers.summary: Predicting the motion of vulnerable road users (VRUs) such as pedestrians must cope with partial observations and distribution shift, so calibrated uncertainty matters alongside accuracy. `eCoMAE` is a masked pretraining method for multivariate time series that pairs block-wise masking with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma decoder and three mechanisms tying predictive evidence to what is observed: uncertainty-weighted consistency on positions visible in both views, evidence suppression on masked positions, and representation consistency across random masks. On the `IMPTC` intention benchmark under leave-one-environment-out weather shift it **raises out-of-distribution accuracy from 0.7971 to 0.8068 and lowers out-of-distribution AURC from 0.0718 to 0.0648**, and it gives the best fine-tuned trajectory error on `IMPTC`, `Waymo`, `nuScenes`, and `inD`.

papers.title: Accumulating Pruning Constraints: New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT
papers.abstract: We present deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT on $n$ variables exactly in time $\Ostar(2^{(1-\gamma)n})$, for a fixed $\gamma>0$, on several classes of instances whose clause density may grow with $n$. Our main tool extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm. When the search gives a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values of the variable yields a pruning constraint that is satisfied by some optimal assignment. Accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of the assignments. The classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on graphs generated by a stochastic block model. In a semirandom formula, the pairs of variables that may share a clause are arbitrary, and the clauses on these pairs are random. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms are still exact on every input, and the time bound holds with high probability over the input. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances. Beyond these classes, the pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and we expect them to be of practical relevance for general formulas, in particular for sparse ones, where each constraint involves only a few variables.
papers.summary: Solving Max 2-SAT exactly in less than brute-force time over all assignments, while using only polynomial space, is open for most dense instance classes. The authors extend the classic DPLL branching algorithm: whenever the search assigns a variable its less promising value, comparing the two options yields a pruning constraint that some optimal assignment must satisfy, and accumulating these constraints along a branch discards all but an exponentially small fraction of assignments. This gives **deterministic polynomial-space algorithms running in time 2 to the power (1-γ)n for a fixed γ greater than zero** on formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expanders and stochastic block model graphs. The pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and the authors expect them to help on general sparse formulas.

papers.title: A physics-informed uncertainty-aware surrogate for $p$-$n$ junction diodes
papers.abstract: We develop an uncertainty-aware physics-informed surrogate for a one-dimensional $p$-$n$ junction diode, conditioned on device length, doping and bias. Using the internal state of the device as predicted by the surrogate we develop a test-suite of quantities of interest including the terminal current, depletion width, peak field and stored charge. The formalism and the quantities are can be extended to asymmetric junction and two-dimensional diodes as shown by means of benchmark analysis. For the one-dimensional symmetric junction surrogate, we obtain 0.11% median $L_1$ error on the electrostatic potential, and 1.5% and 0.61% on the electron and hole densities. Finally, we develop an uncertainty analysis which determines the validity of surrogate answer within the user-specified tolerance.
papers.summary: Simulating a p-n junction diode from first principles is costly when device length, doping, and bias all vary. The authors train a physics-informed neural surrogate that predicts the internal electrostatic state of a one-dimensional diode conditioned on those parameters, then derive terminal current, depletion width, peak field, and stored charge from the predicted state, with benchmarks showing extension to asymmetric and two-dimensional junctions. The symmetric one-dimensional surrogate reaches **a 0.11% median L1 error on electrostatic potential** and 1.5% and 0.61% on electron and hole densities, and an uncertainty analysis flags whether a prediction falls within a user-specified tolerance.

papers.title: Enhancing Atrial Fibrillation Detection Through Hyperparameter Optimization
papers.abstract: This study explores the role of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) in enhancing the detection of Atrial Fibrillation (AF) using both machine learning and deep learning models. We evaluated a range of standard classifiers - Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost classifiers, alongside deep learning architectures including Recurrent Neural Networks, Deep Neural Networks, and Siamese Neural Networks. To fine-tune these models, we applied four HPO methods: Genetic Algorithm, Hyperband, Optuna, and SMAC3. The experiments were conducted using inter-patient and intra- patient data splits to assess model generalization and robustness in the presence of class imbalance, which is reflective of real-world AF occurrence. Our results, based on PhysioNet electrocardiogram datasets, showed that the Hyperband-optimized XGBoost model outperformed all others, achieving a peak F1 score of 96.95%. These findings highlight the critical role of suitable HPO strategies in enhancing the accuracy and robustness of AF classification outcomes in clinical settings.
papers.summary: Detecting atrial fibrillation (AF) from electrocardiograms depends heavily on how classifiers are tuned, yet hyperparameter optimization (HPO) strategies are rarely compared systematically for this task. The authors tune Decision Tree, Random Forest, and `XGBoost` classifiers along with recurrent, deep, and Siamese neural networks using four HPO methods: a genetic algorithm, `Hyperband`, `Optuna`, and `SMAC3`, evaluated under both inter-patient and intra-patient splits of `PhysioNet` ECG data with realistic class imbalance. **A `Hyperband`-tuned `XGBoost` model performed best with a peak F1 score of 96.95%**.

papers.title: How Much Should a VLA Trust Its Reasoning? Step-Level Guidance as a Measured Action-Value Function
papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) policies write a reasoning trace and then decode the action from it. A wrong trace yields a wrong action, and even a correct-looking trace can mislead the plan. Existing remedies ask whether the reasoning is right. We ask how strongly it should steer. CoC-CFG applies classifier-free guidance between the policy's context and the same context without the reasoning span. One weight per Euler step attenuates or amplifies the reasoning, and w=1 recovers the original policy. We treat the choice of this weight as a Markov decision process whose action values are measured, not bootstrapped. With the expert frozen and the noise fixed, applying a weight for one step and finishing the plan under the current controller returns that weight's value exactly. Q-adaptive guidance fits these values with small critics and improves the controller conservatively. In the Alpasim driving simulator it outperforms every fixed weight and online RL (SAC, GRPO) in open loop, and in closed loop it passes 262 of 300 scenes, against 252 for the original policy. On held-out frames of the Waymo end-to-end driving benchmark, its first three stages outperform every fixed weight, four adaptive-guidance methods, SAC and GRPO. On the hidden test set, a frozen Alpamayo 1.5 with rule-based camera and vehicle conversions and Q-adaptive guidance sets a new state of the art among published methods: 8.135159 rater feedback score, against 8.079 for the best published method.
papers.summary: A reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) policy writes a reasoning trace and then decodes an action from it, so a flawed trace yields a bad action, and prior fixes ask only whether the trace is correct rather than how strongly it should steer. `CoC-CFG` applies classifier-free guidance between the policy's full context and the same context with the reasoning span removed, with one weight per Euler step that amplifies or attenuates the reasoning, and choosing that weight is framed as a Markov decision process whose action values are measured by rolling out the frozen expert rather than bootstrapped. `Q-adaptive guidance` fits small critics to those values and updates the controller conservatively, beating every fixed weight plus `SAC` and `GRPO` in the `Alpasim` simulator and passing 262 of 300 closed-loop scenes against 252 for the original policy. On the hidden test set of the `Waymo` end-to-end driving benchmark, **a frozen `Alpamayo 1.5` with Q-adaptive guidance reaches a rater feedback score of 8.135 against 8.079 for the best published method**.

papers.title: Efficient Learning of Mechanism Designs and Compositionality
papers.abstract: Learning mechanism behaviour requires a representation of how connected parts jointly constrain motion. We study whether exposing reusable constraint subassemblies improves prediction from limited data. Assur-KB represents planar mechanisms through irreducible modules, boundary interfaces, and solve dependencies while retaining source geometry. Our theoretical results characterize transfer through module interfaces and establish physical limits arising from missing interface information and accumulated sensitivity. To test the representation claim directly, the experimental design compares matched mechanism-curve pairs across training budgets within the same multilayer-perceptron family. This controlled comparison establishes the utility of the complete representation in the evaluated learning setting. Assur-derived features provide a geometric-mean $1.8\times$ advantage in sample efficiency over flattened adjacency and position inputs across budgets of 50-10,000 mechanisms. Separate experiments establish invariance under tested joint relabelings, higher valid-generation rates under dyadic composition, and a coarser structural index over 10.02 million mechanisms. In summary, the theory and experiments identify how physical constraint structure supports limited-data prediction and which interface conditions govern compositional reuse.
papers.summary: Learning to predict how a planar mechanism moves from few examples requires a representation that captures how its linked parts jointly constrain motion. `Assur-KB` describes mechanisms through irreducible constraint modules, their boundary interfaces, and solve dependencies while keeping the source geometry, and the accompanying theory characterizes when knowledge transfers across module interfaces and what physical limits arise from missing interface information and accumulated sensitivity. In controlled comparisons across training budgets of 50 to 10,000 mechanisms within the same multilayer-perceptron family, **Assur-derived features give a geometric-mean 1.8x sample-efficiency advantage over flattened adjacency and position inputs**, along with invariance under tested joint relabelings and higher valid-generation rates under dyadic composition.

papers.title: Human--AI Interactions as First-Class Data: A Formal Interaction Model and Runtime for Explainable AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.
papers.summary: AI assistants embedded in notebooks, scientific workflows, and development tools treat each prompt-response exchange as transient, which makes interactions hard to reproduce, replay, or analyze. The authors propose the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (`HAIDL`), a formal model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired syntax that records each interaction as a structured object holding computational context, user request, prompt payload, response, feedback, provenance, and model metadata. `HAIDL-X` implements it as JupyterLab middleware that captures user-bot state, builds contextualized prompts, talks to AI providers, collects feedback, and stores interactions in a repository, and a learning layer maps these objects and notebook execution traces into **reproducible measures of engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas**.

papers.title: FIDE: Fiber-Informed Differentiable Experimental Design for Reference-Relative Law Dynamics
papers.abstract: Aggregate measurements generally leave an evolving population law underdetermined, so different measurement systems can be equally adequate for a scientific task while constraining different aspects of the law. We study how to resolve this residual design freedom in baseline-preserving settings, where an existing dynamical model remains the working baseline outside quantities explicitly valued by the task. \textbf{F}iber-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{D}ifferentiable \textbf{E}xperimental Design (\textbf{FIDE}) completes each candidate's aggregate constraints by information projection relative to a common frozen reference, then ranks scientifically adequate designs by the dynamical revision required to realize the resulting completed paths. The resulting \emph{Full action} is the minimum mean-squared velocity correction needed to realize a completed path; equivalently, its square root is the sharp reference-relative expectation-rate discrepancy over a gradient-normalized Sobolev class. This defines a conditional minimum-revision principle for baseline-preserving design rather than a generic truth-recovery objective. Experiments show that this preference changes sensor selection, can help or harm withheld downstream predictions depending on baseline reliability, can be used prospectively from aggregate predictions, and remains computationally usable for a $32$-dimensional configuration law.
papers.summary: Aggregate measurements rarely pin down an evolving population distribution, so several measurement systems can serve a scientific task equally well while constraining different parts of the dynamics. Fiber-Informed Differentiable Experimental Design (`FIDE`) completes each candidate design's aggregate constraints by information projection onto a common frozen reference model, then ranks adequate designs by the minimal mean-squared velocity correction needed for the baseline dynamics to realize the completed path, a quantity whose square root equals a reference-relative expectation-rate discrepancy over a gradient-normalized Sobolev class. Experiments show this minimum-revision preference **changes which sensors get selected and can help or harm withheld downstream predictions depending on how reliable the baseline is**, while remaining computationally usable for a 32-dimensional configuration law.

papers.title: HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.
papers.summary: Large language models are now used to generate search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO), but the harness that discovers those operators is itself usually fixed. `HEMO` makes that harness a self-evolving target: it keeps a persistent harness state and revises one module at a time, covering which past experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how search steps are orchestrated, with a discounted upper-confidence-bound scheduler steering updates toward the modules currently paying off. A persistent memory filesystem carries candidate outcomes and diagnostics across harness versions so later states build on earlier experience. Across **eight MOCO tasks and two structurally different evolutionary backbones** it outperforms conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based operator-design baselines and transfers to related tasks.

papers.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information
papers.abstract: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts with a learned world model. We obtain that, when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, which floors its TD target and attributes this floor to the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, to be trained and improved with this signal, solves a memory task with reduced context.
papers.summary: Memory in reinforcement learning poses two costs: attention must score every stored item to find the relevant one, which strains robots under latency and energy limits, and when a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must travel back across the whole sequence. The authors argue both are governed by the value of information, which they estimate from archived rollouts with a learned world model. Read at the observation, this quantity gives **a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action**, which floors its temporal-difference target and credits the observation that earned it, while read at the decision it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, which the authors intend to train and improve with this signal, already solves a memory task with a reduced context.

papers.title: AI Cosmos: An Agentic Infra for Situated Learning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance during learning, yet these gains do not necessarily reflect learners' ability to thereafter apply the knowledge and skills independently. We present AI Cosmos, an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that organizes learning around two complementary principles: scenario-based participation and cumulative assets of practice. AI Cosmos organizes learners and role-specialized agents within learning scenarios that integrate task-relevant knowledge and, when needed, executable workbenches. An asset-memory loop preserves the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies. We evaluate scenario-based interaction through two preregistered randomized controlled studies examining the acquisition of legal reasoning and programming competence, holding the same underlying LLM across conditions. AI Cosmos achieves greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.
papers.summary: Learners who get help from a large language model often perform better during the task without being able to apply the skill independently afterward. `AI Cosmos` is an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that places learners and role-specialized agents inside scenarios bundling task-relevant knowledge and, where needed, executable workbenches, and an asset-memory loop stores the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies. In **two preregistered randomized controlled studies that held the underlying LLM fixed across conditions**, it produced larger learning gains than a conventional LLM for legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.

papers.title: Hybrid AI Patterns: Thirteen Ways to Couple Language Models with Rules, and How to Choose Among Them
papers.abstract: Language models handle text well, and rule engines give conclusions with proofs. Systems that combine the two are usually described by example, and the same coupling turns up under different names in agent frameworks, guardrail toolkits and neuro-symbolic research. This document defines thirteen patterns for coupling a language model with an executable rule language, in the catalogue form introduced for object-oriented design: intent, motivation, applicability, participants, collaborations, consequences, implementation, known uses and related patterns. Four patterns concern what crosses the boundary between model and rules, five who controls whom, three how the model takes part in the reasoning, and one how knowledge is kept over time. Five invariants hold for every combination, and five failure patterns name the couplings that break them. We relate the catalogue to published pattern catalogues and taxonomies of hybrid and neuro-symbolic systems and show where they overlap with it. A decision guide leads from a problem to a pattern. It rests on our measurements, including the cases in which a model alone did as well as the hybrid or better, and it reports what each design cost.
papers.summary: Systems that pair a language model with an executable rule engine are usually described by example, and the same coupling appears under different names in agent frameworks, guardrail toolkits, and neuro-symbolic research. The authors define **thirteen patterns in the intent, motivation, applicability, participants, and consequences form of object-oriented design pattern catalogues**: four about what crosses the model-rules boundary, five about who controls whom, three about how the model takes part in reasoning, and one about keeping knowledge over time, plus five invariants every combination must hold and five failure patterns that break them. A decision guide maps a problem to a pattern and rests on the authors' own measurements, including cases where a model alone matched or beat the hybrid, with the cost of each design reported.

papers.title: UPPAAi: Towards LLM-Assisted Modeling, Verification, Analysis and Synthesis
papers.abstract: For more than three decades, UPPAAL has supported the modelling and analysis of real-time and cyber-physical systems. Yet building a suitable model, formalising the intended properties, choosing analysis techniques and interpreting counterexamples remain iterative tasks that demand substantial expertise. Large language models (LLMs) can offer plausible explanations and even solutions, but they are not necessarily correct. We present UPPAAI, an extension of UPPAAL in which users construct, explain, debug and specify models in dialogue with an LLM. The guiding principle is that the user requests, the LLM proposes, explains and orchestrates, and UPPAAL verifies. UPPAAI exposes the UPPAAL editor, queries and verifier through a Tools API. We report on seven case studies, from explaining to a newcomer to learning a controller, covering timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata and strategy learning. LLMs proved to be extremely helpful in not just generating solutions but also pro-actively suggesting relevant UPPAAL features it was not asked about.
papers.summary: `UPPAAL` has supported modelling and verification of real-time and cyber-physical systems for over thirty years, but building a model, formalising properties, picking analysis techniques, and reading counterexamples still demand deep expertise, while large language models offer plausible but not necessarily correct help. `UPPAAI` extends `UPPAAL` so users construct, explain, debug, and specify models in dialogue with an LLM under the principle that the user requests, the LLM proposes and orchestrates, and `UPPAAL` verifies, with the editor, queries, and verifier exposed through a Tools API. Across **seven case studies spanning timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata, and strategy learning**, the LLM generated solutions and proactively suggested relevant `UPPAAL` features it had not been asked about.

papers.title: EPC-RawDC: Equivariant Physics Constrained 3D Diffusion with Raw Data Consistency for CBCT to CT Image Synthesis
papers.abstract: Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for image guided and adaptive radiotherapy, but scatter, noise, reconstruction artifacts, and inaccurate Hounsfield units limit its quantitative use. Recent diffusion approaches for CBCT to CT synthesis remain largely image driven, with limited use of the underlying acquisition physics. We propose EPC-RawDC, a conditional 3D latent diffusion framework that combines volumetric generative modeling with two complementary constraints derived from the same scanner specific CBCT forward model. First, geometry equivariant projection constraint exploits the rotational equivariance of the CBCT forward operator by supervising the synthesized CT through correspondingly transformed reference projections. Second, raw data consistency uses noisy projection measurements of the individual acquisition as scan specific supervision during training. The framework was evaluated on two independent clinical cohorts with distinct scanner geometries and projection sources. For JUST, the physics constraints used measured clinical raw CBCT projections acquired with an Elekta system, whereas for SynthRAD2025 the projection data were simulated from the reference CT using a Varian geometry with Poisson photon statistics. EPC-RawDC achieved an SSIM of 0.97 in both cohorts and improved PSNR over DDPM by 2.66 dB on SynthRAD2025 and 2.10 dB on JUST, while reducing mean MAE by 20.3% and 19.0%, respectively. On SynthRAD2025, projection consistency and equivariant errors were reduced by 55.0% and 41.4% relative to DDPM. These results demonstrate that combining a volumetric diffusion prior with scanner geometry and scan specific projection measurements improves quantitative CBCT to CT synthesis across both simulated and measured projection domains. Code available after publication at https://github.com/ALZAHRAALTALIB/EPC-RawDC.
papers.summary: Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) guides adaptive radiotherapy but suffers from scatter, noise, reconstruction artifacts, and unreliable Hounsfield units, and existing diffusion models that translate CBCT to CT mostly ignore the acquisition physics. `EPC-RawDC` is a conditional 3D latent diffusion model with two constraints derived from the scanner-specific CBCT forward model: a geometry-equivariant projection loss that supervises the synthesized CT through correspondingly transformed reference projections, and raw data consistency that uses each scan's own noisy projections as supervision during training. On two clinical cohorts with different scanner geometries it reaches an SSIM of 0.97 and **improves PSNR over `DDPM` by 2.66 dB on `SynthRAD2025` and 2.10 dB on `JUST`**, while cutting mean MAE by 20.3% and 19.0%.

papers.title: Rethinking Pre-pretraining
papers.abstract: We report that allocating compute to synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) never outperforms pure natural-language training in our compute-matched experiments. This holds across four PPT curricula (k-Dyck, neural cellular automata (NCA), declarative reference corpora, and code) and three training regimes: data-constrained, data-unconstrained, and a high token-to-parameter-ratio regime (881M parameters trained on 50B tokens). When natural language is scarce, repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum on natural-language validation loss, with no consistent downstream accuracy advantage from PPT. We find that PPT gains reported in prior work are sensitive to the weight initialization scheme. In an NCA reproduction, we recover a 5.4% perplexity improvement from PPT under the original initialization scheme. An alternative scheme improves both methods, but the no-PPT baseline more, closing the gap between them. However, when PPT receives additional compute rather than a share of the natural-language budget, gains persist at small natural-language budgets even with improved initialization, but disappear by 1B tokens. Finally, models forget what they learn during PPT in subsequent natural-language training; interleaving the same data throughout training prevents forgetting, but does not significantly improve natural-language performance. Our results suggest limited benefits of synthetic pre-pretraining as a distinct training stage and motivate rethinking how such data are used in language model training.
papers.summary: Synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT), where a language model first trains on formal data such as Dyck languages or cellular automata before natural text, has been reported to help in earlier work. In compute-matched experiments across four curricula (`k-Dyck`, neural cellular automata, declarative reference corpora, and code) and three regimes including an 881M-parameter model trained on 50B tokens, **allocating compute to PPT never beat pure natural-language training**, and repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum when natural text was scarce. Earlier gains turn out to be sensitive to weight initialization: an alternative scheme improves the no-PPT baseline more and closes the gap, gains persist only when PPT gets extra compute at small budgets and vanish by 1B tokens, and models forget PPT content during later training unless the data is interleaved, which prevents forgetting but does not improve natural-language performance.

papers.title: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization
papers.abstract:
Activation steering changes what a language model generates by editing its hidden states at inference time. Its most common form adds one vector, the difference of class means (DiM), to every hidden state. CHaRS (concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering) uses optimal transport instead: an entropic plan pairs the clusters of the two classes, and each hidden state moves along a mixture of the cluster displacements, weighted toward its nearest clusters. We study this family of clustered optimal-transport maps for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B, and ask what the plan adds to DiM and whether that survives INT8 and NF4 quantization.
  We prove an identity: whatever the plan, the displacements averaged with the cluster sizes as weights equal DiM, so a clustered map can differ from DiM only for tokens whose routing weights depart from the cluster sizes. In the CHaRS protocol they stay close, and CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens, which routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters, leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite at steering strength 3 (toxic-bert), where DiM already removes 76-85% of it. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At equal strength the variant has somewhat higher perplexity, but at matched toxicity it is slightly more fluent than DiM. Yet a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity, so the role of treating tokens differently remains open.
  Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting it adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.
papers.summary: Activation steering edits a language model's hidden states at inference time, most often by adding a single difference-of-means (`DiM`) vector, while concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering (`CHaRS`) instead uses an entropic optimal-transport plan to pair clusters of the two classes and moves each hidden state along a mixture of cluster displacements. Studying this family for toxicity mitigation in `Gemma-2-2B` and `Granite-3.1-2B`, the authors prove that the size-weighted average of the displacements always equals `DiM`, so a clustered map differs only for tokens whose routing weights depart from cluster sizes, and under the `CHaRS` protocol it is statistically equivalent to `Mean-AcT`, which adds `DiM` at every layer, in all eight pre-specified tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens **leaves 37-39% less toxicity than `DiM` on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite** at steering strength 3, though a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less, so the value of treating tokens differently remains open. The variant keeps its advantage under INT8 and NF4 quantization, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting adds no significant toxicity.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) systems in healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics are often trained on logs that record variables which legal, ethical, or logistical constraints later prevent collecting at deployment time, a setting called runtime confounding. Because earlier decisions shape later states, observations, and action assignments, the missing information can bias learning in ways that compound over time rather than staying confined to a single decision point. The authors contribute policy learning algorithms for this setting, semi-parametric efficient off-policy evaluation procedures, and **diagnostics that quantify the price of runtime confounding**.

papers.title: Localizing Concepts in Visual Autoregressive Models
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal routing of visual concepts is crucial for the safe and controllable adaptation of generative models. While concept localization has been widely studied in diffusion models, the emerging paradigm of next-scale visual autoregressive models remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce LoCo, the first model-agnostic framework to localize where and when specific concepts emerge within autoregressive models. Driven by the native coarse-to-fine nature of next-scale generation, our method precisely maps conceptual knowledge across three distinct dimensions: Layer, Scale, and Position. To systematically localize and evaluate concept routing without context bias, we propose LoCoBench, a comprehensive dataset spanning 10 diverse categories. Extensive probing on image and video autoregressive models like Infinity, HunyuanImage-3.0, and InfinityStar shows that the localized positions are both interpretable and causally related to concept emergence. Building on these insights, we apply our localization method to three key applications: concept erasure, model personalization, and adversarial concept injection. Experiments demonstrate that our targeted intervention achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially reducing computational overhead while preserving benign utility. Overall, our findings offer insights into how conceptual knowledge is routed during autoregressive generation, introducing a practical pathway for more interpretable, efficient, and secure adaptation.
papers.summary: Concept localization has been studied extensively in diffusion models but not in next-scale visual autoregressive generators. `LoCo` is a model-agnostic framework that maps where and when a concept emerges across three dimensions of such models, namely layer, scale, and position, and `LoCoBench` is a companion dataset spanning 10 categories built to probe concept routing without context bias. Probing `Infinity`, `HunyuanImage-3.0`, and `InfinityStar` shows that the localized positions are interpretable and causally tied to concept emergence, and **targeted interventions built on them reach state-of-the-art results for concept erasure, personalization, and adversarial concept injection** at substantially lower computational cost while preserving benign capability.

papers.title: Agentic process evidence
papers.abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
papers.summary: AI agents now open pull requests, choose dependencies, interpret test failures, and change infrastructure across the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), yet their reasoning and tool calls vanish when a session ends, and the git log records only what changed, not which model acted, which tools it called, or who was accountable. The authors frame three procedural problems: the agentic coder as a supply-chain vector, enforcing organizational policy guardrails, and keeping the agent aligned to its assigned task. They propose Agentic Process Evidence (`APE`), **a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation that links agent sessions to their outcomes**, which supports in-toto style attestation, enables Policy-as-Code control with human review only where needed, and is aligned with relevant regulations.

papers.title: Learning Safe Flow Matching Robot Policies from Binary Feasibility Oracles
papers.abstract: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.
papers.summary: Flow-based action generation in robot foundation models does not guarantee that the produced actions respect physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance, and in practice the feasible set is often reachable only through a black-box oracle that answers yes or no. The proposed differentiable safeguard queries that binary oracle to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass and extracts local boundary information to supply constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass, and it is applied identically during training and inference with discrete-time flow matching. On obstacle-aware manipulation tasks the method reaches **100% constraint satisfaction** while keeping task performance intact, without any explicit or differentiable constraint model.

papers.title: Upcycling Language Models for Multiple Specialized Domains
papers.abstract: Effective multi-domain adaptation of large language models requires prioritizing relevant domain knowledge while minimizing interference from irrelevant domains. Existing approaches commonly use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to train a separate adapter for each domain and combine these adapters within one model. However, they either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or dynamically weight adapters while still activating all of them including irrelevant ones. Additionally, while efficient, their low-rank structure limits performance. In contrast, upcycling is a model expansion method that adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer offering larger capacity than LoRA approaches. In this paper, we propose Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling) for multi-domain adaptation. We introduce a new domain-aware supervision that allows the router to effectively learn to distinguish domains by selecting the appropriate experts. During fine-tuning on each new domain, we update only the corresponding expert and router while freezing all other parameters. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest average performance across the adapted domains compared to baselines while retaining general performance. With just 256 examples per domain for router supervision, DS-Upcycling achieves 90-98% routing accuracy after adaptation compared with 43-70% for routers trained without our approach.
papers.summary: Adapting a large language model to several domains at once with per-domain Low-Rank Adaptation (`LoRA`) adapters either weights all adapters equally regardless of input or activates irrelevant ones, and the low-rank structure caps performance. Domain-Specialized Upcycling (`DS-Upcycling`) instead expands dense Transformer layers into experts with a router, adds domain-aware supervision so the router learns to pick the right expert, and fine-tunes each new domain by updating only its own expert and the router while everything else stays frozen. The method attains the highest average score across adapted domains among the compared baselines while retaining general capability, and **just 256 router-supervision examples per domain yield 90-98% routing accuracy versus 43-70% without the supervision**.

papers.title: Reward-Adaptive Co-Evolution of Policy and Rubric
papers.abstract: Rubric-based rewards provide fine-grained, interpretable supervision for open-ended reinforcement learning, where holistic scalar rewards struggle to capture multidimensional response quality. Static rubrics can lose discriminative power as the policy distribution evolves, while existing policy--rubric co-evolution methods rely on globally prescribed update schedules that ignore heterogeneous reward informativeness. We introduce RACE, a Reward-Adaptive Co-Evolution framework. At the group level, per-rollout-group training-signal routing classifies groups as informative, diversity-collapsed, or rubric-failed, updating the policy only with informative groups while caching rubric failures. At the phase level, event-triggered phase switching enters rubric optimization upon persistent reward saturation and returns when rubric-reward improvement plateaus. Rubric phases train the generator on cached pairs using a frozen judge and a scale-normalized pairwise-margin reward. Across both levels, online threshold adaptation adjusts routing and switching thresholds through proportional control. Under a unified evaluation protocol, RACE achieves the highest average performance and outperforms the strongest fixed-alternation baseline on all eight tasks, while improving rubric discrimination.
papers.summary: Rubric-based rewards give fine-grained, interpretable supervision for open-ended reinforcement learning, but static rubrics lose discriminative power as the policy shifts, and existing co-evolution schemes update rubrics on fixed global schedules that ignore how informative each reward actually is. Reward-Adaptive Co-Evolution (`RACE`) classifies each rollout group as informative, diversity-collapsed, or rubric-failed and trains the policy only on informative groups while caching the failures, switches into a rubric-optimization phase when reward saturation persists and back when rubric gains plateau, and adapts both thresholds online via proportional control. Rubric phases train the generator on the cached pairs with a frozen judge and a scale-normalized pairwise-margin reward. Under a unified protocol `RACE` posts the highest average score and **beats the strongest fixed-alternation baseline on all eight tasks** while also improving rubric discrimination.

papers.title: Coupled Guidance for Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.
papers.summary: Guidance steers diffusion sampling for both stochastic robotic controllers and controlled image synthesis, but transplanting diffusion guidance into flow-matching models has proven unstable. A theoretical analysis shows why: the naive translation breaks the coupling distribution the flow-matching model was trained with, weakening control over sampling accuracy. `Coupled Guidance` is derived from a geometric view that exploits that coupling structure, and across a collision-avoidance task in `ManiSkill3`, four dexterous manipulation tasks from `Adroit`, and inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring on `ImageNet-128` and `CelebA-HQ-256`, it **improves sample quality and guidance stability on every task with no added overhead**.

papers.title: D-MOD: Diffusion mode estimation for accelerated MRI
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are powerful priors for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but most current methods are posterior samplers, which return a random draw from the posterior. A reproducible and high-quality reconstruction often requires averaging many samples, resulting in a high computational cost. We introduce D-MOD, a fast algorithm that instead provides a posterior mode. It uses a minorize-maximize algorithm on a lower bound of the smoothed log-posterior, which provably increases the objective. Each iteration draws S noisy samples of the current estimate at the current noise level, denoises them with a pretrained diffusion model, and combines their average with the measured k-space through a conjugate-gradient (CG) solve. We anneal the noise levels, as the distance between the bound and its target decays quadratically with noise. On fastMRI brain (T1, T2, FLAIR), a single D-MOD reconstruction exceeds, in PSNR, the 10-sample finite-MMSE estimates of DPS, DAPS and SNORE-P and stays within 0.31 dB of the strongest baselines (DiffPIR, DDS). This approach thus provides a fast deterministic reconstruction algorithm (11-73 times faster than MMSE estimates), which is useful in a clinical setting.
papers.summary: Diffusion priors for accelerated MRI reconstruction are usually deployed as posterior samplers, so a reproducible, high-quality image requires averaging many draws at high computational cost. `D-MOD` instead seeks a posterior mode through a minorize-maximize scheme on a lower bound of the smoothed log-posterior, where each iteration perturbs the current estimate with noise, denoises the samples with a pretrained diffusion model, and reconciles their average with the measured k-space through a conjugate-gradient (CG) solve, with noise levels annealed because the bound tightens quadratically as noise shrinks. On `fastMRI` brain scans a single reconstruction exceeds the 10-sample estimates of `DPS`, `DAPS`, and `SNORE-P` in PSNR, stays within 0.31 dB of `DiffPIR` and `DDS`, and runs **11-73 times faster than the sampling-based estimates**.

papers.title: It Takes Two to Probe, Thousands to Retrieve: Putting Vision--Language Probes to the Retrieval Test
papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) are tested for fine-grained understanding with image--text matching probes, a model must prefer the correct image or caption over handcrafted negative. In retrieval, the correct item must beat thousands of alternatives. We measure how these two evaluation methods relate by using two probing benchmarks, \svo{} and SugarCrepe, for retrieval tasks. For 100 image and caption queries we judge the top-10 retrievals from full dataset of six VLMs, with human annotators and an LLM assessor. We than compare how well models rank pool of items on the same queries, while changing only where the negatives comes from: the benchmark, a random draw, or the judged-incorrect retrievals of other models. On \svo{} the accuracy of retrieving a positive over handcrafted negatives is significantly higher than for retrieved ones (the correct item is preferred in 85\% against 77\% of the time). Using pool of ten retrieved negatives leads to same accuracy as when one uses pool of 200 to 430 random negatives. On SugarCrepe the order is reversed: its handcrafted negatives are harder than the retrieved ones. Incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores on \svo{}, where the top-ranked item is correct for 54--90\% of the queries under human labels against 6--21\% under the benchmark's labels. However, we detect no association between passing the probe for a query and retrieving a correct item first. The LLM assessor o3 agrees with individual annotators ($\kappa$ 0.57--0.61) slightly less than they agree with each other (0.64--0.68).
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are usually probed for fine-grained understanding by asking them to prefer a correct image or caption over one handcrafted negative, whereas retrieval requires the correct item to beat thousands of alternatives, and how the two evaluations relate has not been measured. The authors convert two probing benchmarks, a subject-verb-object benchmark and `SugarCrepe`, into retrieval tasks, have human annotators and the LLM assessor `o3` judge the top-10 retrievals of six models for 100 queries, and then rerank the same queries while varying only where the negatives come from. On the subject-verb-object benchmark handcrafted negatives are easier than retrieved ones (85% versus 77% preference for the positive), ten retrieved negatives are as hard as 200 to 430 random ones, and incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores, since **the top-ranked item is correct for 54-90% of queries under human labels against 6-21% under the benchmark's labels**. On `SugarCrepe` the handcrafted negatives are the harder ones, and passing a probe on a query shows no association with retrieving a correct item first.

papers.title: Does System Size Matter in Uncertainty Quantification for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials?
papers.abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) commonly use uncertainty estimates to flag out-of-distribution (OOD) configurations and select structures for active learning. A key question is whether the resulting structure-level uncertainty scores remain comparable across different system sizes. A common practice is to aggregate per-atom uncertainties by their mean or maximum and compare the resulting score against a fixed threshold, implicitly assuming such comparability. We test this assumption across several in-distribution (ID)/OOD pairs by characterizing both aggregations as a function of atom count. The two aggregations exhibit distinct size dependencies. Mean aggregation remains size-independent for homogeneous systems but loses sensitivity to defects in large cells. In contrast, maximum aggregation grows with system size for ID systems while remaining approximately flat for defect-containing systems, narrowing the ID-OOD gap in a manner consistent with extreme-value statistics. Although highly uncertain atoms in large structures may indicate novel local environments, retraining on these structures yields little improvement, in contrast to retraining on OOD structures constructed to lie outside the training distribution. Our results reveal a practical limitation of size-unaware uncertainty criteria and motivate size-aware calibration for more reliable OOD detection in large-scale atomistic simulations.
papers.summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) rely on uncertainty estimates to flag out-of-distribution (OOD) atomic configurations and pick structures for active learning, typically by aggregating per-atom uncertainties with a mean or maximum and comparing to a fixed threshold, which silently assumes the score is comparable across system sizes. Testing that assumption on several in-distribution (ID) and OOD pairs as a function of atom count shows the two aggregations behave differently: the mean stays size-independent for homogeneous systems but loses sensitivity to defects in large cells, while **the maximum grows with system size for in-distribution systems yet stays flat for defect-containing ones, narrowing the ID-OOD gap in line with extreme-value statistics**. Retraining on large structures flagged only because of highly uncertain atoms yields little improvement compared with retraining on structures deliberately built outside the training distribution, motivating size-aware calibration for OOD detection in large-scale atomistic simulations.

papers.title: Escaping Path Mirages in Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at https://umlic.github.io/papers/BGP/.
papers.summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning struggles in stochastic long-horizon settings because compounding value errors lead agents to overcommit to trajectories that only succeeded by chance in the dataset, a failure the authors call path mirage. Branch-aware Graph Planning (`BGP`) identifies high-variability points in the data as graph nodes and learns goal-conditioned edges through segmented learning, so the planner can steer around unreliable branches and reduce avoidable stochasticity along a path. On a range of `OGBench` tasks `BGP` **substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned methods**, including in highly stochastic long-horizon environments.

papers.title: DynaRev: Benchmarking Web Agents under Dynamic Goal Revision
papers.abstract: Web agents are typically evaluated with goals fully specified before execution and fixed thereafter, whereas real users often revise their requirements during interaction. To study such interactions, we introduce DynaRev, a benchmark of 181 tasks to evaluate web agents under dynamic goal revision. DynaRev uses semantic milestones to deliver revisions at task-defined stages, covers additive revisions, unconditional overrides, and runtime-conditioned overrides, and evaluates correctness, responsiveness, and efficiency through trajectory-grounded evaluation. Five-model evaluations show that agents often satisfy only part of the task requirements, with performance varying across task sources, revision types, and models. Further analyses reveal varied milestone timing, mixed effects of dynamic delivery, and contrasting revision-handling outcomes, with gains from instruction rewriting while preserving browser state and losses from browser resets. DynaRev provides a testbed for studying how web agents adapt to evolving user goals. The code and data are available at https://github.com/zsq259/DynaRev.
papers.summary: Web agents are normally evaluated with goals fixed before execution, but real users often change their requirements mid-task. `DynaRev` is a benchmark of 181 tasks that delivers goal revisions at semantically defined milestones during execution, covers additive revisions, unconditional overrides, and overrides conditioned on runtime state, and scores correctness, responsiveness, and efficiency from the agent's trajectory. Evaluating five models shows that **agents frequently satisfy only part of the requirements**, with results varying by task source, revision type, and model, and that rewriting the instruction while preserving browser state helps whereas resetting the browser hurts.

papers.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Quantile Demand Forecasting in E-commerce with Doubly Censored Data
papers.abstract: In recent years, a growing number of online retail companies have embraced deep learning models for demand forecasting, leveraging their scalability in processing large-scale datasets. Accurate demand forecasts enable improved planning and allow operational flexibility to adjust sales accordingly. Moreover, quantile estimation has gained widespread application as it offers valuable uncertainty quantification, thereby enhancing the robustness of decision-making processes. However, limited research has addressed the effective quantification of uncertainty when target labels are ambiguous. In retail, actual sales can be capped by stock and boosted by temporary promotions, whereas the target is underlying demand. Such scenarios are characterized by double censoring and no deep-learning pipeline yet exists for such data. In this paper, we introduce a straightforward framework for learning quantiles from doubly-censored observations and propose a tailored evaluation metric. Our approach is supported by theoretical guarantees, and we empirically demonstrate that our metric correlates well with the oracle calibration measure. Experimental results show that our estimator surpasses existing baselines. Finally, inventory simulations and real-world applications confirm the practical utility of our method in retail operations.
papers.summary: Online retailers increasingly forecast demand with deep learning and want quantile estimates for uncertainty, but the training targets are ambiguous: observed sales are capped by available stock and inflated by temporary promotions, while the quantity of interest is underlying demand. No deep-learning pipeline existed for this doubly-censored data, so the authors introduce a framework for learning quantiles from doubly-censored observations together with a tailored evaluation metric, both backed by theoretical guarantees. Empirically the metric **correlates well with the oracle calibration measure**, the estimator beats existing baselines, and inventory simulations plus real-world deployments confirm its practical utility.

papers.title: Mode Dynamics: A Framework for Neural Network Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce Mode Dynamics, a framework that connects coordinated parameter motion during neural network learning to changes in model outputs. Starting from a recorded parameter trajectory, we decompose its updates into collective modes and map each mode to its state-dependent output effect. The framework organizes this link through three mechanisms. Decomposition identifies collective modes in parameter motion and their time-varying amplitudes. Reconstruction tests whether the effects induced by those modes recover local and accumulated output change. Concentration quantifies how behavioral contribution is distributed across modes. Controlled scalar regression and next-token experiments directly test these mechanisms. They show that small sets of leading modes reconstruct behavior, induced effects depend on the training path, and modal complexity varies with task and data. We then evaluate the framework on held-out image and language-model outputs using CIFAR-100 autoencoding and a public Pythia-70M pretraining trajectory. Across these settings, the results connect compact modal subspaces of recorded parameter motion to evolving behavior.
papers.summary: Neural network training moves parameters in coordinated ways, but how that collective motion translates into changes in model outputs is not well characterized. `Mode Dynamics` takes a recorded parameter trajectory, decomposes its updates into collective modes with time-varying amplitudes, maps each mode to its state-dependent output effect, tests whether those effects reconstruct local and accumulated output change, and measures how behavioral contribution concentrates across modes. Controlled scalar regression and next-token experiments show that **a small set of leading modes reconstructs behavior**, that induced effects depend on the training path, and that modal complexity varies with task and data, with further evaluation on held-out outputs from `CIFAR-100` autoencoding and a public `Pythia-70M` pretraining trajectory.

papers.title: The generative paradox: the Anti-Prompt paradigm for human capability
papers.abstract: Generative AI in education is usually judged by the output of human-AI teams. That focus overlooks a second outcome: what people can still understand, challenge, repair, and adapt when assistance changes or disappears. We call this tension the generative paradox and distinguish four manifestations: performance, assistance, ownership, and capability stock. We propose developmental function allocation, which complements operational function allocation and meaningful human control by treating retained human capability as a design objective alongside current joint performance. The Anti-Prompt paradigm reverses the default interaction order: when immediate generation would preempt a consequential human act, AI should first create the conditions for human construction. We distinguish the validity of a product, responsibility for its construction, and evidence of capability after support changes. Representative Anti-Prompts, a canonical interaction sequence, and stress tests spanning mathematical reasoning, experimental science, software diagnosis, and lesson design make these distinctions concrete. We conclude with falsifiable predictions about retained capability and a system-level hypothesis about the reproduction and distribution of expertise.
papers.summary: Judging generative AI in education by the output of human-AI teams overlooks what people can still understand, challenge, repair, and adapt once the assistance changes or disappears, a tension the authors call the generative paradox and break into four manifestations: performance, assistance, ownership, and capability stock. They propose developmental function allocation, which treats retained human capability as a design objective alongside joint performance, and the Anti-Prompt paradigm, under which **AI should first create the conditions for human construction whenever immediate generation would preempt a consequential human act**. Representative Anti-Prompts, a canonical interaction sequence, and stress tests across mathematical reasoning, experimental science, software diagnosis, and lesson design illustrate the distinctions, and the work closes with falsifiable predictions about retained capability and a system-level hypothesis about how expertise is reproduced and distributed.

papers.title: FARE: Factor-Aware Retrieval with Error-Guided Fusion for Retail Forecasting
papers.abstract: Retail sales forecasting underpins inventory planning, yet promotions and calendar events reshape short-term demand. Although each factor usually has historical occurrences, the complete factor combination of a target week often has few precedents. The challenge is therefore to retrieve informative partial matches and weight them by their reliability, which varies across series. We propose FARE(Factor-Aware Retrieval with Error-Guided Fusion), which ranks historical weeks separately for each known target-week factor and merges the selected weeks into a factor reference under a fixed budget. Guided by shrunk errors from completed development weeks and the current disagreement among candidates, a first gate mixes this factor reference with a shape reference from similar sales histories, and a second gate controls how strongly the mixture corrects a backbone forecast. Both gates remain fixed during testing. On Favorita, M5, Rossmann, and Rohlik, FARE reduces the weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) of five backbones by 11.46%, 4.06%, 14.63%, and 10.16% on average. With Chronos-2 frozen, FARE also outperforms conventional and existing enhancement methods, including supervised residual correction and retrieval augmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/HousonGu/FARE .
papers.summary: Promotions and calendar events reshape short-term retail demand, and although each individual factor has historical precedents, the exact combination present in a target week rarely does, so forecasting becomes a problem of retrieving informative partial matches and weighting them by a reliability that differs across series. Factor-Aware Retrieval with Error-Guided Fusion (`FARE`) ranks past weeks separately for each known target-week factor, merges the selected weeks into a factor reference under a fixed budget, uses one gate informed by shrunk development-week errors and candidate disagreement to blend that reference with a shape reference drawn from similar sales histories, and uses a second gate to decide how strongly the blend corrects a backbone forecast. On `Favorita`, `M5`, `Rossmann`, and `Rohlik` it **cuts the weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) of five backbones by 11.46%, 4.06%, 14.63%, and 10.16% on average**, and with a frozen `Chronos-2` it also beats supervised residual correction and existing retrieval augmentation.

papers.title: A Negotiation-Aware Hybrid LLM Framework for Intent Interpretation and Service Discovery
papers.abstract: Increasingly, users express their needs as natural-language intents rather than structured requests. These intents may be incomplete, high-level, or internally conflicting. A conflicting intent either violates fundamental properties of the cloud paradigm or states mutually inconsistent requirements. Classical composition approaches are designed for structured, low-level, and complete requests. They cannot interpret such intents, discover suitable services from provider catalogs, or negotiate conflicting requirements with users. To address this gap, we propose a negotiation-aware framework for intent interpretation and service discovery. The framework first refines the natural-language intent and dynamically detects conflicts. It then structures the intent into a provider-independent TOSCA template. For each specification, it retrieves candidate service offers through deterministic matching grounded in cloud provider offerings. Some conflicts arise during interpretation. Other requirements prove unsatisfiable during discovery. Both are resolved through iterative natural-language negotiation with the user. We evaluate the framework on 70 diverse intents against single-shot and enhanced-prompting baselines. It improves recall and F1 for both conflict detection and service discovery. It also eliminates hallucinated offers and resolves conflicts at a cost proportional to their number.
papers.summary: Users increasingly describe what they need from cloud services as natural-language intents that can be incomplete, high-level, or self-contradictory, which classical service composition methods built for structured, complete requests cannot interpret, match against provider catalogs, or negotiate. The proposed framework refines the intent and detects conflicts, structures it into a provider-independent TOSCA template, retrieves candidate offers per specification through deterministic matching against real provider catalogs, and resolves conflicts found during interpretation or unsatisfiable requirements found during discovery through iterative natural-language negotiation with the user. On 70 diverse intents it improves recall and F1 for both conflict detection and service discovery over single-shot and enhanced-prompting baselines, **eliminates hallucinated offers**, and resolves conflicts at a cost proportional to their number.

papers.title: Fisher Contrastive Learning to Mitigate Feature Suppression: A Case Study in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) learns representations by contrasting augmented views of the same sample, but it can exhibit feature suppression, where dominant or easy-to-learn factors suppress other class-relevant signals, degrading the performance of representations, particularly in high-dimensional data with heterogeneous features. We introduce Fisher Contrastive Learning (FCL), which uses a regularized Fisher trace criterion to address feature suppression. FCL learns embeddings by maximizing the discriminative strength of Fisher discriminant functions, producing representations that preserve class-relevant information implied by the augmentation process. We prove that the representations learned by FCL could alleviate the feature suppression effects. We demonstrate FCL on simulated benchmarks designed to induce feature suppression and on a real-world biomedical application, pretraining on large white blood cell microscopy image dataset and transfer learning for diagnosis of acute promyelocytic leukemia in an external cohort. In all experiments, FCL outperforms the self-supervised baselines and yields more robust and discriminative representations.
papers.summary: Self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) can suffer from feature suppression, where dominant or easy-to-learn factors crowd out other class-relevant signals, which is especially damaging for high-dimensional data with heterogeneous features. Fisher Contrastive Learning (`FCL`) replaces the usual objective with a regularized Fisher trace criterion that maximizes the discriminative strength of Fisher discriminant functions, and the authors prove the resulting representations can alleviate feature suppression. On simulated benchmarks built to induce suppression and on a biomedical pipeline that pretrains on a large white blood cell microscopy dataset and transfers to acute promyelocytic leukemia diagnosis in an external cohort, **`FCL` outperforms the self-supervised baselines in every experiment** with more robust and discriminative features.

papers.title: Closing the Log Gap: Minimax-Optimal Regret for Episodic RL
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the regret minimization problem in episodic tabular MDPs. Our algorithm achieves the first expected regret bound scaling as $\sqrt{H^3 S A K}$ for sufficiently large $K$, where $H$ is the episode length, $K$ is the number of episodes, and $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, respectively. Our method is the first to match the minimax lower bound \emph{without extra polylog factors}. We introduce a variant of UCBVI which does not maintain strictly optimistic estimates, and uses MOSS-style exploration bonuses whose logarithmic terms adapt to both visit counts and estimated variances. A key challenge is controlling the propagation of errors caused by under-optimism, which we accomplish in an occupancy-weighted way, avoiding logarithmic overhead that would be incurred by uniform-over-rows concentration. Our analysis develops time-uniform and variance-aware concentration bounds that may be of independent interest. As a corollary we also develop an algorithm for $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-PAC best-policy identification, which is the first to match the $\Omega\big(H^3 SA\log(\frac{1}{\delta})\varepsilon^{-2}\big)$ minimax lower bound up to constants in some regimes.
papers.summary: Regret bounds for episodic tabular Markov decision processes have so far matched the minimax lower bound only up to polylogarithmic factors. The proposed algorithm, a variant of `UCBVI` that abandons strictly optimistic estimates and uses `MOSS`-style exploration bonuses whose logarithmic terms adapt to both visit counts and estimated variances, achieves **expected regret of order sqrt(H^3 S A K) for sufficiently large K, the first bound to match the minimax lower bound with no extra polylog factors**, where H is the episode length, K the number of episodes, and S and A the numbers of states and actions.
