The analysis controls the error propagated by under-optimism in an occupancy-weighted way and develops time-uniform, variance-aware concentration bounds, and as a corollary the authors obtain an (epsilon, delta)-PAC best-policy identification algorithm that matches the corresponding lower bound up to constants in some regimes.

papers.title: EventSeeColor: Learning to Reconstruct Color from Monochrome Events
papers.abstract: Event cameras capture visual brightness changes under challenging lighting conditions. However, traditional event-based image reconstruction targets grayscale intensity and produces images without scene color. Color distinguishes surfaces with similar intensity. Reconstructing color from events can reveal appearance differences that reconstructed grayscale images cannot express. Although monochrome event cameras do not directly measure color, their event-triggering patterns depend on surface reflectance, illumination, and the sensor's spectral response. These patterns may contain cues that support color reconstruction. In this paper, we present EventSeeColor, which uses event-reconstructed grayscale and aligned events to jointly guide a diffusion colorizer. Grayscale-derived semantic context supports color inference, while region-balanced chroma supervision and local RGB refinement improve color distribution, brightness, and texture. In the combined evaluation on two real event datasets, EventSeeColor achieves the best structural similarity, learned perceptual scores, and chromatic-region color difference among the external methods.
papers.summary: Event cameras record brightness changes robustly under difficult lighting, but existing event-based reconstruction produces only grayscale images and cannot distinguish surfaces that share similar intensity. Although monochrome event sensors do not measure color, their triggering patterns depend on surface reflectance, illumination, and spectral response, and `EventSeeColor` exploits those cues by feeding event-reconstructed grayscale and aligned events to a diffusion colorizer, using grayscale-derived semantic context for color inference together with region-balanced chroma supervision and local RGB refinement. In a combined evaluation on two real event datasets it **achieves the best structural similarity, learned perceptual scores, and chromatic-region color difference among external methods**.

papers.title: Hidden Disparities in Ranking: Category-Aware Fairness via Distributional Stability
papers.abstract: We study the problem of fair ranking in recommender systems. We provide a formal probabilistic framework in which ranking policies are distributions over permutations, and the utility of a user is the exposure given to the items they interact with, relative to that of an ideal ranking. We consider utility parity across user groups, as well as its category-aware refinement, conditional utility parity, which requires parity within each category of items. Following a recent view of fairness as distributional stability, we show that both criteria are equivalent to the stability of the utility under changes in the composition of user groups. Optimizing over mixtures of ranking policies leads to a second-order cone program, for which we provide generalization bounds. A numerical study validates our theoretical findings.
papers.summary: Fair ranking in recommender systems asks whether users from different groups receive comparable utility, where utility is the exposure given to the items a user interacts with relative to an ideal ranking. The authors model ranking policies as distributions over permutations and study utility parity across user groups together with a category-aware refinement, conditional utility parity, which demands parity within each item category. **Both fairness criteria are shown to be equivalent to the stability of utility under changes in the composition of user groups**, and optimizing over mixtures of ranking policies yields a second-order cone program with accompanying generalization bounds. A numerical study supports the theoretical results.

papers.title: Locating and Closing Information Gaps in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-step Web tasks often require several LLM agents to gather and combine evidence. The communication graph of a fixed workflow restricts which agents can read each other's outputs: evidence retrieved by one agent may never reach the agent that needs it, leaving an information gap and an incomplete or incorrect answer. Adding a connection can deliver the missing evidence, but can also lead the receiver to adopt an incorrect upstream conclusion that displaces a correct answer; the final output alone does not separate the two. We propose Selective Probing and Link Insertion for Closing information gaps in multi-agent Execution (SPLICE), which locates information gaps per query and decides what to adopt after adding an edge. After the original workflow runs, SPLICE uses the query and node outputs to locate a possible gap, adds one directed edge from a source to a receiver to deliver the relevant evidence, and re-executes the receiver and affected downstream nodes, producing a candidate answer. The adoption decision reads both the final answers of the two runs and the process changes the edit caused inside the workflow: how far the receiver moved, where its new content came from, and whether the change reached the final answer. A selector trained on these process features chooses between adopting the candidate answer and retaining the original. On five benchmarks, SPLICE raises the task score on Web tool use by 8.0% and the mean score on four reasoning and planning benchmarks by 5.7% relative to the static skeleton, at 1.25 to 1.44$\times$ the skeleton's cost, and transfers zero-shot to four unseen backbones.
papers.summary: In fixed multi-agent workflows for multi-step web tasks, the communication graph can keep evidence gathered by one large language model agent from reaching the agent that needs it, and simply adding a link risks spreading an incorrect upstream conclusion that displaces a correct answer. `SPLICE` (Selective Probing and Link Insertion for Closing information gaps in multi-agent Execution) runs the original workflow, locates a likely gap from the query and node outputs, inserts one directed edge from a source to a receiver, re-executes the receiver and its downstream nodes, and then uses a selector trained on process features such as how far the receiver moved and where its new content came from to decide whether to adopt the candidate answer or keep the original. **On five benchmarks it raises the web tool-use task score by 8.0% and the mean score on four reasoning and planning benchmarks by 5.7% over the static workflow**, at 1.25 to 1.44 times the cost, and transfers zero-shot to four unseen backbone models.

papers.title: Understanding axial attention in TSFMs through single location regression
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) increasingly rely on axial attention mechanisms, but despite their empirical success, the theoretical properties of axial attention remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we extend the Single Location Regression framework introduced in Marion et al. [2025] to 2D structured data, in order to study sparse information settings where a target depends on a small number of tokens. We formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-type predictor and rigorously analyze its statistical properties and training dynamics. We prove that under a specific asymptotic regime and with knowledge of the underlying oracle parameters, our predictor achieves Bayes optimality, whereas a class of semi-linear simplifications strictly fails to do so, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity. We prove that for a specific temperature scaling, Projected Gradient Descent converges globally to the optimal oracle parameters. Extensive numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and highlight the critical role of inverse temperature scheduling in empirical convergence.
papers.summary: Axial attention is widely used in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), but its theoretical properties are poorly understood. The authors extend the single location regression framework to two-dimensional structured data, where a target depends on only a few tokens, and formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-style predictor whose statistical properties and training dynamics they analyze. **With oracle parameters the predictor is Bayes optimal in a specific asymptotic regime, while a class of semi-linear simplifications provably is not**, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity, and projected gradient descent is shown to converge globally to the oracle parameters under a particular temperature scaling. Numerical experiments confirm the theory and identify inverse temperature scheduling as critical for convergence in practice.

papers.title: Bridging Semantics and Structure: A Theoretically Grounded Framework for Link Prediction on TAGs
papers.abstract: Link prediction on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is a fundamental problem with applications in knowledge discovery, recommendation and beyond. Recent progress has highlighted the promise of combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Language Models (LMs) in order to leverage the complementary structural and semantic signals. However, due to the distinct inductive biases of GNNs and LMs, the design of an optimal fusion strategy remains an open research question. In this work, we present Bridge-LP, an intuitive, simple, efficient and theoretically grounded framework that unifies graph and language representations. It is built around three theoretically-justified design components: (D1) jumping connection of textual proximity, which enables robust LM training; (D2) compressed embedding, which encodes neighborhood information long exploited by classical link prediction heuristics, thereby enriching structural signals in a learnable way; and (D3) cache embedding training strategy, which reduces computational complexity. Together, these mechanisms establish an end-to-end cross-modal framework that scales to large graphs while capturing richer graph-text interactions. We conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, comparing against 40 existing models across 9 diverse datasets. Experiments show that Bridge-LP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, delivering up to a 43.06% improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and setting a new benchmark for language-graph integration.
papers.summary: Link prediction on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) benefits from combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Language Models (LMs), but their differing inductive biases leave the right fusion strategy an open question. `Bridge-LP` unifies the two with three theoretically motivated components: a jumping connection of textual proximity for robust language model training, a compressed embedding that encodes the neighborhood information used by classical link prediction heuristics, and a cache embedding training strategy that cuts computational cost. **Against 40 existing models across 9 datasets, it consistently outperforms prior approaches with gains of up to 43.06% in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)**, while scaling to large graphs.

papers.title: Towards Full-Text Scholarly Argument Mining using Entity-Anchored Claim Extraction
papers.abstract: Argument mining in full-text scholarly articles remains an important yet challenging task. This difficulty stems not only from the need to model long-distance dependencies but also from the substantial effort required to annotate sentence-level argumentative components throughout lengthy documents. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach that leverages scientific entity mentions (e.g., tasks, datasets, and models) to identify and structure claims in scholarly literature. We validate our approach through a case study involving 50 full-text research papers on sentiment analysis. We first establish a reliable human gold standard (Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.80$), identifying 113 claim-bearing sentences and extracting 199 structured claim records from 300 candidate sentences. To address the annotation bottleneck, we employ a majority-voting ensemble of large language models (LLMs) to generate a silver-standard dataset comprising 1,487 claims. Encoders fine-tuned exclusively on the silver-standard dataset outperform those trained on a small human-annotated gold-standard dataset and demonstrate strong zero-shot transfer to NLP papers outside the training corpus.
papers.summary: Argument mining across full scholarly articles is hard because claims depend on long-distance context and annotating every sentence in long documents is costly. The approach anchors claim identification on mentions of scientific entities such as tasks, datasets, and models, validated in a case study of 50 full-text sentiment analysis papers where a human gold standard with Krippendorff's alpha of 0.80 yielded 113 claim-bearing sentences and 199 structured claim records from 300 candidates. To relieve the annotation bottleneck, a majority-voting ensemble of large language models produced a silver-standard set of 1,487 claims, and **encoders fine-tuned only on this silver data outperformed those trained on the small human gold standard** while transferring zero-shot to NLP papers outside the training corpus.

papers.title: DYNAS: A Dynamic Network Penetration Testing Framework Using Deep Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: As network scale and uncertainty complicate automated penetration testing, reinforcement learning (RL) environments must support controlled evaluation under defensive and non-stationary conditions. We present DYNAS (Dynamic Network Attack Simulator), which combines parameterized large-scale scenario generation with stateful intrusion detection responses, explicit scan false-positive and false-negative noise, temporary service unavailability, and duration-based action timeouts. We further introduce Pen-DHRL, a recurrent manager--worker policy that selects persistent subgoals using IDS-conditioned global context. We compare Pen-DHRL with GNN, Invariant, and Attention baselines across four scenario variants and multiple training regimes. Under IDS-disabled training followed by IDS-enabled evaluation, Pen-DHRL obtains approximately 64\% and 24\% higher reward per step on Bridge and Dynamic, respectively, and approximately 26\% and 30\% more captured hosts on VarA and VarB than the next-best baseline. With all defensive dynamics active from the beginning of training, Pen-DHRL achieves positive mean episode returns in all four scenarios, whereas the flat baselines produce negative mean returns in all 12 architecture--scenario combinations; staged curriculum training produces positive mean returns across all 16 evaluated combinations.
papers.summary: Automated penetration testing with reinforcement learning (RL) needs environments that capture defensive responses and non-stationary network conditions at scale. `DYNAS` (Dynamic Network Attack Simulator) generates parameterized large-scale scenarios with stateful intrusion detection system (IDS) responses, scan false positives and false negatives, temporary service outages, and duration-based action timeouts, and the accompanying `Pen-DHRL` policy is a recurrent manager-worker hierarchy that selects persistent subgoals from IDS-conditioned global context. Compared with `GNN`, `Invariant`, and `Attention` baselines across four scenario variants, `Pen-DHRL` earns roughly 24% to 64% higher reward per step and 26% to 30% more captured hosts when trained without the IDS and evaluated with it, and **with all defensive dynamics active from the start of training it reaches positive mean episode returns in all four scenarios while every flat baseline goes negative**; staged curriculum training yields positive returns across all 16 evaluated combinations.

papers.title: EpiAgent: Epistemic Self-Play for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Epistemic game theory explains an agent's strategic behavior via the beliefs it holds about others and how these beliefs are updated as the interactions unfold. Modern LLM-based agents, however, often lack an explicit mechanism for learning and updating such beliefs to guide decisions under incomplete information. To bridge this gap, we propose EpiAgent, a framework that equips LLM-based agents with an explicit, learnable epistemic layer, which maintains beliefs over others' private information and combines these beliefs with the agent's available information into an epistemic state for action selection. Concretely, the agent's policy is decomposed into two coupled stages: Epistemic Update, which updates these beliefs from interaction histories, and Action Planning, which selects actions conditioned on the updated epistemic state. By formulating their dependency as a bi-level optimization problem, we introduce Epistemic Self-Play, an algorithm that alternately optimizes the two stages through self-play, utilizing an intrinsic prediction reward to evaluate how well inferred beliefs predict subsequent observations. Empirical results across both mixed and competitive scenarios show that EpiAgent consistently outperforms prompting-based and RL-based baselines. Further analyses reveal the benefits of dedicated epistemic training, improvements in belief inference accuracy, and the contribution of learned beliefs to action planning. These results demonstrate the value of an explicit, learnable epistemic layer for effective multi-agent interactions.
papers.summary: Large language model agents usually lack an explicit mechanism for forming and updating beliefs about other agents' private information, which epistemic game theory treats as central to strategic behavior under incomplete information. `EpiAgent` adds a learnable epistemic layer that splits the policy into an Epistemic Update stage, which infers beliefs from interaction history, and an Action Planning stage conditioned on the resulting epistemic state, and trains the two through `Epistemic Self-Play`, a bi-level optimization that alternates between the stages using an intrinsic reward for how well inferred beliefs predict subsequent observations. **Across mixed-motive and competitive scenarios it consistently outperforms prompting-based and RL-based baselines**, with analyses attributing the gains to better belief inference accuracy and to the learned beliefs' contribution to action planning.

papers.title: Mobilizing the Archive: Bitext Extraction at Scale from Archival Documents for Extremely Low-resource Languages
papers.abstract: While mining parallel sentences from web pages has proven effective for low-resource machine translation, the majority of the world's languages have little to no web presence. What they do have, though, are resources that are the result of centuries of efforts by linguists, such as grammars, dictionaries, and other documentation materials. We propose extracting translation examples from such linguistic resources, which offer parallel data for languages under-represented online and could potentially scale to thousands more languages. We develop a pipeline to achieve this, leveraging an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model as well as a vision language model (VLM), to ensure identified content to be aligned with visual layout information. We demonstrate the utility of the extracted bitexts for bootstrapping translation systems across 20 languages, both by training machine translation models and by applying in-context learning for large language models. For in-context learning, we observe improvements of +15.78 and +6.94 chrF2++ over zero-shot translation for into low- and high-resource languages, respectively.
papers.summary: Mining parallel sentences from the web does not help the many languages with almost no online presence, but those languages often have grammars, dictionaries, and other documentation produced by linguists over centuries. The authors build a pipeline that combines an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model with a vision language model (VLM) to extract translation examples from such scanned resources while keeping the extracted content aligned with the page layout. Using the resulting bitexts for 20 languages, they bootstrap translation both by training machine translation models and by in-context learning with large language models, where **in-context examples improve chrF2++ by 15.78 points when translating into the low-resource languages and by 6.94 points into high-resource ones** over zero-shot translation.

papers.title: ScienceJudge: Pattern Perturbation Augmentation for Sentence-Level Scientific Claim Verification
papers.abstract: Sentence-level scientific claim verification determines whether each sentence in an AI-generated scientific paragraph is supported by a given multimodal evidence bundle. Fine-grained reporting errors often preserve fluent and plausible statements while introducing subtle evidence-claim deviations, making them difficult to detect under sparse and imbalanced supervision. We propose Pattern Perturbation Augmentation (PPA), which models reporting errors as label-specific faithfulness breaking transformations and induces reusable error patterns from labeled examples. PPA applies these patterns to supported claims to construct controlled hard negatives and expands their coverage through pattern-level, operation-level, and cross-domain augmentation. Based on these augmented views, we develop ScienceJudge, which integrates PPA-trained vision-language predictors and instruction-guided LLM predictors through class-weighted ensemble inference. On the local development set, ScienceJudge improves the average score from 0.8124 to 0.8692, achieving a Macro-F1 of 0.8466 and a Paragraph Exact Match score of 0.8919. Our submitted system ranks first on the official NLPCC 2026 Task 10 Track 1 leaderboard with a final score of 0.6890.
papers.summary: Sentence-level scientific claim verification checks whether each sentence of an AI-generated scientific paragraph is supported by a multimodal evidence bundle, where reporting errors tend to stay fluent and plausible while subtly diverging from the evidence, and labeled examples are sparse and imbalanced. `PPA` (Pattern Perturbation Augmentation) treats reporting errors as label-specific faithfulness-breaking transformations, induces reusable error patterns from labeled data, and applies them to supported claims to manufacture controlled hard negatives, expanded through pattern-level, operation-level, and cross-domain augmentation. `ScienceJudge` combines `PPA`-trained vision-language predictors with instruction-guided large language model predictors through class-weighted ensembling, lifting the development-set average score from 0.8124 to 0.8692, and **the submitted system ranked first on the `NLPCC 2026 Task 10` Track 1 leaderboard with a final score of 0.6890**.

papers.title: Judged in Company: In-Context Batching Makes LLM Verdicts Depend on Other Items
papers.abstract: To save cost, practitioners often ask a language model to grade many independent items in one prompt. This assumes that verdicts are separable: that the verdict on an item does not depend on the other items in the prompt or on its position among them. Across three judgement tasks (harm in social-media comments, short-answer grading and review star ratings) and five open-weight models with 4-9B parameters, assigning the same 2,000 items to different random batches of 25 changes 11-22% of decisions on harm and grading, 6.5-13.3 points more than renaming the item keys or rewording the instruction, while AUROC against human labels differs from single-item grading only by -0.033 to +0.010; for four models with 14-32B parameters, 6-15% of decisions change, 4.2-9.1 points more. We show that flip rates decompose exactly into components of order, slot and membership, and that under a threshold model they grow with the square root of the variance that the context contributes, so that effects that are small for scores are large for decisions. Most of the latent dissimilarity between partitions comes from the order of the neighbours and the slot. The main effect of which items share the prompt, the part that voting over permutations of a batch cannot remove, accounts for 0.11-0.22 of it, and majority votes over nine permutations still leave 52-60% of the flips. Batched verdicts also differ systematically from single-item verdicts: even the majority of fifteen random batches disagrees with them on 8.4-17.8% of decisions. Editing a single generation shows that both the model's own earlier verdicts and the neighbours' texts carry the effect. On the easy task, star ratings, only 2.9-3.9% of decisions change. We recommend grading ambiguous items one per prompt, recovering most of the cost with a cached prefix, and reporting agreement with single-item grading whenever items are batched.
papers.summary: Grading many independent items in a single prompt assumes the verdict on each item is separable from its neighbors and position, an assumption tested here across three judgement tasks (harm in social-media comments, short-answer grading, and review star ratings) and nine open-weight models. **Reassigning the same 2,000 items to different random batches of 25 flips 11% to 22% of harm and grading decisions for 4B to 9B models and 6% to 15% for 14B to 32B models**, far more than renaming item keys or rewording instructions, even though AUROC against human labels barely differs from single-item grading. The authors decompose flip rates exactly into order, slot, and membership components, show under a threshold model that flips grow with the square root of the variance the context contributes, and find that majority voting over nine permutations still leaves 52% to 60% of the flips while batched verdicts disagree systematically with single-item ones. They recommend grading ambiguous items one per prompt, recovering most of the cost through a cached prefix, and reporting agreement with single-item grading whenever items are batched.

papers.title: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On : Phenomenon-Based Task Construction, Certification, and Evidence-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in software that can change while they act: an appointment moves, a policy is revised, a record is updated. Testing agents under such changes is harder than it looks. When an agent fails, the cause may be the agent, but it may also be a change that did not fire as intended, an update the agent never received, or a grader that scored the episode wrongly. We introduce EnvOS, a framework for building and certifying environments that change mid-task. Before any agent runs, EnvOS checks that each change fires correctly, that the task remains solvable, and that the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior; after each run, separate code re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. We apply it to stale information, where a value the agent has already seen changes before the agent acts on it. In clinic booking, Claude Opus 5 succeeds on 0/16 tasks when nothing extra is shown, 2/16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15/16 when the updated value is shown; the gain over the reminder holds after correcting for all tests (p = 0.00293). In insurance-claim approval, Opus 5 re-checks on its own and succeeds on 10/10, whereas Claude Sonnet 5 rises from 1/10 to 9/10 when the current policy is shown again, a gain significant in its pre-registered test but not after correcting for all tests. Whether an agent caught a change thus varied with the model and the interface. We also stress-test the grading itself: on corrupted episodes designed blind from the rules, the EnvOS pipeline accepted none of 26 as clean, and on an externally generated set it caught 25 of 39, against 4 for simple log checks. Because every EnvOS environment is generated from a seed and graded by an audited automatic verifier, the same environments are natural candidates for training agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.
papers.summary: Computer-use agents operate in software that can change mid-task, and when they fail it is hard to tell whether the agent, a change that never fired, an update the agent never received, or a faulty grader is responsible. `EnvOS` builds and certifies environments that change while the agent acts: before any run it verifies that each change fires, that the task stays solvable, and that the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior, and after each run independent code re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. Applied to stale information in clinic booking, **`Claude Opus 5` succeeds on 0 of 16 tasks with no extra cue, 2 of 16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15 of 16 when the updated value is shown**, while in insurance-claim approval `Opus 5` re-checks on its own and succeeds on 10 of 10 whereas `Claude Sonnet 5` rises from 1 of 10 to 9 of 10 only when the current policy is shown again. Stress tests of the grading pipeline accepted none of 26 blind-corrupted episodes as clean and caught 25 of 39 externally generated ones versus 4 for simple log checks, and because the environments are seeded and verifier-graded the authors propose them for reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.

papers.title: LLM-guided Planar Loco-Manipulation for Quadruped Robots
papers.abstract: Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45. Project website: https://anonymousprojects-dev.github.io/LLM-guided-LocoManipulation-Quadrupeds/
papers.summary: Navigation in cluttered spaces with movable obstacles can require a robot to push things aside rather than find a collision-free path, which classical planners handle with hand-coded rules and learned methods restrict to low-dimensional commands or fixed action sets. The authors fine-tune a language-conditioned task planner with `LoRA` on synthetic data to map a natural-language task and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, each choosing a skill, an object, and a geometric target, which low-level reinforcement learning policies execute on a quadruped. The planner beats a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation, with comparisons showing that structured representations let models trained from scratch compose skills while pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets, and **an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy reaches 93.3% success in simulation versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline while cutting completion time by over 60%**. On hardware the hierarchy produces the correct skill composition in 44 of 45 trials and end-to-end success in 34 of 45.

papers.title: Reaction precedents extend retrosynthetic prediction beyond training coverage
papers.abstract: Reaction precedents guide retrosynthesis, but how far they can compensate for gaps in task-specific training coverage remains unclear. Using 2.71 million reactions, we restricted training and retrieval coverage by transformation or time, then expanded only the retrieval corpus with model parameters fixed. For transformations excluded from training, mean Top-1 accuracy increased from 13.0% to 58.0% on a historical test set and from 4.9% to 23.1% on a temporally held-out test set. For temporal coverage gaps, retrieval expansion enabled a model trained on records before 2017 to match or exceed a non-retrieval model trained on records before 2025 on both test sets. Without task-specific fine-tuning, precedents improved all 14 representative general-purpose models on both test sets and USPTO-50K; the strongest with precedents surpassed all eight representative specialized models. These findings show that inference-time reaction precedents can extend retrosynthetic prediction beyond task-specific training coverage without parameter updates.
papers.summary: Retrosynthesis models draw on reaction precedents, but how far retrieval can substitute for missing task-specific training coverage was unclear. Using 2.71 million reactions, the authors restricted training and retrieval coverage by transformation type or by date, then expanded only the retrieval corpus while keeping model parameters fixed. **For transformations excluded from training, mean Top-1 accuracy rose from 13.0% to 58.0% on a historical test set and from 4.9% to 23.1% on a temporally held-out set**, and retrieval expansion let a model trained on pre-2017 records match or exceed a non-retrieval model trained on pre-2025 records. Without fine-tuning, precedents also improved all 14 general-purpose models tested on both test sets and `USPTO-50K`, with the best of them surpassing all eight specialized models.

papers.title: Distributional Reward Calibration and Budget-Neutral Credit Assignment for Multimodal RLVR
papers.abstract: We revisit advantage estimation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and observe that any token-level advantage admits a two-stage factorization: a \emph{sample-level baselining} step that converts scalar verifier rewards into a comparable sequence-level signal, and a \emph{token-level credit assignment} step that distributes that signal over the trajectory. Existing estimators typically address only one of these stages: affine baselines preserve the shape of each task's reward law, so heavy tails and binary cliffs propagate into the gradient, while token-level credit rules tie the size of each token's update to raw confidence scales and need not conserve the total credit issued by the verifier. We propose \textbf{TACE} (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation), a two-stage estimator that addresses both stages. At stage~(S1), we replace linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal, which gives a common population reward law across tasks and caps finite-sample outliers deterministically. At stage~(S2), we rank-calibrate a stop-gradient evidence contrast within each trajectory and renormalize the clipped token weights to have mean one, so credit is redistributed across tokens while its total mass and sign are conserved. We prove population-level inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation, boundedness, and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines and unnormalized token weights do not satisfy. On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE obtains the strongest results on a majority of the benchmarks but does not dominate every setting.
papers.summary: Advantage estimation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) can be factored into a sample-level baselining step that turns scalar verifier rewards into a comparable sequence-level signal and a token-level credit assignment step that spreads that signal over the trajectory, yet existing estimators tend to fix only one of the two. `TACE` (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation) replaces linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal, giving all tasks a common reward law and deterministically capping outliers, then rank-calibrates a stop-gradient evidence contrast within each trajectory and renormalizes clipped token weights to mean one so that credit is redistributed while its total mass and sign are conserved. The authors prove inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines lack, and **on a multimodal reasoning suite `TACE` scores best on a majority of benchmarks without dominating every setting**.

papers.title: Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert Review: Application to Online Cell-Type Labeling
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models can accelerate cell-type annotation in digital pathology, but safely scaling their use requires determining, with error control, which model-generated labels can be accepted without expert review. This is challenging in evolving workflows because cell morphology and type composition may change across tissue regions and slides, making one-time calibration unreliable. We propose Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert review under Distribution shift (CARED), a distribution-free framework that leverages randomized expert audit to achieve long-run error control for AI-assisted annotation under distribution shift. For each incoming batch, CARED uniformly selects a subset of cases for expert review and uses the acquired labels to calibrate later decisions. Among unreviewed cases, CARED determines a subset of them to safely skip expert labeling, while suggesting candidate labels for the others for downstream resolution. We prove that this workflow provides long-run control of cumulative error over both the full stream and the cells outside of the audit sample, without stationarity or exchangeability assumptions. We further enhance the framework by introducing class-conditional guarantees to ensure error control within important but rare cell types, together with a utility module to target more automatic resolutions, smaller candidate sets, and greater biological coherence, without compromising validity. Experiments on pancreas, lung, and ovary annotation streams, together with a stream constructed from real expert annotations, show that CARED controls the cumulative errors while a substantial fraction of cells (up to 70%) bypass expert review.
papers.summary: AI models can speed up cell-type annotation in digital pathology, but deciding which model-generated labels can skip expert review with error control is difficult when cell morphology and type composition shift across tissue regions and slides. `CARED` (Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert review under Distribution shift) uniformly samples a subset of each incoming batch for expert review, uses those labels to calibrate later decisions, and among unreviewed cases decides which to accept automatically and which to pass on with candidate label sets. The framework provably controls long-run cumulative error over the full stream and over unaudited cells without stationarity or exchangeability assumptions, adds class-conditional guarantees for rare cell types, and includes a utility module that favors more automatic resolutions and smaller candidate sets. **On pancreas, lung, and ovary annotation streams and a stream built from real expert annotations, it keeps cumulative error under control while up to 70% of cells bypass expert review**.

papers.title: Confidence-Aware Speed-over-Ground Estimation from Doppler Spectra via Reconstruction-Based Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation from ground-facing Doppler spectra is essential for mobile platforms such as railway systems. Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.
papers.summary: Estimating a vehicle's speed over ground from ground-facing Doppler radar spectra matters for platforms such as trains, but classical signal-processing methods degrade when signal conditions worsen. The proposed method trains an autoencoder on rail-domain Doppler spectra, attaches a speed estimation head to its latent features, drops the reconstruction decoder at inference, and adds a lightweight confidence head that predicts frame-level error bounds, with noise augmentation during training for robustness. **Experiments show better speed accuracy than classical baselines together with confidence estimates that flag unreliable predictions under adverse conditions**.

papers.title: Statistical Analysis of Synthetic Data with Verification: A Linear Regression Framework
papers.abstract: Synthetic data are widely used for training modern AI systems. However, their statistical understanding remains limited. It is well recognized in statistics that repeated self-training on synthetic data can amplify errors inherited from pre-trained models, leading to model collapse. Verification plays a crucial role in selecting high-quality synthetic data to help prevent model collapse and improve model performance. We study verified self-training in a linear regression framework, where a pre-trained estimator generates synthetic data with injected generation noise and a verifier selects samples according to a verification threshold. Post-training on the accepted samples updates either all coordinates (full fine-tuning) or only an active subset (partial fine-tuning). Our analysis reveals three potentially counterintuitive effects. We establish that tighter verification does not always lead to lower prediction risk. We also find that a suitable level of injected generation noise can reduce prediction risk, while excessive noise can increase it. Moreover, full and partial fine-tuning can respond differently to the same verification rule, since pre-training error in the frozen coordinates affects both sample selection and post-training risk. We analyze these effects by deriving finite sample risk bounds for four separate regimes determined by the relative scales of the verification threshold, generation noise, and pre-training error. The bounds precisely characterize how verification affects prediction risk across these regimes. In particular, we quantify how the generation noise, the effective accepted sample size, and the covariance of the accepted covariates affect prediction risk. The analysis extends to iterative verified full fine-tuning, where sufficiently tight verification reduces the initial error contribution at a geometric rate.
papers.summary: Repeated self-training on synthetic data can amplify errors inherited from the generating model and lead to model collapse, and verification is commonly used to filter synthetic samples, but its statistical effects are not well understood. The authors study verified self-training in a linear regression setting where a pre-trained estimator generates samples with injected noise, a verifier accepts those passing a threshold, and post-training updates either all coordinates or only an active subset. Finite-sample risk bounds across four regimes, defined by the relative scales of the verification threshold, generation noise, and pre-training error, show that **tighter verification does not always reduce prediction risk, moderate injected noise can lower it while excessive noise raises it, and full and partial fine-tuning can respond differently to the same verification rule**. In iterative verified full fine-tuning, sufficiently tight verification shrinks the initial error contribution at a geometric rate.

papers.title: When Requirements Interact: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding via Interdependent Specifications
papers.abstract: To succeed in real-world long-horizon software development, coding agents must satisfy multi-dimensional task specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, and do so without breaking existing dependencies. However, current works lack specification in both quantity and diversity, often emphasizing primary goals while ignoring complex constraints. Synthesizing tasks to bridge this gap presents two challenges: naively adding specifications risks reducing tasks to trivial checklists rather than compelling joint reasoning, and verifying these subtle interactions risks overlooking hidden flaws or rejecting valid alternatives. To address these challenges, we introduce CodeSpecWeave, a framework for synthesizing tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in real developer seeds, a synthesis agent iteratively develops both coupled task requirements and executable tests, while a review agent audits solution trajectories from multiple models to guarantee test reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1, largely outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, we curate CodeSpecWeave-Bench, a rigorous benchmark comprising 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications, which clearly separates frontier models and reveals significant headroom in handling interdependent engineering constraints.
papers.summary: Real-world long-horizon software tasks impose many interacting specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, that existing coding-agent training data rarely capture, and naively piling on requirements either reduces tasks to checklists or makes verification unreliable. `CodeSpecWeave` seeds tasks from real developer activity, has a synthesis agent iteratively co-develop coupled requirements and executable tests, and uses a review agent that audits solution trajectories from multiple models to validate the tests, yielding 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. **Reinforcement learning on these tasks yields substantial gains over the base model with `DeepSWE-v1.1` and largely outperforms existing baselines**, and a companion benchmark, `CodeSpecWeave-Bench`, with 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications separates frontier models and shows considerable headroom on interdependent engineering constraints.

papers.title: Learned Terminal Costs for Short-Horizon Model Predictive Control of Autonomous Trucks in Interactive Highway Traffic
papers.abstract: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.
papers.summary: Heavy-duty trucks on highways need cooperation from surrounding traffic for critical maneuvers, and neither Model Predictive Control (MPC), which enforces constraints but suffers at the short horizons that are computationally affordable, nor Reinforcement Learning (RL), which captures long-term behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and turns overly conservative under sparse collision penalties, is sufficient alone. The proposed hybrid solves a finite-horizon MPC by dynamic programming and uses a pre-trained RL model to estimate the terminal cost. In simulation with reactive surrounding traffic, **the hybrid achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration**, compared against MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with a base-policy terminal cost estimate, and pure RL.

papers.title: From MS/MS evidence to adaptive spectroscopic characterization: Reinforcement learning guided by candidate molecular structures
papers.abstract: Small-molecule identification from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) may require complementary measurements. Herein, we propose a structure-informed deep Q-network (SI-DQN) that uses existing MS/MS evidence to decide whether further characterization is needed, which measurement to request, and when to stop. The policy combines spectral representations and candidate rankings with score-weighted descriptors of the candidates' chemical features and structural differences. The policy was evaluated on 79,462 held-out samples with simulated MS/MS, infrared (IR), and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra from the Multimodal Spectroscopic Dataset. Evaluation used fixed hard candidate sets containing the correct structure and equal normalized acquisition costs. Averaged across three training runs, SI-DQN increased Top-1 accuracy from 80.10% to 93.78% for positive-ion MS/MS starts and from 70.44% to 93.31% for negative-ion starts. The corresponding mean additional measurement counts were only 0.227 and 0.340 per sample, respectively. Complete acquisition achieved 97.72% accuracy with four additions, whereas SI-DQN reduced the additional measurement count by 94.3% and 91.5%. Relative to a rule-based policy, SI-DQN reduced the composite loss combining terminal ranking error and acquisition cost by 19.3% and 25.5%. Adding structural information to DQN further improved accuracy while reducing requests across all three training runs. At comparable ranking uncertainty, SI-DQN increased request rates relative to DQN more strongly in groups with high structural disagreement, where larger reductions in composite loss were also observed. Together, these results support using the ambiguity among candidate structures after MS/MS analysis to guide further characterization, providing a quantitative basis for balancing identification performance against subsequent measurement effort.
papers.summary: Identifying small molecules from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) alone is often ambiguous, raising the question of when to request complementary measurements and which ones. A structure-informed deep Q-network (`SI-DQN`) uses the MS/MS evidence, candidate rankings, and score-weighted descriptors of the candidates' chemical features and structural differences to decide whether to acquire infrared (IR) or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and when to stop. On 79,462 held-out samples from the `Multimodal Spectroscopic Dataset` with hard candidate sets and equal acquisition costs, **Top-1 accuracy rose from 80.10% to 93.78% for positive-ion starts and from 70.44% to 93.31% for negative-ion starts while requesting only 0.227 and 0.340 extra measurements per sample**, cutting measurement counts by over 90% relative to full acquisition and reducing a composite loss by 19.3% and 25.5% relative to a rule-based policy. Requests concentrated in groups with high structural disagreement among candidates, where composite loss also fell most.

papers.title: TaskFrame: Connecting Task-Level Planning with Frame-Level Control for Game Agents
papers.abstract: Building general game agents requires both high-level task reasoning and low-latency action control in rapidly changing visual environments. These capabilities favor models with substantially different computational profiles, making them difficult to realize within a single model. In this work, we present TaskFrame, a hierarchical planner-controller framework that connects task-level planning with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control. A vision-language task planner decomposes a high-level goal into an ordered sequence of atomic instructions and is optimized through supervised learning and dependency-aware GRPO. The hidden states of special goal tokens that terminate each atomic instruction provide continuous goal embeddings that are cached and reused across control steps. A causal Transformer controller combines the embedding of the active goal with recent observations to predict discrete keyboard and mouse-button actions and continuous camera motion at every game step. We train the system in three stages: planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment. Experiments in Minecraft show that TaskFrame is competitive with general-purpose vision-language models on instruction decomposition, and that in closed-loop evaluation the agent achieves a higher combat success rate than the evaluated baselines.
papers.summary: General game agents need both slow, deliberate task reasoning and fast frame-level control, two capabilities with very different compute profiles that are hard to fit into one model. `TaskFrame` splits them into a hierarchy: a vision-language planner decomposes a goal into an ordered sequence of atomic instructions, trained with supervised learning and a dependency-aware variant of `GRPO`, and the hidden states of special goal tokens are cached as continuous goal embeddings that a causal Transformer controller combines with recent observations to emit discrete keyboard and mouse-button actions plus continuous camera motion at every game step. Training proceeds in three stages: planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment. In `Minecraft`, the planner is competitive with general-purpose vision-language models on instruction decomposition, and **the closed-loop agent achieves a higher combat success rate than the evaluated baselines**.

papers.title: Neighborhood Elites: Quality-Diversity Search for Uncertainty Quantification in Question Answering
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, yet they produce wrong answers indistinguishable from correct ones. In question answering (QA), such an error propagates unnoticed into downstream tasks. Perturbation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) addresses this by probing a model over a set of input rewrites and reading uncertainty from how much its predictions vary. Yet this set is usually built generically, by free paraphrasing, token-level perturbation, or adversarial search. Such rewrites leave two things uncontrolled that matter in QA: what kind of change is made to the context, and how explicitly the context supports the answer. When neither is controlled, the composition of the set is determined by the generator rather than by design, and the estimate inherits whatever that generator happens to produce. Quality-diversity (QD) search is built to cover a predefined exploration space, so we recast input perturbation as a QD problem and propose \emph{neighborhood elites (NE)}, a neighborhood constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across two axes, the kind of edit and the explicitness of support. We compare NE against three other neighborhood constructors, holding the editor, QA model, uncertainty measure and search objective fixed, and against three scores read from the original context. Across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, NE improves failure detection against every other constructor in at least 24 of the 25 dataset-model pairs, reaching 0.726 AUROC and 0.211 AUPRC lift over the base rate. Additionally, NE detects failure better than semantic entropy computed over decoder samples, by 0.074 AUROC and 0.062 AUPRC lift, and this advantage widens as the neighborhood grows.
papers.summary: Perturbation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) estimates how reliable a large language model (LLM) answer is by rewriting the input several times and measuring how much predictions vary, but the rewrite sets are usually produced by generic paraphrasing, token perturbation, or adversarial search, which leaves uncontrolled what kind of edit is made and how explicitly the context supports the answer. The authors recast perturbation as a quality-diversity (QD) search problem and propose `neighborhood elites` (`NE`), a constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across those two axes, edit type and explicitness of support. With the editor, question answering (QA) model, uncertainty measure, and search objective held fixed, **`NE` improves failure detection over every other neighborhood constructor in at least 24 of 25 dataset-model pairs** across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, reaching 0.726 AUROC. It also beats semantic entropy computed over decoder samples by 0.074 AUROC, and the gap widens as the neighborhood grows.

papers.title: Latent Prediction Yields Cross-Subject Alignable Representations in Sensory-Evoked fMRI
papers.abstract: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a central analytical tool in cognitive neuroscience. Here we ask whether self-supervised learning (SSL), which has been scarcely explored in this domain, can yield representations that support strong downstream performance. To do so, we adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on brain data alone. The encoders never see the stimulus images or any representation derived from them. Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.
papers.summary: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data usually relies on supervised pipelines trained end-to-end with access to the stimulus images and language. The authors instead adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) for self-supervised learning (SSL), training participant-specific encoders on brain data alone with no access to the stimuli or anything derived from them. On the `Natural Scenes Dataset` (`NSD`), the learned embeddings are competitive with parameter-rich supervised pipelines on brain captioning and image reconstruction. **Encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, without images or shared stimuli**, after which a decoding head trained on one participant transfers to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance.

papers.title: Latent Path Exploration via Potential-Guided Subtrajectory Balance
papers.abstract: Continuous latent reasoning enables language models to perform intermediate computation without generating explicit reasoning traces. Advances in stochastic latent reasoning allow multiple paths to be sampled in continuous space, but stochasticity alone does not ensure effective exploration. A key challenge is guiding stochastic transitions between intermediate latent states toward useful reasoning paths. We introduce SubLAT, which couples a relative answer potential with Subtrajectory Balance to learn stochastic latent exploration. The relative potential evaluates the answer support of sampled states against replacement states, with a correctness signal at the terminal state. Subtrajectory Balance relates potential differences to forward and backward transition densities across subtrajectories of different lengths. The model is jointly trained with answer supervision, CoT supervision, and representation distillation. Experiments on arithmetic and deductive reasoning show increasing solution coverage with larger sampling budgets across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, as well as improvements on several structural OOD benchmarks. Trajectory analyses reveal progressive divergence among sampled latent paths and higher mean relative potentials for correct trajectories across arithmetic benchmarks.
papers.summary: Continuous latent reasoning lets a language model compute intermediate steps without emitting explicit text, and stochastic variants can sample multiple latent paths, but randomness alone does not steer those paths toward useful ones. `SubLAT` couples a relative answer potential, which scores sampled latent states against replacement states with a correctness signal at the terminal state, with `Subtrajectory Balance`, which ties potential differences to forward and backward transition densities over subtrajectories of varying length. Training combines answer supervision, chain-of-thought supervision, and representation distillation. On arithmetic and deductive reasoning tasks, **solution coverage increases with larger sampling budgets** both in-domain and out-of-domain, with gains on several structural out-of-distribution benchmarks, and trajectory analyses show sampled latent paths progressively diverging while correct trajectories carry higher mean relative potential.

papers.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
papers.abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.
papers.summary: Datacenter LLM serving is limited by facility power, so energy per token matters alongside latency; speculative decoding lets a drafter propose several tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass, but every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, so the energy saved depends on the acceptance rate. The authors measure speculative decoding under production conditions (`SGLang` with CUDA graphs) on H100 and H200 GPUs at batch sizes up to 64 across five corpora, and find that every drafter accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on the low-resource language Romansh than on English. On dense models, verification rather than drafting dominates the energy cost, and **the saving shrinks as batch size grows because batching has already amortized the weight read that speculation would divide among accepted tokens**. At large batches, block drafters push verification into the compute-bound regime where the saving becomes a loss, so meeting a tighter latency target with speculation costs extra energy and leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

papers.title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
papers.abstract: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.
papers.summary: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive one at a time and must be accepted or rejected immediately; with irrevocable decisions no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio, and allowing removal of previously accepted items is the standard relaxation. This work combines removal with two further extensions, bound awareness (knowing an upper bound on item sizes) and recourse (reinserting previously rejected items), and establishes close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under all three. **Substantial improvements over the best known competitive ratio are possible when the size bound is not too restrictive and only a few uses of recourse are available.** The authors also introduce adaptive online algorithms that need no size bound yet achieve guarantees comparable to the bound-aware setting.

papers.title: DolphinRouting: Cluster-Level Binary Routing for Disaggregated LLM Inference Serving
papers.abstract: Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation isolates the two phases of large language model serving, but request-level path selection must account for prefill work, cache reuse, and decode demand. We present DolphinRouting, which learns this choice from end-to-end SLO feedback under a given P/D resource allocation. Requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both worker pools, and output-length information. Offline policy search learns one binary action per cluster. Online feature extraction, cluster assignment, and table lookup select local or remote prefill. We evaluate DolphinRouting on a real PD-disaggregated cluster using three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data. Across the mixed workload and real data, DolphinRouting with $k$-means reduces P90 TTFT by 5.7--7.9\% and P90 TPOT by 2.6--10.1\% relative to Dynamo.
papers.summary: Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation runs the two phases of LLM serving on separate worker pools, which leaves a per-request choice of where to prefill that depends on prompt length, cache reuse, and decode demand. `DolphinRouting` learns that choice from end-to-end SLO feedback under a given P/D resource allocation: requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both pools, and output-length information, an offline policy search assigns one binary action (local or remote prefill) per cluster, and online serving reduces to feature extraction, cluster assignment, and a table lookup. On a real PD-disaggregated cluster with three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data, **the k-means variant reduces P90 time-to-first-token by 5.7 to 7.9 percent and P90 time-per-output-token by 2.6 to 10.1 percent relative to `Dynamo`**.

papers.title: Self-training for cross-centre coronary vessel segmentation in X-ray angiography using pre-contrast frame subtraction
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for coronary vessel segmentation in X-ray angiography often perform poorly on data from centres that were not represented in training. Apart from differences in equipment, the labels of the largest public dataset (ARCADE) are incomplete, as only the segments defined in the SYNTAX score are annotated. In this study, we evaluated whether self-training with pseudo-labels can improve performance on external data without additional manual annotation. Pseudo-labels were generated from two sources, namely the predictions of an nnU-Net model trained on ARCADE and a contrast map obtained by subtracting a pre-contrast frame from the same sequence. The nnU-Net predictions were extended along the contrast map, and pixels detected only in the subtraction image were assigned an ignore label and excluded from the loss. Six models were trained and tested on ARCADE and on two external datasets (XCAD and XACV). All first-round models initialised with the baseline predictions performed better than both the baseline and a control model fine-tuned for the same number of epochs. The model trained on the XCAD pool improved the macro-averaged Dice score by 2.7 points (95% CI 2.3-3.2), while the control decreased it by 0.6 points. A second round of self-training did not lead to further improvement. When an external model trained on 50 fully annotated images was used to generate the initial labels, the XCAD Dice score increased from 0.623 to 0.745 without any XCAD labels, although performance on XACV did not improve because large main vessels were missed. These results suggest that the benefit of self-training depends largely on the sensitivity of the model used to generate the initial pseudo-labels.
papers.summary: Deep models for coronary vessel segmentation in X-ray angiography degrade on data from centres absent from training, and the largest public dataset, `ARCADE`, annotates only the segments defined in the SYNTAX score, so its labels are incomplete. The authors test self-training with pseudo-labels built from two sources: predictions of an `nnU-Net` trained on `ARCADE`, extended along a contrast map obtained by subtracting a pre-contrast frame from the same sequence, with pixels found only in the subtraction image given an ignore label that is excluded from the loss. Across six models tested on `ARCADE` and two external datasets, `XCAD` and `XACV`, every first-round self-trained model beat both the baseline and a fine-tuning control, the `XCAD`-pool model gaining 2.7 macro-averaged Dice points while the control lost 0.6, and a second round added nothing. **When an external model trained on 50 fully annotated images seeded the pseudo-labels, `XCAD` Dice rose from 0.623 to 0.745 without any `XCAD` labels**, though `XACV` did not improve because large main vessels were missed, suggesting the benefit hinges on the sensitivity of the initial labeller.

papers.title: Causal-prior-constrained deep learning for rapid-intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones
papers.abstract: Rapid intensification (RI) is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations. Here we introduce CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep-learning system for 24-h RI warning in the western North Pacific. It integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph into a unified model. The graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change provide an auditable causal prior for training. Discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017, it identifies causal pathways linking atmospheric and oceanic conditions, the cyclone's dynamical and structural state, and its 24-h intensity change. On a forward holdout covering 2020-2024 and 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble achieves a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems; the three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105. It also attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates under our USA 30-kt standard and the published RITCF standard. Ablations show that the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021, with a significant contribution in one ensemble member. A deep-learning model constrained by observationally discovered causal structure thus offers a new route to physically informed RI warning.
papers.summary: Rapid intensification (RI) of tropical cyclones is dangerous and hard to forecast, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to separate in observations. `CausalVisionRI` is a deep-learning system for 24-hour RI warning in the western North Pacific that combines infrared satellite imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and a causal graph discovered from 522 cyclones spanning 2000 to 2017, using the graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-hour intensity change as an auditable prior during training. On a forward holdout of 3,004 records from 2020 to 2024, **a five-member ensemble reaches a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 against a fixed development climatology, while three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105**, and it attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates. Ablations attribute 0.032 BSS across the holdout to the graph pathway, rising to 0.063 over 2020 to 2021.

papers.title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs strain device memory through large model weights and attention states, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing systems separately provision memory for model weights and attention states, imposing fixed fixed boundaries that cannot adapt to the changing memory demands of workloads. Under heavy workloads, insufficient state capacity limits request concurrency and reduces throughput; under light workloads, idle memory in one region cannot be reallocated to another, wasting device memory. Meanwhile, modern LLM architectures introduce heterogeneous tensors with diverse layouts and lifetimes, further complicating memory management. These problems motivate unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. However, a shared pool alone does not make memory directly reusable across tensors with different allocation granularities and execution layouts. This paper presents Rimuru, a modern LLM serving system that unifies memory management through elastic expert offloading. Rimuru establishes a shared page pool to enables elastic memory sharing across heterogeneous tensors. To accommodate different allocation granularities, Rimuru introduces memory views that allow each tensor type to interpret the shared memory space using its own page size and page table. Furthermore, Rimuru combines huge-page alignment with a multi-level page allocator that splits and merges pages, enabling cross-type capacity reuse. A page-table-aware fused MoE kernel directly accesses non-contiguous expert weights, avoiding copy overhead. Building on these mechanisms, Rimuru employs a workload-aware adjuster that dynamically reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demands. Implemented on top of vLLM, Rimuru remains compatible with modern LLMs. Evaluations show that Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.
papers.summary: LLM serving systems provision device memory for model weights and attention states separately, with fixed boundaries that cannot follow workload shifts: heavy loads starve state capacity and cap concurrency, light loads leave idle memory stranded, and modern architectures add heterogeneous tensors with differing layouts and lifetimes. `Rimuru` replaces the fixed split with a shared page pool that is rebalanced at runtime: one pool across tensor types, per-type memory views so each tensor type reads the pool with its own page size and page table, huge-page alignment with a multi-level allocator that splits and merges pages, a page-table-aware fused mixture-of-experts (MoE) kernel that accesses non-contiguous expert weights without copies, and a workload-aware adjuster that reallocates pages across tensor types at runtime. Implemented on top of `vLLM`, **it reaches up to 19.03 times baseline throughput and cuts time-to-first-token by 98.1 percent on average**.

papers.title: Hammering with Vampire in Lean
papers.abstract: We present Vampire-Hammer, a hammer for the Lean interactive theorem prover that discharges goals using the Vampire automated theorem prover and reconstructs proofs checked by the Lean kernel. Vampire-Hammer uses the Lean-auto framework to process goals and premises before dispatching them to Vampire for proof search.
