This review provides a unified perspective on RL and PDE-constrained optimization, and surveys model-free, model-based, and multi-agent RL approaches to PDE control, with particular emphasis on sample efficiency, generalization across parametric variations, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. Two demonstrative examples, the stabilization of a chaotic system and a flow control problem, illustrate the performance and pitfalls of RL agents in practice. Finally, we discuss evaluation and benchmarking practices, current limitations, and open research directions toward reliable, data-efficient, and scalable RL for scientific computing.
papers.summary: Controlling systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) is difficult because of high-dimensional states, distributed actuation, nonlinear dynamics, and strict real-time constraints. This review connects reinforcement learning (RL) to PDE-constrained optimization and surveys model-free, model-based, and multi-agent RL approaches to PDE control, with emphasis on sample efficiency, generalization across parametric variations, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. **Two worked examples, stabilizing a chaotic system and a flow control problem, illustrate both the performance and the pitfalls of RL agents in practice**, and the authors close with evaluation and benchmarking practices, current limitations, and open directions toward reliable, data-efficient RL for scientific computing.

papers.title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines usually serve a separate reranker next to the answering model, duplicating model residency and passage processing. `Glance` instead adds a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to the generator, so short relevance probes branching from the shared prefill cache score every candidate passage without re-prefilling each query-passage pair, letting one resident 9B backbone handle generation, general decisions, and reranking at roughly 0.1 GiB of extra memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of fine-tuning on `MS MARCO`, it reaches nDCG@10 of 0.741 on `SciFact` and 0.345 on `NFCorpus` versus 0.721 and 0.326 for `bge-reranker-v2-m3`, and **its selected context raises answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder selection on 300 `HotpotQA` questions** under the same base generator. Reranking quality keeps improving up to 200 candidates scored from a single prefill, though evaluation so far covers only two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset, and one backbone family.
papers.highlight_summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines usually serve a dedicated reranker next to the answer model, so every candidate passage is encoded once for scoring and again for generation on two resident backbones. `Glance` instead gives the generator a rank-16 LoRA adapter plus a 256-dimensional pointer head, letting one resident 9B backbone score every candidate from a single shared prefill and then answer with the adapter switched off.

- The candidates are prefilled once as a shared state, a short relevance probe of roughly 30 tokens branches per passage from the cached context (including the recurrent DeltaNet state on the hybrid `MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B` backbone), and the pointer head reads one score per passage without ever prefilling a separate query-passage pair, at about **0.1 GiB** of extra memory per decision skill.
- After **39 minutes** of `MS MARCO` fine-tuning on 4,000 queries, the `packed_all` format reaches nDCG@10 of **0.741** on `SciFact` and **0.345** on `NFCorpus`, against 0.721 and 0.326 for the `bge-reranker-v2-m3` cross-encoder, with every zero-shot variant already beating BM25 before any retrieval training.
- On 300 `HotpotQA` distractor questions, the trained adapter's top-3 context raises answer F1 by **+0.045** (0.684 to 0.729, paired bootstrap 95% CI 0.014 to 0.076) over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator, and an activated-adapter variant lets the answer continue directly from the passage cache instead of re-prefilling.
- Scaling the shared prefill helps rather than hurts once trained: quality keeps rising to **0.717** nDCG@10 at 200 candidates (43k tokens) versus 0.659 for the cross-encoder, while the zero-shot adapter peaks at 20 candidates and collapses at 200.
- The cross-encoder stays far faster per query (31 to 60 ms versus roughly 400 ms or more), evaluation covers only two BEIR datasets, one QA set and one backbone family with no significance tests on the BEIR gaps, memory grows with candidates times context length (56 GiB at 100 candidates), scores shift somewhat with passage order, and in the cache-reuse variant the generator sees all passages rather than the reranked subset.

papers.title: Rural Readiness: Domain Generalization with Adversarially Chosen Domains
papers.abstract:
Predictive models trained at well-resourced data-rich institutions often fail when deployed in new populations. Motivated by the goal of building clinical diagnosis and decision-making algorithms for data-scarce rural populations using the general knowledge learned from data-rich hospitals, we formulate the fundamental question of \emph{domain generalization with adversarially chosen domains}, which asks a learner to perform on any unseen target domain nearly as well as the worst hypothesis consistent with the evidence from the observed source domains.
  Assuming only that the hypothesis class contains a "universal" predictor with small error on all $k$ source domains, we characterize the sample complexity of this objective up to logarithmic factors. Letting $d$ denote the VC dimension of the hypothesis class, we find, somewhat surprisingly, that the sample complexity reduces significantly from $\Omega(dk)$ to $O(d)$ under a small relaxation of the learning goal in which, roughly speaking, we allow the learned model to compete with hypotheses that perform well on 99% instead of 100% of the source domains. By applying this insight to the meta-distributional setting, in which source domains are selected according to a distribution on distributions, we obtain a corresponding improvement over known sample complexity upper bounds. We also study the effect of data access to the target domain and show that a small labeled sample from the target domain does not improve the worst-case sample complexity on the source domains.
papers.summary: Models trained at data-rich hospitals often fail when deployed in data-scarce rural populations, which motivates a formal problem of domain generalization with adversarially chosen domains: the learner must do nearly as well on any unseen target domain as the worst hypothesis consistent with the observed source domains. Assuming only that the hypothesis class contains a universal predictor with small error on all k source domains, the authors characterize the sample complexity up to logarithmic factors in terms of the VC dimension d. **Relaxing the goal so the learner need only compete with hypotheses that do well on 99 percent rather than 100 percent of source domains cuts the sample complexity from order dk to order d**, which also improves known upper bounds in the meta-distributional setting where source domains are drawn from a distribution over distributions. A small labeled sample from the target domain is shown not to improve the worst-case sample complexity on the source domains.

papers.title: Nonlinear Dynamical Systems as Scalable and Efficient Physical Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The rapid growth in the size of state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) models has led to increasing compute demands, spurring the development of energy-efficient hardware accelerators. Physical systems trained to perform ML inference, known as physical neural networks, have been proposed as accelerators in part because of their potential to be highly energy efficient. However, the ML inference accuracies reported in most investigations of physical neural networks have been substantially below the state of the art for conventional digital neural networks. In this work, we show in simulation studies that by applying modern ML training practices, including model compression, various candidate physical neural networks based on nonlinear dynamical systems can achieve accuracies as high as 99.2% on MNIST handwritten-digit recognition. We also show for one dynamical system that using it as the core building block of a parameter-efficient ML architecture inspired by MLP-Mixers enables accuracies of up to 86.4% on CIFAR-10 image classification (92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation), compared with 64% for the same system without the mixer architecture. The mixer approach achieved its accuracy while using $>5\times$ fewer trainable parameters than the baseline. Finally, we present back-of-the-envelope estimates for inference energy efficiency and speed when using an example physical dynamical system, suggesting that orders of magnitude improvements may be possible over digital-electronic neural networks.
papers.summary: Physical neural networks, in which a physical system is trained to perform machine-learning inference, promise large energy savings over digital hardware but have so far reported accuracies well below conventional digital networks. In simulation, the authors apply modern training practices including model compression to several candidate systems based on nonlinear dynamical systems and reach up to 99.2 percent on `MNIST`. Using one such system as the core block of a parameter-efficient architecture inspired by `MLP-Mixer`, **accuracy on `CIFAR-10` rises from 64 percent to 86.4 percent, or 92.2 percent with pretraining and knowledge distillation, while using more than five times fewer trainable parameters**. Back-of-the-envelope estimates for one example system suggest inference energy efficiency and speed could improve by orders of magnitude over digital electronics.

papers.title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
papers.abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.
papers.summary: The clinical intake interview is a primary diagnostic instrument in psychiatry, requiring the clinician to build rapport while untangling overlapping presentations. The authors train a language model with multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulated intake environments spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning, then test it in a randomized, double-blind crossover study in which 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients and a separate panel of 15 psychiatrists scored de-identified transcripts. **The trained agent beat its identically prompted base model in 76.7 percent of 60 matched scenario pairs**, with gains in patient-centered communication and differential diagnosis appropriateness, and on 256 adversarial presentations derived from Delphi-consensus safety taxonomies it more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks, from 30.5 to 12.9 percent. The authors note residual gaps that still call for safeguards and clinician oversight.

papers.title: FIRME: Registry-Anchored Memory Graphs for Evolving, Heterogeneous Investor Knowledge
papers.abstract: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that integrates observations across sources and periods without losing identity or provenance. In a knowledge graph, recurring observations may use different surface forms, fragmenting relationship histories and preventing evidence from accumulating. We introduce Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (FIRME), a registry-anchored memory graph that reconciles incoming observations to persistent canonical relationships and retains their source, time, and context. Within periods, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, directly or through a fixed product-topic ontology. Across periods, canonical identities and persistent aliases direct recurring observations to the same relationship history; deterministic updates summarize reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation. We evaluate FIRME on proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts. Compared with a historical registry that retains canonical identities and semantic fallback but omits alias memory, FIRME increases final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8-12.1 percentage points across four dataset-backend settings under a fixed-judge and fallback-review protocol. A blinded human audit of 200 incoming observations per setting finds Correct Match Rate gains of 9.0-16.5 points and reattachment-recall gains of 22.5-29.0 points, with higher observed merge precision in all four samples. A separate audit finds valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 outputs from full within-period fusion in the investor-call setting. Extraction-faithfulness and round-trip diagnostics assess source grounding and preservation of extractor-derived graph content.
papers.summary: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that merges observations across sources and periods without losing identity or provenance, yet recurring observations expressed in different surface forms fragment relationship histories in a knowledge graph. Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (`FIRME`) reconciles incoming observations to persistent canonical relationships while retaining source, time, and context: within a period, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, and across periods canonical identities with persistent aliases route recurring observations to the same relationship history. On proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts, **it raises final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8 to 12.1 percentage points over a registry that lacks alias memory**, and a blinded human audit finds larger gains in match rate and reattachment recall along with valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 fused outputs.

papers.title: Preserving Utility in Continual LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Projections
papers.abstract: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.
papers.summary: Unlearning removes the influence of sensitive training data such as private or copyrighted text without retraining, but requests arrive continuously over a model's lifetime, and most LLM unlearning methods degrade sharply under sequential removal because successive updates interfere with one another. Continual Orthogonal Projection (`COP`) is a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each new update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from earlier forget sets, which **provably guarantees first-order non-interference with prior deletions** while storing only a low-rank basis per layer rather than past gradients or forget data. It plugs into any unlearning method that takes gradient steps on a differentiable loss without changing its objective, and on the `TOFU` and `RWKU` benchmarks it preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, avoiding the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.

papers.title: The Precision Wall: An Optimizer-Dependent Boundary for Optimization under Power-Law Measurement Spectra
papers.abstract: In low-rank matrix sensing of a rank-$D$ factor $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$, replacing isotropic Gaussian designs with power-law measurement covariance $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$ leaves the Burer--Monteiro landscape free of spurious local minima, yet division-normalised first-order optimizers stall above a critical exponent $s^\ast$. We trace this failure to a numerical precision wall. At the ground truth, the smallest non-gauge expected Hessian eigenvalue scales at leading order as $V^{-(s+1)}D^{-s}$. When this curvature drops below the effective denominator floor $\epsilon_O$ of optimizer $O$, normalisation noise overwhelms rare-direction gradients, yielding the leading-order boundary $s^\ast_O(V, D) = [\log(1/\epsilon_O) - \log V]/\log(VD) + \delta_O$, where $\delta_O$ is a metric-dependent detection lag. With $\delta_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ calibrated on four configurations and frozen, this formula predicts Adam's onset within $0.45$ across all 16 cells of a held-out grid ($V \in \{64,128,256,512\} \times D \in \{4,8,16,32\}$), separates fixed-$VD$ pairs, and distinguishes denominator-precision walls from conditioning and sign-quantisation walls. The approximation fails at $D = 2$, reflects a finite-$D$ spectral crossover, and saturates below $\varepsilon_0 = 10^{-8}$ at a dynamical floor.
papers.summary: In low-rank matrix sensing of a rank-D factor with V rows, replacing isotropic Gaussian measurements with a power-law measurement covariance leaves the Burer-Monteiro landscape free of spurious local minima, yet division-normalized optimizers such as `Adam` stall once the power-law exponent s exceeds a critical value. The authors trace this to a numerical precision wall: the smallest non-gauge expected Hessian eigenvalue at the ground truth shrinks polynomially in V and D with exponent s, and once this curvature drops below the optimizer's effective denominator floor, normalization noise swamps the gradients in rare directions. The resulting closed-form boundary, with a single metric-dependent lag term calibrated on four configurations and then frozen, **predicts Adam's stall onset within 0.45 across all 16 cells of a held-out grid of V and D values** and separates denominator-precision walls from conditioning and sign-quantization walls, though the approximation fails at D equals 2 and saturates below a floor of 1e-8.

papers.title: MetaRefine: Score Refinement with Multi-Level Features for Image Assessment
papers.abstract: An image's original dimensions, aspect ratio, and composition provide important cues that can affect its technical and aesthetic quality. Image assessment methods use resizing, cropping, padding, or patch sampling to accommodate different input sizes. However, these operations can alter or obscure original geometric and compositional cues. Existing assessment models also encode rich multi-level visual evidence that can be further extracted and exploited to improve existing models. This motivates us to combine visual evidence with original-image geometry for score refinement without changing the original scoring pipelines. In this paper, we introduce MetaRefine, a metadata-aware score refinement architecture whose lightweight residual heads predict score corrections from geometry, multi-level visual features, and the frozen model's original score. Across 100 configurations on 21 datasets, MetaRefine improves PLCC in 88 configurations and SRCC in 85, with average relative gains of 7.55% and 7.10%, respectively. It reduces MAE in 90 configurations and RMSE in 89, with average relative reductions of 23.27% and 21.93%, respectively. The median parameter overhead is only 1.11%. MetaRefine can further improve state-of-the-art (SOTA) assessment models on multiple benchmarks.
papers.summary: Image quality and aesthetic assessment models resize, crop, pad, or patch-sample their inputs, which can alter or hide cues carried by an image's original dimensions, aspect ratio, and composition. `MetaRefine` is a metadata-aware refinement stage whose lightweight residual heads predict score corrections from the original geometry, multi-level visual features extracted from the frozen assessment model, and that model's own score, leaving the base scoring pipeline unchanged. **Across 100 configurations on 21 datasets it improves PLCC in 88 and SRCC in 85, with average relative gains of about 7.5 percent, and cuts MAE and RMSE by over 20 percent on average**, at a median parameter overhead of 1.11 percent, and it also lifts state-of-the-art assessment models on several benchmarks.

papers.title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
papers.abstract: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.
papers.summary: Research taste is the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known, and this study asks whether frontier models acting as research agents have it. Six models, working alone or in teams, each read seven recent NLP papers, proposed minimum viable experiments (MVEs), set pass thresholds, forecast outcomes, and ranked their proposals; a separate executor then ran all 415 MVEs, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judged the results. **Of the 415 MVEs, 194 were judged sound, valuable, and new, but only 73 were also judged non-obvious and beyond the seed paper**, and while the agents' first choices matched the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, they were not shown to beat simply choosing the experiment written first. Forecasts beat a base rate but were no more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper, teams cost more without clearly better proposals, and the evaluation harness and full dataset are released as `rTaste`.

papers.title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.
papers.summary: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could sharply reduce the physical qubit overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computing, but they need decoders that are both accurate and fast enough to keep pace with hardware, and neural decoders had not been demonstrated for them. `Neural triage decoding` allocates computation adaptively based on syndrome consistency: a local neural message-passing network makes a fast first prediction, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections on the remaining shots. **On ultra-high-rate codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, the `Triage` decoder matches near-optimal algorithmic decoders in accuracy while cutting latency by roughly one to two orders of magnitude.** The design is motivated by an analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder that reveals a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor, and the authors also show neural decoders are robust to mismatched error priors.

papers.title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
papers.abstract: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{https://github.com/AgenticOrgLab/AgenticUniversity.git}.
papers.summary: Large language models can tutor, generate content, and adapt learning paths, but turning these pieces into a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner requires aligning goals, activities, and assessment and using learning evidence to decide what comes next. The authors propose `Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization` and instantiate it as `Agentic University`, where learners join as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program that links personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, with learner feedback and performance steering subsequent support. In evaluation the system showed advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality, and **users achieved mean assessment gains of 12.19 points versus 5.61 on a 50-point scale** while reporting stronger cognitive support.

papers.title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure -- Past experiences and future strategies
papers.abstract: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.
papers.summary: The EGI Federation has delivered federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years, and this report reviews its early AI work in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins for physics and environmental science and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. It argues that since 2023 the focus of AI in science has moved from training models to adapting and applying them to specific domains, projects, and questions. **The resulting strategy for 2026 to 2030 rests on three enablers: AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data, and applications across the continuum; human skills; and trust for running AI in high-risk settings**, backed by projects such as federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms, and AI competence centres. The authors also propose a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures, and EOSC in which EGI specialises in customising and operating AI for research over the long term.

papers.title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
papers.abstract: We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand $r$, the goal is to estimate $Z=\int_{D}r(x)\,\mathrm dx$ on $D\subset\mathbb R^d$. Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on $\mathbb R^d$ and do not respect the domain constraint $x\in D$. We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in $D$ by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on $D$, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of $Z$. For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating $r$. We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.
papers.summary: Estimating a high-dimensional integral of a non-negative function over a bounded convex domain is hard because quasi-Monte Carlo ignores where the integrand concentrates, importance sampling needs a proposal that captures it, and existing learned diffusion samplers are defined on unbounded space and ignore the domain constraint. The authors build the proposal from reflected diffusions that stay inside the domain by construction: a reflected forward process transforms the target toward the uniform distribution on the domain, a neural score model learns to reverse it, and a change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields both a training objective with no extra boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of the integral. For non-smooth integrands they derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient from the Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, so neither reflected transition densities nor derivatives of the integrand are needed. **On numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems the authors report strong performance and favorable scaling with both the dimension and the number of Monte Carlo points.**

papers.title: Algebraic World Model: From Exploration to Proofs
papers.abstract: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.
papers.summary: AI systems now produce machine-checkable `Lean` proofs for hard mathematics, but they typically start from predefined definitions and specifications, which raises the question of whether they can reason rigorously about an unknown world. The Algebraic World Model (`AWM`) explores an unfamiliar environment, writes executable Python hypotheses that it continually tests and revises against observations, organizes them into typed objects and shared rules simplified through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the result in `Lean 4` to prove reachability and impossibility. **On two impossible game levels it produced closed, kernel-checked `Lean` proofs ruling out every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while `Claude Opus 5.5` and `GPT-6 Astra` equipped with coding tools produced none in twelve baseline runs**, and given only feedback that a cheaper win existed it revised its rules to reach six of six correct bounds. Across all 25 public `ARC-AGI-3` games the learned models let `Lean` replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels, predict unseen transitions, and detect changed mechanics, and with `Claude Opus 5` as the underlying model `AWM` clears every level with a score of 99.9 using 43 percent of the human baseline's actions.

papers.title: Discovering Interpretable Acoustic Features in Autoregressive Voice-Cloning TTS Models
papers.abstract: Voice-cloning TTS models synthesize an unseen speaker's voice from brief speech prompts, but it remains unclear which acoustic properties they represent and use. We introduce a feature-based interpretability framework for autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models, analyzing features from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), PCA, and random directions via sparse probing, steering, and quantitative auto-interpretability. We focus on Qwen3-TTS and extend probing and steering to $5$ additional models to test generalization across architectures. These models encode concepts like pitch, energy, noise, and accent, but sparse prediction and steering are effective only for some concepts. Strong probing does not always translate to steering or vice-versa. SAEs are useful for sparse probing of human-labelled concepts and novel-concept discovery, while PCA is competitive for dense probing and steering. Auto-interpretability finds $684$ automatically validated SAE features in Qwen3-TTS covering speaker clusters, speaking style, and recording conditions beyond known concepts. Overall, we perform a comprehensive interpretability study of autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models.
papers.summary: Voice-cloning text-to-speech models reproduce an unseen speaker from a short prompt, but which acoustic properties they internally represent and use has been unclear. The authors build a feature-based interpretability framework for autoregressive voice-cloning TTS, comparing features from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), PCA, and random directions through sparse probing, steering, and quantitative auto-interpretability, focusing on `Qwen3-TTS` and extending probing and steering to five more models. These models encode pitch, energy, noise, and accent, but sparse prediction and steering only work for some concepts, strong probing does not imply steerability or vice versa, and SAEs excel at sparse probing and discovering novel concepts while PCA is competitive for dense probing and steering. **Auto-interpretability surfaces 684 automatically validated SAE features in `Qwen3-TTS`** covering speaker clusters, speaking style, and recording conditions beyond the known concepts.

papers.title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as computational models of human language processing, but which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity has been unclear. Using ridge reduced-rank regression, the authors identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM embeddings across three naturalistic listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI and six model conditions covering autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized models. **Full linear encoding performance is recovered using only 1 to 3 percent of the original embedding dimensionality**, these subspaces generalize across held-out participants and partly across datasets, and principal component analysis needs far more dimensions to match, showing that the brain-predictive directions differ from those capturing the most variance in the embeddings themselves. Characterizing the learned subspaces also surfaces interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity relative to the LLM representations.

papers.title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
papers.abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.
papers.summary: Safety alignment for large language models is concentrated on English, which leaves low-resource languages poorly protected, and existing open datasets are small or ignore region-specific harmful topics. The authors propose a template-based augmentation pipeline that extracts safe templates from harmful prompts, translates them, and fills the slots with culturally authentic harmful and benign entities, releasing `MSafeTemp`, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages for multilingual safety training and evaluation. **English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, and culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses.** Training on the template-augmented data yields more diverse and higher-quality alignment data and improves safety performance beyond English.

papers.title: IndicIPR-QA: A Benchmark for Extractive Question Answering on Indian IPR Laws
papers.abstract: Legal Question Answering (QA) over statutory texts is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially in low-resource settings with complex legal systems. It requires answers that are precise and grounded in the law. However, to the best of current knowledge, no existing extractive QA benchmark provides exact answer spans from statutory texts across all seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Acts. This paper presents IndicIPR-QA1, an extractive QA benchmark for Indian IPR laws. The proposed dataset contains 4,462 QA pairs from 1,116 statutory contexts across seven Acts. Questions and answers are generated using GPT-4o and validated through nine automatic quality checks, single and multi-model LLM evaluations, and a 200-pair human audit. Section-level partitioning prevents source-context overlap across the training, validation, and test sets. Further analysis examines answer span length, lexical overlap, and multi-clause structure across the corpus and individual Acts. BM25 achieves a token-level F1 score of 20.21, while fine-tuned InLegalBERT reaches 85.02 under a unified sliding-window inference protocol. The large performance gap between BM25 (20.21 F1) and InLegalBERT (85.02 F1) shows that simple word matching is not enough to answer these legal questions. Performance also varies across the seven Acts, indicating substantial differences in answer-extraction performance.
papers.summary: Extractive legal question answering over statutory text is difficult in low-resource settings with complex legal systems, and no existing benchmark provided exact answer spans across all seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Acts. `IndicIPR-QA` contains 4,462 question-answer pairs drawn from 1,116 statutory contexts, generated with `GPT-4o` and validated through nine automatic checks, single- and multi-model LLM evaluation, and a 200-pair human audit, with section-level partitioning to prevent context overlap between training, validation, and test splits. **Under a unified sliding-window inference protocol, `BM25` reaches a token-level F1 of 20.21 while fine-tuned `InLegalBERT` reaches 85.02**, showing that lexical matching alone is insufficient, and performance varies substantially across the seven Acts.

papers.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
papers.abstract: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.
papers.summary: Particle-based kinetic plasma simulations need a field solve at every step, and grid-based neural operators must first deposit the particles onto a mesh, which aliases the particle noise that dominates their inputs. `NEOPIC` instead learns a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles and is evaluated at their positions, so no mesh, tree, or deposition step is needed and it can replace the field solver inside particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier, or tree codes with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. The authors prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator for any particle count, derive an error decomposition into sampling, learning, and time-stepping terms, and show the method scales linearly in the number of particles with constants set by the architecture alone. On two- and three-dimensional electrostatic benchmarks such as Landau damping and two-stream instabilities, **a single model trained on several mini-apps from different reference codes captures all of them and stays stable for twice the training time window**.

papers.title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied Drawing
papers.abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.
papers.summary: Studying how vision-language-action (VLA) models scale with data requires large, varied robot datasets that are costly to collect on physical hardware. `BURGER` is a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a prompt-driven pipeline that generates continuous drawing trajectories in simulation and the real world, where each instruction admits many valid drawings and stroke orders from the same blank canvas. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations across 282 drawing tasks, the authors evaluate five VLA models on language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, finding distinct failure patterns and that **some models benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects**. A trained policy deployed on a Franka Panda arm draws reactively under human intervention.

papers.title: Homebrewed SLMs: Autoregressive and Masked Diffusion Language Models Built at Home for Portuguese
papers.abstract: Building a language model of one's own no longer requires a data centre. This tutorial trains one from scratch, tokenizer included, on one consumer GPU, and shows how to tell whether it is good for the tasks of a specialist domain. It proposes no new method. It releases a tested Python package and two notebooks in Brazilian Portuguese with autoregressive and masked diffusion generation on one network, a preregistered comparison protocol, legal tasks built from text alone with a Kneser-Ney floor and public yardsticks, reference numbers for models of 11 to 12M parameters, and a catalogue of defects that only measurement revealed. On Brazilian prose and federal laws, at minutes per run, the autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs over the same text and then memorises it, while masked diffusion improves up to 256. At their best points on test, the diffusion bound exceeds the autoregressive likelihood by 0.06 bits per byte, within the preregistered minimum effect. On held-out laws and on acts published after training, the model ties a 6-gram floor in likelihood on the same windows, and it loses to the floor at continuing those acts. It beats the floor at detecting tampered text, and fills cross-references more often than the floor and public models of 160M and 630M parameters, only in decrees, a genre absent from training, where those scorers stay near or below chance, and in filling the blank only when each group weighs the same, since per item it ties the 630M model. On laws, the public models, trained with about 5x10^2 to 10^5 times its compute, lead in tampered text and continuation. The blind human reading is preregistered and not part of this version.
papers.summary: Training a small language model from scratch, tokenizer included, on a single consumer GPU is now feasible, and this tutorial shows how to do it and how to judge whether the result is useful in a specialist domain. It introduces no new method but releases a tested Python package and two Brazilian Portuguese notebooks supporting autoregressive and masked diffusion generation on one network, a preregistered comparison protocol, legal-domain tasks built from text alone with a Kneser-Ney n-gram floor, and reference numbers for models of 11 to 12 million parameters. On Brazilian prose and federal laws, **the autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs and then memorises the text, while masked diffusion keeps improving up to 256**, though the final gap of 0.06 bits per byte falls within the preregistered minimum effect. On held-out laws the model ties a 6-gram floor in likelihood and loses to it at continuation, beats it at detecting tampered text, and fills cross-references in decrees more often than public 160M and 630M models, although those models, trained with orders of magnitude more compute, lead on tampered text and continuation.

papers.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
papers.abstract:
Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost.
  In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography.
  In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.
  RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.
papers.summary: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check computations run by a more powerful AI system; debate is efficient but assumes one of two provers is honest, and known ways to drop that assumption cost far more compute. Rewindable interactive proofs (RIPs) let the verifier snapshot the prover's state, rewind to an earlier point in the interaction, and continue, which is natural when the prover is a model whose state can be checkpointed. The authors construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers, with **an honest prover running in time linear in the original computation and a verifier running in nearly linear time in the input length after one-time preprocessing**, using no cryptography. An implementation with a preliminary `MNIST` experiment shows the protocol can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.

papers.title: TRACER, a time-to-event EHR foundation model for disease detection across health systems
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained on longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can predict clinical diagnoses years in the future, making them a potential tool for disease screening. We developed TRACER (Temporal Risk Assessment with Clinical EHR Representations), a decoder-based foundation model pretrained on data from over 4.5 million patients from four health systems, and evaluated it on 16 incident diseases at 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons in more than 2 million patients from two health systems excluded from model development. In contrast to typical evaluations that focus on global metrics (e.g., AUROC), we measured performance at the low false-positive rates that are realistic for screening. We found that TRACER retained its discrimination in external health systems, and at 95% specificity, the patients it flagged were up to eight times more likely to be diagnosed within a year than unselected patients. Evaluating at this operating point also revealed what global metrics alone did not: detection and false-alert burden varied across diseases and health systems, even when discrimination appeared stable. Our results illustrate the potential of foundation models for screening and underscore the need for evaluation in health systems excluded from development to assess disease detection and false-alert burden at levels appropriate for intended clinical use.}
papers.summary: Foundation models trained on longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can forecast diagnoses years ahead, but they are usually judged on global metrics such as AUROC rather than at the operating points screening programs actually use. `TRACER` (Temporal Risk Assessment with Clinical EHR Representations) is a decoder-based model pretrained on more than 4.5 million patients from four health systems and evaluated on 16 incident diseases at 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons in over 2 million patients from two health systems held out of development. Discrimination held up externally, and **at 95% specificity the patients it flagged were up to eight times more likely to be diagnosed within a year than unselected patients**. Evaluating at that operating point also exposed variation in detection rate and false-alert burden across diseases and health systems that global metrics masked.

papers.title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $\sigma=\alpha\mu+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. Code and analysis tools are available at https://github.com/ShwStone/DecodingPredict.
papers.summary: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will generate from its prefill-phase hidden states is a key primitive for inference scheduling, yet reported predictor accuracy collapses whenever the target model, dataset, or sampling settings change. The authors attribute this to the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding and model decoding as a stopped stochastic process whose per-step stopping probability ramps up over hundreds of steps, which yields a per-prompt normal law for decode length and an affine relation between its standard deviation and mean. This normal law reproduces per-prompt mean absolute error and the central mass of the length distribution to within a few percent, and under fixed conditions a broad range of predictors, from MLPs to Mixture-of-Experts variants, converge near the bound, so **system error dominates model error**. They propose a benchmarking protocol that fixes model, data, and sampling parameters and reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Mobile Money Scan Messages in Ghana: A Comparative Evaluation of Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and Randon Forest Classifiers
papers.abstract: Mobile money (MoMo) is Ghana's preferred retail payment channel, recording GHC518.4 billion in transactions in December 2025 and over 26.7 million active accounts (Graphic Online, 2026). This growth has coincided with increased social-engineering fraud over Short Message Service (SMS) and Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD), where fraudsters impersonate network operators, agents, relatives, or regulators to obtain personal identification numbers (PINs), identity data, or funds. We present a supervised machine-learning pipeline for classifying scam and legitimate Ghanaian MoMo SMS messages using a labelled corpus of 220 messages across 18 scam and legitimate subcategories. Domain-specific normalisation of currency amounts, phone numbers, and USSD codes preceded TF-IDF vectorisation of unigrams and bigrams. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation and a 20% held-out test set, we trained and evaluated Multinomial Naive Bayes, linear support vector machine (SVM), and Random Forest classifiers using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Held-out accuracy, F1, and AUC were 1.00 for Naive Bayes and linear SVM; cross-validated accuracy averaged 96.6% (+/-3.3), 94.9% (+/-4.6), and 92.0% (+/-4.2). Discriminative n-grams reflected imperative urgency ("send," "claim," "please send") and PIN solicitation ("PIN," "pincode"); legitimate messages featured confirmatory and cautionary language ("balance," "successful," "do not share"). Findings are contextualised in Sub-Saharan African SMS fraud detection, small template-based corpus ceiling effects, and a pathway toward larger naturalistic multilingual corpora. Interpretable classical classifiers achieve high accuracy on structured MoMo scam text and suit carrier- or handset-level filtering in low-resource, on-device settings.
papers.summary: Mobile money (MoMo) is Ghana's main retail payment channel, and its growth has brought social-engineering fraud over Short Message Service (SMS) and Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD) in which scammers impersonate operators, agents, relatives, or regulators to extract personal identification numbers (PINs), identity data, or funds. The authors build a supervised pipeline on a labelled corpus of 220 messages across 18 scam and legitimate subcategories, normalising currency amounts, phone numbers, and USSD codes before TF-IDF unigram and bigram features feed `Multinomial Naive Bayes`, linear `SVM`, and `Random Forest` classifiers. **`Multinomial Naive Bayes` and linear `SVM` reached perfect held-out accuracy, F1, and AUC, with cross-validated accuracy of 96.6% and 94.9%**, and discriminative n-grams reflected urgency and PIN solicitation versus confirmatory and cautionary language in legitimate messages. The authors note the ceiling effects of a small template-based corpus and argue that interpretable classical classifiers suit on-device filtering in low-resource settings.

papers.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
papers.abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.
papers.summary: Long-context models re-run a search for relevant memories at every forward pass, while recurrent compression avoids that search only by deciding in advance what to keep; neither exploits the fact that useful memories at neighbouring steps largely overlap. The proposal treats retrieval as a persistent local traversal through an address space, separating a memory's content from its address, and derives a cost-regularised indexing objective that keeps high-value information within local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible, producing both attractive and exclusion pressures between memories. As a proof of principle on `MiniGrid Memory` with a five-token context, **a persistent local traversal head reaches 0.95 mean return after 0.59M training steps, versus 0.94M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than 2M for categorical addressing**. The experiment tests only the simplest fixed-geometry instance and leaves learned geometry and repeated retrieval for future work.

papers.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
papers.abstract: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.
papers.summary: As AI systems improve at mathematics, benchmarks are moving from olympiad problems toward research-level questions; the `Ramanujan Challenge` posed number-theory formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically but whose proofs may require non-obvious mathematics, including unpublished results and open conjectures. The authors analyse the submissions, comparing AI models, computer algebra systems (CAS), and formal tools, and find correct proofs conceptually distinct from the official solutions along with **a proof of one of the published open conjectures**. Judging complex proofs reliably at scale proved to be a second challenge, so they introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural-language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with one-shot LLM judging, the pipeline cuts false-positive verdicts on natural-language proofs from 23% to 6% and raises judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%.

papers.title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
papers.abstract: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.
papers.summary: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence, and as sequencing becomes cheaper this labour-intensive interpretation has become a bottleneck. `ClinGeX` is a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases it reached **71.7% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, against 45.7% for the strongest comparator**, and in a counterbalanced study with 45 clinical genomic professionals on 135 cases its assistance raised case-level concordance across variant analysis, rare-disease interpretation, and oncology decision-making well above routine and `DeepSeek`-assisted conditions while reducing reported interpretation time. A one-month non-interventional assessment with 11 professionals reported frequent adoption of its conclusions and time savings.

papers.title: FARMS: A Verifiable Foundation for Automated Computational Science
papers.abstract: Automated computational science could accelerate discovery by selecting, adapting and developing numerical methods. This prospect requires mathematical knowledge that AI systems can interpret and reuse with explicit guarantees. Here we present FARMS, a faithful and efficient foundation that transforms computational mathematics into AI-ready computing knowledge. FARMS connects formal statements to source context, algorithmic meaning and quantitative guarantees through source preparation, reusable representations and semantic review. Across 171 targets in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical partial differential equations, 157 were accepted by the pipeline, with mean estimated costs of US \$0.85-2.29 per target across sources. Lean-checked implications from explicit source premises connect selected statements to computational skills, illustrated by a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression. FARMS therefore supports an affordable, reusable knowledge foundation for trustworthy automated computational science.
