papers.summary: Automating computational science, where AI systems select, adapt, and develop numerical methods, requires mathematical knowledge those systems can interpret and reuse with explicit guarantees. `FARMS` turns computational mathematics into AI-ready computing knowledge by connecting formal statements to their source context, algorithmic meaning, and quantitative guarantees through source preparation, reusable representations, and semantic review. Across **171 targets in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical partial differential equations, 157 were accepted by the pipeline at an estimated cost of 0.85 to 2.29 US dollars per target**. Lean-checked implications from explicit source premises link selected statements to computational skills, illustrated with a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression.

papers.title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns
papers.abstract: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. These interactions were analysed with a counselling communication pattern system at sentence level. We investigated two key questions: (1) to what extent LLM-generated responses replicate authentic conversational dynamics and (2) whether counsellors' communication behaviour differs when interacting with human versus LLM-simulated clients. The findings highlight both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across scenarios, showing the potential of LLM-based role-playing exercises to enhance counselling competencies and to identify areas for further refinement in virtual client simulations.
papers.summary: Counselling training relies on role-plays in which peers act as clients, and large language models could take that role if they reproduce realistic conversational dynamics. The study recorded sessions in which novice counsellors worked first with human peers acting as clients and then with clients simulated by `Mixtral 8x7B` under 4-bit quantization, and coded every sentence with a counselling communication pattern system. It asks how far LLM responses replicate authentic dynamics and whether counsellors communicate differently with human versus simulated clients, finding **both similarities and differences in the counselling patterns used across the two settings**. The authors read the results as support for LLM-based role-play exercises while pointing to areas where virtual client simulations need refinement.

papers.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
papers.abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.
papers.summary: Foundation models are usually trained in separate stages, with pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) each using different data and learning algorithms. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, the authors place every stage under one likelihood-based procedure they call `unified training`, which **reframes the whole training lifecycle as a question of which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case**. They build a system that mixes static data and RL generations inside a single trainer. In controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities and gives a stronger starting point for continual learning.

papers.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
papers.abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $\pi_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics
papers.summary: Robotics simulations cover only a narrow slice of real-world tasks because building them takes expert effort that does not scale. `Gym-Anything for Robotics` treats simulation creation as a coding-agent task, selects target domains from U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, defines what makes a good simulation and task, and runs an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each one against those definitions. The resulting `RoboWorld` suite holds 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training reinforcement-learning environments, and **even the best frontier models fail every test task, averaging a reward of only 0.06**. The authors then show that in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads simulator state, self-assisted learning from a model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations for vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as `pi_0.5` each substantially improve performance.

papers.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) post-trains a language model against a teacher that is the same model conditioned on a privileged reference, but existing methods fix that teacher either for all of training or for each whole response. A teacher-intervention pilot study shows that the preferred teacher varies token by token within a single response and can be identified through majority voting and KL-based selection. Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (`MTA-OPSD`) builds a pool of candidate teachers and lets every token pick its preferred teacher during training. On mathematical reasoning tasks with `Qwen3` models, **it consistently beats prior OPSD approaches, with average gains of up to 5.9 points over the base model**.

papers.title: PIVOT: Progressive Intervention via Online Teacher Correction
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited by sparse outcome-level feedback on hard reasoning tasks: when all rollouts in a group fail, rewards provide no learning signal. Stronger teachers can provide additional guidance, but this raises a central question: how can such signals be incorporated into RLVR to support successful rollouts while remaining learnable for the student? We distinguish two complementary mechanisms: trajectory-level intervention, which improves access to reward-bearing trajectories, and token-level supervision, which provides dense targets to guide student learning. Our controlled experiments show that either mechanism alone can remain insufficient, motivating their combination. We therefore introduce PIVOT, which inserts teacher-generated corrections into student rollouts and applies token-level KL supervision to these segments alongside the RLVR objective. Beyond their combination, we systematically analyze where to intervene and how to supervise, yielding a recipe for effective guidance. Across hard logic games and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, PIVOT consistently outperforms existing methods, nearly doubling mean avg@8 on logic games from 19.5% for the best-performing baseline to 35.6%.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stalls on hard reasoning problems when every rollout in a group fails and the outcome reward carries no signal. The authors separate two ways a stronger teacher can help, trajectory-level intervention that gives the student access to reward-bearing trajectories and token-level supervision that supplies dense targets, and show in controlled experiments that either alone can fall short. `PIVOT` inserts teacher-generated corrections into student rollouts and applies token-level KL supervision on those segments alongside the RLVR objective, with a systematic study of where to intervene and how to supervise. Across hard logic games and mathematical reasoning benchmarks it outperforms existing methods, **nearly doubling mean avg@8 on logic games from 19.5% for the best baseline to 35.6%**.

papers.title: Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation
papers.abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand parameter capacity by activating a small subset of experts per token. Expert selection directly affects model capabilities under a fixed active-expert budget. Dense evaluation of all experts reveals weak agreement between single-router rankings and expert-utility evaluation rankings, especially in middle and deep layers. Richer signals for selection and computation incur additional cost: selection based on internal expert activations requires preliminary computation, while processing multiple full representations separately through the same expert repeats its computation. We propose Multi-View MoE to improve expert selection with multiple routers and reuse their preferences to modulate expert computation under a fixed expert budget. Its Multi-Router submodule aggregates sigmoid scores from independently initialized routers. These routers develop highly differentiated expert preferences during training, allowing experts strongly favored by one router or jointly supported by several routers to be selected. Multi-View further uses each selected expert's relative scores across routers to mix learned latent views into its input, reusing routing preferences for both selection and computation. Each selected expert executes one forward pass, preserving the active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and all-to-all communication volume. On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points over the baseline. Multi-Router alone yields a 0.6-percentage-point gain and improves the rank correlation between router scores and evaluated expert utility, with relative increases of 8.1% globally and approximately 58% in the layer with the lowest single-router alignment. Controlled mixing interventions show the model uses input differences that depend on both the expert and the token.
papers.summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate a few experts per token, so which experts get selected directly shapes capability under a fixed budget, and dense evaluation of all experts shows single-router rankings agree only weakly with measured expert utility, especially in middle and deep layers. `Multi-View MoE` aggregates sigmoid scores from several independently initialized routers, which develop differentiated preferences so that experts strongly favored by one router or jointly supported by several are selected, and then reuses each selected expert's relative scores across routers to mix learned latent views into its input. Each selected expert still runs a single forward pass, preserving active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and all-to-all communication volume. On a 24-layer 10B-parameter model with 1B active parameters trained on 708B tokens, **the full method improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points**, with the multi-router component alone giving 0.6 points and raising rank correlation between router scores and expert utility by about 58% in the least-aligned layer.

papers.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.
papers.summary: Scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web requires reliable verification of task completion for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning, but vision-language model (VLM) judges see only the supplied observations and generated inspection programs see only accessible state, so either can miss decisive evidence. `VeriCUA` is a platform-agnostic framework that treats verification as agentic exploration: the verifier inspects available context to build a task rubric, chooses GUI or code checks for requirements that remain unresolved, and combines what it finds under explicit evidence rules, using one shared procedure for online and offline settings. Experiments show **higher agreement with reference labels than the compared baselines across platforms and observation modalities, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online**. Analyses tie these gains to complementary evidence sources and test-time exploration.

papers.title: Multistatic ISAC with Deep Learning-Based Clutter Suppression for 5G and Beyond
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems using 5G and beyond signals of opportunity enable joint wireless sensing and communication using shared infrastructure and spectrum resources. While multistatic ISAC can increase sensing coverage with spatially distributed receivers, dense and dynamic clutter can significantly degrade bistatic range and Doppler estimation, leading to errors in target localization and velocity estimation. This paper presents a multistatic ISAC framework with clutter suppression for high-fidelity estimation of target position and velocity. Distributed clutter is modeled with randomly located scatterers with varying Doppler spreads and radar cross sections to capture dense and dynamic clutter effects. A broad range of conventional signal processing baselines are evaluated for clutter suppression, showing limited robustness under strong clutter conditions. To address this limitation, deep learning-based clutter suppression methods are introduced to improve robustness against dense and dynamic clutter by employing residual and attention-enhanced deep neural network architectures that directly enhance target responses from clutter-contaminated observations. These methods substantially outperform conventional approaches in target position and velocity estimation across diverse clutter conditions in multistatic ISAC.
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems reuse 5G and beyond signals for joint wireless sensing and communication, and spreading receivers across multiple sites extends sensing coverage, but dense and dynamic clutter corrupts bistatic range and Doppler estimates and therefore target localization and velocity. The authors model distributed clutter as randomly placed scatterers with varying Doppler spreads and radar cross sections, and evaluate a broad range of conventional signal-processing baselines for clutter suppression, which prove fragile under strong clutter. They then introduce residual and attention-enhanced deep neural networks that enhance target responses directly from clutter-contaminated observations, and report that **these networks substantially outperform conventional approaches in position and velocity estimation across diverse clutter conditions**.

papers.title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
papers.abstract: When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator's rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent's activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in. Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks. On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls. At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%. On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations. The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix. A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm.
papers.summary: When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can pressure another into breaking its operator's rules, and output filters only catch what has already been written. In six controlled multi-agent scenarios a peer presses a target agent for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret such as a deploy token, and a linear probe on the target's activations, read at each model call before any output, picks out the call that leaks. On held-out `Qwen3-32B` episodes at a threshold flagging 5% of benign calls, **the probe catches 82% of leaking calls, against 26% for a zero-shot decision-model monitor at a similar flag rate**, and a probe on `gpt-oss-20b` reasoning reaches an AUROC of 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels rather than from activations, and the probe also fires on permitted disclosures and gives only short-range warnings, so halting on every alarm would stop most benign episodes.

papers.title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
papers.abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.
papers.summary: Autonomous research systems built on large language models can draw conclusions their evidence does not support. The authors build a laboratory in which multiple LLM-based agents review one another's work, generate and reject research questions, demand independent theoretical checks, and design experiments meant to challenge their own claims, with the power to halt or redirect an investigation. Applied to ensembles of quantum spins in diamond, the agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a family of microwave pulse sequences, then designed experiments to separate competing predictions. **When repeated reference measurements revealed signal drift, the agents declared the first experiment inconclusive and revised the protocol without loosening acceptance criteria**, and the revised run supported the theory.

papers.title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder
papers.abstract: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.
papers.summary: Proactive conversational assistants must decide both when to interject and what short, memory-grounded hint to offer, a job usually split between a gating model and a larger generator. Evaluating the two stages jointly on 28,058 decision points, the authors find that generation scores reported behind an oracle gate overstate end-to-end performance, that a gate's compute savings shrink from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one, and that the user memory profile matters far more than retrieval or model size. **Removing the memory profile costs 24.7 exact-match points, while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match.** They then train a single 1B decoder that gates from an intermediate layer and generates in the same forward pass, matching or exceeding the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31 to 1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline, while a human evaluation of 1,144 ratings supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the 1B pipeline but below the 8B one.

papers.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
papers.abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.
papers.summary: Distortion-free watermarks for large language models tend to lose their signal under speculative decoding or sacrifice output diversity. `TextSeal2` merges two or more watermark keys, including publicly shared ones, into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through the Gaussian copula from `AutoMark`, avoiding the detection dilution of its predecessor `TextSeal`, which routed each token to one of two keys by coin flip. Under speculative decoding, an additional memoryless exponential race run on the leftovers of the draft races verifies keyed drafts so that replacement tokens stay watermarked with the same keys, the acceptance rate is unchanged, and output follows the target model exactly. Across three LLMs, **it detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than `TextSeal` at a false-positive rate of 0.001** with equal output diversity, matches `textGrain` without post-logits optimization, and leads both by 18 and 22 points respectively on 200-token answers under speculative decoding.

papers.title: Difficulty Calibration Across Time for Membership Inference in Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Modern diffusion models are trained on massive datasets that often include copyrighted or private images. Membership inference attacks (MIAs) address this by testing whether a given image was in a model's training set. The standard approach scores an image by its reconstruction loss and flags low-loss images as members. This often fails because some images are simply easier to reconstruct than others, so a simple unseen image can score a lower loss than a complex training image. Difficulty calibration separates memorization from how difficult an image is to begin with. We show how to calibrate along two axes of time: training time and diffusion time. First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC), which compares a fine-tuned model's loss against an earlier checkpoint. This cleanly isolates newly memorized data and gives near-perfect auditing, even without text captions. Since earlier checkpoints are not always available, we next present Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC), which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. Our key observation is that an image's difficulty persists across noise levels, whereas memorization is localized in time. By comparing the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps from the same model, TSC attenuates image difficulty using the model's own trajectory. Empirically, our methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin, and unlike most existing attacks, generalize across different model parameterizations such as $x$-, $v$-, and $\epsilon$-prediction models. Code is available at https://github.com/MichaelJoseph777/TSC.
papers.summary: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) test whether an image was in a diffusion model's training set, typically by flagging low reconstruction loss, but inherently easy images can score lower than complex training images. The authors calibrate difficulty along two time axes: Reference-Model Calibration (`RMC`) compares a fine-tuned model's loss against an earlier checkpoint to isolate newly memorized data, while Temporal Self-Calibration (`TSC`) needs only a single model and compares the loss at a target diffusion timestep against neighboring timesteps, exploiting the observation that image difficulty persists across noise levels whereas memorization is localized in time. **`RMC` yields near-perfect auditing even without text captions**, and both methods beat the prior state of the art by a wide margin while generalizing across x-, v-, and epsilon-prediction parameterizations.

papers.title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.
papers.summary: Continuous diffusion models admit a deterministic probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE) that reproduces their marginals and underpins fast sampling and consistency distillation, but no analogue existed for discrete diffusion. Exponential residual flows (`ERFs`) augment each token position's discrete state with a continuous residual that evolves under piecewise ODEs driven by the current state and the forward and backward rate matrices, with the discrete state changing whenever a residual hits zero. **The construction provably preserves the marginals of the original discrete diffusion**, and a practical discretization specialized to masked and uniform diffusion supports consistency distillation and improves over prior approaches on benchmarks including code and text generation.

papers.title: Testimony from Timelines: Evidence-Grounded Significance Testing of Temporal Clinical Hypotheses
papers.abstract: Ask a language model whether sales tend to dip after a product recall, or whether one side effect tends to follow another after a vaccine, and it answers in a fluent sentence that reads like a finding, with no test behind it. Assertions about how events unfold across many cases fill the Web, and each is a temporal hypothesis that only a significance test over the right records can settle. The verifier must specify the null, select the test and decide which records bear on the hypothesis, and any of these choices can go wrong while the conclusion still comes out right. Yet benchmarks for language-model data analysis grade only the conclusion, with the relevant data handed over. We study the problem in health, where a wrong verdict is costly, and present STRATA, a benchmark that grades every decision on the way to a verdict: 8,735 hypotheses over the clinical timelines of vaccine adverse-event reports, with gold plans, evidence sets, p-values and verdicts derived under a released codebook and reproduced by a deterministic oracle. We also propose ART (articulate, retrieve, test), a staged paradigm that exposes each decision as an inspectable output. Extensive experiments with five model configurations show that systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, a verdict-evidence gap that accuracy alone conceals. ART closes most of this gap and brings a 31B open model to within 0.01 of the frontier models under the same paradigm; the frontier models succeed once given the codebook.
papers.summary: Language models readily assert how events unfold across many cases, such as one vaccine side effect following another, without the significance test that such a temporal hypothesis requires, and existing benchmarks grade only the final verdict with the relevant data pre-supplied. `STRATA` is a benchmark of 8,735 hypotheses over the clinical timelines of vaccine adverse-event reports, each with a gold analysis plan, evidence set, p-value, and verdict derived under a released codebook and reproduced by a deterministic oracle, so every decision on the way to a verdict is graded, and the companion `ART` (articulate, retrieve, test) paradigm exposes each decision as an inspectable output. **Across five model configurations, systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, a verdict-evidence gap that accuracy alone conceals.** `ART` closes most of that gap and brings a 31B open model to within 0.01 of frontier models under the same paradigm, while frontier models succeed once given the codebook.

papers.title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
papers.abstract: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.
papers.summary: Aligned language models refuse harmful requests asked directly yet often comply when the same request is spread across a multi-turn conversation, a brittleness traced to safety behavior being concentrated in a model's first few output tokens. Rather than fight this shallowness, the `ShallowDefend` framework (Assess, Decide, Respond) has the defender occupy that high-leverage span first: it assesses user intent, commits to an explicit parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule that checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, needing no judge or annotation, though the format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. **Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks, the defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison while preserving utility at a modest helpfulness cost**, and per-token KL analysis plus interventional probes show the committed decision is a causal control point.

papers.title: Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models
papers.abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.
papers.summary: Spatial perception requires more than recognizing single images: an observer must maintain a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action, and it is unclear whether visual foundation models supply representations that support this. Using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments, the authors test four capability levels, spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability, with matched controls separating readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. **Strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval**, a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer unchanged to predicted features, and goal-dependent action selection responds to goal changes without reliably improving progress. Object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout, motivating evaluation of spatial representations by whether information is maintained, updated predictively, and used for action rather than only by what can be decoded.

papers.title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
papers.abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.
papers.summary: World models can control an environment well without faithfully capturing its dynamics, which limits their use for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. `world2vec` learns mechanistic world models directly from observations and actions, without reward information, by fitting latent dynamics that reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons. **It uses at least an order of magnitude fewer parameters than `DreamerV3`, `TD-MPC2`, and `LeWM`** while achieving state-of-the-art control of continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors.

papers.title: From extreme weather to agricultural consequences with agentic AI
papers.abstract: Extreme weather is forecast days ahead, yet its consequences for agriculture remain hard to predict: a forecast says where a storm will strike, not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could tell span many sources. We present WxCrop, the first agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and the first that combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss reliably for past and forecast dates. We demonstrate it in Florida on hurricanes, freezes and dry heat, with a loss model calibrated on insurance records for each, and the same procedure extends to other hazards and areas. Three checks show reliability: the hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98, recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2%, and independent production records confirm the county rankings (rank correlation 0.63). Users ask the agent for each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value, every number sourced, so that governments, growers and scientists respond to agricultural disasters quickly.
papers.summary: Weather forecasts say where a storm will strike days ahead but not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records needed to answer that are scattered across many sources. `WxCrop` is an agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices vetted by causal analysis and combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss for both past and forecast dates, with a loss model calibrated on insurance records for each hazard. Demonstrated in Florida on hurricanes, freezes, and dry heat, **its hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98, and recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2%**, while independent production records confirm county rankings with a rank correlation of 0.63. Users query each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value with every number sourced, and the authors say the procedure extends to other hazards and regions.

papers.title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
papers.abstract: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.
papers.summary: Luggage re-identification (ReID) associates observations of the same bag across disjoint camera views in airports, train stations, and border crossings, serving forensics, abandoned-luggage detection, and lost-luggage recovery. Existing methods match cropped images by appearance under relatively clean conditions, while real deployments face occlusion, clutter, and crowds and rarely exploit the complementary shots and views available from multiple video streams. The authors study an end-to-end pipeline that detects and re-identifies luggage from multiple streams, evaluating on a benchmark dataset captured in real-world environments **how to select and merge different views and shots of the same item and how training on datasets from different environments affects overall ReID performance**.

papers.title: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
papers.abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.
papers.summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in a distribution estimated from a finite record, but a divergence ball around the empirical distribution can only reweight observed outcomes while a transport ball also hedges against realizations the data-generating process could never produce. The authors instead center a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball on a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, so the adversary can up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Because the resulting problem admits only a few scenarios and a random sample of that size would likely miss the rare realizations where the worst case concentrates, they build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new importance-weighted realizations from the learned nominal steered toward the current worst case. **On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering on the learned nominal lowers cost under distribution shift at comparable in-distribution cost when data are scarce** and the model class can extrapolate, with the advantage fading as the record grows or the shift departs from the learned structure.

papers.title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
papers.abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
papers.summary: Pixel-space generative Transformers assign one token per image patch, so finer detail demands more tokens and ever more expensive global attention, even though low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. `SpecSlot`, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer, expands each spatial anchor into several slots that each own a disjoint band of discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients, lets only the lowest-frequency slot per anchor join global attention while all slots interact locally, and adds a spatial head for local correction, keeping the generative state, target, and loss in pixel space. On `ImageNet-256` it matches a FLOPs-matched `JiT` control on final FID while converging faster, and **on `ImageNet-512` it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs** and comes within 0.69 FID of `JiT-B/16` at 38.2% lower cost. For text-to-image generation it surpasses `JiT-B/8` on `DPG-Bench` by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
papers.highlight_summary:
Pixel-space generative Transformers spend one token per image patch, so finer output detail means a longer global-attention sequence and quadratic cost growth. `SpecSlot` breaks that coupling by expanding each spatial anchor into K slots that each own a disjoint radial band of discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients, and routing only the lowest-frequency slot per anchor through global attention while all slots mix locally within the anchor.

- The model reads W anchors from non-overlapping input cells, expands each into K slots, runs a global-global-local-local (GGLL) schedule three times where slot 0 is the only cross-anchor carrier, and decodes with a 50%-lapped DCT synthesis plus a zero-initialized spatial correction head, all under a pixel-space rectified-flow loss; at W256/K4 on 256px images the global sequence holds **288** tokens instead of **1,056**.
- On `ImageNet-256`, W256/K4 reaches **FID 6.59** against 6.68 for the FLOPs-matched `JiT-CM` control (a statistical tie that converges faster), using **40.9% fewer FLOPs** than `JiT-B/8`, which still leads the panel at FID 4.34.
- On `ImageNet-512`, it scores **FID 9.14** versus 11.98 for `JiT-CM` (**2.84 better** at 3.9% fewer FLOPs) and lands within **0.69 FID** of `JiT-B/16` at **38.2% lower cost** and 1.6× higher throughput, with the authors attributing the larger margin to each anchor covering four times more pixels while the global sequence stays fixed.
- Transferred to text-to-image, the same architecture beats `JiT-B/8` on `DPG-Bench` (**62.21 vs 61.15**) at **40.6% lower forward cost**, though `JiT-B/8` keeps the `GenEval` lead (29.78 vs 26.99), and ablations show that moving the global carrier to any other slot worsens FID while full-global attention still wins (5.84 vs 6.59) at 74.8% more compute.
- The headline gains are measured against an implementation-defined compute-matched control rather than a published JiT size, the paper concedes the cause of the larger 512 margin is not isolated, extra spectral slots show diminishing returns (effective slot utilization falls from 0.803 at K2 to 0.495 at K8), and evaluation is limited to base-scale models on ImageNet-1K and 256px text-to-image.

papers.title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
papers.abstract:
The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions.
  This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.
papers.summary: The Neural Thickets hypothesis holds that pretrained language models sit in dense weight-space neighborhoods of task-specific experts that random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. Reproducing the reported gains, the authors show the geometric story is unnecessary: perturbing a single decoder block recovers much of the improvement, and **adding a random bias to the output logits of a fully frozen model matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks**. They formalize the alternative as Perturb-Select-Vote (`PSV`), which generates perturbed predictors, selects strong members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions, linking the effect to sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection, with a first-order analysis showing small weight perturbations act mainly through induced logit shifts. In vision, logit `PSV` substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations add little, making it a training-free alternative to perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

papers.title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
papers.abstract:
An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private.
  We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations.
  We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.
papers.summary: Differentially private mechanisms usually scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, letting a few atypical records dictate noise even when the rest of the data would permit far less, and removing those records first must itself be done privately. Propose-filter-release (`PFR`) privately filters its input so that a mechanism that only protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, becomes differentially private in the standard sense on every input. **It requires only a concave friendliness score measuring how well a record fits a dataset and a release mechanism that is private when the changed record fits the rest**, guaranteeing differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, which makes it a general primitive comparable to `propose-test-release` with `FriendlyCore` as one instantiation. The authors instantiate it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the Kullback-Leibler divergence of user histograms, effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.

papers.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
papers.abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.
papers.summary: Data attribution methods for language models are usually judged on downstream tasks such as fact retrieval, but existing evaluations vary several dataset properties at once, so it is impossible to isolate why an attribution algorithm fails. The Controlled Attribution Benchmark (`CATT`) fine-tunes LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge to obtain unambiguous ground truth for fact tracing and lets one dataset property change at a time, revealing that document redundancy and lexical distractors consistently degrade attribution. Rather than propose a new estimator, the authors examine two neglected design choices, the loss used for gradients and how per-token scores aggregate into a document score, and find that causal evidence inside a training document is highly localized but averaged into noise by standard whole-document aggregation. **Replacing cross-entropy gradients with negative log-odds gradients and aggregating only the top token scores improves ground-truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines**, and the log-odds correction also improves counterfactual retraining performance on `FTRACE-TREX` for every method tested, by up to 4.9x.
